# Preface.

Those who will inquire of us concerning the reasons why we were moved to produce such a simple and unnecessary book as this is, and to present it to the world, will receive little certain by way of answer. We must almost confess that we ourselves do not know how the resolve to undertake this work was first awakened in us and has been maintained until now. We have never been of the mind to test our meager strengths on a writing of this kind. Rather, we had decided to devote the remainder of our spare hours, which the mercy of the **Highest** <note>Referring to God.</note> might still grant us, to entirely different investigations that seemed to us more pleasant and more useful to the world. We cannot boast that sensible men have asked us, or even pressed and compelled us, to publish a **Moral Theology** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre." This refers to the study of Christian ethics and how a believer should live.</note>. No one has hitherto, as far as we know, placed such great confidence in our ability that he imagined we would be able to bring about anything better in this **discipline** <note>original: "Wißenschaft." In the 18th century, this term referred to any systematic branch of scholarship or knowledge, not just the natural sciences.</note> than what so many famous men have shared with the world until now. And no one has therefore urged us to contribute our part toward the building of the **sanctuary** <note>original: "Heiligthum." A metaphor for the collective body of Christian truth and the Church.</note>, according to the strength bestowed upon us by the **Lord**, from this side. We ourselves have never held that the world stood in need of a new book on morals. We have only wished that people

# Preface.

...towards making better use of the existing excellent works—in which the nature of **godliness** <note>original: "Gottseligkeit." A central concept in 18th-century German theology, referring to a life of active piety and devotion to God.</note> is explained and the duties of mankind are recounted and proven—than has been done so far. And if we had, through weakness of understanding or lack of insight, fallen into the error of thinking that much could still be discovered and recorded in this part of **sacred learning** <note>original: "geistlichen Gelehrsamkeit." This refers to the academic study of theology and spiritual matters.</note>, that much could be better and more correctly ordered, or more thoroughly proven, then certainly the grace of the **Highest** <note>A common 18th-century epithet for God.</note> and our own awareness of our manifold failures would have preserved us from the prideful opinion that we were fit to remedy these deficiencies. What absurd pride would have to possess us if we allowed ourselves to dream that the Providence of the **Highest** had intended us to give the doctrine of godliness a new luster, or even more strength, after the core of the wisest teachers in all Christian **congregations** <note>original: "Gemeinen." Refers to the various denominations or church bodies of the time.</note> has, as it were, lavished all their intellect and diligence on its clarification? Perhaps others will judge the causes that prompted this superfluous book better than we ourselves, if we merely recount the occasion that imperceptibly brought us to its preparation.

A learned and capable man, who has made himself known through several edifying writings and now governs a school in this land with renown and benefit, lived here for several years by himself and requested that I assign him a task that could both ease the burden of securing his livelihood and occupy his mind in a useful way. After some reflection, I suggested to him whether it would please him to bring into order—and to arrange somewhat better than many had transcribed from my mouth—that which I have frequently presented to the youth here, who are being prepared for the service of the **Lord’s Congregation** <note>original: "Gemeine des HErren." Referring to students training for the ministry/pastorate.</note>, regarding the **Moral Theology** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre." Literally "teaching of customs," the standard term for Christian Ethics.</note> of the Holy Scripture. He accepted the proposal: and the current publisher offered, upon my recommendation, to provide the costs for the printing and to reward the efforts of my friend, if I would oversee his draft and allow my name to be mentioned on the title of the book. I agreed to this without thinking how far the consequences might lead that must flow from this plan. I looked toward nothing further than how I might help a capable man, whom I would gladly see serve the **Church**

)( 2

...ness of this land, I might provide help for a short time until the Lord showed me a way to care for him better. And nowhere did anything appear that could cause me concern; the means I had chosen to achieve this good intention would indeed benefit one, but become detrimental to many others. The publisher feared no harm and expected to find buyers. I believed that it would not be particularly difficult for me, alongside my other business, to look through the **sheets** <note>original: "Bogen." These were large pieces of paper printed with multiple pages of text, then folded to create sections of a book.</note> one after another and either improve them or increase them with some additions. And when this question occasionally presented itself to me: What will the world, which is already overwhelmed with useless books, say to the fact that a man, to whom this is not unknown, contributes his own to this hated multitude? I answered it with another question: Could it not be that a book which appears unnecessary in itself becomes necessary and useful to some people by chance, or rather through a holy and wise **government of God** <note>original: "Regierung GOttes." A theological term for Divine Providence, the belief that God actively guides all events in the world.</note>? What else was there to fear?

The work began. The skillful man of whom I spoke collected from all sorts of—partly failed, partly incomplete—**transcripts** <note>original: "Abschrifften." These were handwritten notes taken by students during Mosheim's lectures.</note> that which I had spoken from memory to my listeners several times concerning the nature and parts of **godliness** <term>Gottseligkeit: a central 18th-century Lutheran concept meaning active piety and a life lived in devotion to God</term> and put it together sensibly. I began to shorten his work, then lengthen it, then change it this way and that. Hardly had I reached the third sheet when I grew tired of this annoying effort. My friend had spent more diligence and effort on a foreign work than I had expected. My negligent and simple writing style had been so decorated and elevated by him in many places that I almost no longer recognized it. My thoughts were hidden and mixed among many others that he had added from his own stock. What I had presented in few words had been at times much more extensively and thoroughly explained and executed by him. Had the work been printed in the state it had reached through the laudable diligence of this learned man, it would perhaps have been more eagerly received and more gladly read by many: However, I could not well without a...

# Preface.

...to separate those disputes from one another with which Christians, as well as **philosophers** <term>Weltweisen: literally "the worldly-wise," a common 18th-century term for secular philosophers or academics</term>, are accustomed to plague each other. The wise saying of that great King occurred to me more than once: **I applied my heart to know wisdom, and folly, and prudence, but I perceived that this also is labor.** <note>original: "Pred. Salom. I, 17." This refers to Ecclesiastes 1:17 in the German Lutheran Bible.</note> And this word moved me all the more powerfully the more often I had experienced the truth of it within myself. What is it, I said to myself, that you are seeking? Your heart clings to certain plans that you will perhaps never carry out, and which, if you have the luck to carry them out, will promote the pleasure of a few people more than your own welfare and peace, or that of most Christians. While you wander through the vast kingdom of learning, making acquaintances here and there, the time slips away unnoticed—time which you are obligated to use for the general benefit as much as possible. Would it not be acting wisely if you spent at least a part of it in the contemplation of such things that require less labor and effort, and promise more satisfaction and benefit to yourself as well as to other people?

If the scholar should say that you could have undertaken something more important and necessary, then these very holy truths, which you will strive to understand more clearly, will give you the strength to listen to his judgment with **serenity** <note>original: "Gelassenheit." A key term in German Pietism and mysticism, referring to a state of calm, detached surrender to God's will.</note>. Is the Lord your judge, or men who, just like you, must present themselves before the judgment seat of the Redeemer, even if they far surpass you here in recognition and science? In this way, the resolution gradually took firm hold in me to continue and complete the work I had begun. And I must confess, to the glory of divine wisdom, that in the progress of the work I often found a sure means to dispel the coldness and sluggishness of the soul toward what is good—a state which is often the tiresome fruit of our earthly affairs and learned investigations.

We wish to leave the question undecided: whether in this matter one should revere merely the ways of general divine **Providence** <note>original: "Vorsehung." The belief in God's ongoing intervention and guidance in the world.</note>, or a mark of the special government and oversight of the Most High over His own? Everyone remains free to think of it as they please. We worry that we might infringe too closely upon humility if

# Preface.

<meta>catchword: shows,</meta>

We believed a special leading of the Lord has guided us to undertake a work which we never intended to begin, much less to complete. It is enough for us to be convinced that the Lord watches over the earth and directs the plans of men to His glory. We have said enough, and perhaps more than enough, about the occasion for this work. It is time to say something about its nature.

We have resolved to collect what the Holy Scripture mentions regarding **godliness** <term>Gottseligkeit: a central 18th-century concept describing a life of active, heartfelt piety and devotion to God's will</term> and the **conduct** <term>Wandel: literally "walk," referring to one's moral behavior and way of life</term> of those who wish to be called children of God, to connect these points, to explain them according to our way of thinking, and to prove them thoroughly. Therefore, we call the entire work a **Moral Teaching of the Holy Scripture** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre der heiligen Schrift." While "Sitten-Lehre" can mean ethics, in this theological context it refers to the systematic study of Christian conduct.</note>. We do not mean to imply by this that every single thing we have presented is expressly written in the divine books, or as if we only wanted to explain those passages that describe and direct the life of true Christians. We only want to say that the foundation of our entire work is the Scripture, that most of what we have presented flows necessarily from it, and that we have brought forward nothing that cannot be reconciled with what the Scripture clearly and distinctly says. The intelligent world knows that books are usually named after what constitutes their most prominent part and core. In certain matters, we have had to call upon **reason** <term>Vernunft</term> for help, so that the truth of the teachings found in the Scripture might appear all the more clearly to those who seek wisdom. And we are certain that no one can present and explain the moral teaching of Christians in its full concept without following our example in this regard.

We will begin the start of the second part with two investigations, the utility of which will extend across the entire teaching of the external works and duties of men. In the one, we will deal with the laws of God; in the other, with the deeds of men, insofar as they relate to the laws of God. In both, we will not be able to refrain from touching upon various questions that have given cause for disagreement among the teachers of piety <term>Gottseligkeit: a central concept in 18th-century German theology, referring to a life of active, heartfelt devotion to God</term>. We assure in advance that whenever our conviction draws us away from certain teachings, we will always remember with reverence the merits and gifts of those who maintained them.

Regarding the other circumstances of this work—the style of writing, certain presentations through which we have sometimes sought to stir the attention of the readers, and other things—we wish to say nothing. We have directed our primary concern toward distinctness and clarity. For the sake of this, we have often intentionally used more words than we might have needed if we had been writing for people who did not need to learn. # Preparation

### §. I.

The **Moral Theology** <term>Sitten-Lehre: literally "teaching of morals," used here as a synonym for Moral Theology</term> of the **Holy Scripture** is a collection of those teachings and truths of the Holy Scripture, arranged according to both Scripture and reason, which instruct a person on how they may pass from a state of sin and natural unrighteousness into a state of grace and peace with **God**, and thereafter must prove and demonstrate their inward faith and renewal through outward good works.

->Explanation.<-

In every science, it is necessary to form an orderly and distinct concept of it. This must be observed all the more diligently in the **Moral Theology of the Holy Scripture**, because the term Moral Theology is used sometimes in a broader and sometimes in a narrower sense. We take it here in the broader sense, and understand by it all those teachings of the Holy Scripture that concern the inward improvement of a person as well as those that direct them toward the upright fruits of faith and **sanctification** <term>Heiligung: the process of a believer being made holy through the Holy Spirit</term>. Everyone is free to assign a greater or lesser meaning to their words, as long as they do not leave the reader in doubt as to what their meaning is. Others use this word in a narrower sense. There are some who use it only to indicate those teachings which deal with the natural corruption of man and show the means to escape this misery. To these, they add **Ethics** or **Christian Jurisprudence**. And with this term, they indicate instruction regarding exter-

<column-break/>

nal life-duties, which must be observed by sanctified people according to the prescription of the Law of **God**. There are others who restrict the term **Moral Theology** even more narrowly, and mean by it merely the teaching of virtues and vices. These count the first part of the study of morals, which concerns the inward improvement of the soul, as part of the **Doctrine of Faith** <term>Glaubens-Lehre: also known as Dogmatics, the systematic study of the core tenets and doctrines of the Christian faith</term>. I grant everyone the right to make such arrangements of this holy science in their mind as seems convenient and useful to them. And every sensible person will, in turn, grant me the right to believe that it is best to use the term spiritual **Moral Theology** or **Ethics** to designate everything that belongs in the Holy Scripture to the inward cleansing and improvement of our souls and to the external order of our conduct.

One can consider all sciences in a twofold manner. First, insofar as they exist in the understanding of a person and are, as it were, attributes...

Those who view the sciences as perfections of the intellect say that they are aptitudes (*) or skills of the mind. Those who look at them from the other side call them disciplines, teaching structures, or orderly arrangements of the truths that make up a science. We have described **Spiritual Moral Theology** <term>geistliche Sitten-Lehre: the study of Christian ethics and the soul’s progress</term> here in such a way that we have set aside the consideration of the individual person; we have not considered it as it exists within people—especially within believers—but rather how it exists outside the human intellect, such as when it is presented or handled in books and writings. People have long been accustomed to viewing the spiritual sciences not only as perfections of the mind, but also as properties of a **sanctified and reborn** <term>geheiligten und wiedergebohrnen: a Pietist reference to the "New Birth" or spiritual conversion</term> intellect. However, they argue that the instruction and presentation of a science, as well as the orderly arrangement of the truths belonging to it, are merely accidental and do not belong to its essence. They claim that something which is merely accidental and occurs by chance cannot provide a *category* <note>original: "genus," a logical term for a general class or type</note>, as one is accustomed to say, in a technical description. They argue there must be something certain and constant from which one should recognize what the nature of a thing actually consists of. But why all this academic cleverness if one merely wants to instruct the inexperienced on what the matter actually is that one wants to explain to them? I believe that all sciences are viewed by a teacher in terms of how they can and must be conveyed to those who wish to understand them. And whoever looks at them this way cannot view them as anything other than orderly, coherent collections of certain teachings and truths intended to serve a common purpose. It is all the same to me whether one wants to admit or deny that such a collection is a "category" properly so-called. It is enough for me that an inexperienced person can easily grasp what a science is when it is described to him in this manner.

I mention all of this to no one's contempt, much less to stir up new and vain quarrels. I know who those are from whom I deviate here, and I consider myself their pupil and apprentice in countless things. I say only what seems good to me.

...seems so: and I mention this for the purpose of removing, according to my meager ability, the obstacles that often hold back those of average understanding when entering a branch of knowledge.

The description I have given of the **Moral Theology** <term>Sitten-Lehre: literally "teaching of customs," referring to the study of Christian ethics and conduct</term> of Holy Scripture is, I believe, clear, distinct, and brief. It could have been made more extensive, but perhaps it would have become more obscure as a result. What a "collection of certain teachings and truths of the Holy Scripture" is, is clear in itself. I only need to say why I added that this collection is arranged according to **Scripture and Reason**. A collection of certain teachings arranged according to reason, leading to a main objective, is precisely what is otherwise called a **system** or a **science** <term>Wissenschaft: in this 18th-century context, it refers to any structured, academic body of knowledge</term>. All things and propositions that serve a certain purpose necessarily stand in a connection with one another and have an order among themselves that follows from the nature of things themselves. Reason discovers this natural kinship and order through reflection and deliberation: it gathers the teachings that lie apart: finally, it places them as their character and the nature of the entire science to which they belong requires. This also happens in Moral Theology. The Spirit of the Most High has not erected a coherent building, nor a technical science in the Holy Scripture. He has allowed the teachings belonging to faith and life to be presented here and there in various books. It is our duty to gather these truths scattered throughout the entire Holy Scripture and to bring them into such a state that both we and other men—

<column-break/>

—can overlook at once what the will of the Lord is, and more easily grasp our duties and the reasons for them. Reason has so much power that it can judge how one piece of divine wisdom relates to another, and in what connection it stands with the first fundamental truths. It makes use of this capacity granted to it by God and uses its knowledge to arrange the divine truths in an orderly fashion. In this way, the spiritual sciences become collections arranged according to reason. Their general state and arrangement can be different without truth losing anything thereby. The concepts, insights, and tastes of men are manifold. Therefore, it happens that one person makes and finds this order, another that order, according to how he envisions the matters or has perhaps been instructed. But the internal order, which flows from the nature, the value, and the use of the teachings, must be the same everywhere and remains unchangeable.

There are people who cannot tolerate divine truths and teachings being brought into such a proper state. It is thought that the holy truths lose something of their power or their dignity if they are linked together and ordered according to certain rules, just like the parts of human scholarship. These people would judge more modestly if they looked more at the matter itself and its purpose, and thought less of the faults of certain people and various abuses that one will never be able to completely abolish. ## §. II.

The divine truths pertaining to life stand in the closest fellowship with the doctrines of faith that have been revealed to us. Many are therefore accustomed to present the doctrines of faith and of life in a single order: And the oldest teachers of our churches held this custom. It seems better to me to present moral theology separately. For many parts of it would otherwise have to be forced into an unnatural order. Not to mention other reasons.

-># Regarding Spiritual Moral Theology<-

Those who still made some distinction presented what they wished to say about the conduct of Christians in special explanations of the Ten Commandments, which were, however, only regarded as parts of the doctrine of the divine law.

The successors of these first witnesses of pure truth <note>Likely referring to the early Protestant Reformers who prioritized "pure" biblical teaching.</note> have considered it advisable to depart from this habit. The famous **George Calixtus** <note>Georg Calixt (1586–1656), a Lutheran theologian known for distinguishing between fundamental and non-fundamental articles of faith.</note> made the beginning of distinguishing **Moral Theology** from the **Doctrines of Faith**, and treating the former separately. His dispute with the well-known apostate, **Barthold Neuhaus** <note>Barthold Nihus (1590–1657), a convert from Lutheranism to Roman Catholicism.</note>, and other conflicts into which he fell, forced him to break off from his commenced work and leave the execution to his students: **Dürr**, **Rixner**, **Haegel**, and **Meyer**. When subsequently **Natural Law** <term>Natural Law: A system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than the rules of society.</term> was better researched by various great people and brought to greater certainty and order, one became established in this method. Over time, **Spiritual Moral Theology** was made into its own science, presented separately, and only that which is indispensable was brought into it from the Doctrine of Faith.

And it seems to me that this was not only permitted, but also well and usefully done. It is true: faith and life belong together. He who separates one from the other disrupts the order of **GOD**. However, in themselves, these are yet two distinct things that can very well be weighed and considered separately. Between the **Sovereign Rights** and the highness of princes, and between the duties of

<column-break/>

subjects, there is the closest connection. These flow from those, and those cannot exist without these. And what prevents, nevertheless, that the doctrine of the power and rights of princes, and the duties that fall to the subjects because of these rights, could be described and presented separately? Why then should the doctrines which represent the greatness of **GOD**, His works, and His love toward mankind, not likewise be considered alone, and the **duty of men** that arises from it be viewed for itself? 

Yet it is not only permitted to present these two otherwise closely linked parts of divine truth separately; it is also useful. First, one gains the opportunity to thoroughly and properly elaborate on certain pieces that are necessary to know, which one does not otherwise easily recall if one retains the old order. The doctrine of the **love of GOD**, of the **powers of nature and grace**, of the **special duties** that one must observe in trade and conduct and otherwise, and many others like them, are of such a nature that one does not find much opportunity within the Doctrines of Faith to elaborate on them according to their merit. One can seek this opportunity and, through reflection, finally find a place among the doctrines of faith where one can put them. But will not the thread of divine truths be, as it were, torn thereby? Will not the understanding of the person we wish to instruct be stopped in the course of his thoughts and hindered [from seeing] the natural connection of the divine...

<margin>A3</margin>

...wish to become, and touch upon other things besides. That is to say, we must take to our aid a good portion of the divine truth that is prescribed to our understanding. If we come to the external arrangement of a Christian’s conduct, everything again relates back to the knowledge of Christ and the benefits he has earned for us. All duties of our life must come from faith. It is not possible to bring the heart to the practice of Christian duties if it has not first been prepared and made capable for them through repentance, faith, and conversion. All good works are the fruits of **rebirth** <term>Rebirth (Wieder-Geburt): In this context, the spiritual transformation or "being born again" that a believer undergoes.</term>. And this, in turn, is founded upon **justification** <term>Justification (Rechtfertigung): The theological concept of being declared righteous before God through faith.</term>. Justification, however, is founded upon the redemption of Christ.

<margin>A3</margin>
**All moral teaching is, for another thing, nothing but an inevitable consequence of the doctrine of faith and, in part, its very purpose.** Revelation instructs us that we owe everything we have—spirit, life, breath, understanding, body—to the Lord. From this doctrine follows this irrefutable conclusion: We are bound to love, revere, and obey the Lord. A rational creature **must always look toward his Creator, search out His will, and strive to please Him.** The Spirit of God reveals to us in the Holy Scriptures the infinite gifts and benefits for which we have the redemption of our Savior to thank. Can anyone who has rightly grasped these truths conclude otherwise than this: I must apply all my strength to prove myself grateful to such a holy and loving Redeemer? I am bound to surrender myself to Him as His own.

<column-break/>

I am duty-bound to sacrifice all the powers of my spirit to Him and to arrange my life in such a way that I promote His honor and build His kingdom. The doctrines of faith are, in a word, the greatest possible motivations that drive us to practice the duties of **godliness** <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"</note>. If one takes these away from the divine laws, they will seem even more unpleasant and burdensome to us than they otherwise appear to corrupt mankind. Those who still strive to live according to them will not do so with the willing and joyful spirit that the Lord demands—not out of love for Him—but out of fear and compulsion. Their obedience will be an obedience of the law and of servitude, and not an obedience of faith and evangelical freedom. In relation to moral teaching, the doctrines of faith are exactly what the weights are to a clock. The clock stands still when the weight is removed. And our strength and desire to do good becomes sluggish and powerless if we do not look to the doctrine of the grace of God that has been bestowed upon us in our Savior.

This may have been part of what moved the first teachers of our churches <note>Referring to the early Protestant Reformers.</note> not to separate the entire divine truth—which serves both faith and life—into two parts, but rather to treat them in a single order. In the older theological instructions, that which belongs to the life and conduct of men was partly drawn into the teachings on the law and good works, and partly treated in specific main sections added to the doctrines of faith, such as those concerning the authorities <note>The "Obrigkeit" or secular government.</note>, the domestic estate <note>The "Hauß-Stande" or family life/household management.</note>, and the preaching office.

->## On Spiritual Moral Teaching<-

...distinction. Those who still made some effort to distinguish the two presented what they wished to say about the conduct of Christians in special explanations of the Ten Commandments; yet these were still regarded merely as parts of the doctrine of divine law.

The successors of these first witnesses of the pure truth have deemed it advisable to depart from this custom. The famous **George Calixtus** <note>Georg Calixtus (1586–1656) was a German Lutheran theologian who was the first to treat "Ethics" as a discipline separate from "Dogmatics."</note> made the beginning by distinguishing **Moral Teaching** <term>Sitten-Lehre: Generally translated as Ethics or Moral Theology; the study of how a Christian should live.</term> from the **Doctrines of Faith** <term>Glaubens-Lehre: Dogmatics; the study of what a Christian must believe.</term>, and by treating the former as a specific subject. His dispute with the well-known apostate, **Barthold Neuhaus** <note>A Lutheran physician and poet who converted to Catholicism, sparking a fierce polemical exchange with Calixtus.</note>, and other controversies into which he fell, forced him to break off from his work before it was finished and to leave the completion to his students: Dürr, Rixner, Heigelius, and Meyer. When subsequently the **Natural Law** <term>Recht der Natur: The concept of a universal law of right and wrong discoverable by human reason.</term> was better investigated by various great men and brought to greater certainty and order, this new method became firmly established. In time, Spiritual Moral Teaching was made into its own science, presented independently, and only those elements from the Doctrine of Faith that are absolutely indispensable were included in it.

And it seems to me that this was not only permitted, but was also a good and useful development. It is true that faith and life belong together. He who separates one from the other disrupts the order of God. However, in themselves, these are nonetheless two distinct things that can very well be weighed and considered separately. Between the sovereign rights and the majesty of princes, and the duties of

<column-break/>

subjects, there is the closest connection. The latter flow from the former, and the former cannot exist without the latter. And yet, what prevents the doctrine of the power and rights of princes, and the duties that fall to subjects because of these rights, from being described and presented separately? Why then should the doctrines which present the greatness of God, His works, and His love toward men, not just as well be considered alone, and the duty of men that arises therefrom be viewed on its own? 

Indeed, it is not only permitted to present these two otherwise closely linked parts of divine truth separately; it is also useful. First, it provides the opportunity to *thoroughly and properly explain certain pieces which are necessary to know, which one otherwise does not easily recall if one retains the old order. The doctrine of the love* of God, of the powers of nature and of grace, of the special duties that one must observe in business and daily conduct and otherwise, and many other such things, are such that one does not find much opportunity within the Doctrines of Faith to explain them as they deserve. One can seek out such an opportunity and, through reflection, finally find a place among the doctrines of faith where they might be placed. However, would not the thread of divine truths thereby be torn, as it were? Would not the understanding of the one whom we wish to instruct be halted in the course of his thoughts and hindered from perceiving the natural connection of the divine truths?

One can, secondly, establish a much **better, more pleasant, and easier order in many things if one presents moral teaching** of the Holy Scriptures as a distinct science. I have not yet encountered any arrangement of the truths belonging to faith into which all teachings serving life and conduct could be brought without force <note>The author suggests that forcing ethical rules into a system of theology often feels unnatural or cluttered.</note>. Those who have attempted to bring the entire will of God concerning the **salvation** <term>Seligkeit: Refers to the state of being saved or eternal blessedness.</term> of mankind into a single orderly collection have soon omitted necessary things, or had to make additions and appendices, or placed various matters in the wrong positions. Is it not better to avoid such errors and to treat moral teaching alone in such a context as suits the whole matter, and which neither gives the understanding too much work, nor requires all kinds of circumlocution and forced connections? I pass over some other reasons.

What has been noted by some otherwise deserving men, so that this separation of the teachings of faith and life might be abolished again, is of no particular weight. The most prominent reason brought forward, as far as I know, is this: 

<column-break/>

People would not correctly see the influence of divine truths upon life and conduct if one were torn from the other in the presentation. One would thereby become accustomed to viewing both parts of revealed truth as distinct sciences that have nothing in common with each other: thereby both the **doctrine of faith** and **moral teaching** would lose something. The former would be regarded by many as mere intellectual knowledge that served nothing but to occupy the thoughts; the latter, on the other hand, would be robbed of the greatest motivations that must flow from the doctrine of faith. I praise the zeal of those who judge in this way: but their judgment itself seems to me not to be sufficiently founded. It is as if one assumed in advance that those who presented moral teaching in particular did not think of the truths of faith and forgot the connection that unites both most closely. If there are some who do this, they sin and give right to the reproach we have mentioned. However, by righteous and experienced **Evangelical teachers** <note>In this context, "Evangelical" (Evangelische) refers to the Lutheran tradition.</note>, this has not occurred thus far. Those of our churches who have until now treated moral teaching alone have always laid faith as the foundation and viewed the duties of life as indisputable consequences of faith. And those who have taught the doctrine of faith alone have not entirely forgotten life. One can therefore let this fear go, as if one were doing harm to both parts of divine truth when one considers each for itself.

# §. III.

The source of this entire science <note>In the 18th century, "science" (*Wissenschaft*) referred to any systematic branch of knowledge or disciplined study, including theology and ethics.</note> is the **Holy Scripture**. From the clear passages and places of this holy book, everything that belongs here must be determined and concluded. Healthy **reason** is indeed not entirely excluded from it; it agrees exactly with the commands of God. Moreover, the holy men <note>Referring to the biblical authors.</note>, in their presentation of moral teaching, have presupposed much that we, as rational human beings, can and must know. Regardless of this, everyone must take careful care not to turn spiritual moral teaching into a kind of "rational wisdom," or to subject the laws of the Lord to the judgment of a bold and poorly ordered intellect.

->Explanation.<-

The source from which we draw moral teaching is the Holy Scripture. In particular, those parts of it belong here in which either the way to the **inner improvement of souls** is shown, or the will of the Lord regarding the life and conduct of mankind is revealed. What a subject is bound to do, he recognizes from the written will of the lord who has sovereignty over the land in which he lives. We all live in the kingdom of the power of our God; we are creatures whom He Himself has made and formed as His subjects. What is therefore incumbent upon us must become known to us from the book which the Author of our nature and the eternal Lawgiver of all rational creatures had composed and recorded for the benefit of mankind. In this world, one does not tolerate arbitrarily chosen laws. He who wishes to live in a certain civil society must not grant his freedom more than

the will of the person who is the head of the society allows. In the kingdom of God, a self-concocted delusion about the best and most useful way of life is likewise of no value. We have <gloss>page 220.</gloss> the laws of our Creator before us. It must now be said what rights are granted to **reason** in the **Moral Theory** <term>Sitten-Lehre; the study of ethics and Christian conduct</term> of Holy Scripture. **Reason** serves first in the explanation of the passages of Holy Scripture and the laws of God, from which this holy science is derived. It investigates, according to certain rules, the meanings of the words that occur in them; it makes the underlying concepts clear. We shall say more about this matter shortly.

Reason is, secondly, authorized to produce exact, distinct, and clear descriptions of the duties, virtues, and vices which the Spirit of God commands us either to accept and practice, or to flee and discard. The servants of the Lord, through whom He speaks in the Scripture, exhort us to **humility**, **gentleness**, **patience**, and **love** toward the brothers; conversely, they plead and entreat us to renounce **pride**, **quarrelsomeness**, **haughtiness**, **envy**, and other vices. But we do not see that they describe these virtues and vices in great detail, or mark their boundaries. They did not find this necessary. They presupposed that they were writing to people who possessed enough reason to form such concepts for themselves, and who could otherwise see in the life of **Jesus Christ** and His witnesses the actual depictions of the duties and virtues that befit a follower of the **Savior**.

<column-break/>

Meanwhile, it is well known that both he who intends to instruct others, and he who wishes to edify himself, must accurately know the nature and condition of the things he requires of himself and others, and must be able to set apart that in which they are related and that in which they are distinct. Whoever is not practiced in this will very often confuse things that must be distinguished, and will generally make for a poor teacher.

**Reason** therefore rightly strives to present the true nature and properties of the elements belonging to the life of the saints, and to categorize each one correctly and orderly. To that end, it gathers together what is said here and there in Holy Scripture concerning them and connects it in a skillful manner. It makes use of what wise and understanding people have observed to present the actual essence of every good and evil inclination, and of every blameworthy or laudable quality of the soul, and introduces it into the Moral Theory of Holy Scripture, so far as it does not conflict with the nature of the same. Finally, if it is not yet certain enough, it takes the life of Jesus and His true members <note>The "members" of Christ refers to the community of faithful believers or the Church.</note> as an aid, and sketches the virtues as they were practiced by them in deed.

<margin>|</margin> Thirdly, **reason** serves us so that we may derive specific duties from the general laws of God, and apply what is said generally in the Scripture to the diverse cases and events occurring in life. Everything a human being has to do or omit in all ways of life, stations, times, and circumstances is not recorded in the Scripture...

Far less are all of life’s events recounted in it <note>Holy Scripture</note> into which we might fall, nor are all the difficulties resolved at once that might manifest in each situation regarding the Law of God. What would Holy Scripture have become as a book if it had pleased God to decide every single question of conscience therein and to instruct everyone according to their particular circumstances? He has therefore left it to human diligence to apply that which He has ordained in general to oneself and others in particular, and to draw from His general commands the consequences that must serve as a rule and prescription in specific occurrences. This is the business and the labor of sound **reason**. This shows what specific duties necessarily flow from the laws of the Lord, which everyone has to observe according to their calling and station. This considers times, places, persons, and things, and provides instruction on what the will of the Lord requires of people according to their differing natures. This resolves the doubts from general fundamental truths that can arise in manifold incidents and leads the wavering understanding through lawful and clear consequences to a certain and secure conclusion.

**Reason** has so much light, **fourthly**, that it can demonstrate and prove the justice, the equity, the wisdom, the excellence, and the utility of the laws of the Lord. # Preparation

Interpretation must call upon four things for help if one does not wish to err: 1) the fundamental truths of the **Doctrine of Faith** <term>Glaubens-Lehre: the systematic study of Christian beliefs</term>; 2) the first and general truths of **Ethics** <term>Sitten-Lehre: the study of moral conduct and duties</term> itself; 3) **Reason** <note>original: "Vernunft"</note>; 4) certain human books and writings.

<margin><note>Red bracket marking point I</note></margin>

I) Whoever wishes to rightly explain the passages of the **Holy Scripture** <note>original: "Heiligen Schrift"</note> that deal with ethics must never lose sight of the fundamental truths of the **Christian Doctrine**. I wish to say with these words exactly what others are accustomed to expressing in this way: the **Holy Scripture** must be explained according to the **Analogy of Faith** <term>Analogie des Glaubens: the principle that individual scriptural passages should be interpreted in harmony with the whole of the Bible and established doctrine</term>. No explanation can be valid or accepted that conflicts with the first principles upon which the entire structure of **Christ’s** doctrine rests. It is not unknown to me that many in our times, who think themselves wise, mock this rule and laugh at the spiritual scholars who appeal to the **Rule of Faith** <note>original: "Richtschnur des Glaubens"</note> in their explanations of the **Holy Scripture**. However, I also know that people of this sort either do not understand what this word means to sensible people, or they do not wish to understand it. Perhaps some poorly executed descriptions of the **Analogy of Faith**, or the haste of certain people, have given them the opportunity to invent false opinions. The **Rule of Faith** consists of those places in the **Holy Scripture** which are clearer, more distinct, and easier than others—those places in which the divine truths are presented most thoroughly and extensively—and at the same time the doctrines that lie so openly in these passages that everyone who has not lost their freedom of spirit can se-

<column-break/>

-e them. Let us be told if we do wrong when we maintain that according to these places, and according to the precept of the doctrines revealed therein, the remaining passages of the **Holy Scripture** must be explained? Is it not established that the obscure places of a book must be explained as the clear and distinct ones would have it? Do not all sensible people who interpret human writings take as a basis those passages where the author's meaning is presented in detail, and judge from them the sense of those places where the same matters have been handled more briefly? Are there not in all sciences certain general fundamental doctrines upon which the whole building stands? And do not those act reasonably who always look to these first truths when they wish to know whether these or those doctrines are correct and can be accepted as pieces of the science to which they are reckoned? 

A teacher of ethics, therefore, must not act otherwise in the explanation of the passages of the **Holy Scripture** that he requires for his purpose. He must always see to it that he does not attribute to them any meaning that cannot be reconciled with the general truths of the religion of our **Savior** <note>original: "Heyland"</note>. **Jesus** says in Luke 11:41, "Give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" <note>original: "Gebet Allmosen von dem, das da ist, so ist euch alles rein."</note>. Is everything then accomplished if one merely shares with the poor? Is generosity toward the needy the path to reconciliation with **God** and to true holiness and purification? This explanation pleases those who wish to boast of their works before **God**. However, it is impossible to reconcile it with so many other passages of the **Holy Scripture**...

Evil desire can remain in the heart and the inclination to sin can remain in the will, even if we were to have ourselves mutilated or our eyes put out. **Jesus** would therefore have proposed an ineffective means for improvement and would have overturned what he emphatically teaches elsewhere if he had commanded us to chop off hands and feet—and thereby make ourselves unfit for the service of **God** and the world—simply to prevent all opportunity for offense <note>The author argues for a metaphorical interpretation: "cutting off" means removing sinful influences, not literal self-harm</note>.

A creature must be very proud and in love with itself to imagine that it is capable of perfectly coming to know its **Creator** for itself, and of bringing a Being that has no limits into the narrow confines of its understanding. Therefore, one acts absurdly when one dares to explain what is in the holy books about **God’s** essence and the mysteries of His will in such a way that our understanding might encounter nothing insoluble within them. To me, this seems just as wise as if a man tilling the field <note>The author uses a "down-to-earth" analogy to show that some things are simply beyond a person's specific tools or station.</note> wanted to twist the basic principles of mathematical sciences until they suited his work and trade, or if a child used its toys to explain a book on architecture. And how would it be possible for mysteries, which human intellect <note>original: "Wiß," an archaic term for wit or intelligence</note> cannot grasp at all, or only with the extreme effort, to instruct people on what they should do or leave undone? This consideration provides us first with this rule of interpretation: **An explanation of Holy Scripture that is so dark that it cannot be grasped by every person's understanding—an interpretation that is not so clear and manifest that it shows all people the way they must go—cannot be correct.** I am amazed when I read the books of certain people <note>The author likely refers to "Enthusiasts" or "Mystics" of the era who used obscure, metaphorical language.</note> who have wanted to give new and unusual instructions for holiness, and I almost do not know whether I dare believe that they have truly persuaded themselves that they have uncovered the true sense of **Holy Scripture**. My understanding, when I begin to read, becomes as dark and obscured as if it were thrust down into a deep cave. Meanwhile, the bold manner with which these people teach, and the images they throw before my imagination, cause me to gather my wits and become eager to truly fathom their meaning. I gain nothing by it, and find ever deeper abysses into which I am sunk. Finally, I conclude thus: **God** is Light, Clarity, and Life. ### IV)
Whoever wishes to thoroughly interpret the passages of **Holy Scripture** that deal with **moral doctrine** <term>Moral Doctrine (Sitten-Lehre): The study of ethics and right conduct based on religious principles.</term> may, to that end, make use of certain human books. I intend this to be understood only regarding those passages found in the **New Testament**. It is agreed that the **Apostles** of our **Savior** used their words in the sense they had in the common language of the **Greeks** in those times: with a few exceptions to which they had to give new meanings to represent certain doctrines of faith that were unknown to the world until then. How else would those for whose benefit they wrote have been able to understand their books? If this is so, it is simultaneously proven that secular **Greek** writings can contribute much to researching the true sense of the words in the **New Testament** and placing them beyond all doubt.

But nowhere can these books, in my opinion, perform greater service than where the deeds, duties, virtues, and vices of men are discussed. I have already said above that it did not please the **Spirit of GOD** to give precise descriptions of these things. And yet, for many reasons, we cannot do without them. If the **Spirit of GOD** spoke in the common language and left the words their ordinary meaning, then these passages are the most fit to make us certain of what the names **Meekness**...

...courage, humility, gentleness, mercy, and others are truly called. One might object: surely there is a great difference between the virtues of nature and those of grace, between the heathens <note>The author uses "heathens" (Heiden) to refer to non-Christian classical philosophers, specifically the Greeks and Romans.</note> and the Christians? How then is it possible to learn the nature of Christian virtues from what the heathens said about the good qualities of a human being? This difficulty is easily resolved. This distinction between the virtues of grace and those of nature does not concern their internal essence; it lies only in other characteristics and factors that make those virtues stemming from grace more excellent. **JESUS** commands mercy; **Plato** does the same. In what do they agree? And in what do they differ? Is the virtue that **JESUS** calls by the name "mercy" of a completely different nature than that to which **Plato** gives this name? Not at all. What **Plato** calls thus is a constant intention to serve the miserable and to offer a hand in their suffering. And our **Savior** means nothing else by this word. What is it then by which these two virtues are separated from one another? First, it is the origin. The mercy of that heathen sage comes from

<column-break/>

nature: the compassion that **JESUS** demands stems from grace: it flows from faith and the love of **God**. Secondly, it is the object. <note>The original German "Vorwurf" here refers to the "object" or "subject matter" toward which the virtue is directed.</note> The compassion in which the disciples of **Christ** practice extends much further than the mercy of nature. It desires to advise both the soul and the body; it applies to friends and enemies alike. Finally, it is the intention. He who is merciful as **JESUS** requires does not seek himself, but the honor of the **Lord**. A Platonic sympathizer only wants to dampen the stirrings of his nature that are unpleasant to him, or to acquire a new level of honor for himself. If one applies this to the other virtues of Scripture, one will easily understand how far the use of heathen books is permitted in the explanation of the same. Many virtues of the heathens are in themselves the same as the virtues of Christians: but the origin, the scope, and the purpose separate the latter entirely from the former. In the interpretation of the words of Scripture that belong to the vices, one does not need nearly as much caution. Who would deny that the greed, pride, thirst for revenge, ambition, and stubbornness which the Scripture condemns were known to the sages of the heathens?

## Explanation.

A teacher who presents the doctrines of faith <note>Glaubens-Lehren: refers to dogmatic theology or the core tenets of what a Christian must believe.</note> agrees in the main matters with the one who deals with the doctrines of life <note>Lebens-Lehren: refers to ethics, morality, and how a Christian should live.</note>. In the presentation of the doctrines of faith, a clear explanation and a correct proof are absolutely necessary if a rational conviction is to arise in the souls of men. A moral teacher <term>Sitten-Lehrer|A teacher of ethics or conduct</term> must take exactly the same path. He must first explain; he must correctly distinguish between virtue and vice; he must assign to each its proper place and boundaries. He must afterward confirm everything with solid proofs from the Holy Scriptures.

First, I say, he who wishes to <u>properly instruct others in their duties</u> must explain them <u>as clearly as possible</u>. The concepts underlying the words used to designate virtue and vice are not known to us by nature. They must, therefore, be very poorly understood by most people unless one comes to their aid with a clear explanation of them. And anyone who has associated even moderately with ordinary people knows from experience what erroneous and false imaginations most people form of the things they should avoid or do.

<column-break/>

Take, for example, the word humility <note>original: "Demuth"</note>, and ask some of those who do not think themselves the worst of Christians what is indicated by this word? What confusion and lack of understanding will one encounter in their answers? How different will the sketches of this virtue be? And how many will not know at all what they should answer? One can take this as a constant rule, which will seldom deceive: Ordinary people create for themselves such descriptions of their duties, of virtues, and of vices, which accord either with their foolish opinions on the nature of Christianity or with their natural inclinations and desires. Let the description of greed and extravagance <term>Verschwendung|unrestrained spending or prodigality</term> be given by two people, one of whom is devoted to the former vice, the other to the latter: One will be astonished at the difference in their descriptions. The greedy man will be careful when he is to say what greed is, so that he does not create a portrait of himself: And the spendthrift will represent his vice in such a way that no suspicion may fall upon him. # Regarding Spiritual Moral Teaching #

Teaching must be derived solely from the Law of the LORD. Whatever is commanded in the Scripture in clear words, or can be derived from a divine Law through a clear and correct deduction, must be accepted and observed. Whoever wishes to convince us of our duties in any other way is mistaken: And whoever wishes to burden us with things that cannot be confirmed by any Law of GOD, to him we owe no obedience.

The Kingdom of Jesus had not been established in the world for long when people already began to introduce two false methods of proof into **moral teaching** <term>moral teaching: original "Sitten-Lehre," the study of ethics and Christian conduct</term>, which gave rise to much disorder. First, people appealed to the authority of men when they wanted to convince Christians of the duties of their conduct. To encourage them, they presented the pronouncements of certain prestigious teachers, the opinions of those wise according to the flesh, and the decrees and laws of assemblies of clergy and bishops. The further the Church moved from its first origin, the more this habit became entrenched. In the times when the school-teachers <note>This likely refers to the "Scholastics," the medieval academics who dominated church philosophy</note> ruled the Western congregations, anyone who could reinforce his exhortation with a passage from **Augustine** <note>original: "Augustino" — St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers</note> or with a law from a so-called **Council** <note>original: "Concilii" — formal meetings of church leaders to decide on doctrine</note> was considered to have proven his point excellently. What happened as a result? People were led away from GOD, who alone is our Law-giver, toward "flesh and blood" <note>A biblical idiom meaning human nature or human authority as opposed to divine revelation</note> and were strengthened in the dangerous opinion that one must obey the advice of one's superiors without examination and must believe whatever the Church believes.

<column-break/>

A proof in moral teaching that is taken only from the authority of other men is invalid and does not deserve the name of a proof. A second kind of people did indeed appeal to the Scripture when they wanted to convince men of their duty: but they forgot the clear Laws of GOD and wanted to determine through extensive digressions what they could have demonstrated with plain passages. I will explain myself more clearly. It was assumed beforehand that in the entire history of the Old and New Testaments there was a twofold meaning: a historical one and another hidden one, which only the "Scripture-wise" could see. They then derived the duties of men from this secret meaning and imagined they had proven them so powerfully that even the most stubborn could hardly resist. This absurd way of proving things was passed down from those Jews who lived before Christ to the teachers of the Christian congregations. To see this, one only needs to compare the writings of **Philo the Jew** <note>original: "Philonis des Juden" — a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegory to fuse Greek philosophy with Jewish Scripture</note> with the writings of Barnabas, **Clement of Alexandria**, **Eusebius**, **Gregory of Nyssa**, and other teachers of the early Church. In both, there is the same way of proving and presenting moral teaching; and one can very easily see that the latter took the former and his peers as their model and master. Since the greatest leaders of the Church had accustomed themselves to this manner, it is easy to suspect what the lesser ones would have done. I will say briefly what happened. From the first days of Christianity until the time of the Reformation, there was almost not a single teacher of morals and of **Godliness** <note>original: "Gottse-ligkeit" — the text breaks here to be continued on the next page</note>...

However, in general, one can say this much to everyone: The Kingdom of God consists not in words, but in power and conviction: but it also does not disdain the service that a hallowed gift of speaking well and pleasantly can provide. Divine wisdom demands simplicity and clarity: but it is also too high and noble for one to wrap it in worthless rags and speak of it as one would of things that mean nothing.

I say secondly: All parts of **moral teaching**, all duties that are demanded, must be thoroughly and clearly proven. We are all subjects of the government of the Almighty God, who can give us laws. And no further exception applies once it is evident that a Law of God exists regarding a matter. But we must also be convinced that this or that, which we are commanded to observe or omit, is the actual will of our King. One may provide the most vivid and pleasant outline of the virtues, one may paint the abhorrence of vice in the most terrifying way for men, one may apply every effort to this work that can rightly excite and move the human imagination; yet all this labor is worth nothing if one cannot clearly and distinctly show the corrupted man that one is proclaiming nothing to him but the will of God.

All proof in the entire **moral**—

### regarding spiritual moral teaching ###

Teaching must be derived solely from the Law of the Lord. Whatever is commanded in Scripture with clear words, or can be derived from a divine law through a clear and correct logical deduction, must be accepted and observed. Anyone who wishes to convince us of our duties in any other way is mistaken: and we owe no obedience to anyone who wishes to burden us with things that cannot be confirmed by any Law of God.

The Kingdom of Jesus <note>original: "JEsU"</note> had not been established in the world for long when people already began to introduce two false methods of proof into **moral teaching** <term>moral teaching: original "Sitten-Lehre," referring here to the study of ethics and Christian conduct</term>, which gave rise to much disorder. First, people appealed to the authority of men when they wanted to convince Christians of the duties regarding their conduct. To encourage them, they presented the pronouncements of certain respected teachers, the opinions of those who are wise according to the flesh <note>a biblical reference to worldly or human wisdom as opposed to spiritual wisdom</note>, and the decrees and laws of the assemblies of clergy and bishops. The further the church moved from its first origin, the more this habit became entrenched. In the times when the scholastic teachers ruled the Western congregations, anyone who could strengthen his exhortation with a passage from **Augustine** <note>original: "Augustino"</note> or with a law of a so-called **council** <note>original: "Concilii"</note> was considered to have proven his point excellently. What was the result? People were led away from God, who alone is our Law-giver, toward flesh and blood, and were strengthened in the dangerous opinion that one must obey the advice of one's superiors without examination and must believe whatever the church believes.

<column-break/>

A proof in **moral teaching** that is taken only from the authority of other men is invalid and does not deserve the name of a proof. Another group of people did indeed appeal to the Scripture when they wanted to convince men of their duty: but they forgot the clear laws of God and wanted to establish through extensive digressions that which they could have demonstrated with plain passages. I will explain myself more clearly. It was assumed beforehand that in the entire history of the Old and New Testaments there was a twofold meaning: a historical one and another hidden one, which only the scholars of Scripture could see. From this secret understanding, they subsequently derived the duties of men, and imagined that they had proven things so powerfully that even the most headstrong person could hardly resist. This absurd way of proving things was passed down from those Jews who lived before Christ to the teachers of the Christian congregations. To understand this, one need only compare the writings of **Philo** <note>original: "Philonis"; a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria</note> the Jew with the writings of **Barnabas**, **Clement of Alexandria**, **Eusebius**, **Gregory of Nyssa**, and other teachers of the early church. In both, there is the same way of proving and presenting **moral teaching**; and one can very easily see that the latter took the former and his like as their model and master. Since the greatest leaders of the churches had accustomed themselves to this manner, it is easy to suspect what the lesser ones would have done. I will say briefly what happened. From the first days of Christianity until the time of the Reformation, there was almost not a single teacher of morals and of **godli-**

...ness, who did not tolerate this habit. The Reformation also brought more light to this matter. The most prominent teachers of the pure churches <note>A common term used by Protestant writers to refer to the Lutheran or Reformed churches following the Reformation</note> have gradually become more cautious; they have preferred the certain foundation of divine laws over the clever fables and inventions of men when they wish to improve souls. Yet how could it have happened that such a deeply rooted habit would be eradicated all at once? One still finds some among the older and newer teachers, even in our own church, who retain something of that old affliction. And perhaps, even in the clarity of our own day, a small remnant of this weakness remains here and there. I do not think I am mistaken in calling this way of convincing people of their duties weak, ineffective, and absurd. It seems to me that a proof which stands on an uncertain foundation and cannot truly engage a well-ordered mind may rightly be called such. Who gave us the instruction that all books of the Old Testament <note>original: "alten Bundes," literally "Old Covenant"</note> have a twofold meaning? Who told us that the deeds of Moses are partly history and partly contain certain laws and exhortations that one must seek out through meditation? And who gives us the assurance that those are not deceiving themselves who seek so many lessons from these deeds—lessons that no one can perceive who wishes to stick to the ordinary rules of interpretation?

I will not be properly understood unless I add some examples.

<column-break/>

I will take these examples from the books of **Gregory of Nyssa** <note>A 4th-century Christian bishop and theologian, one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" known for his mystical and allegorical interpretations</note> regarding the *Life of Moses*, which are nothing more than an allegorical proof of the primary duties a Christian must practice. This great teacher wants to convince the people of his station that while one may indeed read the books of the heathens and the worldly-wise, one must not forget the Holy Scriptures and Christian doctrine. This truth is correct in itself and can be proven from such passages of Holy Scripture that everyone can understand. But Gregory finds this truth in the life of Moses and proves it through a very particular explanation. Moses is adopted as a son by the daughter of the King in Egypt: but his own mother suckles him. From this it is clear, says Gregory, that a Christian must read worldly books in such a way that he still seeks his primary instruction from the Christian Church. Scripture tells us, he says, (*) that although Moses was with the Egyptian princess, he was nevertheless made great by the milk of his own mother. This shows us that we must not entirely wean ourselves from the milk of our mother, the Church, when we read the books of worldly scholars for our instruction; rather, we are obligated to learn and observe the laws, ways, and orders of the Church alongside them. For through these, our soul is strengthened and nourished, and lifted above that which is transitory. What a proof! Who would have thought that the Egyptian princess was an image of worldly books, and the mother of Moses—

I wish to add one more reminder, which, if I am not mistaken, is unrecognized by some and not much regarded by others: A teacher of morals <term>Sitten-Lehrer: A teacher focused on ethics and outward conduct</term> finds more work and effort in presenting his proofs to people than a man who wishes to demonstrate the teachings of faith. Most people believe it is harder to present the doctrines of faith <term>Glaubens-Lehren: The theological dogmas of Christianity</term> in such a way that conviction arises, than it is for the teachings of life <note>original: "Lebens-Lehren," referring to practical moral instruction</note>. They give this reason for this opinion: The doctrines of faith are mysteries that go beyond reason. Reason rebels against the obedience of faith and does not so easily accept what is proven to her from the Scripture. But the teachings of life are in accordance with our concepts. The law of nature, which is engraved in our souls, comes to the aid of the work of a moral teacher. And therefore, one is much more easily convinced of the fairness and justice of the divine commands that concern one's conduct <note>original: "Wandel"</note>. We readily admit that for a certain kind of person, this is correct. Namely, those who imagine themselves to see sharply and have made an idol of their intellect are more easily brought to accept that part of Christ's teaching which organizes human life, than to believe the mystery of the Cross. Those proud sages who lived in the days of the first Christians praised the moral teachings of the Christians, while the Word of the Cross was to them, by contrast, a

But in all people, whether they be wise or foolish, learned or unlearned, there is a wicked habit of the heart that stands in the way of our conviction regarding the will of God. This heart always stirs whenever repentance and conversion <term>Bekehrung: A turning away from sin toward God</term> are proclaimed. Reason and Scripture may join together and seek to overcome the evil heart, yet it always finds its corners <note>original: "Winckel," meaning loopholes or hiding places</note> where it can flee. The clearest laws of the Lord are twisted when they stand against our inclinations. Generally, it seems to me, therefore, that a man who explains the laws of God <note>original: "Geseze GOttes"</note> finds more work and effort among corrupt people than a teacher of truth that is presented to the intellect. From this, I draw this rule: A teacher of morals <term>Sitten-Lehrer: One who instructs others in ethics and godly behavior</term> must apply every diligence to make his proof convincing and strong, so that the rebellious heart may be more easily conquered. He must regard parables and spiritual interpretations not as proofs, but only as ornaments that one can occasionally use when one wishes to make a matter clearer. Finally, he must think that nothing is more becoming to a man who speaks and exhorts in the name of the Lord than to support his discourse with clear words and laws of the Lord, and to convince the world that it is not he, but the Lord, who demands obedience.

### §. VI.

No one is better suited to present this holy science <note>In this period, theology and ethics were often referred to as "sciences" or organized bodies of knowledge.</note> than a man who has allowed himself to be sanctified through the grace of God. An unconverted teacher can, to be sure, recognize divine truth and, by presenting it, lead others to the kingdom of God, provided he does not falsify it. However, a convert has many advantages over the former because of his spiritual experience, because of his **unspotted conscience, because of his faithful and sincere zeal, and because of his pure heart.**

---

**The pure and holy intention of a converted teacher gives him the fourth advantage over an unconverted one.** His only concern is that the honor of God may grow and that sinners may be snatched from destruction and ruin. This purpose makes him alert and watchful. It makes him perceptive and tireless. He strives to learn all the obstacles that stand in the way, and at the same time, all the means to overcome these obstacles. He ponders how he might arrange his thoughts in an orderly way, how he might set up his instruction convincingly, how he might urge and move the sluggish will, how he might perceive human weakness from all sides, and how he might leave nothing behind that could serve against it.

<column-break/>

He calls upon the assistance of the Most High for his endeavor: And to whom has this ever been denied who has sought Him sincerely and fervently? Where there is a holy and pure intention, there is a righteous zeal <term>Eyfer: In this context, a godly passion or intense commitment to spiritual duties, rather than mere anger.</term> to achieve it. An unconverted person has no other purpose than to make himself liked and respected, or to pass the time that he must spend on the instruction of other people by virtue of his profession. Whoever seeks nothing more than this does not need to be so cautious, so careful, or so industrious when he is to instruct others in their duties. Disorganized chatter, decorated with all sorts of child’s play, often moves the imagination of the simple-minded more than the most thorough instruction. And to those people who only teach because they must teach, it is all the same how and what they present, as long as the time passes. What, therefore, will an unsanctified teacher of ethics do? One who seeks honor in this way will conform to the corrupt taste of the inexperienced whom he encounters in his time. He will not take much trouble to improve and purify it. He will seek to tickle the ears with fables, high-flown rhetoric, vain human trifles, and stories, because most people like to hear these things. A thorough and well-composed discourse causes trouble for the majority because it requires attentiveness. People would rather lend an ear to those who talk shiftlessly and bind themselves neither to order nor rules, because they can be followed without much burden to the understanding. Both will never think about how they should convince the intellect or win over the will. Their purpose does not require such labor; and it matters little to them whether they convert or confuse.

Another advantage occurs to me that a sanctified teacher of morals has over one who is carnally and worldly minded. ***A converted teacher will be more eloquent than an unconverted one.*** Perhaps one wonders at this opinion. What has eloquence to do with godliness? Has it not already been said that the Spirit of God does not teach the art of speaking? Nevertheless, I hope that I will be proven right as soon as I have explained what I have proposed. We must imagine two people who are not particularly unequal in their natural gifts; both have intellect and skill, and have learned as much of human sciences as is necessary to improve and maintain these gifts. Where there is too great an inequality of natural skill, the presentation of an

<column-break/>

unconverted man can often be better and more lively than the instruction of a righteous man. But of these two people I have described, one has sacrificed himself to God. The other clings to the world and allows himself to be governed by his evil lusts. I maintain that the former will speak much better and will instruct much more wisely, elegantly, and skillfully than the latter. No people are more eloquent than those who are convinced of the things they wish to teach others, and who are not hindered by any internal disorder of the spirit in the clarity of their thoughts or the arrangement of their words. The orators of this world agree with us on this point. One speaks in a forced and vexing manner about a thing that one does not believe to be true. And one does not know how to help oneself—finding neither the right words nor the natural placement of thoughts—when one is inwardly troubled and driven to and fro like a boisterous sea.

<margin>//</margin> But when the heart speaks, when conviction speaks, the words find themselves. One does not have to search long: one does not have to set them down and cross them out: one does not have to hunt for the best expressions in the books of eloquence. The power that has occupied the heart suggests the noblest and most suitable words, and causes the speech to flow without stumbling. And where a stillness of the soul and a free and pure spirit dwell, there the presentation generally becomes just as orderly and correct as the state of the heart is. These advantages belong to the righteous who fear the Lord. The Spirit of the Most High has made them certain of the truths they proclaim. And this light of the intellect opens their

->§. VII.<-

He who knows the Scripture, who has exercised his understanding, and who has finally surrendered himself to **God** for His service, will easily find the middle path between the errors <note>Original: "Abwegen," meaning "off-paths" or "byways."</note> that tend to lead people astray in the presentation of moral teaching. There are different kinds of errors in this science. Some think only of internal sanctification and forget the external duties of life, which were nonetheless prescribed by **Christ** and the Apostles. Those who walk this error can generally be called <term>Mystical Moral Teachers: Groups like the Pietists or Quietists who were sometimes accused of ignoring worldly responsibilities in favor of inner prayer</term>. Others, by contrast, forget the internal cleansing of the heart and demand nothing but external works and virtues. This was the mistake of the school-teachers <note>A reference to "Scholasticism," the medieval method of theology and philosophy that some reformers felt had become too focused on logic and ritual.</note> before the <term>Reformation: The 16th-century religious movement that emphasized faith over ritual works</term>; and it is still the mistake of all those who seek justification through their works. He who remains with the Word of **God**, and allows himself to be led astray neither by his imagination nor by his reason, will easily avoid these two errors.
