## Explanation.

All sorts of wrong paths have been chosen by those who have instructed people in the doctrine of morals <term>Sitten-Lehre: A traditional term for ethics or the study of Christian conduct and character</term>. To speak of them all would be too extensive and against my intention. I will only mention the most prominent ones. One only needs to read the Holy Scripture superficially to be convinced that we are directed, above all things, to seek the change and conversion of our heart, and afterward to make this inward renewal and sanctification manifest through works of love and godliness <note>Original: "Gottseligkeit." This refers to a life lived in active devotion and piety toward God.</note>. On the one hand, God did not create us for solitude. He wants us to live with one another, to maintain the bond of all human society, to offer one another a hand, and through godliness and the rightful use of the goods He has bestowed upon us, to make our lives as happy as possible. No one can doubt this who has rightly viewed the commands and laws of God concerning His service and the love we owe to ourselves and other people. But the **Lord**, who is holy, is also not served by people who are outwardly pure and inwardly impure. He desires no virtue that is founded on fear, coercion, self-interest, and other earthly intentions. He wants the service we bring Him to flow from faith and a true love. He requires that true love for Him should bring about love for the brothers and a proper love for ourselves. Who, therefore, would believe that in all times people have been found who separated these two things from each other, and viewed either only the inter-

<column-break/>

nal sanctification, or only the external virtue, as the goal of the divine doctrine of morals, if daily experience did not teach us this?

There are people who almost forget that they live in a world occupied by people, and speak of nothing but inward contemplation, purification, enlightenment, and union with God. Those who still have anything to do with the world, they say, with the business of the earth, who still seek out other people, who still carry on trade and commerce, or who still love the creatures <note>In this context, "the creatures" refers to any created thing—people, nature, or objects—as opposed to the Creator.</note>, are imperfect and have remained entirely behind on the way to right holiness. The world would hardly have enough deserts and wildernesses or hidden places and chambers to receive all the people seeking their salvation if everyone wanted to listen to these people. There are others, on the other hand, who hardly think that an impure heart is an abomination before the **Lord**, and therefore place the whole essence of godliness in the external services and duties we can perform for God, ourselves, and others. Paul and the other apostles would have spoken in vain that we must be renewed in the spirit of our mind, Ephesians 4:23 <note>Original: "Eph. III, 23." The author likely intended Ephesians 4:23, which discusses the renewal of the mind, as Chapter 3 does not contain this specific phrasing.</note> if it were to depend on the judgment of these people. It will be permitted for me to call the former the **Mystical** moral teachers, and the latter the **Scholastic**. I do not wish to do anyone wrong with these words, nor have their meaning extended too far. I only make use of them so that I may speak more briefly and not be in need of long descriptions. We are certainly called to seek union with **God** and our **Savior** through faith and repentance. Can we fulfill these commands if we flee from everything external, leave work and business aside, sink the spirit into a constant silence, give the senses no room to bring external images into the soul, and strip the intellect of its thoughts and its very capacity to think? that we should assist one another and maintain the society that **God** has established here below? Does sanctification then cancel out the purpose of creation? And is a **Christian** then a person who has lost all claim to the goods that **God’s** love has shared with us—an inhabitant of the world who is only there to guard the spot he has chosen for meditation? Is a servant of the **Lord** then a man who must serve no one, simply to keep himself pure from all defilement?

One seeks in vain in the conduct and the teaching of **Jesus** and his **Apostles** for a basis for such separations. Our dearest **Savior** did not withdraw himself from the society of men. Rather, he went to those places where the crowds of people were the largest. An invitation to the innocent enjoyment of some friends, arranged at **Cana** <note>A reference to the Wedding at Cana (John 2), where Jesus performed his first miracle by turning water into wine.</note> in honor of two newly-weds, was not unpleasant to him. He ate with tax collectors and the greatest of sinners. And thus he left us a model <term>Fürschrift: Literally a 'writing-template' used by students to learn calligraphy; here meaning a divine blueprint for living</term> for life that is of a completely different nature than that which the **Mystical Moral Teachers** praise. The **Apostles** did exactly as **Jesus** did. They did not lock themselves in dark chambers, nor did they seek out remote wildernesses and caves, but instead went where the greatest gathering of people was. One would have to consider the lifestyle of **Jesus** and these faithful witnesses to be sinful if the people of whom we speak were to be proven right.

I know that many of the first **Christians**, who meant well, chose this way of worship and recommended it to others.

One rails against heretics: What more is needed? What is the use of tormenting oneself for a long time and struggling against one's own nature? ### §. VIII.

There are two other wrong paths in spiritual ethics. One side is too strict. It does not imagine humans as humans, but as angels who have already departed from this world. It demands more than the law of the **Most High** requires of us. It places burdens on others that it cannot carry itself. The other side is too lenient and grants the corrupt heart more than is right. It restricts the laws of the **Lord** and gives them far too narrow an interpretation. Whoever follows the laws of the **Lord** exactly, while keeping the nature of mankind constantly before their eyes, will not find it difficult to avoid these two wrong paths.

***

## Explanation.

In almost all Christian congregations, one hears complaints and grievances about moral teachers who are either too harsh or too lenient. And our churches do not lack such accusations either. Many of these complaints are groundless. Everyone wants Christianity to be arranged according to their own imagination.

<column-break/>

# Regarding Spiritual Moral Teaching

-><meta>catchword: one</meta><-

He who seeks solitude immediately scolds those who do not stay away from large gatherings. A person who is by nature soft-spoken and of a somber spirit believes that one concedes too much to human vice <note>The original "Unart" refers to a lack of discipline or a bad habit.</note> when people are allowed to speak often and at length, or to express their thoughts vividly. Another, who can tolerate no changes, immediately speaks of "love of the world" and "vanity" when he sees others having their clothes made in the fashion common to their times. On the other side, the same errors occur. A vain courtier, who spends the best part of his time with gossip, finery, sleep, and follies, complains bitterly about the ministers of the Gospel who tell him that his way of life is not the way of **Christ**. He believes that one does not properly distinguish between people and things, and demands more than one should. An unmerciful man, when exhorted to love, often gives us the answer that love "begins at home" <note>Literally: "love starts with itself."</note>, and that **Jesus** does not demand that one should hate and forget oneself. A foolish boaster, who squanders his inheritance through vain splendor and luxury, complains vehemently about those who wish to change him and lead him to the kingdom of heaven. "What," he says, "is this harsh moral teaching <term>Sitten-Lehre: the study of Christian ethics and how one ought to live</term> being proclaimed to me? Does not Christianity consist in the internal essence of the spirit? Can I not do what I want outwardly with what is mine? Where has **Jesus** ever forbidden my love for cleanliness, order, and adornment? Are faith and love lost if I dress better than others, or decorate my house more expensively than is customary?" Thus do corrupt men play with the words "harsh" and "gentle" in moral teaching!

<column-break/>

And just as unfair are the complaints of those who sometimes think the yoke of **Christ** <note>A reference to Matthew 11:30: "For my yoke is easy and my burden is light."</note> is being made too soft, and at other times believe it is being made too hard and heavy. Yet, there are also legitimate grievances in this matter. One can indeed be harsher than one ought to be. One can also be gentler and softer than is fair. And there is no lack of examples of such moral teachers who have erred in either one direction or the other.

One can be either too harsh or too gentle in the presentation of moral teaching in two ways. First, one can commit these errors in regard to the people to whom one proclaims the law of **God**: and afterward, in regard to the moral teaching itself that one presents. In regard to the people, those are too harsh or too gentle who make no distinction between those they instruct in their duties, and who say and proclaim the same things to the converted and the saints as they emphasize to sinners and the unconverted. The law of the **Lord** remains always the same and unchanged. The differing state of men can neither abolish the commands themselves nor the obligation of men to obey those commands. But the sinner is bound to fulfill the entire law for himself, in all its parts, or else expect its curse. But the reborn and the righteous man, to whom faith has credited the obedience of his **Savior**, is only obligated to perform what he is able to accomplish through the grace of the **Lord**. For the deficiencies and errors he commits, the perfect satisfaction <note>A theological term referring to Christ's payment for human sin on the cross.</note> of **Jesus Christ** comes to his aid. Regarding **Moral Teaching** <term>Sitten-Lehre: the study of Christian ethics and how one ought to live</term> itself, one can be either too sharp or too lenient in various ways. Nothing is more common among the common crowd than the opinion that forced devotion, which one indulges in at the time when one wishes to partake of Holy Communion, is what the Scripture calls repentance and the renewal of the mind. And one cannot deny that some teachers, through an incautious presentation or for other reasons, have strengthened many in these false imaginings. There is more to the transformation of the spirit, which the Spirit of **God** calls the **new creation**.

**God** demands true regret and sorrow from all sinners: however, the measure of regret is nowhere prescribed and is directed according to the circumstances of the person. *The sins being repented are likewise unequal.* And the regret bears a resemblance to the magnitude of those sins. Generally, those fall into the vice of a far too great mildness in external **ethics**, who consult reason, the carnal mind, and the inclinations with which we are born when explaining divine laws. Our heart, which is evil, and our reason, which is weak and darkened, are not the rules by which the **Lord** guided Himself when He revealed the way of salvation. He wanted to have Saints who were as holy as He Himself, 1 Peter 1:16. <note>“Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.”</note> and Perfect ones, who were similar to Him. Matthew 5:48. <note>“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”</note> We are therefore bound, in His commands, to look upon His perfection and holiness, and not upon our misery and weakness. The words used by the **witnesses of the Lord** <note>Referring to the Apostles and writers of the Holy Scripture.</note> must be accepted in their full power and meaning. If the understanding that emerges does not please our spirit, or if our flesh has something to criticize in it, the emphasis of the commands must not be weakened for that reason. We would need no law if we were so pure and wise that we could guide ourselves according to our own will.

deviate to the other side, and are stricter in the prescription of life's duties than is fair. First, those belong here who demand more from people than has been commanded of them by the **Lord**, and who burden their brothers with weights that **God** has not bound. A servant of the **Lord** is nothing but a teacher of his brothers, and no lawgiver. No one can burden us with anything that is neither expressly imposed in the law of **God**, nor flows through a clear and easy consequence from a law of the Most High. Where the **Lord** ceases to command, there begins the freedom of those who are His subjects and creatures. Those who preach much to us of constant fasting, of physical discipline, and of retreating from the world, must first demonstrate—before we are required to follow them—that they have the right and the command to announce such things to us, which **Jesus** and His witnesses never demanded.

Furthermore, those are to be counted here who depict the life of a Christian in such a way that one could not remain a member of the world, nor observe the ordinary business of life, if one wished to follow their opinion. The religion that **Jesus** revealed and commanded to the world does not abolish society, which **God** established upon the earth, but rather binds it faster and stronger. And whoever therefore wishes to shape us so that we must vacate the world in order to become Christians, misses the true purpose of **ethics**. # On Spiritual Moral Teaching

A closer consideration of the life of **Jesus** will always lead us back to the right path and provide a living impression of **God’s** will. **Jesus** commanded us to love our enemies. There is disagreement over how much this commandment imposes on a person. Some push the matter too far, forgetting the distinction between friends and enemies, and believe they have made great progress in self-denial when they exhibit a cold and brittle demeanor toward their loved ones, while showing an exceedingly strong love and devotion toward their enemies.

Others give this duty an all-too-lenient interpretation. They believe it is enough not to actually offend their enemy in deed. Both false opinions find their dismissal in the life of **Jesus**. Those who, in their love, completely prefer their enemies over their friends—showering the former with goodness and benefits while letting the latter languish in need—cannot justify this behavior with the example of **Jesus**. **Jesus** forgives the most painful injustice of his enemies with an unfeigned love; but does he, for that reason, push his friends aside? Does he not rather give them a preference over the others? And this very example refutes the others, who convinced themselves it was enough to inflict

<column-break/>

no evil on enemies. **Jesus** repays evil deeds with good deeds.

The third rule: In moral teaching, one must pay heed to the circumstances of people and their nature, and desire nothing that conflicts with the constitution of this world or is contrary to human nature. I do not call "nature" here the natural capacity of humans to do good, nor their corruption <note>The author is clarifying that he is not speaking of "Original Sin" or "Total Depravity," but rather the physical and social realities of being human.</note>. I call "nature" the natural constitution of their body and spirit. A commandment that would shatter the world and dissolve the bond of human society cannot come from the Creator and Author of the world. The current circumstances of the world require soldiers and armies to maintain public peace. It cannot, therefore, be inherently blameworthy to choose this way of life. A command that exceeds human nature, or resists those drives within it that come from **God**, cannot be the will of the **Lord**, who loves our preservation. The natural drives of most people require the state of marriage. And those who accordingly force a large portion of people into a celibate life <note>A critique of the Catholic practice of clerical celibacy or perhaps extreme asceticism.</note> are harsher than the **Lord** of nature, and they sin.

### Explanation.

Two significant errors are committed in the comparison of natural and revealed moral teaching <term>moral teaching: the German "Sitten-Lehre" refers to the study of ethics and the rules of conduct</term>. In the first, some Christian communities fall into the trap of mixing the moral teaching of the Scriptures with that which reason provides. The other error is committed by those who want to know nothing of reason in spiritual moral teaching. Both opinions are accepted too hastily, or at least poorly considered. One side has stretched the relationship between revelation and reason too far, wanting to make the path of holiness easier and shorter than it truly is. The other has imagined that there is nothing but blindness in our understanding, and that knowledge based on general truths and nature is merely a deceptive will-o'-the-wisp. True reason and revelation both originate from one Author <note>The author refers to God as the source of both human logic and holy scripture</note>, who cannot contradict Himself in His thoughts and commands. Reason is greatly corrupted by the Fall <note>Referring to the theological concept of the Fall of Man, which supposedly damaged human intellect</note>; however, it is not entirely suffocated or abolished. Some light remains to us. The Fall has left us certain indisputable and universal truths. And these cannot possibly conflict with the truths that revelation presents to us.

I place the first distinction between spiritual and rational moral teaching in the fact that the foundation of both sciences is not entirely the same. The foundation of moral teaching is the law. The moral teaching of reason appeals solely to natural law. It makes this general conclusion: What accords with the first truths of pure and sound reason and with the constitution of the world, that must happen; what conflicts with it, must be avoided. Spiritual moral teaching does not reject this law or this type of proof. ### §. X.

**The purpose of JESUS’s moral teaching is our holiness:** And this is **twofold.** We should first be improved and **purified** in the depths of our hearts, and be freed both from the darkness of our understanding and from our inability to do good and the evil inclinations of the will. Secondly, we should learn from it how we may also please God with our outward conduct, and through our deeds and works promote the glory of God, the best for other people, and our own blessedness. From this, one will easily judge the false intentions that some imagine regarding moral teaching.

---

### Explanation.

The purpose and intention of a science <note>In the 18th century, "science" (*Wissenschaft*) referred to any organized body of systematic knowledge, including theology and ethics, not just the natural sciences.</note> is actually the benefit that should and can be drawn from it by the one who learns it. To speak precisely, a doctrine or science has no "purpose" or "intention" in itself. Where an intention is to exist, there must be deliberation, choice, reason, and testing present. However, it is customary to call the advantage that one can expect from a science its purpose or intention. And my intention is not to abolish words that have long been in use and can easily be explained. Whoever asks: "What is the purpose of moral teaching?" actually means to say: To what end does one seek to learn this science?
<column-break/>
To what should it serve us? What benefits are we to expect when we have practiced and allowed ourselves to be instructed in it?

This purpose is **holiness, or our change and improvement.** Whoever wishes to say with others: "It is the renewal of the divine image," <note>This refers to the *Imago Dei* (Genesis 1:27), the theological concept that humans were created in God's likeness but lost it through sin; "spiritual moral teaching" aims to restore this likeness.</note> only differs from us in his words. **The holiness for which we must strive** is twofold: an internal one of the soul itself, and an external one of our deeds, performances, and actions. Spiritual moral teaching deals with both, and intends to improve the conduct as well as, primarily, the soul of mankind.

# 64
## Preparation

Purifying people and putting them in order.

**To sanctify oneself means**, if this figure of speech is considered generally, nothing other than **to dedicate and surrender oneself entirely to a matter or person.** And to be holy is to belong completely to a certain person or matter, and, as it were, to pertain to them. I wish to present the matter somewhat more clearly. This will serve to help one better grasp the force of several figures of speech in the Holy Scriptures. The word which has been given as "holy" in our language signifies two things in the writings of the ancients. It signifies, on the one hand, **something that is particular to a matter or person; it signifies, on the other hand, something that no one may violate.** In the first sense, those things which belonged to the gods or the authorities alone—the temples, the town halls, the servants of princes, the vessels used in divine service or in secular matters concerning the whole commonweal—were called holy. In the second sense, laws, heralds, ambassadors, and other things or persons that no one was permitted to harm were called holy. In the beginning, this word was used very broadly. Over time, its meaning was more precisely narrowed, and it was applied only to such people and things that belonged either to the gods honored by the land, or to the highest earthly power in the land, or to the entire people. One meaning of this word flows from the other and is grounded in the other. Whatever was dedicated to the gods or the authorities was at the same time secure from all attack and

<column-break/>

injury, and therefore holy in both senses. And what no one was allowed to offend without placing themselves in the utmost danger either belonged to the service of the gods or concerned the welfare and prestige of the entire people. However, these two meanings are not always united in divine and human writings. At times only this one, at times only that one, must apply in certain passages. And whoever, therefore, wishes to correctly understand the meaning of an ancient book must imagine the nature of the things for which this word is used, in order to conclude what sense lies beneath it. I am not writing a scholarly book: otherwise, I would be able to demonstrate what I have just said with countless passages from the ancients. One may seek the same among others who have taken the trouble to collect and explain the remnants of extinct languages <note>The author refers here to classical languages like Latin, Greek, and Hebrew which were the foundation of 18th-century scholarship.</note>. I mention this only to make the meaning of the word "holy" and "holiness" in moral teaching <note>Original: *Sitten-Lehre*. This refers to the study of ethics and the practical application of Christian virtues in daily life.</note> all the clearer.

In that part of the Holy Scripture which pertains to moral teaching, these words generally mean as much as being dedicated and surrendered to God: And holiness is either the inward sacrifice of the heart to God, and the living resolve to dedicate all inclinations of the soul to the fear and love of the Highest <note>A common Pietist title for God, emphasizing His absolute sovereignty.</note> and to arrange one’s whole life according to His will; or it is the fruit and effect of this resolve, which shows itself in the stifling of dominant bad habits and in the piety of one’s conduct. **God is called holy in many places, and calls Himself holy.** One may in the—

purifying and putting people in order.

*To sanctify oneself, if this manner of speaking is considered generally, means nothing other than to completely dedicate and yield oneself to a thing or person.* And to be holy is to belong perfectly to a specific person or thing as if being their own property. I wish to present this matter somewhat more clearly. This will serve to better grasp the power of certain expressions in the Holy Scripture. The word which has been rendered as "holy" in our language meant two things in the writings of the ancients. <note>The author is likely referring to both the Hebrew term *kadosh* and the Greek *hagios*, both of which carry the dual meaning of being "set apart" and "forbidden/sacred."</note> *First, it means as much as something that is a person’s or thing’s own property: second, it means something that no one is allowed to violate.* In the first sense, those things that belonged to the gods or the authorities <term>Obrigkeit: The secular government or ruling power</term> alone were called holy—the temples, the city halls, the servants of princes, the vessels used in divine service or in worldly matters concerning the entire commonwealth. In the second sense, the laws, the heralds, the ambassadors, and other things or persons whom no one was permitted to harm were called holy. In the beginning, this word was used very broadly. Over time, its meaning was more strictly limited, and it was applied only to such people and things that belonged either to the gods whom the land worshiped, or to the highest earthly power in the land, or to the entire people. One meaning of this word flows from the other and is grounded upon it. Whatever was dedicated to the gods or the authorities was at the same time secure from all attacks and

<column-break/>

violations, and therefore holy in both senses. And whatever no one might offend without putting themselves in the utmost danger either belonged to the service of the gods or concerned the welfare and reputation of the entire people. Nevertheless, these two meanings are not always united in divine and human writings. At times, only this one must apply; at others, only that one, in certain passages. And whoever, therefore, wishes to rightly understand the meaning of an ancient book must imagine the nature of the things for which this word is used, in order to conclude what kind of sense lies beneath it. I am not writing a scholarly book: otherwise, I would be able to demonstrate what I have just said with countless passages from the ancients. One may look for these among others who have taken the trouble to collect and explain the remnants of extinct languages. I mention this only to make the meaning of the word "holy" and "holiness" in ethics <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre"</note> all the clearer.

In that part of the Holy Scripture which belongs to ethics, these words generally mean as much as being dedicated and yielded to God: *And holiness is either the internal sacrifice of the heart to God, and the living resolve to dedicate all inclinations of the soul to the fear and love of the Highest and to arrange one's whole life according to His will; or it is the fruit and effect of this resolve,* which manifests in the stifling of dominant wickedness and in a pious way of life. *God is called holy in very many places, and calls Himself holy.* One may in this... <meta>catchword: sen (likely from "senden" or "seiner")</meta>

these passages do not deviate from the meaning of this word which I have just indicated. The Highest Being, who is subject to no one, can dedicate, surrender, and devote Himself to no other thing except Himself. God can accept no foreign prescription or rule for His perfections and actions. But God has, so to speak, dedicated Himself to Himself and to His own perfection, which is infinite. He never deviates—neither in His counsels, nor in His deeds and words—from His unchangeable justice, wisdom, goodness, and other attributes. If we were permitted to speak of the Lord, whose greatness has no measure, in a human manner, we would say: God has taken Himself as the pattern according to which He directs Himself. He always has the eternal law of His unchangeable nature and perfection before His eyes, and directs everything He decrees, everything He undertakes, and everything He says according to this model. He is His own lawgiver and the law itself, and He never transgresses the eternal model of His majesty and perfection. However imperfect these ways of speaking and expressions may be, they will nevertheless be suitable enough to explain in general what the Scripture means when it calls God holy. ***God is holy; that is, He always acts as His perfection requires, and in all His works and words He always projects an image of the virtue and excellence that dwells within Him eternally and unchangeably.*** Following this example and model of the Lord, those humans who wish to belong to Him should likewise be holy. God looks upon Himself and directs Himself according to His divine nature. Man,

<column-break/>

in turn, should look toward God and compose everything he thinks or undertakes according to His will. God is and remains dedicated and surrendered to Himself. Man is bound to dedicate and sacrifice himself in turn to the Highest and to follow His laws. Whoever does this is called holy, and dedicated to God. ***Whoever fails to do this is unholy; he has not set God before himself as the regulator of his movements and deeds, but rather himself or corrupt creatures.***

***In God there is a twofold holiness: an internal and an external one.*** He is internally holy in His essence. One cannot easily explain this with words that match the greatness of God. How poor, how imperfect, how lowly are our languages when we are meant to represent the majesty of our Creator in them! One must be satisfied if one can only convey a small concept of it to man, while reminding him that he must, as much as he can, separate everything small and trivial from his words and thoughts. In God, there is an eternal and constant purpose to always act according to His perfection, and an eternal stillness and undisturbed rest from all things that could oppose this purpose. ***God is externally holy.*** What He says, what He does, what He commands, and what He establishes corresponds most precisely with this internal purpose. He is just as pure, righteous, and perfect in his works as the water that flows from the purest spring is as clear as the source itself. The special duties are best considered according to the different types of connections in which people stand. We are members of the general society that God has established upon the earth. We are members of the state, or civil society, in which we reside. Finally, we are members of the spiritual society, which is called the **Church**. Each of these connections requires a particular behavior from us.

In the description and presentation of these duties, we wish primarily to look to the **Holy Scripture**. We do not wish to forget **reason** and the things that can be derived from it. The matter itself will sometimes require us to seek counsel from it and touch upon certain things that have been handled among the wise of the world <note>Original: "Weisen der Welt." This refers to secular philosophers, such as the Greeks and Romans mentioned on the previous page.</note>. Yet the main purpose shall be directed toward the book that God has caused to be written for the instruction of the human race.

There are so few duties toward spirits and invisible creatures <note>Likely referring to angels or spiritual entities, which were common subjects in 18th-century moral philosophy.</note> that it is not necessary to place them into a separate section. And what one perhaps owes to irrational creatures <note>A standard term for animals, which were viewed as lacking the "rational soul" of humans.</note> is likewise easily and briefly determined. The specific duties can best be considered according to the different types of connections in which people stand. We are members of the general society which God has established upon the earth. We are members of the state or civil society in which we reside. Finally, we are members of the spiritual society which is called the church. Each of these connections requires a particular conduct from us.

In describing and presenting these duties, we wish primarily to look to the Holy Scripture. We do not wish to forget reason and the things that can be derived from it. The matter itself will occasionally require that we seek counsel there and touch upon certain things that have been dealt with among the wise of the world <note>A reference to secular philosophers, such as those from classical antiquity.</note>. Yet the main intent shall be directed toward the book which God has allowed to be set forth for the instruction of the human race.

### Explanation.

One does not require much light or wisdom to convince a person who is willing to see that he is no longer the same being he once was when he was first created and formed by God. Anyone who wishes to show that a certain miserable and imperfect piece of work was not made by a highly practiced and skillful artist need only compare the master's known skill with the object that is claimed to be his 
<margin>1.</margin> work. Likewise, we need only compare the infinite perfection of God with our own miserable condition to be certain that the human race was of a much different character when it first came, so to speak, from the hand of the Most High. Can any sensible person imagine that the people who now inhabit the earth—these weak, these impure vessels, so inclined toward sin and naughtiness <note>German: *Unart*; in this context, it refers to a fundamental deviation from moral excellence or "bad behavior" in a spiritual sense.</note>—are the very same creatures that a God (who is Perfection, Purity, Holiness, Light, and Grace itself) brought into being when He wished to reveal His greatness and goodness? Would it not be easier to believe that the most nonsensical writing was the work of a man who never committed a single error against reason and was held by all to be a model of wisdom? One of two things must be true: either a blind chance has put us together and no wise or powerful hand formed us; or, we are corrupted and have lost the 

<column-break/>

perfection that the wisest power once shared with us when it saw fit to place rational creatures into the world. One cannot believe the first option for any longer than it takes to observe oneself somewhat closely. As miserable and frail as we are, the wisdom of an eternal and wise Author <note>German: *Urheber*; here meaning the Creator or First Cause.</note> still shines out from the midst of our misery. Every limb on our body proclaims the honor of its Author. And the joining together of these parts for a specific purpose shows those who concern themselves with it ever more traces of an unfathomable wisdom. However disorderly, however simple, however incorrect most people may think, they nevertheless *do* think; and however perversely they may will, they nevertheless *do* will and desire. But can anyone truly conceive of that which we call thinking, willing, and desiring within us, and at the same time believe that these qualities come from a cause that can neither think, will, nor desire? Thus, the other option remains. We must confess: that we have, in a certain way, become what we were not before, and have lost the pure and blissful state that the highest power shared with us at our first origin.

These are not thoughts that first arose only after the revelation that God granted us through Christ became known in the world. One...

# On the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

...to falsify and corrupt the good.
It is known that this opinion pleased many nations before **Christ**, and everywhere gave birth to an absurd worship and countless errors. There was no agreement when this fable <note>original: "Gedichte" — in this context, it refers to a constructed philosophical or mythological narrative rather than a poem.</note> was dissected and explained in all its parts. How can those agree who rely on nothing but an imagination? Yet they did agree on this: that the corruption of man stems from a particular being that is distinct from the Father of Light and of Good. I do not wish to dispute these absurd thoughts at great length now. Even those who have taken pleasure in giving them a new color <note>meaning those who have attempted to modernize or refine these old Dualist arguments.</note> have confessed that one could not accept them until one had overturned the eternal and unchangeable truths of reason. (*) And what more is needed to grasp their weakness? I will only remind you of one thing that pertains to the purpose I have set for myself here. Those who accept this opinion to resolve the question of the origin of evil in man do not touch upon the main difficulty upon which everything depends. We want to know: how can a creature of **God**—that is, of an eternal, unchangeable, and necessary Being—be corrupt? They answer us: There are two gods, one good and one evil. The evil that makes our nature so hideous comes from the latter. The former has nothing to do with our malice. Are we improved by this? Is the primary doubt removed by this? Not in the least. We ask: how from a **God**,

<column-break/>

who is necessary and eternal, can sin come? They admit that sin comes from a god: but they add that this god is, by his nature, evil. And that is exactly what our reason cannot comprehend. We cannot unite the concept of a **God** with the concept of what is called sin, evil, and corruption. We cannot believe that a being so evil in himself could simultaneously be **God**. We therefore desire that one should point out to us a source of evil outside of **God**. And yet they place the very origin of corruption within a **God**. They lead us exactly where we do not wish to go. They leave the difficulty standing that we want to see removed, and dismiss us with an answer that does not belong to the matter. Evil comes from an evil god. But it is still a god from whom it springs. And my reason wants to know nothing of any god when it seeks to uncover the origin of the corruption that dwells within me.

As unfounded and foolish as these opinions are, they nonetheless serve as proof to us that a man who knows nothing of Revelation can perceive and recognize his own corruption. He cannot find a way out when he is to state the causes of this corruption: He is at a loss <note>original: "Er versteht sich [nicht]" — the context implies he fails to understand or explain himself consistently.</note> when he is to explain the magnitude of this corruption, and counts much as innocence that actually belongs to our misery: He does not know that this very corruption is rightly imputed to us by **God** as a sin: But the hideousness itself, which has taken hold of his nature, is so visible—

# The First Chapter

...evident, so that it cannot escape his contemplation. One can use this to decide the question that is debated among theologians <note>original: "Gottes-Gelehrten," literally "those learned in God."</note>: *Whether Original Sin can be recognized from the light of nature <note>The "light of nature" refers to human reason and observation without the aid of divine revelation or scripture.</note>, or not?* It seems this dispute is mostly settled as soon as the ambiguity of the word "Original Sin" is noted. This word signifies either merely the corruption of human nature, or it signifies at the same time the guilt that clings to man because of this corruption and makes him a sinner. Those who use this word do not always remind us which of these two meanings they are assigning to it. Thus it happens that others sometimes interpret their opinion against their will. If Original Sin means nothing more than the corruption of our nature, then those who maintain that reason has clarity enough to perceive it are correct. If this word means more—if it is meant to simultaneously indicate the guilt that is imputed to us because of our misery—then those who deny that Original Sin is known through revelation and reason simultaneously have won the argument. Who, by themselves, is capable of grasping that an evil which we did not bring upon ourselves could nevertheless accuse, condemn, and make us punishable? It is true, reason understands the infinite holiness of **God**; it concludes therefore, or could at least conclude therefrom, that the **Lord** cannot love such creatures as we are by nature. But reason recognizes just as clearly the infinite justice and mercy of **God**. These perfections awaken in it the assurance that so just and kind a Being will not hold men to punishment because they 

<column-break/>

are born miserable and unhappy. This opinion maintains the upper hand in the heart of the man who has no revelation, and almost extinguishes the great concept we must form of the holiness and innocence of **God**. Nature does not demand to seek the means by which these perfections are united: and it also does not have so much power that it could find it. It thus looks merely at the goodness and equity of the Most High and remains at this conclusion: whoever is innocent of the disease with which he drags himself along need fear no punishment because of it. The love we all bear for ourselves, and the desire to be happy, strengthens these thoughts. And what clings more firmly to us than the opinions which self-love comes to assist?

The Scripture declares itself so clearly regarding the natural corruption of man that one could desire nothing clearer. *All passages belonging to this matter can be divided into three categories.* The first comprises those places in which man is presented as a creature that has lost a great happiness and glory. In the second are the verses that depict man as a being that carries a seed of malice <note>original: "Unart," meaning an innate badness or deviation from a good nature.</note> and corruption in the heart, which requires only a small rain to break forth and bear fruit. In the third belong those expressions that describe man in such a way that one must consider him generally as entirely corrupted and sinful. We wish to look at those of each kind that primarily strengthen our doctrine.

From the first category, the words of **Paul** are particularly remarkable:

Romans 3:23. *For all have sinned, and come short of the glory that we should have before GOD.* One will understand the emphasis of this passage somewhat better if it is translated: *We lack the glory of God.* The Greek word <term>glory</term> <note>original: δόξα (doxa)</note> signifies that which brings one honor, prestige, and renown. The bright radiance that surrounded the face of Moses when he came down from Mount Sinai—the glow that was a public testimony of his communion with GOD, and which awakened so much honor, fear, and love among the unrefined Israelites—is called his glory. Exodus 34:29. The rays, the light, the brilliance of the sun, which formerly moved so many nations to the idolatrous worship of this star and constitutes its greatest adornment, is called its glory. 1 Corinthians 15:41. And what, then, is the glory of GOD? It is that in which the perfection of His being consists: the infinite beauty of His nature, which must ignite and maintain love and reverence in those who behold it; the incomparable virtues, of which we encounter so many adorable traces in the world and in the works of nature and grace. This glory of GOD is what man lacks. With these words, the Apostle says two things: First, this: Man formerly possessed the glory of GOD, or something of the glory of GOD. How can someone lack something that he never had before? And how can it be advanced as a reproach against him that he did not inherit a certain good, if nothing of it belonged to his fathers? Man, therefore, was previously adorned and decorated with the glory of GOD. What

<column-break/>

this is intended to say is clear from the preceding: Man was endowed with certain perfections of GOD, as far as his finite and limited nature was capable of them. If he had remained as he was formed, one would have seen in him manifest, though imperfect, sketches of the holy attributes that make God great and glorious in the eyes of those who know Him. Thus, Paul says here exactly what the Scripture otherwise says in other words: Man bore the image of GOD. Whoever has the glory of GOD is indeed similar to Him whose glory has been communicated to him. The second thing that Paul reports is expressed in the words themselves: Man has lost this glory of GOD. That which he formerly possessed of divine attributes according to a certain measure—the holiness, the righteousness, the light, the wisdom which the first creation bestowed upon him—is lost. One must not doubt that this sentence concerns all people who inhabit the earth. Of whom the Apostle speaks, he indicated in verse 9: *Both Jews and Greeks, all are under sin.* In Paul's time, all inhabitants of the world were divided into Jews and Greeks. With the word "Greeks," they designated all those who were devoted to idolatry and despised the Jewish faith. And according to the modes of speech that were customary in the Apostle's time, he said exactly what we would now present with these words: All people, whoever they may be, are sinners and have forfeited the glory that the Creator wished to make hereditary among mankind.

# The First Chapter

Regarding the second category of passages in Holy Scripture that speak of the corruption of mankind, we wish to cite two utterances of our Savior himself and explain them with a few words. The first is found in *John 3:6*: *That which is born of the flesh is flesh.* This passage becomes immediately clear if only the ambiguity of the <margin>p. 224.</margin> word **flesh** is removed. In the language of the holy men who composed the Scriptures, **flesh** very often signifies the human being, who consists of flesh and blood. And this very same word, when it is placed in opposition to the word **Spirit**, indicates the <term>depravity</term> <note>original: "Unart"—in this context, it refers to a fundamental moral corruption or a state of being contrary to one's original, good nature.</note> that dwells in natural man. One does not need to prove this with scriptural passages, as it is known to few people. At this place, our Savior uses the word **flesh** in both senses. This is the source of the obscurity of his words. First, he uses the word **flesh** and understands it to mean human beings: *what is born of the flesh*. That is, what is procreated and born of natural men according to the laws of nature ordained by God. Afterward, **flesh** signifies for him the sinful inclination that has its dwelling and finds its nourishment in the human being who is procreated in the ordinary way. *That is flesh*; that is, it is afflicted with and occupied by an inclination toward evil, an impulse toward depravity, and a readiness to sin. Whoever doubts whether we are explaining the words of our Savior correctly need only compare the contrast with these words: *That which is born of the Spirit is Spirit.* In these latter words, can **Spirit** indicate anything other than spiritual, holy, and divine inclinations, movements, and desires? One may therefore judge whether the **flesh**, which is 

<column-break/>

placed in opposition to the **Spirit**, could mean anything other than what we have just noted. Whoever would assign the same meaning to the word **flesh** in both parts of our Savior’s words would produce an absurd interpretation. For instance, if the word **flesh** meant "human being" both times, this doctrine would emerge: *What is born of a human being is a human being.* Is this not already known? Does such a statement harmonize with the purpose of Jesus? Is it fitting for the highest Teacher of Truth? If one chooses the other meaning and believes that **flesh** signifies human depravity both times, then we would have this doctrine: *Depravity comes from depravity; sin is a daughter of sin; evil desires procreate evil desires.* This, again, is something that was partly unnecessary to mention and partly unsuited to the matter at hand. We cannot leave this passage of Christ’s without first mentioning that he simultaneously indicates the origin of the flesh, or depravity, within it. *What is born of the flesh*, he says. Thus, natural birth—ordinary procreation—is the mother, the source, the origin of corruption. Evil lust is propagated along with nature itself and therefore lies within nature itself. Those who derive our depravity from external things, and who persuade themselves that we are born pure and blameless, may see how they can reconcile their opinion with these words of our Redeemer. We believe with him that that which is born is flesh.

The second passage of our Redeemer about which we wish to say something is this: *Out of the heart come evil thoughts—*

We ask all who are willing to use their reason: does not this truth flow naturally from these words of our Savior: that the heart of man is unclean and has an inclination toward sins, vices, and evil deeds? If the heart is the spring from which those things burst forth that make a person distorted and punishable—as our Savior expressly says—then must there not lie at its very foundation nothing but disorder and impurity? Can I then believe that a well, from which murky and unhealthy water flows, is situated in a pure and well-constituted soil? Can I then believe that a tree which bears poisonous fruits rests upon a good and healthy root and draws nothing but good sap from its earth? Jesus does not say expressly here that this evil condition of the heart is natural and innate. We never desire to stretch the words of Holy Scripture beyond their power, nor to prove more from them than can be proven without effort. Would to God that no one had ever exceeded the measure in this matter; then we would have fewer half-conclusive proofs and perhaps fewer despisers of divine truth. I will add to this the words of the Apostle Paul, with which he describes his own misery. *Romans 7:18*: *I know that in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing.* No one, I hope, will believe that Paul was an extraordinary human being in respect to corruption, or that he possessed a unique nature that distinguished him from the rest of humanity. What he says of himself, therefore, must be understood as applying to all mortals. He describes himself, and at the same time all people as they are by nature, as a dwelling place of evil. At first glance, it seems as if he only wanted to say that he has a lack of good, rather than an actual inclination toward evil. It appears as if he were presenting his heart merely like a field on which no good seed has been sown. However, the sequence and the remaining circumstances of his speech refute this explanation. Were he speaking merely of a lack of good, he would not have said in the following verses that a sin dwells in him (v. 20) and that there is a law in his members that rebels against the law of his mind (v. 23). # On the Natural Corruption of Man

...what we will say is as well known to reason as it is to those who wish to judge humans only from revelation.

---

The understanding shall be considered first. It is well known that this word refers to the power of the soul to perceive and comprehend the things that come before it, to deliberate upon them, to represent them clearly to oneself, and to compare them with one another; and finally, to judge and conclude what is to be held as true or false, and what is to be done or left undone. Regarding the diseases of this faculty of our souls, there are as many complaints as there are people who have truly known themselves. For every book we have that provides rules to improve the understanding and to think with certainty, we have just as many testimonies that men do not doubt the misery and weakness of their intellect. And who can calculate the number of these books? Among the worldly scholars, the question has been raised: Does our understanding truly possess all the power it needs to comprehend clearly, think securely, and judge rationally, but can no longer properly use this power for various reasons? Or is this power in fact no longer present within it, but lost? It matters little to us now which opinion one chooses to embrace. A man who is truly poor, and another who indeed has a treasure but can in no way reach it, are equally unhappy. Both are needy and miserable. Whether one says that man is stripped of the ability that a healthy understanding ought to 

<column-break/>

possess, or whether one maintains that this ability lies within him like a treasure that no one can access, it remains certain that he is sick and impoverished in his understanding. In this matter, we imagine the understanding in its greatest perfection, as it was once possessed by a human being. The strength of wit <note>original: "Witzes" – in this period, "wit" referred to general mental sharp-sightedness or intellectual capacity rather than humor.</note> is very unequal among men, as is unknown to no one. One person sees far and has the power to penetrate into the depths of things. Countless others remain stuck to the outer shells of matters and have no more insight than their trade and business require. However, no matter how sharp the understanding may be in a person, no matter how quickly he may think or how certainly he may conclude, he still has his weak and dull sides, which the most sharp-sighted person perceives much sooner than a simple one.

The understanding of a human being does not need to be as great as the understanding of a spirit <note>Likely referring to angels or purely intellectual beings.</note>. It does not need to see into everything that is in God and His essence, or understand and grasp everything God has made, everything that can be comprehended, and everything belonging to the invisible world. Our understanding could be pure, healthy, and perfect in its own kind, even if we did not know the internal composition of the stars, even if we could not recount the various kinds of God’s creatures, could not rightly compare the infinite with the finite, and could not resolve many questions that can be raised about the decrees of God, about that other world, or about the natures that perhaps dwell upon the moon. # The First Chapter

Gifts that the Lord imparts to His creatures must only be in accordance with their calling, their station, and the purposes for which He formed them. And no one can rightly complain that they have not received more from Him than is necessary for these ends. It is therefore no proof of the imperfection or weakness of our intellect that we do not comprehend everything, nor understand the nature and properties of all things. Even the angels admire much in God and His ways that they do not fully perceive, yet they are endowed with an understanding that can be called perfect and without flaw in its own kind. If one wishes to demonstrate that our <term>mental acuity<note>The original German uses "Witz," which in this period referred to general intellectual capacity or "wit" in the sense of sharp reasoning, rather than humor.</note></term> is weakened and corrupted, one must show that we do not currently possess as much skill of the intellect as our circumstances here below require, and as is necessary for the satisfaction of our spirit and our happiness in the world. And this is easily demonstrated.

We assume from the start that a powerful and wise Being placed us in this world. By assuming this, we simultaneously assert that we were made inhabitants of this world for certain purposes and not without cause. We will never fully fathom all the reasons that moved God to provide this world with such creatures as ourselves. And this is also not necessary for our happiness. But we can see this much: that we are here to live in a certain community with other creatures who are like us, to promote the general good of our entire race, and to build our own preservation, peace, welfare, and satisfaction.

<column-break/>

The rest that we might say on this, we now leave behind with diligence. If we had enough understanding to reach these purposes without offense, then the complaints man makes about the defects of his intellect would be imaginary and unfounded. A piece of dust that the Lord, out of His free will, has made into a rational creature must not imagine that nothing should be hidden or unknown to him. He must be satisfied if he has the power to recognize his happiness and to find the means that can serve him toward it. However, we are far from having that much capacity of understanding. And therefore, we rightly conclude that we have suffered a great loss in it.

<margin>N 3</margin>
Should our understanding be healthy, it would have to rightly know itself and those natures with which it has a certain community. It would have to form clear concepts of the duties incumbent upon it without difficulty or toil, distinguish its luck from its misfortune, always easily find the path to its welfare, and be able to proceed upon it unhindered. It would have to proceed with certainty and safety in its conclusions regarding its welfare. Finally, it would have to know the things that can bring it harm or advantage in the world, and know the creatures with whom it is surrounded as far as they can harm or benefit it. Which man can boast of these gifts? And who, therefore, can imagine that he still possesses the same understanding and intellect that the most holy and loving Being imparted to him at the first creation?

# Chapter One

Gifts which the Lord <note>original: "der HErr"</note> imparts to his creatures must only be in accordance with their calling, their station, and the purposes for which he has formed them. And no one can rightly complain that he has not received more from Him than is necessary for this. It is, therefore, no proof of the imperfection and weakness of our understanding <term>Verstand: the faculty of logical reasoning and comprehension</term> that we do not grasp everything, nor understand the nature and properties of all things. Even the angels admire much in God and His ways that they do not rightly perceive, and yet they are endowed with an understanding that can be called perfect and without fault in its kind. One must show, if one wishes to demonstrate that our intellect <term>Witz: in the 18th century, this referred to general mental capacity or cleverness rather than humor</term> is weakened and corrupted, that we do not now possess as much skill of understanding as our circumstances here below require, and as is necessary for the satisfaction of our spirit and our happiness <note>original: "Glückseligkeit," meaning a state of blessedness or supreme well-being</note> in the world. And this is easy to demonstrate.

We assume beforehand that a powerful and wise Being placed us in this world. In assuming this, we assert at the same time that we are made inhabitants of this world for certain purposes and not without cause. All the causes that moved God to provide this world with such creatures as we are, we will never fathom. And this is also not necessary for our happiness. But we can see this much: that we are here to live in a certain community with the rest of the creatures who are similar to us, to promote the general good of our entire race, and to build our own preservation, peace, welfare, and contentment.

<column-break/>

The rest, which we could say, we now intentionally leave behind. Had we enough understanding to reach these goals without offense, then the complaints that man leads concerning the defects of his understanding would be imaginary and groundless. A speck of dust, which the Lord by free will has made into a rational creature, must not imagine that nothing must be hidden or unknown to him. He must be satisfied if he has the power to recognize his happiness and to find the means that can serve him toward it. However, we are far from having so much capacity of understanding. And therefore, we rightly conclude that we have suffered a great loss in it. <margin>NB <note>Latin "Nota Bene," meaning "Note well" or "Pay attention"</note></margin> If our understanding were healthy, it would have to know itself and those natures correctly with which it has a certain community. It would have to form clear concepts of its duties without burden or effort, distinguish its happiness from its misfortune, always find the way to its welfare easily, and be able to proceed upon it unhindered. It would have to proceed with certainty and safety in the conclusions that concern its welfare. It would, finally, have to know the things that can bring it harm or advantage in the world, and know the creatures with which it is surrounded as far as they can harm or benefit it. Which man can boast of these gifts? And who, therefore, can imagine that he still possesses the very understanding and intellect that the holiest and most loving Being imparted to him at the first creation?

Who is he that knows himself and his nature correctly? I will now say nothing of the body...

And one would think, since this has happened, the world should think more rationally and orderly. But experience teaches us that the masters of this art often commit the greatest errors against their own principles, and convict the lesser ones that another art is still needed if one truly wishes to help the human understanding.

How should one manage it, so that a person makes what is inherently correct and useful so much a part of themselves that it is always present and available whenever they have need of it? This is the question for which the key has not yet been found. First, it is very laborious and difficult for us to find the first fundamental principles <term>Grund-Lehren</term> <note>The author refers to the basic axioms or starting points of logical reasoning from which all other truths are derived.</note> from which our conclusions and judgments about even ordinary things must be derived. Do we not see daily that the wisest often base their actions and deeds on such propositions as are in themselves absurd and foolish? Even if we have found these first fundamental truths with great effort, other difficulties arise that give even the best of us trouble. First, we do not perceive all the consequences that flow from such a truth. Our eyes can be helped by a telescope <note>original: "Fernglas." In the early 18th century, the telescope was a powerful symbol of how technology could extend human senses, but the author laments that no such "lens" exists for the mind.</note> when they are weak: but for our intellect, no means has yet been found by which it might be made fit to see into the distance and observe the chain of things that are related to one another right to the end. Sometimes the similarity of things or the ambiguity of words deceives us so strongly that we imagine this or that follows naturally from a certain proposition, when it is actually quite far removed from it. And when this deception becomes somewhat old within us, it often pleases us so much that we would rather lose life, property, and honor than let go of our opinion. In the midst of reflection, we are often overcome by a certain natural sluggishness or blindness that ruins everything we have built with care. This sometimes causes us to rush to a conclusion sooner than we should: and this is the origin of the greatest errors. Sometimes it makes us

<column-break/>

take something as settled which we do not yet know; sometimes it causes us to skip certain things in the sequence of our thoughts. And thus we acquire a science without a foundation, which is soon overturned again. What is more? A small disorder in our body, which even the wisest does not notice, often disturbs the most correct thoughts and leads us down a path that is dangerous and deceptive, without our knowing it. One may seek the remaining defects that cling to our power of judgment among those who have diligently described the weaknesses of humanity. Even if we have overlooked nothing in our deliberation and have governed our intellect so skillfully that it passes a wise judgment, we are still not safe. Two dangerous enemies remain who defeat us with cunning and overturn the best thoughts. One is our internal desires and inclinations: the other is the people and things with which we are surrounded. The intellect can be withdrawn from our inclinations in a certain way: and in this state, it often does everything we demand of it. It sees, it understands, it deliberates, it finds. We believe ourselves to possess the light and the truth itself as long as we are in this state of calm, and we assure ourselves we will remain with it forever. And yet this pleasure often lasts no longer than the time set aside for reflection. Scarcely do we let go of the reins and let reason <term>Vernunft</term> <note>While "Verstand" (intellect) handles logic, "Vernunft" (reason) is often viewed in this period as the higher faculty that connects knowledge to the will and moral action.</note> enter into its natural connection with the will <term>Wille</term>, then the light is lost or darkened once more. ## §. III.

Therefore, we do not contradict those who grant man sound reason and encourage him to make use of it. There is indeed something in us that can be called sound reason, regardless of how one chooses to define the word reason. And those who speak now of sound reason, and then of corrupted reason, are not at odds with themselves. In part, they use the word reason in a different sense when they combine it with the word "sound" than when they add the word "sick" or "corrupted." In part, it seems to me, they are looking at one thing from two sides when they call reason sometimes sick and sometimes sound.

### Explanation.

What we have said about the limited powers of our understanding can be misapplied by some who willfully wish to be called simple and blind. The follower of the Bishop of Rome <note>A common Protestant way of referring to the Pope.</note> will perhaps say: "This is exactly what we have preached for so long to you who are called Protestants. Our reason no longer suffices to distinguish truth from falsehood. God has therefore appointed a visible judge in Rome who can tell us without danger of error what we should believe or reject." Peter Daniel Huetius <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a famous French bishop and scholar who argued that human reason is too weak to find truth without divine revelation.</note>, that so-famous French bishop, wrote his book on the weakness of the human mind with no other intention than to serve his

<column-break/>

Church. If the Pope is to be all-important, man must first be entirely humbled and turned into a being who wanders here as if in a dream, not knowing whether he is asleep or awake. The enthusiast <term>Schwermer</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Schwermer" or enthusiasts were religious radicals who believed in direct, personal revelation from God, often rejecting traditional reason or church structures.</note> will want to take advantage of this very same point. "Yes," he will say, "that is the right path to wisdom. Man and his knowledge <term>Erkäntnisse</term> amount to nothing. For this reason, God has planted a certain light in our hearts that must give us counsel when something important arises. Let us just be still and cease our thinking and judging! The word that dwells within us will reveal what is to be done or believed." Because of these and other people, we must, before we go further, demonstrate—

# Chapter One

...show that man is not so entirely abandoned by reason as many make him out to be. We are wretched and corrupted; yet, a sound reason still remains within us.

Never has there been more dispute among Christians concerning reason and its power than in our own days. On one side, some have granted everything to reason in order to harm faith and religion. On the other side, some have denied reason all its capacity for that very same purpose. Conversely, some have based everything on reason so that they might confront the scoffers of revelation and serve religion. And yet others have wanted to know nothing of it, precisely because they believed that the more they attributed to reason, the more would be taken away from revelation. It takes a great deal of time before one can read all the treatises that have been written on this matter. Even more time and effort are required if one wishes to weigh everything against each other, consider it exactly, and choose something certain. Many of those who have labored in this dispute strive for one goal and eventually all arrive at one goal. But the paths they take to get there are so manifold that one often imagines their opinion is headed elsewhere, and one does not know whether it is advisable to follow them. It is no small mark of our misery and corruption that the creatures of God, who are rational, quarrel so vehemently with one another as to whether the gift bestowed upon them by God is worth something or nothing. Whether reason should be heard or not heard? Whether it must remain idle in matters of religion, or has something to

<column-break/>

do? How little dispute there would be among us over these things if we had not lost something of the original clarity of the understanding! People are just as divided when they are asked to explain what they actually mean by the word "reason." We are convinced that we possess something that makes us fit to judge correctly of ourselves and of things—both visible and invisible. # Chapter One

In my opinion, the human reason, in both senses, can be called now **weak**, now **strong**, now **sick**, now **healthy**, depending on how it is viewed and considered.

Our understanding, or the power of our souls to comprehend, compare, think, and judge, is in a certain sense healthy, and in another weak, sick, and wretched. <note>The following passage is underlined in red ink in the original</note> *It is healthy because it can correctly comprehend many things, and can recognize, perceive, and understand them without error: It is sick because it cannot recognize, understand, grasp, or even imagine the nature of countless things.*

An eye that distinguishes and sees nearby things very well, but does not clearly recognize those that are somewhat distant or poorly positioned, has its strength and its weakness: it is, in a certain way, sick and, in another way, healthy. Our understanding is of the same nature. This faculty of which we speak is healthy in itself because it can correctly deliberate upon many things, conclude with certainty, think in an orderly fashion, and safely derive one truth from another: It is sick and weak because it is hindered by various internal and external causes from using and applying its power correctly, and thus it errs in countless ways. What does it help if one has the strength within oneself to occasionally find this path and stay upon it, yet is daily blinded by all manner of things so that one does not see the path, and allows oneself to be led astray by various deceivers to wander foreign and erroneous roads? How often are those, who are otherwise gifted with the greatest understanding, accustomed to passing off what seems true to them as truth and certainty, and making their ill-considered and even worse-proven notions and thoughts into propositions of sound reason?

Reason, when it signifies the universal truths that are known to all men and the fundamental doctrines of the sciences, is ordinarily presented as healthy and uncorrupted. At the very least, if I recall correctly, I have read no one who has judged otherwise. However, I believe it can just as well be said of this reason, in a certain sense, that it is healthy, and in another, that it is sick and powerless. This reason is healthy. **That is to say, the truths and doctrines of which it consists are certain, indisputable, and unchangeable.** Whoever grounds his conclusions upon them, and allows himself to be neither blinded nor hurried, can be assured that he will not miss the truth. It is, on the other hand, unhealthy and weak when viewed from another side.

<column-break/>

I wish to say this: It is not as perfect as we might wish and require. Many universal truths that could be of use to us are hidden and invisible. In most sciences, many fundamental principles <term>Grund-Sätze: literally "ground-sentences," the foundational axioms upon which a field of study is built</term> are still missing which we would need to bring them to perfection. In many of them, we have accepted certain opinions that are not yet proven as infallible truths. And thus the reason, so highly lauded and praised as healthy, is in a certain way very powerless and imperfect.

To make this clear, I imagine a body that is deprived of some limbs and parts, yet is healthy in the members it does have. This body is healthy on one side. Nothing is lacking in the strength and perfection of the limbs it possesses. It is sick on another side. Namely, it lacks some pieces that belong to a perfect and healthy body: It has lost an eye; it has lost a hand or something else. Such is our reason. What is revealed and known to men of universal truths and doctrines is correct, healthy, and an infallible means to increase in knowledge. But how much is lacking? How often does the wise man wish in his investigations that he might have more light? How often does he borrow something here or there, which he does not really know, just to satisfy his desire for knowledge? ### §. IV.

In spiritual matters—I mean those things which concern God, our communion with him, and the salvation of our souls—this weakness of our understanding reveals itself even more strongly. Most of those who have no other light than their reason hardly think of investigating these things and walk as they are led. <note>Ephesians 4:18, 5:8</note>. Those who still think of them are deceived by themselves and fall into wandering paths, which must seem absurd and foolish even to themselves, <note>Romans 1:27</note> if self-love did not blind their eyes. <note>Colossians 2:11</note>. If revelation seeks to enlighten such people, then divine wisdom appears to them as foolishness, <note>1 Corinthians 1:23, 2:14</note> and their own ignorance appears to them to be a true enlightenment. If they are brought so far—either through birth and education or other causes—that they do not actually resist divine revelation, then their knowledge nonetheless remains of no use to them where it is not quickened by a divine power. Namely, it is dead, without spirit, power, life, and effect, until the Lord himself opens the eyes and makes the knowledge that dwells within them salutary and effective. <note>1 John 1:20, 2:6</note>.

Their misery is accordingly twofold: There is a vanity of the mind present: That means: Their understanding is once and for all filled with ridiculous, strange, irrational, and vain opinions. And they walk according to this vanity: Their will directs itself according to these dangerous and harmful errors and carries out their conduct just as the corrupted and darkened understanding desires it. The understanding, which in itself is clear, is covered over with false and erroneous opinions, which they have thoughtlessly allowed themselves to be taught, as if with a cloud and fog. Whatever is darkened once had a light: only the darkness causes the light to serve no purpose. *Who are alienated from the life that is from God.* This is the second thing that makes them hideous and disfigures them. ### Chapter One

...is, is a way of life that pleases God and is acceptable to Him; a life that accords with the will and the precept of God, which He Himself has given through reason. And to be *alienated from the life that is from God* means to have an aversion to a virtuous and God-pleasing way of life, and to reveal this inward aversion through one's deeds and life. Paul shows in verse 19 in what manner this occurred among the peoples <note>original: "Völckern," referring to the Gentiles or Heathens.</note> of whom he speaks. I cannot depart so far from my purpose as to be able to explain this passage in full right now. One sees from this that: *To walk in the vanity of one's mind*, and: *to be alienated from the life of God*, are ways of speaking that agree in their primary meaning. The cause of this sorrowful condition is twofold: *Through the ignorance that is in them*: this is the first cause. *Through the blindness of their heart*: this is the second cause. These latter words have moved us to consider this passage of Paul's somewhat more extensively here. They serve our purpose, namely, because they depict the natural state of men, which is the blame for why we can fall into such pitiable circumstances as the heathens were in. The Apostle wishes to teach us this: Natural ignorance, with which we are born, and the blindness—or rather the insensitivity—of our heart, have caused these heathens to fall so low and to become so absurd and foolish in their understanding, and so perverse and stubborn in their will. Thus, in the understanding of the natural man, there is first by nature an ignorance. He does not see the truth that must lead him to salvation <note>original: "Seligkeit," referring to eternal happiness or the state of being saved.</note>.

<column-break/>

He brings no light, no knowledge, no clarity with him when he is born: it is dark and thick in his understanding. Reason, which is still there, sleeps, as it were: and how many are those who have the desire to awaken it? Therefore, he is easily brought to "vanity of mind," to stay with Paul’s phrasing. Therefore, he easily lets himself be talked into the most absurd and foolish things by a deceiver or a madman, and often unexpectedly becomes even more mad and senseless than his teacher. What things did the priests of idols formerly put into the heads of those heathens born in blindness, which they afterwards defended as eternal truths? And what dreams and follies do people still engrave among certain Christians, which they impress so deeply upon themselves that they are ready to sacrifice their blood for them? The miserable state of our understanding with which we are born, or the ignorance that is in us, is to blame for this. The other cause that worked the corruption of these heathens is in the will. *Through the blindness of their heart*, says our translation. In the style of writing of our holy books, the "heart" mostly signifies the power of the soul which we otherwise call the "will." in this place, we are bound to assign this meaning to the word "heart," because the heart and its natural sickness are clearly distinguished from the sickness of the understanding and the ignorance that dwells within it.
