It has this meaning in very many places. This hardness or insensitivity is precisely the spiritual sickness of the will, which the Spirit of God otherwise tends to call spiritual death. In our will, there is no impulse, no movement toward the good or toward the love of virtue. In regard to the things that please our Creator, our will behaves as if it had no feeling at all, no inclination, and no desires. This sorrowful condition promotes the fall and the total corruption of the natural man. Since nothing good can take hold in us because of the insensitivity of the heart, evil ideas and examples have all the more power over our soul. Our heart follows its natural impulse and obeys the desires it has inherited. Even if the most reckless things are suggested to us: if they are only pleasing to the flesh <note>In this context, "flesh" (German: *Fleisch*) refers to the carnal or fallen human nature that seeks worldly rather than spiritual satisfaction.</note>, the evil heart practically forces the understanding to accept them, and uses these irrational opinions to defile one's entire conduct and to spend one's life in a state of mad overconfidence and the most shameful vices. Do we not see here a sorrowful picture of the natural man? And are the causes that Paul gives for the spiritual misery and the sinful conduct of most men not confirmed by daily experience?

We will now come to those who know nothing of revelation, yet apply all the powers of their understanding

<column-break/>

to learn to know God, His will, themselves, and their duties. We maintain that these people, however enlightened by nature they may be, are still too weak to grasp the greatness of God and the purposes for which man was created through their reason. We willingly concede that a person who has a desire to reflect can recognize His power and wisdom from the works of God that he sees, and through the powers of nature can find many truths that contribute no small amount to the well-being and happiness of mankind. However, this capacity of nature, useful in itself, cannot perform the services for us—for various reasons—that we require to come to God. First, it is not sufficient to investigate all the truths that belong to a complete edifice of spiritual wisdom. Let us count the pieces that we can determine without the aid of revelation and calculate them against those about which reason can give us no instruction; it will then be shown that the latter account is far greater than the former. I see so much order, wisdom, and power upon the earth that I cannot refrain from believing that the cause from which these things come must be much more powerful and wiser than I can grasp or express. I conclude from this: My duty is to honor this infinite Being. Yet my spirit is not satisfied with this. It searches further. It asks: How must I honor this Being? Where do I find the teacher who leads me where I wish to go? My reason <note>German: *Vernunft*. In Enlightenment-era theology, "Reason" was viewed as a gift from God but one that was severely limited by human fallibility and the "fall" of man.</note> tells me clearly: A creature such as I must walk carefully, virtuously, and sensibly, and resist his evil inclinations. The truths, secondly, which we believe we see and recognize most clearly, nevertheless often become dark and uncertain in our eyes so long as we support them merely with reason. A proof that seems clearer to us today than the sun will perhaps seem imperfect and fragile tomorrow, if we either turn our eyes to another side or perceive a change within ourselves. It may be that a natural philosopher <note>German: *Weiser der Natur*. This refers to a scholar who studies God and the universe through the natural world rather than through scripture alone.</note> today trusts himself to testify to the immortality of his soul even unto the pyre, and regards the proofs that support it as pillars that cannot break; and this same man can speak of this matter with uncertainty tomorrow, and can say neither truly 'yes' nor 'no'. Whence does this come? From two things. First:

<column-break/>

from our internal evil desires and inclinations. If these are contrary to a certain truth, if they conflict with an insight we otherwise held to be irrefutable, they weaken—when they are stirred and become heated—even the most correct logical conclusions. One concludes in certain moments when the desires are at rest: I would have to be insane if I did not believe this world were the work of a just, wise, and powerful Being. And what happens after a few hours? A strong desire to sin and to indulge in disorder awakens. This darkens the light that illuminated us shortly before so quickly that we hardly regard all the reasons we held to be so strong as anything but conjectures that might perhaps deceive. This comes, secondly, from this world itself, which appears to us miserable mortals as a place where light and darkness take turns with one another. We are too small and lowly to oversee the entire constitution and arrangement of the works of God and to rightly judge the wise connection of all things that exist. Hence it seems to us as if there were an eternal and constant struggle between good and evil, between wisdom and blind chance, between order and disorder on this earth. This creates uncertainty and confusion within us. If we look to one side, we are full of reverence and wonder; if we turn to the other, we become lost and doubtful. ...doubt constantly. At its proper time, the earth brings forth what is useful for the sustenance and pleasure of animals and humans. When I observe this, I become certain that a powerful and wise Being governs. But there is also no end to the misfortune here below. That land is scorched by the sun; this one is stiff with perpetual frost and cold. Here the ground moves and buries cities, villages, and countless people in its womb; there the sea rises from its banks and swallows half-countries. In certain remote lands, which we cannot yet reach, many peoples live in the utmost misery and in a pitiable state of body and spirit. In other stretches of land, where greed <note>German: *Gewinnsucht*. This likely refers to the colonial and commercial expansion of the 18th century, driven by the desire for profit.</note> has driven us, dwells an incredible multitude of people whom one would take for a kind of cattle, if they did not show their reason partly through certain arrangements and partly through their deceptions.

When I imagine these and many other things, I suspect—so long as revelation <note>German: *Offenbarung*. The concept that God reveals truths to humanity through scripture or divine intervention which cannot be reached by logic alone.</note> does not offer me its hand—that this world arose by chance, and I doubt whether the order present in the world is sufficient to convince me of the contrary.

The world is full of lifeless and living creatures, of herbs, plants, trees, and animals that serve for the pleasure, preservation, and health of mankind. A mere student of nature and reason, as long as he considers these alone, sees these things as blessings from a loving Being who wishes to make humans happy. But there are also poisonous, harmful, and deadly things in the world, which

<column-break/>

often overtake and execute humans in the greatest security. The earth is full of poisonous snakes, of vexatious vermin, of cruel and raging beasts, of unhealthy herbs and trees, which make life unsafe and laborious in many places. The sea contains an incredible number of monsters and terrifying creatures that seem to exist only for the purpose of consuming the weak and making humans fearful.

When reason <note>German: *Vernunft*. The faculty of the mind used to form conclusions; the author argues here that reason is paralyzed by the "problem of evil" in nature.</note> looks upon these things, it stands still and does not know if it has concluded correctly when it thought to see the hand of a wise and good Creator in the things that benefit us here.

There is a certain light within us that lets us not doubt that a human is bound to live an orderly and virtuous life and to do wrong to no one; and at the same time, there is within us a natural and violent impulse to do the opposite and to direct all our deeds toward our own benefit and pleasure alone.

Reason, left to itself, does not know how to compare these two things. It has sometimes firmly resolved to strive after virtue and respectability; and it is not long before it hears, as it were in the innermost depths of the heart, the question: Why then am I by nature inclined to indulge my desires? And who is fit to answer that correctly without the assistance of a revelation?

# On the Natural Corruption of Mankind

...men <note>Likely the conclusion of a word such as "come" or "taken" from the previous page.</note>. The wise men of whom we know have allowed themselves to be led astray by self-love and the pride of nature, so that they dared to break through with their own wit <note>In this context, "wit" (*Wiz*) refers to human ingenuity or intellectual cleverness.</note> and attempt to fathom the depths of all wisdom. One philosopher laid this foundation, and another laid that, based on teachings we can find through our own reflection; then, they added so many of their own unfounded fancies that a misshapen and strange work resulted—one that only gave others the opportunity to mock and laugh at them. 

Most of the wise, who presume to recognize so much of **God** and of religion through the powers of their own understanding that they can turn it into a complete science, remind me of certain foolish master builders. One has a few columns, some prepared timber, and various well-hewn stones at hand. From these pieces, one believes a perfect house can be assembled. However, when it comes to the actual work, it becomes clear that much more is needed before the task can be completed. One should, therefore, before proceeding, first think of how to procure what is missing. Instead, one clings to the original plan and takes whatever can be found first, simply to join what one already has in a specific way. Glue, useless beams, discarded stones, crooked wood—in short, everything one encounters is brought into the work and joined with the good and elegant supplies. What comes of it then? A dwelling that collapses at the first wind, and a house that passers-by laugh at and call a masterpiece of ignorance—

<column-break/>

—and folly <note>original: *-sen*, completing the word *heissen* (to be called/named) from the previous column.</note>. Most of my readers will have enough skill to interpret this parable for themselves regarding the people of whom we speak.

We would need to add almost nothing more to settle the point we wish to prove: that a human being who follows only his own reason is not capable enough to recognize **God**, His ways, His essence, and His will. However, we wish to go a bit further and confirm the matter more through examples. The wise men who lived before our **Savior** will be able to provide the best testimony in this investigation. No one will deny—unless he knows nothing of these people—that the heads of the ancient philosophical schools were people of uncommon sharp-mindedness, and possessed great insight and gifts of understanding. Even if there are many among the modern wise who are no worse or less capable than they were, we can certainly find none whom we would have reason to place above them. 

If it is therefore proven that these great and sharp-sighted people partly arrived at childish and absurd opinions, partly remained stuck in doubt and uncertainty, and partly patched things together where one idea cancelled out the other, then no one can deny any longer that human understanding is too weak to raise itself to **God** and to discover anything correct and certain in spiritual matters. **Paul** says of all these people that, in their imagined wisdom, they were fools: *Claiming to be wise, they became fools.* <note>original: "Da sie sich für Weise hielten, sind sie zu Narren worden."</note> **Romans 1:22**. The cleverest of them all is ***Socrates***. He argues that there is a single, powerful, and wise being, and he constantly insists on virtue, honor, and justice. But this very same sensible man honors the gods of the Greeks no differently than the lowliest day laborer, and he desires no change in the common worship, despite its absurdity. He thinks differently than the common people about the gods he prays to. He considers them spirits to whom the highest **GOD** has entrusted a portion of the government of this earth; yet, he still wants the service itself to be maintained. One might think he merely conformed to common opinions out of fear. However, there are many traces of superstition throughout his entire life: and in his final speeches, one sees that he truly meant well by the established religion. When asked why one should stick with the old ways, he answers: one could find nothing better; and if **GOD** himself did not tell man how He wished to be honored, they would never arrive at a true certainty.

...who formed this world and created a multitude of intermediary spirits <note>original: *Mittel-Geister*; these are the "daemons" or lesser deities in Platonic thought</note>, who make up a sort of staircase between **GOD** and mankind and bring the prayers of mortals before the highest **GOD**. I conclude from this that Plato himself either presented his opinions only as conjectures, or provided such poor reasons for them that his students did not think it advisable to follow him.

***Aristotle***, who was honored for so long as a divine teacher even among Christians, is even more simple-minded and perverse in his propositions concerning **GOD** and spiritual matters. What is **GOD** according to his opinion? Nothing more than that which starts the motion in a clock. A being that sits calmly above all the stars and, in a certain way that he himself cannot explain, sets the world in motion, spends his time in constant contemplation, and does not even think of the people or the things that occur beneath the moon <note>The "sublunary" realm, which in ancient science was the only place where change and decay happened</note>. # The First Chapter

Can it not be a matter of indifference whether I know that He <note>Referring to God</note> exists or not? (*) What is our soul? A small part of a certain corporeal and fire-like spirit that is spread throughout the whole world, and is therefore mortal and transient. (**) What must I, as a rational person, do? Everything that can make me satisfied here, bring me into high regard, and make me beloved, whatever it may be. Would we be much more blessed than the irrational creatures if these things were truly so?

The Stoic <term>Stoic; a member of the ancient Greek school of philosophy that taught that virtue is the highest good and is based on knowledge and reason</term> speaks **magnificently of God and of virtue.** Those who do not know the language and the inner workings of these people's doctrine easily believe that they were not so very far removed from true wisdom. Whoever becomes more closely acquainted with them sees no reasons why he should hold them in particularly high esteem. God, in their opinion, is a fiery spirit who is as closely united with this world as the soul is with a body. He possesses great perfections and attributes: and for that reason, He deserves the respect and veneration of men. And yet, He is so subject to destiny and fate that He must absolutely follow its dictates. Of what use to me is a God from whom I have neither punishment to fear nor reward to hope, and who can do nothing more or less than what must happen according to eternal and unchangeable providence? (***) Into the moral philosophy <note>original: *Sitten-Lehre*</note> of the Stoics, I can

<column-break/>

not find my way at all. Their teachings are lofty, and in appearance, beautiful and excellent. Virtue is everything: a wise man needs nothing more to make himself happy: through it, he is just as content in the hands of the executioner as an Eastern king is in his palace. And what then moves me to strive after virtue? Does God reward it? He can neither chastise nor reward. Is my spirit immortal? Not at all. It either passes away immediately when the body decays, or at least cannot endure for long. What reasons then do I have to distress and constrain my nature, which gladly wants to obey its desires? Virtue is its own reward. This is true: but it is no reason to encourage ordinary people toward virtue. One cannot be convinced of this truth except through experience. It serves, therefore, only to maintain those who are already virtuous and have tasted the reward of virtue in their goodness, but not to awaken the wicked from their security. But what is the purpose of the entire moral philosophy of the Stoics? I am much mistaken, or it does not hang together with the rest of these people's propositions. Reason tells me I should be virtuous. But does not reason itself say, according to the propositions of the Stoics, that everything in the world proceeds according to an unchangeable destiny? Does it not say that the evil and the godless are a necessary piece of this world, belonging to its perfection? Does it not likewise admonish—

### On the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

If the wicked man is what he is by necessity, then the virtuous man will be nothing different. To what end, then, are so many teachings, reminders, and exhortations necessary? With **Epicurus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (341–270 BC) who founded Epicureanism, a school of philosophy that sought happiness through the absence of pain and fear</note> and his followers, I cannot get along at all. I cannot become his disciple unless I first renounce my reason and overturn what I consider to be indisputable. I ask him: From where did this world originate? He answers: Once, an infinite number of small particles of matter, which had swarmed around for a long time, unexpectedly fell together. That was the origin of all things that we see. If I am to believe that, I must first accept two propositions that conflict with all the rules of reason. I must first posit: That from disorder, confusion, and lack of understanding, order, constancy, and wisdom can arise and have arisen. Who can deny that there is wisdom and reason in man, and order and constancy in the entire constitution of the world? And yet, was there none of these things in those specks of dust and tiny bodies <note>The author is referring to Epicurus's theory of atomism, where the world is formed by the random collision of atoms</note> which, in the opi-

<column-break/>

nion of **Epicurus**, formed this world by chance? I must, secondly, imagine that a matter of importance can come to be and happen without a cause. The **Epicurean** may torment himself as long as he wishes; he will never be able to tell me what cause united and brought together the long-scattered specks of dust. This cause cannot reside within the specks of dust themselves. And apart from them, this man wishes to know of no other cause. It is therefore nothing that effected and brought about such a great thing, or else this world arose without a cause. He will perhaps cite chance as the cause. But with that word, only the ignorant can be dismissed. A chance without a cause is nothing and a foolish fancy. The rest of the teaching of this sage is just as absurd as the beginning. His gods are like little cardboard figures, who look as if they had flesh and blood and yet have none; who spend their time in certain remote regions in idleness and games, and do not even know whether animals other than themselves live in the world. His moral philosophy <note>original: *Sitten-Lehre*</note> has this main principle: I must do everything that can create pleasant sensations for me or, at the very least, put me beyond pain and unrest. One may explain and excuse this doctrine for as long as one wishes: it will still be easy to prove that it is the path to all vices. We have said enough to demonstrate that the greatest mind, which has no light other than its reason, cannot find the truth regarding divine and spiritual things.

# Chapter One

The doctrine concerning the **blindness of humanity** in spiritual matters is essentially this: a wise man, when left to his own natural devices, is so blind that he cries out "folly and lack of understanding" whenever the **revealed truth** is proclaimed to him. His own wit <note>original: *Wiß*; here meaning intellect or cleverness</note>, especially if he has already been captivated by human wisdom, is not powerful enough to perceive the excellence and beauty of the teaching that alone leads to salvation, unless the grace of the Most High comes to his aid. There is so much majesty, beauty, and excellence in this revealed doctrine that any person who is not entirely corrupted must feel some sense of reverence and 
<margin>Hb</margin> 
high esteem for it. We have examples enough of people who were far removed from Christ and yet could not help but praise and admire many parts of his teaching. However, closely bound to everything that is great and glorious in this holy and soul-saving doctrine is much that appears small, lowly, and contemptible in the eyes of the world. A teacher of a beautiful system of ethics <note>original: *Sitten-Lehre*</note>, who confirms his preaching with miracles, grants his disciples the power to perform wonders, and spreads his teaching without worldly power or status, is something charming and extraordinary. But a **miracle-worker** who is subjected to the punishment of a slave <note>original: *knechtischen Strafe*; a reference to crucifixion, which was reserved for the lowest classes in the Roman Empire</note> and crucified, who had nothing but poor and despised followers, and who yet earned salvation for the whole world through his cross—this is offensive and vexing to the "wise" man. The high regard that the former considerations brought him is turned into contempt by the latter. He does not know how to reconcile majesty and lowliness in the person of Jesus Christ. We

<column-break/>

generally judge the value of things according to what we hear and see, or according to the opinions of this world. And the **Cross** and the lowliness of Jesus do not agree with these worldly opinions. Therefore, one feels entitled to despise and reject his entire teaching. If one has previously filled one's head with another kind of wisdom, this happens even more readily. It costs the natural pride and self-love of corrupt man too much to admit that he has hitherto walked in darkness and has allowed himself to be deceived and fed with husks and refuse <note>original: *Trebern und Unraht*; a biblical metaphor referring to the food of swine, symbolizing worthless worldly pursuits</note> instead of pure grain.

The **Apostles** of our Savior experienced this when they proclaimed the crucified Redeemer to the **Greek sages**. They found an entrance among common and lowly people, who were not tempted by human cleverness to resist grace and truth. But they found resistance, disobedience, and mockery when they opened the mystery of the **Gospel** <note>original: *Evangelii*</note> to those who believed they could see further than the Greek masses <note>original: *Pöbel*; the common people</note>. Paul says that he preaches the crucified Jesus as "foolishness to the Greeks." **1 Corinthians 1:23**. And in the **Acts of the Apostles**, one finds examples that confirm this. **Acts 17:32**; **Acts 26:24**. These holy men did not wonder at this. They recognized, by the divine light granted to them, that a natural and puffed-up wise man could not act otherwise. Their newly converted congregations were sometimes offended by this stubbornness and refractoriness of the presumed wise men. They therefore took the opportunity to show them that one

"The natural man," he says, "perceives nothing of the Spirit of God; it is a folly to him and he cannot recognize it. For it must be spiritually judged." 1 Corinthians 2:14. In my opinion, more scholarship has been applied to clarifying the meaning of this passage than was necessary. What a "natural man" is can best be determined by the contrast. The **spiritual man** is set in opposition to the **natural man**. No one doubts that the spiritual man is a person who has received the Spirit of God and has been enlightened by Him. And so *the natural man can be none other than one who lacks the Spirit of God, who possesses merely a soul or spirit capable of thinking, reflecting, and pondering, and who judges the things that come before him solely through this power of the mind.* This person, first of all, perceives nothing of the Spirit of God—or, as one might translate, of the teachings of the Spirit of God, of the preaching of the Gospel, which was presented to the world by the Apostles. He understands the meaning of their words, but he does not "perceive" the teaching; that is, he does not recognize the excellence, the blessedness, the sufficiency, and the glory of this doctrine. Misery enough! What are we if we cannot distinguish the chaff from the wheat, nor separate the gold offered to us from false ore? Yet we are even more miserable. Paul goes further and says that the wisdom of the Holy Spirit is **folly** to such a man. He is in a bad state who does not know what is good; but he

And if only he still had the ability to help himself out of this wretched state! Even that is lacking. Paul says thirdly: "He cannot recognize it," meaning he does not have the strength to escape his natural ignorance and blindness. And why not? Because, says the Apostle, "it must be spiritually judged." The meaning of these words is simple: whoever is to rightly judge the truth taught by the Spirit of God, as is fitting, must be enlightened by this Spirit himself. *It is therefore no wonder that those who do not have the Spirit of God, nor wish to submit to Him, proceed in such a blind and foolish manner.*

I wish, however, as a further proof, to cite two passages of Holy Scripture. I have chosen those that are generally not commonly used in this matter. The first stands in 1 John 2:20: <note>The original text cites "Joh. I. 20," referring to the First Epistle of John, Chapter 2.</note> *You have the anointing from Him who is holy, and you know all things.* It is all the same whether one understands "the one who is holy" here to mean the Spirit of God or our Savior, Jesus Christ. The <term>anointing<note>In this context, "anointing" (Salbung) refers to the internal influence of the Holy Spirit, which was often compared to the sacred oil used to consecrate kings and priests in the Bible.</note></term> signifies, in John's way of writing, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, who is compared to an oil in the Scripture. Jesus earned this anointing for us; and the Spirit of Grace imparts it to us. One can therefore leave the interpreters the freedom to understand the word "holy" as referring to either one. The anointing is, as John says, the means through which the believers to whom he writes had obtained the knowledge of all things—that is, of the main points of Christian doctrine. Can one then know nothing of the truth without having received the anointing? Who would claim this? One can know the entire doctrine of faith and yet be unanointed. In John’s way of writing, "to know," or "to know God," means the same as to know in a living, powerful, and salvific way. And so in his words lies this teaching: No one can rightly know God, no one can be called truly enlightened, except the one whom the Holy Spirit has powerfully touched and awakened in <term>regeneration<note>Regeneration (Wiedergeburt) or "new birth" is the spiritual transformation where a person is thought to be moved from their "natural state" into a state of grace.</note></term>. If the people to whom John writes 

<column-break/>

know everything through the anointing, then it follows that those who are not anointed know nothing.

I take the second passage from this very same letter of John, chapter 3, verse 6: *Whoever sins,* says John, *has not seen God, nor known Him.* It is clear that he speaks of Christians who were instructed in divine wisdom and had been received into the community of the saints. To these, he says, the knowledge of God is lacking if they defile themselves with willful sins. The members of the first congregations did not lack the literal knowledge of divine truth. No one was admitted to baptism except those who were rightly instructed in the main points of Christian doctrine. And the conviction of those who confessed the Christian religion was not to be doubted at all. Who would have accepted a doctrine that brought about shame and harm if he had not been convinced of its truth? John must therefore be speaking of the powerful and <term>salvific<note>Salvific (seligmachend) refers to knowledge that actually leads to salvation or the "saving" of the soul, rather than just academic knowledge.</note></term> knowledge. According to his declaration, one can be a well-instructed and well-founded Christian and yet still have a lack of this knowledge. We wish to conclude. **A Christian who sins does not know God and is blind in spiritual matters. He who sins is still in the state of nature.** Thus, those who are still in the <term>state of nature<note>The "state of nature" (Stand der Natur) refers to the human condition after the Fall, characterized by an inherent inability to please God or understand spiritual truth without divine help.</note></term>, and enjoy no divine assistance, also have a lack of true and living knowledge of spiritual and divine things.

# The First Chapter

### §. V.

Anyone who wishes to be convinced by visible evidence of the blindness and lack of understanding of man in spiritual and divine matters need only consider the varying behavior of so many people regarding religion and divine service. One part of the inhabitants of this world elevates their reason above all else and believes they possess within it a certain means to pull the truth out of its depths. Another part acts as if they had no understanding at all, following now their imagination, now the authority of other men who, through various proofs, pass themselves off as enlightened and wise. Each group is again divided into all sorts of harmful branches. From the first kind arise <term>Atheists<note>original: "GOttesläugner," literally "God-deniers."</note></term>, enemies of revealed religion, doubters, <term>Socinians<note>A non-trinitarian movement that prioritized rational interpretation of the Bible, named after Faustus Socinus.</note></term>, and others. To the latter belong the followers of the <term>Bishop of Rome<note>A common Protestant term for the Pope, used here to suggest that the Roman Catholic Church relies on human authority rather than direct spiritual enlightenment.</note></term>, who are the only ones who imagine that the Spirit of God dwells nowhere but in a certain visible church; the <term>fanatics<note>original: "Schwermer," a term used for radical religious groups who claimed direct, emotional inspiration from God.</note></term> and false prophets; and those people who make an internal or external light the guide for their doctrines and deeds.

### Explanation.

One will find nothing to object to in the proof we have given so far of the inability of the human understanding in spiritual matters, unless one intends either to pervert the matter of which we speak or to act unfairly. However, we will not be satisfied with that alone. In order to make this truth all the more certain, we wish to add a new proof taken from things unknown to no one, which can therefore be judged all the more easily. We conclude thus: Men are split into countless sects and opinions regarding religion; their un-

<column-break/>

derstanding must therefore be very weak, darkened, and suited for nothing less than the knowledge and judgment of pure truth. If there were enough power and strength to distinguish the light from the darkness, then at least the greatest part of mankind would recognize and accept it. If some were found everywhere who could not help themselves, the clever and sensible would, with little effort, strengthen these weak ones and set them on the right track. One would therefore find harmony and peace everywhere, and especially among those who boast of a revelation.

...agreement in the most important aspects of religion. And when is there more discord and disagreement than when the question is raised: What must I believe, what must I do, to be saved? Can it be said that even a twentieth part of the people who live here below have a uniform rule of faith and life? It seems to me, therefore, that this discord is proof enough that we are, by ourselves, <term>powerless heroes<note>original: "ohnmächtige Helden." A sarcastic or ironic term for humans who believe they are strong enough to find truth on their own, but ultimately fail.</note></term> when we must break through the darkness in which we are born to find the way to GOD.

This conclusion becomes even stronger and more important to those who look at the basis of all the disputes conducted regarding faith and religion. As diverse and manifold as the thoughts and doctrines of men are concerning matters of faith, there is—when everything is carefully weighed—only one single source from which they all stem. We miserable mortals cannot agree among ourselves whether our <term>intellect<note>original: "Verstand." In this context, it refers to the human capacity for logical thought as opposed to divine inspiration.</note></term> is worth anything in spiritual matters, or whether it is worth nothing at all. From this comes all the quarreling and all our disagreement. The light of our intellect is weak, yet it is not completely extinguished. To help this weakened intellect, the love of GOD has lit a greater light for us and given us a <term>revelation<note>The "Offenbarung," referring to the Bible or direct divine communication.</note></term>. This revelation presumes the things that we can easily find through our intellect. It confirms that which is made known to us through nature. It provides us with certain and infallible grounds for the truths that <term>reason<note>original: "Vernunft."</note></term> presents to us as if in a twilight. Finally, it compensates for the deficiencies and errors found in <term>natural religion<note>The belief that God can be known through nature and reason alone, without the need for supernatural revelation.</note></term>.

<column-break/>

Can we desire more? And how happy would we be if we sought to understand the meaning of this divine revelation with faithfulness and zeal, subjected ourselves to its pronouncements in simplicity and composure, and waited patiently for the time that will resolve the doubts that still appear here and there? What do we do instead? We create many vain worries and unrest for ourselves. Sometimes our pride leads us so far that we hold the instruction GOD gave us through his witnesses in contempt. We want to be our own teachers and masters. Sometimes we allow ourselves to dream that our <term>wit<note>original: "Witz," meaning cleverness or human ingenuity.</note></term> is the key to revelation, and that GOD intended to tell us nothing more than what a man who is not born <term>foolish<note>original: "aberwißig," meaning senseless or mentally deficient.</note></term> could discover for himself. Sometimes an innate laziness misleads us into believing that GOD has opened the secret of His will only to certain people, and that the "great heap" <note>An archaic term for the common masses or the general public.</note> is clever enough if it entrusts its salvation to the eyes of others. When pride and imagination come together, one easily becomes so bold as to think that revelation is nothing but a staff with which one first learns to walk, and thereafter one has more strength in oneself than can be found in the Scriptures. And where does it all lead in the end with all these opinions? To this single question: Does our intellect have the right and power to judge spiritual things or not? Those who grant the intellect this right cannot agree on how far it extends. And those who deny it are nonetheless at odds with one another as to which means they should use to get to know GOD instead of the intellect. He who could resolve this would soon make one single flock out of all the contrary-minded societies.

The third pretends that, after a serious and sharp investigation, it has *found that no one can say who is right* or wrong among these, or how far their opinions agree with the truth; the intellect of man is far too blunt for anything certain to be decided by it. If one takes together what we have reminded you of so far, it will show that the atheists themselves best refute themselves and convince the world that no one who does not believe in a GOD is fit to explain the origin and nature of the natural world through his understanding. I conclude thus: If it were possible to state the causes of all visible and invisible things without a GOD, then so many cunning minds, who have attempted this for so many hundreds of years, would finally have found an easy and clear path to this mystery. But I see nothing less than unity among the people who have ventured this: I find that the first foundation of all the buildings they have raised against the Most High is sandy and loose: I notice that most are not even capable of properly presenting their thoughts and explaining them with clear words.

This convinces me that nothing has been accomplished by them so far. And I need nothing more to believe that it is impossible to carry out what these people venture to do.

Those who are called **Deists** <note>Deism was a popular 18th-century philosophy that believed in a Creator who designed the universe like a clockmaker but does not intervene in human affairs.</note> are split into almost as many types and species as those who deny GOD entirely. If this disagreement concerned secondary matters, one could excuse it with the incapacity of men and our natural weakness. They all admit there is an eternal being to whom the world and man are subject. And yet, when they are asked to say what the attributes of this being are, their unity turns into a bickering that has no end. They all want to have the appearance as if they believed that man should not live according to his pleasure, but has certain duties to observe toward GOD and other people. And if one asks them: How must GOD be honored? and what sorts of elements belong to natural **morality**? then one will see how uncertain and divided they are. No agreement has yet been made among them on the single question: *What is man?* <note>original: "Was der Mensch sey?"</note>—whom they should surely know best. They argue among themselves: Whether man is entirely mortal, or partly immortal? Whether he is free or subject to the rule of **fate**? Whether he has something to hope for and fear in another world, or not? What, then, will they be able to say about other things, of which they are even less aware...

If this were true, then reason must possess an uncommon strength; and those who grant it so much power must attribute more to it than even the despisers of God and the enemies of revelation do. The latter at least admit that much cannot be rightly seen or recognized by man. A skeptic, on the other hand, believes that he can sufficiently examine and recognize everything. He pretends that he has traveled with his thoughts, as it were, through the entire visible and invisible world; that he has precisely investigated all regions, creatures, occurrences, deeds, and actions; that he has come to know himself and all other people thoroughly; and that he has calculated and measured the powers of our spirit and intellect without deception. How far does the right of the external Word or the Scripture extend? Where does the jurisdiction of the internal Word begin? How is an imagination, a trick of the brain, or a passing thought to be distinguished from the inspiration <term>inspiration</term> <note>original: "Einsprache." This refers to the belief that God speaks directly into the heart or mind of the believer.</note> of the inner Word? There are almost as many opinions on these questions as there are people of this order. Who can expect unity among such people who accept no certain rules and think as their imagination dictates to them? The lovers of the external light <note>Likely referring to those who wait for outward signs, miracles, or literalist interpretations rather than an internal feeling.</note> fare no better. It is no different when one mixes with these people than if one comes among a tribe of savages, each of whom thinks himself as good as the rest of his kind and wants to walk his own path. A person who expects more from God than He has promised him cannot remain at one with those who want to have the same claim and hope for the goodness of God as he does.

It is difficult to get along with these people and bring them onto a better path. If one presents them with the clearest passages from Scripture, one receives the answer: The Scripture must be understood and interpreted according to the direction of the divine light which they feel internally or externally. And what further is to be done,

<column-break/>

when one has been dismissed in this way? If one attacks their error through reason, one finds no hearing at all. Most of them believe that what is called reason is the voice of the ancient serpent <note>A common theological reference to the Devil in the Garden of Eden.</note> that once seduced Eve into the Fall. One must therefore deal with such people as if with children, and above all seek to win their love and confidence before engaging with them further. In my view, the bickerings they have with others of their kind provide the best opportunity to first prepare and awaken their minds. They themselves complain that many who mean well allow themselves to be over-hasty and are not skilled at distinguishing true inspirations or promptings from false and deceptive ones. They go further and admit that there are godless and malicious people who sell the evil counsel of their darkened and impure hearts to the world instead of divine truths. One can coax even more from them, if they are not entirely stubborn. One can bring them so far that they admit that some, who were certainly filled with a divine light, had sometimes felt the attacks of their human weakness and mixed self-conceived opinions with the teachings that the Spirit had given them. They thus confess that not all are enlightened who wish to be held as such, that one can take a delusion of the imagination for a true divine light, and that even the truly enlightened have a tendency toward error and do not always see when they think they see. Whoever concedes this will also have to admit that one needs certain means and signs to distinguish the rays of the true...

# The First Chapter

...divine light from the deceptive appearance of the malice of other men and his own imagination. And what more is needed to darken and extinguish this whole alleged light? One can deceive oneself: One can be led astray. In this fundamental principle, we agree with these people. Where the danger of deception exists, a wise man must look for secure and certain aids <note>The author uses "Hülfs-Mittel," referring to tools or methods used to reach a correct conclusion.</note> to escape the misfortune into which he might fall. On this point, we shall likewise have nothing to dispute. The internal or external light is therefore not enough on its own to lead us. Apart from it, we have need of another light that makes us certain whether the true light of God shines within us or others, or whether it is a blinding decoy <note>original: "Blend-Kerze." Literally a "dazzle-candle," used here to describe a false light that blinds rather than illuminates.</note> lit by a sickness of the mind or malice of the will. And where then must this new light be sought, which is to be the judge of the other light? Is it within us? Or is it outside of us? Is it within us? Then the old worry is present again: whether we are not being deceived. All internal movements, considered on their own, could be the effects of my weakness and imagination: and thus one cannot provide testimony for the other. Is it outside of me? Well, then we must turn either to the Scripture or to Reason to emerge from doubt. Reason is of no use. We will concede this for a time. The Scripture thus remains; it must deliver the verdict on whether that which is held by me as a revelation, or presented as such by others, is indeed one. It is the yardstick <term>yardstick</term> <note>original: "Richtschnur." A builder's plumb line or measuring cord used to ensure a wall is straight.</note>,

<column-break/>

according to which everything that appears to be divine must be tested. If that is so, then I do not know what use an internal or external light would be to me, even if God were willing to give it to me. As soon as something stirs within me, I must hurry to the Scripture and ask whether my stirring is a work of God or not? And therefore everything that I need to know must already be recorded in this divine book, because I must test everything that seems to come from God against it. If that which is internally or externally given <note>original: "eingegeben," referring to the idea of divine inspiration being "poured in" or suggested to the mind.</note> to me agrees with the written revelation, then it is correct. But to what end is it given to me by God, since I can know it regardless? Why does the Lord, who loves me, cause me unnecessary trouble? And why make the path to salvation <term>salvation</term> <note>original: "Seligkeit," referring to eternal happiness or the state of being saved.</note> more convoluted than it need be? He instructs me in the Scripture. This would be enough for me. And yet He does not let it be enough: He tells me the same thing once more in another way. And so He burdens me with a task that I do not even need. I must take that which He presents to me from the depths of my soul, or flows into my understanding from the outside, and retain it, weigh it, summarize it, and finally compare it with His written revelation? And what more do I learn than I could have heard from His Word anyway? Is the simplest path not the best? And does a ruler act wisely who, after having given clear laws, lets these very laws be whispered <note>original: "einblasen." Literally "to blow in," as in breathing an idea into someone.</note> to his subjects daily in another form through a speaking trumpet <term>speaking trumpet</term> <note>original: "Sprach-Rohr." An early megaphone or acoustic tube; here used as a metaphor for direct divine communication.</note>, and forces them every day to investigate whether this whispering comes from the legitimate Lord or from a rebel?

If the supposed inspiration does not agree with Scripture, then it is, without question, false and reprehensible. If I find nothing in Scripture from which I can conclude whether the inspiration is true or false, then I must let my reason rest and may claim neither one nor the other. I could be deceiving myself. And where I lack the means by which I can escape deception, I can do nothing else but remain still and suspend my choice. Can I believe that a wise, holy, and loving Being would have given or promised me a gift that serves me for nothing, and which, if it were there, would only keep me occupied in constant and at the same time useless labor?

Those of the other kind remain, as we said above, in the world and seek from other people the certainty that neither Scripture nor Reason, in their opinion, can provide to them. God, these people say, has shared five pounds <note>This refers to the "pounds" or "talents" from the Parable in Matthew 25; it is used here as a metaphor for spiritual capacity or the gift of understanding.</note> of knowledge with a small number of people whom He has appointed as His messengers and envoys; the rest He has barely provided with one pound. He has protected the former so that they cannot fail and can turn neither to the right nor to the left. To the rest of the human race, He has granted only enough knowledge that they can grasp what those leaders say and conclude, and can conduct themselves accordingly in faith and life. Is it not difficult to believe that man, who is so proud by nature, could so humble himself and persuade himself that he is nothing but a dark chamber in which others of his kind must carry the light? Man, who otherwise wants to be so sharp-witted, for whom it seems so burdensome

Over this, people will likely argue for as long as there are those who have no desire to instruct themselves. The Latin <note>Refers to the Roman Catholic Church.</note> believes that the Spirit of the Most High rests alone on the head of his bishops. The Oriental <note>Refers to various Eastern Christian traditions, such as the Coptic or Syriac churches.</note> is satisfied with neither and holds that one must seek counsel at Mosul or Cairo, where his patriarch lives. Those of the Roman persuasion insist most strongly that the Church or the heads of the Church must be regarded as the sole possessors of truth. # The First Chapter

JESUS and his Apostles did it differently. They desired that the peoples to whom they proclaimed the truth should use their understanding and judge for themselves. And praise be to GOD! that the peoples were obedient to these commands. We would still be heathens or Jews if those to whom JESUS was first proclaimed had stuck to the idea that one must believe his teachings without contradiction and must be ignorant in matters of religion. And to this category belong most Christians, who wander along according to the course of nature and the world, and yet still think they must have a religion. Whether one looks at faith or at life, one encounters this misery everywhere. The faith of Christians is neither obscure and rambling in its teachings, nor difficult and lofty in the proofs by which the teachings are strengthened. One can, in a short time—even if one were ever so poor in intellect—grasp the true understanding of the relevant teachings. And at most, one needs twice as much time to learn and comprehend what both nature and the Scripture say to demonstrate the truth of these teachings. A man of such a vast spirit should surely also know GOD, His calling, and the duties that rest upon him. And yet in these things, he is often more simple-minded than an average citizen who has spent most of his life in heavy manual labor. # Of the Natural Corruption of Men

...raised an idle doubt in our modern skeptics, he finally sometimes entrusts his conscience to a man to whom he himself would entrust nothing of importance in worldly matters. One daily sees scholars who, through their toil and labors, have earned a claim to immortality, who have read what a man can read, who have weakened and ruined their health through reflection, and yet who would find infinite trouble if they were to speak of a single piece of faith in a truly sensible and thorough manner. They have never truly thought about this matter and have used their intellect elsewhere.

An artisan <note>original: "Künstler"; in the 18th century, this often referred to a skilled craftsman, mechanic, or engineer rather than just a fine artist.</note> sometimes sees, I know not how far in advance, what effects must arise from the assembly of certain boards, wheels, and weights. He predicts it, and does not deceive himself as to what would happen if he reduced the weight by half, if he placed this wheel in another place, or if he added four wheels instead of two. Thus, he makes in his mind a series of consequences and conclusions that others find difficult to grasp and judge. And yet, when I wish to convey to this same man the easiest proof of the perfections of GOD, or to show him the connection of the first basic doctrines of Christianity, he complains that it is difficult for him to follow my thoughts: he says he is too simple-minded to understand and retain such long and far-fetched conclusions in their proper order. That usurer <note>original: "Wucherer"; a moneylender, often used here to imply someone very shrewd in financial matters.</note> and merchant over there knows countless advantages <note>Here used to mean "tricks of the trade" or "profitable strategies."</note> which he could not have learned without careful consideration. He knows what every turn of phrase in the world means and in how many ways it can be inter-

<column-break/>

-preted and explained. And when a settlement or a written contract <note>original: "Hand-Schrift"; here referring specifically to a legal document or promissory note.</note> is delivered to him, he sees in an instant whether the words mean what they are supposed to mean, and whether an ambiguous expression or a word with multiple meanings could provide an opportunity for fraud. Ask this man what love is, what humility is, what obedience is, what repentance is. Ask him to give his opinion on the best-known parts of Christian moral teaching. And one will immediately see that one can be skilled in the language of the world and understand nothing of the language of the Spirit of GOD.

### Chapter One

[...to] be is in itself vicious and evil. Woe to those who ruin their understanding through wine and heated drinks! But in my life, drunkenness is so intertwined with other things that I might almost call it a virtue. I have much work, and even more cares. ->§. VII.<-

This natural misery and corruption of our understanding is constantly increased by all kinds of causes if we are not on our guard. Some of these causes are within ourselves; some are outside of us. Within ourselves dwell evil desires, a punishable self-love, and an extraordinary laziness, which is the mother of blind imitation. Each of these things contributes to the further darkening of our understanding. <note>original: "1 Petr. II. 11. Joh. XI. 48. Joh. VII. 48." ->Explanation.<-

Our understanding, which by nature is so weak and poorly constituted, must also constantly deal with internal and external enemies that unceasingly strive to do it harm and injury. If one thinks one of these adversaries has been subdued, another is already present who is just as harmful. And we ourselves have opened the door to him. We are generally so reckless that we only seek to drive out one enemy by another. Thus, it often goes with us as it does with people who take poison to rid themselves of a fever, or who throw themselves headlong from a height to escape from prison. We wish to recount the most prominent of these causes that increase the

A religion may be as silly and distasteful as it will, it will always find followers among men. One will always encounter people whose inclinations agree with some doctrines of the deceivers. And no more is needed to bring them to a blind following. Their heart will outvote the understanding and finally move it to submit and hold as true what the desires wish to be held as true.

Secondly, we find in our
<margin>p. 219.</margin>
souls a blameworthy **self-love**, and from this arise so many false and foolish conclusions that they can hardly be described. By this word, I understand the excessive desire dwelling within us to gain and keep everything that can bring us pleasure, delight, peace, comfort, and prestige. Where this desire dwells, there is one of the worst enemies of reason. And who among mortals is free from it? Let something be as absurd and foolish as it may: if it can serve as a means to lift us from the dust <note>A common idiom for rising from a lowly social or economic position.</note> or make us rich, it gradually becomes for us a certain truth. And let something be as reasonable and grounded as it may, it will soon seem incorrect and uncertain to us if those who proclaim it to be true are in danger of losing their prestige or their possessions. What was clearer and more distinct than the truth of the doctrine of **JESUS**? And yet the leaders of the Jews could not see this bright light of the Gospel. Why not? Self-love blinded them. They feared that they would lose their earthly glory and would be no higher than the rest of the people if they recognized Christ as the **Messiah**. They reveal their hearts quite sincerely in John chapter 11, verses 47 and 48. *What are we doing?* they say. *This man does many signs. If we leave him thus, everyone will believe in him: then the Romans will come and take away our land and people.* What a conflict between reason and unreason is in these words? And this conflict is awakened solely by the love which these people bore for themselves. They admit that **JESUS** is a great

<column-break/>

miracle-worker. They further concede that his miracles were fit to convince the entire Jewish people. Does that not say clearly: **JESUS** is a messenger of God? Whoever says one performs such signs that could draw a whole nation to his teaching gives him testimony that a supernatural power works within him, which neither human understanding nor power could hold back. Thirdly, there is in our souls an uncommon laziness and sluggishness. We have no desire to use our understanding; we shrink from investigating the nature of things themselves. We listen to nothing more unwillingly than the voices of those who awaken us to search for ourselves and to test what may be truth or falsehood. What can this sluggishness that clings to us produce other than a daily growth of our blindness and folly? Because we have no desire to reflect, we accept without consideration everything that is said to us with a certain zeal. # On the Natural Corruption of Man

...and must pay for their laziness with the loss of this precious gift. <note>The "precious gift" refers to the faculty of reason and judgment discussed on the previous page.</note> Those who at the age of twenty had the capacity to judge reliably and sensibly are often, by the age of thirty, unable to go any further with their thoughts than their senses allow, because they have spent ten years on things that required no reflection. This laziness of our nature, which constantly pulls the intellect toward the earth, is the mother of that great and rash credulity and blind imitation which causes so much harm among men. We do not wish to think and reflect for ourselves, yet we still want to know the truth; that is to say, we want to obtain a good without the labor that is required for anyone to make it their own. This conflict of our inclinations is great. However, our deceptive heart knows a means to resolve it in a certain way and to unite these two disagreeing desires. It burdens others with the task of thinking and deliberating in our stead, and reserves for itself nothing but the intention to approve and accept what has been thought out by them and found to be in accordance with reason. We experience daily that those whom we have trusted most in this matter make the grossest errors; yet we do not allow ourselves to be awakened from our sleep by this. We simply switch people. What we did not find in one, we expect to find in another. Let whoever will present themselves—so long as we are maintained in our laziness, we will believe them. From this comes that wretched and yet so common conclusion in the world: "This is true, because I heard it from a man who took the trouble to reflect seriously on the truth."

# On the Natural Corruption of Mankind

...makes the Highest Being a tyrant. A harsh and severe mind does not forgive easily; and such a person generally imagines the Highest to be exactly as he is himself. The greater part of Asia believes that the world is governed by an unchangeable fate <note>The author is referring to "Fatalism," a philosophical view commonly attributed by 18th-century Europeans to "Eastern" or "Asiatic" cultures.</note>, that things cannot happen otherwise than they do, that he who is destined to fall by the sword must so fall, that the hour of death cannot be postponed for a single moment through prudence or reason, and that whatever a human being does, he does by virtue of an eternal and immutable decree of **GOD**. I do not wonder that this opinion has spread so far and is so steadily maintained. The peoples who live toward the rising of the sun <note>Meaning the East or "Orient."</note> are idle, delicate, voluptuous, indifferent, and hostile to labor. And the opinion of a strict and inevitable fate fits this constitution of body and mind uncommonly well. What can be more pleasant to one who shuns effort and work than the assurance that it is all the same whether he exerts himself or not, because the decrees of **GOD** have already determined everything that shall happen, and his own laziness and delicacy are ordained and commanded by the same?

<margin>p. 295. 459.</margin>

Such a soul accepts everything that happens to it as truth, and makes from those things it first receives the fundamental doctrines according to which it judges everything else that is later taught to it. And yet, there are few things held in such poor regard among men as the education of youth. We are allowed to grow up however we wish, and people are satisfied if we learn to observe external propriety and grasp something of the sciences that the station and way of life each person chooses seem to require. Our first years are generally entrusted to such people who possess hardly even a meager knowledge of divine and human things, let alone reason and wisdom, and who, moreover, suffer from various maladies of the understanding and the will. What can these people instill in us other than lack of understanding and folly? They imperceptibly instill in us the false opinions with which they themselves are afflicted; they teach us to look at and judge the things of this world according to their own perverse and corrupted manner; they give us, through words as well as examples, certain unintelligent rules for living which are perfectly designed to nourish evil inclinations, the pride of nature, rash self-love, and other vices.

A man of reputation tells us something with emphasis. Who asks for long whether it be true or not? His status moves our imagination, and his words penetrate our ears with a certain force. One hopes that they will become extraordinary people who will one day be elevated above others through their virtue just as much as through their status. And what happens? ...to accustom themselves to believe those who put forward something that gives a new addition to their power, rights, and majesty, however much it may conflict with reason in itself. We laugh at Alexander the Great and some of the ancient Roman Emperors, who wanted to be held as gods and allowed ignorant peoples or base flatterers to dedicate temples, altars, feast days, and sacrifices to them. ->§. VIII.<-

Our will, which is the second power <note>original: "Kraft"; here meaning a faculty or capacity of the soul.</note> of the rational soul, can boast of perfection just as little as the understanding. Considered in general and on its own, it has its great defects and infirmities: and in regard to divine and spiritual matters, it is entirely corrupted. For one, it accepts blind and deceitful leaders. It follows the promptings of the senses and often fails to use the light of the understanding <term>Verstand: the cognitive faculty used for logic and processing information</term> that God has assigned to it. Secondly, even if it asks the understanding for counsel, it lacks the capacity to remain in stillness and peace long enough for this internal judge to perform its office and to have precisely examined and weighed the matters at hand. And even if it manages to restrain itself, it ultimately lacks the strength to consistently choose and practice what the understanding has found to be wholesome, good, and useful. It rushes headlong excessively: and if it happens not to rush, its desires often mislead it into doing the opposite of what it ought to do.

->Explanation.<-

The misery and incapacity of our understanding has, I believe, been considered extensively enough. Whoever desires further instruction must seek it from those who have diligently examined the powers of our understanding according to reason <term>Vernunft: the higher intellectual capacity for grasping universal truths</term> and have demonstrated its infirmities through indisputable experiences. Now we must consider the other power of our souls, which is called the will. By this word, one generally understands
<column-break/>
the faculty of the soul either to desire or to abhor what appears to us to be either good and pleasant, or evil and harmful; and thereby to form the resolution to do all that can bring us to the enjoyment and possession of things that seem good and useful, and free us from the power of harmful and evil things. A spirit that was created not merely for contemplation, but for action...

## Section VIII.

Our will, which is the second power of the rational soul, can boast of perfection just as little as the understanding <term>Verstand: the faculty of cognitive reasoning and intellect</term>. Considered generally and on its own, it has its great flaws and maladies: and in respect to divine and spiritual things, it is entirely corrupted. First, it adopts blind and deceptive guides. It follows the promptings of the senses and often does not use the light of understanding that God has assigned to it. Secondly, if it asks the understanding for counsel, it nevertheless lacks the capacity to keep itself in stillness and quiet until this internal judge has performed its office and has precisely examined and weighed the matters at hand. And even if it restrains itself that much, it ultimately lacks the strength to always choose and practice what the understanding has found to be wholesome, good, and useful. It hurries itself excessively: and if it does not hurry, the desires <term>Begierden: passions or irrational appetites</term> often mislead it into performing the opposite of what it ought to do.

### Explanation.

The misery and incapacity of our understanding has, I believe, been weighed at sufficient length. Whoever requires more instruction must seek it from those who have diligently tested the powers of our understanding according to reason and demonstrated its maladies from indisputable experiences. Now the second power of our soul is to be considered, which is called the will. By this word, one understands

<column-break/>

in general the capacity of the soul to either desire or to loathe what appears to us as either good and pleasant, or evil and harmful, and thereby to form the resolution to do everything that can lead us to the enjoyment and possession of the things that seem good and useful, and free us from the power of harmful and evil things. A spirit that was created not merely for contemplation, but for action...

We will first consider the will alone and on its own. We will then look at the inclinations and desires that have their seat in the human will. (I) **The will is perfect and without lack, which always follows reason and arranges its inclinations and conclusions according to the prompting of an enlightened understanding.** (II) **The will is sick and imperfect, which either leads itself—if it has the power to govern itself—or either will not or cannot obey reason.** These two fundamental doctrines will soon show us whether we have cause to boast of our will, or to lament its misery and impotence. *A well-ordered will, created according to the counsel of the Most High, follows the wise and thorough instruction of a pure and healthy reason.* This obedience of the will toward reason comprises three things within itself:

*(I) The will must never undertake anything without asking reason, and must not let itself be led by any other usurped and deceptive guides. (II) The will must allow reason time to precisely test and investigate the things that occur, and not choose anything until the same has orderly weighed and considered everything. (III) The will must firmly resolve to choose and to do what the judgment of pure reason has found to be useful and wholesome, and must execute this conclusion.*

I do not need to prove that these things are required for the obedience of the will toward reason. The matter speaks for itself, and no sensible person will be able to doubt it. One need only think of the parables given shortly before of a traveler and an ignorant child <note>The author previously used these metaphors to illustrate how the soul requires a guide (reason) just as a child or a traveler in a strange land does.</note>, in order to recognize that nothing unfounded has been included in this obedience. We wish, therefore, only to consider the condition of our will according to this rule. We possess none of those three things which belong to the perfection and right arrangement of our will. And we can therefore say with truth that there is just as much to find fault with in this power of our souls as there is in the understanding.

# The First Chapter

...to have [dominion] over the spirit and to allow oneself to be captivated by external things. Every human brings certain natural desires and inclinations into the world, which have their seat and origin in the composition of the blood and other internal parts of our body, which we do not yet fully know. One person has a natural drive for comfort and quiet; another is never left in peace by a certain internal restlessness. This one loves solitude, while that one is never more satisfied than in the greatest commotion. One is displeased when commanded to stop working, while another is startled by the striking of the clock that calls him to his business. One almost hates the very air in which he was born, believing that under a foreign sky he might rest more softly; another believes he would die if he left the place where he was born and raised. These innate inclinations steer our will with incredible force. If something presents itself to us that matches—or seems to match—them, we are ready to apply every effort to obtain it. 

We do not even think for a moment that we have an **internal counselor** <note>The "internal counselor" (inwendiger Rahtgeber) refers to reason or the conscience, which the author argues should be consulted before acting on impulse.</note> whom we are first bound to consult, to see whether our efforts will lead to our advantage or harm. A merchant who desires gain is told that in the **New World** <note>A common 17th and 18th-century reference to the Americas, often associated in the European mind with limitless gold and silver.</note> it is as easy to collect silver as it is to pile up stones here. This is enough to set his whole life in motion. The sea, which he must first cross, seems to him but a moderate river; and the months he must spend suspended between air and water...

<column-break/>

...seem to him like hours that pass in haste. Reason has nothing to do with his resolution, and he takes great care not to inquire of her, because she might perhaps raise objections. We want, in a word, what our natural desires want. 

Our senses, which are moved by external things, are the other cause that moves us to will and act thoughtlessly. Whatever the senses accept and charm, that charms our spirit and brings our will into *heat and unrest*. <note>Underlined in red ink in original.</note> The wise have so often reminded us that the senses are deceptive judges and represent things to us much differently than they are in truth. We have been so often instructed that we perceive only the outermost surface of things through our eyes, and therefore cannot trust them. It has been proven to us that what was often imagined to be beautiful has been found to be ugly and misshapen. We have been taught that the pleasure of the ears is based on nothing permanent, and that the remaining senses can give us no assurance of the true nature of things. 

It has been shown to us with countless examples that those who allow themselves to be led astray by appearances and give no room to reason when something is to be decided, have become the authors of their own greatest misfortune. And yet, one has hardly been able to win over even a few among men through all these presentations, so that they might first reflect a little in many matters before they fall in love with what their senses have presented to them as pleasant and magnificent. # The First Chapter

<columns>
As soon as things present themselves to us that are suited to awaken pleasant or unpleasant movements in our body and senses, we immediately proceed to a choice and a conclusion. The consequence often shows us afterward that those things which delight the external man <note>The "external man" refers to the physical body and sensory desires, as opposed to the "internal man" or the soul.</note> for a time are enemies of his true peace, while those that sadden and deject him for a few hours are the means to his lasting contentment. One must choose a **way of life** <note>original: *Lebens-Art*; this refers to one's vocation, career, or general state in society.</note>. He who is not entirely foolish believes this choice is so important that he must do nothing in haste. What happens then? One gathers together the things that seem laborious or easy, vexing or pleasant in the dealings of the world, and demands of his **understanding** <note>original: *Verstand*; in this period, the "understanding" was seen as the faculty that processes sensory data, whereas "reason" (*Vernunft*) was the higher faculty of moral judgment.</note> only to know this: In which way of life will I enjoy the most pleasure of the senses? The understanding directs its judgment according to the natural desires and the bodily constitution of the one asking for advice. And hardly has it passed judgment, the **will** hastens thoughtlessly to execute it. Afterward, one often learns that the best part was left out of the inquiry, and through a reckless love of pleasure, one’s true happiness has been destroyed. It happens to us very often, just like those inexperienced people who had never seen fire. They concluded from the warmth they felt from it that a thing which produced such a pleasant sensation for the body must be present everywhere and should be taken into their huts and beds. One can easily imagine how soon they were convinced through pain and conflagration that those things which refresh and captivate from one side are suited from another <insert>to cause agony and misfortune</insert>

When things present themselves to us that are suited to awaken pleasant or unpleasant movements in our body and senses, we immediately proceed to make a choice and a conclusion. Afterward, one often learns that the best part was left out of the inquiry, and that through a reckless love for pleasure, one has destroyed his true happiness. ### §. IX.

I conclude from this poor condition and weakness of the will that it is partially deprived of **freedom** <note>original: *Freyheit*; here meaning the moral liberty to choose the good.</note>, which is the very soul of the will's entire perfection. In my view, the essence of freedom lies in those qualities and powers of which we have denied the will full possession. If its nature were to be expressed in a few words, it is a faculty of the will to always carry out what an enlightened and healthy understanding, after sensible and orderly reflection, has found to be good, wholesome, and useful. This faculty is not entirely abolished and lost in humans. Were it otherwise, we would be subject to a **blind necessity** <note>A philosophical term for "determinism," where humans have no choice in their actions.</note>: and neither GOtt nor humans could hold us accountable for why we acted in such a way and not another. However, it is very weakened in all humans: in some, it is hardly perceptible; in many, alas! it is almost entirely stifled through the habit of sinning.

A power is in its perfection when it is arranged and used according to the purpose and order of the wise **Creator** <note>original: *Schöpfer*.</note>. And the capacity of man is corrupted, imperfect, and miserable when it behaves and is applied against the intention and order of the **Lord** <note>original: *HErren*; here referring to God as the sovereign master of his creation.</note> who bestowed it. And he is thus not free who allows himself to be moved to decide or execute something—without asking the **Understanding**—by the desires that rule within him, or by the appearance of things that touch his senses. He is further free who has the power to hold back the forces of his **Will** until the **Understanding** has viewed the matter from all sides and carefully compared it with the primary purpose for which man was created. For an imperfect contemplation is the mother of an irrational and unfounded judgment: and this gives birth to nothing but monstrosities <note>original: *Mißgeburten*; metaphorically referring to ill-conceived actions or "malformed" moral choices.</note> that stain one's conduct and bring man into misfortune. And he thus has no **Freedom** who ambushes the **Understanding** in the middle of its work and, before it has weighed everything, allows himself to be led to choose and perform something. He is, finally, free in whom the power dwells to carry out that which has been found good and reasonable by the **Understanding**, and who does not allow himself to be led astray or pulled back by any other representations. And he is thus a servant of his lusts or of other people, whom an indistinct concept, a sensation that feels pleasant to the body, or a reason that has the appearance of truth, can immediately steer elsewhere.
