Part I. X

...be called a master of himself and his deeds, who stands constantly in danger that a coarse brush might paint over the most delicate and best-captured images of his soul, and that a pleasant stirring in the blood <note>A reference to the 18th-century medical and philosophical belief that "animal spirits" or movements in the blood caused sudden emotions or passions that could override rational thought.</note> might hinder and overturn his best intentions? These three things are comprised within the description of **Freedom** that I have given. Whosoever removes one of them, removes everything and falsifies the entire concept. And the more one takes into consideration the things we mentioned above and envisions the human being, the less desire and capacity one will feel to deny or reject any part of it.

The matter will become even clearer once we have proven that the other concepts one might form regarding the **Freedom of the Will** conflict with certain and infallible truths. We wish to demonstrate this as briefly as possible. In a matter of such great significance, one cannot be overly clear or orderly. One can envision **Freedom**, insofar as it is considered a perfection of the **Will**, in a threefold manner. The first concept is the one we have provided: and it need not be repeated. Aside from that, one can place **Freedom** in a capacity of the **Will** to choose, from its own power, that which seems good to it, without concerning itself with what the **Understanding** might have to say about it. I do not ask now whether the **Will** possesses such a capacity? I will reveal my opinion on that hereafter. I only ask here: whether, if such a capacity were present,

<column-break/>

one could seek the essence of **Freedom** within it? And I believe I am right to answer that with a "No." Such a quality is an imperfection. A man who has a light that he can use to illuminate the darkness, and yet chooses to grope and walk along in blindness, would hardly be considered wise or perfect by anyone but a madman. But **Freedom** is a perfection. Such a quality is contrary to the order and intention of **GOD**, who has given the **Understanding** to the **Will** as a guide. But **Freedom** is a quality directed toward the promotion of **GOD’S** intentions and orders. Such a quality must lead mankind upon an unknown path, which could just as easily end at the seat of misery as at the dwelling of happiness and prosperity. But **Freedom** is a perfection of the **Will** that is intended to offer man a hand in finding true happiness <note>original: *Glückseligkeit*; a term implying both earthly well-being and eternal blessedness.</note>. Finally, one could say that **Freedom** is a capacity of the **Will** to resist the clear conviction of the **Understanding** and to do, or not do, what a pure and healthy **Reason** <note>original: *Vernunft*; the higher faculty of human thought.</note> has found to be good and wholesome. Again, I will set aside the question: whether the **Will** possesses such a capacity? One can spend much time, if one has the patience, listening to everything that can be and has already been remarked upon regarding this question from both sides. We only ask: whether that which is called **Freedom** can be made into such a quality or power of the **Will**? And we maintain that this is not possible. What would **Freedom** become if we...

# The First Chapter #

...accept this opinion? It would be a capacity to overturn the order of God, to build one’s own misfortune, and to defy one's Creator, as it were. A will that tears itself loose from the sovereignty to which it is subject according to the intention of the Most High, which extinguishes the light itself that is shown to it for its own safety, and which finally regards its blind desires more highly than the counsel of true wisdom, is corrupted to the extreme and can be presented as nothing less than perfect. Since these latter two concepts of freedom cannot stand, then the one we have provided alone will maintain possession among all those who wish to judge this matter with reflection.

And why do we need many lengthy explanations? Our Savior has confirmed it Himself and placed it beyond all danger of inaccuracy. He says to the Jews: The truth would make them free; and immediately thereafter: *If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.* <note>original: "Joh. VIII. 32. 36." This refers to the Gospel of John, chapter 8, verses 32 and 36.</note> These two passages, taken together, constitute this thesis: The truth, or the doctrine that the Son of God proclaims, puts man into the state of freedom, or gives him the means to regain his lost freedom. In the first instance, Jesus presents the truth as the means to make oneself free; in the second, He calls Himself the sole acquirer of freedom. This difference in presentation is reconciled and resolved in the manner we have stated. Are these words, therefore, not an obvious proof of the truth of what we have said so far regarding the

<column-break/>

nature of freedom? He is free, according to the pronouncement of our Savior, who gives ear to the truth, grants it a place in his soul, and is ready to follow it in his deeds and actions. <margin>Thus</margin> there is no freedom where no knowledge of the truth and of that which is good, salutary, and useful is found. Thus there is no freedom where the will undertakes, without reflection and consideration, whatever seems good to it. Thus there is no freedom where an unhappy power reigns to resist the truth that reveals itself in the understanding. He is truly free whom the Son of God has set free through His teaching. And he who has become a partaker of this blessedness, whose desires and inclinations are brought into order, he wills that which reason and revelation recognize as good, and he allows himself to be led and governed by an enlightened understanding. Perhaps some believe that I am here mixing together two distinct things: spiritual and natural freedom. They might say: Jesus speaks of spiritual freedom, while here the subject is natural freedom. This reproach will fall away of its own accord when one reads what I shall shortly report concerning the misery <note>In this context, "misery" or "depravity" (Elende) refers to the weakened state of the human will in theological terms.</note> of the will in regard to spiritual things. **Natural and spiritual freedom are not different in regard to their nature and essence.** One can very well use what is said in Scripture about spiritual freedom and bondage to illustrate and strengthen the general concept of freedom.

# Of the Natural Corruption of Mankind. #

Whether this attempt to clarify this piece of human knowledge <note>original: "Erkenntniſſes"</note> agrees or disagrees with others, may be investigated by those who care to know the various thoughts of men on this matter. I am just as little inclined to recount what others teach about it as I am to refute them. I will say only this: those come closest to my view who define freedom as a power to will that which one recognizes as good. (*) I am in perfect agreement with these famous men regarding the nature and essence of freedom. We both place this quality in the obedience that the Understanding <term>Verstand: the faculty of reason and judgment</term> is duty-bound to render to the Will according to the order of God. We disagree only on the boundaries of the concept of freedom. They expand it more broadly; I draw it more narrowly. And if two people, not particularly skilled at looking closely into a matter, wanted to engage in a dispute over this disagreement, a useless war of words could result, which would confuse the matter more than clarify it. Between me and those excellent people—with whom I am otherwise not to be compared in many things—it will come down only to this single question: <note>The following passage is underlined in the original text</note> Whether freedom should be considered a natural property of the Will in general, or as a perfection of the same? They are devoted to the first opinion; and I, not without cause, choose the latter. It seems to me that true freedom is something so noble, great, and excellent, that one can hardly

<column-break/>

grant it to all men in its full scope. I find an internal resistance to saying that a raving sinner—who obeys his desires and imaginations without reflection, a man who desires only as much knowledge as he needs to practice the countless fleshly lusts with which he stains himself—possesses a good as precious as true freedom is. And, unless I am very much mistaken, this must nevertheless be asserted by those who have chosen the description of freedom that I have cited. I do not know if I am mistaken in adding one more thing, which seems to come to the aid of my concept. The Will itself must be distinguished from Freedom, which is a property of the Will. However, does it not seem that the Will itself and its Freedom are being conflated when one says that freedom is a power to will what one recognizes as good? Considered in itself, the Will is a faculty <term>Vermögen: a natural capacity or power</term> to choose what the Understanding presents to it as good. Is Will and Freedom then the same thing? Or do we wish, in order to avoid this reproach, to describe the Will as it is in itself, without the slightest regard for the things that one wills and desires? One can do this: however, in that case, one does not look at the Will as it actually finds itself in the soul, but rather as it can be imagined in the intellect of those who wish to remove it from its natural seat and consider it entirely in isolation. To anyone who wishes to reflect a little on what I have presented thus far, this will seem quite easy and comprehensible. It is known that an incredible number of people are so miserably raised that the power of the understanding <term>Verstand: the faculty of reason and judgment</term>, which the Lord has bestowed upon them, is nearly smothered and destroyed. There can be no freedom in the will where there is no prudence <term>Klugheit: practical wisdom or the ability to discern the best course of action</term> in the understanding. How much freedom, then, should one attribute to a large part of the human race? It is known that many thousands hardly think of the fact that they are obligated to sharpen the wit they have by nature and to make it fit for their own use and the benefit of other people. From youth onward, one overburdens his understanding with all sorts of irrational, vain, and absurd opinions, which one afterwards, when one has grown older, regards as so many infallible rules by which one must guide oneself. Since it goes this way for most people, is there reason to say that they possess a complete freedom? It is known that only a small number of people are scattered here and there in the world who [resist] their desires...

...must behave differently. And how many such cases are there? In matters that have some importance and concern the true happiness and misfortune of men, reasons are always found that must tip the balance. Since this is conceded by both sides, the remaining disagreement concerns only a secondary matter, which can give rise to no great consequences, whether it be decided one way or another. The will is always bound to take counsel with the <term>understanding</term> <note>original: *Verstand*; in this era, this refers to the logical, analytical faculty of the mind.</note>: in things that mean something, the <term>motives</term> <note>original: *Bewegungs-Gründe*; literally "reasons for movement."</note> are easily found. What then remains to be decided? Whether there are certain trifles where the reasons can hardly be specified? And whether in such minor occurrences the will, out of its own power, can prefer and choose one thing over another? Are these questions so significant that one must believe no one can answer "Yes" or "No" to them without danger? A prince has decided all things in his laws that have some connection to the welfare of the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: *gemeinen Wesens*; the collective public good.</note>, and commanded the subjects to undertake nothing before they have carefully examined these laws. Meanwhile, some small cases occasionally arise that cannot be settled according to the prescription of the laws. The citizens fall into a dispute: whether, in such things that can harm no one, it is within their power to do what seems good to them, or whether they may undertake nothing at all? Does this dispute deserve that one party should look upon the other as a band of rebels working for the destruction of the general welfare? I remind you of a second point: Those who consider the will as a scale that always needs a weight

<column-break/>

if it is to lean to one side, and thus deny it the power to proceed to an action without an inspiration from the understanding, yet concede that the will can also be set in motion by natural causes that do not come from the understanding. I see this from the answers with which they dismiss the objections made against their teaching. Among other things, they are told: Two coins can be presented to a person that are so similar that no one can perceive a difference. This person will nevertheless, if commanded, choose one of these two coins, even though he can discover nothing for which one should be preferred to the other. <note>This is a classic philosophical problem similar to "Buridan's Ass," exploring whether a person can make a choice between two identical options without a logical reason.</note> Is this not a clear proof that the will has the power to act for itself at times, and does not always require an impulse arising from the understanding? To this objection, this answer is given: In this case, there will still be a cause present that sets the will in motion, even if one is not aware of it. The person will choose the coin that lies most conveniently for him. Granting that this is correct; then it is nevertheless clear that the understanding does not always rule the will. The cause that works here lies in the physical position of the body, with which <term>reason</term> <note>original: *Vernunft*.</note> has nothing to do. One must therefore not say that the ground from which the movements of the will arise always resides in the understanding: One must admit that sometimes the understanding, sometimes something else external, is the cause of the deeds of men. What might be objected against the answer itself, from which I derive this conclusion...

After careful reflection, I have come to the opinion that our will is indeed provided with a <term>faculty</term> <note>original: *Vermögen*; a standard philosophical term for a power or capacity of the soul.</note> to undertake something out of itself, and does not always need certain <term>motives</term> <note>original: *Bewegungs-Gründe*; literally "reasons for movement."</note> to be stirred from its state of rest. The experiments I have conducted with myself in many matters, in the most rational way possible, first moved me to believe this: and afterwards, a certain contemplation made me firmer in this belief. I have found from often-repeated experience that I possess the faculty to, as it were, blind my <term>understanding</term> <note>original: *Verstand*; the analytical, logical part of the mind.</note>; to hold it back from all deliberation and contemplation regarding certain things that occur; and, when I have brought it into that state, to act or not act out of a mere impulse of the will, and to prefer one thing over the other. A friend asks me to spend a few hours with him on a walk. I am master enough over my understanding that I can, so to speak, command it to be still and not even think about whether it would be beneficial for me or not to comply with my friend's will. My understanding obeys: and I say, when it is completely quiet, "Yes" or "No" out of a <term>free choice</term> <note>original: *freyen Willkühr*; referring to an arbitrary or spontaneous decision not forced by logic.</note>, according to what seems good to me. I have tried this in very many other things that seemed of no particular importance, and have always felt the same effect. In matters of some size and significance, it has never wanted to work. experiments, deceived myself? Or is my soul in some things not similar to the souls of other men? The latter is dismissed of its own accord; as for the former, someone will hardly persuade me of it. I have watched over myself completely and kept watch on all the stirrings of my spirit as precisely as possible. If one can indeed deceive oneself and err when one examines everything that goes on in one's soul so sharply and deliberately, then it is difficult to determine anything in matters such as this. And would both sides not do best if they left the matter in doubt? My experience will perhaps be countered with two things. One will say: there was a cause present in my understanding that pulled the will to one side, even though I did not notice it; there are often certain representations in the soul that the soul itself does not perceive. I shall answer to this that this can be no proof against me, because one will never be able to demonstrate that the movements of my spirit remained unknown to me at the very time when I spared no diligence to observe even the slightest stirring of my thoughts. A general <term>tenet</term> <note>original: *Lehr-Satz*; a formal principle or axiom.</note>, which one might bring forward for this purpose, is, as is known, not capable of overturning a sensation and experience that has revealed itself so often and always in the same way. Secondly, it will be alleged: the very intention I formed, to undertake something without deliberation, was in these cases the motive that brought me to a certain conclusion. He who resolves to accomplish something without reflection brings his will into movement just as well...

It seems to me that God, in His wisdom, must have bestowed upon the human will such a <term>faculty</term> <note>original: *Vermögen*; the capacity or power of the soul to act.</note> to move itself at times from within, without the assistance of the <term>understanding</term> <note>original: *Verstand*; the faculty of logic and analysis.</note> or other external reasons. All sorts of cases arise in which it is in no way possible to determine which side is the most certain and secure. Finally, one finds natural doubters who are ingenious to their own unrest; they find so much to deliberate and worry about in every matter that their lives would end sooner than their delibera-

This is the reflection which strengthens me in the opinion that the experience I spoke of shortly before was no dream or imagination. There would be no end to countless things and reflections if the will were not endowed with the power to choose and conclude without a ground or cause. The faculty is therefore there, provided my thoughts do not deceive me. But a wise man will never use it except when his understanding denies him light and help. And whoever thinks to find the essence of freedom in this power gives, in my opinion, the intelligent an opportunity to say that freedom is anything but a good and a perfection. 

I add nothing but this: that this opinion does not at all conflict with the doctrine so zealously defended in our times, that nothing can occur without a <term>sufficient reason</term> <note>original: *gnugsamen Grund*; a reference to the Principle of Sufficient Reason popularized by Leibniz and Wolff, which states that everything must have a reason for being as it is.</note> and cause. The soul and the power granted to it by God is the ground from which those deeds flow whose causes one cannot [otherwise] find. It is admitted, as we noted above, that a certain posture of the body or something else outside the understanding can bring about certain conclusions of the will. Does he act more absurdly who believes that the inherent natural power of the will is the ground of various actions, just as the natural weight of lead or stone is the ground for the entire movement of a clock?

-># On the Natural Corruption of Humanity. <-

### §. X.

In regard to spiritual matters, the state of our will is even worse. If freedom in human and earthly things is greatly weakened and exhausted, then in spiritual and divine matters it is entirely lost and forfeited. Psalm 14:2–3. Our will lacks the <term>faculty</term> <note>original: *Vermögen*; the inherent power or capacity to act.</note> to desire and to will those things which agree with the order of God and the purpose for which we were created. Romans 7:5. And even if something of such a desire could arise within us, the power is nevertheless not present to carry out this desire and to fulfill the will of God. John 15:5. To assist the weakness of most people, the Scripture has taught us this in a metaphorical manner <note>original: *Gleichniß-Weise*; using parables or analogies to explain complex spiritual truths.</note>. To depict the misery of our will, it has compared us sometimes to slaves and servants (John 8:34; Romans 6:17, 20; 2 Peter 2:19) and sometimes to dead and lifeless people (Ephesians 2:1; Colossians 2:13; Ephesians 4:17).

### Explanation.

We must do two things here to make the matter under discussion clear. We must first present the misery and incapacity of the will in spiritual things, and we must thereafter explain the emphatic metaphors of the Holy Scripture with which it has depicted and explained this misery.

The entire misery with which our will is afflicted in view of spiritual things is called, in a single word, the loss of spiritual freedom or **spiritual bondage** <note>original: *geistliche Knechtschaft*; a core theological concept suggesting that the human will is "chained" by sin and cannot choose God on its own.</note>. There is far less dispute among those who search for divine and human truths over the question of what spiritual freedom is, than

<column-break/>

over the nature of earthly and general freedom. It will be all the easier for us to say what the former is, and we will be able to show all the more clearly that we have every reason to mourn the total loss of this great good. **Spiritual freedom** is a capacity of the will to always provide a willing obedience to the conclusions of the <term>understanding</term> <note>original: *Verstand*; the rational faculty.</note> when it has been enlightened by God in spiritual matters. Here we assume beforehand that freedom is a perfection of the will, and that the ground of it lies in the understanding. We hope that we have sufficiently proven this above. Spiritual freedom requires not an ordinary understanding, but one enlightened by God.

# The First Chapter

...enlightened understanding. This arises from the things with which spiritual freedom is concerned. These things are divine and concern the supernatural and eternal happiness of humanity. Who can be informed of these things unless the Lord Himself has enlightened and taught him? This enlightenment was natural before those from whom all people descend <note>A reference to Adam and Eve and the concept of Original Sin.</note> fell into the Creator's disgrace. After their crime deprived them and all their descendants of the **Image of the Highest**, no one by nature knows any longer how he must walk rightly in order to please the Lord. God has remedied this deficiency through a supernatural revelation, which is contained in the writings of certain men whom He chose as His witnesses to the world. And our distressed condition, which we have inherited from our first fathers, required that He provide these writings with a special power, alongside a clarity that no book written by a human intellect can boast of. He had to place within them a strength—an understanding that is well-designed not only to instruct, but also to move, to captivate, and to convince in the most vivid way: a strength that penetrates the understanding and, through the understanding, directs the will toward obedience. **That understanding is thus called "enlightened" in the darkness in which we are now born,** which learns the law and the will of the Creator from the divine books and—through the power of the Holy Spirit, which is united with their teachings—vividly and correctly grasps where the desires of the will should be directed and according to which

<column-break/>

rules the entire conduct of a person must be arranged if they intend to attain the possession of the future goods of salvation. Here, the word "enlightened" is taken in its strict, proper, and most common sense as found in the Holy Scripture itself. Yet, for whoever wishes, it is also permitted to call those "enlightened" in a lesser and broader sense who merely allow the power of the Holy Scripture to clearly instruct them, but who will not grant its capacity to convincingly move the understanding and the soul any room within their hearts. One cannot deny that a person who does not wish to be an obstacle to himself, and who is not naturally unskilled at grasping and reflecting upon things, can obtain thorough and clear concepts of the doctrines that everyone must know to be saved from the divine books. And what hinders us from **calling a person who has come this far enlightened—indeed, enlightened by God?** He is called enlightened because he knows more than a merely rational person can know and recognize. And he is called "enlightened by God" because the book which made him so wise comes from God and was composed by men whom God moved and preserved from error. **I take the liberty of using the word "enlightened" here in this sense.** I cannot view people here as truly <note>In this context, "truly enlightened" implies a spiritual transformation where the heart follows the head.</note> enlightened. If I did so, I could not accuse their will of any spiritual bondage. A rightly enlightened understanding simultaneously sets the will in motion to follow the light. Freedom. 2 Corinthians 3:17. <note>original: "2 Kor. III. 17." And it is presupposed that when a true and certain knowledge is lacking in the understanding, no true and rightful freedom can exist in the will. I must therefore imagine here a person whom a revelation has clarified and enlightened in a certain way. And the question I have to decide is this: **Whether a person, to whom the will of the Highest is known, possesses enough strength that he can adapt his will to it and carry out its conclusions?**

<margin>1.)</margin> A soul that wishes to boast of such power must first be able to say of itself with truth that it is never inclined to undertake or desire anything without first hearing the opinion of the Highest concerning it. It
<margin>2.)</margin> must further be able to say of itself that it always feels a joy and desire within itself to perform and observe what it has judged to be in accordance with the will of the Lord, and to reject that which conflicts with the order
<margin>3.)</margin> and intentions of God. It must finally be able to say of itself that

<column-break/>

nothing stands in its way of obeying this desire, and that its capacity to worship God perfectly through thoughts, words, and works is just as strong as the longing to make itself pleasing to Him. It will be seen, without my reminding, that these things are so interconnected that all fall away at once if only one is touched and removed. Suppose someone has the capacity to arrange the movements of their soul and all their actions according to the rule of divine law: Would this capacity not be dead, ineffective, and useless if the desire and joy to make use of it were lacking? Suppose that someone has the joy and desire to sacrifice their entire life to the Lord: Would this joy serve for anything if the strength were lacking to obey the impulses toward the good? A capacity without the longing to use it is exactly like a body that is strong in itself but lacks a soul; and a desire that is linked to no power to act and work appears to me like a soul dwelling in a ruined and unusable body. Suppose finally that joy and the capacity to act are present, but one takes away the resolution to decide and begin nothing without the counsel, assistance, and consent of an understanding enlightened by God: To what purpose would these two things serve? Will they not always be misused and applied against the divine intention? Think of a traveler who wishes to arrive soon where he is sent, and has a capable vehicle in his power, but diligently refuses to look at the signposts that were set up for his and other travelers' benefit—

Those who have been prepared from youth by a careful hand to be <term>vessels of honor<note>A biblical allusion to Romans 9:21, referring to individuals chosen or refined for noble and holy purposes.</note></term> in the house of God, and who have been most thoroughly instructed in the will and order of their Creator, scarcely feel any impulse to determine their thoughts, actions, and intentions according to the divine rule that has been taught to them. Our will, in a word, uses its senses as advisors and regards the knowledge that comes from God as a light intended to serve no further purpose than to illuminate an empty chamber. One searches in vain for the joy and desire to fulfill and carry out what the enlightened understanding has designated as good and pleasing to God. Our natural inclinations stand in constant enmity with divine orders and commands. And from where, then, should the longing arise to align oneself with God? # Concerning the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

The frequent repetition of actual sin formerly brought you so far that you had no desire, no ability remaining to undertake anything laudable and virtuous. You did nothing but sin, and this habit of doing evil finally deprived you of all ability to do good. Can we be satisfied with this explanation? We admit that if the first passage of *Paul* <note>Referring to Ephesians 2:1</note> stood alone, it would be difficult for us to reject these interpreters <note>meaning those who argue sin is only a habit</note> based on those words alone. The words can support this interpretation; and whoever has read some of the ancient sages can bring forth passages from them to confirm it. However, the second passage, which is somewhat clearer than the first, removes all doubt and supports those who claim that the internal corruption of man is the cause of spiritual death and inability. *Paul* calls that "the uncircumcision of the flesh" <note>original: *Vorhaut des Fleisches*</note> in the latter passage, which he called "sin" in the first.

<column-break/>

Is it believable that he would have designated actual sins with this name and compared them to a foreskin? In what way do the evil deeds of men resemble a foreskin? The foreskin <term>uncircumcision: a biblical metaphor for the raw, unrefined natural state of a person before being "cut" or purified by God</term> is something natural that belongs to the body of man and cannot be separated from it except through force and effort. And sin, therefore, which can be viewed as a foreskin and called a foreskin, must likewise stick in the nature of man and be so inherent to him that it requires effort to separate it from him. It seems to me that we have the greatest reason to seek this teaching in the passages of *Paul*: The sin that is born with us just like a foreskin, the corruption that dwells in our nature, makes us just as incapable and unfit to think or perform anything good as the loss of life makes a man unable to move his limbs or to either desire or accomplish anything.

The inclinations and desires that have their seat in the will are just as little pure and correct as the will itself to which they belong. Who knows more of a pure longing to please him and to make oneself daily more perfect? Who knows more of a desire to serve others—who are by nature similar to him—and to be helpful toward a righteous happiness and contentment? Who, finally, knows of a right yearning to properly build and strengthen the general welfare of the world and of mankind?

One will gather from what follows that this small effort we have applied to firmly establish the concept of evil and good desires was not applied without cause or benefit.

## On the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

Z 3
<meta>catchword: set</meta>

...given for the attainment of happiness. Consequently, desires must be directed according to this, if they are to be called good. Suppose the thing for which the will yearns is good: if the desire is either greater or smaller than what human happiness and one's specific condition requires, then it cannot be called proper or good. This already shows us that it is necessary to expand the concept of good and evil desires. By virtue of this observation, we must say: a **good desire** is a longing for something inherently good and useful, which aligns with the purpose for which man was created and his specific circumstances, and is neither greater nor lesser than that purpose and the specific state of man requires. 

An **evil desire**, on the other hand, must be called such a longing that desires things which are inherently good in a greater or lesser degree than they are necessary. Experience daily assures us that countless things, which are in themselves excellent and useful, can be applied to a poor use. This same experience convinces us that certain things, which are inherently harmful and disadvantageous to the world, must sometimes be desired so that a greater good may be gained or preserved. Once again, this moves us to add a supplement to the description of good and evil desires. 

**A desire for a good thing becomes evil and reprehensible if the one in whom it dwells is determined to use it for their own harm or the harm of others.** Can one praise the wish of a person who longs for wine and food for the purpose of burying their reason beneath a mountain of them and lulling the active spirit to 

<column-break/>

sleep? Or who, for that end, sharpens their reason so that an innocent enemy might be overthrown? A longing for something inherently evil must be called praiseworthy if it is joined with the intention of ridding oneself and the world of a great evil. 

Can one blame a magistrate <note>The German *Obrigkeit* refers to those in positions of legal or governing authority.</note> who wishes for and promotes the death of a highwayman, or scold a father who, for the sake of better health, leaves his child to the "unmercifulness" of a surgeon? <note>Before modern anesthesia, surgery was a traumatic and painful ordeal, often described in terms of cruelty or lack of mercy.</note> Now everything will be brought together that belongs to a complete concept of good and evil desires. 

A **good desire** is a wish of the soul to partake in and enjoy something inherently useful, insofar as it is necessary for the preservation of our true peace and happiness <term>happiness: translated from 'Glückseligkeit,' which implies a state of blessedness or spiritual well-being</term>. An **evil desire** is an impulse of the soul that either yearns for truly harmful things or desires useful and good things either excessively or for a sinful purpose. One will perceive from what follows that this small effort we have applied to establish the concept of evil and good desires was not used without cause or benefit.

<margin>p. 453. // // // // // x</margin>
To know what kind of desires must exist in man if he were pure and innocent, it is necessary to take man himself into consideration and to contemplate the purpose for which he was formed. A human being is a being joined together from two parts: a piece of artfully formed and arranged earth <note>A reference to the biblical creation of the body from the dust of the ground.</note>, and a rational spirit, which was placed for a time into a world filled with many of its own kind...

The faculty of desire is in itself like a weapon <note>original: "Gewehr"; in this period, the term could mean any tool or weapon used for defense or action.</note> which can harm or benefit, and be used well or poorly. —sists, and is to make both happy according to their kind and nature, must arrange its desires according to the state of both and not forget the one while caring for the other. He who extends this care so far that he thereby exhausts the powers of the body and disrupts the dwelling of the spirit, violates the order of the Most High and makes himself guilty of folly. He is rational who omits nothing that can preserve the structure of a frail and fragile body. He is rightly called senseless who so nourishes and tends his hut <note>A common metaphor in this era for the physical body as a temporary dwelling for the soul.</note> that the spirit within it sleeps and lies numbed rather than living and working. (IV) A rational being consisting of two parts, one of which is far nobler, greater, and more excellent than the other, one being immortal and the other mortal, and one of which is capable of a far purer happiness than the other, must direct its desires with a much stronger zeal toward the things that are advantageous to the former than toward what may benefit the latter. It senses that it feels displeasure from things that can damage or destroy its earthly dwelling, and pleasure from those things that can give it duration and firmness. # Of the Natural Corruption of Humanity

...end would the wise Creator have otherwise united body and spirit in such a way that a movement which destroys or sickens the body also saddens and torments the spirit, while another impulse, which preserves and improves the body, encourages and refreshes the spirit? It is therefore not only natural, but also ordained by **GOD**, that such a being should seek pleasure <note>original: "Wollust"; in this 18th-century theological context, this refers to physical well-being or sensory delight rather than modern "lust."</note> in a certain measure, flee from pain, long for pleasant sensations, and bear an aversion to painful movements.

<insert>A spirit does not sin when it desires, in the proper measure, those things which belong to the comfort, rest, and pleasure of its body.</insert>

These desires agree with the intention of the Highest, who instructs us through the implanted instincts of nature that He does not wish the bond of the soul and the body to be severed before the time He has appointed. (VI) Where two things that are entirely different by nature are linked together, cases must occasionally arise in which the happiness and welfare of both parts cannot be maintained at the same time. It is impossible that an eternal and imperishable happiness can always be sought in such a way that earthly and perishable happiness should never suffer some loss thereby. It is impossible that an earthly and human pleasure can always be maintained in such a way that the hope for an unchangeable fortune is never diminished by it. It is impossible to lead an immortal spirit, which exists in the fellowship of a mortal body, toward glory in such a way that this body always retains its complete well-being. It is impossible to keep a corruptible body in constant rest

<column-break/>

without ever disturbing the well-being and contentment of the spirit created for eternity, which is paired with it. What does a rational being do in such cases, which are not rare? It is bound to stifle the desires that aim at the preservation and welfare of its inferior part <note>The "inferior part" refers to the physical body, which the author considers secondary to the eternal soul.</note> and to maintain only the inclinations that can make its noble and immortal part perfect and happy. It is obligated to forget that from a certain perspective it belongs to a world that is visible, and it must turn its wishes alone toward a state in which a short and fleeting pain can be repaid in an infinite way. (VII) A rational being that lives in a world populated by many of its own kind, who are all bound to a common purpose in a certain way, must direct a portion of its desires toward the best of this great society of which it is a member.

# The First Chapter

### On the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

The perfection of the understanding consists in knowledge and wisdom. The will is happy and perfect only when its inclinations and desires are ordered according to the will of the Creator. From this, we understand what our spirit would primarily crave and wish for if nothing were lacking. It would wish to ever increase its knowledge, its light, and its wisdom. It would strive to more and more perceive the nature of its Creator and the things that come from Him, the connection of all the works of the Highest, and the intentions and plans of infinite wisdom. It would be concerned with nothing so much as how to avoid the punishment of error and how to prepare a peaceful dwelling for truth within itself. It would willingly take upon itself a physical discomfort, a troublesome movement in its blood and vital spirits <note>original: "Lebens-Säften"; referring to the "vital juices" or humors that early modern science believed governed the body's health and temperament.</note>, or unpleasant labor, if these could serve as a means to fill it with a clear and pure knowledge. It would, in a word, eagerly desire to become constantly more enlightened and wise. *Just as inclined it would have to be to increase the perfection of its other power, the will.* It would never cease to long for the agreement of its own will with the will of its Author. It would have to examine the latter, and seek to guide and govern the former as the latter required. There would have to be—if I may speak with the Scripture—a constant drive toward holiness and righteousness, and an everlasting longing within it to become holy, even as He is holy <note>A reference to the biblical command in Leviticus and 1 Peter to "be holy, for I am holy."</note> to whom it owes life and breath. And the more the light of the understanding would increase,

<column-break/>

the more this order of the will would grow. What would a world be like that was filled with spirits in whom such noble and pure desires reigned? Would it not be more than a paradise? Must not the sketch that the imagination can make of it already enchant the spirit and awaken a longing for it? Are these noble desires within us? We either do not know ourselves, or we must answer that these blessed impulses are not present. Where are the people who have brought with them a pure desire to chase after wisdom and to take part in the clarity that surrounds the origin of all things, *our GOD?* Where are the souls who, above all else, long to enter into a friendship with truth and wisdom, *and who would rather afflict the handful of dust <note>The "handful of dust" is a common theological metaphor for the mortal, physical body.</note> with which they are surrounded than neglect their true advantage?* Where are the people who labor to please their Creator *and to make themselves worthy of His grace through a zeal to serve Him?* *Who thinks of light and wisdom? Who respects righteousness and holiness?* Our desires are directed solely toward the body and the lusts that the senses, together with the imagination, can provide for us. Our inclinations have no other purpose than to awaken a brief pleasure in our lowest and least significant part <note>The physical body, considered secondary to the eternal soul.</note> and to bring about vain and foolish ideas in our brains. The best and noblest desires that should exist in a rational being consisting of body and spirit are gone and lost. They must have been there once. Whoever would deny this would offend the majesty of the Creator and the Highest and purest

...maintain. The desire to serve the world, the love for the fatherland, and the concern for the best interests of human society are nothing but beautiful names with which we cover our zeal for our own honor, ease, and abundance, which alone animates the deeds of men. The true desire to promote God's intentions in the world and to maintain and build His kingdom here below was lost along with our original innocence <note>In Christian theology, "original innocence" refers to the state of humanity before the Fall of Man, when desires were supposedly pure and directed toward God.</note>. Those who are so industrious, so heated, so eager, and so untiring in serving the world would be colder than ice if the world they wish to serve were not a land that promised them a satisfaction of their lusts, or if the hope they have for something great, pleasant, and respectable were to die out. Corrupt people! What are we? Deceivers of ourselves and others. People who can easily distinguish between appearance and truth in their peers

<column-break/>

and yet use the very thing they hate in others to make themselves beloved and respected. We are vessels filled with clay, dust, and filth, and yet we wish to occupy the place in the house of the Most High <note>original: "Hause des Höchsten"; likely an allusion to 2 Timothy 2:20-21, which discusses "vessels of honor" and "vessels of dishonor" in a great house.</note> that is dedicated to the most useful and indispensable tools. Our best desires, which should bear the image of their Creator within us as rational creatures, are lost. No one seeks to please God anymore, to sanctify their spirit, or *to expand and maintain the kingdom of the Most High.* The lowliest desires remain. *We look toward our bodies, toward the lust of our senses, and toward the pleasures of our imagination.* In a certain way, these inclinations might not be punishable in themselves: however, they have fallen completely into disorder and corrupt more than they improve or build up.

### §. XII.

There still remain within the souls of men certain desires that are not, in and of themselves or in their nature, punishable or sinful. We possess desires to maintain and refresh our bodies, to please our minds, and to propagate our kind. Who would claim these stirrings within us are evil or hated by the Most High? Most people possess a longing to acquire love and respect among others and to live free from want and misery. In this, too, there is nothing impure if viewed on its own and considered alongside the nature of the society God has planted here. There are inclinations toward certain trades, duties, ways of life, and customs within people. These arise, it seems to me, from a wise arrangement of the Creator, who has provided the members of His city here below <note>The "City of God" or "City of the Most High" refers to the spiritual community of mankind under divine governance.</note> with various gifts and stirrings...

### Explanation.

The desires that still dwell within man are not viewed in the same way by everyone. Many condemn them altogether and speak as if the spirit, which the Lord breathed into the first man, had departed after the Fall <note>In Christian theology, the "Fall" refers to the transition of the first humans from a state of innocent obedience to God to a state of guilty disobedience.</note> and a completely different soul, created by an evil being, had taken its place. Others can see nothing unholy in the inclinations with which we are born and are ready to assert that everything that is natural is also good and just. Neither side has ever been able to find so many friends and followers that their opinions became the doctrines of faith for great nations and countries. And perhaps both parties speak more sharply than they actually think. Most have chosen a middle path and have held the desires of nature to be partly good and partly evil. However, in the writings of those who hold this opinion, not everything is set down so orderly and clearly that one finds no cause for doubt or guesswork. I might almost say that for a long time people have believed they have a right to speak of human desires in a disordered and confused way, tearing down with one hand what they have built with the other. I do not know if I shall avoid these errors which I believe I have found in others. It may be that I fall into even greater ones. The matter is difficult: Who can fathom the human heart? <note>original: "Wer kan des Menschen Herz ergründen?"; a common theological reflection based on Jeremiah 17:9.</note> Yet this very difficulty of the matter can serve as an excuse for a mediocre mind among fair-minded people, should it happen to go astray or fail in the order of its thoughts.

<column-break/>

In my opinion, one must distinguish in certain desires and inclinations of men that still exist between what comes from God and His providence and what the Fall and sin have added. The origin of certain desires comes from the Author of Nature. His wisdom had the holiest and wisest intentions when He planted them into the souls of men. The Fall caused that which was good in itself and intended for a holy purpose to now be evil, sinful, and impure. Man is created to propagate his species, to live in the society of others, and to fulfill the intentions of the Creator. What could have been achieved of these things if no desires or inclinations at all had dwelt in his soul? The Lord, therefore, had to provide His rational creature with certain drives and impulses as soon as He formed him. Of these drives, the most noble have vanished: yet some are still there which, considered in themselves, cannot be called the vices or blemishes of the children of Adam <note>The "children of Adam" is a traditional phrase referring to all of humanity as descendants of the first man.</note>.

We all desire to turn away pain, displeasure, and sadness from ourselves. We all seek to prolong our lives as long as possible. We all feel a fear of the destruction and dissolution of our being. We all wish to refresh the body through nourishment, food, and drink. We all dread hunger, nakedness, cold, thirst, and other evils. Whoever considers these desires within themselves and compares them with the nature of man will—unless some false delusion blinds them or some disease has struck the brain—consider them good and necessary. 

Man is bound, by virtue of an internal drive, to preserve the bond by which God has linked an immortal spirit with a part of animated and skillfully arranged clay <note>This refers to the biblical account of man being formed from the dust of the ground (clay) and receiving the breath of life.</note> for as long as it can be done. Body and spirit are united in a wonderful way so that man might not neglect this connection. That which harms the body awakens a sorrowful movement in the spirit. That which strengthens and preserves the body creates a pleasant sensation in the soul. That which pleases, gladdens, and cheers the soul, and that which delights the imagination through the senses, usually gives the body an added measure of strength, power, and vivacity. 

Was not Jacob, though worn out by age, strong enough to travel to Egypt when his spirit became alive through the news of Joseph's life? Genesis 45:27–28. <note>original: "1 B. Moſ. Does not a person almost die themselves when their friend closes their eyes in death? Are there not enough examples of people whom a sorrowful message has laid in the grave? A creature so wonderfully formed and made by its Creator <term>Urheber: literally 'Author' or 'Originator,' referring to God</term> must necessarily desire that which can refresh the spirit and the body, and must abhor that which can bring torment and unrest to one or the other part of its being. 

In doing this, the creature does nothing other than follow the will of the Creator, who wishes to see its nature preserved for a certain time. It would sin if it tortured itself without necessity and thereby became guilty of its own downfall. A certain society of Christians <note>The author likely refers to ascetic monastic orders or extreme Pietist sects that practiced self-mortification—the act of causing oneself physical pain for spiritual discipline.</note> may see how they shall one day answer for it, when they advise those seeking holiness to destroy and torment the casing of the spirit <note>A metaphorical term for the physical body.</note> and to fill the imagination with nothing but unpleasant and terrifying images.

And for what purpose was the soul granted the power to draw from them a pleasure that renews and enlivens the whole man?

The two sexes, which are necessary for the propagation of mankind, were already present before the desire for the forbidden fruit contaminated the human heart. Both were already provided with those same wisely and artistically arranged organs of generation <term>Gliedern der Zeugung: reproductive organs</term>, the contemplation of which now fills the best researchers of nature with reverent wonder. The bond that unites the two kinds of humans for this end—so that they may live more happily and multiply themselves—was already woven and sealed by the Most High Himself at the time when man was still full of obedience and love toward his Creator. These stirrings, therefore, of which we speak, would have also shown themselves in a certain way in the state of purity and innocence. How, then, can they be forbidden and impure in themselves? One may choose whichever of these inventions one wishes, but one will eventually find oneself forced to encounter one of two of the greatest follies. By this I mean: one must either claim that a complete transformation of the human body and spirit occurred and their entire essence was overturned as soon as they tasted the forbidden fruit, or one must admit that nothing of the ways, intentions, and perfections of the Creator can be inferred from the contemplation of man and of all nature. The former is absurd and nonsensical; the latter will be very pleasing to those who would like to see all natural and revealed religion <note>"Revealed religion" refers to truths known through scripture/revelation, as opposed to "natural religion" known through reason and observation of the world.</note> overthrown and abolished.

The spirit of some is so great that it encompasses, as it were, the whole world, and wishes to make everyone who dwells as a rational creature on the face of the earth into their friends or admirers. Who can count the paths upon which the human race divides itself to obtain esteem, name, love, and reputation? There is, however, a single source from which all these so diverse thoughts and movements flow. The greatest part of mankind wants to be liked, honored, and highly esteemed. The longing for the love of other people is not evil in itself. <margin>p. 243.</margin> *Love is the bond by which the society* of men is held together and strengthened. God, therefore, who wills the unity and connection of His rational creatures—which is the means of their preservation—must have endowed their hearts with an inclination to attract the love of their equals to themselves. *The love of others can be acquired through nothing but kindness, service, and beneficence. I speak of the desire in itself and separate from it all imperfections and vices <note>The author is making a distinction between the pure, God-given "desire for honor" and the "vice of pride" (Superbia) that often corrupts it in fallen humanity.</note> that make it misshapen and sometimes abominable. Who would want to burden themselves to ease the trouble of life for another whose misfortunes the world views as just punishments for his folly and lack of understanding? No one can, in a word, have much hope for the assistance, friendship, and help of other people except the one of whom the world believes he is worthy that another should take a burden upon himself for his sake. Must this not have moved the wise Creator to endow men, who are to live in a society and preserve themselves, with a longing for a good opinion and reputation? And can he be called sinful who, in a lawful manner, seeks a means that promises him from the abundance of other people that which he and his own might lack? His lowliness and the contempt in which he is held close the door to those who possess the means to help. Has the Lord not created us to help bear one another’s burdens? Are we not here to serve and help one another? Can a desire then be displeasing to Him, or can an impulse have an evil origin, which, viewed in itself, is conducive to this purpose? I will pass over various other points that serve as proof of this matter, in order to set them forth and present them properly in another place that is more convenient.

It appears as though it were necessary that in a large and extensive society, which is to remain in a constant state of cohesion, a certain number of people must be provided with the desire to collect more than they need. How soon would a community fall apart if it were composed of people where no one could be made happier, more content, or more peaceful by another? How little love, esteem, friendship, and order would dwell in a gathering where one could perceive no <term>inequality of status</term> <note>The "Great Chain of Being" philosophy: the idea that social hierarchy is a natural and necessary reflection of divine order.</note>, of fortune, and of other things? Whoever grants this will, if I am not mistaken, have to confess that <term>Providence</term> <note>God's intervention and guidance in the world.</note> must have placed in certain people an impulse to enrich themselves and to acquire more fortune than they need, so that they might come to the aid of the indigence of their fellow members. ### Section XIII.

However, the Fall <note>The "Fall of Man," referring to the biblical loss of innocence in the Garden of Eden.</note> has entirely defiled these inherently innocent desires and thrown them into disorder. If we have claimed that a portion of the desires still dwelling in humanity are in themselves blameless and useful for achieving the wise intentions of our Creator, then we have at the same time admitted that the form in which they now appear is hideous and displeasing to the Most High. The work of **GOD** is corrupted. The beauty and innocence of our impulses is not merely stained, but lost. [since] this purpose exists, so must the desires and natural impulses of the same be constituted. It is self-evident that these particular intentions of **GOD** in such a great multitude of people must be manifold and very diverse: And from this, it is simultaneously clear that men must be differently minded and of different natures. Imagine an extensive society whose members all possess the same inclinations and desires, and judge whether the same could remain in a constant connection and union and work toward a general purpose. Where there are many and various intentions, which all converge into one great and general purpose, there must necessarily be found a kind of adversity and strife. Let us remember fire and water, heat and cold, light and darkness. Are these things not the standard images used to represent the greatest discord and disunity? # Chapter One

...to choose damnable desires to reach their goal, making the desires themselves completely sinful and impure.

A desire that is not evil in itself becomes punishable and unjust when it oversteps its bound, and is greater or smaller than what the purpose for which it was given requires. This is understood without need for proof. A ruler <note>original: "Regent" — referring here to a sovereign or governing authority.</note> gives his subjects weapons to protect their lives against a foreign power. Whoever among them forgets this intent and either allows themselves to be mutilated without resistance, or uses his weapons against his friend and fellow citizen, becomes worthy of punishment. God has implanted in us certain inclinations and desires that align with the purposes for which he formed us and placed us in the world. If the measure of these desires is arranged by us as these purposes require, then we have no cause for unrest over the desires themselves. If we let them wander further into excess, or if we suppress them when they should act, then we destroy the work and the intentions of the Most High and become guilty before his judgment seat. And where is a person on this earth who can boast that their desires observe the order prescribed by God, or are governed by them as the counsel of the Creator intended? Are not our *passions like a stormy sea that can never stay within its shores?* Is not everything incorrect and disorderly among us? Are we not either insatiable in our inclinations, or completely inept and perverse in the arrangement of them? Do we not immediately crave something 

<column-break/>

else, once we have received that for which we have long yearned? Does not a new hunger immediately appear when that which has tormented us for several years has barely been satisfied? When do we stand still? When do we stop our desires? When do we say, it is enough? The desire to live is a natural impulse from which no one can free themselves, except those whose reason has been displaced by a disease of the brain. God has provided us with this desire so that we might think of the preservation of our being. We step far beyond this goal. We want to live even when our death could increase the glory of God and establish the welfare of many people. We want to live even when the Lord commands us to leave this stage <note>original: "Schauplatz" — literally "show-place," a common 18th-century metaphor for the world as a theater or stage of action.</note> to others. If the death of many people could prolong our lives, we would gladly buy our preservation through the ruin of others. And we would watch with joy the outcome of a fire that should consume half the world, if we were assured that we alone would rise rejuvenated from the ashes. *The desire for food and drink is natural:* The wish to provide comfort to one's body and some delight to one's spirit is permitted. But how immoderately do these passions behave in corrupted man? Out of a thousand people, there is hardly one who does not take twice as much nourishment as the maintenance of his body requires. And where do we find those of whom it can be said that they maintain measure and order in the pleasures necessary for the refreshment of the powers of the body and the mind? I will take this opportunity to submit a thought to the judgment of reasonable people—one that occurred to me when I read certain proofs for the **immortality of our souls**. Our desires are never quiet but always in motion. They always demand something new. They climb far

<column-break/>

higher than human strength can reach, and would gladly claim for themselves a happiness that no finite creature can receive. Scarcely is one pleasure over when plans are already made for a new one, in which one imagines more satisfaction. And scarcely has one tasted something of this new delight when a longing for another is ignited. Scarcely has one attained this honor when one yearns for a greater one. Our desires are, in a word, without measure or end. Some take this as a proof to demonstrate the immortality of our souls. A spirit, it is said, that has infinite desires cannot be transitory and mortal. A being that is never satisfied with what it has, and always desires more or something else, must in a certain way participate in infinity and can therefore surely expect to last forever. I doubt the strength of this proof very much. The constant restlessness of our desires, the violent and insatiable longing of our spirit, seems to me rather a **sign of the decay of our nature** <note>The author argues that restlessness is a symptom of the "Fall of Man" rather than a natural attribute of an immortal soul.</note> than a mark of immortality. Our spirit, although it is immortal, remains by its nature finite. A finite and limited being must, in my opinion, if it is in its proper order, also be provided with such desires that harmonize with its nature and are thus likewise finite. Infinite desires in a finite and limited being are, as far as I can grasp, an **imperfection** that must arise from a cause other than a wise and holy Creator. # The First Chapter

...unites things that are **contradictory**. What conflicts more with one another than the finite and the infinite? Where such a contradiction exists, there must necessarily be a cause of constant unrest and perpetual discontent. Is it not a misery, a vexation, and a misfortune to always strive—indeed, to be *compelled* to strive—after an infinite good, and yet have no hope of ever attaining possession of it, because the nature in which this longing dwells is not capable of any infinite good? Even in that eternity which will unite us with God, we can promise ourselves no other happiness than one that is appropriate to our nature and the powers of our souls, which have their measured limits. And if, accordingly, the infinite and immeasurable desires that trouble us here were to accompany us even to the throne of the Highest, then surely that same unrest which makes this life wearisome would follow us there, and we would always desire more than we could receive. In the state of innocence <note>Referring to the theological state of humanity before the Fall of Man.</note>, the desires of man were, without dispute, neither more intense nor greater than the condition of his nature and his peace allowed. Our first mother <note>Eve</note> laid the foundation for her misfortune and that of all her descendants when she permitted them to go beyond the goal, and let herself be persuaded by the serpent to desire a perfect equality with God, and thus to crave a greater good than she could hope for. **Genesis 3:5**. From that time on, by virtue of the corruption that has come upon us through her, we wish for more than we can obtain, and we do not know how to find the reins by which our restless and unruly impulses must be restrained

<column-break/>

and held back. Grace, which sanctifies us, wishes to lead us back to that lost moderation and order, and to enclose the extravagant inclinations of man within certain limits. And would not that man be blessed who reached the point where he sought and desired nothing more than what is permitted for him to crave and possible for him to obtain? Do not all sensible people think of means by which they may reach such a state, and thereby become partakers of the peace and contentment that we lack here? Therefore, if the proof of the **immortality of the soul**, which we are dealing with here, were firm and correct <note>The author is critiquing the common 18th-century philosophical argument that because humans desire the infinite, they must possess an infinite/immortal soul.</note>, then the first man would have lacked a great reason by which he could have recognized the imperishability of his spirit: And the more we grew in holiness and renewal, the smaller the natural conviction of the eternal life of our souls would have to become in us. I do not present these thoughts as certain and infallible. Those who possess more knowledge than I may be the judges of how far they are valid. Perhaps I do not rightly understand the opinion of those who consider the insatiable longing of our souls to be a sign of their immortality. I and others with me will be indebted to them for a kindness if they would explain their proof more clearly and thereby resolve these doubts.

# Of the Natural Corruption of Men.

...conduct of men, which in themselves appear most innocent, one will necessarily find them to seem perfectly evil and punishable. What comes from God regarding our <margin>//</margin> desires was granted for the <margin>//</margin> purpose that we should extend the honor of our <margin>//</margin> Creator, preserve ourselves, <margin>//</margin> become useful to other men, and <margin>//</margin> promote and build the general good of the whole world, <margin>//</margin> as much as is within us. No men think of these intentions except those whom the Lord has seized and sanctified for His service through a supernatural power. The rest contemplate nothing but themselves and their own pleasure: and this very pleasure is for the most part only an illusion and more harmful than useful. It is true, the world draws advantage from the desires of men, and our inclinations in a certain way hold together the bond of this great society that lives upon the earth. But no one envisions this advantage when following their own desires, and therefore the good that arises from it cannot be credited to them. It is the Providence of God that governs all things so holily and wisely that our disordered and corrupt inclinations coincidentally become a cause of much good and, against our will and opinion, must serve the advancement of His righteous and partly unsearchable intentions. Without sin, we could seek a certain measure of delight and enjoyment if we had the intention of making body and spirit more capable thereby of honoring God through our labors and helping our brothers. We could strive for a certain standing un-

<column-break/>

-der men, if we did so for the purpose of becoming more skillful at preventing evil, protecting the distressed, and assisting the weak and powerless. We could concern ourselves with the wealth and goods of this world if we had the intention of using our abundance to remedy the want of the needy and to assist those who are held back by necessity and poverty from using and applying the talent <note>original: "Pfund" — literally 'pound,' referring to the 'Parable of the Talents' or 'Pounds' in the Bible, where a master entrusts money to servants to invest.</note> that the Lord has entrusted to them. Who can boast that they desire pleasure, comfort, honor, and abundance for this reason? Does not our own heart tell us that we think only of ourselves, and desire what we wish and seek only to satisfy our ill nature <note>original: "Unart" — a term for a bad habit or a corrupted nature.</note> and either to despise others, or even to rule over and oppress them?

A threefold main purpose is commonly attributed to all the desires of men. We long, it is said, either for a pleasure of the flesh, or for honor, or finally for possessions and wealth. There are thus three main desires or three main vices: the plague of lust <term>Lust-Seuche: carnal desire viewed as a contagious or destructive passion</term>, ambition, and the craving for money. All other vices and desires stem from these three. This division is justified partly through experience and partly through the well-known passage of Saint John, 1 John 2:16. *All that is in the world, namely the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but of the world.* (*) I venture, both

# On the Natural Corruption of Mankind

...our soul alone, or our imagination, or our senses, or some of these parts together, please and amuse us. *There are, first, desires that aim at a pleasure and gratification of the soul.* The spirit can be delighted and pleased in more than one way. And just as the ways our soul can be delighted in itself are manifold, so too are the various types of desires belonging to this category. Cajus <note>Cajus and Titius are traditional placeholder names, like "John Doe," used in philosophical and legal examples.</note> collects an uncountable multitude of books and does not know how to satisfy this craving. What is his intention? He wishes to awaken a constant <term>pleasure (Wollust)</term> in his soul. <note>In this 18th-century context, "Wollust" refers to intense satisfaction or delight of any kind, not necessarily sexual lust.</note> His spirit finds a delight when he can see and compare the different opinions and thoughts of the greatest people, when he notices here the errors of men and there the certain and firm steps of a wise and practiced mind, when he perceives the innumerable ways of presenting the same thing in so many books, and distinguishes that which man knows from that which he does not. Cajus wishes to awaken and maintain these pleasant sensations in his soul. Titius feels an unchangeable drive for silence and solitude in his heart. What does this drive aim for? For a mere pleasure of the spirit. His soul is, I know not how, refreshed when it can rightly observe the ways of men, their useless labors and worries, the value of their inventions, their vain pleasures, and either laugh at or mourn them. Society and the noise of the world are the reason that his spirit cannot enjoy this pleasure. He therefore flees the world and only occasionally enters the gatherings of men to fetch new supplies for the pleasure he wishes to provide for his soul.

From this comes the unquenchable thirst for honor and reputation. ## Chapter One

...regarding this common division, as well as the proof thereof which is taken from Saint John <note>original: "heiligen Johanne". This likely refers to 1 John 2:16, a common theological source for categorizing human desires into the "lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, and pride of life."</note>, I have something to remark. Everyone is free to accept or reject my thoughts: and for that reason, I shall not cease to honor the merits of those who have approved this division until now, because I believe it could be improved in some respects.

**In my opinion, all our desires have only one main purpose. We seek all our pleasure and enjoyment, but in different ways.** I take these words in a broad sense and understand by them not only actual pleasure, but also a freedom from displeasure, from pain, and from dissatisfaction. We work for this reason alone: so that we may bring about pleasant sensations for ourselves and, once we have obtained them, establish ourselves in the enjoyment of the same. No one would desire honor, wealth, or any other good if he did not believe that the use or possession of these things would make him a participant in a <term>pleasure (Wollust)</term>, a delight, a satisfaction, or an enjoyment. <note>The author uses "Wollust" in the 18th-century sense of "intense delight" or "gratification," which can be intellectual or spiritual, rather than just physical lust.</note> Our imagination represents to us that sweet and refreshing movements and sensations will arise and remain in our body or spirit once we have taken possession of this or that thing. This representation sets the whole person in motion. **We desire first. Afterward, we think of the means to satisfy this desire.** Once we have found the means, we use them with zeal to achieve our purpose. The more vivid the representation of the imagination is regarding the pleasure we expect to obtain,

<column-break/>

the more violently we wrestle, strive, and worry. And therefore, the desires and <term>passions (Affecten)</term> <note>From the Latin "affectus," referring to powerful emotions or states of mind that move a person to action.</note> are never stronger, more violent, or more constant in any person than in those gifted with an extensive, fruitful, and vivid imagination. We are capable of a threefold pleasure: **a pleasure of the soul, a pleasure of the imagination, and a pleasure of the senses.** Whoever wishes to divide pleasure only twofold and count the pleasure of the imagination as part of the pleasure of the spirit remains in agreement with me on the matter itself and only changes the manner of presentation. And whoever even wishes to say there is only a single kind of pleasure—that the spirit is gladdened solely through the senses and the imagination—I have no quarrel with him either. He need only grant me that the spirit can be gratified in three ways: **through itself, through the senses, and through the imagination**, and I am satisfied. Perhaps no man lives who does not simultaneously wish for and demand this threefold kind of pleasure, albeit with unequal zeal. However, just as people are very different in body and spirit, some are more inclined to this kind of pleasure and delight, and others to another. And one not infrequently encounters people who are so strongly ruled by the desire for a single one of these types of pleasure that one must almost doubt whether any longing for the others is present in them at all. I will not enter into this investigation now, but rather divide the desires that trouble us according to these different types of pleasure for which we are suited.

John forbids, unless I am entirely mistaken, the most prominent vices and evil customs that were then in vogue among the pagans. The pagans were devoted to drunkenness, unchastity, and other vices that are pleasing to the flesh or the body. These the Apostle calls the "lust of the flesh." One sought to surpass the other in this regard. These so beloved amusements served the corruption of the world. They maintained cruelty, unchastity, laziness, and other harmful vices in the hearts of the spectators.

# The First Chapter

## §. XIV.

This misery of our nature is all the more to be pitied because we lack the means to conquer it or even to weaken it. In certain people, **reason** can sometimes bring about a kind of standstill and take away some of the power of conflicting and restless desires. Others can be brought to labor and zeal by the **Law of GOD** and the fear of punishments threatened therein, placing a bridle on disorderly lusts and inclinations. However, neither the former nor the latter can successfully carry out their intent. The stillness one acquires in this way does not last long. At the slightest opportunity, nature retreats back into its old rights: and the violent force and disorder of the lusts is often made even more vehement by the restraint imposed upon them for a short time. <note>original: "Röm. VIII. 3."</note> Romans 8:3.

### Explanation.

A great evil is nevertheless bearable if one is certain that means are available to overcome it. A sick person is cheerful in his pains if he is assured by the mouth of an experienced physician that there is more than one herb and plant present in the kingdom of nature to kill his internal enemy. But to suffer, and yet know that one suffers without hope of redemption; to be tormented, to know one's misery, and yet see that one can promise oneself no rescue—this is the highest misfortune into which one can fall. In this condition is the person who lives outside the **state of grace.** He is a slave to his lusts and must follow wherever his ruin pulls him. Sometimes he wakes up and wishes for his rescue. Yet the more he looks around for help, the less

<column-break/>

he finds it. He tries what he can to tear his chains apart. He often imagines that he has gained much and is already free on one side. And not long thereafter, a violent and unexpected fall teaches him that nature is invincible and man is a corrupt creature who cannot be improved by himself. Could the disorder of our internal evil inclinations be removed by our own strength, we would have to achieve it either through wise and rational reflection, or by knowing how to impress upon ourselves the decree of the Law: <note>original: "Laß dich nicht gelüsten Röm. VII. 7."</note> *Thou shalt not covet* (Romans 7:7), so that the heart might be turned around by it. These two means are, in themselves and by their nature, excellent and powerful. But we are like those sick people who are already wrestling with death, in whose already infected and decaying bodies
