# On the Natural Corruption of Man.

the noblest means must spoil without effect. Reason and law have in themselves enough strength and power: but in the fallen soul of man, little or nothing. One will be convinced of the truth of this teaching from what follows.

### I.

*Reason cannot free us from the dominion and power of our evil desires.* I understand by reason here a wise and well-founded judgment of our understanding regarding the movements and lusts of our souls. Man has so much power and *strength of spirit* that he can see and recognize the disorder and injustice of his desires. He can—provided he is not simple by nature or blinded by his lusts—comprehend that his heart is a gathering-place of all kinds of inclinations that are capable of disturbing his own peace, weakening the body, consuming the sharpness of the spirit, and bringing and propagating confusion and misfortune among other people. And if he believes that a wise Being placed him in this world for a specific purpose, he will find himself compelled by this to conclude: I must partly abolish, partly restrain these excessive and harmful desires, if I do not wish to offend myself and one day fall into the hands of the righteous Judge of the earth. How could I please **GOD** with a heart that works toward my own ruin and seeks nothing less than to destroy the order of the Lord in the world and to grieve his subjects? These thoughts would have to change and improve us if they could truly take hold in us, take deep root, and reach a living effect

<column-break/>

within our souls. Truth must triumph where it is permitted to use its power properly, and light must illuminate where its rays are not stopped and hindered. Our natural state does not allow this wise judgment of our reason to accomplish anything in us. It is true, the splendor of wisdom seems to penetrate in certain hours and to convince and please us in an indescribable way at the same time. There are blessed moments in which it seems to become bright within us. One sometimes thinks one has perfectly mastered the truth and will, through its power, drive away the entire host of one's selfish and evil desires. # The First Chapter

One is, for a few hours or a few days, calmer and more still: one does not feel the assaults of the passions so strongly for a short time. One becomes confident through this peace and thinks one has won. What self-deception! Our desires act like a clever enemy. They pull themselves together and save their strength until their adversary is lulled to sleep. At the first opportunity that seems favorable to them, they march out from their corners with renewed strength and attack the restless heart. <note>Underlined in red in original:</note> **Truth and reason cannot long endure in the land of such a powerful enemy.** They are, as it were, strangers standing on unknown soil. They therefore give way: and our desires, suppressed for a time, avenge themselves upon us by doubling their strength. We become worse than before and retain nothing from our brief pleasure but a sorrowful memory, which is far too weak to renew the resistance within us. 

Euclio <note>Euclio is a character name borrowed from the Roman playwright Plautus, traditionally used in literature to represent a stereotypical miser.</note>, who lies sick with the <term>money-plague<note>Original: "Geld-Seuche." A colorful term used by the author to describe greed as a pathological or infectious disease.</note></term>, hit upon some rational thoughts eight days ago when he saw the burial of his friend, who had been of the same mind as he. The whole arrangement of the funeral procession, the joyful heirs, the conversations of the companions—who left his friend little glory—and other things besides, unexpectedly brought him to the thought that it was foolish and absurd to worry so much about a thing that would be of no use in the next world and often remains here in the hands of the people to whom one would least grant it. He continued this reflection and found himself quite moved by it.

<column-break/>

Five days pass, and during them, Euclio speaks and acts like a man who has freed himself from the folly of the spirit and wishes to apply his wealth for the benefit of himself and the world. The poor neighbor rejoices and hopes to gain a small piece of property through the generosity of this completely changed man, which he can leave to his orphans. The servants proclaim the good fortune that has dawned in their house everywhere. The minister of the Gospel <note>Original: "Diener des Evangelii," referring to a Lutheran or Reformed clergyman.</note>, whom this man confides in, believes that an extraordinary grace has made his heart a temple of the Spirit of **GOD**. 

On the sixth day, everything changes. A Jew <note>In the 18th-century context of this manuscript, this likely refers to a stock character used to introduce a financial temptation or a high-interest business deal.</note> presents himself and assures the converted miser that there is an opportunity to gain ten percent if one is willing to commit a small sin. A pair of orphans were in extreme distress, and now was the time to seize a small estate, the sole inheritance of their fathers. What becomes of Euclio as he hears this? His blood becomes stirred. The hidden lust breaks forth like a dammed-up stream. Truth and reason must vacate the mind in two moments. He hurries to his chest to count the money. As he deals with this, he sees a supply of devalued and half-valid coinage <note>Original: "abgesetzter und halbgültiger Münze." This refers to older coins that had been officially devalued or were no longer accepted at full face value during currency reforms.</note> that he had long wanted to get rid of. It occurs to him to mix a portion of it into the money being demanded. Out of necessity, the recipients must be satisfied with what he chooses to give. <note>Underlined in red in original:</note> **He thus heaps sin upon sin and has the advantage from his supposed reformation that his old lust rages with a rejuvenated strength.**

# On the Natural Corruption of Humanity

We wish to add a few particular observations to this general consideration, which is daily confirmed by experience; these, I believe, will make the inability of reason to tame the desires even more clear. **The first remembrance.** The greatest number of people possess almost no reason at all—at least, they cannot make use of it to their own advantage. Small is the group who can intelligently judge the impulses that manifest within them and, by the power of universal truths of reason, convince themselves of the incorrectness of those impulses. Most have only heard that there is something noble and good in man called reason, but they have never tested whether this gift also dwells within them and could serve some purpose. The world allows itself to be led by its senses and imagination, and uses the understanding only as far as these reach. How few take the trouble to learn the <term>fundamental doctrines<note>Original: "Grund-Lehren." In this context, the author refers to the foundational principles of logic and morality required for ethical discernment.</note></term> which must serve as a guide if right and wrong, vice and virtue, truth and falsehood are to be distinguished from one another? And how many are there, even among those to whom these fundamental doctrines are not unknown, who know how to use them correctly—applying them both to the discovery of truth and to their own peace of mind? Will there even be found, among three thousand inhabitants of a country, a single one who is capable of proving, through a proper sequence of rational deductions, that the immoderate desire for honor is a punishable and evil quality? How can reason be a universal means to change or soothe the desires, since it is possessed by so few and

<column-break/>

used by even fewer?

**The second remembrance.** Those who have sharpened their reason and are not without a desire to make use of it are hindered by all sorts of internal and external causes from using it for their own good. Perhaps there are some <term>fortunate people<note>Original: "glückselige Menschen." This refers to individuals blessed with a naturally clear disposition or a temperament that is easily governed by the intellect.</note></term> in the world whom the understanding never fails when it is required of them. Perhaps there are some who are equally capable at all times of perceiving the truth and testing whatever occurs and happens according to its standard. The vast majority do not enjoy this happiness. There are more dark and gloomy days in the lives of ordinary men than bright and cheerful ones. By this I mean: our <term>spirit<note>Original: "Geist." This refers to the human mind or higher consciousness.</note></term> enjoys a true freedom for very little of the time that we wander here, and can only occasionally untangle itself from the bonds in which it lies in order to judge thoroughly, orderly, and precisely. We are not always as wise and sensible as we wish to be. Today we see sharply and believe we have found the key to many secrets; tomorrow our <term>wit<note>Original: "Witz." In the 18th century, this term referred to general mental acuity, intelligence, or the ability to make connections, rather than just humor.</note></term> is covered, one knows not how, with a cloud that barely allows a faint reflection of yesterday's light to pass through, and which maintains its place for many days against all our efforts. A small, unexpected change and secret movement in our body disturbs the spirit in its work and deranges the most correct and orderly thoughts. ### Chapter One

...protracted contemplation has been built, and it sets us back so far that we cannot recover our strength for a long time. In the midst of the sharpest contemplation, a certain internally rising fog often settles between us and the light for which we strive, leading us back into old ignorance and forcing us against our will to abandon the investigation. The wisest conclusions escape us in a short time if they are not carefully maintained and renewed. And what would our knowledge and understanding be now if the art of expressing the images and thoughts of the soul through certain signs on paper <note>The author is referring to the invention of writing and printing as the only reason human knowledge survives the frailty of memory.</note> had not been found? Without this means, would we not still lie in the greatest ignorance and, at the end of our lives, have to sigh over the poor benefit that the use of reason has brought about? Can a gift that we can rarely use correctly, which is so easily disturbed in its work, be a certain remedy against an evil that torments us every day and does not even rest when we sleep?

**The third remembrance.** *Nothing is more to be regretted than that reason almost entirely deserts us at the time when its help is most necessary.* What use is a weapon that cannot be found in a time of need, or a medicine that is locked away when one sees death before one's eyes? Our impulses and desires sometimes fall into a strong heat and demand absolutely that we should obey and follow them. Who does not remember that in him very often such a riot of certain natural

<column-break/>

impulses arose, which partly fought with one another and partly surrounded and occupied reason from all sides, so that he himself did not know what was happening to him? And how many are there who never think of these disorders without horror and humiliation, because they let themselves be overtaken by sin therein and stain their lives with spots that many years cannot wipe away? In these so dangerous hours, in this riot of desires, in these violent attacks of lusts, we need reason most of all. This should calm us, drive away the desires, bring the heart back into its old order, and moderate the untamable heat of nature. And where is reason in the wisest man in these cases? Do we even have reason, or can reason even show itself, when the desires truly wake up and awaken one violent movement after another in the narrow space of our corrupt heart? Are not the <term>philosopher<note>Original: "Welt-weise," literally "world-wise." Both have no reason and, in this confusion, require the understanding of another to compose themselves again. And what can another's understanding, however pure it may be, achieve at times with a mind that is truly set in motion and vividly feels the drive of the desires? **The fourth remembrance.** All grounds of reason that are meant to move our corrupt heart must be, as it were, seasoned and mixed with self-love—and even more, with an impure self-love. Tell us what you will against lusts; prove it as strongly and clearly as possible: if we do not see that there is something to be gained or lost, our heart remains lying in its sinful sluggishness. We praise the intellect and the eloquence of those who skillfully depict the ugliness of lusts and vices for us. We rejoice when we ourselves, through our own reflection, have discovered something that can serve to convince those who cling to the desires of the flesh. Meanwhile, we stay on the old path and do not turn back until we see that we might perhaps fall into an abyss if we continue. One must not be too greedy: for this vice makes one hated and ridiculous. One must avoid an excess of wine: for intemperance ruins one's health. One must set a goal and measure for one's pride: for otherwise, one draws many enemies upon oneself who can be a hindrance to the attainment of one's purpose. Some are so corrupt and occupied by their desires that even these reasons bounce off their hearts like blunt arrows and leave behind no mark of any strength. With others, who are somewhat better, they have enough power that one becomes more cautious and finds a certain middle ground through which self-love and desires are satisfied at the same time. The proud and ambitious man retains the disorderly lust in his soul and obeys it: he only changes in that he covers it with the cloak of humility and affability. # The First Chapter

Here he <note>The author is referencing the Apostle Paul, specifically his arguments in the eighth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans.</note> shows partly the impotence of the Law to remedy this evil, and partly the true means that can set the corrupted sinner at liberty. To the Law, he says, it is impossible to help man. And he immediately gives the reason for this: *For it is weakened through the flesh.* These words contain a twofold teaching: The first: The Law, viewed and considered in itself, has power enough to convert us and to bring our desires into order. For it comes from God. It is a means given by Him against the excess of passions. How then could it be weak in itself? The second: The Law has lost the power it possesses in itself; it no longer has the ability to change the heart since

<column-break/>

man became fallen and corrupted. Whence comes this weakness of the Law? From the flesh. It is well known that Paul very often uses this word to indicate indwelling sin <note>In Lutheran theology, "indwelling sin" refers to the "fomes peccati," the lingering spark of corruption that remains in human nature even after baptism.</note> and the corrupted nature of man. This flesh, the evil desire, the inclination toward sin, sets itself against the natural power of the Law and weakens it so much that we can offer no obedience. The love of God has remedied this misery and provided fallen man with another means to put sin and corruption to death. God did that which the Law could not do, and sent His Son, whose death and suffering earned for us the grace of justification <note>The act of being declared righteous before God.</note> and sanctification <note>The process of being made holy through the Holy Spirit.</note>.

### §. XV.

Notwithstanding all this, we could still boast of a certain kind of happiness if these restless desires, which we cannot tame, remained within our souls and applied their power merely to disturb the peace of our minds. But they go further. They are not satisfied with dominion over our spirit. They wish to be fully gratified and do not rest until we have satisfied their impulse and committed the evil deed by which they can be sated. *James 1:15.* <note>Original reference: "Jac. I. 15." This verse describes the progression from desire to sin, and from sin to death.</note> Through this, our spiritual misery becomes complete. When the desire is satisfied and the sin is accomplished, we are left with an anxious heart and a wounded conscience: We heap torment and unrest upon ourselves in those hours when we come to our senses: We become guilty of the ruin and misfortune of other people, plunging some into temporal displeasure and others even into the eternal punishments which divine justice has prepared for sinners.

### Explanation.

It is misfortune and misery enough that the heart of a corrupted person is like a battlefield, upon which one enemy after another appears and tests their strength. It is sad and distressing enough that we can neither close the entrance to these enemies of our peace, nor take away their freedom to set our soul into confusion, disorder, and suffering. What is an intellect that must be an idle spectator to countless accidents that daily occur to the peace of the soul—a peace it ought to protect—and cannot prevent its enemies from lighting one fire after another? What is a will that is forced to obey its adversaries and to fight against its own life? And yet, this would be a misery that could be endured in a certain way if it remained within the bounds of our souls and could finally be soothed through time and our own labor. But our desires demand to be satisfied. And they find this satisfaction no sooner than when the deed toward which they are directed is accomplished. Judas is martyred and tortured by inward avarice <note>The author uses the term "Geldsucht," literally a "sickness for money" or obsessive greed.</note> until he resolves to commit the most abominable vice in order to gain thirty coins, whose luster catches the eye. The lust that is stirred in David when he beholds Bathsheba cannot be stilled by reason: it brings body and spirit into disorder; it gives commands without asking the intellect; it carries out everything that seems pleasant to it, and consents to a crime that is otherwise seldom paired with sensuality—to cruelty, to treachery, and to homicide—so that it may

<column-break/>

retain its dominion and, at the same time, appear permissible in the eyes of the world. <insert>A desire that is truly awakened within the corrupted man summons everything within him to its service: and everything is ready, to our misfortune, to render obedience to its command.</insert> The intellect allows its strength to be taken away and, as it were, blinds itself. It uses its entire power to serve the lust and exerts itself now to gloss over the vice that pleases the reigning desire, now to devise means through which that desire might obtain its goal. The imagination is occupied with magnifying the pleasure that the evil deed one intends to commit seems to promise, and with transforming the moments that a fleeting sensuality can last into months and years. The memory seeks out the buried traces, as it were, of the pleasant sensations one formerly enjoyed during the commission of certain sins, and knows how to reckon up a good number of people who, despite all their sins, reached a peaceful and healthy old age. The will delivers itself with all its powers into the bondage of the desire that draws it along, and wishes neither to crave nor to perform anything except what is pleasing to that desire. The body itself makes itself ready to fulfill the will of the naughty <note>In this 18th-century context, "unartig" (naughty) carries a stronger sense of being "contrary to one's proper nature" or "wicked."</note> lust, and gathers all the life-spirits <note>term: "Lebens-Geister" (vital spirits). In early modern physiology, these were believed to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to animate the limbs and transmit sensory data.</note> together into those members that must be used as instruments for the forbidden deed. Is it any wonder that a creature who is so subjected to the dominion of his desires is led by them into the coarsest misdeeds and cannot [save himself]?

An excellent passage regarding this power of lusts is found in the Epistle of Saint James, **James 1:14–15**. A person, he says, is tempted when they are enticed and lured by their own lust. Then, when lust has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is finished, gives birth to death. One can, in a certain sense, call this passage the **genealogy** <note>original: "Geschlecht-Register," literally a family register or lineage.</note> of the sins and evil deeds into which we are prone to fall. The Apostle refutes those who, even in the early days of Christianity, endeavored to shift the blame for the evil a person commits onto God Himself. In every age, people have been found who wish to make the Almighty the author of sin in various ways. And as godless and absurd as the teachings of such people have been, they have always found many followers, because the impure person wishes to appear pure and blameless despite their wickedness. What will a sinner not believe if they wish to persist in their foul nature and yet be free from the troublesome accusation of conscience? The Apostle first shows that the natural concept we have of the essence of God clears Him of all accusations from people who wish to burden Him with their sins. God, he says, can tempt no one or entice them to evil. For He Himself is not tempted, but is perfectly pure and holy. He then shows that the origin of sin must be sought in the evil heart of man himself and in the lusts <note>In this context, "Lust" refers to any disordered or intense craving, not solely sexual desire.</note> that possess it. He

<column-break/>

distinguishes three things to clearly represent the generation of sin: **the enticement of lust**, **the conception of lust**, and **the birth of sin**. The mother of evil deeds is the inherent badness and evil desire. This is stirred and awakened—sometimes by external images, sometimes by words, sometimes by the imagination, and sometimes by other causes—so that it longs to produce miserable fruits and seduce the person into sin. When it is heated, it entices and lures the person to fulfill and satisfy this longing. It knows how to make all the thoughts and stirrings of the person its own, so that their entire nature seems to encourage them to give it a hearing. What power does a person have to resist such an internal force? They follow. They entertain the sinful thoughts that the lust has excited. They use their intellect, imagination, and memory to adorn and excuse it. They thus give to the lust the "seed" by which it is enabled to reach its goal. The witness of Jesus says: *Lust conceives.* The person, having first been set in motion by it, maintains it, nurtures it, enlarges it, and gives it room to fill their entire heart and simultaneously bring the body into an ultimate, disordered heat. This is the conception of lust. Whoever has come this far is completely defeated. The heart, swollen and occupied by lust, hastens to the completion of the sinful act. **Lust gives birth to sin.** Up to this point, the sinner is unfeeling and drunk with a presumed pleasure. But the fruit which the unrestrained lust has brought into the world leaves them dismayed and confused. This child of destruction is immediately again the

-># Chapter One<-

...calls affections, and see how far they have been defiled by the Fall. We want to retain this word *affection* <note>original: "Affect," from the Latin *affectus*, referring to a state of mind or emotion.</note>, although it is foreign and borrowed from the Latins. I am not unaware of the German words with which some moralists <term>Sitten-Lehrer: teachers of ethics and conduct</term> think they can translate this Roman word. However, it seems to me that none of these are capable of correctly representing the thing meant by the word *affection*. At the very least, I know of no word invented so far that fits perfectly with the description of an *affection* given here. And I do not wish to waste time inventing another that I could use in a way that avoids the confusion of different concepts, which a sensible person must avoid as much as possible.

It is necessary that I first say something about affections in general before I distinguish what is good or evil in them. I will pass over most of the things brought forward and partly debated by researchers of human nature, and present nothing more than what must be known to those who wish to correctly judge what happens within themselves and to thoroughly instruct and safely lead other people. It is admitted among scholars that the diligence of men has greatly confused and obscured this teaching. And whoever wants to be a witness to this himself need only compare three of those who wish to explain it against each other and try to either correctly grasp their propositions or reconcile them. In my opinion, this disorder and confusion arises primarily from two causes. One

<column-break/>

is that people are not in agreement regarding the meaning and description of the word *affection*. One person gives it such an extensive meaning that he includes under it all desires of the will and all changes that occur in the human mind <term>Gemüthe: the internal seat of emotions and thoughts</term>; indeed, he sometimes even counts the external signs of inner movements and certain vices that stem from the affections as being among the affections themselves. Another narrows the meaning of this word much more and makes the number of desires so large that few movements of the soul remain for him that he can count as actual affections. One should therefore not be surprised if one finds a long register of affections in one writer and a very small list in another. Had both sides agreed on what they wanted to call an *affection*, the number would perhaps be equally large, or the difference in number at least much smaller. Many others, for the second cause, base this teaching not so much on experience as on certain opinions that they have accepted as indisputably true and regard as the fundamental principles of all wisdom. Whoever wants to treat such matters thoroughly—matters that occur and are felt within a person—must, I believe, seek the ground of his science within himself. He must carefully observe what he feels within himself, frequently repeat the examination of his own sensations, notice the occasions upon which they arise, precisely note the effects that flow from them, and not judge the nature and origin of human movements until he has learned to know himself correctly. How many are found among the...

...sages of this world who act according to this rule? Most seek certain general truths from which everything else we can know and recognize must be derived, and finally imagine they have found them. Afterward, everything that is to be explained in the nature and life of humans must conform to these supposed truths. If the experience of other people conflicts with them, it must be false. If one occasionally finds stirrings within oneself that seem to say something else than what one wishes to believe, they must be suppressed or overlooked. If the design one has made is lacking here or there, imagination must replace it. How easily could it be proven that in the teaching of the **affections** <note>original: "Affecten"; in this context, the term refers to what we would today call emotions, passions, or psychological impulses</note> this very path has often been taken? Had many been able to be simpler and started with themselves to research the truth in this matter, many who gladly wish to learn from the writings of others would not have to complain that they had encountered more light in their dealings and interactions with the **unlearned** <note>original: "Ungelehrten"; referring to common people without formal academic or philosophical training</note> and in their own hearts than in the books of the learned.

We have described what we call an affection as clearly as the nature of the matter would allow. There is something in the thing to which we give this name that cannot be explained or made clear: this is its inner essence. We can say whence an affection arises, or indicate its origin; we can say what the immediate occasion is that excites an affection; we can finally say what an affection

<column-break/>

works in the soul and the body. Whoever asks us further and wants to know what the essence of an affection actually consists of? What exactly it is that we feel when these or those things express themselves in us and reveal themselves through certain signs? We know little how to answer. We can do nothing more than return a general word with which all changes occurring within us are designated. We say an affection is a **sensation**, a **movement** <note>Historically, the term "emotion" comes from the idea of the soul being "moved" (Latin: *emovere*)</note>. Whoever is not satisfied with this and demands that we climb higher and explain what a sensation or movement is, forces us to confess our ignorance. We cannot describe the changes occurring within us in any other way than according to the effects they bring about in us. They make us either satisfied or discontented. They are therefore either pleasant or unpleasant sensations. One should not demand more from a person to whom the essence of his soul is largely unknown, and who therefore cannot express in words what happens within it when it is now so, now otherwise disposed. And one should not dare to say more, so that one may not hear the reproach from others that the nature and essence of the thing have not been distinguished from its origin and effects. An affection in itself is a movement that cannot be described. **Love, hate, joy, sadness, hope**, are names with which we designate certain sweet or vexing effects in the soul, which we ourselves do not truly know and which we make even darker than they are in themselves when we wish to make them known. ### The First Chapter

If I am not much mistaken, much misunderstanding and lack of clarity has crept into certain writings about the **affections** <note>original: "Affecten"; refers to the passions or emotions</note>, and especially into some books about the love of God, precisely because this has not been considered. How often does it happen that one persuades oneself that they know the subject, when they only know certain things belonging to it, which either come from it or awaken and stir it up?

We have called an affection in general a movement of the soul, in order to avoid the question that is sometimes heatedly debated by some: Which is the seat of the affections? Is it the **understanding** <term>Verstand: the cognitive faculty of the mind</term>? Is it the **will** <term>Wille: the faculty of choice and desire</term>? Is it the brain? We count these movements as part of the will because they stem from inclinations and desires, which no one would separate from the will. Furthermore, we have nothing to do with this investigation and can tolerate someone following this or that opinion. Otherwise, we will not deny that this question has always seemed to us partly somewhat obscure and partly superfluous. What does the word *seat* mean in this context? Is it the same as the origin? And should the question be understood this way: In which power of the soul do the affections arise? Or does *seat* mean the constant residence and dwelling? And does one want to know in which power of the soul the affections constantly rule? It could be that those who cannot agree on this question might drop all hostility toward one another if they explained its meaning with other and more certain words. <column-break/>

Or would a new light dawn for us that served us to know our soul better and to watch over it more closely? I will not even say that one always takes on a difficult and almost daring task when one wants to create certain parts in one's thoughts and ascribe to each its special powers, gifts, and properties within such a simple being as our spirit is, in which all powers always work together at once. One will see from what we are about to say concerning the origin of the affections that our entire spirit takes part in them, although the desires can actually be regarded as the source of the same. We shall only have to speak of that: the rest in our description is clear and can be confirmed by everyone’s experience.

The affections come from the desires and inclinations of our will. <margin>p. 241.</margin> All our desires stem from a single main inclination: the longing to be happy. One can therefore say, if one wants to briefly represent the nature of an affection: An affection is nothing other than a desire set properly into motion, or a violent awakening of the longing to be happy, from which no human can excuse themselves. ### The Fourth Reminder.

**In many people, desires are excited, yet they are not troubled by any affects.** <term>Cato</term> <note>Cato the Younger (95–46 BCE), a Roman statesman famous for his Stoic resolve and emotional control.</note> loves his son. The boy is laid down dead before his eyes. And Cato looks upon the corpse unmoved. <term>Socrates</term> <note>The famous Greek philosopher, often cited in this period as a model of patience and rational calm under duress.</note> considers fame and honor to be almost the highest good. He is insulted, mocked, blamed, and beaten. Socrates laughs at these insults. Cajus is greedy. His ship, sent to China, arrives home rich and safe. And one cannot tell by looking at him that he is set out of his composure in the slightest by this news. Is it not then false to say that affects always arise whenever a person’s desires are set in motion? These examples also do not move us to change our opinion. **People here confuse the affects with the outward signs of the same.** As often as a desire truly awakens, a certain sensation follows according to the unchangeable laws of nature, which belongs to the affects. However, long practice and effort have brought some so far that they are capable of holding back these movements and

<column-break/>

hiding them, so that they do not become known through visible signs. In others, the movement of the blood and the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>original: "Lebens-Geister"; early medical theory held that "spirits" or subtle fluids in the nerves were responsible for movement and sensation.</note> is by nature so heavy and slow that their inner sufferings are not easily betrayed through outward gestures and postures. In many, desires gradually become weaker through age, through reflection, and through various accidents, while the intellect grows stronger. Is it any wonder that in such people only slight traces of the affects can be seen? And perhaps some are so constituted by nature that, when their desires are provoked, it naturally brings about a kind of insensitivity and numbness: perhaps that very thing which we call stillness, composure, or indifference in certain people is the very thing through which the affect reveals itself—the very thing that the awakened desire must produce in them according to their particular constitution. 

We are being told nothing but an unfounded fiction when we are told that it is possible to have, maintain, and feel desires and yet feel no affects. Those great men presented to us to prove this were just what other humans are; they merely possessed this advantage: that they could stop the course of the affects and cut off their freedom to shake and move the body—or they had become cold in their desires. In our thoughts about others, we rely far too heavily on the judgment of our eyes. What we cannot see or discover in them, we believe is not present. Weakness and rashness! Whoever wishes to know man must not merely mark what he sees of him and hears from him: He must study nature...

### The Fifth Reminder.

Meanwhile, not all people are perfectly equal to one another in regard to their <term>affects</term> <note>In the philosophy of this period, "affects" (German: *Affecten*) refer to what we now call emotions or passions—strong movements of the soul that react to external things.</note>. One is more inclined toward this affect, and another toward that one. One is more easily stirred and moved, while another requires a far stronger impulse. This person is set into motion by a cause that the other does not even notice. To one person, when he falls into an affect, it is as if a violent fire were ignited in all his veins; in another, the movement is so gentle and mild that it is scarcely felt by himself, and even less so by others. *Above all, it is to be noted that not all people are subject to all affects.* Some can truthfully testify that they have never been disturbed in their tranquility by certain stirrings. However, this must not be understood as applying to the primary affects, but only to certain <term>secondary stirrings</term> <note>German: *Neben-Regungen*. These are minor or derivative emotional reactions that depend on specific temperaments rather than the universal human condition.</note> which require a particular constitution of the body and spirit that is not present in all people. In my view, some are praised without cause for knowing nothing of certain affects; conversely, some are done an injustice when it is believed that everything that can be called an affect is stirred within them. A rational distinction must be made. *I call the primary affects: love, hate, fear, hope, joy, and sadness.* These movements are unquestionably necessary effects of the desires, and they must arise within a soul

<column-break/>

that has directed its longing toward certain things. Whoever tells us that this or that person has never perceived any of these movements within himself tells us that this person is free from all desires—and that is the same as saying he is not a human being. Many claim of themselves that they have never felt fear. *This boast is vain.* One can believe that in certain cases where most people fall into fear, they remained unchanged; one can believe that they felt the power of this movement less than other people; but it is impossible to believe that they were never troubled by this affect. Have these people then never desired to possess anything? Have they never envisioned a certain goal? Have they never exerted effort to partake in something? Have they never fallen into the danger of being disappointed in their hope? A person who has been constantly without fear must never have felt pleasure or loathing for a thing, and must have walked in this world as if nothing in it concerned him. Where are such people? *It is said of certain people that they are never sad, nor ever joyful.* One should rather say that one could rarely see the common signs of joy or sadness in these people. The affects themselves must truly arise within them because they are human beings who consider some things good and others harmful. It is inconceivable that a creature who loves his own welfare should not be moved in a pleasant way when he attains the things he deems necessary for his happiness, and should not notice an unpleasant stirring when

This is because their desires are more narrowly focused and are not tied to any particular malice. I can easily imagine that there may be people whom *anger* either never afflicts, or does so only very weakly. For I can envision such a natural arrangement of a body that it does not easily leave room for this violent movement. It may well be that Cajus <note>Cajus (Gaius) and Titius are traditional placeholder names used in philosophical and legal texts, much like "John Doe" today.</note> does not deceive me when he assures me that jealousy has never made him restless. He perhaps does not possess as much imagination as this affect requires, or he is of a flighty spirit and only looks at things superficially.

### The Sixth Reminder. 
<note>original: "Die sechste Erinnerung." The author uses "reminders" as numbered points or observations in his argument.</note> 
Whoever asks us why it is that this af-

<column-break/>

-fect arises in us at one time, and another at a different time—why joy stirs today, sadness tomorrow, fear now, and then hope—can easily answer this for himself, provided his understanding is not entirely small or base. This comes from the *difference in mental representations, through which the resting desires are set into motion.* <note>The term used here is *Vorstellungen*, meaning the mental images, ideas, or perceptions we have of the world.</note> Just as the cause is which stimulates and awakens the sleeping pleasure, so too is the affect and the movement that arises from it. Titius is joyful because the thing he desires presents itself to him as near or present. Cajus becomes anxious because the evil he wishes to escape seems to him not far removed. We wish to conclude with a reminder that, while it only concerns words and their usage, will contribute no small amount to avoiding misunderstandings and errors in this very complex teaching.

### The Seventh Reminder. 
<note>original: "Die siebende Erinnerung."</note> 
*The words we use to designate the so-called affects in their proper sense also have a much broader meaning.* They sometimes indicate a certain natural state of a person, sometimes the desire from which the affect arises, and sometimes the person's inclination toward a certain affect. One says: "A person loves this or that," and intends only to indicate: "The person has a desire for this or that thing." One says: "A person hates," and means only this: "The person cannot well tolerate this or that thing." One says: "My friend is full of fear." This is only meant to say: "My friend is of a fearful temperament and can easily become anxious."

# The First Chapter

People say: "Hope never abandons me." By this, they mean: "I always believe that my circumstances will eventually improve." ->§. XVII.<-

The desires that drive us are of two kinds. Some wish to possess or keep certain things because the intellect has concluded that they are beneficial to our <term>welfare</term> <note>Original: *Wohlfart*. In this historical context, it refers to general well-being, health, and prosperity.</note>. Others demand to see certain things removed from us because the intellect has judged that they would build toward our misfortune and misery. *Therefore, there can be no more than two primary affects, which are the foundation of all other movements of our souls: Love and Hate.* The former 
*arises from the first type of desire; the latter from the second.* Both can be stirred and awakened in different ways, and thus produce all manner of specific movements. If it appears that the thing we love is about to be lost, an unpleasant movement soon arises which we call *Fear*. If it looks as though we shall reach our goal or remain in possession of the good, we feel a pleasant stirring called *Hope*. If we judge that a thing we vehemently desire will never be obtained, we struggle with a most vexing movement to which the name *Despair* has been given. If we lose what we have sought, or fear greatly that we shall lose it, our soul deals with a movement called *Sadness*. Conversely, if we receive that which seems useful and great to us, we are ruled by that contented stirring usually designated by the word *Joy*. We know from ex-

## Explanation.

The general instruction we have given regarding the nature and the production of the affects will not be sufficient to understand everything we have to say about the corruption and the <term>sanctification</term> <note>German: *Heiligung*. In this context, it refers to the moral and spiritual process of making one's emotions holy or aligned with divine will.</note> of these movements. We must step closer, look at the most prominent affects one after another, and explain the cause and nature of each. We will limit ourselves in this treatise as our purpose requires. One can seek that which we deliberately do not touch upon in the books of the <term>philosophers</term> <note>Original: *Welt-Weisen*, literally "world-wise ones." The author suggests that while secular thinkers have mapped the heart, this text focuses on the spiritual implications.</note>, who have made it their business to fathom the hearts of men.

The affects are nothing other than movements that arise from desires. This has been shown thus far. One must therefore look at the nature of the desires and the causes by which they are stirred—now this way, now that—if one wishes to classify them correctly and consider them according to their origin and effects. <insert>Our will can do nothing</insert>

Accordingly, two main desires govern our soul: A desire to obtain or keep things that are considered good, useful, and serving; and a desire to turn away those things that could hinder the happiness we seek. This is enough said to demonstrate that there can likewise be no more than two primary affects. An affect is nothing other than a violently awakened and heated desire. <insert>Our will is only capable of two main desires.</insert> Who then will be able to create more than two main affects, from which the remaining movements (which are usually so called) have their origin? We wish only to remind the reader of one thing, and then explain the matter itself as it appears to us. That which we wish to remind you of is this: many—I had almost said most—who wish to make the nature of Love and Hate clear, do not look in their explanations at this movement itself, but rather at its origin, or at the effects that flow from it. If I am not much mistaken, this is, as it were, a silent confession that the movement itself which we call Love can indeed be felt, but not described. These words concern only a certain kind and genus of love—namely, that which we bear toward other living creatures who are capable of happiness. Furthermore, they present to us not the essence and actual nature of love, but only a fruit and effect of it. The pleasure taken in another’s well-being and happiness springs from the love with which I am devoted to someone; it is not the love itself. One must first believe that interaction and fellowship with a person can add to our own welfare; further, one must feel a certain pleasant sensation and movement in the soul, which sets the blood and the **vital spirits** <note>The "vital spirits" (German: *Lebens-Geister*) were believed in 18th-century physiology to be a subtle fluid or gas that traveled through the nerves to mediate between the soul and the body.</note> into a stir and motion whenever one either sees this person or thinks of them. From these two things grow the joy and pleasure in their welfare and happiness. *David* could have felt no pleasure in *Absalom's* <note>original: "Absolons"</note> fortune within himself if he had not believed that the well-being of this son was necessary for his own welfare and satisfaction, and if, by means of this opinion, he had not noticed a sweet and indescribable movement within himself. With these and other similar descriptions, which can be easily gathered, the languages ordinarily used in common life agree. In most manners of speaking in which the word "love" occurs, it means either regarding something as a piece of the **highest good** <note>The "summum bonum," or the ultimate goal of human existence.</note> which one strives after—this is the origin of love—or it means: to accommodate oneself to someone’s will and to do everything one can to promote

<column-break/>

the preservation and prosperity of the same. And these are the fruits and effects of love.

In our opinion, love itself is nothing other than a quiet, secret, but pleasant movement of the soul, which no one can properly explain or describe to another. This movement may perhaps be as diverse as there are people who are moved by it. I cannot say what I myself feel when I love; how then shall I be able to describe what others perceive within themselves? And by what means or rational conclusions shall I determine that *John* and *Peter*, who love at the same time, notice the same sensation and movement within themselves, since neither of these two can properly represent in words what is happening inside him? This movement arises as soon as a person has convinced himself—rightly or wrongly—that this or that person or thing constitutes a part of his perfection, peace, and well-being; it produces from itself all kinds of labor and efforts to maintain, please, protect, and improve this presumed good, which are too well known to need recounting.

He considers that resurrection of the dead as the beginning of the most perfect bliss, and he longs for this time when the power of the unjust over the saints shall cease and the body will accompany the spirit into the purest glory. The faithfulness and truth that essentially dwell in the God whom he serves assure him that this time will certainly dawn. The years that will pass between his death and the last day of the world seem to him, in the face of this certainty, to be mere moments. In this faith, he feels a lively movement of the soul that completely possesses him and fills him with courage, joy, and purely pleasant sensations. One is accustomed to call this movement—when it has risen as high as it did in Paul and leaves no room for doubt—**confidence** or **trust**. This word, however, does not indicate the movement itself, but rather its source and origin. One feels a truly exceptional and pleasant stirring of the soul when one considers a matter, though it is still distant, as if it were already actually there and present. **Hope** is never without a kind of fear. If the certainty of the thing one desires becomes so great that the fear ceases, then hope is transformed into confidence and trust. In ordinary language, and in the Scripture itself, both words—hope

<column-break/>

and confidence—are often used interchangeably, one being substituted for the other. A cautious interpreter must take note of this so as not to make a mistake in his explanations.

Our good, which we value above all else, is often entirely withdrawn from our eyes. All probability of regaining it vanishes, and we thereby become completely incapable of that pleasant stirring called hope. This state of the mind <note>original: "Gemüht"</note> gives birth to a most sorrowful and soul-harming movement, which sometimes leads men into extreme ruin. It has been given the name <note>The OCR reads "Rahmen" (frame), but the context suggests "Namen" (name).</note> of **despair**. This word is not always used in common speech as we use it here. Despair is sometimes attributed to those who cease to hope in matters of moderate importance and feel restless and unpleasant sensations because of it. Such a movement we call merely a "sadness." Despair, according to our concepts, is something more violent—a forceful movement that manifests when we judge that the things in which we place our highest good and happiness are lost. It is also said that this or that person despairs when they merely give up the hope of obtaining something they sought, even if they feel no particular pain or torment of the spirit. One must not be led astray by these different meanings of the word "despair." Everyone is free to assign a greater or lesser value to the words they use, provided they do not forget to explain this to those who read or hear them.

to provide information. We consider it advisable to distinguish between **sadness** and **despair**. We use the former word for those movements that disturb us regarding the loss, or the danger of losing, such things upon which our highest happiness is not strictly founded, and which can be moderated or soothed by other ideas. We use the latter as the name for the movements that manifest within us when those things are gone which we consider absolutely necessary for our highest welfare, and which bring about truly sorrowful and most harmful effects. At the same time, we are not so unreasonable as to accuse those of haste or imprudence who represent despair as a kind of sadness or call it the highest and most perfect sadness. What this means is easy to explain. Judas can see the grace of the Most High and future blessings only as the greatest treasures, which infinitely surpass the money he otherwise loves. The sin he committed through the betrayal of his Savior grows so large in his spirit that he is convinced he has completely lost all claim to these goods and all hope of winning them. Through this, his spirit becomes darkened. The desire for salvation <term>Seligkeit: a state of eternal spiritual happiness or blessedness</term>, which becomes quite active in these circumstances, joins with the most terrible and painful movement of the soul one can imagine. Immediately, his soul is taken up with a pleasant movement that penetrates bones and veins and restores the strength and cheerfulness of his early years to his weakened and exhausted body. This entire instruction is simple. One person or another will perhaps believe that more should have been said. Whoever knows more of this matter than I do retains the freedom to improve my thoughts and can believe that I will always be eager to learn something more from them.

## §. XVIII.

Our spirit is moved in the same way when the matter is viewed from the other side and man is placed in opposition to those things which he regards as obstacles to his peace and welfare. The desire to be happy, which rules us all, compels us to demand the downfall and absence of those things that we consider harmful to us.

Anger is a particular <term>affect [a strong physical and mental emotion or passion]</term> that presupposes a certain condition of the body and the spirit and is therefore not common to all people. ### Explanation.

That which we have said concerning those affects arising from the primary emotion of love mostly includes what belongs to the explanation of the emotions arising from the other primary movement of our heart: hate. We have therefore earned the right to be briefer here than before. A person judges that certain things are an obstacle or harmful to their happiness, their peace, their honor, or their welfare. Upon this judgment there follows immediately an abhorrence and aversion toward these things, or an insuperable desire to free one's happiness from these enemies. This desire often rests: and we ourselves sometimes do not know that it dwells within us. We count among these <term>affects</term> <note>The author uses 'Affecten' to refer to what we now call emotions or passions of the mind.</note> **jealousy**, **envy**, **shame**, and the **desire for revenge**. <insert>In the heart of a</insert> jealous man, a double desire is stirred, which awakens its own violent movement, to the unrest of the one who feels it. He considers the possession and the affection of a certain person toward him as his highest happiness and finds a sweet and pleasurable sensation therein. It is already understood that this is called "loving." He then learns that another wishes to share the possession of this good with him or even draw it entirely to himself. This stirs in him a repugnance toward the enemy of his welfare, which carries with it a restless and vexatious movement. One easily sees that this is "hatred." These two movements—the one pleasant, the other burdensome—join together as they are stirred, so that they produce from themselves a torment of the soul and a most contrary movement, to which, as circumstances fall, fear, anger, and sadness sometimes add themselves, to the even greater misfortune of the person. From this, one can perceive what tortures those who are commonly called jealous. The suffering they feel is a painful and very burdensome movement of the soul, the spirits, and the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>original: "Lebens-Säfte." This refers to the historical medical theory of "humors," where bodily fluids like blood and bile were thought to dictate a person's health and personality.</note>, which reveals itself in people who feel a strong hatred toward a person who wishes to disturb them in the pleasant and joyful possession of another whom they violently love. What sad accidents does this miserable plague not produce? What does

<column-break/>

history and experience tell us of the lamentable and absurd things committed by those who have allowed this movement space in their souls? It often happens that, along with love for the person one adores, hatred also unites in a new way. Then the effects of this <term>affect</term> become even stranger and more harmful. Love, when thus combined with hatred, can become cruel and commit things that the most violent hatred otherwise could hardly bring about.

<insert>In envy, I see precisely this unhappy union of hatred and love.</insert> No one could feel the evil called envy and resentment if he were not of the opinion that certain things were beautiful, excellent, and suited to the promotion of his welfare. Why would Joseph's brothers grudge him his preference in their father's favor if they did not believe that a father's love could make the one who enjoys it happy? One must, therefore, love beforehand if one is to feel envy. To this love is joined a vexation, a repugnance, a hatred against the one who possesses the goods that seem useful, advantageous, and conducive to our satisfaction. Is there not in the heart of Esau, who begrudges Jacob the paternal blessing, a hatred against his brother who, as he believes, has wrongfully brought the same upon himself and his descendants? These two movements—love for a thing and hatred toward a person to whom the thing has fallen—awaken, when they become lively, the unrest of the soul called envy. Our answer, therefore, to...

### The First Chapter

...to the question: "What is **envy**?" the answer will be this: It is a violent and vexing movement of the soul, which arises in those people in whom the love for a certain thing and the hatred against the person to whom it has fallen are stirred at the same time.

The **desire for revenge** is a fierce and agonizing fire that attacks the soul of a person who is certain that another has deprived him of something which is absolutely necessary for his happiness. This is enough said to convince anyone willing to see that in this restless and sorrowful movement, love plays as much a part as hatred. The vengeful person is of the opinion that he was happy until this or that was taken from him, and he cannot stop loving and highly valuing the lost thing. He is just as strongly possessed by hatred toward the person who is the cause of the loss he has suffered. Both movements awaken a burning desire to make the other person just as unhappy as himself, which is accompanied by a restless and sensitively agonizing movement. We are told that the indigenous inhabitants of <term>America</term> <note>The author refers to the indigenous peoples of the Americas, reflecting the 18th-century European perspective on "savage" cultures.</note>, whom people are accustomed to calling savages, are all naturally afflicted with this harmful and sorrowful emotion. These poor people must therefore be plagued by a powerful love for what they call honor or highness, which produces a violent hatred toward their neighbors (who often happen to rob them of their supposed happiness) and thereby generates cruel and bloodthirsty movements in their hearts.

<column-break/>

In **shame**, if we examine the matter closely, we will find this very same community of hatred and love. He who feels shame loves honor, and hates partly that which enticed him to commit something that attached a blemish to it, and partly himself, for allowing himself to be led into damaging the good opinion held of him. From this arises an unpleasant movement of the heart that a person cannot hold back. One punishes a young person with serious words who has committed an offense against decency and propriety. Immediately, a vexing emotion rises in his heart, which testifies to its presence through a change <note>Likely referring to blushing or a change in facial expression.</note> and certain gestures. Whence does this come? The transgressor believes that no small part of his happiness consists in the good judgment people have of him, of his virtue and reason, and he therefore longs for this good. This desire is so violently awakened by the forceful reminder of his father or teacher—showing him that he has deprived himself of some of this desired honor—that love makes itself felt. At the same time, he wishes that what has happened had not happened, and feels a repugnance toward the opportunity that caused his lapse, and toward his own weakness. Both together make him so dismayed and restless that he cannot hide the dejection of his soul. Shame is an unpleasant movement of the heart which manifests itself when the desire to be of some value, or the love of honor, [joins] in a person with a kind of hatred toward those who have removed him from the good opinion of men...

# On the Natural Corruption of Mankind

...is united in our mind. Our purpose allows us to break off the explanation of those human movements called *affects* <note>original: *Affecten*; referring to the passions or emotions</note> here. It is, we freely admit, imperfect. This arises partly because it is nearly impossible to bring the stirrings revealed in man under such certain rules that no or only few exceptions occur. Who can rightly fathom the heart of mortals? How little are we equipped to categorize the so manifold dispositions <note>original: *Gemüths-Arten*</note> and temperaments of the earth's inhabitants—which awaken a multitude of stirrings that are in certain ways both similar and dissimilar—so that no one need doubt into which order he should place the people he encounters? How then shall we manage with these movements, which always contain something that corresponds to these dispositions and the other qualities and circumstances of people? It is indisputably true that all who wish to speak of man, his nature, and his properties, imagine not so much mankind in general, but rather the type and kind of people with whom they have become acquainted. And who can correct this error?

<column-break/>

Men are equal: Who will deny this? But birth, the body, education, the climate <note>original: *Luft* (air), often used in this period to denote the environmental and geographical influence of a region</note>, way of life, the country, sustenance, and other things besides, which are infinitely varied, have so much power over them that they become unequal in many ways. One must therefore be satisfied in such matters with an instruction that is only somewhat suited to the nature of the entire human race. That which we have given will, hopefully, be of such a nature. And whoever is unwilling to tolerate this kind of imperfection within it must consider how he might provide himself and others with greater powers of the soul than we possess here. Another kind of imperfection in our presentation arises from the nature of the intention we have set for ourselves. Not everything that can be said about the *affects* is found here: But as much is found as is necessary for our purpose. No one will be able to reproach us for having overlooked or omitted anything until he has convinced himself, through a sensible consideration of our entire project, that the things he seeks here in vain necessarily belong to it.

### §. XIX.

These movements of the soul, which are called *affects*, are by no means evil so long as they are considered in themselves. They stem from the desires that necessarily had to exist in such creatures as humans are, since the Lord willed that they should be mindful of their preservation and happiness. And whoever pays close attention to them and their effects <note>original: *Würckungen*</note> in man has reason to admire the wisdom of the Creator, who made man capable of them...

## Explanation.

The nature of the <term>affects</term> <note>original: *Affecten*; referring to passions, emotions, or strong inclinations of the mind</note> has been explained insofar as our work requires. Now it must be shown to what extent they belong to our corruption. Are these sensations entirely evil? Or were they only corrupted and distorted by the Fall of the first humans? Much depends on this question. The entire conduct of a Christian must be arranged according to the answer given to it. The true nature of what Scripture calls <term>self-denial</term>, <term>sanctification</term>, and <term>renewal</term> cannot be demonstrated until it is settled whether the affects are consequences of the first sin or a fundamental part of human nature. It is all the more distressing that Christians are divided here, as in a thousand other things. Most believe there is something good and something sinful in the affects: the former comes from God, the latter from the corruption which the transgression of divine law has brought upon us. Others claim that everything that can be called an affect is blameworthy: and that one can only be called a true disciple of Jesus if they have acquired a perfect stillness and tranquility of the soul, knowing the affects only from their old sensations and from the example of other people. One has always

<column-break/>

found people of this latter kind among Christians. Yet in the times closest to us, their number has greatly increased and grows almost more than it should decrease. Discord has also mingled among this group. Difficulties have been presented to them against their opinion, which many found significant and did not dare to fully resolve. Thus it has happened that some have restricted their doctrine somewhat more precisely and stepped a few steps closer to those who insist not on the eradication, but on the improvement of the affects, while the others have only become more stubborn in maintaining what they once accepted.

It is commonly believed that the <term>Stoics</term> <note>An ancient school of philosophy that taught that the path to happiness is found in accepting the moment as it presents itself and not allowing oneself to be controlled by the desire for pleasure or the fear of pain.</note>, a kind of pagan philosopher <note>original: *Welt-Weisen*; literally "world-wise ones"</note> best known for their strict moral teaching <note>original: *Sitten-Lehre*</note>, were the first to claim that the affects were entirely useless and that a wise man must free himself from them completely. Those who wish them well say that this reproach is based merely on a misunderstanding: that one should have nothing... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "nichts" (nothing) indicates the beginning of the next page.</note>

...did not take heed that the **Stoics** spoke with a particular language and gave a new meaning to the words common in the world: They had not taken the word **affect** <note>original: *Affect*; here referring to a strong emotion or passion that moves the soul</note> for a sad or joyful movement of the soul arising from a desire, but rather meant by it the violent, vehement, and harmful effects of these movements. We do this all the more gladly because we shall find therein an opportunity to provide a reminder that can be useful in many other disputed questions. Whoever looks at the first principles of the doctrine which the Stoics presented as wisdom will find the greatest reason to believe that they prescribed a complete eradication of the affects to their students. A wise man must consider <term>virtue</term> alone as good, excellent, and useful, and look upon the remaining things of the world as worthless trifles that were not made for him. Whoever tells us that we must grant no place in our souls to any wish, any longing, any craving—whatever it may be—teaches us at the same time that every affect rising within us is evil and a testimony of our folly, because it betrays the presence of a desire. The doctrine of the removal of the affects is thus connected to the first principles of Stoic wisdom. How does it happen then, that despite this, sensible men have dared to speak in favor of these people? It is because some among them, in the execution and explanation of their principles, deviated from the fundamental rules of their doctrine and spoke more mildly than the internal logic of it could tolerate. Their adversaries attacked the building they had erected primarily from this side, which is the weakest, and found no small amount of popular approval. ### Chapter One

and therefore concluded that ignorance and envy had cast a stain upon the Stoics, which they had long since wiped away. This was all the easier to achieve because even during the time when the Stoic schools were still active, people here and there were inclined—based on the words of a few individuals—to attribute a better doctrine to the entire sect than was generally ascribed to it. And yet, I am certain that those among them who did not seek to please the world regarded the others—those who aligned themselves more with ordinary thoughts—as corrupters of true wisdom and unfaithful heirs of the original founder of the Stoic doctrine. Is this not the common course of the world, which is still a constant cause of much confusion? Certain people put forward a new doctrine and find followers. Others show that this same doctrine is entirely incorrect and runs contrary to reason and Scripture. As the dispute progresses, it becomes clear that one is too weak to defend everything that was asserted so strictly in the beginning. This brings about elucidations, explanations, and restrictions of the general propositions, as well as modest rejections of certain accusations. Later, some people look to these "softened" versions when they are to judge the correctness or incorrectness of the disputed doctrine. Others, however, stick to what was first established and what accords with the essence of the entire teaching. This is the source of so much strife and disagreement among those who are asked to give their opinions on certain spiritual and worldly matters. Would the Roman Church have so many defenders

<column-break/>

if there were not people who paid more attention to the gentle interpretations of certain members of that Church than to the primary foundational doctrines and the entire context of their faith? The world will have to deal with this disorder as long as its inhabitants are humans who allow themselves to be guided by reputation and who are over-hasty in their judgments.

Certain doctrines of the early Church—whose leaders we are accustomed to calling the "Fathers"—are accused of being infected with this same teaching, which is attributed to the Stoics not without reason. They show all too clearly that they took pleasure in Stoic doctrines. Nevertheless, I do not quite venture to say that they truly meant everything they wrote in their hearts exactly as their words sound. These early Christian teachers lacked adversaries who could have made them more cautious and careful in their ways of speaking and their presentations. I find that in other places they spoke more sensibly and, as it were, took back what they had presented as truth elsewhere. Why then do great and wise people divide the affects into indifferent and evil? Two things are to blame for this. First, one does not look at an affect in itself, but adds partly the cause and source, and partly its effects. We are ready to say this as well, if we have previously changed the description of an affect and made it more extensive. Hatred against others is certainly evil. In itself? Not at all. Who will praise envy? It is certainly evil. Only note that this culpability does not lie in the movement itself, which is called envy, but in its origin. Envy arises from the impure pleasure of seeing another deprived of a certain good which one desires for oneself. And so it is with most of the remaining affects that are called evil. The mere desire for certain things that one found to be good would soon have grown cold again and been stifled by the power of the senses and other things. The mere aversion toward a thing considered harmful would easily have been lost amidst all sorts of changes. Our heart resembles a clock that stops if it is not kept in motion by a weight. Our God therefore arranged us so artfully and wisely that the soul's desire for a useful and wholesome thing would always be accompanied by a sweet sensation, and the abhorrence of a cause of our misfortune always by a vexing movement. We call these two stirrings hate and love. My spirit must, through a certain natural consequence—which I recognize only dimly in this misery—be enlivened and refreshed as often as I behold things that, in my opinion, can contribute something to my perfection and peace. And through just such a consequence, my mind must feel a displeasure and torment when I encounter things that, as I believe, can weaken or take away my pleasure. My spirit must, according to an unchangeable order—I know not how—be delighted when I come closer to the goal of my wishes, and fall into dissatisfaction and pain when I lose my pleasure from sight. What would I be if my being were not arranged in this way? Would I not be a creature that was changeable and inconstant in its desires and driven now here, now there? Would I not fall upon this today and that tomorrow, and be fit for nothing less than a proper improvement of my welfare? But what would I be if my opinions about what is called good and evil were never straying, and my spirit allowed itself to be charmed neither by false conclusions nor by the representations of the senses to choose misfortune for happiness? # The First Chapter

It is not necessary to imagine another world than this one, or a society of people who can neither rejoice nor grieve, neither love nor hate, neither hope nor fear, and to consider the behavior of such creatures in order to see the truth of these things more clearly. We know that such "poems of the soul" require more detachment from the senses and strength of spirit than can be demanded of most people. One can come closer to what we wish to make clear here. Are there not people present in the world in whom years or other accidents have so weakened the <term>affects</term> <note>original: "Affecten." In this 18th-century context, "affects" refers to the passions or emotions that move the soul to action.</note> that they can hardly be felt anymore? What are such people? Worn-out tools that can serve no matters of any importance. Their desires hardly stir anymore. Their will is partly inconsistent and fickle, partly immobile and stubborn. They long for certain things in this hour; they show a hint of aversion at other times. How quickly these desires pass! Often, they are near their end in the very moment they are born. Why is this? The sweet or unpleasant movements, which in other people enliven desires—which are the oil that maintains the fire of passions and inclinations, and which pull and drive a person to seek the goal of their wishes—can no longer reach their proper strength in them. Often they remain, without ground or cause, fixed in a certain purpose that must bring harm and disaster to them and others. Why is this?

<column-break/>

One cannot, through any presentation, truly stir within them that which is called joy, sadness, or hope in other people. Therefore, their opinion remains unchangeable. Let one not mistake all constancy and loyalty in elderly people for wisdom and virtue. It is often the insensitivity of the soul that makes them so hard and unmoving. What would the world be if it were populated by nothing but such people? How little would we have been suited for the purpose for which our holy and just Creator formed us, if we had been created that way by Him? Who would have had the power to bring us out of our stillness and move us to run toward the goal ordained for us?

How little our understanding knows how to help itself when it is meant to explain and describe internal sensations? In our Jesus, we see divine, holy, and blameless affects. # The First Chapter

Our current <term>affects</term> <note>In this period, "affects" (German: *Affecten*) referred to what we now call intense emotions, passions, or psychological impulses.</note> are of a completely different nature. What happens to us when such a movement suddenly takes over our heart and disturbs its peace? Does it not seem as if a violent stream were breaking its banks and flooding everything? Does it not seem—especially in those of a lively spirit—as if a fierce fire is ignited, filling the entire space of our souls with a thick and unpleasant smoke? The understanding, the light that is supposed to guide the whole human being, becomes dark and, as it were, surrounded by a poisonous mist. One cannot see for oneself and does not know what to choose. And those who still see and wish to guide us through their reason cannot find the way to our heart. Tell someone who is angry, fearful, or vengeful everything that wisdom and reason itself can suggest: will it not return empty as long as the emotion rules the soul? Will it not bounce off like a blunt arrow from a rock and leave behind hardly a trace of its power? How shattered must the spirit of a person be who needs the reason of another and yet cannot make use of that which is offered for his use? Under these circumstances, the will knows neither measure nor goal. It has lost its guide and sees itself forced to follow the power of blind and raging desire, which falls now to this side, now to that. The body falls into disorder and must often pay for the mistakes of the troubled soul through pain and malaise. Have not many, whose steady and healthy bodies seemed to promise a long life, found the grave

<column-break/>

quite early because they could not resist a burgeoning emotion? Even he who is most gently affected by these stirrings feels enough to be certain that these violent and impetuous movements cannot come from a just and loving Being who loves the welfare of His creatures. Would **GOD**, who endowed our spirit with wit and understanding, have placed a dangerous fire at its side, through which this priceless treasure could be made useless and ruined? Would the **Lord**, who commanded our preservation, have placed a hidden poison within us, which could unnoticed wear down the powers of the body and gradually bring about our downfall? Should this violent roaring—which makes us incapable of thinking for ourselves and separates the powers of the soul (which ought to work in constant union) so that one stands still while the other is in motion—should this be an arrangement of the Highest, who demands order, knowledge, truth, understanding, and stillness?

It is true: an emotion, considered in itself, testifies to the power and goodness of the Creator. But its violence and vehemence, the way it touches and seizes the soul, and the disorder it leaves behind even after its departure, is proof of its corruption and the unholy state of humanity.
