I admire in this work the wisdom and caution of the **Artist** <note>The "Artist" or "Craftsman" here refers to God as the Creator of the natural world and the human soul.</note>, and I understand that the land would neither nourish its seeds nor benefit man if this water stood still and the artfully placed channels were blocked. After some time, this water rushes in with force and suffocates that which it was intended to sustain and prepare for the use of man. Its fury often goes so far that people fall into danger and sometimes only barely save their lives. Can I conclude anything else from this than that the **piece of art** is ruined and the wise arrangement of the **Master** has been destroyed by an accident? No one will be so ignorant and simple as to not easily apply this parable to the current state of our **affects**.

One can be convinced of the corruption of the affects in another way, if one pays attention to the *measure of their power and effects in man.* A thing that is intended by a wise artist to support other things and keep them in order will, as long as it remains undamaged, always provide as much power as the condition of the thing it is meant to serve requires. The mainsprings, wheels, and weights that are intended to maintain the movement of a watch always harmonize in their effects with the purpose for which the work is intended, provided they are not hindered or damaged. And if the watch goes incorrectly and against the intention of the maker, no one doubts that the pieces and parts within it, which should maintain a regular motion, are corrupted and falsified. We

<column-break/>

have proven that the **Lord**, who has joined us together with an astonishing wisdom, has placed the **affects** <note>original: "Affecten"</note>—or rather the capacity of the soul to enter into those movements called affects—within us for this purpose: so that our **desires** <note>original: "Begierden"</note> might thereby be kept in motion and we might become all the more capable of working toward our **welfare** and **happiness**. The **clockwork**, if I may speak so, the weight, the measure of the affects, would therefore always—if man were in his proper state—be guided by the desires and the worth or worthlessness of the same. I will explain myself more clearly. For a desire directed toward a great and excellent thing, an affect would have to follow that is violent, strong, and in accordance with the nature of the thing desired. The loss of a thing indispensable to our welfare would have to be accompanied by a special and uncommon sadness, in order to awaken the person to apply all their strength against such evils. The probability of winning something that could truly make us more perfect and happy would, according to the order of **God**, have to awaken a strong and lively hope to encourage our zeal to obtain this good. Desires, on the other hand, which are occupied with common, poor, and little-useful things, should bring about moderate, slight, and only half-lively movements. ### On the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

Desire cannot die or diminish. What are a few years, more or less, in a life that is for the most part composed of trouble, labor, and displeasure? We know that even the wisest cannot entirely rid themselves of the wish to live. But should this desire linger long within them? Should the assurance that one might spend a few more days in the company of a plagued body have the power to throw the heart into an extraordinary surge and awaken an immeasurable joy? And yet, what is more common? A minister of the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelii" (Latin for "of the Gospel")</note> has exhausted almost all the strength of his spirit at the bedside of a withered old man to stir in him a longing for a better dwelling. He has accomplished enough that the dying man shows no horror and awaits the end, which he cannot postpone, with a certain composure. He is satisfied with this state. He knows that the noblest desires in the impure human are but faint, and that love, hope, longing, and abhorrence remain lagging in even the best minds, even if the heart is not ill-disposed. After a few moments, the physician announces that signs of a lengthening of life are present. There is hope that the body, already attacked and wobbling here and there, might yet resist the encroaching decay for a few months, though not without pain. This word awakens the desire to live. ## Explanation.

We have one more thing to consider to fully understand the corruption of the **affects** <note>The author uses "affects" (Affecten) to describe powerful, often irrational emotional impulses or passions that overwhelm reason.</note> in man as he is now. Through their violence and intensity, they increase the ill-disposition into which we are born. They turn people who could still be useful to the world into senseless slaves of themselves, who run wherever they are directed by the blind command of pleasure and diligently plunge into the abyss from which they should instead save themselves. They are like a violent movement in a sick and wasted body, which generally increases the disease and completely strips away what remains of one’s strength. Must one not consider that quite evil and sinful which expands the dominion of sin and makes man increasingly incapable of heeding the call of grace, which wants to save him, or even the voice of reason, which can still see a little? 

We will now pass over the harm that these movements cause in the human body and in life as a whole. How much has already been written and recalled regarding this? It has been demonstrated that these movements, where they are not restrained in their power, wear down the noblest strengths of man and imperceptibly consume the "oil in our lamps," <note>An allusion to the biblical Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matthew 25), where oil represents spiritual readiness or life-force.</note> if I may speak so: That the strongest health cannot withstand their repeated attacks: That they gradually take the strength from those senses which are so necessary to lead this

We have countless examples of such people who, in the heat of a passion, were struck by a stroke or other terrifying evils; some were snatched away immediately, while others were made into visible witnesses of human misery for the short time they had left. 

The history of all nations tells of wars, the ruin of common wealths, rebellions, murders, and countless other evils that were first stirred by nothing other than a violent affect. And I truly believe that no race lives on the face of the earth that does not know of some misfortunes that would have been avoided if their fathers or ancestors had known how to master their emotions. Whoever looks at the affects from this perspective alone must confess that they cannot be considered good or pure in ordinary men. Yet, this shall not be touched upon further now. # The First Chapter

...retain the [most probable] meaning, and signify nothing more than making something worse and putting it into a poorer state. We have no hesitation in joining this latter view. It is unnecessary to investigate whether passages of Scripture can be found where this word can mean nothing else than falling into eternal ruin and damnation. One can concede this. In our passage, it certainly cannot well take on this meaning, which is otherwise less common. If Paul said simply that man was corrupted by seductive lusts, the thoughts of those from whom we differ would become very probable. But he does not speak of man in general: He <margin>p. 84.</margin> speaks of the **old man**. It has been proven that the **old man** <note>A theological term referring to the fallen, sinful nature of humanity inherited from Adam.</note> is the depravity, the corruption, the evil inclination that we have inherited from the oldest and first man. Of this inherited depravity, it cannot well be said that it delivers itself into the power of Satan through the lusts of seduction. This way of speaking would be anything but natural, intelligible, and consistent with the facts. The depravity of nature is in itself already worthy of damnation and does not first need to seek the path to it. And it itself is not actually damned or corrupted: The man in whom it dwells hastens to hell when he indulges in it. We do not wish to touch upon some other things that could be mentioned. But it can be said exceedingly well that this innate malice and depravity is further strengthened and made worse—or corrupted—by the power and violence of evil **lusts** and **affects**. And we are therefore certain that this is the true meaning of the Apostle.

<column-break/>

He compares the impure and sinful desire that dwells in us by nature with a man who, through age and other things, is sick, wretched, and near to putrefaction. And the evil and disordered lusts and **affects** <term>affects: powerful emotions or passions that bypass reason.</term> he considers like the things that completely devastate this infected and corrupted man. It is known that such bodies, consisting of impure parts inclined toward decay, when they are set into internal motion, are always more inflamed, made foul-smelling, and prepared for total ruin. Such a body is, as it were, the heart of man. The power of lusts and affects heats the sick being of the same more and more, and thereby causes his wretched state to be increased, and the nature, which is already sick and impure, also loses the appearance of life.

The truth of this doctrine will become clear from what we wish to report concerning the damage that the affects inflict in particular upon the powers of the soul. The power of the **understanding** <term>understanding: the rational faculty or intellect.</term>, which should govern the **will**, is always more weakened and darkened by these movements. All people become aware that an affect that is only moderately strong takes all power from the understanding to bring its concepts into order, to consider them clearly, and to judge thoroughly regarding them. It is no different than if a darkness arose within us as soon as a rightly awakened lust brings our heart into a violent motion. Even virtue, scholarship <note>German: *Wissenschaft*. According to today's opinions and customs, if the world knows that one can calculate his interest, leave something behind for his descendants to squander, and pay for the praise with which he is honored—what will he not become? As he observes this, he falls into a desire to likewise enrich himself and, as best as possible, to collect treasures. In the beginning, this desire is not so very violent. He still retains time and space to reflect and, in certain moments, has enough power over himself to use the rational teachings he has been taught against the attack of greed <note>German: *Geldsucht*, literally "money-sickness" or an obsessive craving for wealth.</note>. The pleasure wishes to master his mind entirely, but cannot quite succeed because his imagination is not yet completely corrupted and occupied. What happens? Euclio <note>Euclio is the protagonist of the Roman play *Aulularia* by Plautus, traditionally used as the archetype of the paranoid miser.</note> unexpectedly becomes the owner of an estate that a close relative had gathered for a completely different purpose and, through death, was forced to leave to the one he least intended it for. This coincidence awakens in him an indescribable joy. And from this moment on, his previously faint desire becomes strong and powerful. The pleasant sensation he felt in this movement leaves behind a certain fertile seed, from which, at the slightest opportunity, one desire after another grows, completely filling and subduing his soul. He wishes to enjoy such pleasure daily: and by virtue of this wish, he remains in constant movement and

<column-break/>

attention to find the means by which he was first so refreshed and enchanted. After some time, he loses a large part of the goods he had acquired with such satisfaction. One can easily imagine that his soul became troubled and grieved by this. Does this adverse <term>affect<note>German: *Affecten*. In 18th-century psychology, "affects" were intense emotional states or passions—like rage, terror, or greed—that were seen as "disturbances" that overwhelmed a person's rational mind.</note></term> lift the desire? Not at all. Rather, it adds a new element to it, making it much more active and intense. In the pain that overcomes him, he compares the current unpleasant sensation with the pleasant one that delighted him before, and takes from the former an impulse to strive all the more strongly for the latter. Both affects, however much they conflict with one another, unite in a certain way toward one work. They simultaneously smother all reason and tear the person away, seeking nothing more than what can satiate and satisfy the desire. Fear, hope, confidence, and other affects are added: and each of these movements contributes something to maintain and increase the fire. Finally, it reaches the point where it seems as if nothing more lived in the person but the desire to become rich. Nothing is so small or insignificant that it could not encourage it. He sees the rays of the sun, which resemble gold. Opportunity enough to awaken his pleasure and set it in motion! Clothes, books, measure, weight, numbers—everything he seeks and hears has something about it that can steer him toward his main inclination. So it goes with us humans. Through the affects, the diseases of our will are housed and maintained, and the lusts that fight against the soul are grounded as deeply as possible within it. The will of man, which allows itself to be ruled by them...

...is imperceptibly torn completely loose from reason <note>German: *Verstand*. In the philosophy of this period, *Verstand* refers to the faculty of the mind that judges, analyzes, and guides moral action.</note> and proceeds without light or guide, led by chance and external things. In such people, one sees a constant cycle of desires and affects <note>German: *Affecten*. These are intense emotional stirrings or passions—like anger, fear, or joy—that can overwhelm a person’s ability to think clearly.</note>, which impart new strength and power to one another. The desire begets an affect. The affect presses the desire deeper into the soul and makes it easily emerge again. The stirred desire immediately leads back to an affect. This, in turn, breathes new life into the desire. And where is the man who can, by his own power, end this game and command silence and rest to these alternating and mutually supporting desires and affects?

Efforts have been made through reflection to find the cause of why the affects are so capable of strengthening the desires of the will while simultaneously corrupting the power of our souls. Certain wise people explain the matter thus: Every affect creates a sense of pleasure and amusement for the soul. Even those driven by vexing movements—by grief, by sadness, by fear—nonetheless feel something that seems pleasant and sweet to them. This pleasure <note>German: *Wollust*. In this 18th-century context, the word refers to an intense, visceral satisfaction or sensual delight, not necessarily restricted to sexual lust.</note>, which accompanies every affect, leaves certain traces behind in the soul, which constantly renew themselves as soon as we encounter something that even slightly corresponds to the matter that previously stirred the affect. The renewal of these traces of experienced pleasure always awakens the desire itself. And as often as this happens, so often is it engraved deeper into the heart and, so to speak, more and more with

<column-break/>

the nature of man himself united. From this, it follows that desires which have reached the state of affect cannot, in time, be weakened or even eradicated by any art or reflection. From this, it follows that inclination or aversion toward certain people or things, which has been transformed into a strong love or a true hatred, becomes almost immortal and very often flows with the blood into the latest descendants. This kind of investigation is so difficult that the cleverest fail in it and must confess that something will always remain that we cannot resolve as clearly as we wish. All the less can it be considered a shame to those who are the authors of this opinion <note>The author is likely referring to contemporary psychological theories of the early Enlightenment, such as those of Malebranche or early Pietist introspective psychology.</note> if we demonstrate that it must be improved. If we may trust our own experience and sensation and the words of other people, then what is laid down here as a foundation is false: that every affect, whether pleasant or vexing, awakens a pleasure in the soul. Surely a heart beset by fear, sadness, grief, anxiety, and hatred feels no pleasure. And he who has truly felt these stirrings wishes for nothing less than to harbor them within himself again. Rather, he flees every opportunity for them: and we know people who would rather wish for death than to experience once more a certain unrest of the mind and sadness which they have left behind. Could this be the case if it were true that all affects generated and brought about a kind of pleasure within us? Are we not by nature inclined to fall back into the state in which we were previously pleased?

# The First Chapter

...found and enjoyed a kind of sensual pleasure? <note>German: *Wollust*. In this 18th-century context, the word refers to an intense, visceral satisfaction or delight, not necessarily limited to modern sexual connotations.</note> Perhaps what we are about to say will give less occasion for such an objection. All sensations, whether they be pleasant or unpleasant, impress themselves far more deeply upon the imagination and the memory than the other things we otherwise comprehend, experience, and notice. The wisdom of our Creator has arranged this so that we might become all the more attentive to avoiding things that harm us and to striving after those that can benefit and preserve us. One who has forgotten everything he has labored to learn over many years still remembers without effort the pleasure or displeasure that befell him long ago. Affects <note>German: *Affecten*. These are intense emotional stirrings—like anger, fear, or joy—that can overwhelm a person’s ability to think clearly.</note> are movements of the soul that are always united with a joyful or sorrowful sensation. And naturally, they must therefore leave behind noticeable footprints <note>German: *Fußstapfen*. The more often they stir within us, the deeper these footprints necessarily become. And if they gain the upper hand, they become like the indelible features that the hand of an artist has engraved in stone and bronze. This is sufficient, I believe, to find the cause we seek here. The impression that pain or sensual pleasure tends to give to certain powers of our spirit can be renewed and stirred by the slightest occasion. We know from experience that a word, a sound, a facial expression, and sometimes something we do not even know ourselves, can lead us back into times of sadness or pleasure and refresh the memory of old sensations. With this re-

<column-break/>

-membrance, the causes from which the pleasant and painful movements arose must simultaneously occur to us again. The causes of the affects are the violently excited desires. Is it then any wonder that these are always awakened as often as the traces of the pleasure and displeasure excited thereby are torn open again within us, and, when this happens often, imprint and embody themselves, as it were, into nature itself? Is it any wonder that a person who has allowed himself to be driven about by various affects falls, by that very means, entirely into the slavery of his lusts and gradually renounces all obedience to reason? <note>German: *Vernunft*. For Enlightenment-era writers, Reason was the divine faculty that should govern human behavior; to "renounce obedience" to it was to lose one's humanity.</note> One has felt truly joyful once and retained a deep mark of this affect in the soul. A small circumstance, a conversation with a friend, a glimpse into a muntere company can therefore easily bring this sensation back to the mind. As soon as this has happened, we think at the same time of the thing that previously brought us joy—that is, of the satisfaction of a certain violent desire. Is it possible for this to take place within us and for the desire itself not to be excited, from which this past delight sprang? And does one not immediately understand that this same desire must thereby become more familiar, more pleasant, and more beloved to us, and gain ever more power over our soul? Those who are not entirely unskilled in thinking will add the rest for themselves. Out of the multitude of passages that belong to this matter in the holy books, we wish to choose only three and explain them with brief remarks. The first is this: **Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts.** Romans 6:12. To perceive the true emphasis <note>German: *Nachdruck*. This refers to the rhetorical weight or specific theological force of the words.</note> of these words, one must note that the Apostle is not speaking here of the evil effects of sin in the whole person, but solely of its dominion in the body, which is mortal. The preceding words, which we do not wish to touch upon now because they belong to another place, deal with its dominion over the soul. He depicts the innate depravity <note>German: *Unart*. In this 18th-century theological context, it refers to a "naughty" or "crooked" nature—the fundamental corruption of the human character after the Fall.</note> of mankind under the image of a tyrant who has, in a certain way, lost his old dominion through the conversion of the Romans, yet constantly works to pull spirit and body back under his yoke. He asks the Romans to resist these efforts of sin and to defend the obtained freedom of the body and the spirit against its cunning and violence. To ensure they fail all the less, he shows wherein the dominion of sin consists. We look here merely at what he says of this dominion in the body. According to the Apostle’s pronouncement, sin reigns in the body in two ways: first through lusts, and thereafter through the misuse of the limbs <note>German: *Glieder*. Often translated as "members" in older Bibles, referring to the physical parts of the body used to perform actions.</note> for evil, godless, and unjust deeds. He clearly notes the first kind of dominion in these words: **That you should obey it in its lusts.** Lusts are presented here as the servants of a ruler, sent out to report his will to the 

<column-break/>

subjects. Whoever obeys such servants does the will of the master himself. Our evil and disorderly desires are indeed such messengers of the corruption dwelling within us, which, as often as they stir, make known to us the wish and inclination of the tyrant who has taken possession of our nature. Whoever, therefore, leaves them space and power obeys sin and lets it reign in his body. Whoever, on the other hand, resists them—so that they cannot properly show themselves or present the opinion of their master—cuts off the opportunity for sin to regain any of what it has lost. The following words deal with the second kind of dominion: **Neither yield your members as weapons of unrighteousness unto sin.** <note>original: "Auch begebet nicht der Sünden eure Glieder zu Waffen der Ungerechtigkeit." This is Romans 6:13.</note> The meaning of these words is obvious to everyone. The Apostle wishes to say this: Do not carry out the will of the inward lust through your limbs, and guard yourselves against using your body for evil and punishable actions. We touch upon these words only in passing so that the connection of the Apostle’s speech and his intention might become clearer. Otherwise, we are only concerned with the words first cited, in which the Romans are exhorted to give no hearing to lusts as the servants of indwelling sin. In this context, it refers to the deep-seated cravings or desires that tempt the soul.</note> in this passage of the Apostle primarily as the violent effects of desires that shake the body and bring it into disorder, or as the **passions** <note>German: *Affecten*. These are not just feelings, but intense emotional and physiological "movements" that the author believes physically agitate the human frame.</note>. No soul is so pure and perfect that sinful thoughts and disorderly movements do not occasionally arise within it. These do not yet give sin a true dominion over the soul, much less over the body, provided they are immediately smothered and driven back into their corner. But if one allows these rising stirrings to have free rein—if one grants them time to truly settle—what will happen? They will inevitably produce passions and violent movements that pull from the soul into the body and confuse the whole person. And when these are present, then sin reigns in the mortal body through the lusts which we have obeyed. Thus, it seems to us the Apostle’s meaning is this: Whoever yields so much to evil desires (which no mortal can prevent) that they are able to transform into actual and powerful passions, has once again granted his old enemy dominion over the body in which he lives. Whoever fears this misfortune should strive to ensure that desires do not go far, nor disturb and attack the body through the passions.

It remains only to investigate what is meant by these "businesses of the flesh" or "works of the body." Generally, one understands these to be sins and evil deeds. It is believed that the holy man [Paul] intends that one should avoid and abandon the sinful works that arise from the corruption (which is called the "flesh" or "the body") and are carried out through the visible and external body. And whoever looks no further than the words themselves, judging them more by our common language than by the Apostle’s style of writing, has reason enough for this explanation. However, we feel obliged to deviate from this common opinion and to believe that "business" or "works of the flesh" here indicate nothing other than the ruling and violent **lusts**, which break out into passions and strong movements. We wish to confirm this explanation through a twofold reason. The first is handed to us by the word **kill**, which Paul uses regarding the works of the flesh. No matter what one says, the manner of speaking: "**to kill the actual sins and works of the flesh**," will always remain harsh and awkward. Furthermore, there is no place in the writings of the Apostle where an example of such an expression can be found. On the other hand, it is common in his letters for believers to be encouraged to **kill their lusts and desires**. And this way of speaking is consistent with the matter at hand. An emerging lust can have its life or power—its ability to lead a person into sin—taken away through the power of the Spirit, through reflection, and through prayer. One can no more inflict death upon an actual sin that is being committed than one can take away the movement of a ball from a distance as it runs down a level path from a height, or to stop the bang and the effect that must follow from a piece of artillery that has just been fired. But an evil desire, a powerful passion <note>German: *Affect*. And they thereby lose more and more of their life until at last, like a crucified person, after many vain efforts, they slowly die away. ## Chapter One ##

...how they might sharpen the power of the intellect <note>original: *Verstand*; the faculty of reasoning and understanding</note> that dwells within them and make it truly useful, nor how they might adorn and equip it with necessary and useful knowledge <note>original: *Wissenschaft*; here referring to systematic learning or a body of knowledge</note>. Others accumulate a stockpile of knowledge but do not prepare the intellect in such a way that it can properly make use of it. The former are like those who leave a naturally good field entirely overgrown and uncultivated. The latter are like those who, in a field that has neither been cleaned beforehand nor otherwise properly prepared, thoughtlessly cast in a seed that must choke without fruit. Even if this latter sort has some advantage over the former, it is only small and insignificant. What purpose does it serve to fill the memory with a multitude of things which, because of the incapacity of the intellect, serve no purpose and often bring more harm than benefit? How much of an advantage does he who possesses a weapon, but does not know its use or application, have over someone who has no weapons at all? Are they not both unable to protect themselves? Whether one neglects their intellect in this way or that, one will be to blame for the increase of corruption in the will <note>original: *Wille*; the faculty of choice and action</note>. ...wants to improve his understanding <note>original: *Verstand*; the faculty of reason and discernment</note> only to a certain degree—namely, only so far as it is consistent with his evil desires—and diligently leaves the rest of it stuck in its darkness.

Many who have cleansed their understanding and acquired a useful knowledge <note>original: *Erkenntniß*</note> do not wish to use their acquired goods where they are most needed. These people strengthen and increase the corruption of their will, just like those who are pleased to remain in simplicity. We have often been accustomed in time to use our understanding and apply it usefully. We have often been shown early enough that the ordinary course of human affairs is very perverse; that the world is a dwelling for such creatures who work with pleasure at their own ruin; that most take on bitter toil so they may please others who are more foolish than themselves; that people <note>The following six words are underlined in red ink</note> <term>cannot be so tormented by any tyrant</term> as they are driven to and fro by their own opinions, which are nonetheless absurd and at times childish; that things are in fact quite different than they outwardly appear to our senses; that the value of most things, the possession of which people buy through sorrow and danger, lies in their sick imagination <note>original: *Einbildung*</note>; that those who seem the greatest, most noble, and most respectable for the most part only represent a foreign persona, and are very little different from common stage-actors. We have not only grasped these truths but found them to be perfectly correct. We cannot help, when we look at the world’s stage <note>original: *Schau-Platz der Welt*; a common 18th-century metaphor comparing public life to a theatrical performance</note> from a distance, over—

<column-break/>

—the movements and gestures of the performing persons, laughing, or rather pitying the misery of mortals who want to walk on stilts so that they may fall all the sooner, and work themselves out of breath to snatch a wind that is harmful to them. To this point, we can boast of a certain luck. It is a great thing to know the world rightly and to see the goal toward which the paths of men run. Whoever would use this knowledge and direct themselves accordingly would certainly have gained a great advantage over their will and would soon be able to cut off the progress of emerging desires. How many of those who have come so far direct themselves accordingly? Certainly so few that one would have to search far to find them. He who has become so wise and understanding for the most part runs the same street in the world upon which those walk who never concerned themselves with truth and reason. We follow the opinions of the world. We fall in love with the child's play of the world. We are of exactly the same mind as certain philosophers <note>original: *Welt-Weisen der Griechen*; literally "world-wise ones of the Greeks"</note> who in their schools zealously ranted against ambition, guarded their students against common delusions, and laughed at the common folk, yet afterward, when the time of the public games came, presented themselves to the rabble as a spectacle and fought and sweated just as heatedly as a day-laborer for a crown of oak or laurel leaves. Our wisdom belongs in our private chamber, and perhaps before a small number of friends to whom we gladly wish to show our intellect. In the world, we forget that we comprehend more than others and—

And it is to be wondered at that men rarely fail to follow the consequences that flow from the false opinions they have adopted. # The First Chapter #

## Of the Natural Corruption of Mankind ##

...thinks never better and more correctly, than when he must determine the lineage of his presumption <note>original: *Uberwiz*; refers to an arrogant or excessive cleverness that leads one to overcomplicate the truth</note> and count the branches that shoot forth from the root of a single unfounded proposition. Imagine, for example, that someone allows themselves to be seduced by this unintelligent delusion: *That man is happy whom many people praise and extol.* How fertile will this same thought become in a short time within the mind of the one who has accepted it? How many other thoughts and false conclusions will it give birth to? How easily and how quickly does this person recognize the means that might contribute to his imagined happiness? How swiftly does he judge whether this or that is useful or detrimental to his purpose? How ingenious is he, partly in inventing new and unknown paths, and partly in confronting those who wish to hinder him? A single opinion that is held for truth corrupts a good portion of the understanding and makes it useless. And just as many false thoughts flow from such an error, so too do many blameworthy and disorderly desires arise in the will. Is it not indisputable that the will must long for those things that present themselves to the understanding as beautiful, great, praiseworthy, pleasant, and useful? The deeper that time, social interaction with other people, and other accidents engrave these opinions and their consequences into the imagination and memory of men, the more impure reason becomes and the more powerful become the desires that are founded upon them. What is to be done with a man who has dragged himself along for many years with false concepts and arranged his deeds accordingly? Must one not look upon him like a crookedly grown tree, to which one can no longer give a bet-

<column-break/>

-ter position? Must one not be satisfied if one can only slightly hinder the progress of his follies and moderate the heat that drives him in a certain way? Judge from this how unhappy the condition of those must be who have either never practiced their understanding, or who will not or cannot use their practiced understanding? They are inclined to fall into all the nets that their lusts, other people, and their own senses set for them. Every opinion that has some following in the world finds an open entrance into their soul. It establishes itself firmly therein and spreads its lineage with incredible speed as far as it can go. It then works with all its children to corrupt and defile the will. Every false concept gives birth to an unreasonable and sometimes highly sinful desire. Every one of these desires, when it is set in motion by something, stirs up an affect <note>original: *Affect*; in the 18th century, this referred to a strong, often uncontrollable emotional state or passion like anger, fear, or lust</note>. Every affect clouds the understanding, falsifies the imagination, and enlarges the appearance of the error from which it grew. In this way, the understanding and the will damage one another in turn. Our imprudence allows everything that the presumption of men has found to be "wholesome" to sneak into our soul and multiply there. This army of vain dreams seizes all the strength of the will for itself, so that it might better protect and fortify itself. The will follows and makes itself poor in strength in order to completely suppress the understanding. The understanding is then so "grateful" that it, in turn, spares nothing to rob the will of all its power. Thus we make ourselves into miserable servants, who... <note>The text cuts off here as the author prepares to describe the nature of this self-imposed servitude.</note>

I do not wish to dwell any longer on the explanation of a matter that every person can perceive within themselves and learn from their own foundations. Where are the wise who have neither allowed themselves to be deceived by an empty imagination, nor applied the errors of their understanding to the complete ruin of their will? I will take an example from the people of my own station <note>The author is referring to the "learned class" or academia.</note> in order to awaken those who read this to think more attentively about themselves and to notice their own false steps. What is more common among the learned than this delusion? <insert>**A scholar must possess many books.**</insert> <note>This sentence is underlined in red in the original.</note> Should we not, before we allow ourselves to be pleased by this idea, apply our understanding to test how far it may or may not be valid? And yet, what is done less by the vast majority of those who belong to the realm of the sciences? One says "Yes" before even grasping the sense of this opinion, and allows the understanding to derive as many consequences from it as it desires. This understanding, as we have already reminded ourselves, never fails less often than when it seeks to pull new errors out of uncertain and deceptive concepts. And immediately thereafter, a chain of conclusions is ready, hanging by a link that we do not yet know, and yet joined together correctly enough. What sort of register would result if we wanted to recount everything that must necessarily follow from this imagination? I must muse day and night on how I might increase my supply. That is the first consequence. And it is already

<column-break/>

equally fertile with all sorts of other opinions as soon as it exists. I must read everything I can. I must not spend a long time considering and reflecting upon what I read. How else would I finish the multitude of books that belong to my science? Titius <note>A traditional placeholder name in Latin texts, similar to "John Doe," used here to represent a hypothetical scholar.</note> deserves my respect and love, for because of the very quantity, he no longer knows what books he possesses. I perform a service to the world if I offer him my hand to climb higher. Cajus <note>Another placeholder name, representing a second hypothetical scholar.</note> can be of no use. How much knowledge can a man have whose books barely cover half of a narrow wall? It would be a shame for me if I took his welfare to heart. All of these are natural consequences of the opinion we have named. And we do not refuse at all to give them space within us. The will must immediately accommodate itself to these conclusions and thoughts.

<margin>Vertical red line alongside this paragraph</margin>
One can see, without my reminder, what sort of desires and inclinations must grow out of these concepts and imaginations. These draw the entire will under their mastery and lead us from one vain—indeed, harmful and sinful—effort into another. These labors and efforts, which awaken the desires, pull ever more darkness and fog around the understanding. Many die away before they notice the slavery of their will, and they propagate a portion of their folly to their descendants. Many see their weakness only when time has worn them down, and they regret in their final years that they applied their understanding poorly and thereby worsened their will.

# The First Chapter

### §. XXIII.

Our wretched and in many ways afflicted body finally makes our ruin complete. Both the natural constitution of our bodies and the changes to which they are subject contribute their part to this. One person is hindered from thinking in an orderly and correct manner by thick and heavy blood. For another, the weakness of the instruments <note>original: "Werckzeuge"—referring to the physical organs and senses</note> through which the spirit must act stands in the way of persevering in contemplation and achieving a clear and pure understanding. Another is prevented by different causes from learning to know himself and the things that surround him for his own good. One receives, in the very blood from which he is formed, the seeds of those vice-ridden inclinations that will disturb his entire life thereafter. Another sucks in the desire for certain vices with his first nourishment <note>A reference to the contemporary belief that character traits could be passed through a wet-nurse's or mother's milk.</note>. The heat of youth makes us unfit to reflect and to accept the counsel of the wise. The strength of maturity <note>original: "männlichen Alters," the prime of life or "manly age"</note> breeds a punishable stubbornness in many. The frost of advanced years makes us sluggish and sleepy in giving ear to the truth, and unfit to change our inclinations. How old is the complaint that the body now stifles, now confuses, and now hinders and halts the spirit in its work?

### Explanation.

Sin, which robs the spirit of its happiness, has simultaneously corrupted the body and prepared it for pain, for all kinds of sickness and evils, and for its end and decay. From this arises the sorrow and the misery of the days we spend here in the land of our trial. And from this very source grow new and powerful obstacles that hold us back from seeking our true welfare and from working our way out of the abyss in which we lie. The condition of our

<column-break/>

body increases the general corruption of mankind and strips a soul that observes itself of all hope of accomplishing anything useful against its own nature. We find ourselves compelled by the very subject we are handling here to present this in a somewhat more detailed manner. It shall, however, be touched upon rather than fully elaborated. The matter is too well known for it to be necessary to be long-winded.

# On the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

**Part I. Qq**

...union between the body and the soul, such that one of these two parts, of which we consist, takes part in the happiness of the other; that the one conducts itself according to the state and condition of the other; that the spirit is confused and distressed by the sensations of the body; that the body suffers through the movements of the spirit; that a free, pure, and contented spirit may breathe endurance, strength, and health into a weak and sickly body; and that a corrupt, heavy, and ill-disposed body may hold down a spirit that is not in itself unskillful, and disturb its order. Men disagree on what ground this so intimate union of two such different beings arises, by what bond it is maintained, and according to what laws the spirit holds a certain dominion over the body, and the body over the spirit. We shall leave the explanation of this mystery of nature to those who are more sharp-witted than we are, and accept only that which is admitted by all: that body and spirit agree in their effects and functions and, in some unknown way, obey one another. We need nothing more for the illustration of what we intend to say, and for that reason, we need not endorse any of those opinions that have been invented until now to explain the mutual dominion of the body and the spirit. We wish to begin with a general reminder. From this, we shall proceed to some particular observations. Through sin, the body has become subject to death, and it carries the causes of death within itself when it is born. Therefore, it must exist, as it were, in a constant, violent

<column-break/>

state of motion. It increases; it decreases. Both require that it be attacked and unsettled in a certain way. It rises to a certain size, and immediately thereafter, it falls again. It consists of parts that easily come asunder, and it is surrounded by nothing but things that can cause such a separation. It requires new nourishment daily. This is sometimes too weak, sometimes too strong, and sometimes unhealthy. And even the best nourishment, where it is meant to serve, must awaken labor, movement, and sensation in its parts. The joints, the vessels, the instruments of the senses <note>original: "Werckzeuge der Sinnen"—referring to the physical organs like eyes and ears</note>, and the remaining parts of this artful structure <note>original: "künstlichen Gebäudes"—a common early modern metaphor for the human body as a complex, divinely engineered building</note> are thus gradually weakened and worn out. Pains appear, as do vexing sensations and illnesses, which disturb its peace and stillness even more vehemently. The pieces of which it is composed gradually separate and approach their downfall step by step. A body that is to dissolve and fall back into the dust from which it was formed—which must first expand to a certain length and size, and then immediately incline toward decline and destruction—can never be still, never persist in an unchanging state. It must always be driven, moved, and unsettled, now from this side, now from that, first by this accident, and then by another. We therefore suffer violence daily. Even the most natural movements are always accompanied by a certain intensity that besets and causes detriment to the body in various ways. External things, our duties, and the preoccupations of our senses ensure that we feel the burdens and the violence of these constant changes and movements so...

scarcely perceive them. They are nonetheless there. And every person can say of themselves that they dwell in a casing <note>Original: "Gehäuse," referring here to the physical body as a temporary shell.</note> in which there is never peace, and which destroys and devastates itself from within. One may judge whether a soul that resides in such a dwelling—and which, by virtue of the closest union, must feel what occurs therein—can ever be in a true state of stillness and order, can ever use its power correctly, or can ever think, will, desire, and work unhindered. In former times, the <term>philosophers (literally: "world-wise ones")</term> who considered this world or the stars to be animated by spirits were asked: how is it possible that the spirits residing in those bodies, amidst such rapid, violent, and constant motion, could enjoy any rest or stillness, and thereby be partakers of happiness? Soon, I believe, we may put this very same question to those men who boast of the strength of their reason, who believe they are capable of thinking purely, orderly, and wisely, and who promise much regarding the power and skill of their spirit: Is it possible that a soul bound to a body—which is shattered and disquieted by perpetual motion, in which one wheel and weight drives another, and most often with unequal force; in which the secret enemy of life daily awakens a new rebellion that always causes harm and wears down or weakens one piece after another—is it possible that such a soul can ever truly be itself, ever truly play the master, or ever truly gather and use its strength? Perhaps just as little as a person who, in

<column-break/>

a ship that is being tossed to and fro and is filled with busy sailors, can solve a difficult problem in <term>geometry (the art of measurement)</term> or set a poem to a pleasant melody. If I do not explain myself clearly or correctly enough in a matter that is not so strongly noticed, I shall nonetheless have said enough that my meaning can be understood. It was not so poorly or incorrectly spoken, what Plato and his followers once said—provided it is separated from their other teachings to which it belongs as a consequence: That the spirit lies in the body as if stunned and half-slumbering; that it does not know what is happening to it; that it occasionally rouses itself and sees a piece of the truth, but soon falls back again and is lulled to sleep by the noise of the senses; and that this state will not end until the bonds that united it with the body are loosened by death. I fear that those who wish to know the least about this often experience it the most. Let this not be misunderstood. The skeptic finds no support here. We admit that the soul can recognize, distinguish, and use truths; we say only that it is hindered by the restless state of its mortal body from using its power correctly and from recognizing and judging everything clearly and vividly. From this, one can see in general how much the current weak body contributes to the corruption of man.

### On the Natural Corruption of Mankind. ###

One must look partly at the natural constitution of our body, and partly at the changes to which it is subjected, in order to recognize how much it contributes to the increase of our misery and corruption. The former, the natural constitution, makes the understanding in many quite dull and useless; in others, sleepy and sluggish; and in most, very fickle and inconsistent. In some, it makes the will stubborn and rebellious; in others, malicious and daring; and in many, depraved, unchaste, ambitious, and so forth. One sees this so frequently, and one complains so vehemently about it, that we would be applying a superfluous effort if we wished to spend much time proving it. In some, even with the greatest labor, one cannot awaken a distinct and clear recognition of the most necessary and useful things. In others, one can indeed bring in some light, yet they lack the capacity to maintain it. In one hour, one rejoices over their growth, and in the next, one finds cause to lament their forgetfulness. We know that there are not so very many who have a right to complain about such an incapacity. In truth, most of those who complain about their poor understanding, about the lack of memory, or about the sluggishness of their spirit, should rather sigh over the negligence of their will and their evil heart, which does not want the understanding to be enlightened any further than their wicked lusts can tolerate. Nonetheless, there are some who are by nature witless, dull, unfit for thinking, slow to grasp, and in a word, resemble other men only in their form and in

<column-break/>

certain natural instincts. From whence stems the misery of these people? From the arrangement of their body, from the unskillfulness of the tools <note>Original: "Werckzeuge," referring to the organs, senses, and brain through which the soul interacts with the world.</note> through which the soul works within the body, from the quality of the blood, and perhaps from several other things that will always remain unknown to us. The spirit lies imprisoned in such a body and at times hardly thinks of its deliverance. We say even more: many are unbelieving, many are doubters, many are spiritual dreamers and self-imagined prophets, because their body, their blood, and the constitution of their brain force the soul in a certain way and displace it from its freedom. Would that those who are called to work on the improvement of such people never forget this! Would that there were always so much light among the servants of the Lord <note>Referring to the clergy or ministers.</note> that they might distinguish the errors of a thick and corrupted blood, the weaknesses of a shattered brain, and the imaginings of a desolate head burdened with vapors <note>A reference to the "humors" theory of medicine, where bodily fluids or gases (vapors) were thought to cloud the mind.</note> from the doctrines of malice and a perverse heart; and that they did not use coercion, punishment, and long proofs where medicinal remedies would perform better service. Lucilius <note>A generic name often used in philosophical dialogues, possibly referencing Seneca's correspondent.</note> cannot feel the power of the proofs within himself with which we rescue the honor of religion. Shall we scold him as a malicious man and a blasphemer? It may be that he is not unworthy of this name. Yet it is also possible that a certain sickness, which no physician knows how to name or describe, takes away the sharpness of his soul. Let us, before we condemn him, take heed of the rest of his being and see whether his conduct corresponds with his unbelief. Cajus sees in all things doubts—

### The First Chapter ###

Doubt and uncertainty: He confesses that he is very close to joining those who consider the effort to investigate the truth to be futile and useless. Yet perhaps he would be more steadfast and certain if his soul did not dwell in a body that is changed by every wind, which is sluggish and sleepy, and which cannot allow the spirit as much time and space as it needs to precisely observe and contemplate the things that occur. We have had the opportunity to deal with some people whose wavering, sickly, and strangely constituted bodies forced them, against their will, to torment themselves with constant doubts. And we have noted in our dealings with the world that none fall more easily into this mental illness <note>German: *Gemühts-Kranckheit*. In this period, the "mind" or "disposition" was seen as inextricably linked to the physical humors of the body.</note> than people in whom a mediocre understanding, a strong imagination, and a sensitive, weak, and pampered body come together. Titius <note>The name "Titius" was commonly used in early modern academic texts as a placeholder name, similar to "John Doe," to represent a hypothetical person.</note> speaks of nothing but apparitions and, in his opinion, maintains a perpetual communion with heaven and its inhabitants. Another takes it into his head that the Lord has called him to improve the world and to establish a new spiritual kingdom. Both are harmful to the common good. Both draw the simple-minded into harmful snares and into danger of their souls. One thinks to bring these deceivers to better thoughts with reasons, with logical conclusions, and with passages of Scripture. But has one also noticed that they are subject to certain troublesome physical ailments and have perhaps drawn an impurity of the blood upon themselves through unsuitable nourishment? Has one also considered whether they might not be natural

<column-break/>

fools, in whose formation nature committed an error? We are convinced that many who are called fanatics, "enlightened ones," dreamers, and enthusiasts <note>German: *Schwärmer* and *Enthusiasten*. These were derogatory terms for radical religious groups who claimed direct personal revelation from God rather than following established church doctrine.</note> are nothing but sick people, who would perhaps come to health if they were brought into the quiet, accustomed to an orderly way of life, and supported for a time with healthy food. We can cite more than one example of such people who became sound in faith as soon as they began to take better care of the corrupted health of their bodies. And on the heads of some people who have incited one unrest after another and brought hatred and persecution upon themselves—not without cause—we have observed with wonder certain signs from which one could conclude that their internal parts must be arranged either contrary to nature or at least differently than in other men.

Unbelief, heresy, and superstition, which cause so many lamentable occurrences in our world, are of a twofold kind. One kind of these great mists belongs to the illnesses of the soul, which spring from a blind and corrupted reason or a wicked will. The other kind can be reckoned among the secret illnesses of the body, which hide from the keen sight of the best physicians and—one knows not how—lead the spirit astray and infect it. The former type must be conquered and driven out through Scripture and reason. The latter is often forced to give way merely through gentleness, through compassion, through care, and through patience. We wish to set these and some other things aside, because they [make up] only the smallest number...

# On the Natural Corruption of Man #

...concerning the number of people, and proceed to something that concerns us all and therefore serves our purpose better.

We know that we do not always view and judge visible and invisible things in the same way, and after a few days, we often consider great and excellent that which today seems mediocre and slight to us; and conversely, we lightly value what currently seems to us to be of no common worth. How often do we almost think that we were recently enchanted, when we believed we perceived merits and beauties in this or that person, in this or that writing, or in this or that matter, which now appear to us as flaws and blemishes? We further know that we do not have the same skill <note>German: *Geschicklichkeit*. In this context, it refers to a natural aptitude or mental readiness.</note> for thinking and reflection at all times. There are hours in which a light, as it were, surrounds us, in which we see the innermost nature of things, perceive the consequences of many truths in the most correct order, recognize our own shortcomings, and behold the follies of this world with the greatest clarity. How happy, how wise do we imagine ourselves to be in those hours! And indeed we would be, if this state were unchangeable and our soul could rise and work with an equal strength at all times. However, this light only allows itself to be seen at certain times. Other hours follow in which we hardly know where to begin to understand the nature of a thing, in which all wit <note>German: *Witz*. In the 18th century, this did not just mean humor, but intellectual acuity and the ability to find connections between ideas.</note> seems to desert us, in which the nearest consequences of a known truth remain dark and

<column-break/>

hidden to us; yes, in which we do not even know how to find the words necessary to reveal to others what we think. How dismayed we often become over this change! And how displeased a wise man would be in these moments, if hope did not sustain him that these mists would dissipate and a new light would break forth from the current darkness? We know that we are often disturbed in the midst of our best contemplations and do not even know how it happens to us. We follow with much pleasure the thread of a conclusion that we have intelligently spun, and think ourselves to be at the end of a labyrinth <note>A common philosophical metaphor for the search for truth amidst confusion.</note> into which we have ventured to pursue the truth. And before we know it, our work breaks off and leaves us standing in uncertainty. We look around: we seek help: we go back and want to set out on the path once more: we look for a guide and escort. All in vain. We are forced to yield and be content with the resolution to start anew at another time, and only suspend the work until we have gathered new strength. So it goes with us. And we believe that even the wisest will not exempt themselves from the number of those who feel these changes. No man can doubt that this unequal constitution of our intellect and our power of thought—these sudden darknesses of our souls, this alternating of day and night—is an extraordinary hindrance to us in finding the truth and improving ourselves through it. If [at all] hours the things of this world were [placed] before our... <note>original catchword: "Augen" (eyes)</note>

Can a person of such a nature assure himself that he will hunt down and seize the truth? Perhaps at the time when we believed ourselves to be sharp-sighted, some unknown delusion deceived us.

So think some who reflect upon these changes of our understanding within themselves. And from where comes this change, which is as vexing to us as it is dangerous? It arises mostly from the differing condition of our body, which, through all sorts of causes we ourselves do not recognize, is made now more capable, now less capable of serving the soul. The spirit is active, alert, and lively when the <term>tools<gloss>German: *Werckzeuge*. # On the Natural Corruption of Mankind #

...can make adversaries of the soul, which desires to think of his and her own best interests?

We could, if it were necessary to be more extensive, add many other observations to this reflection. We have already shown above that the intellect tends to align its opinions with the constitution of the body, and that many have no other reason for asserting this or that than because it happens to suit the characteristics of their physical frame. We could strengthen and elaborate on this here with several examples. Nowhere can this be seen more clearly than in religions, or the various types of divine worship among superstitious and unconverted peoples. The gods of the nations are commonly of the same character as the nations that revere them. They are rough, unpolished, coarse, and cruel, so long as their worshippers remain harsh, wild, bloodthirsty, industrious, and enemies of luxury. However, they improve over time. Their worshippers become softer, more delicate, more sensitive, and more polite: the gods align themselves accordingly and likewise take on a more refined nature. Compare the Jupiter of whom Homer sings against the one who was worshipped in the times of Plato and Socrates. In many things, they do not resemble each other at all. The former depicts the natural hardness and rowdiness of the people who lived in the times of destroyed Troy; the latter is much more civil and gentle because, in the meantime, his people had transformed and, so to speak, put on a different body. The Northern peoples were driven by the natural constitution of their bodies toward freedom, toward labo-

<column-break/>

-rious and violent efforts, and toward war and robbery. And their chief god, Odin <note>original: "Othinus"</note>, was exactly the same. According to their opinion, he was constantly hunting: he strangled, robbed, and murdered. And of all virtues, none was less known to him than compassion, gentleness, mercy, and mildness. We wish neither to dwell upon this anew nor to cite anything else that belongs here, so that we might not be unnecessarily long-winded in a matter that is not entirely unknown.

How much our body *contributes to the wickedness of our will* is perhaps even better known than what it inflicts upon the intellect. The seeds of our evil and naughty inclinations, which pursue us even unto the grave, very often lie more in our vital humors <term>humors<gloss>In historical medicine, the "Lebens-Säfte" or vital juices—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were believed to dictate a person's health and temperament.</gloss></term> and blood than in our souls. Many would cease to be thieves, robbers, blasphemers, adulterers, or those filled with envy and sudden rage if the art of medicine knew of a means to transform the blood that we have received from our parents. And by all appearances, no one can boast that his body contributes nothing to the lusts that move and disturb his soul. The gross vices of many people are nothing but diseases they have inherited: and experience teaches us, alas, daily, that with such innate vices, often as little can be achieved as with those genealogical and hereditary illnesses. We must remember this regarding certain people who constantly relapse and cannot be drawn away from their <term>wickedness<gloss>original: "Unart," referring here to a fundamental flaw in one's natural disposition or character.</gloss></term> by any effort, so that we may not pass an unjust judgment. # On the Natural Corruption of Mankind #

...well-intentioned heart can be paired with a lifestyle that appears, on the surface, to be reprehensible. Our God is just. He will not count an innate disease of nature—a vice that dwells more in the blood than in the soul, a heat <note>In the medical theories of the time, "heat" in the blood was thought to trigger impulsive or sinful behavior independently of a person's character.</note> communicated to us through no fault of our own—as a crime against those who honestly watch over themselves, who seek to please Him through their zeal for self-improvement, and who wash away their daily shortcomings with true faith in the blood of their Savior.

The natural changes that occur in our body provide us with another opportunity to illustrate how the physical power of the body increases our wickedness. Who does not know that the state of our body changes with our years, and that a person takes on quite different forms and ways of life depending on how their body is constituted? This varying condition generates certain vices and imperfections which one can call "natural." Who has not heard of the vices of youth, of the prime of life, and of old age? In childhood, everything is weak and unsuited to clear and thorough knowledge, because the limbs have not yet properly settled, nor have the organs <term>Werckzeuge</term> <note>Literally "tools"; the author refers to the physical structures of the brain and body as the "instruments" the soul must use to think and act.</note> through which the spirit works reached their proper strength and perfection. How much does this first stage of our life contribute to our corruption? In it, we are soft, tender, and weak. Our brain receives all images that one wishes to incorporate into it, and retains longest that which it has accepted in these times. It is, so to speak, new, raw, and unworked; therefore, one can proceed with it as one pleases

<column-break/>

and shape and arrange it however one sees fit. The memory is fresh; it easily retains and grasps the first thing presented to it without effort or labor. What a cause of many vices and errors, which subsequently follow us until the very last moment! Let people care for us as they will; let them set ever so many guardians and watchmen over us: the world itself, in which we live, infects us in these years. The senses are powerfully moved and occupied by external things. Our sensations are as vivid as can be. These, in turn, pull along the imagination; the imagination carries its concepts forward to the soul. We are corrupted through our eyes, our ears, and through the weakness of the internal organs that serve the soul, before anyone even thinks we could be corrupted. Youth is full of heat and fire. The blood is constantly in motion and allows the whole body no rest or stillness. From this comes the lack of reflection, an unsteady and flighty nature, an irrational haste, an uncontrollable drive for sensual pleasures and those things that please the senses and stir the lusts, and a foolish fickleness. What disorder do these lusts of youth not create in our spirit? What a web do they not spin to ensnare us for the remaining days of our life? To what sins and harmful undertakings do they not seduce us? We finally settle down. The circulation of the blood becomes more orderly. Experience gives the understanding more knowledge and insight. # The First Chapter #

[...the joints] of our body no longer want to move and bend as they did in our younger years. Have we gained much through this? We have lost one evil and received another in its place. The natural rigidity of the body works, in an unknown way, to produce a certain stubbornness <term>Eigensinn</term> <note>While *Eigensinn* is often translated as "stubbornness," the author uses it here to describe a psychological state where the mind becomes as inflexible as the aging joints.</note> of the soul, to which one is accustomed to give the name of a "composed nature" without right or reason, and which only leads to other vices. In our younger years, we fall from one folly to another. *Childhood and youth are vanity*, says Solomon. <note>Ecclesiastes 12:10. The original German cites *Prediger Salomo*, the Preacher Solomon.</note> And he judges wisely. The increase of years causes us to remain stuck in one or several follies and to turn all the powers of the spirit toward a few desires, which we had previously distributed among many. Can we boast of this as an advantage? Can a man say he has become healthy if he finally falls into consumption <term>Schwindsucht</term> <note>A historical term for tuberculosis or any wasting disease.</note> after being plagued for a long time first by this weakness and then by that one? How often do the names which the world is accustomed to give to our changes deceive us? "My frivolity is over," says Porcius. <note>Porcius is likely a stock name for a character in a moral dialogue, used to represent a man who mistakenly believes he has achieved virtue.</note> "How happy am I! My spirit is steadfast; my soul knows what it seeks. I know the goal for which I strive. My desires have their certain purpose. I am no longer a flighty spirit. How shall I rightly thank Heaven, which has freed me from the tyranny of lusts and set a limit and measure to the inconsistent nature that led me from one vice into another?" Blind man! Is your current steadfastness perhaps not a natural consequence of the change that increasing age has brought about in

<column-break/>

the body? Is this supposed virtue perhaps not a hardness, a stubbornness, an impulse that inevitably inclines us toward certain desires, whereas before we wanted now this, now that? What then is the single and certain goal for which we strive? Is it not wealth, honor, a kind of sensual pleasure, providing for our own, the longing to rise, the yearning to elevate one's house and make it respectable? Are these the new goods that entry into the years of manhood has procured for us? Or are they new vices that are appropriate to the age in which we stand? *Everyone knows what to say* regarding the weaknesses of old age. According to the confession of the entire world, the power of the spirit decreases along with the body in most people. In the elderly, the brain becomes rigid, dry, and incapable of accepting and retaining new concepts. <note>The author reflects the pre-modern medical view that a "moist" brain was flexible and capable of learning, while an "old, dry" brain became physically unable to change.</note> The memory loses itself imperceptibly. Imagination finally fails us in all its services. The limbs fall away from one another and make the whole house <note>A common biblical and philosophical metaphor for the human body as the "house" of the soul.</note> dilapidated. And this natural change brings forth new imperfections and vices of our spirit. The most common are stubbornness, fearfulness, and greed. And what fruits do these not pull along with them, which persist through the whole of life? It seems as if the stubbornness of the elderly is a natural effect of their rigid limbs and bones, hardened by time. Fearfulness may arise as much from their experience as from their trembling and wavering body. Greed springs not only from fearfulness and other causes but also from the feeling of weakness and

It is too late to strive for the knowledge of God, for virtue, and for godliness when one's strength has dissipated and the spirit must yield to the encroaching weakness of the body. It is too late to properly grasp the great truths of religion and to impress them upon the soul when the soul is being abandoned by the body and is itself weary of its fragile dwelling. ### §. XXIV. ###

Now it will be easy to conclude that man, as he now is, can neither find nor promote his true happiness <term>Glückseligkeit: a term referring to both earthly contentment and eternal salvation.</term> through his own power. The ignorance, darkness, and weakness of the understanding, which he can never conquer, prevents him from thinking, inventing, or deciding anything fruitful and good. And even if something of such things has become known to him through the diligence of other men, through revelation, or through his own reflection, he still does not have the capacity to present the same to the will in such a way that it receives a true desire to obey. The evil inclinations that stir in the will and, as often as they are properly awakened, bring about violent movements and passions <note>original: "Affecten"</note>, rebel without ceasing and darken all the light that might still fall into it. Should a desire to improve oneself ever arise, it is nonetheless so faint and powerless that it dies before it is even properly born. The body of death <note>A reference to Romans 7:24: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?"</note>, the corruptible and weak body which begins to consume itself internally from its birth, contributes its part to making us entirely incapable. Let no one deceive himself. We can neither know nor create and attain our salvation and improvement through ourselves.

On the Natural Corruption of Mankind.

## Explanation.

We will find almost nothing to explain here, and even less to elaborate upon. What has been pointed out here is nothing but a simple and natural conclusion that flows without any force from what we have discussed at length regarding the natural state of man. We have made a short excerpt of what has been proven: We have derived from it what the simplest person can see: What should we add? Man is fit for nothing, neither in soul nor in body. He lives in a world where he finds daily opportunity to grow worse, and almost nowhere finds help to improve himself. Reason, which should help him, serves him for nothing except to learn to recognize his misery. The will and its lusts have torn themselves away from the rule of the intellect. The images that enter daily through the senses stir up one storm of desires after another and deprive the power of imagination—which is so necessary to us—of its health. The shattered and damaged imagination <note>In the 18th century, "imagination" (Einbildung) was viewed as a physical and mental faculty that processed sensory data; if corrupted, it led to spiritual and moral error.</note>, with the assistance of ignorance, indwelling sin, and the daily rising passions <note>original: "Affecten," referring to strong, often irrational emotions or impulses.</note>, takes ever more power over the intellect. At last, the intellect sees nothing more except what the imagination and impure lust present to it. Meanwhile, it still believes it rules. It commands; it orders; it governs; it lets itself dream as if the will obeyed it. And in reality, it is like a slave who may say and reveal nothing more to his fellow-servants than what the master has put in his mouth. It is a servant of its own bad nature

<column-break/>

and of the corrupt will, and obeys merely while it believes it is governing and ruling. The will, in turn, is a servant of its body, of other people, and of the foolish opinions that rule in the world. One serf rules the other within the wretched human being, and he hardly knows that he lies under a constant yoke. Those who should improve us are often themselves fallen deepest into the bondage of sin and corruption. 
<margin>Note Well</margin>
What is said to those who are educated most carefully? Are they taught to be virtuous, to serve the Lord, to despise the world, to rule their senses, to exercise their reason, to triumph over opinions, to govern their lusts? Are they shown where the path to true rest and contentment lies? In a word, are they shown how they should become better? Far from it. What is called "to educate" means nothing other than to guide young people in how they might make themselves pleasing to the world—which nevertheless "lies in wickedness"—how they should obtain vain praise through their manners, gestures, and some outward virtues from those who are themselves worthy of no praise; how they should adorn their evil inclinations with the cloak of virtue, reason, and decency; how they may deceive the eyes and ears of other people and be regarded for what they are not; how they may restrain themselves in the presence of others and never grant their passions free rein except when they have escaped the oversight of others. <meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding the inherent corruption of humanity. # Chapter One

The world—call it what you will—is in truth a **hospital**, wherein he is called healthy who knows how to hide his pains and weaknesses most skillfully; or a **theater**, upon which everyone shows themselves to others in a foreign guise, so that they may corrupt one another more and more and contribute their share to the general misfortune under which we lie. What conclusion can one draw from all of this? Is it not this? No human being is by nature fit to find true **happiness** <note>original: "Glückseligkeit," a term implying not just joy, but a state of blessedness or supreme well-being.</note>. And even if someone were fit for it, they would still lack the strength to seize it for themselves. And if someone were capable of that, they would still lack the power to protect and preserve their acquired treasure from the robbers with which the world is full, and from the enemies who constantly lie in wait for us.

<column-break/>

Is it possible that a person—who can barely half see, who has neither the desire nor the strength to set his feet correctly, who is additionally surrounded by companions who delay him with a ridiculous **farce** <note>original: "Possen-Spiel," referring to a crude comedy or buffoonery.</note>, and who is finally blinded at every moment by the dust raised all around him—is it possible that such a person can hope to reach the place of his rest, which lies very far from him, through an unpathed and overgrown field? Whoever has the sense to judge, let them consider how far all of us, who wander here for a short time, differ from such people? The infinite vortex of business, of quarrels, and of pleasures <note>original: "Wollüsten," which in this context refers to worldly lusts or sensory indulgences.</note> that we call "the world" numbs us too greatly; otherwise, we would soon see that no image fits us better.

Others know their misery to a certain extent and seek to escape it, but only through means that are inadequate and only increase their agony. In many, these two qualities come together. One finds people who, in a certain way, both know and do not know their condition at the same time. One finds others who constantly change, thinking of themselves for a time, and for a time appearing to forget themselves entirely. Whoever wishes to keep the usual ways of speaking and say: "Some people live in a **state of security** <note>original: "Stande der Sicherheit," a theological term for a person who is unconcerned about their sinful state and lacks spiritual awareness.</note>; others live in the **state of spiritual bondage** or of the **Law** <note>original: "Stande der geistlichen Knechtschaft oder der Gesetzes," referring to those who are aware of their sin through the moral law but are not yet liberated by grace.</note>," differs from us only in words.
