# On the Natural Corruption of Mankind

...they would be, if we presented them with such words that indicate the ground from which this distinct condition of men tends to arise.

### Explanation

Who does not know that humans, despite the fact that they are all sinners and corrupt, are nonetheless not all called corrupt in the same manner, and bear the name of "sinner" in different senses? The natural order of our thoughts now leads us to the consideration of this distinction, which is otherwise known to everyone. We have finished with the representation of the state of nature into which we are born, and have demonstrated, if we are not mistaken, that we are all sick and miserable. What remains but for us to show that this defiled nature does not behave in the same way in everyone, but rather brings forth different effects according to the diverse disposition of men? It is commonly said that sinful men live in a twofold state: some of them spend their days in a state of **security** <note>original: "Sicherheit," referring here to a state of spiritual complacency or false confidence where one feels no need for repentance.</note>, others in a state of **spiritual bondage** <note>original: "geistlichen Knechtschaft," a condition where one feels the weight of sin but is unable to break free from it.</note>. Men who live in these two states are then subdivided again into certain kinds. The security of some is entirely crude, carnal, and irrational; the security of others has a somewhat better appearance and is more moderate. The bondage in which some lie is strict, mournful, and burdensome; for others who are stuck in the same misery, it looks somewhat more tolerable and endurable. We have nothing to object to regarding these names and divisions.

<column-break/>

And since people have become accustomed to them almost everywhere, it would be partly a futile and partly a harmful task if one sought to abolish them. On the other hand, no sensible person will interpret it poorly if we, as it were, interpret and explain the same using words that are somewhat more familiar and easier to understand. We believe that one will more quickly grasp the different dispositions of men if one says that some **know their misery**, while others **do not know it**, because these words require no new description and are clear and bright in themselves. If we deceive ourselves in this opinion, we have at least deceived ourselves innocently; and those who see our error will nonetheless have no reason to accuse us of a gross and punishable oversight. We wish to consider men under this twofold image in such a way that we partly make known their condition itself, as much as is necessary, and partly investigate the causes from which it arises.

Many people do not know the misery of the nature in which they are born. **Self-love**, with which we are all stained, paints our condition for us—if not as beautiful, then at least as quite good and tolerable. We find opportunity to constantly satisfy our desires. We are plagued by no worry, fear, or grievance. What do we lack then? Such—

Should we become our own tormentors? He consents to everything that his desire demands and wishes. He longs to become rich: therefore, whatever serves that end is permitted and blameless. Sucking the blood of the poor through ungodly usury <term>Wucher</term>, depriving widows of the small remnant of their fortune, denying property entrusted to him, hunting the weak and forsaken out of their paternal inheritance, and wherever something is even more shameful than these things—these are mere pieces committed by him without offense or contradiction of his conscience <term>Gewissen</term>. He holds that a certain office would be more fitting for him than for another who is far more skilled for it. It takes no more than this to move him to belittle this innocent person and stain them with all sorts of invented vices. The wretch does not know himself and therefore lives amidst his sins in an astonishing peace of mind <term>Gemüths-Ruhe; a state of internal tranquility, here used ironically to describe spiritual apathy</term>. This security <note>original: "Sicherheit," a theological term for a false sense of spiritual safety or complacency</note> of men disguises itself in many forms. In many, it is so adorned that one should almost make it into a virtue and hold it for a particular happiness.

The causes of this wretched state are manifold. In the hearts of many who live therein, there reigns a hidden and secret unbelief <term>Unglaube</term> which they themselves do not perceive. Would he not see that his service to God is vain, and nothing but a habit that has become easy and pleasant to him through frequent repetition? VIII. 13.", referencing Luke 8:13</note>. We are all worshippers of ourselves and do not let ourselves be easily moved to believe that we have no cause for this adoration. This good opinion of ourselves prevents us from examining our true condition. Is it necessary to ask how a matter stands when one suspects only the best? And who is accustomed to concern themselves much with the health of a person whom they consider strong and invulnerable? ...examples of those stubborn and morose saints to be seen, who in the caves of a secluded rock formerly made their reason dull, their imagination sick, and their bodies partly weak and partly insensible through diligent effort. Whoever views them from the other side believes that they have a desire to represent, in their conduct, the vices of the ancient world that lived before the Great Flood <note>The biblical Deluge of Noah's time.</note>. Is this not to be at war with oneself and at the same time partly to know and partly not to know oneself? Those people in Athens run together daily at the market and seek merely to please their ears and their curiosity with new reports <note>A reference to the biblical description of the Athenians' love for novelty</note>, and at the same time they are superstitious in all things and build altars to known and unknown gods to be safe.
<margin>Acts XVII. 22. 23. 24.</margin> Countless members of the Roman Church <note>The author is writing from a Protestant perspective, critiquing Catholic practices of the time.</note> divide their time between all kinds of supposed holy exercises and the greatest vices. The morning is sometimes spent in the arms of an unchaste mistress, the afternoon at the altar of a saint or with a spiritual walk. Man very often makes himself into a diligent and fearful servant only so that he may fulfill his desires more freely and carelessly and transgress the will of the **Lord** with more boldness. One sees that one needs all the grace and mercy of the Most High and does not want to lose it. Hence comes anxiety and fear. One believes that one can stand before His throne with the heart that one brought into the world, and does not know its deep wounds. Hence comes rest and security. **GOD** appears in

<column-break/>

the eyes of these people to be what the princes and rulers of this world are, who are satisfied with certain external services rendered at the right time and allow their servants to use the time they can spare from them well or ill. Far different from these are those who constantly change and step from one state into another as accidents and circumstances change. Gaius <note>original: "Cajus," a standard Latin name used here to represent a generic individual</note> heard a speech on the first day of the year that awakened him and brought him to the point where he resolved to bid farewell to his lusts. This resolution lasts for the first month. His conduct is withdrawn. His face is serious. His speech is deliberate. His caution not to offend anyone is extraordinary. His house is a school of godliness <term>Gottseligkeit: a state of living in a way that is pleasing to God</term>, in which work, devotion, prayer, and exhortation alternate with one another. The poor man never addresses him in vain. And no one leaves him without edification. On the last day of the month, all this ceases. How so? An old friend calls on him and wants to spend his time pleasantly. Immediately, everything is reversed. There is laughing, playing, joking, eating, drinking, reviling, mocking, deceiving. One hardly thinks about wanting to improve oneself. This continues until the time approaches in which one is accustomed to observe the memory of the sufferings of **JESUS** <note>This refers to the season of Lent or Passiontide leading up to Easter.</note>. This circumstance of time makes a new change. One returns to the previous silence and seeks to atone for the committed folly through devotion and order. Does it remain long with this intention? No longer than until a new incident brings a change in the external circumstances...

# Of the Natural Corruption of Man

...makes. If this supposed zeal lasts a long time, it certainly ceases when the days dawn that are dedicated to the memory of the Resurrection of **Jesus**. The spiritual joy that people strive to awaken in others during this time draws earthly joy after it. And the latter uses the finery of the former for its own justification. Why is it necessary to follow man further and present his perpetual fluctuations? We worry that more than enough Christians can be found who, from their own conduct <note>The word "Wandel" refers to one's habitual way of living or moral behavior.</note>, could add what we have intentionally chosen to omit. The world complains about the great number of the fickle <note>original: "Wanckelmuͤhtigen"</note> and the inconstant, who want one thing today and another tomorrow, and thereby bring the best plans and orders to nothing. Of those who are spiritually inconstant, there are certainly no fewer. What a multitude would emerge if all those were to be gathered who at one moment zealously preach against vice and call for repentance <note>original: "Busse"</note>, only to praise those very same vices with their own example which they had shortly before rejected; who at one moment strive to win the grace of the Most High through tears and humility <note>original: "Demuht"</note>, and immediately thereafter seek to win the love of His enemies through jest, lust, and decadence?

<column-break/>

We shall cease here from speaking of the natural state of corrupted man. Many will find more in this reflection than they seek; and many will seek more in it than they find. To some, it will seem too brief and deficient here and there; to others, it will seem too long-winded in many places. What is to be done? We do not consider ourselves so skillful that we could satisfy every taste and opinion. And is there anyone in the world who could handle such matters in a way that meets everyone’s particular insight and demands? We have achieved our purpose if, from what we have said, one is convinced that man has forfeited his innocence and happiness <note>original: "Glückseligkeit," implying a state of blessedness or supreme well-being</note>, and that he is unable to help his own corrupted soul. If anything else has been said too much or too little, let it be returned to us as a minor error, and let one be content with the main point. Perhaps some had suspected that we would treat here of vice <note>original: "Laster"</note> and its various kinds. We had intended to do so. However, after more mature reflection, we have concluded that we will be able to present what pertains to this matter more conveniently in another place.

### §. I.

A clear and rational depiction of the corruption and misery in which man finds himself can, by itself, awaken him to think earnestly of his rescue and improvement, provided he does not lack the attentiveness or the understanding to rightly grasp and comprehend it. We love ourselves naturally: and therefore we will certainly not fail to think of our happiness, once we have been convinced that we are unhappy and miserable. How is it then that so many, despite such clear and bright presentations of their impure and evil state, remain lying in the depths of their corruption? It is due to certain things that fetter man, as it were, so that he is unable to rise and obey the truth. These can most easily be divided into causes found within man himself, and those encountered outside of him. Following this order, we shall speak of the principal obstacles that oppose the conversion of men.

# Explanation.

<margin>more on page 253 <note>original: "plura p. 253"</note></margin>
If the heart of man is to be truly won and guided toward obedience, then the understanding <term>Understanding (Verstand): In this period, this refers to the rational faculty of the mind that must be convinced before the heart or will can follow.</term> must first be enlightened, convinced, and adorned with a true and thorough knowledge of **God**. One can, through certain vivid presentations and exhortations, stir the will of a person so that he resolves to undertake this or that. However, it is not possible to awaken a truly powerful, emphatic, and lasting purpose in him unless the understanding has first been convinced of his duty and the reasons for the obedience that is required. Whoever considers this will soon see the reason why we identify ignorance—the gross and unbelievable ignorance in spiritual matters that manifests itself almost everywhere in the kingdom of our **Savior**—as the first source of the ruin of mankind. How shall we bring people to repentance <term>Repentance (Busse): Not just feeling sorry, but a fundamental change of mind and direction.</term> and conversion who know neither **God**, nor their own condition, nor their calling, and who have never truly grasped the truths through which the **Spirit of the Lord** works in souls? We can spare ourselves the trouble of explaining this more extensively. It is admitted everywhere. It is confessed that a thorough and righteous knowledge of divine things must be present in those who are to be truly strengthened and maintained in godliness. One grieves over the simplicity and the ignorance of most Christians. One

<column-break/>

makes every possible arrangement to remedy it. We will therefore take for granted that which is universally accepted, and only show in particular what belongs to a true knowledge of divine things, and how few can boast of it. Once we have demonstrated this, one will be able to judge for oneself how much this lack of knowledge contributes to the maintenance of ungodliness and the sinful nature of man.

A true and righteous knowledge consists of two things: a pure, clear, and correct concept of certain teachings, and an ability to convince oneself and others of the truth of these things with sound reasons. One can call the former "perception"; one can call the latter "conviction." Those who wish to speak in the language of our Church <note>Likely referring to the Lutheran scholastic tradition common in Germany at the time.</note> would say that true knowledge requires both perception and assent <term>Assent (Beyfall): The intellectual agreement that a doctrine is true, following the initial understanding of it.</term>. Whosoever lacks one of these two pieces says without ground or reason that he knows or possesses knowledge. Those who are provided with clear and distinct concepts but cannot state the reason for them seem to us, in truth, to be no better than those who can tell a story prettily but do not know whether it actually happened or was merely invented. Their supposed knowledge serves for nothing. It gives neither counsel, nor comfort, nor strength when the hours of temptation approach and disturb the peace of our lives.

Those who are familiar with today's world know that those who proclaim unbelief attack the hearts of the innocent who believe in this way, and, where they do not find the heart better armed, they commonly overwhelm it at the first assault.

Whence comes this evil? From more than one cause. Partly from the **poverty of the people**, which does not allow them much time to spend on the learning of religion; partly from their **lethargy and laziness**, which desires to know nothing that causes the intellect any effort. Primarily, however, it stems from the fact that neither in the books wherein religion is treated, nor in the speeches to the people, nor in the instructions of the youth is it common to explain the main truths of religion correctly and to prove them thoroughly. What is written of this in the common textbooks of the youth is very little; and this little is, moreover, presented in a disorderly and obscure manner. Those who speak publicly and exhort the people dwell upon the doctrines that belong to religion itself, and seem assured that their listeners are sufficiently grounded in the main truths and only need to be preserved from errors and vices. One certainly has some reasons at hand with which one thinks to justify what we label a mistake. However, that which has become known to us of these reasons will very little impress people who look further than words. And we are certain that all sensible people will agree with us here, as soon as they have only heard what is being put forward.

**It is entirely unnecessary,** it is said, **to instruct the people in the first foundations of religion.** Do we preach in Rome or in Athens, where people sacrificed to idols? Or do we teach in a country where the faith must first be proclaimed? We speak to Christians who already believe. What purpose does it serve to prove something of which no one doubts? ...born and raised in the country. <margin>p. 531.</margin> But what kind of Christians are they? The name of "Christian," which our listeners bear, must not blind us. ## The Second Chapter

...[that a migh]ty Being created this world and constantly rules it, without mentioning those who have called this into doubt, or leading the simple folk astray?

No, someone might further object, this is too high for ordinary people. We will not be understood if we speak of such things. The reasons that serve as proof for the main truths of religion are partly too difficult, and partly too long-winded, to be grasped by people who are accustomed to using their senses more than their intellect. Why should we make ourselves unintelligible and thus weaken our own office? Those who speak this way have forgotten the word of the Apostle: **God has not left himself without witness.** Acts 15:17. <note>original: "Apost. Gesch. XV. 17." The author likely intended Acts 14:17, which states God "left not himself without witness."</note> If this is true—if the Lord Himself has left a clear testimony of Himself and His perfections in the world—then what is being said must be false; and a wise man, who has not looked upon the world merely superficially, must be able to explain and demonstrate this testimony even to the most unpracticed of men. Anyone who is willing to look around will find more than he believes possible to convince even the simplest of the truth of the faith (which they often profess more with their mouths than with their hearts) without needing any elaborate artifice.

<margin>NB</margin> Is it so difficult to make known the works of the Lord with which we are surrounded, so that the glory of the Creator may be explained? Is it difficult to use the astonishing order of nature—which moves us so little only because we see it daily—as a proof of the **Omnipotence** <term>Allmacht: the quality of having unlimited power, a common attribute of God in 18th-century theology</term> and **Providence** <term>Vorsehung: the protective care of God as a spiritual power</term> of God?

<column-break/>

Is it difficult to lead a person upward to the origin of all good gifts through himself—through the wise construction of his limbs, through the singular arrangement of his entire being, and through the very light which he enjoys with pleasure? What must we do so that men may "feel and find" the Lord? Acts 17:27. Nothing more than to open their eyes, or rather, to show them how to use their eyes with reason, and how to view that which seems common and ordinary to them as visible signs of the presence and governance of God. Is anything easier than to seek out the marks of their divine mission from the life and deeds of **Jesus** and His **Apostles**? And does it require a great intellect or deep reflection to grasp this conclusion: <margin>NB</margin> "He who gives himself life again after a short time, after having been executed in a cruel manner, has completely removed all cause to doubt the truth of his teaching"? To all appearances, those who tell us that the proof of the truth of religion exceeds the understanding of the simple folk are looking at a certain kind of reasoning which has been devised with great effort by some sharp-witted scholars to strengthen the authority and honor of the faith. We agree with them completely that most of these scholarly proofs can hardly be explained or conveyed properly to those who only deal with common worldly affairs and who have made their reason, as it were, a servant to their senses. However, we also do not wish for such proofs...

### The Second Chapter

...prepared to gain something from simple people: translations which are often so dark and unpleasant that even a sensible person, who looks more at the subject matter than the delivery, becomes tired and annoyed by them. How many books, excellent in their own language, look in our now so common translations no different than if they had been hatched in wild, confused, and disorderly heads? Every nation has its own language, which is arranged according to its own mind, its way of thinking, its taste, and its customs; it loses much of its charm if it is explained merely with the words of another language. He who translates from a foreign language must never forget this. He must allow the person whose thoughts he wishes to make known to another nation to speak as that person would have written if he had written in the language of that nation. He must, as it were, make him a citizen of a foreign land, where he should not become contemptible but rather give pleasure. And what do our translators do, who give us the writings of the **English** and **French** against **unbelief** <note>original: "Unglauben," referring here to Deism or atheism prevalent in the 18th century.</note> to read in German? They leave them their native clothing and merely hang a German cloak around them. By this I mean: they let them speak our language according to a foreign manner, and merely join German words together according to a foreign way of thinking and writing. Is it any wonder that these otherwise great men appear displeased in this costume and are often only half-understood by those who read them? But why is it necessary to elaborate on this at length? Those who wish to use this excuse 

<column-break/>

to gloss over their own negligence can prove with that same reasoning that it is altogether superfluous to instruct the people in religion. If it is unnecessary to publicly prove the first doctrines and truths of faith because this has been done in many books that anyone can read, then for that same reason it serves no purpose for us to preach about other things. Is there any part of faith or life that has not been handled very well and thoroughly in well-known writings? Why then do we plague ourselves so much? Let us merely sing and pray in our assemblies, instruct the youth in reading, clear up their understanding a bit, and afterwards tell the people what they should read for their instruction? These excuses are not invented. We have heard them more than once and in part read them. It would benefit no one if we were to name those in whose works we have encountered them.

**II.** This ignorance of the people in the main tenets of religion causes many to remain in their darkness and corruption and to give no ear to the call of grace. # On the Remedying of Human Corruption.

...[instruc]ted. To **come to God** means in the Scriptures as much as to be converted, to submit oneself to God from the heart, and to accept His will as the guideline for one's entire conduct. Our Savior himself makes use of this way of speaking, which in his time was undoubtedly very common and well-known among the Jews. *Whoever comes to me,* he says, *I will not cast out. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.* <note>original: "Joh. VI. 37-44." These are quotes from the Gospel of John.</note> If a person is to come to God in this way, if he is to cast off the world and the corruption in which he was born, and if he is to dedicate himself and his soul to the Lord in constant service, then he must believe. It will be granted to us without any need for proof that this means the same as being rightly convinced and persuaded. Anyone who wished to interpret it otherwise would give the words of the Apostle an absurd meaning. And of what must he then first be rightly convinced? Of the foundational truths upon which all religion rests. He cannot rightly follow revealed religion, nor surrender to the Lord's will, before he first believes **that there is a God**. The word **God** cannot be taken here in any other way than as it is normally used in the Scriptures. He must believe that there is an eternal, holy, powerful, and infinite Being, a wise and perfect Creator of all things, whom no mortal can sufficiently revere. This general faith is not yet enough to turn the heart fully toward the path of repentance. One must, if one wishes to come to God, also be particularly and vividly

<column-break/>

assured that this God takes heed of humans and their nature; that His eye sees our condition and our behavior; that He distinguishes among His rational creatures and, according to an immutable justice, proceeds with each according to their merit. One must believe that *He will be a rewarder of those who seek Him.* <note>A reference to Hebrews 11:6: "for he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him."</note> These few words contain more than an entire doctrine. Whoever believes what Paul says here views God in a certain connection with the people who dwell here below. He believes regarding God that humans are His creatures and subjects; that He has prescribed a certain rule of life and conduct for these subjects; that He has attached punishments and rewards to this rule; that He observes the conduct of humans and watches their ways; that in Him is a justice that can never fail; and that He pronounces judgment upon His creatures according to this justice, so that the righteous can unfailingly hope for a reward for his faithfulness, and the sinner must fear a certain punishment. He believes regarding man that the Lord has granted him such strength of spirit that he can distinguish between evil and good; that a certain law is engraved upon his soul; that he is provided with an immortal spirit that can be either satisfied or tormented after its departure from the body; that no one is his own master who may give himself laws according to his own pleasure, but rather everyone must apply and use what he has or can do according to a certain order that comes from the Author of our life; and that everyone is bound to seek the Lord, which is to say, to strive to [please] his Creator...

And who is so simple that he should not immediately see that from this flows precisely what we seek to prove here: that the lack of conviction regarding the main truths of faith is one of the general causes that keeps many people from coming to the Lord and surrendering their heart to His grace?

In matters that do not touch or occupy our senses, our **will** usually follows only the concepts and opinions of the **understanding**. One must never assume that the will will resolve itself toward a matter with emphasis, where the understanding does not, so to speak, compel and drive it through its light and conviction. One can know that something is praiseworthy, good, and useful; even more: one can know it so well that one does not even allow a doubt to arise against it. Finally, one can believe in a certain sense that something is excellent and soul-healing <note>original: "heilſam" - literally "wholesome," but in a religious context, it refers to that which benefits the soul's salvation</note>, and yet always remain cold and indecisive about striving for it. Hardly has one obtained this from the understanding, but at the same time a fire is lit in the will that leaves us no rest until we have made a beginning of the work. Are we of such a nature? And who will deny that we are not so constituted?

He cannot, even if he wanted to, deny that he must not fail in his loyalty and obedience in any case. These two are exhorted to lose a portion of their pleasure and property to please their master. ### §. III.

In the matters that belong to religion itself, the ignorance of most Christians is no less. How many will we be able to pick out from most congregations who have a truly clear and distinct concept of the truths of our most holy faith and can correctly explain what they imagine themselves to know and understand? How many will we find who can demonstrate what they know only moderately for their own and others' conviction? And where shall we seek those who see and grasp the excellent connection of all doctrines of which religion consists, which is so highly necessary for true Christians? And if these things are missing in most, it is also certain that the true form of religion, its natural beauty, which alone is capable of touching the heart and awakening a love for it, must be something foreign and unknown among Christians. Can one expect anything else than that people of this nature walk slowly when invited by the Lord, and listen to the voice of grace just as unmovingly as an unintelligible cry that wants to disturb them in their rest and bring them to a task which, in their opinion, they can leave undone?

## Explanation.

We wish to persuade ourselves that the lack of conviction regarding the main truths that serve as the foundation of religion would not hinder many from their conversion <term>Bekehrung: The internal process of turning one’s heart toward God.</term>, if only they were properly grounded and instructed in faith itself, which alone is the path to life. Divine truth, when properly received and grasped, has an attractive power, and sometimes brings forth the most excellent fruits even on a field that is otherwise unprepared. One finds examples everywhere of people whose profound ignorance of the basic principles of religion did not stand in their way of coming to GOD. Grace triumphed as soon as it found a pure heart in which the seed of the Word could take root, spread, and multiply. And many only truly learned and understood afterwards—once they were already sanctified and reborn—what they should have, according to the natural order, grasped and learned before they set out on the path of salvation <term>Seligkeit: Refers to both the state of being saved and the eternal happiness/blessedness that follows.</term>. *The word of truth is the only means of conversion.* If this word is correctly understood and received by a sincere heart, it works infallibly: and the saying of JESUS cannot deceive: Those who are pure of heart (those who are only without malice, without wickedness, without preconceived notions, without resistance), they shall see GOD. Matthew 5:8. He who moves one part simultaneously displaces all parts and makes the entire structure misshapen and unusable. He who has grasped this general agreement of all parts of religion, both among themselves and with the whole being, is in a position to save his faith against all efforts of error and to satisfy his heart with an irrefutable certainty. He who sees nothing of this will waver at every attack and often loses the noblest and best things unawares, because he does not notice the necessity and the utility of them.

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption
Part I., Zz

[...that they] should provide their subordinates with a rational and coherent outline of religion? In their opinion, it is enough that the brain does not remain empty, and that things are grasped in the way the common textbook of their country presents them. And so it happens that we do not learn the **science of salvation** <note>original: "Wissenschaft des Heils"; a term for systematic theology or the study of how one is saved</note> nearly as well as a trade or a piece of human scholarship, which is handled skillfully by masters and brought into a proper order. 

And this causes more harm than many can imagine. We are dealt the pieces of religion individually, so to speak—like clothes, wares, coins, and similar things that do not hang together—and are commanded to keep and preserve them all well. We would do this if divine truths were as pleasant to us as the things we need in the world for necessity or pleasure. But since we value the latter far more than the former, we pay little attention to them, and thus, from these individual and disconnected pieces, we imperceptibly lose first this one, then that one. The further we go in our life, the more we miss. And at the time when we need our knowledge the most, there is often hardly enough left for us to understand the speeches of those who are meant to comfort us and prepare us for our departure <note>A reference to receiving the "Last Rites" or final spiritual comfort on one's deathbed.</note>. Would this evil not be prevented if religion were entrusted not so much to our **memory**, as to our **reason**? Would we so easily lose first this and then that necessary doctrine if they were all, as it were, bound together, well-pre-

<column-break/>

-served, and handed over to us properly ordered among themselves? Would not, if our memory became weak in some things, the internal awareness of the relationship of one doctrine to the rest renew the half-extinguished concepts and strengthen our knowledge? Does a person not retain things much more easily that are interwoven like the links of a chain, than all sorts of things where one hardly seems to touch the other? 

We will pass over the other evils for now that must grow out of this way of learning religion. We have already touched upon some of them: and in what we are about to mention, one will again find something that belongs here. A **Christian** should rightly recognize the beauty of the whole religion and the usefulness of all the doctrines and duties it prescribes. That would certainly be no small remedy against our laziness and hardness. Who loves what he does not know? And who, on the other hand, can refrain from loving and esteeming that which shows itself to him as beautiful, useful, excellent, and lovely? 

Perhaps the spiritual knowledge of the Christians who belong among us is in no way worse off than in this regard. The majority of the crowd thinks of their religion as nothing other than an imposition, a tribute, or a tax <note>The author compares religious duty to "Schatzung" and "Steuer" (taxes/tributes), suggesting people view faith as a burden rather than a gift.</note> that the lord of the land has imposed on them to their annoyance, which they finally pay off and yet would gladly not pay at all. ## Chapter the Second

...comprehends and adopts, and can devise such easy excuses to justify its faults. A proper collection of the **doctrines of faith** <note>original: "Glaubens-Lehren"</note>, which are revealed in the Scriptures, is the most excellent means to keep the soul in **equanimity** <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a state of calm, detached peace and spiritual composure</note>, peace, and contentment, if they are correctly understood and firmly grounded. What worry can our imperfection and weakness cause us that could not be dampened by this divine wisdom? What grief can this life and the possession and use of the goods granted to us here below awaken in us, for which one could not fetch a useful medicine from this storehouse? What fear and sadness can the contemplation of that world [the afterlife] excite that would not find its **counter-image** <note>original: "Gegen-Vorstellung"; a conceptual remedy or balancing thought that resolves a doubt</note> here? God has forgotten nothing in it by which our evils could be diminished, our doubts stilled, and our hope and confidence strengthened. And what do the majority of those who call themselves Christians consider this holy **science** <note>original: "Wissenschaft"; here referring to a systematic, rational study of theology rather than modern laboratory science</note> to be? As a necessary evil to which one must subject early youth before they take up the matters that serve for the maintenance of life. One allows it to happen, because it cannot be otherwise, that our own children are just as plagued with the learning of it in their childhood years as we were formerly martyred by it, and comforts oneself that the time of freedom will not be so very long in coming. One cares little whether they learn much or little, and is quite satisfied when one has lived to see the moment when they leave school and may join those who, according to common opinion, have finished learning,

<column-break/>

And those who are perhaps so fortunate that their children fall to righteous teachers who prepare their subordinates with zeal and labor for the service of **the Lord**, very often regret the suffering that they had to endure without necessity from their first years, and think of all sorts of ways to lighten their effort. How much will one make of a religion in the years of understanding [adulthood] that was grasped in such a way? Generally, one forgets most of it and retains only that which can, in some way, come to the aid of the desire to sin, when it is torn out of its context and misunderstood. The part of religion that belongs to the life and conduct of Christians is suited in all its parts to promote the peace of the mind, the health of the body, and the prosperity of men; to make their days pleasant and agreeable, to lengthen their years, to increase their reputation, to make their lineage and descendants happy, and to enhance the taste of permitted pleasures. # On the Maintenance of Human Corruption.
->Zz 2<-

...what welfare, what contentment can be called? The world is divided in its opinions regarding the **doctrine of godliness** <note>original: "Gottſeligkeit"; meaning piety or a life lived in devotion to God</note>. One part views it as a form of wisdom that is indeed beautifully and excellently composed, but impossible to practice. The other views it as a burden that the free will of the Most High has laid upon humanity to give them something to do in the world. The former group thinks it was preached for the purpose of keeping the coarse world in fear, so that they might at least not abandon all diligence in doing good. They claim Jesus showed what we *must* be if we were able to become perfect, not what we *should* become in the world, where no perfect people reside. His teaching, they say, is a picture that serves to shame the **pride** <note>original: "Hochmuth"</note> with which men are infected, but not a pattern according to which one must live if one intends to be saved. Those who wish to be wiser than the common crowd even add—so that they are not taken for teachers of ungodliness—that it is not advisable to make this truth known. The people could be offended and entirely corrupted by it. One sensible person might whisper this into another’s ear, but publicly, it must be said no differently than before: that the Lord has given laws and will demand an account from those who dare to transgress them. Could the enemy find a more poisonous weed to corrupt the wise in the field of the Lord than this? The second kind, which is the strongest, places the practice of godliness among the hardships that cannot easily be separated from this life. They explain the words **divine service** <note>original: "Gottesdienst"; often translated as worship, but here used in the sense of 'serving God' like a servant</note> and **serving the Lord** in the

<column-break/>

unpleasant sense in which the word **service** <note>original: "Dienst"</note> is used when one denotes the duties that a subject is forced to perform for his sovereign. They imagine God as a regent who is concerned that his citizens take on all sorts of toil in his service, and who promises something as a reward to those who bear it. If most people were asked: would it not have been more pleasant for them if the Lord had not so restricted their desires? Would they not be satisfied if the Lord allowed another Gospel to be preached to them, one that gave **freedom to sin**? Would not most answer that they would accept such a change as a benefit?

Such are the people whom we are to lead to heaven. So little do they know the way of the Most High. And what else can result from this but a **fleshly security** <note>original: "fleiſchliche Sicherheit"; a theological term for a false sense of spiritual safety while one continues to live according to worldly desires</note> and a persistence in their **inherited corruption** <note>original: "angeerbten Verderben"; a reference to the state of original sin</note>? We proclaim the doctrine of Jesus, which alone can move and purify the heart. And those who hear us are so poorly instructed in it that they are not even capable of understanding the power of our words. Those who teach and exhort cannot always begin from the very first letters of the alphabet; they must imagine that they are dealing with people who, at the very least, have not been neglected in the foundational principles of truth. They therefore only touch upon many things without following through or explaining them in detail. They derive new proofs from the old truths that ought to be known to Christians.

### §. IV.

To the ignorance that so disfigures most Christians, all sorts of errors and perverted opinions are added, with which many are afflicted to their great harm. What will the truth achieve when it is mixed with lies and darkness and is even made a servant of malice and ruin? The holiest and most important parts of the **doctrine of faith** as well as the **doctrine of life** are misunderstood by those who wish to be called Christians, explained incorrectly, and misused to cover their evil inclinations and deeds. What is more wholesome than that which we teach according to the Scripture concerning the corruption of man, **justification**, **redemption**, the **worthlessness of good works** <note>original: "Nichtigkeit der guten Wercke"; a core Protestant teaching that human actions are "nothing" or have no merit in achieving salvation compared to God's grace</note>, faith in Jesus, and the general and infinite mercy of God? And are not all these blessed teachings so twisted and interpreted by **complacent** <note>original: "sichern"; specifically refers to "spiritual security," a state where a person is falsely confident in their salvation and therefore indifferent to their own sin</note> and corrupt men, as if God had given them for the purpose that everyone might use this world according to his pleasure?

## Explanation.

Ignorance is no small evil: Error is an even greater one. An ignorant person still possesses a pure understanding, to which one can convey what is beneficial to him, if one finds time and opportunity to instruct him. The erring person is worse off. <note>Underlined in red ink:</note> His understanding is already corrupted. Whenever one wishes to work upon him, one always finds a secret resistance. An idol already stands erected in his soul, which he worships. This must first be torn down before the image of truth can have a place. The heart is already in love with a certain delusion, which it wishes to keep: and this love must first be dampened. How much more difficult must the work be here? He who teaches an ignorant person has a desolate and empty field to sow. This is labor. He who works on an erring person must first clear a ground that is overgrown with weeds before he can scatter the seed. This is much more extensive and troublesome. <note>Underlined in red ink:</note> He who knows that he has to deal with people plagued by false opinions must prepare himself for no ordinary patience. And if these opinions are moreover of the kind that stand in fellowship with the desires <note>original: "Lüsten," referring to carnal or worldly cravings</note> of the heart, then twice as much is required. <note>Underlined in red ink:</note> He who does not know that the people he seeks to win are mired in error is even worse off. He sows even into the wind and does not see the cause that robs him of the hope of harvest.

It would be misfortune enough for us if we only had to complain about the ignorance of

<column-break/>

our Christians. What a plague? <note>Underlined in red ink:</note> The kingdom of light is covered with Egyptian darkness <note>A biblical reference to the "plague of darkness" in Exodus, used here to describe a total lack of spiritual understanding</note>: and the disciples of the Lord, who is a light to enlighten the Gentiles <note>original: "Heyden," Luke 2:32</note>, sit in the night of an intolerable ignorance. But that is not all. The little that most still know is interpreted so perversely and incorrectly, so poorly and erroneously understood, that it cannot be called knowledge, but error. In most places, care is taken that young people grasp the right understanding of divine truths and learn to know the Lord as He is. And hardly have we escaped discipline and instruction, but our evil and naughty heart brings everything to naught and gradually gives those doctrines of godliness a form that suits our evil lust. We carefully retain the words and phrases we have learned. We speak with the Scripture; and we would be annoyed if someone wanted us to speak otherwise. This keeps our teachers in the opinion that our thoughts and concepts are healthy and in accordance with the pure truth. Meanwhile, among many, nothing is less true than this. <note>Underlined in red ink:</note> The heart has corrupted the faith, accepted errors instead of truth, and devised for itself principles of which Scripture knows nothing. Man is often quite unhealthy in faith, even though his speech is so cautious and pure that one can suspect nothing evil. # On the Maintenance of Human Corruption.

...who believe that [religion] does not concern everyone, but only certain people. And this class of people is spreading in our days among those who possess power and prestige, further than many realize. One shrinks from saying openly and clearly what one thinks in the heart: And yet, at certain times, when the tongue has escaped the oversight of the intellect, one says more than a wise man needs to see into the depths of the soul. # Chapter Two

## Explanation.

We mentioned above that those who falsify the doctrine of faith and bend it toward sin either attack its entire structure and defile it, or interpret specific parts against the **Lord’s** intent to strengthen their own wickedness. The same can be said of the **Ethics** <term>Sitten-Lehre: In this context, it refers to the system of moral philosophy or the code of conduct regarding right and wrong behavior as taught by Christ.</term> that **Jesus** prescribed for His disciples. Those who have interacted with the world know that some subvert its entire constitution and arrange it in a way that best serves to maintain their own sense of security, while others misunderstand—or rather, choose to misunderstand—this or that piece of it. Those of the first type mostly possess an expansive power of imagination and can comprehend and compare much within it, provided they themselves are the authors of the opinions they maintain. We mention this latter point for a reason. One very often encounters people who merely repeat without understanding what they have heard from others wittier than themselves, yet remain speechless at the first question from a person of understanding. How full is the so-called "great and polished world" <note>This refers to high society or the "beau monde" of the 18th century, which the author views as spiritually superficial.</note> with people of this sort? The second type is generally not so skilled at thinking and reflecting, and they leave the fundamental truths belonging to **godliness** <term>Gottseligkeit: A state of being truly devout or pious; it implies a life lived in accordance with God's will.</term> standing undamaged. The former are commonly more harmful than the latter; yet both types stand immensely in the way of the progress of godliness, both in themselves and in others. One will easily understand this from what we shall say about both.

The first group chooses different paths

<column-break/>

to weaken the **Lord’s** law. We agree that the **Lord** has commanded nothing in **Revelation** <term>Offenbarung: The truths of faith made known by God through Scripture, which are seen as supplementing or clarifying natural reason.</term> that runs contrary to the **Law of Nature** <term>Recht der Natur: The moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, often used in Enlightenment-era debates to justify various behaviors.</term>, which is engraved in our hearts. And the reasons for this truth are well known. Many are accustomed to deriving this incorrect conclusion from it: "Therefore, everything is permitted according to the revealed law that the Law of Nature does not forbid." And this false conclusion, wherever it takes root, gives birth to a multitude of other errors that run through the entire system of ethics and corrupt its best part. "Who," says the sinner, "has given the clergy the power to make the way to heaven as narrow as they usually do? Everything that **Jesus** says must be understood as sound reason dictates. The Law of Nature allows for taking more than one wife. It permits letting go of a person with whom one cannot live contentedly and choosing another, more suitable companion. It does not forbid making one’s enemy so lowly and weak that he can no longer do harm. It allows one to seek their rights through force when gentleness has been used without fruit. It sets no specific time for the service of **God**. It tells us nothing of a public service that must be offered to the **Lord**. It gives all people an equal right to the goods that this world can bestow, and thus threatens no punishment to those who use this right and take something from a lawful owner of great treasures through cunning." Would **Jesus** then [command] the opposite...

We do not need to merely imagine this, because the world everywhere is filled with people who conduct themselves according to this rule, and yet hope to be saved by it. In this opinion, two things are mixed together that are widely different. It is one thing to command nothing that conflicts with another law; and it is quite another to order and establish nothing more than what has already been set forth in another law. Revelation has neither abolished nor overturned any of the laws that Reason teaches. Does it follow, therefore, that Revelation has added nothing to the Law of Nature <term>Recht der Natur: Also known as Natural Law; the idea that certain rights or moral values are inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</term>, or that it has declared everything free and permissible which now seems free and

What great need would there have been for a revealed Ethics <term>Sitten-Lehre: A system of moral philosophy or code of conduct.</term> if the **Lord** had permitted us to do everything that does not currently seem to run contrary to general justice? And who does not know how much men, in their current state of debasement, disagree over the things that are permitted or forbidden according to the Law of Nature? Those who have worked most successfully and zealously on the explanation of this law have, until now, been unable to find a means to reconcile minds on this question: What are the first principles from which all statutes of the Law of Nature must be derived? And is it not clear that as long as this question remains undecided and is not settled to everyone's satisfaction, the

<column-break/>

We wish to say nothing of a certain kind of people who use the phrase "Law of Nature" in a completely different sense than most do, meaning by it the natural drives and inclinations of man. According to the belief of these people, there is no universal Law of Nature by which all men must abide; each has his own, and this refers to this single fundamental law: One may do everything to which one is naturally inclined, provided one does no harm to one's peace of mind, welfare, and health. How small must the holiness of Christians appear in the eyes of a man who wishes to compare the teaching of **Jesus** with such a "Natural Law" that has been fashioned by evil desire? Whoever has to deal with people who speak so many words about the Law of Nature and its agreement with the Christian doctrine of godliness <term>Gottseligkeit: True piety or a life lived in devotion to God.</term> must first inquire exactly what they intend to indicate by it. It often has as many meanings as there are people who use it. **Everyone calls that the Law of Nature which he desires to do.** Doctors are often accused of generally praising those things as healthy and wholesome which seem most pleasant to their own taste; and unless we are very much mistaken, one can say the same of many of those who always appeal to the Law

The love of **GOD** and of one's neighbor are the two main sources from which all virtues and duties commanded by our Savior spring. No wise man of this world has built, or could have built, his system of ethics on such a secure and clear foundation. And yet, the evil heart of some men takes this very opportunity to excuse its insolence and disobedience.

<margin>From the same [author], Chapter III, page 422.</margin>
Everything depends on the love of **GOD** and of one's neighbor. Wherever this dwells, there is everything that can be called godliness and Christianity. We have adorned our spirit with this ornament: to this we hold fast. We clearly sense that we have a strong desire to please **God** and to be useful to our neighbor: this is enough. We cannot deny that we commit much that seems to cancel out this twofold love. However, that comes from our weakness, which we can never fully uproot. One must judge us by our heart, which is pure and filled with love, and not by our deeds, which are, alas! testimonies of human misery. The **Lord** demands the soul. That, we have surrendered to Him. Our conduct <term>Wandel: A person's entire way of life, behavior, and moral path.</term> cannot be led so perfectly according to the law because we are human. What audacity, to use the Most Holy to defend one's injustice and rebelliousness! Is it believable that people who have read the Scriptures have not noticed therein that **Jesus** commanded us to judge the nature of trees by their fruits,

<column-break/>

and taught that none shall enter the kingdom of heaven except those who have done the will of the Father in heaven, Matthew 7:21.

What we teach according to the Scriptures regarding the imperfection of the holiest people and the impossibility of fulfilling the Law is misused just as shamefully, and even more so. We need only touch upon this point, because many upright teachers have already zealously spoken and written against it and continue to do so. The Scripture, they say, clearly states that we shall not cast off sin before our end and shall always remain far removed from perfection. This teaching is correct. What follows from it, then? This—unless we are very much mistaken—that one cannot demand too much from man, and must regard his sins and faults as unavoidable weaknesses. Is it any wonder that a dangerously ill person often falls into a faint, or insults and mocks those standing around in the onset of his fever? This all-too-common excuse of people who gladly wish to remain sinners is no better than if someone afflicted with an innate illness were to say that he has no reason to alleviate his ailment as much as possible, or to counter its violent progress through diligence and medicine. Because we wander in this tabernacle <note>original: "Hütte"; a common biblical metaphor for the mortal human body, as seen in 2 Corinthians 5:4.</note>, we cannot be fully restored. Is it therefore permitted to grant sin all power over us and to make it stronger daily through laziness, security, and inattentiveness? The Scripture cuts off our hope for perfection in this life: but at the same time, it gives us an instruction—

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption.

...for, if I serve the Lord alone and in stillness? <note>The author is contrasting the "quietist" approach of solitary prayer with public religious duty.</note> He, on the other hand, who loves to feast his eyes in a large company and seeks a convenient way to serve God, falls upon the other extreme and concludes that it is enough to appear in the assembly of the saints at certain times to fulfill his duty. God demands that we often appear before His face and reveal the concerns of our souls to Him. He himself remains omniscient and immutable, whether we observe this command or not. He does not need us to reveal our condition to Him. We alone draw benefit and fruit from our prayer. And yet man is so foolish that he imagines the Lord is being done a favor by our devotion. He goes even further in his folly: he believes the Lord allows him to use this world freely and satisfy his desires, as long as he waits upon Him at the proper time. God has, as he believes, struck a kind of compromise <note>original: "Vergleich," suggesting a legal contract or settlement.</note> with man, the content of which is this: whoever wishes to do everything here below that pleases him shall be obligated to speak or recite a prayer at certain times. Whoever neglects this shall atone for his sins in the next world. "Do we not do," says the evil heart, "that which is pleasing to the Lord? Will it then be a crime if we, in turn, sweeten this life for ourselves as much as possible?" God has established orders among men and commanded that everyone behave according to their station <note>original: "Stand," referring to the rigid social classes of the 18th century.</note>, that the greater should command the lesser, and the lesser should obey the greater.

<column-break/>

How culpably do people interpret these commands! The "greater" man believes he is entitled to humiliate the others, who do not equal him in power, as deeply as possible, and to squeeze out all their nourishment and life-sap, as it were. The world was created for him, or so he believes. Its goods are the inheritance of the mighty. To the rest, nothing more belongs than what the former are willing to leave to them. And when the needy and wretched man languishes under labor and plague, he can accuse no one but the Lord, who made him a servant and a curse to the world. Has it not come so far in the world that the courts proceed much differently against a "lesser" person who has committed an offense than against a high and respected person? Is it not openly said that it does not mean much if a person without station or dignity is attacked a bit too harshly? That it is unnecessary to observe the strict rules of justice against people who are worth nothing? And no one thinks that this runs contrary to the teaching of our Savior. The "lesser" person, on the other hand, allows himself to be used for all kinds of sins and injustices under the guise of obedience to superiors, which Scripture imposes upon him. The high-ranking civil servant <note>original: "Staats-Bediente"</note> often excuses all the untruths he speaks, all the effort he applies to embellish unjust claims, and all his vigilance in using the circumstances of the time to the advantage of his Lord and the disadvantage of others, by citing the loyalty he owes to his Prince. Another, who does not have as much power, does not shrink from exploiting the despised people entrusted to his supervision—

What does it help? The malice of men is never exhausted in darkening the light of truth and annihilating the labors of Her messengers.

## §. VI.

<margin>p. 462. Part II and following <note>original Latin: "seq."</note>
p. 152.</margin>
What should we say of the customs and **way of life** of today’s world? Those who wish to look upon it with diligence will soon realize that it must prove a hindrance to many in obeying the voice of the Savior, which calls them to repentance <note>original: "Busse," a term referring to both inner remorse and the turning back to God</note>. Among the powerful, the esteemed, and the wealthy, a manner of living has been introduced which—even where it is not inherently sinful and forbidden—certainly weakens the strength of the soul and fills the spirit with various lusts and follies that resist the workings of grace <note>original: "Gnade," the divine influence for regeneration</note>. Even those who walk most orderly set aside a portion of their time for their labors and business. The constraint they have placed upon themselves during these hours is afterwards sweetened in vain company, through disorderly conversation, through absurd joking, through gaming, and other things. For the **Lord**, nothing remains but those moments in which the spirit is exhausted and already robbed of its strength. Many who are blessed with goods think of nothing else than how they might enjoy themselves according to the taste of their times, and how they may show themselves pleasing to others who are like-minded. What hope is there that grace will triumph over such hearts?

## Explanation.

It has been proven and established through long experience that the customs and habits of nations contribute in no small measure to their fortune or misfortune. Small or modest societies have, through an orderly, serious, and reclusive conduct, secured for themselves the love of their neighbors, along with power, might, and esteem. Yet they later fell or were even destroyed. And it has always been observed that a change in the way of life contributed the most to this misfortune. As soon as

<column-break/>

luxury <note>original: "Ueppigkeit," implying excessive indulgence</note>, sensuality, disorder, and laziness mixed among the mightiest peoples, their honor was darkened, their power diminished, and the beginning of their downfall was made. Rome and Greece would perhaps still be what they once were, if they had not fallen in love with the foolish and vain customs of certain Eastern peoples <note>original: "Morgenländischen Völcker," a term historically used to refer to the Orient or Near East</note> and adopted the very habits that had previously made it easier for them to victory over foreign nations. The customs of men stand in a close relationship with religion...

# The Second Chapter

...of a greater relationship. Truth and godliness <note>original: "Gottseligkeit," referring to a life lived in active devotion to God</note> might be presented ever so clearly, yet they suffer when a people accustoms itself to an irrational and absurd way of life. Social propriety <note>original: "Wohlstand," which here refers to the "good form" or "decency" expected in high society</note> should be guided by religion; but generally, religion must submit to the authority of social propriety and take on such a form as the common course of the world desires. One could show this from the history of the Jews and the Christians, were one inclined to digress. For now, we only wish to touch upon one part of this general teaching, and show how much our current manners and customs hinder the progress of godliness. Should we eventually find the time and opportunity, it will be easy for us to go further and specifically demonstrate that the customs of Christians stain religion itself and, here and there, disguise and corrupt its various holy truths. It often happens that the teaching of Jesus Christ and the ordinary way of living come so close together that either the latter must be changed or the former abolished. In such cases, which are not so rare, negotiators are always found who wish to establish a compromise and unite religion with the customary manners of the world. Peace is made: but always to the detriment of godliness and faith. Religion must lose some of its rights so that the essence of the world may keep its free course. How artfully does human reason know how to twist the clearest words of the Savior when it seeks to give vent to its own desires, or to ease the conscience of the great ones of this world?

<column-break/>

We say that the customs and ways of life, which in today's world are passed off as skillful and decent, prove a hindrance to those accustomed to them, whether in accepting the call to repentance <note>original: "Busse," a term for the internal change of heart and turning toward God</note> or in growing in godliness. In asserting this, we do not wish to involve ourselves in side-issues; it is enough that we carry out the matter itself. One might ask us: whether the manners and customs of our fathers were better and more useful for godliness? If we wished to answer this question, we would have to undertake a burdensome and extensive comparison of past and present times. And how few are capable of handling such a matter with the necessary clarity and conviction? Perhaps we would lack the understanding, and perhaps we would also lack sufficient reports to demonstrate anything certain in this regard. One might ask us: in what way, according to our thoughts, should the outward way of living be arranged? And that is a matter which cannot easily be brought under general rules. If the souls of men are possessed with a true fear and love of God, they will understand without effort what is appropriate for their circumstances or not. One might ask us: how to ensure that the disorderly nature of today’s world is abolished and better customs introduced? That is just as much as if someone inquired how the evil generation of mankind could be converted and improved? We set these and some other things that could be included here aside, and do not wish to exceed the boundaries—

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption.
### Part I.

...to cross [the boundaries] that we have drawn for ourselves.

The customs <note>original: "Sitten," referring to the morals, manners, and social habits of a people</note> of the high-born and the lowly, the wealthy and the poor, the powerful and the insignificant have always been distinct among all nations. And how could they be anything other than very different? To act with proper order, we must pay attention to this well-known distinction. First, we wish to illuminate the life of the distinguished, the great, and the powerful; afterwards, we shall come to the lowly and the insignificant. Those who are great, wealthy, and distinguished in the world lead a life in which everything is arranged for pleasure, carnal gratification <note>original: "Wollust," which in this 18th-century context refers broadly to sensory indulgence and luxury rather than just sexual lust</note>, the constant variety of such pleasures, comfort, and status. To enjoy as much pleasure as is ever possible, to spend one’s life in a certain kind of idleness, to keep the spirit always lively and cheerful, to gratify the senses through daily variety, to make oneself beloved and agreeable to others, and to perform religious services as quickly as possible: this is the desire, the life, and the purpose of those who are held in high regard. All things that are nowadays called "knowledge" and the "art of living" <note>original: "Wissenschaft und Art zu leben," referring to the social education and etiquette required of the elite</note> aim toward these goals. Let us be more brief. Everything in our customs that is called beautiful, decent, or elegant is based on two desires: **On the carnal pleasure of the senses and the imagination, and on the addiction to honor <note>original: "Ehr-Sucht," or the excessive pursuit of status and reputation</note>.** We have more than once zealously endeavored to find other causes for the things belonging to the conduct of today's world, and we have always labored in vain. One constantly seeks to provide the senses with a new delight. From this come our luxurious meals, at which nothing

<column-break/>

is neglected that can gratify all the senses and inflame the desires. From this come the gatherings in which there is gambling, dancing, joking, and all manner of things that no one would pass off as evidence of wisdom. From this come our spectacles <note>original: "Schau-Spiele," referring to theater and public performances</note>, which in most places can still be called schools of folly and vice. From this come our amusements, which are varied in countless ways because the senses and the imagination soon grow weary of a thing they constantly enjoy. From this come the social visits to others, through which we commonly seek to provide a delight for the ears of our imagination. We are eager to maintain honor and standing among others. In this corrupt world, one generally achieves this through two things: through the public opinion of our assets and wealth, and through our affability. He can have an indisputable hope for honor and status who has once convinced others of the opinion that he is fortunate, rich, and wealthy. Therefore, we do everything that can serve this purpose. The world must believe through and through that we are perfectly happy, that we sit in abundance, and that our income is inexhaustible. # The Second Chapter

...of a greater kinship. No matter how clearly the truth and godliness <note>original: "Gottseligkeit," referring to a life of active piety and devotion to God</note> are presented, they still suffer when a people becomes accustomed to an irrational and absurd way of life. Prosperity <note>original: "Wohlstand," which in this context means social well-being, wealth, and the established status quo</note> ought to be guided by religion; however, in general, religion must submit to the dictates of prosperity and take on whatever form the common course of the world demands. One could demonstrate this from the history of the Jews and the Christians, if one were inclined to digress. We wish now only to touch upon one part of this general teaching, and show how much our present manners and habits hinder the progress of godliness. If we find time and opportunity, it will be easy for us to go further and specifically demonstrate that the customs of Christians stain religion itself, and here and there disguise and corrupt its various holy truths. It often happens that the teaching of **JESUS** Christ and the ordinary way of living come so close to one another that either the latter must be changed or the former must be abolished. In such cases, which are not all that rare, negotiators are always found who wish to establish a compromise and unite religion with the customary manners of the world. Peace is made: but always to the detriment of godliness and faith. Religion must lose something of its rights so that the essence of the world may keep its free course. How artfully human reason knows how to twist the clearest words of the Redeemer when it seeks to give vent to its own lusts, or to ease the consciences of the Great ones of this world?

<column-break/>

We say that the customs and ways of living, which in today's world are passed off as skillful and decent, become a hindrance to those who are accustomed to them—either in accepting the call to repentance or in growing in godliness. In asserting this, we do not wish to involve ourselves in side-questions; it is enough that we carry out the matter itself. One might ask us: whether the customs and habits of our fathers were better and more useful to godliness? If we wanted to answer this question, we would have to undertake a burdensome and extensive comparison of past and present times. And how few are equipped to handle such a matter with the necessary clarity and conviction? Perhaps we would lack the understanding, and perhaps also the sufficient information, to demonstrate something certain in this regard. One might ask us: in what way, according to our thoughts, should the external way of living be arranged? And that is a matter which cannot easily be brought under general rules. If the souls of men are occupied with a true fear and love of **GOD**, they will comprehend without difficulty what is appropriate to their circumstances or what is not. One might ask us: how to ensure that the disorderly nature of today’s world is abolished and better customs introduced? That is essentially the same as if someone inquired how the evil race of men could be converted and improved. ### On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

...at the very least into all sorts of snares, which make their progress in goodness difficult for them. One who is constantly occupied with providing their senses with desired pleasures in many ways—one who always worries about how to please others and conform to this world—one who daily prescribes tedious laws for their body, their sight, their tongue, and all their limbs just to appear to be what they are not—that person must always be burdened with many foreign thoughts that are detrimental to godliness <term>Gottseligkeit: a state of living focused on God and piety</term>. At what time should the spirit be lifted up and prepared to receive grace? In the morning? During these hours, the heart is already thinking about the changes, duties, and supposed necessities of the day. No sooner does one wake than the restless questions of vanity stir: "How shall I dress today to please? Will this or that suit me better? What shall I undertake to spend the time with pleasure? Whom must I visit today? Who might call on me? What pastime shall I provide for those I expect?" How often is the entire morning barely enough to arrange everything that the day seems to require? In the evening—or, according to our modern customs, at midnight, when the games or other amusements end? Then, body and spirit are so exhausted from the strain with which one has tormented oneself that the best [spiritual] impulse must immediately be stifled and fail. Even assuming there were nothing impermissible in all those things belonging to the lifestyle of the high-born and the wealthy—supposing everything were innocent that is now counted toward a respectable and noble character—nevertheless

VIII. 15," referring to the Parable of the Sower</note>

Those who do not seek to invent new pleasures and ways of life, but merely stick to what others have devised and made into a habit, are not much more fit for the work of the Lord than the former. The same purpose, the same effort, the same obstacles and unrest. One yearns for pleasure and honor: one believes both can be obtained by observing the usual manners and customs: one pays close attention to those who are regarded, so to speak, as masters of a respectable and beautiful way of life: one conforms to their example, sometimes with annoyance, sometimes with harm: one often spends a portion of one's time reflecting and calculating how to provide the funds that this imitation requires. In this deliberation, the evil will clouds the understanding and causes one to fall into unjust and harmful paths. One lets one day after another pass in disorder and often does not come to one's senses until the outcry of the deceived <note>original: "Hintergangnen," referring here to creditors or people who have been cheated or left unpaid</note>, who demand what is theirs, awakens us. All means that we use to satisfy and satiate our desires <note>original: "Lüste"</note> have this nature: they always refresh and further excite the very desires they are meant to satisfy. They are like the water with which a person suffering from dropsy <term>dropsy: an archaic medical term (edema) for swelling caused by fluid retention; it was often used as a metaphor for insatiable greed or desire</term> seeks to quench his thirst, which only excites new thirst. As often as a desire is satisfied, we feel a pleasant sensation. This leaves behind certain traces and a memory, by which we are always enticed to renew the previously felt pleasure. Whoever is wise, let him judge from this the effects of worldly customs and lifestyles upon our soul. It is clear that they serve nothing else than to satisfy our sensual pleasure <note>original: "Wollust," here meaning hedonistic luxury or delight in the senses</note> and ambition. This presentation of the harm that the lifestyle of the high-born and wealthy brings to godliness will—as well-founded as it is—not move everyone to immediate agreement. A proof that is meant to encompass an extensive subject, involving many types and categories, penetrates few minds with power and emphasis. A person always exempts themselves from the number of those one intends to move, because it is difficult to grasp everything so clearly and thoroughly in such brevity that everyone sees themselves as affected. For these reasons, we find ourselves compelled to touch upon the matter of which we now speak piece by piece, as much as can be done, or to designate more precisely what we count here among the hindrances to **Christianity**. Perhaps we can better advise the weakness with which most are afflicted through nothing so much as a clear and distinct description of the conduct of those people whom **God** has placed higher in the world than others. One often sees the consequences of a matter immediately, as soon as one truly learns to know it: and the understanding is generally reached more quickly when the imagination also finds something to do during a proof.
