...others may judge whether people can be found who resemble these images, if not in all things, then in the most prominent ones.

*Pompejus* <note>The author uses this classical name as a pseudonym for a typical high-ranking official or courtier of the time.</note> occupies a position among the primary servants of a distinguished court. His intellect has placed him in the favor of his lord, and his loyalty and vigilance keep him there. He knows the strengths and weaknesses of the country and knows how to use the former skillfully and how to hide the latter from the eyes of the world. He works tirelessly and sometimes squanders his strength with great diligence so that nothing is overlooked. This is his way of life: He denies himself sleep early in the morning and hurries to the business that awaits him in great quantities. He considers everything carefully, thinks, decides, and executes until the time comes when he must either give the Prince an account of what has happened and what should happen, or appear in an assembly of other officials. The day is more than half over before he returns. He almost always dines in the company of others and strives to be cheerful and alert among them. And for this, means are at hand: the blood is heated by foreign wines and well-prepared foods, and the head is weighed down with all sorts of vapors. He is granted no rest after the table to compose himself. Social propriety requires that he allow all sorts of people to come before him who wish to recommend themselves to his favor, ask after his health, or present something related to his office. And these people take up the few hours that pass until the time when he must either attend the assemblies at court or—

<column-break/>

—seek opportunity elsewhere to gather his spirits and put them back in order. Sometimes he joins those who are gambling. Sometimes he speaks now with this person, now with that, about things that mean nothing. He is seldom permitted to entertain his thoughts alone or to seek his pleasure as he wishes. A man of his kind must always be in motion. He returns home late and exhausted and finds so many things yet to be done that he must postpone his necessary rest for several more hours. Thus, most of his days pass. Some are even more laborious and vexing. Others are somewhat quieter but just as detrimental to the true peace of the soul. When he is perhaps able to attend a church service, he rises from the table where he has been occupied either with the investigation of a tangled matter, or reading and weighing all sorts of petitions, or examining a new draft or proposal—that is to say, he is burdened with nothing but worldly thoughts. He leaves with the intention that, as soon as the hour of devotion is over, he will continue the work he has started and, in the meantime, forget nothing of what he has noted. And he carries out this resolution as soon as he can. Half of the day belongs to the state, along with a portion of the night. The other half belongs partly to the refreshment of the body and partly to the worldly wisdom and the way of life common among the great. What remains for the Lord? When does *Pompejus* have the time and strength to examine the innermost parts of his heart and to watch over his desires? When does he find the quiet hours necessary for the earnest contemplation of time and eternity? He is great in the eyes of the world. His loyalty is [the cause of] favor and—

# Chapter Two

...honor that he receives. Lord! How much capacity does the constant noise in which he lives allow him to honor your grace and to become submissive to the power of your Spirit?

Charinus <note>Like "Pompejus" on the previous page, "Charinus" is a name borrowed from classical literature—common in the 18th century—to represent a specific social type: the wealthy, private gentleman.</note> is well-bred and was prepared in good time for the service of the world. He is moderately instructed in some sciences and can spend several hours with pleasure over a book written with wit and understanding. His fathers left him a considerable fortune. And he has greatly increased this store through a respectable marriage and orderly household management. He desires no office or service. Court life seems to him a magnificent slavery. The other positions he might perhaps obtain seem to him laborious and tedious. He wishes to enjoy his property in an independent state <note>A "stand" or "state" refers to one's social class or vocation. Charinus chooses to be a private "rentier" rather than a working official.</note> and live according to the desires of the great ones of the world. The honorary title he bears was only accepted so that he might occupy a certain place in society and not have to yield to everyone <note>In the strict social hierarchy of the time, a title was necessary simply to avoid being seated at the bottom of the table or yielding the path to others.</note>. How does Charinus live? Half the year is spent at home, half with others. He has handed over the management of his affairs to people of whose loyalty he is certain. At home, he always sees a number of friends who take part in his pleasure and wish to enjoy the world with him. And he is glad to see them. A quiet and solitary life seems to him to be the shadow of the grave and of death. His house is well-built and decorated. His rooms are adorned as often as human vanity has devised a new type of finery

<column-break/>

devised. His table is so furnished that everyone, whatever their taste may be, can rise from it satisfied. He lacks nothing in order to drive away all restless and morose thoughts from his daily arriving guests. Now he fishes, now he hunts, now he plays games, now he jokes, now he creates a new and unexpected pleasure. He knows how to adjust himself to each person’s temperament and to say to everyone what they like to hear. No one must say that they have not been particularly honored and pleased by him. So that he may never find a lack of things to say to each according to their particular inclination and to tell for amusement, he spends several hours every morning reading such books in which travels to remote lands, strange occurrences and histories, lively ideas, foolish worldly affairs, and secret events of great lords and their courts are told. His memory is a storehouse from which everyone can take what is fitting and pleasing to them. And he strives to present everything with liveliness and eloquence. The time he spends with others passes in the same way. Everyone strives to receive and please him no worse than they were received and pleased by him. Daily changes, festivities, new companies, and pleasures. Charinus has the reputation in the world that no one knows how to live better than he, no one can entertain his guests more skillfully, no one can more pleasantly sustain and cheer a whole company. How much glory does he have before the Lord? Does he also remember that every human being was created for a certain purpose...

And when does the Lord find it so quiet and empty that he can enter into him and *sup with him?* <note>original Latin reference: Offenb. Joh. III. 20 (Revelation 3:20)</note>

Theagenes <note>Like "Charinus" on the preceding page, "Theagenes" is a name borrowed from classical literature—a common literary device in the 1700s—to represent a specific social archetype: the ambitious young courtier.</note>, a young man of status <term>Stand: one’s fixed social rank or class</term>, has dedicated himself to the service of the court, and through his intellect and friends has already obtained the management of a small office, and the certain hope of a greater one. It is necessary that he establish himself in the advantages he has already gained and move further ahead. He must therefore seek to acquire the reputation of being a man of a proper and pleasing nature, able to accommodate himself to anyone, and one who rightly understands the "art of living." He must, in a word, know how to fit into the world and adopt the customs that belong to the "well-being" of people of his kind. He does what he must, and sets as his models those who are praised by most as people knowledgeable of the world. The day begins at nine or ten o'clock in the morning in his chamber and ends at two o'clock at night. The first hours of the day are spent partly on the "awakening of the life-spirits" <note>A contemporary medical-philosophical concept referring to the stimulation of the nerves and vitality after waking.</note> and partly on finery <term>Putz: elaborate dress and grooming</term>. What a mistake it would be if someone could find a flaw in his clothing! During this time, a friend occasionally visits him who

<column-break/>

speaks with him of yesterday's pleasure, of the gain and loss of a game <note>Likely referring to high-stakes gambling or cards, a common courtly pastime.</note>, of new reports from the court, of incoming news of war, state, and peace, of the best way to "shorten the time" <note>A literal translation of "Zeit-Verkürzung," meaning pastimes or entertainment used to ward off boredom.</note>, and other even worse things. And how lucky it is if the conversation goes no further, nor attacks the honest names of other people, or even faith and godliness? If he remains alone, he reads a book that does not particularly tire the mind: a newspaper, a poem, a piece of a romantic or heroic tale. If he does take up something serious, it concerns his office, his income, or his future advancement. Why bother with the rest of the "rubbish" that people call science, the knowledge of God, and reason? He appears at court at the proper time, in adornment that is popular among people of good taste, and lets it be his chief concern that he might please. And what is necessary for this purpose? He must put forward nothing that has the appearance of wisdom or reason. Above all, he must say all sorts of things to the "weaker sex" <note>A common 18th-century idiom for women.</note> that flatter their imagination, turn their weaknesses into virtues, and praise their clothing, ribbons, lace, and head-dresses; he must always have a ridiculous story at hand, a report of a new fashion, or an example of "civic simplicity" <note>Used here sarcastically to mean the perceived lack of sophistication in the middle classes.</note>; he must know how to play the part of one "enchanted" where necessary, and never allow it to be said that he lacked clever ideas. He must speak with everyone according to their particular temperament and seek at every opportunity to investigate their secrets...

## The Second Chapter

...find. One must never find him otherwise than cheerful and alert; that is, he must always bring forth things that no one can cite as evidence of his wit, and which in a company of clever people would certainly be called follies and useless words. It must cost him nothing to call an absurd deed sensible, an ugly person beautiful, a childish joke a brilliant idea, a vain display a majestic and engaging nature, and an obvious vice a virtue. There is no greater mistake than if he were carelessly to lead someone to the opinion that he is not happy, not satisfied, or not calm and composed. After the meal, it is his duty to run about and, as they say, "pay his respects" at various places. Thus, he stays here for a while, there for a few moments, and strives everywhere—through excessive politeness, through a forced modesty, through calculated gestures and postures, through several well-considered questions, and through a short conversation about the weather and wind or other common things—to leave behind the reputation of being a skillful, polite, and refined man. He can never feel a lack of words on these occasions. The first thing that presents itself to him can bring about the conversation that decorum <term>Wohlstand: in this context, it refers to the social propriety, etiquette, and "good breeding" expected of the upper classes</term> requires. Toward evening, he seeks a gathering either at court or elsewhere, in which he can speak more freely and recover from the burden of the day. He knows the houses where gaming <note>referring to gambling or card games</note> takes place, or where many people gather to pass the time with one another. At times there are plays or other public amusements. A person

<column-break/>

of his kind must miss nothing of such things. At times, he invites to his home those with whom he found opportunity to enjoy himself, and provides them with the very same pleasure he enjoyed with them. Most often, he falls into a company of such people who wish to amuse themselves with games or who love strong drink. What use would reason, religion, modesty, and thoughtfulness be there? He does as the others do and lives according to the rules of "liberty" <note>The author uses "liberty" (Freyheit) ironically here to mean a lack of moral restraint</note> that prevail in such meetings. He speaks just as boldly against religion as against the love of one's neighbor, especially when spirits are heated. And most often, after midnight, he takes a burdened body, a wasted and confused head, a stained conscience, the sinful intention to continue this way of life, and sometimes a debt made at play back into his chamber. Is it not absolutely necessary that, with this way of life, the seed of truth and godliness that was instilled in his young heart must be choked? Charinus <note>Charinus is another name used by the author to personify the "man of the world." And is it possible that the Spirit of the Lord could find a place in such souls to work?

Chariclea, a woman of means and noble birth, intends to lead her life as is customary among people of her rank. She is so married that this intention finds few or no obstacles, and she has so much wit that she can imitate others in this matter or even surpass them. The arrangement is easily made.

The day consists of fourteen or fifteen hours. The first three are spent awakening the spirits numbed by sleep, playing with dogs or birds, and at the dressing table <note>Putze: This refers to the "toilette," the elaborate and lengthy process of grooming, hair-styling, and dressing common among the 18th-century elite</note>. Two hours are used either to visit others or to talk with those by whom she is visited. The remaining five must pass either in gaming <note>referring to card games or gambling</note> or in other cheerful company. She likes no one around her more than those who can laugh with her at the clothing, behavior, and gestures of other people, pour out antics and silly jests, provide new reports of worthless things, and keep the heart in constant motion and cheerfulness. If someone comes who speaks more modestly and happens upon the topics of reason, virtue, and godliness, she is deaf and full of other thoughts, or knows how to find more than one reason to withdraw from the company of such a tedious schoolmaster. The care of the household belongs, as she believes, only to people of low birth and spirit. The education of children is in the hands of those appointed to it; and she insists that they be led toward a freedom and liveliness appropriate to their station and be spared from strict lessons of virtue. It is easy, she thinks, to ruin a noble and exalted spirit in youth and make it slavish if it is challenged too sharply and enclosed in narrow bounds. # On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

Are these impulses not from the greatest enemies of our souls? Those who engage in trade and commerce commonly allow themselves to be so strongly consumed by the greed for profit <note>original: "Gewinnsucht"</note> that they consider almost nothing a vice if it serves to satisfy that greed. Those who must seek their livelihood through the labor of their hands become just as base in spirit as the physical objects they handle; under the constant exhaustion of the body, they gradually lose both the strength and the desire to lift their spirit toward devotion and contemplation. The Word of the Lord is heard out of habit. And even when it is heard with some attention, it cannot work for long in such hearts, which either hurry back to their business immediately or ease the hardship of their lives with sinful and disorderly amusements.

### Explanation

The Kingdom of God has from the beginning found more acceptance and love among the lowly and despised of this world than among the wealthy and powerful of the earth. And as far as we can judge people—whose hearts are otherwise closed to us—things are no different in our own times. Nevertheless, godlessness and disorder among those belonging to the lower classes are great and are growing rather than decreasing. In one place, one sees a bit more outward decency and discipline than in another; there, people complain less than here about open horrors, shame, and vice. Yet where is the blessed region where one has no cause to lament the blindness, ignorance, laziness, and coldness of the majority, and to long for improvement? Where are the congregations of which one could boast that they consist of more truly pious and righteous people than of the wicked and "mouth-Christians" <note>original: "Mund-Christen" — a term used to describe those who are Christian in name only, professing faith with their mouths but not living it in their hearts</note>?

<column-break/>

Even where things are at their best, there is more appearance of godliness than power. In most places, the ministers of the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelii"</note> must sustain themselves with the thought that the eyes of the flesh cannot discover the hidden seed of the Lord, and that the Savior <note>original: "Heyland"</note> has established an invisible kingdom everywhere in the midst of a perverse generation. This misery is nurtured and maintained by many causes; among these, the way of life of people who must earn their bread through labor and toil seems to us to be not the least significant. One may judge from what we intend to mention whether we are mistaken in this opinion. If it seems to some that we have said either too much or too little, let them remember that no one can compose such general descriptions without provoking these thoughts in some. How is it possible to describe the so manifold ways, habits, temperaments, and customs of—

## Chapter Two

...unite people in such a short description, so that everyone might overlook the whole essence of the world at once and find nowhere anything to take away or to add?

We wish to begin with two primary observations <note>The author uses "Erinnerungen" (reminders/observations) to frame his argument</note> that extend across almost our entire Church and which will give those who wish to reflect a significant light to understand the basis of the disorderly conduct of many people. The first: Most people living in the middle or lower classes are only moderately or poorly instructed in religion during the first years of their lives. The second: The lesser families and social ranks spare no effort to abolish the difference between the classes of this world, and to move as close as possible to the higher ones through their outward appearance. Here one sees two fertile mothers of many disorders and vices that prevail among men. We have already dealt with the damage caused by ignorance above. People who hardly grasp the first letters of Christian doctrine in their younger years, and are placed into burdensome service with this meager knowledge, must in a short time lose even the little they know. And what benefit can these unprepared souls later draw from reading the Bible and public exhortations? In what way can they be won over and brought to a true change of heart and will? Is it not obvious that the majority lets the reins of their inclinations loose in this dangerous state—

<column-break/>

—and places godliness in the mere observation of external exercises of worship? We do not wish to repeat here what was mentioned shortly before regarding this matter. The blind desire to imitate people of higher status has now become a general plague and sickness. The proud man imagines that he has been wronged by Providence, that he has been placed lower than his gifts and merits require, and that a spirit of his kind and sort was suited for greater things. One does not exactly want to argue with God. However, one creates an idol for oneself upon which one can pour out one's resentment without danger: and this one calls Fortune <note>original: "das Glücke." In this context, it refers to the personified concept of Luck or Fate, often depicted as a fickle goddess</note>. How many curses and complaints are cast out against this shadow, which our imagination has turned into a ruling being? It is blind, perverse, frivolous, fickle: it acts neither according to right nor fairness: it takes pleasure in constant confusion and disorder: it makes gods out of stones and blocks <note>Meaning: Fortune elevates unworthy, "stiff" or "dumb" people to high status</note>: and those who could be gods <note>i.e., those with true merit and talent</note>, it banishes to a corner where they are hardly seen, and even less greeted. Is it a sin and wrong to resist this strange regent, and to create justice for oneself against its peculiar stubbornness as far as possible? And what advice is there for this? To abolish the orders themselves, which are once firmly established in the world, is impossible, or at least far too difficult for those who are not satisfied with them. Out of thousands, barely one succeeds in swinging himself from his low rank into a far higher one. There remains therefore nothing...

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption #

...nothing remains but to approach those whom one cannot reach in any other way through clothing, manners, and other things. This is, so to speak, a way to defy unfair fortune and publicly testify that one considers its rule to be unjust, judging oneself worthy of a far higher status. Most people look at the type of person closest to them and model themselves entirely after their pattern and example, regardless of whether their wealth or other circumstances can support the intentions of their puffed-up heart. Many strive to climb even higher and to unite the lowliness of their status and trade with the fortune and splendor of the high-ranking. No one wants to remain what they are. It is obvious what evil consequences arise from this plague. Such a swollen spirit, intent on nothing more than satisfying its desire for honor <note>original: "Ehr-Begierde"; refers to a vain ambition for social status</note>, at first suffers neither punishment nor admonition. Even if it could still endure one of these two, the sense of what is good is nearly stifled because it is too heavily burdened with foreign concepts belonging to the world. What shall we say of the sins and vices that grow from this? One deceives and cheats those whom one should never look upon with anything but pure respect and love. One borrows and lends without thinking about whether and how the debt can be repaid. One disturbs the peace of one's house and lineage. One tears up the foundation of one's earthly prosperity. One makes oneself an enemy and traitor to one's own people, and prepares steps toward the pit of misery for those for whom one should be building houses. One

<column-break/>

awakens the envy and enmity of one's fellow citizens, and thereby robs oneself of a support in days of adversity. One even leads one's own children onto the path of debauchery and luxury, which may one day lead them to ruin. What words are sufficient to describe the ugliness of a desire from which so many evil consequences arise? And in what way shall we move people to repentance and godliness <term>Gottseligkeit</term> <note>A central term in German Pietism, referring to a life of active, sincere devotion to God</note> who are afflicted with such a harmful sickness of the soul? The great and high world is in constant motion, striving to climb higher and to distance itself from the low and humble through various arts and inventions. The low and humble world grows ever more fervent in its desire to move closer to the great and high, and pursues them tirelessly, no matter how arduous the path may be. What must we fear, we who see this? Nothing but that both will finally plunge down into the abyss and lose their eternal prosperity alongside their earthly well-being.

Those who belong to the low world can be divided, to some extent, into two main categories. Some conduct trade and industry; others seek their bread through the labor of their hands. Both ways of life are filled with toil, worry, and grief. He who trades first tests the power of his spirit and then drives the body and its limbs to carry out the thoughts and conclusions of the soul. He who must earn his nourishment with his hand tires the body incessantly and, through this constant motion, takes away

A slight change in the weather, in the seasons, in opinions, and in many other things can become a cause of poverty and misery for him. People who live in such uncertainty are constantly driven to and fro by the two movements that have such strong power over our souls—I mean, fear and hope—and hardly reach a true stability of the heart. Meanwhile, they wish and long, by virtue of an implanted drive, to escape this unrest and to reach a true stillness and contentment of the heart. What new cares does this wish create? But that is not all. One further believes that the use of these pleasures must be unrestricted and completely unbound, and must not cease until reason is fully conquered and driven from its seat. A pleasure that concludes in manifest **frenzy** <note>original: "Raserey"; a state of wild, irrational excitement or madness</note> is the best, in the opinion of the world. Where measure, rule, and order are observed, there is constraint: And what is a pleasure that is accompanied and tempered by fear and constraint? The cheerful gatherings of this world are thus nothing but societies of people who have resolved—amidst bold, irrational, and unruly chatter or other offensive pastimes—to consume so much strong drink until they have lost everything that makes them human, and have become similar to irrational creatures, or at the very least, to those people whom one is accustomed to lock up and imprison in well-ordered countries

<column-break/>

so that they may harm no one. He has honor enough who has become foolish later than the others, or who has brought enough reflection away from the gathering that he does not miss the place where he is accustomed to rest. What is man? No one denies that reason is a gift from the Lord, which we cannot do without in this world. And yet so many thousands believe their happiness and prosperity would suffer if they did not plunge themselves into delusion, witlessness, and insanity as often as they could. Is it any wonder that from such people so few can be brought to <term>godliness</term> <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"; a life of active piety and devotion</note> and be strengthened within it?

Those who deal and trade in <term>commerce</term> <note>original: "Kaufmanschaft"</note> are diligently led from an early age so that they might be truly seized and possessed by the <term>lust for gain</term> <note>original: "Gewinn-Sucht"; an obsessive or addictive pursuit of profit</note>. All instruction given to them during their years of apprenticeship refers to this purpose. And he believes he has raised his apprentices correctly who has driven all other desires from their hearts through the single desire for profit, and has instilled in them the opinion that true honor is earned solely through the skill of making one's advantage. Whoever is brought this far views all ways and means that can lead to this goal as fair and permissible, whether they conflict with justice or not. Such is the nature of man. Once someone has persuaded us that this or that is our highest good, he has simultaneously made us so heartened, or rather so reckless, that we do not shrink from any sin or injustice that might serve as a means

# On the Sustaining of Human Corruption.

...[doing] that which justice hates and forbids, one flatters oneself in the silence of the heart that the matter was played out cleverly. One then resolves to use the same means currently employed to deceive a neighbor at the very next opportunity. Whatever is gathered together in this manner is afterwards called the blessing of the **LORD** <note>original: "Segen des **HErren**"</note>: and that Holy Being, who finds abomination in the deceitful, must be called the helper and ally of those who have grown rich through the transgression of His laws, simply because He does not choose to use His omnipotence to destroy the evil counsel of those hungry for gain.

A wise observer can perceive from this how difficult it must be to lead the hearts of those to the **LORD** who have been trained in commercial business from their youth. One must always suspect two enemies of true godliness to be present within them: an unmeasured lust to plunder and gain, and a love for all the injustice that can produce profit and utility. A person who has spent the entire day—now calculating, now exhausting the mind with all kinds of schemes to sell their wares well, now straining the power of the spirit to notice the weak side of the buyers, now uttering many useless words against their own conviction and conscience, now even confirming a false testimony with an oath—sits down in the evening to read a prayer from a book to which they are accustomed, or a passage from the Bible without any reflection. They lie down with the evil intent to begin the coming day exactly as they concluded this one, and leave their bed with a fresh

<column-break/>

desire to enrich themselves through craftiness and sin. They even call upon the **LORD** to grant them grace in trade—which is to say, they wish for Him to sharpen their wits to ensnare those who deal with them, and to blind those who are not inclined to believe their words. Is this way of life close to the Kingdom of **God**? Those who have spent six days in this manner arrive on the seventh at the gatherings appointed for divine service, bringing with them the entire burden that makes their soul unfit for true devotion. The heart calculates, fears, hopes, and deliberates, even while the ear hears and the mouth sings a hymn. Is it to be expected that they will return home edified, touched, moved, and sanctified? To the two evil desires we have noted, others are later added as matters progress, which are no less dangerous and obstructive. Should the resolution one has taken to become rich succeed, then for most people of this sort, wastefulness and luxury are embraced. None are more willing to squander much than those who have gathered a great fortune without great toil and labor. And none know less how to use their goods rightly than those who have convinced themselves that human happiness consists in wealth and abundance. If the hope one had for great treasures seems to fade, the desire to seize something through outrage and entrapment becomes all the more heated. With this is joined envy over the prosperity of others who have been more fortunate. And what can these two impulses not do in the soul of a corrupt person...

The body is so exhausted and fatigued by the day's work that it denies all help to the soul, which still wishes to think of **GOD** in the evening, in its endeavor. How can a spirit rightly compose itself and withdraw from the world when it dwells in a sleepy and weary body? It must fall into slumber against its will. It is already half-dreaming when it thinks it is practicing devotion <note>original: "Andacht"</note>. It believes it is praying, yet knows not what it says. Often, during reading or prayer, it feels a certain pleasure and imagines this to be the peace of the Kingdom of **GOD**. Yet that which seems to be a spiritual delight is, in truth, nothing but a natural sensation that usually awakens from the rest following a heavy exertion. <note>The author warns that the feeling of "peace" a laborer feels while praying at night might just be the physical relief of finally sitting down after a hard day.</note> The days of public worship are without labor and could therefore, if used rightly, compensate for the damage inflicted upon the soul during the week by the constant fatigue of the body and the troublesome care for nourishment. To understand this, one must note that for people who spend their lives under much labor and toil, the mere rest of the body and a quiet idleness are regarded as a special pleasure. We, who do not have to exhaust ourselves so much, become fretful if we must sit without movement and have no one beside us with whom we can pass the time. It is much different with these people. Their limbs are always stiff and weakened by work, and their spirit is dull and, as it were, so enclosed that it has neither the strength nor the desire to move much. Therefore, a mere standstill of all movements of the body and spirit appears to them as something enticing and pleasant: and they are capable, to our wonder, of spending many hours as if they were clocks from which the weights had been removed. Whoever remembers this will soon comprehend the cause of the great modesty and silence observed in most during the hours of devotion. Just as the causes by which the world is moved to attend the worship service, so also is the fruit and effect of these devotions. The former are carnal and natural; the latter is, for the most part, poor and inconsistent.

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption.

### §. VIII.

Apart from man himself, there is a greater number of various causes that maintain and strengthen him in the state of sin and corruption. Our understanding can take countless paths through this land of trial, in which the providence of the LORD has assigned us an uncomfortable lodging <note>The author uses the metaphor of an "uncomfortable lodging" or inn to describe the temporary and often difficult nature of earthly life.</note> for an indefinite time: And on all these paths, we encounter tempters who lie in wait for the true peace of man. In order to maintain order, we wish to divide these external causes, by which man can be prevented from coming to God, into two main categories: general and specific causes. By the former, we mean such obstacles that are dangerous to all people, regardless of what kind or category they may be. The latter are those which do not make repentance and conversion <term>Repentance and conversion: from the German *Busse und Bekehrung*, referring to the internal transformation and external turning back toward God</term> unpleasant and vexing to everyone, but only to those who either have reason and prestige, or are lowly and insignificant.

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption. 407

They finally allow us to use the name of **Satan** <term>Satan: from the Hebrew for 'adversary,' here referring to the chief fallen angel and tempter</term> to frighten the world from the pulpit and in a few other cases; yet that is all that people are willing to concede. We took this preference of the contemporary world to heart before we set pen to paper, and we have carefully considered the most prominent arguments usually brought forward to justify it. We can conscientiously assure you that this was done with all necessary freedom of spirit and with the intention that we would not mention the power of **Satan** over humanity at all, if only we found that the opinion of those who dislike hearing of it could be adorned with—if not proven by—plausible reasons. We could have done this without placing ourselves under suspicion or mistrust. In a book dealing with moral philosophy <term>Moral philosophy: from the German *Sitten-Lehre*, the study of ethics and human conduct</term>, an instruction on the power of **Satan** would have been missed without causing any offense. However, the closer we came to the conclusion of this examination, the more certain we became that either the truth, the divinity, and the authority of our holy books must be denied, or a certain power over the corrupted minds of unbelievers must be granted to the unclean spirit. We have therefore decided to rather bear the displeasure or contempt of some people—who never wish to take the trouble to examine this matter accurately and sincerely—than to betray the truth in a certain way through our silence. We agree entirely with those who complain that many things are attributed to **Satan** that actually arise from entirely different causes.

<column-break/>

We regret the superstition and blindness of many people who attribute everything called evil to an invisible power, failing to remember that the tinder <note>original: "Zunder," meaning highly flammable material used to start a fire; a metaphor for human lusts</note> of all sins that can be committed lies within our own hearts and inclinations. We admit that the evil spirit must serve as a pretext for many people to excuse their ungodliness and wickedness. Finally, we ask those who labor in the Word <note>referring to the clergy and theologians who preach and teach</note> to use this name cautiously, and to give the children of this world no opportunity for mockery, nor the common man any cause for gross errors and hollow excuses through their constant complaints about the infinite power and strength of **Satan**. We cannot concede more than this. And those who demand of us that we should no longer warn people about **Satan** at all are asking us to turn the **Scripture** into an uncertain book from which nothing could actually be determined or proven. This will be shown by what we are about to point out.

The true doctrine of **Satan** and his power was obscured and corrupted early among men. -># On the Maintenance of Human Depravity<-

A [new] way of introducing **worldly wisdom** <note>original: "Welt-Weisheit"; a term used in the 18th century to describe secular philosophy and natural science as opposed to theology.</note>, and to break the yoke of the old **school-philosophy** <note>original: "Schul-Philosophie"; referring to Scholasticism, the medieval method of learning that dominated universities for centuries.</note> under which the learned had lain for so long, first opened the way to these dealings. These great men investigated nature with purer eyes than had been done before, and found that much which had hitherto been passed off as supernatural and attributed to **Satan** was without cause. At the same time, they applied themselves to improving the old doctrine of spirits and to providing a clear concept of the difference between a spirit and a body, and of the true nature of these two opposing essences. Those who considered this matter with the greatest ingenuity finally concluded, along with the world-famous <term>des Cartes</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher whose "dualism" strictly separated the mind (thinking) from the body (matter).</note>, that a spirit is a *thinking being*. They believed that one could not distinguish a spirit from a bodily nature more clearly or plainly than by teaching that the primary power of a spirit consists in **thinking**. 

How rarely does man rightly use the freedom granted to him? This new light blinded some instead of enlightening them. Many arrived at the thought that since a spirit could do nothing but think, one must deny it all other effects and reject everything that had been taught until now regarding the power of the **evil spirit** over the minds and bodies of men. Against this undertaking stood so many clear and distinct passages of **Scripture** and so many histories of sorcerers, alliances with Satan, ghosts, possessions, apparitions, and other such things that no one wished to doubt. Thus, they attempted to overturn this twofold

<column-break/>

foundation of the old doctrines. The latter, which was taken from history, could be contested without danger. Without much long-windedness, they denied the credibility of all these tales, asserting that our fathers and ancestors had all been led astray by the **superstition** of their times, and had accepted as truth that which sick, fearful, gullible, and deluded people had dreamed. 

And this pretense was made uncommonly probable by various things. The **legal scholars**, who were encouraged by the freedom of thought that was gradually being supported more and more, pointed out the gross errors that had previously been committed during the investigations against **witches, hags, and sorcerers**. They proved tangibly that many people had been miserably executed who had never seen Satan except in their sleep. The **physicians** applied themselves to demonstrating that many uncommon illnesses had been groundlessly labeled as enchantments or possessions by Satan. These doctors received all the more applause because they confirmed what they taught through action, healing many such occurrences with herbs and plasters—cases which people had previously tried to lift only through **prayer and fasting**. Finally, the researchers of antiquity stepped forward, uniting erudition and reason to convince the world that all the strange events that the heathens had attributed to the gods—all prophecies, miracles, and oracles—had been wrought through the **deceit and cunning of priests**. Even the **theologians** themselves were not entirely idle.

Where this light stands still, it is a mark of wisdom to boast of one’s own ignorance. Of what use is it to plague ourselves and others with far-fetched conjectures that we can strengthen with nothing but our own imagination? What the **Scripture** has clearly revealed to us consists of the following things. It teaches us:

(I) In general, that **Satan**, either himself or through his angels and assistants, can entirely occupy the heart of **unconverted men** and prepare it for his service. 

(II) In particular, that he can further darken and blind their already dull and dim **understanding**. 

(III) That he can incite and move the **will**, which is by nature inclined toward evil, to actual **sin**. 

(IV) Finally, that those whose souls **Satan** has taken over and possessed have lost all **freedom and strength**; they do not so much act themselves in things that run against the law of the **Lord**, but rather allow the **tyrant** <note>Satan</note>, under whose yoke they have fallen, to work through them. 

The **Lord** did not need to make more known to us than this, so that we might be on our guard. Had the **Spirit of the Lord** revealed more to us, we might have been more learned, but not wiser regarding **salvation**. And for what would this knowledge have sufficed? Nothing but to satisfy our **curiosity** <note>original: "Fürwiß," meaning an excessive or meddlesome desire for knowledge</note>. Yet perhaps curiosity would only have been further awakened and stirred by it.

Scripture tells us what is to be determined here in two ways: once quite clearly and distinctly; then somewhat more obscurely and hidden, yet in such a way that even the simple-minded can discover its meaning without artifice or effort. There are many passages in the books of the New Testament in which the works of the evil and unbelieving are attributed to Satan himself. Let us select a few from them. **Jesus** says in the parable in which he represents his kingdom as a field where wheat and weeds grow together, that his enemy would mix these weeds among the wheat he had sown. **Matt. XIII. 25.** <note>The Parable of the Tares (weeds). In this context, the author uses it to show that false doctrines are "planted" by a spiritual enemy.</note> He is himself the interpreter of these images and informs us that the enemy signifies the devil, the wheat the holy and pure doctrine he made known to the world, and the weeds erroneous and godless opinions. Is it then Satan himself who makes such dangerous and hideous doctrines known to the world? We know that this generally happens through wicked and malicious people. **Jesus** thus calls them Satan, and actually means those whom he otherwise usually calls false prophets. Can we conclude anything else from this than that the spirit of darkness works in the souls of those who want to mingle their ungodly chatter with the holy doctrine of the Redeemer and plunge the world into sin and godlessness through errors? At the time when the Jews were preparing to take **Jesus** captive and deliver him to the heathens, he let these words be heard, among others, in his speech to his disciples: The prince of this world, or **Satan**, comes and has

<column-break/>

nothing in me. **John XIV. 30.** <note>original: "Der Fürst dieser Welt"</note> **Judas** was nearby with the deputies of the priests and the Roman soldiers to seize him and present him as a criminal to the court of his enemies. These words undoubtedly refer to this crowd. And why does **Jesus** name the prince of the world instead of his enemies and accusers? Because they were driven by **Satan** to carry out this unjust work. It is permitted in all languages to name the author of a thing in place of those whom he uses to carry out his designs. **Paul** wishes, among other things, at the end of the letter to the Romans to this newly planted congregation: The **God** of peace will tread **Satan** under your feet shortly. **Rom. XVI. 20.** What these words mean is shown by the name the Apostle assigns to **God** here. He calls him a **God** of peace, a **God** who loves peace and those who seek peace. And this designation is reason enough to believe that **Paul** here wishes that **God** might soon dampen and suppress the disunity and disputes that had arisen in the **Roman** church. This discord undoubtedly came from restless people who, by all appearances, did not want the law of **Mosaic** customs <term>Mosaic customs: the religious laws and rituals derived from the Torah of Moses, which early Christians debated over following.</term> abolished, or wanted other things arranged according to their own stubbornness. And yet **Satan** is identified as the author of it because he held possession of the souls of these brawlers. It seems to us that the simple understanding of these words is this: The **Lord**, who is an enemy of all quarreling and desires peace among men to be built...

It is absurd, he says, (*) to imagine that God’s enemy, against His will, misleads and deceives most people, and that God afterwards delivers these deceived souls to Satan for eternal punishment. This sentence can be understood in two ways. Firstly, it could mean: Christians teach that God, as powerful as He may be, cannot prevent Satan from misleading people. Secondly, it could be explained thus: Christians teach that God does not like to see Satan achieve his evil purpose with most people. The Latin words: **against God’s will** <note>original: "Invito Deo"</note>, are so ambiguous that they can support the latter interpretation as well as the former. It certainly seems that the Jew intended to say the first. And if that is so, we answer him that he is ignorant of the doctrine of Christians. We all teach that our God, who is endowed with infinite power, could completely chain Satan and, if He pleased, render him entirely powerless to harm the world. ## The Second Chapter ##

...to investigate his objections. It is true that the Lord, who loves our happiness <note>original: Glückseligkeit</note>, does not like to see anyone in the snares of Satan. However, the entire proof falls apart. Could a sensible person conclude this: "God would prefer it if no human gave ear to Satan—to whom He allows, for just reasons, to lay snares for humanity—therefore, He is not almighty"? Those who only wish to look around the world will easily be able to find their way into the doctrine of Christians, which seems so unbelievable and strange to this Jew <note>Referring to Spinoza, whom the author frequently identifies by his Jewish heritage to frame him as an outsider to Christian truth.</note>. 

A prince who loves justice and godliness sees in his land a multitude of wicked mockers who exert every effort to draw disciples and propagate their poison. He has enough power to root out this gang and to hinder them in their wretched undertaking. And yet, he does not do it. After mature reflection, he has found it more advisable to oppose godliness with reasons and causes rather than with force and punishments. Meanwhile, it grieves him as often as he hears that many of his subjects fall away from the faith and join the enemies of the Most High. Will a wise man, upon hearing this story, find reason to doubt the truth of the matter? Will he take occasion from this to deny the power or the wisdom of this prince? How often must we request the masters of reason—who wish to soar above the clouds—to simply remain on the earth and to accept instruction from those who are far simpler than they are? 

The second ground relates to divine justice: Can it be believed that a just God would let Satan mislead humanity un-

<column-break/>

punished, and on the other hand punish those who have the misfortune to fall into his snares? Pure, gross ignorance and blindness! The Latin word <term>Impune: unpunished or without penalty</term>, which we translated as "unpunished" in the first sentence of this conclusion, can again be explained in a twofold way. It can mean: "without punishment"; and thus the meaning would be: God does not punish the malice that Satan exercises upon humanity. Or this word can also be rendered as: "unhindered." If one translates it thus, this sense emerges: God lets Satan carry out his work freely and does not prevent him from misleading people according to his pleasure. 

The contrast seems to confirm the former translation. Yet, whether one chooses this or that interpretation, the statement remains false and incorrect. **It is false that the Lord allows the malice of Satan to go unpunished.** He is reserved for the judgment of the great day <note>Jude 1:6: "And the angels who did not keep their positions of authority... he has kept in darkness, bound with everlasting chains for judgment on the great Day."</note>. And **it is false that He allows him all freedom to exercise his willfulness.** The Lord destroys his designs as often as they stand against His holy purposes and protects His own against his cunning and malice. 

The other point agrees just as little with the doctrine of Christians. Spinoza speaks as if we believed that God misleads the people who are misled by Satan, simply because they let themselves be deceived by him, even though they cannot escape his ambushes. Is it not impudent to reproach Christians with such doctrines, which perhaps none of all the dreamers <note>The author uses "dreamers" to refer to radical sectarians or enthusiasts whose theological errors he contrasts with "true" Christian doctrine.</note> who appear in such great numbers among the confessors of the...

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

...endured in the name of **JESUS**? Could we, who speak with the greatest reverence of the holiness and justice of our Creator, arrive at the opinion that **GOD** would eternally punish an unavoidable misfortune—a misfortune that He Himself neither can nor will hold back? One must represent a doctrine as so foolish and absurd when one neither wishes to tolerate it nor can contest it with valid reasons. The unbelievers, who live outside the Kingdom of God, would feel the weight of divine justice anyway, even if no Satan were present in the world. *He who does not believe is already judged.* **John 3:18**. And those who allow themselves to be seduced by his inspiration to greater misdeeds than they would otherwise have committed through the wickedness of their nature, have a harsher judgment to expect. This is because they have despised the offered grace which would have saved them from the power of this enemy, had they submitted to it.

We cannot say whether all those who do violence to the Scripture—so that the doctrine of the cunning and strength of Satan may be removed from it—presuppose this thoughtless fiction <note>original: Gedichte; here meaning a fabricated story or poetic invention</note> of Spinoza, or something else. Very few allow the reasons for their audacity to be seen clearly: And perhaps there are many among them who themselves do not know what makes them so bold to explain a book, which they consider divine, far more freely than a sensible man has ever explained a Greek or Latin poet. Perhaps in some it is nothing but pride 

<column-break/>

and sacrilege, in others a secret unbelief that they themselves do not properly perceive, and in still others a brazen arrogance. The Day of the **Lord** will make everything clear and reveal the counsel of hearts. We wish here only to show in brief how those who find the light—which manifests in the cited and explained passages of Holy Scripture—annoying, tend to behave. They divide themselves into two classes. One will not grant at all that this doctrine is in the Scripture and gives those passages, which we understand as referring to Satan, a completely different interpretation. The other admits this but wishes to remedy the difficulty in another way. We want to hear both and represent their opinion more sincerely than many among them tend to represent our doctrine, or rather the doctrine of Holy Scripture.

Those of the first class would, by all appearances, explain their thoughts in this way if it pleased them to conform to our way of thinking: **Jesus** and the apostles spoke and wrote in the language that was common among the Jews in their time. A sensible man who wants to win over a people can never do it otherwise. This language was filled with all kinds of figures of speech that referred to the opinions of the Oriental <note>original: Morgenländischen; referring to Middle Eastern or Near Eastern cultures</note> peoples, among whom the ancestors of the Jews of that time had lived for such a long time. And these figures of speech could be abolished all the less because the doctrines on which they were founded were themselves held to be true and correct by many Jews, at least among the common man. ### Chapter Two

The whole world has chattered more about spirits and their effects than the people of the **Chaldeans**. It is they who first made **Satan** the **Lord** of the world and equal to **GOD**. Whatever seemed difficult or mysterious to their wise men in nature or in man, they generally derived from a good or evil spirit. This vain science of spirits had become known to the **Jews** in **Chaldea**. And the majority of them had thoughtlessly adopted it, insofar as it seemed to suit their religion. Therefore, from that time on, their entire language was changed and organized according to the dictates of this teaching. What was formerly attributed to **GOD** or to nature—all unusual illnesses, all melancholic thoughts, all rising evil lusts and desires, all disordered visions of an agitated imagination, all violent emotions <term>Affecten; strong passions or overwhelming feelings</term>—this was now declared to be the work of a malicious spirit <note>original: unartigen; here meaning ill-natured or wicked</note>, who found pleasure in stirring up one storm after another in the bodies and minds of men. We do not mean to say that the entire people of **GOD** were infected with this plague. Without doubt, the wiser ones surely noticed that more darkness and superstition than light and truth were to be found in this doctrine. The **Sadducees** admitted this publicly. However, the common man is everywhere the master of language, and dictates the rules of speech to the learned. The wise men themselves among the **Jews** thus had to speak as if they believed everything that had given rise to so many new figures of speech unknown to the ancient **Jews**. In this state,

<column-break/>

our Savior found the people of the **Hebrews**. It was not advisable to interfere with the established language or to purge it of its Oriental refuse <note>original: Morgenländischen Unraht; referring to the "clutter" of superstitious ideas brought from the East</note>. A new language might have been even more unbearable to the people than a new teaching. He therefore prudently deferred to habit and usage, and spoke as was customary among the **Jews**, without partaking in the opinions from which those idioms were derived. He and His apostles called an extraordinary illness a "possession of **Satan**," and the sinful and sorrowful thoughts—which thick blood, an excess of vital spirits, or a damaged imagination had awakened—they called "inspirations and temptations of **Satan**." We, who explain His holy discourses, must not look at the shells of the words, but at the kernel that lies within them. **JESUS** spoke as the **Jews** did, but thought like those who believe nothing of all the alleged powers and effects of spirits. He spoke of spirits like an **Essene** or a **Pharisee**, yet believed like the wise among the **Jews** who laughed at the nonsensical superstition of these two sects. Is it not an old and universal command of all wise men: One must follow the common man in language, but follow the wise in one's opinions? If these people are right, then the rest of us are mistaken in taking the words of **JESUS** and His apostles in too strict a sense, and in not considering that they were forced to present their teachings in a tainted and impure language.

## On the Maintenance of Human Corruption ##
-> Part I <-

We want to answer. Many arguments <term>Beweisthümer; formal proofs or logical demonstrations</term> are of no better quality than dilapidated houses that have been given a fine appearance and look through artifice. Whoever looks at such buildings only in general easily believes them to be solid, comfortable, and lasting. But whoever examines them piece by piece loses all desire to live in them. So it is with this supposed proof. One needs only to dissolve and take apart the various components of which it is composed, and its weakness will be plain to see. In it, some things are laid as a foundation that agree fairly well with the truth; and upon these, one later builds all kinds of completely groundless conjectures <term>Muthmassungen; suppositions without evidence</term> to blind people who lack foresight. It is true that the nations into whose hands **God** gave the **Jews** for a time <note>A reference to the Babylonian Captivity</note> were afflicted with all kinds of absurd opinions regarding spirits and their effects in the underworld and in mankind. It is true that they blamed everything that seemed difficult and obscure to them on a spirit, and especially attributed all uncommon illnesses of the body and mind to the **Devil**. It is true that the **Jews** learned many of these false opinions among them and brought them back to their homeland. It is true that from the language of the **Jews**, which they spoke at the time of our **Savior**, one can collect a considerable number of such figures of speech <term>Redens-Arten; idiomatic expressions</term> that refer to the teachings and opinions of the **Chaldeans** and **Babylonians**. It is finally true that both **Jesus** and many other **Jews** made use of these figures of speech without thereby

<column-break/>

approving of or accepting the opinions from which they first arose. Among the known languages of the world, there is almost none in which some figures of speech are not found that stem from old and, through time, weakened—even completely erroneous—doctrines. And the wise among the nations who speak these languages express their thoughts through them, even though they are far removed from these doctrines. The rest of what is derived from these things we have conceded is, if not false, then unproven, and is presented without ground or cause as being just as certain as the preceding. It is false—or at the very least, it is unproven—that no one among the **Jews** at the time of **Jesus** could speak according to the rules <note>original: "Regul-mäßig"; here meaning speaking in a way that aligns with social or linguistic norms</note> without attributing all extraordinary occurrences in nature, in the body, and in the spirit of man to **Satan** or the spirits. How can people who do not belong to the most simple-minded imagine such things, which can be refuted by daily experience? This much is certain: when an entire people has publicly confessed to a certain doctrine, everyone who does not wish to be called a heretic <term>Irrgläubiger oder Keßer; a misbeliever or heretic</term> is bound to speak as this doctrine requires. Suppose a nation had decided to believe that **God** was provided with a certain body just like men, and to cast out those who would represent **God** as a pure and spiritual being. Those who wished to live among this people would be forced to speak of **God** in such a way that they would not lead anyone to the opinion that they were dissatisfied with the established doctrine. # Chapter Two #

Those who demand of us that we should believe that among the **Jews** in the times of **JESUS** and the **Apostles** one had to speak as if spirits ruled the whole world, must first demonstrate to us that this doctrine was an article of faith <term>Glaubens-Artikul; a fundamental tenet of religion</term> among the **Hebrews** which the entire people accepted unanimously. They do not dare to prove this. Rather, they admit that not all **Jews** held this to be true and that every person had the freedom to attribute much or little to spirits. With what appearance of truth can they then pretend that the laws of the **Jewish** language would not have allowed one to speak of illnesses and evil thoughts differently than our holy books speak of **Satan**? Does the language of an entire people conform itself to the opinions of a few people? Or would an intelligent person, residing among a people who establish nothing certain about the nature and powers of spirits, be forced to represent spirits as gods of the world who must be worshiped, simply because a certain party is found that does not doubt it? Those who are not willing to be satisfied with this easy and clear proof can be convinced by the **Jewish** historian **Josephus** <note>original: "Joseph"; refers to Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> and by the **Jew** **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note>, who wrote around the times of which we speak, that one spoke and was permitted to speak differently among the **Jews** than these people choose to believe. It is further false that those who were not taken in by the common superstition regarding spirits—that is, all those who were called "Great" and "Respected" among the **Jews**—spoke of particular and unusual occurrences in the same way the Scripture

<column-break/>

speaks of them. All the world knew that the **Sadducees** derived from natural causes that which the **Pharisees** and the common man held to be works of **Satan**. And no one persecuted them because of it. They were admitted to the divine services <term>Gottesdienste; public worship</term>. They were entrusted with offices and positions in the **Great Council** <note>The Sanhedrin, the supreme judicial and administrative body in Jerusalem</note>. The **High Priest** himself was often a **Sadducee**. And what then should have moved these people to speak differently than they thought, and to carry out a spiritual deception <term>Gauckeley; a performance of trickery or illusions</term> with their words and figures of speech? Could our **Savior** and His witnesses not have followed the example of these people and mentioned evil spirits as little as they did, if He had held this doctrine to be erroneous? Finally, it is false that everything we teach from the Scripture regarding the powers of spirits over mankind consists only of a few figures of speech <term>Redens-Arten; idiomatic expressions</term> that can conveniently be directed toward another meaning. They act as if we alone could point out a few ways of speaking from the Scripture to bolster our doctrine of **Satan**. This certainly means wanting to deceive oneself and others. We do not appeal to a few words and expressions that might perhaps be interpreted differently, but to complete and clear sentences that are composed with lucid words in many places. Is it a mere figure of speech when **Paul** says: The **GOD** of this world blinds the souls of the unbelievers, so that they cannot see the light of the truth? Is this not rather a clearly presented doctrine? Is it a mere figure of speech, or an ambiguous word, when the same **Apostle** says the **Ephesians** did not [wrestle] with flesh and

Is it not true that the wise, who wish to be foolish for a time so that they may win over the weak, must at least indicate in the books they write for the instruction of the whole world where they speak according to their own opinion and where they speak according to a foreign and false opinion? This has happened nowhere in the books called **Scripture**.

## The Second Chapter

Jesus and his witnesses speak at all times of **Satan** and his workings in such a way as if they were presenting that which they themselves held to be indisputably true and established. They do not note with a single word that they were merely accommodating themselves to the concepts of the simple-minded. Would they have acted like wise and sensible people in this matter, if that were true which is put forward as truth by those whom we here refute? Would their books and writings be of much use to us if they had, without thought or reflection, sown weeds and wheat among one another? And is there a single doctrine of the **Scripture** that could not be rejected under this pretext—that Jesus and his witnesses sometimes presented the truth and sometimes error, yet left behind no signs by which these two so contrary things could be distinguished? (II) The doctrine of **Satan** is, in the opinion of these people <note>The author refers to the Enlightenment rationalists who viewed the Devil as a metaphor for psychological illness.</note>, a harmful superstition that must be cleared from the minds of men if the common and specific peace of the world is to be maintained. Can one say, without violating the majesty of our **Savior** and the honor of his witnesses, that they had no reservations about presenting such a harmful and simultaneously absurd doctrine not only as their own, but also confirming it through their miracles and signs? Would even a naturally clever and honest man who wishes to improve a people seek to spread their ungodly and poisonous fables on every occasion, satisfying himself with the hope that after seventeen hundred years some masters of **Reason** would fight against them?

<column-break/>

(III) Is it believable that a man who has the heart to attack the religion of a people at its very seat, who touches upon the doctrines that are called into question by no one and accepted as divine by all—is it to be believed that such a man would leave a silly and yet detrimental superstition in peace, which is pleasing only to a certain number of people? Jesus set himself against the opinion, which almost all of **Israel** acknowledged in his time, that divine service consisted of sacrifices and the other customs that **Moses** prescribed. He took from the common teaching of the **Sabbath** the great prestige it had among the Jews. He scolded the heads and teachers of the people, who were regarded as messengers of the Lord, as fools and blind men, and cared little what kind of storm this undertaking would draw together. And should this divine teacher not have ventured—I will not say to attack, but only to pass over in silence—a doctrine that was no piece of public faith and could be accepted or rejected by everyone at will? What unintelligible things does the guild of today’s wise men give us to believe? We are to imagine that the Jesus who feared nothing, nor needed to fear anything—whom no king, nor High Priest, nor governor frightened, who acted in the Temple as a lord in his own house—that this Jesus would let all courage and heartiness fall when he was to tell the common man that the **Devil** was nothing but a bogeyman <note>original: "Schrecken-Bild" (image of terror)</note> that the ignorance of the **Orientals** <term>Orientals: In this context, "Morgenländer" refers to people of the biblical Near East, whose languages were often dismissed by 18th-century European scholars as being naturally prone to exaggerated metaphors and myths.</term> had carved? (IV) Is it wisely acted, when

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

...a man who wishes his teaching to be accepted in an entire country—does he merely repeat what pleases the common crowd and care little for what the great and respected men in the land believe? Does this not mean making himself despised and ridiculous to the best part of the people? The people are accustomed to following the great in their opinions. And whoever has brought these to his side can be certain that the rest will follow. Those among the Jews, in the times of **Jesus**, who were rich, landed, favored by the **Romans**, and great at the courts of the descendants of **Herod**, sided with the **Sadducees** <note>A Jewish sect known for denying the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits or angels.</note>, who mocked the **doctrine of spirits** <note>original: "Geister-Lehre"; referring to the belief in angels and demons.</note>. Would he not have acted far more wisely if he had at least introduced a middle-doctrine that would have been pleasant to the great and not particularly displeasing to the rabble? And would he not have made himself much more beloved thereby? No man who wishes to convert the world is accustomed to mixing the **silly whims** <note>original: "albernen Grillen"</note> of lowly people among his good and useful teachings without necessity, and thereby turning the minds of the clever and sensible away from himself. (V) All of this set aside, and granting that which runs against all appearance of truth—that **Jesus** had cause to teach of spirits in the Jewish fashion among the Jews—why then did his witnesses repeat and present this same thing among the **Heathens**, among the **Romans** and **Greeks**? ## The Second Chapter

...to persevere in the faith. They do not wish to deny that everything the **Scripture** says of **Satan** must be accepted in the literal sense <note>original: "Verstande... den der Buchstabe an die Hand gibt"</note> provided by the text. Nor can they easily tolerate those who would make our **Savior** a servant to the spirit-dreams of the **Jews**, or who claim that he spoke according to the corrupted tastes of the **Jewish** people. In their opinion, **Satan** did indeed perform all those things reported of him during the time of **Jesus**. He tormented bodies, poisoned the minds of men, and laid snares and nets for the saints. However, they believe he can now do none of these things anymore. His power is finished since the doctrine of **Jesus** has triumphed and become known everywhere. Perhaps he still plays his games in places where the name of **Jesus** is unknown. But among **Christians**, he can no longer stir, because the omnipotence of **God** has banished him to the abyss. Those who believe this grant us that **Satan** could destroy the souls of men and draw them under his dominion, and that wherever no greater power stood in his way, he was always ready to give proof of this power. We, in turn, grant them that in the times of **Jesus**, he enjoyed more freedom to torment the bodies of men than in the times following, because the **Lord** wished to make the glory <note>original: "Herlichkeit"</note> of his Son known to the world. The question that remains for us to decide is this: Does the **Lord** still permit **Satan** to blind the minds of wayward **Christians**, who live outside the state of grace, and to entice them to sin? We answer this with "yes," and hope that the reasons we are about to provide will justify this answer.

<column-break/>

Firstly, what is it that moves those who hold a different opinion to believe that all power has been taken from **Satan** to work upon the souls of the wicked? Is this clearly revealed in **Scripture**, that after the days of **Jesus**, **Satan** was to lose all authority? Or is it a mere conjecture supported by certain arguments? A passage of **Scripture** containing such a claim can hardly be named. What, then, are the reasons that drive one to such a conjecture? Is it perhaps considered belittling to our **Savior** that **Satan** should rule in the midst of his own people? This reason must fall away, because it proves more than it is intended to prove. If it redounds to the dishonor of our **Redeemer** that his enemy now overcomes men, then it would follow that this could never have happened at all. And yet the **Scripture** tells us that this did happen in the early days of **Christianity**, that **Satan** at that time caused unrest and disorder among **Christians**—and what is more, that he overcame one of the **Apostles** of **Jesus** and made him his servant <note>A reference to Judas Iscariot.</note>. Either this is false; or, if it is true, then one does not infringe upon the honor of **Jesus** by believing that he [Satan] can still gain followers in the midst of the visible kingdom of **Christ**. Is there anything else they wish to protect themselves with? They know of nothing else. And he who gives no reason for his opinions cannot accuse those who refuse to trust him of any injustice. Secondly: If the **Lord** had intended for the power of **Satan** over the wicked world to cease after a short time, would He not have left us some news of this?

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

...have? Is it becoming of a wise **Ruler** <note>original: "Regenten," referring to God</note> in the books that he wrote for the comfort of his **Subjects**, to speak of a certain danger that will soon pass as if it would never end? The **Lord** has nowhere given us such a report. With what justification can we restrict his general reminders and warnings according to our own pleasure? Perhaps one will object: The **Lord** also mentioned nothing in the **Scripture** stating that the power of **Satan** over the bodies of men would decrease after the days of **Jesus**; and yet this has occurred. One might therefore believe the same regarding his power over souls, with good reason. We answer in two ways. First, it is false that there is nothing in **Scripture** from which one could conclude that after the times of **Jesus**, the power of **Satan** over the bodies of men would fall. The Spirit of the **Lord** never warns against physical possessions <note>The author uses "Besitzungen" here to mean demonic possession of the body.</note>. He speaks only of spiritual possessions. And **Satan** was not permitted to take the body of an obvious sinner—such as the man guilty of incest <note>original: "Blut-Schänder," referring to the case of incest mentioned in 1 Corinthians 5.</note> from **Corinth**—until an **Apostle** had handed him over to him.

<column-break/>

These two things were evidence enough that the **Lord** had decided no longer to allow **Satan** to torment the bodies of many people. It was not necessary thereafter for the **Lord** to have us informed of it. Matters of this kind become easily known to us through our senses and reason, and therefore do not need to be made known through **revelation**. It is quite another thing with the efforts of the evil spirit to seduce souls and bring them under his subjection. These are discovered by neither ear nor eye. And the intellect likewise lacks certain signs to distinguish the impulses of nature from the enticements of another spiritual power. The **Lord** would therefore have had to reveal it to us if men no longer had anything to fear regarding the snares of **Satan**. Thirdly, if **Satan** still has the power, through the permission of the **Most High**, to tempt the godly, how can one persuade oneself that all access to the hearts of the wicked is closed to him?

***

->§. X.<-

The whole world agrees that a wise and cautious **education** <note>original: "Erziehung"</note> lays a secure foundation for a sensible and virtuous life for most people. We could therefore promise **godliness** <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"</note> one victory after another, if only people would make it their concern to prepare the tender hearts of the **youth** in good time for the reception and high regard of the same. And what is held in lower regard among us? Most do not even think about properly forming the hearts of their children, or having them formed by others. It is allowed to keep the ugly shape that it has by nature.
