## Chapter Two

Those who still think of it <note>Referring to the instruction of the young.</note> seek nothing more than to teach them the art of how they might please the world, gain honor and reputation, and gather wealth. Is it any wonder that godliness <term>Gottseligkeit: a state of living in accordance with God’s will; piety.</term> cannot find a seat or abode in minds that are guided in such a way?

->Explanation.<-

A good portion of life passes before our spirit reaches its right strength and our body its full firmness. In these years, most are so soft and pliable that one can lead and turn them like the young branches of trees, however one wishes. And well is it for him who falls under a wise hand that strives to properly set the naturally evil heart and to lead the spirit toward a certain and rational purpose! A body that is accustomed in these times to endure hardship, work, and toil becomes durable and steady afterward. And a spirit that is filled early with noble and wise teachings and guided toward the oversight of itself rarely loses entirely the seeds of reason and virtue in its life which were entrusted to it. Our brain, which is then still like wax in which one can press all the images one wants, accepts without resistance the concepts presented to us and maintains them until the latest years against everything that would erase them. No time, no changes, no cases of good or bad luck completely extinguish the things intelligently taught to a tender mind. And the examples of those who, through a violent illness or high age, lose everything they learned in the first years are so rare that they are almost counted among the wonders of nature <note>The author refers to "wonders of nature" here as rare anomalies or freaks of nature.</note>

<column-break/>

counted. One can therefore have the grounded hope that those who are equipped in time with wise and rational teachings will hardly fall entirely into ruin and misery, or lapse into a truly godless walk of life <note>original: "Wandel," referring to one's conduct or way of living.</note>. There always remains in their understanding and memory a certain light which never truly goes out. Time, business, cares, pleasures, bad examples, dissolute company, and other things can darken it. Yet, nonetheless, it breaks through again in certain moments and reminds the person whom it serves that he must walk differently than he walks. All of this has been detailed by so many clever and sensible people and confirmed by such general and infallible experience that it is quite superfluous to make many words of it. We are neither inclined to treat the benefit of a wise education in general, nor to give general rules of education. What could we say of these two pieces that has not long before us been presented and explained by others much more skillfully and elegantly than could be done by us?

# On the Maintenance of Human Depravity #

...has already been proven, and we need only derive from it this conclusion as a clear and indisputable consequence: if our youth were raised as they rightly should be, we would see more righteous Christians among us. And the fact that we find so few truly godly <term>Gottseligkeit: a state of living in devotion to God; piety or "living well" before God.</term> people among us stems largely from the thoughtless and perverse upbringing of the young. We will not touch upon the other advantages that flow from a good instruction of children and spread throughout the whole world at this time. If it is established that godliness is supported by it, then it is simultaneously clear that it is useful for countless things. We wish to proceed in an orderly fashion in the explanation of this matter. We will first show that a good upbringing can perform very important services for godliness. We will then investigate whether our common discipline is conducive to what is good, or whether it instead hinders the progress of true Christianity among us?

**(I) We posit that education can be a means to promote and propagate godliness among Christians.** One must not interpret this statement incorrectly. The grace of the Lord alone can change our soul, enlighten our understanding, and sanctify our will. Therefore, let no one understand us as if we believed that a clever and sensible discipline could make us into true and God-pleasing Christians. Whoever asserts this makes godliness a work of nature <note>The author is being careful to avoid the "Pelagian" heresy—the idea that humans can achieve salvation through their own efforts or education without divine grace.</note>. We mean only this: through a righteous and well-ordered upbringing, the human mind <term>Gemühte: the seat of emotions, will, and spirit; the inner disposition.</term> can be prepared to

<column-break/>

receive grace all the more willingly. Wise instruction can clear away many of the obstacles that otherwise resist the Lord’s call within a person. In one’s earliest youth, the heart can be prepared like a field <note>The "heart as soil" is a common biblical metaphor referring to the Parable of the Sower.</note>, so that it later receives the seed of truth without resentment, preserves it better, and allows it to work and labor more freely within itself. We do not think that anyone will find the slightest cause for offense in this teaching. If a word, a way of speaking, or a proof should escape us in the explanation of this that seems to conflict with it, we ask in advance for forgiveness for this error, and that it be attributed not to our will—which is sincere—but to the weakness of our understanding. Who rules so perfectly over their intellect, their imagination, and their memory that these powers of the soul should never deviate somewhat from the boundaries prescribed for them?

**// Two things belong to godliness: // Illumination and Sanctification. The latter is // never without the former, the former is never without the latter. //**

What is illumination without sanctification? Just as much as a light that serves and shines for no one. What is sanctification without illumination? Nothing but a blind resolution to work in the darkness and to walk without light. Both must come from God. We have retained nothing more than the wretched capacity to resist the power of the Lord, who wishes to awaken these good gifts in us. This capacity to resist manifests naturally in all people. Our understanding opposes its inherited blindness and darkness to the illuminating grace. Our will prefers the power of its lusts

### Chapter Two ###

...and desires against the grace of sanctification. The more we increase in years and physical strength, the more power and strength is gained by nature, which is full of enmity against **God**. If there is no one who opposes our evil desires in time, they gradually become like swift and violent rivers that can be stopped or held back neither by skill nor by force, which submerge and tear down everything that stands in the way of their course, and additionally draw many small streams and rivers to themselves, whereby their power is increased. We wish to say this: the evil lusts of nature, to which all freedom is allowed, become almost invincible over time and take many other desires into their company, which are excited by the course of the world, interaction with other people, and many other things. Thus, a resistance of age and habit is gradually paired with the resistance of nature, which is just as difficult to overcome as the former. Whoever might be helped by a parable or image to understand this matter more clearly should remember those who come into the world with hereditary and natural diseases. # On the Prevention of Human Depravity #

...the internal aversion of nature against the will of the **Lord** is broken, and care is taken that the stubbornness of the heart is not strengthened by any new helpers from the outside. <note>The author suggests that external influences, like bad company or worldly habits, act as "helpers" to our innate sinful nature.</note> Whoever wishes to raise their youth for the **Lord** must never lose sight of this goal. In our times, the world is so full of such erroneous teachings that one hardly knows how to be cautious and on guard. Yet, before we expect it, to our significant dismay, a host of harmful and absurd opinions appears, having taken the place of ignorance and shielding the person against all efforts toward godliness. The former—ignorance and blindness—must be rooted out with all one's might; the latter—the errors that creep about—must be prevented with great care. ### Chapter Two ###

...presume <note>The German text begins with "muhten," the conclusion of the verb "vermuhten" (to presume or imagine), continuing the sentence from the previous page.</note> that a clear and detailed concept, a convincing and moving <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "Wissenschaft"; in this period, it refers to systematic learning or a body of knowledge rather than modern laboratory science.</note> of such a doctrine would arise in the mind of a person who falters and complains of difficulty and darkness whenever he is led toward something that has no resemblance to his business, pleasures, and worldly labors? Will one be able to clearly instruct a person in his duties, and thoroughly convince him of the truth, if he is not master of his thoughts, and who, as soon as he is meant to keep them in order and fix them upon something certain, falls into a slumber that lasts as long as the discourse continues? We observe, not without astonishment, that this is little or not at all attended to, and that youth—aside from those dedicated to the sciences—are allowed to grow up as if their understanding had been granted to them only so that it might crawl about upon this earth. And we therefore fear that those who seem to us to be the best instructed have often grasped little more than the words with which the noblest and greatest truths of faith are usually explained. Our people read the **Scripture** and increase neither in faith nor in love. They hear public exhortations and remain as poor and empty of knowledge as they were from the beginning. They look through certain books that treat of <term>godliness</term> <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"; a central Pietist concept meaning an active, heartfelt, and practical devotion to God.</note> and can never recount to anyone what they have found within them. All these defects we generally excuse by the great weakness of the understanding, with which most people seem to us to be naturally afflicted.

<column-break/>

Let us rather say that the neglect of their understanding is mostly to blame for this misery. There are few people naturally gifted with so little wit and reason as we imagine. Their inability to think and reflect arises because we have not sharpened or awakened their understanding in the years of childhood. People would follow our sermons with devotion, they would read the **Scripture** with more edification, they would better understand the books that treat of godliness, and one could demand of people that they should devote themselves to prayer, if one made it a priority to rescue the souls of young people from the slavery of their senses and to form them so that they might follow a matter with their understanding—even if it does not touch their eyes and ears—and could rightly use the powers of their spirit. Do we always judge our simple folk as fairly and reasonably as we should? We advise against those who wish to instruct a thirty- or forty-year-old **farmer** in <term>geometry</term> <note>original: "Meß-Kunst"; literally the "art of measuring."</note>. Why? The spirit of this man has lost the capacity to comprehend this high science. It is already worn out and far too accustomed to visible things. Perhaps he would have grasped this science and even more, if he had been guided toward it in his younger years and his understanding had been rightly prepared. We say it is in vain to send a fifty-year-old man to a <term>wrestling school</term> <note>original: "Ring-Schule"; a school for physical training or athletics.</note>: his limbs would be too stiff and the tendons and joints so frozen that they could not be brought to any great speed or agility.

If he had been led in his youth to where they now wish to lead him, he would not now be without the skill to make it difficult for another wrestler to achieve victory over him. And the world praises these judgments. And yet we want a man—to whom it was never shown how he must use the powers of his mind, who was never accustomed to bringing his thoughts into order and maintaining them there for a time, who never occupied himself with anything other than coarse and visible things, who never considered or judged anything except what he perceived through the eyes, the ears, and the other senses—we want, I say, such a man, when he has come of age, to devote himself to <term>devotion</term> <note>original: "Andacht"; in this context, it refers to a focused, meditative state of prayer and religious reflection.</note>, which requires a withdrawal of the senses from the world; we want him to be edified by a sermon that hardly anyone can grasp except one who knows how to govern his thoughts, and to read a book with attention and pleasure that no one can understand without deep reflection.

The errors to which the entrance to the minds of youth must be closed are of a two-fold kind. Some lead to **unbelief**; others to **superstition**. We take the word "superstition" here so broadly that we include under it everything that can be called an irrational worship of God and an absurd opinion of religion. One kind of these errors, where it is deeply rooted, is as harmful to true <term>godliness</term> <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"; a central concept in 18th-century German piety meaning living a life pleasing to God.</note> as the other. Those who long torment themselves over the question: "Whether unbelief can cause more misfortune and unrest in the world, or superstition?" strike me just like two doctors who are called to a wretch

<column-break/>

wounded by a snake, and at his bedside fall into a dispute whether the bite of an Asiatic or American snake is more dangerous—without remembering that the patient will die before they have ended this unnecessary strife. Is it not better that we leave these and some other questions to be decided by those who do not know how to pass their idle time in their private chambers, and instead think about how both unbelief and superstition may be kept away from the souls of men? These two plagues of the human race are in a constant labor to overcome each other, and yet they gain little against one another. One rather preserves and strengthens the other, instead of being able to suppress it. The more unbelief gains ground, the more shamelessly it lets itself be seen in its true form. And this form is so hideous and terrifying that those who truly perceive it would rather fall into superstition than surrender themselves to such a monster. The more superstition increases, the more it exposes its secret malice and hidden claws, which it otherwise used to veil with a decent cover. And this makes most people so dismayed that they fall in heaps to the side of unbelief. One sees this strange struggle very clearly in our times. Unbelief has attracted so many disciples in certain countries and received such immeasurable freedom as never before. Many have therefore thought that it would be all over for the power of superstition. And they were far wrong! # The Second Chapter

...permits that he always wishes to punish, teach, and improve, encourages the heart of the one he wishes to improve toward resistance, and stirs up love for our natural qualities and the pride that clings to us all. And where these are awake, hardly anything good and useful can be accomplished. One must, as often as the opportunity presents itself, vividly and eloquently present the examples of such people who have been plunged into *misfortune and unrest through these desires*. One must investigate whether some naturally good inclinations do not stand alongside the evil and blameworthy ones, and strive to strengthen them. Whoever can bring it so far that he opposes the dominant lusts with an internal enemy—that is to say, another desire—has gained much, and can be certain that in many cases one power will suppress the other. One sees, for example, that in the soul of an ambitious youth there is simultaneously a natural love for <term>stillness</term> <note>original: "Stille"; here meaning a state of inward peace and external retirement from the chaotic "noise" of public life.</note>. There is no surer means to dampen that ambition than to draw out and maintain this inclination toward quietude. These two lusts are, in any case, difficult to reconcile with one another; and one has every reason to believe that in time they will cause a thousand wretched nights and difficult hours for the one in whom they simultaneously reign. Therefore, let nothing be neglected to awaken and strengthen the one that is not blameworthy in itself. One should praise, as often as one can, the pleasures and the *advantages of a life led without noise* and unrest. One should vividly depict the torment of the mind and the sorrow that tends to follow on the heels of those who seek honor, and de-

<column-break/>

-prive those who have attained honor of their peace, making life bitter for them. One should collect examples from history of great people who gave up the highest services and offices to find the peace in a lonely cottage that they could find nowhere in the great world. One should give the apprentice, once he has grown in understanding, the writings of those who have contemplated the nature of the world in silence and have regretted in their solitude the madness of humanity, who give up the true pleasure offered by a modest station for an imaginary one. One must *finally punish the mistakes into which youth* falls out of an impulse of inherent desire with leniency and modesty. The pain and resentment resulting from sharp chastisement awakens more love than hatred for the desire that led the person to sin.

We would become much more long-winded than we wish to be if we wanted to present everything that ought rightly to be done to preserve the hearts of young people against the charms and temptations of the world. It will be enough for our purpose to pull together the most necessary points and to ask those who are capable of using their intellect to take apart and more fully explain what has been mentioned in general. One must, in good time, show GOD, the world, humanity, oneself, and <term>godliness</term> <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"; a term for lived piety and a life oriented toward the divine.</note> in their true and proper form to those whom one wishes to withdraw from the corruption of this world. These few words comprise everything we can say. Why should we deny it?

# Chapter Two #

...shows that he always wants to punish, teach, and improve, he stirs the heart of the one he intends to reform to resistance, and rouses the love for our natural characteristics and the **pride** that clings to all of us. And where these are awake, it is difficult to accomplish anything good or useful. One must, whenever an opportunity arises, eloquently and vividly present the examples of those people who have been plunged into misfortune and unrest by these desires. One must investigate whether some naturally good inclinations do not stand alongside the evil and blameworthy ones and strive to strengthen them. Whoever can bring it so far that he opposes an inner enemy—I mean another desire—to the ruling passions has gained much, and can be certain that in many cases one power will suppress the other. One sees, for example, that in the soul of an ambitious young man there is at the same time a natural love for stillness. There is no surer means to dampen that <term>ambition</term> <note>original: "Ehrgeiz"; literally "honor-greed," referring to an excessive craving for status and public recognition.</note> than to draw out and maintain this inclination toward rest. These two desires are, in any case, difficult to reconcile with one another; and one has every reason to believe that in time they will cause a thousand miserable nights and difficult hours to the one in whom they rule simultaneously. Therefore, one should neglect nothing in awakening and strengthening the one that is not in itself blameworthy. One should praise, as often as one can, the pleasure and the advantages of a life led without noise and unrest. One should vividly depict the torment of the spirit and the sorrow that follows on the heels of those who seek honor, and 

<column-break/>

to those who have attained honor, tends to make life bitter. One should gather from history the examples of great people who gave up the highest offices and positions in order to find peace in a lonely hut, which they could find nowhere in the great world. When the pupil has grown in understanding, one should give him the writings of those who have contemplated the essence of the world in silence, and in their solitude have pitied the madness of men who give up the true pleasure offered by a moderate station for an imaginary one. Finally, one must punish the faults into which youth falls from an impulse of inherent desire with gentleness and modesty. The pain and resentment resulting from sharp chastisement awakens more love than hatred for the desire that led the person to sin.

We would become much more long-winded than we wish to be if we wanted to present everything that ought rightly to be done to preserve the hearts of young people against the charms and temptations of the world. It will be enough for our purpose to pull together the most necessary points and to ask those who are capable of using their intellect to analyze and explain more fully what has been mentioned in general. To those whom one wishes to withdraw from the corruption of this world, one must show in good time **God**, the **world**, **humanity**, **themselves**, and **godliness** in their true and proper form. These few words encompass everything we can say. Why should we deny it?

-># On the Maintenance of Human Corruption<-

<meta>catchword: God’s</meta>

Most people grow up in such a way that they either do not know these things at all, or know them very imperfectly. And few are gifted with such a power of **understanding** <term>Verstand; here referring to the faculty of reason and discernment</term> that they can later conquer their own imagination, present things to their thoughts as they truly are and not as they appear, and tear themselves away from the **yoke of opinions** <note>A metaphor for the social pressures and conventional wisdom absorbed during childhood.</note> that they soaked up in their youth. Therefore, when we are grown, we thoughtlessly follow those who go before and wish to lead us; we surrender ourselves to the judgment of our senses, thinking, speaking, and acting as is the custom in the world in our times, and even believe that those who do otherwise were either born without reason or have suffered damage to their intellect through all manner of accidents. And how bitter and unhealthy are the fruits, for ourselves and others, that sprout from such a **disposition of the soul** <term>Gemüths-Beschaffenheit; one's inner character or temperament</term>?

<margin>1.)</margin>
One must first show **GOD** in His right form from youth onward to those whom one wishes to make strong enough to resist the lusts of the world. The zeal of men to please **GOD** is governed by the **reverence** <term>Ehrerbietung; a mix of profound respect and holy fear</term> that they harbor for Him in their souls. And this reverence is of the same nature as the concept of **GOD** that has been instilled in them. Whoever either does not know **GOD** at all, or has allowed what he does know of Him to be corrupted by all manner of impure additions—whoever imagines the Lord and Creator of the world to be like a weak and powerless man, or sets a goal and measure to His perfections in his thoughts—must naturally lack a right fear and reverence

<column-break/>

toward Him. And in this state, how great can his desire be to serve Him? He, on the other hand, who as often as he thinks of **GOD** sees an image in his spirit that enraptures him and sets him in wonder, will always find an inclination to revere Him and an impulse to obey His will. Thus, **piety** <term>Gottseligkeit; the practice of a life devoted to God</term> depends heavily on people learning to grasp the glory, majesty, and greatness of the Lord as clearly and vividly as possible in the first years of their lives. Those who raise and lead them must, above all, accustom them to withdraw all thoughts from that which is visible and transitory when speaking of **GOD**, and to seek no likeness or image of Him on earth or in heaven. Initially, one will encounter more than one difficulty in this effort. However, many will also allow themselves to be overcome through diligence and practice. The power of our spirit is so enclosed by the things we perceive, see, and hear, that we do not venture to contemplate a spiritual being in itself, and, as it were, shrink back

# On the Persistence of Human Corruption

Most grow up in such a way that they either do not know these things at all, or know them very imperfectly. And few are endowed with such a strength of **understanding** <note>original: "Verstand"; the faculty of reason and discernment</note> that they can later conquer their own **imagination** <note>original: "Einbildung"; here meaning the subjective, often false, mental images and prejudices we form</note>, representing things to their thoughts as they *are*, and not as they *seem*, and tearing themselves away from the yoke of opinions they absorbed in their youth. Therefore, when we are grown, we thoughtlessly follow those who go before us and wish to lead us; we abandon ourselves to the judgment of our senses, thinking, speaking, and acting as it is customary to think, speak, and act in the world in our times. We even believe that those who do otherwise were either born without understanding or have suffered damage to their intellect through all sorts of accidents. And how bitter and unhealthy for us and others are the fruits that spring from such a **disposition of the mind**?

<margin>1.</margin> To those whom one wishes to make strong enough to resist the lusts of the world, one must first show **GOD** from youth onward in His right form. The zeal of men to please GOD is directed by the reverence they cherish for Him in their souls. And this reverence is of the same nature as the concept of GOD that has been instilled in them. He who either does not know GOD at all, or has allowed what he knows of Him to be corrupted by all sorts of impure additions—he who imagines the Lord and Creator of the world to be like a weak and powerless human being, or who sets goals and measures for His perfections in his thoughts—must naturally lack a right fear and reverence

<column-break/>

toward Him. And in this state, how great can his desire be to serve Him? On the contrary, whoever sees an image in his spirit that enchants him and sets him in wonder whenever he thinks of GOD, will always find an inclination to honor Him and an impulse to obey His will. **Piety** <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"; a state of living in a way that is pleasing to God</note> therefore depends heavily on people learning to grasp the glory, majesty, and greatness of the Lord as clearly and vividly as possible in the first years of their lives. Those who raise and lead them must, above all, accustom them to withdraw all thoughts from that which is visible and transitory when GOD is spoken of, and to seek no likeness or image of Him on earth or in heaven. At first, one will encounter more than one difficulty in this effort. However, many difficulties will also be overcome through diligence and practice. The power of our spirit is so enclosed by the things we sense, see, and hear, that we do not venture to contemplate a spiritual being in itself, and we almost shrink back when someone tries to represent it to us. # The Second Chapter

<columns>2</columns>

...surrounded by **GOD**. The ordinary person does not notice this, even though it lies right before his eyes, partly because he was never taught to pay attention to it, and partly because he has seen it constantly from his youth onward. A careful and rational upbringing can prevent this neglect. Whoever explains the nature of every thing to a growing person, as far as his understanding permits, and reveals to him the wisdom, art, and power shown in all natural things, will gradually make him capable of discovering the **paths of the Lord** <term>Gänge des HErren; a theological concept referring to the observable workings of divine providence in nature</term> upon the earth, and to conclude from His footsteps, which he will perceive everywhere, that He is great, mighty, loving, and holy. A person who is so prepared and raised will find a quiet reminder in all places where he looks that the Lord is present and watches over the ways of men; often, in the midst of disorder, he will be compelled to think of the One who fills the earth with His goodness and has built mankind so wisely that they can enjoy the gifts of His grace with delight.

<margin>2)</margin>
One must correctly introduce the world to those whom one wishes to raise wisely, in which they are to spend their days. How many are there among mortals who truly know the land they inhabit? One person imagines it this way, another that way. And very few know what it actually is. Most would be able to give no answer at all, even if one took great pains to draw their thoughts about the world out of them. They were never told anything about it: And they themselves never took the

<column-break/>

trouble to consider the matter. As far as we have been able to notice, the people who can still say something about it are divided into four opinions. 1) One part believes *this world is a land of delight and pleasure, which GOD prepared to please His friends.* This is how those think who find an abundance of everything here and are not disturbed in their pleasure by any sad occurrences. Whoever presents to them the misery and the plague of so many people who live alongside them says nothing to them that would particularly move them. These weary and plagued people, who can barely earn as much as is necessary to maintain the strength of the body, are, in their thought, there for the purpose that the pleasure of the "blessed ones"—upon whom GOD looked during the creation of the world—might be maintained. Whoever is to live happily needs people who serve his lusts. GOD has therefore chosen the largest part of humanity for misery and poverty, so that the small number of His **favorite children** <note>original: "Schooß-Kinder"; literally "lap-children," referring to those perceived as being God's pampered favorites.</note> might feel no hardship in the paradise He has built for them.

<margin>2)</margin>
To others, this world seems a land of *plague and suffering, a vale of tears, a prison, a house of torture.* This opinion has taken root among those who have been oppressed with poverty, sorrow, toil, and pain from youth onward. And since the largest part of humanity lives in such a state, this view has the most followers. It is of no use to show these people that many live here contentedly and without particular agony. They look only at themselves and believe that the few people who find something good here are nothing more than a very small exception...

# On the Sustenance of Human Corruption

...make an exception to the general rule.
<margin>3)</margin> Another group views this world as a dwelling which, in itself, is neither good nor evil, but can become both depending on how people are minded and constituted. A wise and cunning man can make it into a place of pleasure for himself. A simple and foolish man will always find himself poorly off within it. <margin>4)</margin> Still others view this world as a **stage**, upon which a certain invisible power plays, as it were, and deals out good or bad luck. According to what these people believe, one can live well or poorly here below: but no one can contribute anything to it themselves. **Fate** <term>Verhängniß; often used here to describe a deterministic or pagan view of destiny rather than divine providence</term> rules and takes its pleasure in humbling some, elevating others, tormenting these, and gladdening those. A rational person must adapt to this strange government as best he can and play the part that has been assigned to him. None of these opinions is entirely false or incorrect. Each has its proofs and reasons that seem to give it preference over the others. Yet none hits upon the true foundation of the matter: none explains the true intentions that the **Most High** set before Himself when He resolved to create this world and to populate it with such creatures as human beings. Each, on the contrary, leads those who are devoted to it onto certain detours that hinder true godliness and corrupt the hearts of men. What dangerous consequences flow from the first opinion <note>The "first opinion," mentioned on the previous page, likely viewed the world as a prison or place of punishment.</note> is evident to anyone who is not entirely reckless, without our needing to give a reminder. Those who imagine that they live here locked up in a **house of correction or torture** generally become their own enemies.

<column-break/>

In doing so, they offend against the love and goodness of the **Lord**, and they care just as little for the common good of the world as those condemned to eternal imprisonment care to think about how the chamber in which they are locked might be protected and preserved against all accidents. If the world is a land that conforms to its inhabitants and offers life and good days to the clever, but vexation and suffering to the foolish, then **God** is nothing and man is everything. And if this were true, who could blame the cunning if they strained their intellects to deceive the rest, who cannot see so far, and to elevate themselves through their fall? If the world is a **stage** on which **Fate** rules, then it is in vain to work and to arrange one's life according to a certain rule. Let us use what is there as well as we can, and place the outcome of all things into the hands of destiny, which no one can command. Therefore, one must take care that none of these opinions takes hold of the minds of the youth if one wishes them to be prepared for true virtue and godliness.

What this world is in general and in itself, even the most sharp-witted will not determine with all their effort and labor. **"For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?"** <note>original: "Wer hat des HErren Sinn erkant? Wer ist sein Rahtgeber gewesen?"</note> **Romans 11:34**. Who has surveyed the entire order of the works of the Lord? Who knows how the planet that **God** has given us as a dwelling relates to the other great bodies, which we partly glimpse from afar, and partly do not see at...

# The Second Chapter

...not see? We can say nothing more than what the world is in regard to the people who live upon it. This world is a land which the hand of the **Most High** has laid out and adorned with a singular wisdom, so that within it, as in a mirror, mankind may see the greatness of the **Lord** to whom they belong. At the same time, it serves as a place where they may be tested to see if they are worthy of a far better and more beautiful world, in which the **Lord** Himself wishes to commune with them. It is a vestibule <note>original: "Vorhof"; an outer court or entryway to a temple</note> of eternity, in which we are meant to stay for a time to provide proof of our obedience and to see the **Lord**—whom we shall one day behold face to face—in shadow-images <note>A reference to the theological concept that earthly life only offers a dim reflection of divine reality</note>. Everything that otherwise seems difficult and dark to us here will become easy and comprehensible if we take this description to heart. It pleases the **Lord** to lead the rational creatures whom we call human beings, step by step, toward the clarity He has prepared for them. He acts like a Prince who allows a people He wishes to make happy to first dwell in a distant and dangerous land before He leads them into the beautiful regions He has destined for them; this is done to distinguish those who are worthy of a greater rest from those who do not deserve the grace shown to them from afar. Here, we are surrounded by pleasure and displeasure, by joy and sorrow, by pain and sensual delight, by labor and rest. All these seemingly contradictory things are appointed by the wisdom of the **Lord** for one and the same purpose and intent. We are divided into many different orders and serve in various offices. This man 

<column-break/>

rules, that one obeys; this one is full, that one hungers; this one fills the world with the fame of his name, while that one is buried in the dust in which he stooped during the days of his life. This great variety of offices, stations, and ways of life relates to a single goal. That which is allotted to us—be it highness or lowliness, wealth or poverty, pain or pleasure—is that by which the **Lord** wishes to try our obedience and test us. Whoever is found faithful in the part wherein he is placed, and proves his faith and obedience, shall see the **Lord** and receive the reward for his sincerity and patience in another world. In this, the **Lord** does not lack the means to overcome this trial which His wise counsel imposes upon us here below. Nature shows us the majesty of the **God** whom we serve in a thousand images. Grace comes to the aid of the weakness into which we have fallen and equips us with the necessary strength to overcome this world. We are all people who are being led toward one goal in different ways and manners, and we all live, to a certain extent, in the very same state in which our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note> were. Those who constantly remind themselves of this can never become proud and haughty in the good fortune that falls to them, nor ever become sad and dejected in the misery that strikes them. Those who constantly reflect on this will never despise the wretched man in his want, nor worship the high and mighty in his splendor and luxury. Are we not all in the land of trial? # On the Sustenance of Human Corruption.

...the sweat shed by the worker? Is the health in which one man rejoices anything other than the pain that strikes another down? Is the power bestowed upon the king anything other than the helplessness over which the subject sighs? Sleeping humans! Wake up at last, and learn to know the world in which you live! That which you possess and prize so highly, that which you desire and do not obtain, everything you see, enjoy, and feel, is the fire through which we are to be tested <note>original: "bewehret"; in this context, it suggests being tempered or proven, like metal in a furnace</note> here, so that we may receive the crown of life. How much does it matter to those who are to be tried whether their obedience is put to the proof by a matter of great value or by something of little worth? What would two wise men make of it, if one were directed to prove his serenity <term>Gelassenheit: a key Pietist concept meaning a state of inner detachment, patience, and total yieldedness to God's will</term> in a poor garment, and the other his humility in a magnificent one? Would it not be enough for both of them if they knew that, after enduring the trial, they would receive a great and important reward? Whoever wishes to raise their youth wisely must ensure that this concept of the world is planted in their souls.

<margin>3.)</margin>
One must early on show people in their true form to those whom one wishes to lead to the **Lord** from their earliest youth. Nothing is so certain as this: that we, who live in the midst of men, often know nothing less rightly than our brothers. We are all by nature miserable and needy, weak in body, and simple and lacking understanding in soul. We are all evil and full of senseless self-love <term>Eigen-Liebe: a theological term for the selfish pride that turns a person away from God toward themselves</term>. What have the wits of men not devised to hide these three evil qualities? And how we labor, now in this way, now in that, to blind the world so that it might not see our shame? What are the costly fabrics in which we wrap our limbs, the grand retinues in which we appear, the ornaments with which we deck our dwellings, the servants who must wait upon our nod, the strange disguises of our heads and faces <note>This is a critique of 18th-century fashions, such as elaborate powdered wigs and heavy makeup</note>, the constant changes of fashion, the secret tricks of giving color and appearance to the skin of our bodies and keeping away the wrinkles that age is wont to draw, and many other things besides? Are they not all merely coverings for our shame? Do we not wish, through these things, to abolish the natural equality in which we are all born and to introduce a distinction between ourselves and other men? The world, seeing such artfully adorned bodies, is meant to abandon the opinion that we are formed from the very same earth as the beggar and the day laborer, and to entertain the thought that little or nothing of the misery under which human nature lies has been allotted to us. What is our assumed cheerfulness of spirit, our freedom to speak and to judge all things, our boldness

# The Second Chapter

...to blame and destroy the works, deeds, and labors of other people? Is it an attempt to lead others to believe that our understanding is so broad and spacious that it can grasp more than one world and comprehend the most difficult things? And what shall we say of the efforts of men to cover the small flaws of the body that were perhaps born with them? If we applied half of the diligence we use to beautify our perceived natural defects toward the removal of the actual infirmities of our spirit, what happy people we would be! What is our great politeness and readiness to serve? The sweet words with which we seek to ensnare the hearts of men? The particular effort to meet everyone according to their taste and insights? For most, it is nothing but a trick <note>original: "Kunſt-Stück"</note> to hide the ugly shape of our heart—which desires nothing but advantage and honor—from the sight of men, and to persuade them that we have, from birth, entered into an eternal covenant with virtue and truth. Many are deceived by this zeal of men to hide their faults and consider them greater than they actually are. The wisest, who are otherwise no slaves to their senses and can distinguish the appearance from the truth, still often require all the strength of their understanding to pull a man out of the corners in which he hides himself, and to separate in their thoughts the borrowed ornaments—with which he hopes to attain honor and prestige—from his natural gifts and qualities. Those who are inexperienced and bound by the power of their sen-

<column-break/>

-ses proceed without hesitation and grant those who show themselves in such a disguise the preference they demand. From this arise all kinds of evil consequences that disturb our lives and hinder godliness <term>Gottſeligkeit: a core Pietist term for a lived, inward holiness and devotion to God</term> from conquering our minds <term>Gemühter: the totality of a person's inner life, including will, emotion, and intellect</term>. The lowly make the high into earthly gods and dedicate the fear and reverence—which they owe to the **Lord** alone—to perishable creatures who have raised themselves above others through nothing but vain ornament and borrowed splendor. The high accept the service and the unintelligent humility of the lowly as a tribute due to their merits and virtues, and eventually forget that they have a **Lord** in heaven, with whom there is no respect of persons <note>original: "bey dem kein Anſehen der Perſon gilt"; a reference to the biblical concept that God does not judge by outward status or favoritism</note>. This leads one to be misled into trusting his life, fortune, and honor to the hands of such people who have resolved never to speak anything but good, and never to think anything but evil. The opinion that one has formed of the wisdom and greatness of certain people brings him to follow their disorderly example <term>Exempel: a moral pattern or model to be followed or avoided</term>, and without reflection, he hurries with them to the pit that must swallow the sinner. Whoever wish to walk cleverly and wisely in the world and escape many snares must know the art of undressing people and pulling off the mask under which they wish to hide their true nature. And whoever wishes to rightly grasp this art must be led to it from youth. One must [lead] the young people, who come from the societies of such people who, through their finery, through their splendor, through their politeness, through their clever and sharp-witted...

You have now seen a number of people who please your eyes. As it seems to me, you believe that you have left a gathering of uncommon spirits who have cast off what can be called low and common and have perfectly learned the science of living <note>The "science of living" (Wissenschaft zu leben) refers to the art of high-society conduct and social graces.</note>. But know that all those whom you now admire are far from being what they wish to be. All of them brought the intention into the gathering to deceive others, and prepared themselves beforehand with much art so that they could carry out this intention. Accustom yourselves to cast away through reason what these people presented so beautifully and honorably to your senses, and to consider them in their natural nakedness when you have departed from them. Accustom yourselves, as often as you return to your stillness from other people, to impress upon your mind that you have seen nothing but a fragile ash, which God’s power has united with a rational spirit for a short time, and which human pride has veiled in silk, gold, silver, linen, foreign hair <note>A reference to the expensive, powdered wigs fashionable in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> and I know not what other trifles, so that their natural ugliness might not strike the eye. Accustom yourselves to always think that man would never so adorn and decorate himself if he

<column-break/>

did not know himself that he was misshapen and unclean. And never forget that those who appear most magnificently are those who trust the gifts of their nature and the virtues of their spirit the very least. Did you admire that man who, in shining and magnificent clothing, spoke with a particular earnestness and apparent wisdom of the affairs of the world and critiqued the deeds of kings? Follow this great man into his chamber; then you will see what he is! That precious garment is meant to adorn a body that is stained by all kinds of sins and already attacked by hidden diseases, an understanding that knows nothing more than what it has learned from the newspapers <note>original: "Zeitungs-Blättern"; here referring to the broadsheets and early news-sheets of the era.</note>, and a heart that is equipped by nature with guile and violence. You were enchanted by the beauty, the pleasant manner, and the affability of those women, flashing with Oriental stones <note>original: "morgenländischen Steinen"; likely referring to precious gems such as diamonds, rubies, or pearls imported from the East.</note>, wrapped in an artfully woven garment of all kinds of colors, and bearing a testimony of human skill on almost every limb. Strive, with your understanding, to take away that which does not belong to this person and which has been borrowed from many lands so that she might seem more glorious and beautiful in the eyes of men than she truly is! What will remain after this deduction? A spirit that knows neither itself nor the world, and in lack of understanding and ignorance follows the crowd of those who surpass her in folly and luxury. A heart that can love none but those who flatter its evil lusts, which has set out to praise all other people publicly and despise them secretly, which never [remains]

A handful of earth, skillfully formed by GOD and paired with a corrupt spirit. A creature that is born naked and miserable from other humans, who is needy in understanding, evil in will, and yet proud in spirit; who often changes three times in twelve hours and yet always remains constant in his intentions—that is, looking toward nothing but his own advantage and his honor—and in doing so, uses and seeks out everything that nature and art can achieve to hide this miserable condition and to make himself look significant. We laugh at the ancient kings of the Persians and Indians, who had themselves carved in stone three times as large as they actually were, in order to deceive posterity and to instill the error in future times

<column-break/>

that they were giants and extraordinary people. But is it not the very same spirit that enticed these kings to such folly that governs our entire race? What they wanted, we all want in a certain way. We only employ different means than they did to reach our goal, and we wish to enjoy the honor during our lifetime that they expected after death. Think of this, my child, in your dealings with people, so that you do not forget the Lord, who opens the womb of blessed eternity to you for an unchangeable happiness after a few years, so that you do not commit idolatry, and so that you do not lose your true welfare in the world. You are a human yourself and cannot prevent your senses from sometimes being moved, amused, or captivated by the artificial trickery <note>original: "Gauckeley"</note> of men. But your understanding must always be on guard, so that this illusion <note>original: "Blendwerck," literally "blinding-work"</note> may not last long, and the true image of man never leaves your sight.

### The Second Chapter ###

...and clearly accept and consider a concept of this kind. An adult who is occupied in the world in one way or another has already formed a certain sketch <note>original: *Abriß*; a mental blueprint or outline</note> of his own happiness, which he never allows to leave his thoughts. He weighs everything told to him from reason and Scripture regarding his improvement against this sketch. And whatever seems to conflict with it is to him either madness and irrationality, or a weight and a burden, no matter how good it may be. The way of life <note>original: *Wandel*; refers to one's conduct or "walk" through life</note> that our Savior demands will never again agree with any of the images that people are accustomed to making for themselves of a contented and happy lifestyle. And one can therefore be assured that all people who have already firmly decided in what manner they wish to seek their fortune will find no taste for it, even if one exerts all the powers of the mind to make it popular and pleasant. We depict for people the peace that must dwell in a heart that is sanctified, connected with God, grounded in the hope of infinite salvation, and separated from the fellowship of vice. We are heard; what else? We are praised. And that is all. While we are heard and praised, the already pampered heart makes this objection in silence: "Will not a good portion of the pleasure I enjoy be lost in this so-vaunted peace? Will I feel the delight in it that has hitherto enchanted me when I have grown richer by craftiness and deceit? Will I still feel the pleasant fire

<column-break/>

that the excessive use of certain drinks is accustomed to igniting within me? Will I further hear the fame that has hitherto been granted to me in so many gatherings because of my clever ideas and merry mockeries? Will I retain the hope that so gladdens me, that my kin will look upon the lowly world with as much contempt as I can, owing to my wealth and my honor? Will I be able to continue using the comforts that I have hitherto taken to the harm and disadvantage of many people?" And this inward rebellion puts our entire effort to shame. We praise the strength, the health, the peace, and the joy that a moderate and orderly life provides. And with those who have already tasted the fruits of lust <note>original: *Wollust*; in this context, it refers to carnal or worldly pleasure rather than just sexual desire</note> and who count the inflaming of the blood and the vital spirits as necessary pieces of their welfare in the world, we labor in vain. Why? Our discourse is refuted by the design that the immoderate man has made of a happy life. If that which we can say to clarify the incomparable words of the Apostle is to take hold in a person—*Godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come* <note>1 Timothy 4:8</note>—if this is to take hold and endure, it must be entrusted early to the understanding, before the world infects us and our soul has finished preparing the idols which, because it is united with the body, it intends to worship.

# On the Maintenance of Human Depravity #

...with that which happens in the world, and then judge whether we do not have cause to trace the origin of the wickedness of many people back to their earliest years. In which Christian community is the youth so prepared for obedience toward the Lord and His grace? And yet we still ask: From where do the weeds <note>original: *Unkraut*; a biblical metaphor for sinful impulses or wicked people among the good</note> come? From where comes the crude and ungodly nature of the world? One portion of humanity is not raised at all. Another portion is raised poorly, to the detriment of reason and true wisdom. The vast majority grow up exactly as they were born, retaining all the freedom to nourish and strengthen the bad habits and lack of understanding they brought into the light of this world. Those who should sanctify their young years to the Lord often, through the evil example they provide, make them "children of hell twice as much as they are themselves." **Matthew 23:15.** The disciplines with which their faults are punished do not improve the soul. Furthermore, these punishments are often used so irrationally that wickedness gains more from them than it loses. Those who should correct the parents' mistakes in the schools are, for the most part, incompetent in all matters. What is the small amount of religion they instill in children through coercion and fear? A clutter of words <note>original: *Wörter-Kram*; implying rote memorization of vocabulary without spiritual depth</note> that does not touch the soul and vanishes after a few years. The rest of what they learn serves only to help them find their bread and provide for the body’s nourishment. And where are the means to remedy these evils in the current state of the world? We see almost none, unless those who govern the world under the supervision of the Lord

<column-break/>

wish to use the power they have received from the highest authority for the benefit of mankind. Lord! How often the spirit of Your servants sinks into melancholy and sadness when they see Your little ones wandering like sheep that have no shepherd? Lord! When will the times come when Your anointed ones <note>original: *Geſalbten*; referring to kings and sovereigns seen as divinely appointed</note> will comprehend that the welfare of the nations entrusted to them by Your hand depends on a wise education—and that the lands must be the happiest, the richest, and the most peaceful in which the subjects are led early on to Your service and to a pure fear of God and love of neighbor?

A skill in hiding one’s true intentions and inclinations, and persuading the people with whom one interacts—through favors and other not-so-praiseworthy means—that one is what one is not, so that one may acquire reputation and property. However, that which is commonly passed off as such resembles the true art in very few respects; it is stained with so many false and ruinous teachings that one can hardly see the good that is still mixed within it. Those who want to make their charges quite "perfect" *finally also teach them the secret of becoming rich* without falling under the suspicion of greed, along with the skill of drawing one honorary post and dignity after another to themselves without possessing the merits that are required for them by fairness. And if we should judge the instructions given to them in their youth for this purpose by the behavior of those who rise in the world (though no one knows how) and accumulate goods—as it appears must be the case—then neither the commandments of justice nor the teachings of Jesus Christ have any part in this supposed wisdom. <margin>M</margin> What time then remains to thoroughly instruct young people about God and their duties, to prepare them for faith and love, and to lead them to the denial and contempt of this world and its goods? Little or nothing. It is held to be enough that a young person does not remain entirely inexperienced in the things that are reckoned toward religion...

And when we have reflected on where these evils come from, we have been able to find no other causes than an immoderate love of the world, a blind pride and haughtiness, a violent desire to acquire honor and fortune for oneself, an entirely false and absurd opinion of true happiness, and other such evil inclinations. # On the Sustenance of Human Corruption

It <note>The author refers here to the "laws of politeness" or worldly social custom personified as a teacher.</note> commands its pupils first and foremost to say things that can stir up the **disordered desires** of our nature, which cling to all people. It then requires one to pay heed to everyone’s taste and to arrange the conversation so that everyone finds something therein that serves particularly for their **amusement**. It further commands that whatever might still seem rational and wise be immediately turned into a **jest** and ruined by a witty whim; that innocent and well-intentioned ways of speaking be skillfully twisted into a punishable or absurd meaning; that the pride of men be refreshed by all kinds of tales of other people’s faults and follies; and that one play with **double entendres** <note>original: "zweydeutigen Worten"</note> that can fan the quiet fire of lust without great offense to outward **decency**. There is rarely a lack of people practiced in this art, since the opinion has taken hold that no one lacks common skill who knows how to move others to laughter. Yet, if perhaps no one is found in a gathering who is capable of this, people afterwards complain about the annoyance they felt and lament that they were **bored**. What are our **pleasures** and **delights**? Most are nothing but a blind noise started without **reason**, which does not cheer our spirit but numbs it, and does not refresh our body but tires it. We are permitted to seek a pleasure at times that does not conflict with the law of the Lord, because our soul, as well as our body, would succumb under everlasting labor. However, we are bound therein to arrange it so that we receive new strength through it to serve the world and the Lord with all the more utility, and can return to our ordinary work with an unblemished heart and a cheered body. Can we boast that we hold to this rule, which both **Scripture** and **reason** prescribe? Our delights should be a <term>Artzney: medicine or remedy</term> against the fatigue of body and spirit. Where are those who consider this? A large part of humanity lives as if it were born to amuse itself constantly, and only occasionally had to undertake something else so that it might not become entirely weary of <term>Wollüste: sensual pleasures or luxuries; often carries a connotation of sinful excess</term>, or find a lack of the means necessary for their continuation. # The Second Chapter

...render them unfit for useful duties. How perverse is man? The order of the Lord intends for our work to alternate with rest and permitted amusements, so that we may remain strong enough to bear the portion of toil that His providence has seen fit to impose upon us. The law of our **wickedness** <note>original: "Unart"—this refers to a lack of discipline or a corrupted nature</note> commands the opposite: Man must exhaust himself through violent and reckless desires, so that he may receive a morose spirit and a heavy body and become useless to both the world and God.

Callicles, a man who knows nothing more than what reason and reflection can provide, comes from the isolation in which he has lived his life until now among a few friends, into one of our cities, wanting to learn about the world. A few days after his arrival, he presents himself to some people of reputation and intends to increase his knowledge through conversation with them. He is told that these distinguished men cannot have the honor of seeing him today; they have invited some friends over to drive away the annoyance that their burdensome offices cause them every day, and to enjoy themselves. The foreign sage goes home with pleasure, in the belief that tomorrow he will find those he seeks all the more cheerful and spirited, because they have taken a one-day break from the plague and toil of their lives. He returns the next day at the designated hour and asks to be admitted. The entrance is blocked, just as it was yesterday. The servants bring the news that their masters find themselves

<column-break/>

ill, and could hardly speak with anyone today: Their heads are filled with **vapors** <note>In 18th-century medicine, "vapors" were thought to be internal fumes that rose to the brain, causing confusion or illness; here it describes a hangover or mental exhaustion from over-indulgence.</note>, the body is exhausted, and the spirit is in disorder. Yesterday’s pleasure was somewhat intense and has left unpleasant sensations behind. Callicles thinks he is hearing a poem <note>Meaning he thinks they are telling him a fictional story or a joke.</note> when he is told this. He returns to his inn and wants to inquire more closely with others whether he can trust this pretext. On the way, he passes a house in which a crowd of people is gathered, some of whom are shouting, others jumping; some behaving indecently, others quarreling, some playing, others drinking, and no one is in possession of themselves. He thinks he sees a gathering of **insane** people who ought to be taken under stricter supervision, and asks a passerby what this means. The reply is: "A few good people have come together in this house who have worked many days in a row and now want to refresh and rest themselves." Callicles recognizes from this that what those servants told him might be true, and shortly thereafter is convinced of it by others. By the next post, he sends this news to one of his friends whom he left behind: "My friend! It seems that we have been remarkably deceived in our thoughts about the world. What I have seen of it so far looks, at the very least, completely different from the image we formed of it in our silence. We convinced ourselves that among men, just as among us, rest must follow toil and labor, and that in the hours set aside for pleasure, one would give to the body and the spirit..."

### On the Sustenance of Human Ruin.

...must give the spirit space to recover itself. In the land where I now live, the opposite has been introduced. Here, the labors are the amusements that keep body and spirit in order, and the amusements are the labors that ruin and exhaust the whole person. You know that we have sometimes become sick from our deep reflection and physical exercises, and had to give ourselves rest for a time to prevent greater evils. Can you believe that here the reverse takes place? Here, labor makes one healthy, and rest from labor makes one sick. People remain strong and healthy in body and spirit during their efforts; and in the hours of their pleasure, all the strength they saved during their regular duties is so utterly lost that they lie prostrate for the following days and must call for the physician. We once thought that toil and labor could shorten a person's life. Let go of that opinion. Here, pleasure and rest deliver people into the arms of death. It is a stroke of luck that most people here are so needy <note>original: "dürftig"—referring to poverty or a meager state of living</note> that they can seldom afford to leave their work aside. Could they enjoy and refresh themselves more often, the land would lose most of its inhabitants sooner than one might think.

What shall we say of the remaining circumstances of those delights that we are accustomed to use? We are too cautious to claim that they are nearly all sins. We know that many exceptions must be added to such general propositions if they are to hold any weight. And what use is a general teaching that 

<column-break/>

must be accompanied by a thousand exceptions if it is not to be rejected as false? This we can claim without fear: that most worldly pleasures <note>original: "Wollüste"—while often translated as 'lusts,' in this 18th-century context it refers more broadly to sensual or carnal delights</note> are closely related to actual sins, and are enjoyed by few without some fault against the conscience. We know of almost nothing except the amusements of the senses and the imagination. How few are those who know how to create a pure pleasure for the spirit, and can cheer themselves without the aid of their senses? And is it not true that the senses and imagination are dangerous leaders, who seldom observe measure and order, and often—before we expect it—lead people away from the middle path <term>middle path: "Mittel-Strasse," the classical ideal of moderation or the 'golden mean' between extremes</term>? Our lavish meals are cruel kindnesses. We strive to weaken the health of our guests through an abundance of food. We take pleasure when we see that those who arrived sensible, depart deranged and without reason. We reflect on how we might beguile their understanding and corrupt their hearts with vain and useless conversation. Our games are exercises that can stir up harmful desires in most people. We know people who perhaps would never have thought of secret malice and deception if they had not learned the secret of how to prey upon the unwary during play. What need is there to say many words about the other amusements of our times? Whoever truly knows them, and does not wish to deceive himself, will agree with those who believe that most of them provide opportunity for a wretched unrest of the spirit and a dangerous disruption of one's thoughts.

## Chapter Two

...be able to. O God! How often does the word of the wise King occur to your servants, who see the world in its amusements: *I said of laughter: It is mad; and of mirth: What doeth it?* <note>original: "Ich sprach zum Lachen: Du bist toll, und zur Freude: Was machstu?" — Ecclesiastes 2:2</note>

->§. XII.<-

The piety of men is very often directed according to their knowledge and understanding. And their knowledge is commonly of such a nature as the instruction they have received. He who has been wisely and sensibly instructed recognizes that which he knows thoroughly and clearly. He who has been unskillfully and disorderly taught often knows nothing, even though he believes he has grasped much. We have a twofold instruction in our congregations; one for the young beginners in religion and piety, the other for the adults who have already laid the foundation in the truths belonging to faith and life. Might the decay of piety in many places perhaps be attributed to those to whom this double instruction is entrusted? Would people often understand so little of the truth that leads to piety if it had been conveyed to them clearly and convincingly? The instruction of the youth occurs through questions and answers and is called <term>catechization: a method of religious instruction using a series of fixed questions and answers to teach the core tenets of faith</term>. It seems as if many do not even rightly know the nature and character of this method of instruction and therefore manage it very poorly. Should one then be surprised that those who come out of their school recite nothing but words without power, and know how to recount what they should believe and practice without understanding, yet know not how to rightly explain it to anyone?

### On the Perpetuation of Human Corruption.

...catechized and instructed. This opinion cannot be better proven than by explaining the true nature and the purpose of so-called **catechization** <note>The process of teaching through a series of questions and answers, usually for religious instruction.</note> and deriving several consequences from this presentation. From this, our readers will easily be able to judge whether we have hitherto seen correctly, or whether we have been deceived. We must be granted to be right if what we are now about to mention regarding the nature of catechization is true. For who will deny that many of those who catechize either do not understand this or completely lose sight of it during their work? We, in turn, will gladly confess that we have erred if it can be demonstrated to us that this way of teaching of which we speak is constituted quite differently than we believe.

**Socrates is, unless we are very much mistaken, the principal inventor and author of the instruction that occurs by way of questions.** It may be that some among the Greeks had already stumbled upon this method of teaching before him. And perhaps some wise people among other nations also formerly instructed the youth in this manner. The great obscurity of ancient history does not allow us to assert anything certain about it. However, it remains, as we believe, indisputable that this famous Greek sage first brought it into practice, explained and illustrated it through his example, and—through his prestige—transmitted it both to his students and to others who recognized its benefit. He can rightly be called the first master of a custom who gave posterity the opportunity to adopt

<column-break/>

it and to spread it ever further. This extraordinary mind noticed that the Greek youth in the public schools were poorly instructed in the sciences <note>In the 18th-century context, "sciences" (Wissenschaften) refers broadly to any systematic branch of knowledge, including philosophy and logic.</note> which can be grasped by the understanding alone. He said that after they had learned for many years, they nevertheless knew how to recite nothing but words and names, or else understood the nature of things so imperfectly and incorrectly that their knowledge could be called an error rather than a genuine realization. The causes of this evil could not long remain unknown to such a great spirit. He soon found it came from the fact that people only engaged the memory and the imagination of the young people and took no pains to open their understanding and lead them to think and judge for themselves. A person to whom the same thing is presented for a considerable time must finally grasp it with the memory and, where he does not entirely lack imagination or the skill of the tongue, know how to recite it to others. Is he thereby learned and wise? Not in the least. As long as he cannot judge, test, take apart, compare with other things, and precisely separate from other things that which he has learned—in a word, as long as he does not know how to use his understanding to properly perceive what has been grasped and, as it were, make it his own—his knowledge is a foreign good that actually belongs to his teacher and can be stolen by anyone who has a bit of wit and skill. ## Chapter Two.

...hitherto had only worked with memory and imagination, so that in the future they might not merely be rich in words, but might attain clear and distinct concepts of things.

To understand his intention, one only needs to remember the saying he so often uttered: He was, he said, what his mother was. His mother was a midwife <note>original: "Heb-Amme"</note>. She assisted women so that they might more easily bring their children into the world.

He performed this very same office for the human understanding, seeking to lead people so that the children of their spirit—the concepts of their souls—might be perfectly and successfully born and presented to the world. It is no wonder that this man has been shown such uncommon and constant reverence, both among the pagans <note>original: "Heyden"</note> and later among the Christians themselves.

The world has certainly had very few people who have seen so clearly into human nature, who could so skillfully distinguish a true science <note>original: "Wiſſenſchaft"; in this context, it refers to systematic knowledge or "scientia"</note> from a false and deceitful one, and who knew how to clarify the most difficult things with such sharp intellect; not to mention the other special qualities and natural virtues that have rightly made him great and venerable to posterity.

He found that there would be no better means to achieve the goal he had set for himself than to probe the young people—whom he wished to lead to wisdom and rational science—through cautious and wise questioning, and to persist with it until he had corrected their imperfect and deficient concepts and had imperceptibly torn them out of their ignorance by their own efforts. The means

<column-break/>

was well and sensibly devised, but difficult to carry out under the circumstances of that time. He was not dealing with children, or with pupils who were subject to his discipline. They were already grown, free men whom he wanted to improve—people who, for the most part, were puffed up by status, birth, wealth, and the hope of soon rising; people who had already spent many years in the schools of the most learned and were sick with the imagination that they already knew everything a man could learn who wished to serve his fatherland with profit.

His intention even extended to the teachers themselves, to whom the youth were customarily entrusted. It annoyed him that many among them stuck in the very same darkness in which their pupils walked: And he thought all of Greece would benefit if he convicted the most boastful and famous among these people of ignorance and brought them to the point where they first learned themselves before they taught others.

The work therefore had to be conducted with caution. People of this sort could not be questioned in the same way as pupils and beginners. What would their pride have done if one had treated them like the ignorant and apprentices?

Socrates therefore took upon himself the persona of a student who wishes to learn, and gave those whom he wished to instruct the persona of a teacher from whom he hoped for instruction. # On the Cultivation of the Human Understanding <note>original: "Von Unterhaltung des menschlichen Verderbens"; the word "Verderbens" (ruin/corruption) in the header is almost certainly a printer's error for "Verstandes" (understanding), as it contradicts the entire content of the chapter and the catchword logic of the era.</note>

[...ance,] then brought easy questions into play and demanded an answer to them. From the answers he was given, he took the opportunity to ask new questions, without letting it be known that he thought anyone had answered poorly. As the conversation progressed, he often complained about his **slow wit** <note>original: "schweren Verstand"</note>, which he claimed did not allow him to rise up properly and to see and grasp everything immediately. Under this pretext, he asked for new explanations. In this way, he finally pushed the matter so far that those with whom he had engaged noticed that the **pretended disciple** knew more than the master he had chosen. 

The conclusion of the conversation ended exactly as Socrates wished. Some went away ashamed, others thoroughly instructed and enlightened. There are still many such conversations available, which his students recorded or composed from memory, from which one can see how he went about this type of instruction. They all agree on the main points. And whoever has read them with care can easily extract the general rules according to which this excellent man proceeded. 

His main intention was to **sharpen human understanding**, to make those things truly known to them which they had recognized only darkly and indistinctly, to correct their errors, and to accustom them to accepting nothing without care and reflection. To this end, he first endeavored, through a few questions, to investigate their true opinion of the things he wished to treat. He eased the burden of correctly phrasing and presenting their thoughts through all sorts of **images**

Part I.

<column-break/>

and **analogies** <note>original: "Gleichnisse"</note>, which he took from common life and from those things that had become known to them through the senses and experience. Generally, he used three or even more such images, so that he himself might become all the more certain and they might reveal their opinion all the more clearly. He behaved as if he himself required these explanations because of his own simplicity and weakness, and never let it be noticed that he wished to offer a helping hand to the untrained intellect of his students. 

After a short time, it was found that those whom he questioned either did not know the matters at all or knew them very imperfectly, despite thinking they understood them fundamentally. He then continued and worked, through new questions and explanations, on the improvement and arrangement of their incorrect and dark concepts. He took away what was superfluous. He replaced what was missing. He set right what was disorderly. He polished, trimmed, transposed, and improved for so long until a **clear and pure image** emerged, which exactly and properly agreed with the nature of the thing. 

All of this happened under the appearance of a **desire to learn** <note>original: "Lehr-Begierde"</note> quite imperceptibly and in such a way that the person he instructed did not know himself what was being aimed at. The questions were phrased so simply that they seemed to mean nothing at all, despite the fact that they were all necessary to the main matter. The images and explanations related to the most common things of human life. The student never had to hesitate nor strain his intellect. The answer already lay in the question. He did not have to worry that he would betray his ignorance.

...is conducted. His teacher dictates to him how he must answer. This useful effort to clear the understanding of the ignorant and half-learned turned out very badly for *Socrates*. To whom is his death unknown?
