The **catechization** is a rational and orderly conversation between a teacher and a student, in which the teacher adopts the persona of the student and, through careful and clever questions, seeks partly to explore the true concept the student forms of things that do not move the senses, and partly to correct the errors in this concept, so that the disciple may become like the master and perceive a pure and correct image of truth in his understanding just as well as he does. ## Chapter Two

...compelled to write. If a more convenient opportunity arises, it will be easy for us to present in detail what we must now partly leave to our readers' own reflection. We demand that the catechist <term>catechist: a teacher who instructs through questions and answers, usually regarding religious principles</term> must take on the persona of the student and ask questions as if he himself wished to learn. This is how the first founder <note>referring to Socrates</note> of this way of teaching did it. And the very purpose of this method necessitates it. Anyone who merely wants to know in general what the person they are questioning has learned; whether they can give a general account of their faith; whether the tenets of a doctrine stick in their memory word-for-word—anyone who wants to test the knowledge of young people in things subject to the senses and imagination, I mean in history, geography <term>geography: original German *Erdbeschreibung*, literally "earth-description"</term>, geometry <term>geometry: original German *Meß-Kunst*, literally "the art of measuring"</term>, and other matters—such a person can ask questions like a teacher and view his subordinates as students. His only concern is to see whether the memory of the people he has instructed is rich and filled with the things he wished to instill in them. And this can be drawn out no matter how one chooses to ask. It is quite different for those who wish to investigate how the concepts of youth are actually formed regarding things that only the intellect <note>original: *Verstand*</note> can clearly grasp and use for its own and the world's benefit, and who want to correct the deficiencies and errors of these concepts. These people must position themselves as students in order not to miss the truth. He who asks like a teacher is usually paid in words and is often deceived by those words. He who asks like a student cannot

<column-break/>

be dismissed with mere words. Even against the will of the person he instructs, he draws out thoughts and concepts that reveal the state of the human soul and provide an opportunity to remedy ignorance and errors. He who asks like a teacher inevitably falls, before he even suspects it, into punishing the youth who answer incorrectly. And through this, the learner is frightened, and the conversation, which should flow continuously, falls into disorder. Anyone can see how much this harms instruction without us needing to mention it. He who asks like a student can continue the conversation unhindered and is not so easily misled or upset by poorly conceived answers. He who asks like a teacher can hardly maintain the trust, love, and freedom of the youth, which he so desperately needs for his work. He who asks like a student imperceptibly humbles himself below those he wishes to instruct, and thereby awakens in them the heart and courage to express their thoughts faithfully and sincerely. He who asks like a teacher cannot easily continue the discussion until everything within the student's intellect reveals itself as clearly as necessary. He presumes to possess great knowledge. And this very knowledge will stand in his way during the progress of the work, preventing him from investigating as precisely and thoroughly as the purpose of his effort requires. He who asks like a student can, under the cover of his assumed ignorance, push the matter as far as he pleases without offense or hindrance.

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption #
<note>The original title "Von Unterhaltung des menschlichen Verderbens" likely refers to the theological concept of the "corrupt" or "fallen" state of man, which education seeks to address or "maintain" in the sense of managing and correcting it through instruction.</note>

Who is ever lacking in new questions and objections, if they are someone who truly wishes to learn, or even someone who merely pretends to be ignorant? And finally—so that we do not cite several other causes—what is the greatest and most skillful teacher for a time, when he catechizes? <term>catechizes: refers here to a specific Socratic method of teaching through dialogue rather than rote memorization</term> He is nothing but a pupil and a student. He first endeavors to explore the true opinion of the person he wishes to instruct through his questions, so that he may afterwards either confirm it, if it is correct, or improve it, if he finds it erroneous. Does this not mean being ignorant and wanting to learn? He cannot, therefore, do otherwise than ask questions in the beginning like an ignorant student, and he must hold back his own knowledge until he has heard the mind of the other who is to be instructed by him. We cannot, therefore, deny that we have often been surprised when we hear certain people, who are presented as extraordinary teachers of youth, asking questions only as masters who could look into the hearts of their students and read their thoughts. Yet we have observed so many other errors in common catechizations that we have made this one almost the least among them.

We have established that catechization properly extends only to those things which do not move the senses and imagination. This will seem strange to no one who simultaneously takes into consideration the rest of what we have noted, and who will see from it that by this word <note>the word "catechization"</note> we do not mean every testing of another's knowledge, nor every kind of questioning, but only that testing and questioning through which the concepts of the understanding are properly 

<column-break/>

established and the spirit is to be brought into order. Whoever seeks to explore through questions how much a young person has learned of Biblical history, of the division of the Promised Land, or of the customs of the Jews, can reach his goal without great effort. It is unnecessary for him to pose as a student; unnecessary for him to seek to discover the mind of his pupil through all sorts of detours; and unnecessary for him to refute the mind he has discovered through new questions or to bring it to clarity and distinctness. He does not put the understanding <note>original: *Verstand*</note> to the test, but only the memory and the imagination of the disciple. And the state of these two powers can soon be fathomed, and just as easily improved where necessary, because one can take the human senses to one's aid. However, we do not actually call this work "catechizing," but merely "inquiring" <note>original: *nachfragen*</note> to see whether there is as much of certain things present in a person’s memory as one wishes to find there, and whether the imagination has not failed in the arrangement of its mental images. <margin>}</margin> To catechize means to enlighten the understanding through questions in such matters that fall under the jurisdiction of the understanding and are reached neither through the senses nor through the imagination alone.

That which we have considered in our description of the purpose of catechization simultaneously presents the most prominent rules which he who wishes to preside over this work with profit must always have before his eyes. ->### Chapter Two###<-

Questions seek to explore the true concept that the student forms of those matters pertaining to faith and life. It is proven and established that a person rarely forms a correct representation or image of things that are merely presented and explained to him in a speech. The most clear and upright teacher is often dismayed by the perverse and unintelligible answers of his students when he wishes to hear, at the end of his lecture, how far they have understood him. This arises from various causes, which we do not wish to recount in detail now. Sometimes the fault lies with the teacher; sometimes it is found with the listener. The latter is sometimes abandoned by his attention, and sometimes by his memory. Often he allows his imagination to work more than his understanding during the time of instruction. And not infrequently, his natural inclinations mingle unnoticed into the matter, preventing the understanding from properly working out the image it is supposed to construct. We will not mention that many are held back by a natural sluggishness and dullness of spirit, so that they cannot well follow the teacher. The teacher presents the matter as he himself has grasped it. And how often does this concept not suit the understanding of those he is meant to instruct? What seems easy, clear, and distinct to him often seems difficult, dark, and indistinct to many of those who hear him, because their understanding—if we may speak this way—is formed and arranged quite differently. Often he measures the power of his students' understanding by the strength of the spirit that dwells within himself. Often he lets

<column-break/>

himself be rushed by other errors. One must expect even greater darkness among those who have only learned a matter by heart from a book. The living voice of a man who presents things in an orderly and sensible manner sets the understanding of the listeners into motion and labor. And therefore, at the very least, a kind of dawn <note>original: "Demmerung," suggesting the first glimmer of light in the mind</note> must arise in the human spirit—that is to say, a certain, albeit imperfect, knowledge <term>knowledge: from the German "Erkenntniß," meaning a deeper realization or recognition rather than just facts</term>. Conversely, those who merely entrust another’s words to their memory generally let their understanding rest entirely; they can rarely give back anything else to those who ask them than the very words they have grasped. One can therefore be certain that the vast majority of young people, who are instructed in things invisible and withdrawn from our senses only through words or the writings of another, preserve in their souls either no concepts at all, or at least very confused, dark, and disordered ones. What is the use of this knowledge? It serves nothing but to deceive people who imagine that wisdom dwells where many words are made. A wise catechist <term>catechist: a teacher who uses a dialogue-based method to teach religious principles</term> must therefore, as it were, descend into the understanding of those whom he wishes to fill with an upright and fundamental knowledge of God and divine things. He must explore, through simple but well-considered questions, what kind of concept of the doctrines of religion lies in the souls of his disciples. Whether they understand anything more than the words of the book which has been given to them as a guide for their knowledge? What kind of thought-images <term>thought-images: from the German "Denckbilder," referring to the mental models or pictures a student forms to represent abstract ideas</term> they [associate] with the words, which they...

A person finds more than one cause within themselves that prevents them from revealing the thoughts of their heart without error or misunderstanding. Sometimes the memory refuses to do its duty. And we must first precisely and clearly understand and recognize the thoughts and opinions of a person before we can work on refining their concepts and bring them onto the path of wisdom and truth.

<margin>2.)</margin>
The second Main Law: A *Catechist* <note>A teacher who uses the method of question-and-answer, usually for religious instruction</note> must seek to gradually purify, improve, supplement, and prune the concepts of the youth—once they have been brought to light and explored through questioning—using new and well-formulated questions, until the image of truth in the student's understanding matches perfectly in all parts with the image that lies in his own understanding, or rather, in the matter itself. ### The Second Chapter ###

[The teacher] must show him through his questions what is too much or too little in his thoughts, and let the pupil himself lay a hand on them to take away the superfluous and add what is lacking. He must do this in more than one way. Rarely does the undertaking succeed if one stays upon a single path. He must continue with this for as long as it takes until the apprentice <note>original: "Lehrling"</note> himself has grasped and arranged the concept according to the pattern of pure truth. It is difficult for us to find the words that can clearly explain the essence and nature of this instruction: how much harder, then, must the work itself fall to those who have not practiced it? In all of this, the teacher must never forget that he is dealing with human beings who are not yet truly masters of their understanding, who lie fettered, as it were, under the power of their senses and imagination, and who can hardly tear themselves away from the fog <note>original: "Miß"—likely meaning the obscuring mist or distractions</note> of the visible world. Such people always consult their imagination and follow its will whenever they hear and try to grasp something spiritual and heavenly. These people must be guided through their own imagination and senses toward purer contemplations and thoughts. Whoever speaks only to their pure intellect will remain incomprehensible and unclear to them. One must, therefore, always have images and parables at hand, taken from common life and from the things they know most about, in order to make higher matters known to them through these, and to lead their understanding to thinking and reflection in a playful manner. One must take various such images apart through questions and ex-

<column-break/>

plain them. One must skillfully apply these images to divine things without violating the truth, and make the youth capable—through what they already know and understand—of getting to know divine wisdom without error. Those who are guided and instructed in this way must (unless they are devoid of all natural gifts) come to themselves, learn to grasp religion clearly and correctly, and attain a thorough knowledge <term>Wissenschaft: in this context, a systematic and grounded understanding of faith, rather than "science" in the modern sense</term>. An understanding that is prepared in this way from its earliest years will not easily accept anything presented to it without consideration and reflection. Such a person will draw benefit from public exhortations and be able to edify himself from the reading of godly books. He will clearly present what he knows and be able to edify and uplift not only himself but also others with his knowledge.

It only depends on the artist bringing the material into a different order. He must be a man in whose memory a supply of various words and phrases always stands at his service; whose imagination is extensive and quick, yet remains correct and subject to reason; in whose understanding light, clarity, and distinctness reign; whose will burns with a righteous desire to make people children of the light; and from whose gestures and words nothing but gentleness and love shine forth. How many people can boast that they are equipped with these gifts of the spirit?

The second consequence: **Those who are to serve in this kind of instruction must rightfully be drawn to it and prepared for it from their earliest years, and burdened with no other business or labor.** It costs practice, time, and effort to habituate one's understanding and will so that they can be used in the prescribed manner. A wise, deliberate, and orderly <term>Catechization<note>A method of oral instruction, often using a question-and-answer format, to teach the core principles of the Christian faith.</note></term> requires a soul that is composed, alert, fresh, and has all its powers gathered together; a soul that is neither troubled by foreign thoughts nor forced to count the moments it can spend on the conversation with beginners. The third consequence: **One can catechize none other than those people who have already laid a foundation in Christian doctrine and know how to use their understanding to some extent.** The immature and children can be asked whether their memory has grasped the words in which the points of religion are presented in the usual textbooks, or the verses from the Scripture added for their proof. The fourth consequence. **Catechization is a conversation that, properly speaking, can only be conducted with one person at a time.** In these conversations, we wish to enlighten the understanding of the youth, to draw out their true opinions through questions, and not to let them go from us until we can be certain that they see the truth in its proper form. Is this possible in a conversation held with many at once, interrupted every moment and adjusted by various answers—now this way, now that? A conversation of this kind, in our opinion, mostly leaves the unpracticed confused and uncertain, scatters their thoughts as well as the teacher's, maintains the inattentiveness which is the common weakness of the early years, and prevents the questioners from explaining and carrying out a matter quite orderly and in detail. We know of no congregation among us in which this is considered. We catechize a large number of young people at once. We believe that most of them, if not all, must be questioned. We improve the imperfect answers of one through the answers of another. We present five or six questions about certain things to one person, and then hurry on to the rest. In certain places, a <term>Catechization<note>Oral instruction using a question-and-answer format to teach religious principles.</note></term> looks not unlike a muster of soldiers. <column-break/>

ignorant? Is it possible that a man who goes through a large assembly in such a manner can properly hold his thoughts together? Is it to be believed that so many inexperienced people will comprehend anything in its proper context from such a divided and torn instruction? Either we do not rightly know the nature of man, or our catechizing would have to bear more fruit if we constantly, thoroughly, and skillfully questioned only one or two of the best among the crowd at any one time, and let the others listen until they could be tested in the same way at another time.

The fifth consequence. **One must never set out more than a single piece of Christian doctrine for catechization at one time.** This single piece must be weighed, perceived, and examined from all sides, and impressed upon the understanding with skill. The spirit of the youth is not yet so ready and quick that it can move from one matter to another without disorder and offense, nor can it change its thoughts so that the first do not cause confusion in the following ones. And he who wishes to make many things known at once to people who have not yet reached this proficiency often experiences with frustration that not one of them has been properly understood.

### Explanation.

It has been a long time since we collected a small supply of all sorts of reminders concerning preaching in our church and decided to submit them to the public judgment of reasonable people. It remains to be seen whether the providence of the Lord will assign us a convenient time in the remainder of our life to improve and arrange them so that they can show themselves to the eyes of the world. We wished, therefore, that we could here present and explain the most prominent and necessary points from them. However, we see ourselves hemmed in on all sides and must, against our will, yield to time and the other circumstances that command brevity. They did not explain any specific passage of Scripture. They did not formally execute any doctrine of faith or life. ## The Second Chapter

->486<-

...occurred outside the hours of public worship. This oldest style of preaching has gradually been completely changed by various causes, which we cannot recount at present. Public sermons have gradually become long speeches intended to serve a dual purpose: partly for the instruction of adults in the teachings of faith and life, and partly for the awakening of **godliness** <term>piety or living devotion<note>original: "Gottseligkeit." In this context, it refers to a deep, active religious life rather than just outward ritual.</note></term>. That which people learn of religion in the years of their youth is only the beginning and **ground-plan** <note>original: "Grund-Riß," meaning the fundamental outline or architectural sketch of faith.</note> of the faith, which is thereafter to be expanded, filled out, and brought to perfection. Furthermore, this little that was learned is obscured in many ways as age increases; it is stifled and contaminated by all sorts of false propositions—given partly by human corruption and partly by the **ill-mannered world** <note>original: "unartige Welt." The author refers to a world that is contrary to God's order.</note>—and sometimes even extinguished where it is not renewed, confirmed, and strengthened. Therefore, it is necessary that they learn as long as they live, and are always pointed and led back to those truths which one took pains to plant in their souls during their times of **ignorance** <note>original: "Unverstandes," referring to the intellectual immaturity of childhood.</note>, lest they fall into ignorance, error, superstition, and ungodliness. The earliest Christians were not ashamed to be continually instructed, and they attended the labors of the **catechists** <term>teachers of the fundamentals of faith<note>original: "Catecheten." Those who taught the basic doctrines, often to new converts or children.</note></term> with pleasure. But once that first love had died away and the living zeal that burned in the souls of the first Christians was extinguished, one could no longer bring people to travel to the places where the catechists instructed the beginners outside the time of public worship. Most were held back by **pride**.

<column-break/>

They considered it a shame to sit down among the students or otherwise be instructed by the teachers. Others would hardly allow their worldly business and labors to **pause** <note>original: "Anstand geben."</note> for as long as the hours of the common gatherings for public worship lasted. What was to be done in this state? Out of necessity, the exhortations to the people had to be expanded and composed in such a way that the inattentive and ignorant could find the instruction they needed therein—instruction which they were unwilling to seek anywhere else but at public worship. Thus, arrangements were made everywhere among Christians that a passage from the Scriptures should be read by the orator at the gatherings of the congregation, explained, and applied for the instruction of those present. Most of the listeners were **simple** <note>original: "einfältig," meaning uneducated or lacking intellectual sophistication.</note> and inattentive. So that their simplicity might not hinder the benefit of this labor, it was decided to extract the **main content** from these speeches and to compose the speeches themselves so orderly that they could be broken down into certain parts. Then, both these parts and the main proposition to which they belonged would be recited at the beginning of the instruction and sometimes repeated. It stood to reason, of course, that to an ordinary person, who is not accustomed to training his mind to think, a continuous speech must seem like a **labyrinth**, and that one must therefore present him with a kind of sketch of it and give a thread into his hand that he could safely follow. To prevent inattentiveness, one first borrowed from the art of worldly orators the so-called **introductions** <note>original: "Eingänge." These were designed to capture the audience's attention before the main delivery.</note>, which are actually for the purpose...

# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption #

<note>original: "Von Unterhaltung des menschlichen Verderbens." The author is discussing how religious instruction supports or sustains the human soul in its fallen state.</note>

...that were introduced into the world, so that the listeners might be made attentive and their spirits encouraged. To these were later added the remaining **rhetorical devices** <note>original: "Kunst-Griffe," literally "art-grips" or tricks of the trade used by orators.</note>, which were customarily used in judicial and other worldly speeches to hold minds steady, to bind them to the speaker's delivery, and to lead them back from the distractions into which most people tend to fall when hearing a long speech. Had people observed the necessary care and wisdom in this, and separated the truly good from the superfluous vanity and the false pomp of earthly orators—had they kept what was innocent in the worldly **art of rhetoric** <term>Redner-Kunst<note>The formal study of persuasive speaking, often viewed with suspicion by Pietists who preferred "simplicity."</note></term> and thrown away the childish and the absurd—then no one would have particularly blamed these attempts. Nor would they have complained that the simplicity of Jesus Christ was being distorted by the falsely praised **art of chatter** <term>Schwaß-Kunst<note>A pejorative term for empty, flowery, or overly intellectual speech that lacks spiritual substance.</note></term> of the world, and that the cross of our Savior was being rendered void by the rules of the rhetoricians. The previously common exhortations to godliness were finally, at last, attached to this public instruction. One can, as we hope, understand from this what sermons actually are, as they are now held in most congregations, and from whence the parts come out of which they are composed. We cannot refrain from adding that, by all appearances, the Church would be in a better state if no reasons had been found to exchange the old, short **awakening discourses** <term>Erweckungs-Reden<note>Sermons intended to stir the emotions and provoke a spiritual "awakening" or conversion.</note></term> for long and rambling **doctrinal speeches** <term>Lehr-Reden<note>Didactic, academic sermons focused on explaining theology rather than moving the heart.</note></term>, and if the people could be instructed and strengthened in religion in another way.

<column-break/>

Whoever is not entirely incapable of judging what can and must follow from a matter clearly presented will soon be able to extract the most important rules to be observed in preaching from this presentation. Whoever wishes to speak to a congregation with benefit must always look to two things: *First, the purpose of his work; and second, the people whom he is to edify.* Upon these two things is founded everything he has to do or to leave undone. The purpose of a sermon is twofold. The understanding of the listeners should be enlightened and always further illuminated: their will should be bent under the yoke of the Lord and moved either to begin the path of godliness or to remain upon it. The instruction given to the understanding is always derived from a passage of the books of Holy Scripture. It follows of itself, therefore, that this passage—at least as far as it is to serve for instruction—must be explained thoroughly, yet according to the grasp of the listeners. Whoever can hit the middle ground in this explanation between an overly learned illustration and a powerless and unfounded expansion of the words of the Lord, and can combine brevity of delivery with a convincing clarity, has a gift that cannot be valued highly enough. It is one thing to explain a passage of Scripture from the **pulpit** <term>Kanzel</term>, and quite another to investigate its meaning for oneself or to determine it in scholarly writings. How annoying it often is to hear that many, who wish to be called great **interpreters** <term>Ausleger<note>Commentators or exegetes who explain the meaning of the Bible.</note></term>, and perhaps are so, do not think of this distinction? ### Chapter Two ###

Instruction itself consists of two things: a clear **delivery** and a correct and certain **conviction** of the intellect. The delivery can never be clear enough. The conviction can never be thorough enough. He who wishes to deliver clearly to an entire congregation, which consists of many kinds of people, must know the art of saying little with many words <note>This refers to the skill of explaining a simple concept thoroughly so that all levels of intelligence in the audience can grasp it.</note> and saying one thing in many ways, without awakening disgust and annoyance in the listeners. His imagination must be fortunate. It must cost him no effort to find an image among the things that man knows, to both illuminate and adorn his delivery with it. 

Conviction is of even greater importance. We do not know what we should say when we hear that some think one should not prove anything from the pulpit, while others think it matters little what reasons one uses, if one must indeed prove something. One may not prove anything on the pulpit? How? Do we then have people before us to whom **wit** <term>Witz<note>In this period, "Witz" referred to mental acuity or the faculty of understanding, rather than just humor.</note></term> and reason were given without cause? Or are we entitled to demand of those whom our Savior has redeemed that they should believe our words and build the hope of salvation upon our mere assertions? We walk as we believe. And can a righteous faith, can an honest assent take place in the soul of a person who has not been convinced? Is then a stream of words, which flows without order from the mouth of a chatterer, a ground that can satisfy our heart and cancel the resistance of our evil nature? Should people speak thus, who know that Jesus freed us from the respect of persons and demands that we worship the Father in spirit and in truth?

<column-break/>

Does it matter little what reasons one uses from the pulpit? **Wood, hay, straw, stubble** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:12, where the Apostle Paul warns against building a foundation with inferior materials.</note>—is everything good enough? What does it matter how a person is convinced, as long as they do not doubt? How? Is faith then so poor that we must give it a shine with false gold to deceive the inexperienced? Must we not worry that people are present who either notice the weakness of our proofs themselves or receive word of it through others? And must we not fear that these will later become worse than they were, and throw away trust both in us and in the good cause that was so poorly defended? 

He has opened a great door to unbelief, to Satan, and to sin, who first brought the cursed delusion among teachers that proofs which would move and convince no sensible person in the world could already occupy a respectable place in sermons. We do not wish to hear any artificial, far-fetched, difficult, and learned conclusions. These serve for nothing in the place where the entrance to the Kingdom of God is to be opened to the learned and unlearned alike. However, we also want to know nothing of fables, will-o'-the-wisps, **strokes of air** <note>original: "Luft-Streichen," referring to empty gestures or arguments that hit nothing but air.</note>, and chilly fancies and playthings, when repentance and faith are proclaimed and man is to be snatched from his own self. The will of the listeners shall be won and moved to renounce their natural inclinations and follow the Lord. Whoever wants to do this must know the human heart and understand in what way a turmoil in the...

He must know how to present the word of divine truth in such a way that it ignites and stirs a salutary fire in the sluggish and complacent <note>The original German "sicheren" refers to a state of false spiritual security or complacency, where a person believes they are safe from judgment without having undergone true repentance.</note> heart. He himself must be touched, moved, full of spirit and life. Words, gestures, and movements must testify to a zeal and a pure love for those whom one wishes to encourage. The fire of a spiritual orator <term>Geistlichen Redners<note>A preacher or sacred orator, specifically one whose goal is to move the soul toward God rather than just providing intellectual information.</note></term> resembles a flash of lightning that penetrates the thickest bodies and sets fire to everything it encounters. However, it must not be a blind fire that nature alone has brought about and art has somewhat expanded and enlarged. It must not be a fire that shoots empty rays or plays with mere words that signify nothing. It must come from the Lord and work through the power of truth so that rocks are melted. Let us speak without metaphor: whoever wishes to move others correctly must himself be touched by the grace of the Lord, and heat the will not through an artful noise, not through well-placed words, not through a forced tone of voice, not through feigned gestures, nor through violent movements of the body, but rather occupy and win the understanding through the pure and penetrating power of truth, and through the understanding, win the will.

An Indian mourning woman <note>A reference to professional mourners common in 18th-century ethnographic descriptions, used here as a trope to contrast theatrical, performed emotion with genuine spiritual conviction.</note>, a common stage actor, or a deceptive beggar can stir the passions of men and bring about joy, fear, sadness, and other emotions. Everything that does not serve this double purpose—which we have hitherto not so much presented in detail as merely indicated—is an abomination to the Lord in a sermon and useless to the world.

The second thing toward which those who hope for fruit from their sermons must always direct their thoughts are the people themselves to whom they speak. What is the nature of people? They are mostly all slaves of their senses and their imagination, and sink back again before one realizes it, when one wishes to lift them up and lead them to the contemplation of spiritual things. They are mostly all inept at following a speaker who continues in a closed order <note>Meaning a strictly logical or structured sequence of academic arguments.</note> with their thoughts and gradually drawing the chain of his conclusions and presentations to themselves. It is necessary that sometimes, in the middle of the speech, the listener be re-energized in a skillful and lively manner and be torn out of the slumber into which most unnoticeably fall. It is necessary that the spirit, the cheerfulness, the fire, and the intensity of the speaker redouble and unite with a gentle and quiet affect <term>affect: a controlled emotional appeal or state of mind used in rhetoric to move an audience</term>, when the speech arrives at the most important things, which the listener should grasp and adopt above all else. 

We know that many, perhaps out of a good intention, despise all these things and consider them human trifles <note>The German "Menschen-Tand" refers to worthless trinkets or vanities; here it suggests that rhetorical skill is a worldly distraction from the Gospel</note>, which are unbefitting to the Cross of Jesus and the doctrine of godliness. The doctrine of Jesus, it is said, is strong enough in itself to conquer man. It only needs to be presented and explained, however it may happen. It needs no art. Its simplicity rather puts to shame the art and eloquence of the wise of this world. Have not the Apostles of Jesus triumphed over Rome and Greece, even though they were abandoned by all earthly eloquence? 

We cannot believe that those who find this reproach significant have rightly considered the state of the people to whom we must speak, as well as those who speak. <column-break/>

And we do not doubt that most would much more willingly agree with us if we gave them the instruction to speak without preparation, art, and reflection, rather than our current wish to burden them with the difficult work of seeking out so many means so that they might open the ears of men. What does a person prefer to do more than let his intellect rest? But nothing is more certain than this: that the greatest crowd appears in the congregation without impulse or desire to hear and learn, and brings with them a cold, sluggish, and averted spirit. 

Should we not concern ourselves with this state and let people sleep and dream? Or does reason advise us to apply all our diligence so that we may steer their ears toward our delivery? ## Chapter Two ##

...and win from them that attentiveness which they are naturally so reluctant to grant?

The second piece of advice we can offer is this: One must do everything possible so that those who hear us also understand us. Hearing and understanding are not always found together. There are people who keep their listeners in constant attention and yet speak without benefit or edification. Often, there is something indefinable—in the voice, the pronunciation, the gestures, or the words of an orator—which compels our attention and fills the soul with a delighted admiration. We believe, as long as the speech lasts, that every word has weight, that every sentence reveals a mystery of truth to our spirit, and that a balsam of wisdom flows from the teacher’s mouth. And when we afterwards examine the treasure we thought we possessed, nothing reveals itself to us but an empty shell, an intellect that remains as dark and ignorant as it was before. Thus, a special effort is required to make the speech truly intelligible. Those who wish to strive for this must, first, *maintain a great order in their words and thoughts, set everything out correctly from one another, divide it clearly, and present it sequentially as the nature of the matter* they are discussing requires. Instruction that lacks arrangement and order only burdens the spirit and frequently gives cause for error to be put in the place of truth. Secondly, they must never speak except *with common and well-known words,*

<column-break/>

which immediately awaken a clear concept in the minds of the listeners, and they must strive to connect these words in such a way that the meaning is understood as soon as the words are spoken. In a word, the language must be pure, clear, and not artificial <note>The original "geschminckt" literally means "made up" or "painted," referring to overly flowery or deceptive rhetoric</note>, but naturally beautiful and pleasant. Thirdly, they must *exercise the power of their imagination* <term>imagination: here referring to 'Einbildungskraft,' the ability to create mental images or analogies to explain abstract concepts</term> so that they become adept at *presenting a matter in various ways and, as it were, showing it to the listener’s understanding from all sides.* Those who heap conclusion upon conclusion, doctrine upon doctrine, use no more words than are necessary to explain a thing, and deal with their listeners no differently than a philosopher <note>original: "Welt-Weiser," a common 18th-century term for a secular philosopher or scientist</note> who wishes to prove a certain proposition to another of equal intellect—these have yet to learn that most people cannot make progress on such a narrow path. Finally, they must always keep in mind *that they are seeing people who work very little with their intellect* and much with their imagination and their senses. People of this nature do not know what is happening to them and remain deaf and unmoved as long as they hear a sequence of things that they can only comprehend by withdrawing all senses and thoughts from the visible world. One must deal with them as with children and, as far as can be done without harm to the truth, open their understanding through images and things they know or can at least easily imagine. # On Addressing the Corruption of Man #

...derive a truth for the paper from the first principles of our science <note>In this period, "science" (Wissenschaft) referred to any systematic body of knowledge, including theology and the study of the soul.</note>. However, he has grasped one of the greatest rules of spiritual eloquence who can lead people to the knowledge of divine truth through the things they deal with in their daily lives. This rule was given to us by our **Jesus** through His own example. His witnesses <note>Referring to the Apostles and early disciples.</note> observed this among both the Jews and the Heathens. Are these [modern critics] greater than they? Have they known the human heart better—or perhaps certain imagined wise men who present their obscure and long-winded art of logic and proof as a universal remedy against ignorance and simplicity? 

We have said little of the things required for such a discourse, through which people are not merely entertained, not just persuaded, not simply moved and awakened, but are to be thoroughly instructed and moved toward an upright **godliness** <note>original: "Gottseligkeit," a key Pietist term referring to a deep, active, and sincere devotion to God.</note>. We could expand much further if the space and other matters allowed it. Yet this little bit will already seem more than enough to those who value this work so poorly and lightly—those who view preaching as a mere trade <note>original: "Handwerck"; the author criticizes those who see the ministry as a routine job rather than a spiritual calling.</note> that everyone can practice who does not lack speech and memory; who measure a good sermon not by its purpose, but by the applause with which the common crowd receives it. We must leave these people to the governance of the **Lord** and their own reason. There will always be sensible Christians found to whom that which seems too much to others will still appear too little.

We wish to forget these complaints for now and act as if one found no lack of such people anywhere. If this were indeed the case, would the benefit expected from our public discourses on godliness be certain and hoped for without doubt? 

We confess that we have many reasons to doubt whether this manner of instruction—even if every preacher did his part sincerely—would produce the desired fruit in everyone. It occurs to us that the external form of our churches would look somewhat better if we introduced an easier and more convenient way to maintain and strengthen those who are already adults in the truth. Perhaps we should occasionally allow thorough discourses by skilled and eloquent people for the benefit of the "experienced" <note>Those further along in their spiritual education.</note>, while sustaining the gatherings of the entire congregation only with such short **awakening-discourses** as were customary among the first Christians. 

We submit this opinion to the examination of those who surpass us in knowledge and experience. ## Chapter Two ##

...are provided with the gifts of nature that this work requires? He who wishes to draw the minds of his listeners to himself through a discourse and enlighten their understanding must think purely and correctly, conclude with certainty and clarity, compare cautiously, know human nature exactly, and know how to distinguish appearance from truth. His imagination must be expansive and yet restrained, his memory fortunate, his language clear and elegant, his voice engaging, his heart undaunted, and his whole being and demeanor cheerful and lively. And how great is the number of people whom the Lord has so equipped? One portion of those so constituted would rather use their talent to profit in the service of the world <note>original: "mit seinem Pfunde... wuchern." A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25, where a "pound" or "talent" represents God-given abilities that one must use for His glory.</note>. One portion is neglected and abandoned, and out of poverty must leave their talent unused—if not buried entirely—until much of its value is lost. One portion is poorly guided and so overwhelmed with worthless things in the years of their youth, or rather so corrupted, that the spirit collapses under the weight and has already forfeited its true freedom by the time it should be doing its best service. One portion falls into the hands of superstition, which considers it an honor and a special merit to suppress and, where possible, root out the useful and good gifts that the Lord has granted to some for the common good. The few who still come to the office of teaching <note>the ministry</note> with the skill indispensable for this kind of instruction soon find themselves forced to give up the diligence they previously applied to their public speeches, and to set aside many of the

<column-break/>

good qualities they had acquired with great effort. A man who must speak so often to the congregation and, at the same time, perform so many and varied other tasks as those who preside over our communities, cannot possibly reflect on everything he wants to present with such deliberate reason and wisdom, nor arrange and organize it so shrewdly and skillfully, nor imagine it so purely and elegantly, nor speak it so well and livelily as would be fitting. The strength of his spirit is divided too much and driven apart. His imagination is so occupied by many things—which are almost all of one kind and sort—that it cannot properly expand and almost always remains in one position. His courage is weakened and dejected by interaction with so many miserable and plagued people who seek comfort from him. His memory does not find the time to search out from its treasure everything that might serve his purpose. Most, if they do not wish to neglect many parts of their office, must strive for the proficiency to acquire in a few hours, and sometimes in a few moments, as much provision as is necessary for a speech that is to last an hour. And many must even think of how they might proclaim the word of truth without any preparation or reflection at all. Can it be demanded with the slightest appearance of fairness <note>original: "Billigkeit," meaning equity or reasonableness in a legal and moral sense.</note> that people who are so pressed and pulled to and fro should present—with power, life, and order—not just whatever occurs to them, but nothing but service-oriented and useful lessons for their flocks? The world complains about the many poor, uneloquent, and cold exhortations that in our chur- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Kir-" for "Kirchen" (churches) on the following page.</note>

Whenever we listen to sermons that can impart little light and wisdom, we turn our thoughts from those who speak to the state of our Church, and wish in silence that the Lord might awaken the spirit of His anointed <note>original: "Gesalbten," a term usually referring to those set apart for holy office, like kings or priests.</note> to heal her breaches. We leave those who preach to the judgment of the Lord, because for the most part, we do not know how far their hearts are involved in their poor delivery, and we often regret that they lack the time and encouragement to maintain their congregations with more spirit and power.

**Other difficulties are found among the congregations being instructed.** These congregations consist mostly of people who cannot command their thoughts as far as we and they themselves would like. They often grasp things quite well and orderly at first.

<column-break/>

And nonetheless, before one realizes it, they escape the oversight of the spirit and often take occasion—from a single word, a turn of phrase, a small coincidence, or a movement of the speaker—to stray from the circle <note>The "circle" here refers to the logical flow or the "inner circle" of the topic at hand.</note> and scatter themselves into the world. It is true: after a while, they return from this disorder. However, in the meantime, the thread of the argument is lost, which proceeds in its proper order. And where among our ordinary people are those who could later replace what was lost and deduce from what followed what had gone before? One can take it as something indisputable that in all ranks of the world, from the highest to the lowest, very few people are found who can follow a speaker with their hearing and spirit so quickly and orderly that they grasp his discourse in the correct order with their understanding, retain it correctly, and are able to represent it to themselves again afterwards. **One should ask those who have listened most diligently to a slow and clear speech to recount its core and content. One will immediately perceive from what they say that they have learned and accepted nothing more than a little something, a verse, a piece of a proof, or a few words whose meaning they do not know how to explain.** **Another difficulty arises from the listeners! Our congregations consist of people who are practiced in the truth, and of simple folk who understand little or nothing.** How shall we manage it so that both types are edified and satisfied by our speeches? # On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

...[who] would be able, with his discourse, to encompass this diversity of human minds, both in regard to nature and to grace? We believe this to be just as impossible as a physician devising a single remedy that is useful to all people in all illnesses. We must be content with general teachings, exhortations, warnings, and rebukes, and hope that everyone who hears us will apply these to themselves according to their particular state. We generally and overall point out the sources of doctrine, comfort, punishment, and exhortation. Each person must draw from these for themselves, and arrange both the measure and the preparation according to their own condition. But can we fundamentally hope for that which we must hope for? Is it not well-known that general teachings and warnings are either heard with complete indifference, or are usually applied to other people? The person who is truly meant to change desires to be addressed specifically. Indeed, one has more reason to wonder that so many make use of public instruction at all, than that most hear it as if it concerned a different kind of people.

Do we also remember that for some time now we have refined our language much more than before, increased it with great additions, and improved it in various ways? And that these changes in language usually reach people of low status only after many years? Languages that are in use and constantly spoken transform from time to time and, like humans, pass from one age to another. Simplicity pays little heed to this constant change and usually remains with the language spoken by their fathers. ### The Second Chapter

...collected learning, having practiced in worldly wisdom <term>worldly wisdom: (German: *Welt-Weiſheit*) a common 18th-century term for philosophy</term>, learned history, languages, and other sciences, and learned the art of cornering and fending off an adversary; yet, they have either left their own understanding uncultivated, or at least have not applied themselves to truly knowing the world and the evil heart of men, or learning how to conquer them through the power of the word of truth. This type of person is eloquent and lively when scholars converse about the state and nature of their sciences, but remains mute, sluggish, and heavy when the sinner is to be terrified, the righteous encouraged, the dying comforted, and the rebellious nature is to be hallowed to the Lord. One notices in others that they meet with little success in their office because their wit does not harmonize with their learning. The heart is upright; the understanding is filled with useful and good doctrines; the will is ready to serve with its gift. What then is missing? *A certain skill of the spirit and imagination, which is mostly a gift of nature, to correctly present what one knows and apply it for the benefit of humanity.* One encounters some teachers who continue to play the very same role they formerly played in the world, only in a different suit of clothes; they betray through their manners that they were deeply entangled in earthly affairs and observed the established ways of the world as strongly as any others. People are quietly offended by their conduct. They themselves believe they are blameless. Their conscience reproaches them with nothing evil; therefore, they are at peace. And one can gather from many things that their minds are in fact pur-

<column-break/>

-er than most are willing to believe. What then is the cause of their outward behavior, which appears offensive? They have been torn from the midst of the world, where they had to occupy themselves with all sorts of secondary matters and deal with many people, and placed into a station in which the appearance of luxury, sensuality, and a worldly-minded heart does just as much damage as luxury, sensuality, and worldliness itself. They were given no space to properly settle their souls and bring them into order, nor to cleanse their conduct of certain things that belong to the prosperity of the world but to the detriment of the servants of the Most High. One discovers that many perform their office without courage, life, or joy, and commit the greatest errors because they were born into low status, poorly raised, and brought through the world in misery and wretchedness; through these burdensome circumstances, they have fallen under the dominion of the spirit of bondage and fear <note>original: *Geiſt der Knechtſchaft und der Furcht*; a reference to Romans 8:15</note>, from which they cannot tear themselves away through any amount of imagination or effort. Creon <note>Creon is used here as a fictionalized figure—a "mirror for princes"—representing a ruler seeking to reform his state.</note>, as he considers these and many other things, first arrives at the thought that the teachers at the universities and the people to whom the examination of those called to the teaching office is entrusted must be either lazy or sluggish, or without religion and conscience. Should not those, he says, who are meant to lead the youth dedicated to the Church, be able to tear out the roots of many of these weaknesses if they looked more to their duty than to their comfort and income? Should not the people who sit in the <term>ecclesiastical courts: (German: *geistlichen Gerichten*) administrative bodies responsible for church discipline and the examination of clerical candidates</term> better inquire into the circumstances of those presented to them as future teachers, and without regard for status, reject those afflicted with such defects? After a brief reflection, he recognizes that both the former and the latter, even with the most honest and sincere hearts, cannot achieve what, according to his first opinion, ought to be achieved by them. Teachers can do nothing but instruct clearly and movingly exhort. No one can know whether his effort will bring much or little fruit, because this depends on many circumstances unknown to him, and which he could not change or prevent even if they were better known to him. The others, in the few hours in which they examine the prospective teachers, cannot even properly explore their knowledge. How then could they 

<column-break/>

investigate the powers of their minds, their inclinations, their faithfulness, and their sincerity, which are recognized not through words, but through works? And granted, if they found that the understanding and will of some were ill-disposed—granted, if they looked into the heart and perceived therein a seed of vice and negligence ready to bear fruit—would they, given the state of today's world, be able to do everything they wished to do? Would they, without danger of a greater evil and with the certain confidence that their zeal would succeed, be able to close the door to the house of the LORD to these unprepared servants? The sovereign power of a land alone holds the means in its hands to emphatically keep unfaithful and inexperienced workers away from the Church. ~~If the sovereign power will not use its authority for this end, then the others, who are appointed as guardians and overseers, can do nothing more than implore, warn, exhort, and pray.~~ Creon understands this and resolves to abolish, through new laws, the disorder that has crept into the filling of ecclesiastical offices. He listens to the advice of the experienced, ponders the condition of his land, stirs up his love for the common good, and surveys the obstacles that could be set against his undertaking. After everything has been done that prudence requires in such a case, he causes the following ordinance to be made known:

Since the capacities of the mind are not of an equal size in everyone, a distinction in the manner of instruction must be observed. In order that this distinction may be respected, those being raised for the service of the Church shall be divided into three classes. And the teachers at the academy <note>original: "hohen Schule," referring to a university or theological seminary</note> shall instruct in a threefold manner. Those of the first class shall be practiced and instructed as thoroughly and extensively as possible in all parts of spiritual science <term>geistlichen Wissenschaft: the study of theology and divinity</term>. The middle class will have somewhat less to learn than the first. The last class shall only need to be guided so that they rightly understand the counsel of the Lord regarding the salvation of mankind and can give a clear account of the faith and hope that should reside within them as well as in their future congregations.

(VI) It does not rest in the free will of each person to decide which branches of scholarship—those not entirely necessary for the office of teaching—he wishes to apply himself to. The overseers of the Church will take heed of what each person is primarily suited for according to his natural inclination and ability, and they will assign to him that which he should investigate. Those who are tireless and possess a rich memory will be advised to learn either history, or the languages of the Orient <note>Specifically Hebrew, Aramaic, and Syriac, essential for biblical scholarship</note>, or something else that requires patience and industriousness. ### On the Restraint of Human Corruption.

(XXI) No one shall be admitted to the <term>teaching office: "Lehr-Amt," the professional ministry</term> until he has reached thirty years of age. The heat of natural desires seldom truly subsides before this time. And as long as these still prevail, one must always fear that a man may allow himself to be overtaken by faults that weaken the effectiveness of his work upon the souls of his brothers.

(XXII) Every man shall remain with the <term>congregation: "Gemeine," the local community of believers</term> once entrusted to him for the duration of his life, unless reasons of great importance dictate otherwise. The transfers of the <term>servants of the Gospel: original: "Diener des Evangelii"</term> give rise to manifold weaknesses and offenses, and are very harmful both to the ministers themselves and to the congregations. On the other hand, care will be taken that no one in the place where he stands shall have cause to complain of want or contempt.

(XXIII) Since these institutions must bring immense benefit to the entire country, the whole country shall also contribute something to their maintenance. Those aspiring <term>ministers of the Word: "Diener des Worts"</term> who themselves have the means to live will not refrain from repaying the good they enjoy in the aforementioned houses through a reasonable fee. The needy will be provided for free of charge; in return, they shall strive to earn their place in this salutary work through all manner of useful and good efforts.

This order—notwithstanding all objections raised, whether by the excessive veneration of old customs, the spirit of pride,

<column-break/>

the unwise love of parents for their children, the inclination toward a harmful license, or the fear of great expense—shall be made known everywhere, introduced, and strictly protected against all interference. Its great utility will soon be seen. The formerly misshapen Church will become like a garden of the Lord. The world will no longer be scandalized by so many incompetent people who spend the years of their youth in a sinful frenzy and all kinds of lusts, and afterwards, through new sins, purchase the favor of certain people who are so base in spirit and so destitute of conscience that they betray the teaching and the office of their Redeemer for about <note>This is a biblical reference to Judas Iscariot's betrayal of Jesus.</note>thirty pieces of silver. Mockers will find no more opportunity to laugh at the unseemly arts and secret negotiations formerly practiced and maintained to help a poor and unskilled relative to a good <term>parish: "Pfarre"</term>, now through a marriage, now through a reciprocal favor, now through a sinful trick. The land will be cleansed of the miserable chatterers who fill their memory with foreign knowledge, their heart with vanity, and

## Explanation.

We can speak more freely here, since even those who otherwise seem to grant little good to the servants of the Church have recognized that the poverty and indigence pressing upon most of them brings no small harm to religion. JESUS commanded through his Apostle that those who are taught should share all kinds of good things with him who teaches them, Galatians 6:6. <note>original: "Gal. VI. 6."</note> and that those who preach the Gospel should live from the Gospel, 1 Corinthians 9:14. <note>original: "1. Cor. IX. 14."</note> No one can interpret these and other commands, which indicate the same, in any other way than that the teachers of the congregations should be placed beyond all worry for their sustenance and supported in such a way that they may perform their office without restlessness and burdensome thoughts and calculations. It seems as if this is considered an abolished commandment in many places of our Evangelical congregations. If there are some among those working in the Word who need not complain of lack, then

<column-break/>

there are, conversely, exceedingly many to whom so little is thrown that they can barely clothe themselves and their own and provide for their basic needs. And those who enjoy a bit more and can contemplate the future without torment and sorrow are yet mostly bound to all sorts of business and labors that pull the mind toward earthly things and are obstructive and harmful to the careful administration of their office. How many of those, whose spirit should belong to the LORD alone, must simultaneously act as farmers and traders and maintain a strong communion with the world, if they do not wish to starve and become unfaithful to their own families? The servants of the **Lord**, who spend their days in poverty, cannot raise their children well or have them properly guided. ### §. XVI.

In the multitude of godless and harmful books with which the world is deluged in our days, there also lies a great cause of the encroaching godlessness. We shall say nothing of those writings that shamelessly declare war on God and revealed religion <note>Religion based on divine revelation (the Bible) rather than just human reason.</note>. Very few are led astray by this kind of book. There are others that, in a secret and malicious manner, challenge the teaching of Jesus Christ; they give luster and color to vices and sins; and under the pretext of improving and elevating the intellect, they corrupt the heart and stir up evil desires. The high society as well as the middle class read such works for their pleasure. Even the lower classes can hardly do without them. Through this, a hidden ember is ignited in the souls of many people, which seizes everything at the first opportunity and generally stirs up a loathing and abhorrence for everything that belongs to virtue, reason, and godliness.

->The Second Chapter<-

### Explanation.

The books that threaten the loss and ruin of piety <note>original: "Gottseligkeit" — a term referring to a deep, lived-out Christian devotion</note> in our days are of two kinds. Some unabashedly attack the foundations of faith and religion; others cautiously scatter the seeds of godlessness and unbelief, hiding their true intentions under the cloak of reason and eloquence. Of the first kind, there are not a few present in our times—times in which freedom is united with coercion in a most extraordinary way. Yet, religion has not so very much to fear from these. Most are composed in such a dry and tedious style that readers become weary by the first few pages. Those that are written somewhat better make themselves either unpleasant through their lack of order, or suspicious to people of any reflection through the absurd doctrines and untruths that appear here and there. In some, the manner of teaching is so dry, tasteless, and repulsive that no one has the desire to follow such a stubborn schoolmaster. In others, ignorance and the desire to sin are more clearly revealed than can be tolerated by people who have not entirely renounced shame and modesty. Many books of this genre, both written and printed, have passed through our hands. And as of yet, we have found none among them that did not make us indignant, either through its confusion and darkness, or through its impudent audacity. How does it happen that the spirit of these people—who accuse the largest portion of the

<column-break/>

human race of blindness—appears in such a poor and common dress when it is meant to truly show itself? And how does it come to pass that those who believe themselves to think more cleverly and correctly than the rest of us can seldom properly place and arrange their thoughts on paper? Are we too simple-minded to reach the "wisdom" of unbelief? Are we not worthy enough for such a sharp-sighted race to condescend for our sake? Are the arguments of the enemies of religion so high and difficult that they cannot be properly explained? Or, on the contrary, is their brain so deranged that they mistake a cloud for a light? It is certain that out of a thousand people, not one is able to grasp the meaning of the writings in which religion is fundamentally contested. And since, moreover, these books are rare, since they are expensive, and since they are written in foreign languages <note>primarily referring to French and Latin works of the Enlightenment</note>, we need not be particularly anxious that they will win over many among the Christians or incite them to a contempt for the Most High.

From the other kind of writings we mentioned, more harm grows against piety. The less the authors of these works wish to appear as if they seek to abolish the first principles of religion, the more they endeavor to strike a certain middle ground between faith and unbelief, the more easily they catch those who read them with pleasure and without any worry. One can gather these people under two main categories. Some seek, in an artistic or—

Our children will perhaps live to see the unhappy time when the question may be asked: whether one nation has anything to reproach the other for in this matter? The language of the Germans has for some time become much more beautiful, pure, and extensive. We no longer lack people endowed with spirit and wit. ## The Second Chapter

To the books of the first kind, we reckon the fictional histories and travels, of which a considerable number exist. In these, religion in general and the faith of Christians in particular are secretly attacked and made to look ridiculous—sometimes through a fable, sometimes in a dialogue with a savage, sometimes in the description of a foreign religious service, or through the recounting of the vices and tricks of certain idol-priests <note>original: "Gößen-Pfaffen" — a derogatory term used by the author to describe the clergy of non-Christian or non-Protestant faiths.</note>. The images are so skillfully tailored, the comparisons look so natural, the words are so well chosen and so diligently borrowed from the Christians themselves, that one is not permitted to guess the target at which the arrows are aimed. We include here certain otherwise truthful travel descriptions and histories of foreign peoples, in which no opportunity is missed to exalt the morals, customs, virtues, and ways of life of idolatrous and unbelieving lands and peoples, and to prefer them over Christian ones. The latest world-observers <note>The author is likely referring to Enlightenment-era travel writers and philosophers like Voltaire or Montesquieu, who often used foreign perspectives to critique European society.</note> who have published accounts of their travels seem for the most part to be of the opinion that it belongs to their duties to despise everything that is called Christian; not only to excuse the peoples among whom they have been, but to praise them beyond measure and to send Christians to school under these so-called barbarians. What a seriousness, it is said, is shown by the Turks and Persians? What a reverence toward **God**, whom they have present in every matter? What an order in their divine service? What a silence and composure in misfortune? What a love for the poor and needy? How polite and modest is the

<column-break/>

Chinese? How just is the *Carib*, even if he eats his enemies? How profound is the *Brahmin*? How devout are the *Dervishes* and *Yogis* <note>original: "Drewische und Jaugis" — terms for Muslim and Hindu ascetics respectively.</note>? How much renunciation of the world is found among the *Sufis*, a *Persian* sect? What is to be found among Christians of these virtues? The Christians who come among these virtuous and rational peoples corrupt them further, rather than bettering them. This is read by countless people who have neither the strength nor the desire to think about the causes of things—some for their mere amusement, others for different intentions. And what else can grow in them from this but a poor opinion of the nature and use of the religion of our Savior? Hitherto we have believed that the doctrine of **Jesus**, in all places where it arrives, has conquered the raw and wild customs of the nations, soothed the ill-bred minds, and made—if not friends of **God**—at least human beings out of unruly and desolate people. And it is either all false, what time has left us of ancient spiritual and worldly history, or this opinion is generally correct and well-founded. Now we are expected to believe the opposite. They want to persuade us entirely that where the name of **Jesus** has never been heard, pure and unadulterated virtue can be seen much more clearly than where one hopes to be saved through him. The peoples whom we have hitherto held to be wild and unskilled could be our moral teachers; and where Christianity truly takes root, nothing better than an unfortunate change in outward conduct is to be feared. # On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

...we cannot entirely doubt those who wish to force this opinion upon us. Their testimony agrees in most things they recount regarding the customs of distant peoples. We will not deny that the outward conduct of many heathens and unbelievers puts to shame those who wish to be called followers of the most holy Savior. We will also concede that the tyrants, the mercilessness, and the insane zeal of some peoples who call themselves Christians without cause have made the name of the **Lord JESUS** stink <note>original: "stinckend gemacht" — a forceful idiom meaning to bring into extreme ill repute or to make loathsome.</note> among the inhabitants of the newly discovered world. Furthermore, we admit that the greed, injustice, and intemperance of certain **Europeans** have infected some otherwise fairly well-mannered peoples and filled others with a hatred for the teachings of **JESUS**.

None of this, however, fully clears those of evil intentions or imprudence who, without reflection or distinction, praise the great virtues and laudable customs of non-Christian peoples. Would they not have acted more wisely and better protected their own honor if they had sought to fathom the causes of these "shining virtues" <note>term: "Schein-Tugenden" — literally "apparent virtues" or "shining vices"; a theological concept suggesting that outward good deeds without faith are merely hollow imitations of true virtue.</note> and shown the world that they were nothing but mere habits, which could be attributed neither to reason nor to religion? We have reflected on this matter with some effort and are thereby fully convinced that everything in the customs of the **Peoples of the East** <note>original: "Morgen-Länder" — literally "morning-lands," referring to the Orient or Asia.</note> and other nations that appears so beautiful and virtuous is a natural effect of the air in which they live, their nourishment, the constitution of their bodies, and other similar things. The **Indian** is quieter, more composed, gentler, and more patient than other men. This

<column-break/>

virtue is natural. Is it any wonder that people who eat no meat, who take neither wine nor other strong drinks, and who spend their miserable lives under the strictest servitude, are plagued less than we are by the heat and violence of their spirits and vital fluids? <note>The author is referring to the "humoral theory" of medicine, which suggested that diet and climate directly influenced a person's temperament by altering the balance of fluids like blood and bile.</note> The **Persian** is much more moderate than we **Peoples of the North** and the **West**. He is more serious, more deliberate, more secretive. He spends entire days in one spot. Where is the ground for these customs? In the souls of these people? In their faith? Not at all. One must seek it in the hot and dry air with which they are surrounded. This air constricts the blood and nutrient vessels in the body, prevents the rapid circulation of the blood, makes a person sluggish and composed, and prepares the body so that it requires very little for its nourishment.

The **Turkish** and **Indian monk** <note>The author is likely referring to Sufi dervishes in the Ottoman Empire and Hindu sadhus or "fakirs" in India.</note> renounces all earthly comfort, renounces honor, wealth, and pleasure; he wanders the land without ceasing and speaks everywhere like one in a trance of the glory and greatness of **God**, of the contempt for the world, and of the peace of a heart that has entirely cast off the earth. Is this holiness and devotion? It seems to us that these are people who by nature possess a violent and often disordered imagination (as do most **Peoples of the East**); people for whom an empty stomach causes no particular hardship; people who from their earliest youth have ruined and corrupted their intellect through all sorts of fables and the reading of turgid and bombastically written books; and people who, moreover, consume every day certain juices <note>Likely a reference to coffee, tea, or perhaps opium (laudanum), which Europeans of this period often viewed as mind-altering substances that induced "Eastern" lethargy or mystical trances.</note> according to the custom of their land, which put a man outside of himself...

## The Second Chapter

...can easily fall into such a way of life by placing themselves in that state and exceedingly heating their imagination. The Mohammedan <note>original: "Mahumedaner"</note> observes his prayer hours most precisely and correctly, and often interrupts the most important business so as not to neglect the duty his religion prescribes. Do they all do this? Or are there just as many negligent ones among them as among us? The latter is more than probable, regardless of those who turn this practice into a special virtue and choose not to mention those who transgress it. But even assuming the first were true: Has anyone considered the particular power that habit has in such external exercises? A person who is raised from youth in such a thing and continues in it constantly finally becomes like a clock, which necessarily strikes at certain times and knows nothing of the causes that drive it to do so. Has anyone also remembered that the prayers of the Mohammedans are always connected with bathing and washing? And that this washing in hot countries is a pleasant refreshment and a medicine against all sorts of ailments and hardships? Does one also consider that nothing is easier than this praying, and that neither the elevation of the soul <note>original: "Erhebung der Seelen"</note> nor the gathering of thoughts is necessary for it? *The Oriental* <note>original: "Der Morgenländer"; a term used historically to refer to people from the Middle East or Asia.</note>, who is otherwise unmerciful and cruel in countless ways, nevertheless builds rest houses <note>term: "Ruhe-Häuser" — likely referring to caravanserais, which provided shelter and water to travelers.</note> where travelers can be safe from the heat of the sun, and appoints people who must provide strangers there with water for their refreshment without reward. How does that cruelty reconcile with this work of love? One will soon solve this doubt

<column-break/>

if one only properly imagines the condition of these wealthy benefactors. These people have never experienced hunger, want, nakedness, or other evils. Therefore, they can look on without pity or emotion as the wretches who must serve their lusts languish and perish. However, they have often felt the extreme exhaustion on their travels brought about by the great heat in the part of the world where they live, and have noticed in themselves that thirst is the most troublesome evil of all. This sensation has stirred a natural pity toward travelers and the intention to care for them. They would also provide for the hungry and the naked and add something to the wages of their servants if they had learned in their own bodies the magnitude of the hardship that arises from hunger and poverty. Such is man. He is inclined to alleviate in others the misery that has affected him personally. The suffering that has not touched him, he views much more calmly. We have gone further than we intended to go. We wish to stop and summarize what we could still say of this matter in a few words: There is no virtue, no praise, no laudable quality of the peoples who do not know our Savior for which an intelligent person could not give natural causes based on the nature of the land, the constitution of the government, and other such things.
