# On the Maintenance of Human Corruption.

### I. Part. Uuu

...arrangements of the unbelieving peoples as wise and rational, wherein the vices and misdeeds of the heathens are even preferred over the virtues that our Jesus commanded of His disciples. Writings of this kind have become very common for some time now. Our ancestors looked upon foreign religions and their authors with half-closed eyes. <note>The author suggests previous generations were perhaps too dismissive, but modern writers have swung to the opposite extreme of over-praising them.</note> **Muhammad** <note>original: "Mahomed"</note> was not a deceiver, but a zealot for the honor of God. His zeal misled him so that he believed God and the angels spoke with him at times. In this consists his entire mistake. Otherwise, he deserves reverence and love. His Law-Book <note>The Quran</note> is not a disordered, partly unintelligible, and superstitious chatter. Whoever wishes to look closely will find the core of religion therein, which sound reason teaches all men. **Zoroaster** <note>The founding prophet of Zoroastrianism, an ancient Persian religion.</note> and the **fire-worshippers** who come from his school are ill-reputed, but in fact are purer and holier than those who slander them. What is evil in the fact that they believed God could be compared to a fire and represented under the image of fire? Oh! If only these innocent and honest people had not been driven out of the world into remote corners where they are not even allowed to speak properly! The ancient **heretics**, whom the first Christians would not tolerate among themselves, were

<column-break/>

honest and sensible men. They were hated only because they could not endure the pride of the clergy and were not satisfied with the cold and half-hearted godliness of most Christians. How well the world would stand if these honest confessors had been heard and placed in the stead of the so-called "Orthodox"! Those who must interact with the world experience daily how much the honor of the religion of **Jesus Christ** and true godliness is diminished by these and other similar speeches, which are spoken as boldly and daringly as they are weakly proven. One has gone so far in our days as to represent the virtues, which belong to the essence of our holiest faith, as harmful weaknesses. Jesus teaches His followers mercy, meekness, and love toward the brethren. One of the most sharp-witted people of our times, who has insidiously wasted a good deal of his great knowledge and liveliness in the service of unbelief, gives it to be understood quite clearly that this holy commandment displeases him. What use is it in the world, other than to make men effeminate? The cruelty of the **Arabs**, who do not respect their own lives and without much ado take the lives of others, is much nobler and is wrongly called cruelty and harshness by us Christians. ## Chapter Two

...a manly steadfastness, which to a certain extent despises its own life and stops its ears to the whimpering, lamenting, begging, and crying of those who do not wish to lose their lives. One does no injustice to those possessed by this opinion if one wishes that they might live under a government devoted to this "manly steadfastness." There, they might experience the great "fortune" of those who must always leave their last will and testament behind whenever they go to court, because they cannot know whether the King might choose to demonstrate a sample of his manly courage upon them. <note>The author is being sarcastic here, suggesting that those who admire cold, stoic "steadfastness" in the face of death would feel differently if they lived under a tyrant who could execute them at a whim.</note> We count among this type of writing almost all those published in our times by the people who wish to be called witty and enlightened spirits. One of the most necessary qualities for those who now seek to maintain a reputation for "liveliness" and "vibrancy of spirit" through their works is a certain indifference toward religion and everything belonging to it. A head that wishes to judge everything freely and alertly, and a heart that fears to offend the laws of godliness and measures its words by the rule of reverence toward the **Lord**, are thought—so it is believed—to be poorly matched. And a writing that tastes of the faith of the common man seems "unsalted" to those of high and fine taste. One must, therefore, distance oneself as far as possible from the nets that superstition has spread in the world. Whoever wishes to please 

<column-break/>

perfectly must take even a bit more liberty. He must know how to mock religion in an ingenious way, and as often as an opportunity presents itself, he must covertly seize upon one aspect or another of it to expose it to the laughter of his readers. How fine it looks when—through a word misplaced on purpose, through a false lament, through a cautious mockery, through a funny whim, through a poisonous assumption, through a feigned ignorance, and through many such arts—one can give others the impression that they are only waiting for thirty pieces of silver to openly betray **Jesus**? <note>A reference to Judas Iscariot's betrayal of Christ for thirty pieces of silver, suggesting these authors are modern-day Judases.</note> To prove this, we can refer to most of the writings that are considered works of such spirits—especially among foreigners—who have torn themselves away through their intellect from the "indecent servitude of opinions" <note>The author's sarcastic term for traditional religious doctrines.</note> in which the ordinary world lives, and who receive so much applause among us. One finds few among them who know how to master the minds of men through their eloquence and shrewdness without detriment to religion. And we fear that the time is not so far off—unless the Providence of the **Most High** intervenes—when it will be lamented that our own witty and alert heads also seek to increase their honor through the disgrace of faith and truth. May the **Lord** grant that, after our days, this fear may be called an untimely trepidation with good reason!

Those spirits of the first magnitude, who wish to have the appearance of being above all...

<meta>This page continues the author’s analysis of the rhetorical strategies used by "enlightened" skeptics to undermine traditional religious belief. # On the Maintenance of Human Corruption

...all the errors and imaginings of the human race have climbed, have for some time introduced among themselves a certain **style of writing** that perfectly suits their intentions. They all observe this style so carefully and sacredly that one might believe some members of their order had devised it with great diligence and persuaded the rest to swear by its laws. Thus, those who normally attribute far less to their own intellect than these thinkers do can all the more easily guess the secret of this language. We wish to set forth the most prominent rules of this **witty eloquence**, which we ourselves have noted in the short time we have been able to devote to the writings of these free and exalted souls. This will be quite useful as proof of the opinion we are maintaining here.

(I) Those who want to plant suspicion and mistrust toward the Christian faith and religion in general into the hearts of the world must never openly attack it. One must never speak of **God** without a veneer of reverence, and never mention the duties prescribed by His law without praise. Those who declare themselves clearly against religion and godliness only stir up a storm in the minds of the weak, which tears down and destroys a portion of their designs. And the greatest part of the world belongs to these "weak" ones. <note>The author argues that these writers use "soft power" and subversion rather than direct confrontation to avoid alienating the general public.</note>

(II) Wherever one can, one must intermingle something of one's love for truth, for sincerity, and for freedom, and show the world a heart that, in silence, sighs over the ignorance and

<column-break/>

folly of the human race and longs for improvement out of true compassion. The more confidence one knows how to awaken in oneself, the deeper the arrows one wishes to shoot will penetrate.

(III) One must intimate, with a certain modesty and with gentle words, that one is holding back much of one's insights and thoughts out of prudence. One should often break off in the middle of a certain presentation concerning religion, as if a wise fear were checking the course of the pen and holding back the truth. From this **artful caution**, readers will certainly draw incautious and harmful conclusions. <note>This refers to the rhetorical device of *paralipsis* or *aposiopesis*, where a writer suggests they are "censoring" themselves, prompting the reader to imagine even more radical ideas than those explicitly stated.</note>

(IV) One must certainly not forget to magnify the weakness of men, their inclination toward superstition, their blind imitation, and their reckless haste in spiritual matters. This bears so much fruit that many fall into the delusion that whatever is believed by the majority must be false and brought forth without consideration.

(V) As often as it can be done, one must mention that most religions in the world have much to thank the female sex for their progress and growth. <note>A common 18th-century trope used by skeptics to dismiss religion as something fueled by "feminine" emotion or "irrationality."</note> This sex, it is claimed, seizes upon everything that has even a veneer of religion and can instill their faith into the wisest and most cautious men through various ways. How splendidly can this proposition be illustrated even from the history of the **Old Testament**?

# The Second Chapter

<columns>
(VI.) It is of great use to frequently complain about the **spiritual tyranny** that reigns among men, and to assert that the world will remain blind and mad so long as every individual is not granted the complete freedom to present the opinions of his heart, both orally and in writing. No one has done this more concisely or beautifully than **Anthony Collins** in his book on the *Freedom of Thought*, and in a preface he attached to another book directed against the Christian religion. <note>Anthony Collins (1676–1722) was a prominent English deist. His "A Discourse of Free-Thinking" (1713) was a landmark text for the Enlightenment, though highly controversial among the clergy of his time.</note>

(VII.) The primary arguments commonly used to prove the truths of **natural religion** must frequently be challenged and made to seem suspicious. <term>natural religion: A system of belief based on reason and the study of nature, rather than on miracles or divine revelation.</term> One can either say that these arguments are entirely useless, or one can pretend that they have not yet been properly executed and explained. One can hope for a good effect from both sides. He is unwise who attacks or denies these truths themselves; that only brings hatred, annoyance, and danger. One must only wish that these excellent and holy teachings might be properly strengthened and placed beyond all doubt through new and unshakeable grounds.

(VIII.) It has accomplished little good to place **reason** above religion and to attempt to arrange the latter according to the dictates of the former. Religion has almost always gained ground through this effort. A clever man must reverse the matter: Reason must be subjected to religion. One must say that religion is indisputably true; that it is light and clarity itself. However, it is to be lamented

<column-break/>

that reason can see nothing of this truth, and even less can it prove it. Nothing remains but for one to become a fool so that one may rightfully bear the name of a Christian. One must cast away the best, clearest, and purest truths—which are just as certain as the fact that two times two are four—blindfold oneself, and say with a holy stubbornness that one wishes to believe and maintain the most absurd things in the world. **Pierre Bayle** first attempted this artful trick with no small success. <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) was a French philosopher. The author suggests that Bayle’s "fideism"—the idea that faith and reason are entirely separate—was actually a clever way to make faith look ridiculous by showing it had no logical basis.</note>

(IX.) It is necessary to mock everything that is believed and accepted by the majority in the world, and especially to skillfully laugh at the opinions to which the largest part of the world has joined itself. He has accomplished much who has moved men to believe that nothing is so uncertain and false as that which is held to be truth by the most people.

(X.) On the other hand, one must support all new and previously unheard-of doctrines and propositions, and extol the people from whom they originate as the **lights of the world**. It does not matter whether one believes these opinions oneself or not, or whether they come from a healthy mind or a corrupted imagination. It is enough that the world is encouraged to despise the old and to put the new and unusual in its place. Minds prepared in this way will later dare even more and will not be immediately frightened when someone declares their old faith to be incorrect.

(XI.) No effort should be spared to strip the books of **Holy Scripture** of the honor and prestige they hold among most people. This can be done in many ways without letting one's true intentions be noticed. Can one not, from the history of the **Old Testament**—which is accompanied by few details—distort first this, then that, and present it as if **reason** could not find itself therein? Can one not bring forth something from ancient **pagan history** that looks not entirely unlike Biblical history, in order to diminish the latter? Is it not easy to hatefully describe the disputes of the clerical scholars over certain books and passages of Holy Scripture? Can the manifold opinions of the commentators not be recounted in such a way that average people become confused and decide for themselves to leave the Scripture aside as an uncertain book? Can one not calculate the vast number of **different readings** <note>original: "Arten zu lesen." This refers to the "variant readings" found in different ancient manuscripts of the Bible, a major topic in early biblical criticism.</note> and thereby pose the question of whether it is to be hoped that a mind as small as the human one could find the correct way of reading out of this infinite swarm?

(XII.) All of this must only happen in passing and, moreover, as if under a cloak. The whole matter is lost if one discovers their opinion too freely. One must pretend to be eager to learn and wish to see one's doubts resolved. One must praise certain scholars who have dared to renounce the usual opinions and explanations. ...praises his deep insight and erudition: and by doing this, one imperceptibly changes the great opinion of the true messengers and envoys of the Most High that one formed in youth. (XIV.) One must occasionally speak of the holy doctrines of **religion** with such turns of phrase that evoke a common, contemptible, and unworthy concept in the mind. (XV.) great minds of ancient times to a matter belonging to religion, does not have to fear as much resentment. He achieves what he seeks much more successfully than those who offer their own judgments. And yet, he silently advises those who read him to think in exactly the same way and to respect the events, customs, and doctrines of **Christianity** no more than the **Pagan** ones. It appears as if he only wishes to enliven his dead discourse with a wise and pleasant word from a spirited mind. The discerning reader, meanwhile, already notices where he is aiming: namely, that he is of the opinion that those ancients thought more correctly than we do, and that they, if they were to return, could not sufficiently marvel at our over-cleverness <note>original: "Überwiß." (XVI.) If it is precarious to engage with religion itself, then play with the words, divisions, and other things used by those who teach and present it. ## The Second Chapter

...Christians remained in their first purity and love after those days. This artifice is not yet worn out. It was only devised a short time ago. And those who wish to make use of it can greatly profit from the frequent complaints of wise and upright men regarding the decay of **Christianity**. It is easy to see what those who find a taste for this pretense must necessarily think. They must conclude that the doctrine of **JESUS** is a human and earthly work. Is it believable that the wisdom of **God** would have allowed a doctrine, revealed by Him for the benefit of the whole world, to perish so early?

**(XX)** One must speak of the first ages of **Christianity** in such a way that wicked thoughts must naturally grow from it. The first communities must be composed of nothing but despicable servants, miserable slaves who simply wanted better days, beggars, ruined merchants, day laborers, and a handful of sad and melancholic <note>original: "Gall-süchtiger" — literally "bile-sick," referring to the ancient medical theory of humors where excess black bile caused gloominess</note> people. The teachers who governed the communities in those days must be described as dull, unlearned, wild heads who left behind nothing but testimonies of their simplicity and often did not even know what they wanted themselves. One must attribute stubbornness, pride, immodesty, madness, and other diseases of the mind to the **Martyrs**. The so-called **Heretics** <note>original: "Ketzer"</note>, whom the **Christians** did not wish to tolerate among themselves, must be protected without distinction against all accusations and turned into people who were sacrificed to the ambition and superstition of the first **Bishops**. The more poorly the first youth of the **Church**

<column-break/>

is presented, the greater becomes the suspicion that its foundation was laid only by men.

**(XXI)** Whenever the opportunity arises, one must maliciously introduce and excessively expand upon what certain scholars have reported—with good reason—concerning the uncertainty and darkness of ancient **Church History**, the credulity of some among the first **Christians**, the **pious frauds** <note>original: "gottfeligen Betrügereyen" — referring to the historical concept of "fraus pia," or lies told to promote a religious cause</note> that were so often played, and the multitude of fables that have crept into history. How much honor will the **Christian Religion** have left once the world is convinced that nothing more grounded or certain can be reported of its first state than this: that it was propagated through cunning and deceit alone, and once it became properly known, it looked little better than the religions it refused to tolerate alongside itself?

**(XXII)** Above all things, the overseers and teachers of the churches—the **Clergy** <note>original: "Geistlichen"</note>, as they are called—must be painted as black as possible. The more one applies oneself to showing that their pride, their lack of understanding, their superstition, their enmities, their quarrelsomeness, and other vices have brought the world into misfortune at all times; the more often one repeats that their whole guild <note>original: "Zunft"</note> is worth nothing, nor can be worth anything; the more eloquently and sharply one can tear through the weaknesses they have in common with other men—the more the religion itself, which stands under their supervision and care, suffers. And one finds a hearing in this all the more certainly and easily because it is indeed true that the power and strength of religion is often nowhere less—

**(XXIII) One more main reminder.** One must never write about religion and divine things in a serious and rational manner. The style of writing must immediately become light and merry as soon as one happens upon a matter of this kind. People judge the value and utility of things by the words used to present them. And whatever is presented in the language of buffoons and "merry counselors" <note>original: "lustigen Räthe" — refers to court jesters or witty socialites who mock serious subjects</note> is always relegated to the lowest place in the hearts of men. It is time to make an end of this narration of the rules according to which the "high, free, and unconstrained spirits" <note>original: "hohen, freyen und ungebundnen Geister" — a sarcastic reference to Enlightenment "Free Thinkers"</note> of our times are accustomed to direct their writings, in order to tell the world in a fine and artful way that their great intellect has triumphed over all superstitious fear and has torn itself away from the constraints of the lowly world. One need only leaf through three or four books by these witty people to find examples of this. And yet we still ask: why does godliness grow so cold, and why does corruption so stubbornly resist the power of truth?

Regarding the other kind of books, which give life and nourishment to the sins and evil lusts of men, we wish to say little. To whom is it unknown that a great army of such writings already exists in all languages, and grows daily, which describe the sins and vices—against which our **Savior** threatened damnation—in a

<column-break/>

clear and vivid manner? They praise them ornamentally, in both verse and prose, and recommend them, as it were, to corrupt mankind. **Christian** governments very rarely stir against the unbridled freedom that reigns in these books to the detriment of decency and virtue—indeed, to the misfortune of the commonwealth. The people who are appointed in some places to watch that no godless, filthy, and scandalous works appear are either deceived or ignore this nuisance. The ministers of the **Gospel**, who zealously argue against the fact that drunkenness, unchastity, seductions, deceptions, and many other abominations are publicly praised and adorned with all the ornaments of art and eloquence among **Christians** (who should not even know of such things), these servants of the **Lord** are accused of wanting to suffocate the freedom of the spirits and reintroduce a "Papal Court of Conscience" <note>original: "Päpstliches Gewissens-Gericht" — a reference to the Inquisition or strict ecclesiastical control over private thought</note>. Youth of both sexes read such poems and stories, in which the disordered desires of the flesh are presented for imitation, with a particular pleasure. In many houses, it is even thought advisable to grant them permission to do so, because the mind is supposedly cleared by it and the foundation for a "clever life" <note>original: "Klugheit zu leben" — here meaning social savvy or worldly sophistication</note> is laid. When one considers this, is it any wonder where the "unclean fire" <note>original: "unreine Feuer" — a common metaphor for lust or illicit passion</note> comes from, which suddenly flares up in many still-inexperienced souls and does not subside until it has been tempered and extinguished by lamentable sins? Is it any wonder that so many have a loathing for everything that belongs to truth and godliness?

### Explanation.

We wish here only to remind the reader of as much as is necessary to prevent all misinterpretation. We agree with those who are of the opinion that a rash and superstitious godliness <term>Gottseligkeit: a state of living in a way that is pleasing to God, combining inner piety with outward moral conduct</term> is just as much a blot on religion as a disordered and sinful way of life. We willingly concede that those who seek to introduce a Christianity that conflicts with the orders of the world and the current constitutions of human societies are harmful members of a state and degenerate children of the Savior. We are fully convinced that many people are found among Christians who seek to advance godliness through the loss of truth, and we offer to those who wish to hinder these people in their undertaking in every way all the assistance that love and gentleness allow us to provide. We confess that those who practice an absurd and tasteless godliness can be distinguished from upright and true Christians by certain names. Least of all do we wish to speak for those who leave their congregations, hold secret meetings, mock or disparage the institutions of the church, and place no small part of their holiness in a scornful contempt for the usual divine service and for those Christians who remain with it. We have so often experienced with annoyance, after a sincere investigation, that the hearts of many people of this kind are distinguished from the hearts of other

<column-break/>

men by nothing but a great spiritual pride and excessive self-love; that some among them are sick in their understanding and even sicker in their imagination; and that others are deceived and led astray by their own souls. We only wish to obtain more protection and love among their brothers for righteous and good hearts who unite truth and godliness. We say only that godliness often loses many friends because people who offend no one with new and unusual opinions, who remain in communion with other Christians, and who separate themselves from other men by nothing other than a more cautious and quiet way of life and a more precise exercise of the duties of Christianity, are reviled, mocked, and, I know not how, scolded. How common this error is in our times is well known. And how good it would be if it were committed only by those of whom one can rightly use the word of our Redeemer: *They know not what they do!* <note>original: "Sie wissen nicht was sie thun!" — A reference to Luke 23:34</note> Should we not here and there encounter, even among those called to be guardians and nurturers of godliness, some who are provoked by an ill-considered zeal or something else even more blameworthy into a resentment against the people who are unbearable to the world because they, so to speak, condemn the world through their righteous conduct? It is easy to imagine what will be objected against our reminder. It will be said: The truly righteous and godly,

# The Second Chapter

those who follow the example of the **Savior** are never mocked, persecuted, or slandered. People only oppose those <term>eccentrics: Sonderlinge; specifically referring to religious non-conformists or separatists who lived outside the established church norms</term> who create new laws of godliness <term>Gottseligkeit: a state of living in a way that is pleasing to God, combining inner piety with outward moral conduct</term> and who like to burden themselves, as well as others, with all sorts of weights that were never placed upon us by our **Savior** and his witnesses. Is it really so wrong to point out the mischief such people cause through some sharp words and names, and to warn others not to follow in their footsteps? Is it forbidden to call things and people by their right names? Or should we call a visionary <note>original: "Phantasten"; often used in this period to describe those with "enthusiastic" or mystical leanings that strayed from church doctrine</note> wise, a hypocrite godly, a deluded person a child of the Most High, or a sad and peevish head a righteous Christian?

This answer seems not to be unfounded as long as it is viewed in general. And we do not doubt that it will entirely please those who spend their days without care or unrest of conscience and do not wish to think of the renunciation of the world until they can no longer use it. This type of people always wishes that they might not be disturbed in their sinful stillness by any examples of righteous and honest Christians; and therefore, they are happy to see the honor and reputation diminished of those who might be called such. To us, on the other hand, it seems—

<column-break/>

that regarding this general excuse for the outrage with which the coarse world meets the godly, much remains to be noted. Is it true, as is presupposed in it, that none but the eccentrics and the <term>work-holy: Werckheilige; a derogatory term for those who believe they can achieve salvation through outward religious deeds or legalistic rituals rather than faith</term>—to whom the law of the **Lord** still seems too soft and mild—must endure shame and dishonor among men? Is it true that the truly pious, who walk in the commandments of the **Lord**, remain unharmed? Those who are not devoid of all experience will know that this distinction is observed almost nowhere and that true and false saints are generally mingled together and drawn under the same judgment. And as often as we consider the behavior of people in certain places toward those who live with more order and caution than the common crowd, we cannot refrain from believing that a congregation of the first Christians would hardly find place or peace among them if they were led back into this lower world through a miracle from **God**. Well then, they will never believe that their particular practices, through which they separate themselves from other Christians, grant them a merit or a greater grace with **God**: They will never exalt themselves in their hearts over others who do not wish to follow their example, much less condemn them: They will leave the judgment of men to the **Lord** and seek to bring the righteousness of conduct, which they themselves observe, to others neither through cunning nor through other forbidden means. Among the testimonies to the ungodly conduct of many church leaders are the vexatious disputes that some among them conduct over **religion**, decorating them with the name of "a holy zeal for the honor of **GOD**." An unusual word, an ambiguous turn of phrase, a bit of disorder in a presentation, an incautious metaphor, a slight deviation from the established way of teaching, a doubt about certain opinions that nothing but antiquity makes respectable, or a clearer explanation of a doctrine previously presented obscurely—these are the causes that immediately stir the bile of many who wish to be called the guardians of the church. And who is so cautious and prudent, who is so safe from all missteps of his intellect and memory, who is so masterful of the language in which he writes, or who sees all the consequences of a phrase or proposition so clearly that he should never fall into such small errors? One would have to bear this excessive concern for the truth with the same **patience** with which many other human weaknesses are borne, if those afflicted by it proved through their sincerity and **gentleness** that it was their intellect alone, and not their **heart**, that sinned. ## Chapter Two ##

...and continue their quarrels more treacherously than those who declare themselves against the perceived errors of their brothers in matters of faith? All forbidden strikes taught by the blind spirit of **quarrelsomeness** <term>original: "Zancksucht" — a persistent, argumentative nature that seeks conflict over minor issues</term> in the fencing-school of perdition are employed by them, so that the adversary might be overcome and deprived of both his cause and his good name. And **vituperations** <note>original: "Schmäh-Worte" — abusive language or insults</note>, false conclusions, distortions of the best intentions, slanderous tales, and whatever else an agitated mind heated by anger can devise, are often the finest ornaments in writings meant to rescue the honor of divine truth. These ill-behaved combatants can hardly do otherwise. He who attacks another over a trivial matter, or wishes to wrangle over nothing at all, must obtain through cunning and malice the prestige that his poor cause cannot possibly give him. He must magnify the wrong of his enemy through poisonous falsifications and slanders, so that his own exposure and bad behavior cannot be clearly recognized.

What do the **children of this world** <note>a biblical term for people who are focused on secular life rather than spiritual matters</note> say to these shameful dealings? They mock the "heroes" who begin the fight and scornfully compare them to that **mad knight** <note>a reference to Miguel de Cervantes' character Don Quixote</note> who mistook windmills for giants. And since they let nothing slip from their hands that might strengthen them in their complacency and sin, this misfortune of the Lord's community must serve them for that very same damnable purpose. Those among them who surpass the rest in wit present us with this—as they imagine it—insoluble **knot of doubt**. 

The disputes which Christians wage among themselves with such vehemence and unfairness are either truly important and concern the essence of faith, or they signify nothing and are declared great and important by their founders without cause. If they are indeed important and concern the fundamental doctrines of religion, would we not then be acting most reasonably if we withheld our approval until they were settled to everyone's satisfaction? On which side should we stand? Each **party** <note>original: "Parthey" — referring to various denominations or theological factions like the Lutherans, Calvinists, or Catholics</note> condemns the other. Each wishes to be called the sole possessor of truth. How can we accept a religion that is still so unsettled that its most prominent teachers cannot agree on its first principles? If these dealings are trivial and of no particular importance, then we find just as much reason to restrain ourselves. Should we [place] our salvation in...

# Of the Maintenance of Human Corruption. #

...[into] the hands of such people who are so foolish that they either will not or cannot distinguish a **war of words** <note>original: "Wort-Krieg" — a dispute over terminology or semantics rather than core theological truths</note> from a genuine dispute? Should we trust the word of such teachers who quarrel far more fiercely with one another over minor errors than other men do over those things upon which their entire earthly welfare depends? Should we learn the way to heaven from those who are certainly on the path to damnation, if what they preach regarding gentleness, peace, and love is true? This foundation is so weak and miserable that those who consider it irrefutable should be ashamed, if they were even capable of shame in matters concerning religion. It must either come from a broken brain or have sprouted from a heart that has resolved to persist in sin and malice. But what is more certain than that the people who devised this argument allow themselves to be held in the corruption in which they live by the thinnest of ropes? And is it honorable for those who serve the Lord that they themselves spin the threads—through their disorder and unnecessary heat—from which these fragile ropes of the heart's unbelief are woven?

->§. XXII.<-

Among the people who spend their lives in lowliness and poverty, there are likewise certain specific causes that keep them in the **bondage of sin** <term>original: "Dienstbarkeit der Sünden" — the theological concept that a person is enslaved to their sinful nature until liberated by grace</term> and in their natural wickedness. One of the most prominent is the heavy yoke which most of them must bear in order to find what is required of them, and to meagerly provide sustenance for themselves as well as their families. All the world complains that the times are always becoming worse and more laborious. The **taxes** <note>original: "Auflagen" — can refer to general duties, levies, or financial burdens imposed by authorities</note> are increased from day to day and multiplied now in this way, now in another. The old means of earning something and setting it aside for one’s family have become useless through all kinds of causes. The luxury and extravagance of those who possess power and honor rise ever higher, and with it increases their heartlessness toward those whom the Lord has placed beneath them. The crowd of miserable people who sigh for bread, and who through the most strenuous labor can hardly earn enough to defend themselves against the attacks of hunger and thirst, grows in all places

The day of the **Lord** will make it clear whether they are driven by necessity and other valid reasons to deal so harshly with those who have the same right as they do to the goods of this world and the next, or whether they forget that they also have a **Master** in heaven, with whom there is no respect of persons. *Ephesians 6:9.* <note>The author is citing a biblical admonition to slave-owners and masters, reminding them that God judges everyone equally regardless of social status.</note> We only wish to briefly note the evils that arise from this for godliness <term>original: "Gottseligkeit" — a life lived in devotion to God</term> and religion. People who are so severely plagued and distressed generally become much more cunning, malicious, stubborn, and ill-mannered than they are by nature. Power and malice have been, for as long as the world has stood, engaged in an everlasting war. The former [Power] strives unceasingly to strip the cunning and malice of men of all their strength. And it strives in vain. The more it restricts a person, the more closely it watches his conduct, the more the person sharpens his intellect to obtain through cunning and secret maneuvers what he cannot win through power and boldness. And countless individuals, to whom nature granted neither great wit nor shrewdness, are imperceptibly made skillful by the strict discipline and order under which they are placed, enabling them to deceive the most watchful and to overcome power itself. Can this be hidden from those who have observed the theater of this world with attention? And how difficult it is for the word of the **Lord** to accomplish anything fruitful in such minds, which—almost against their will—have become clever in evil and crafty in deceiving their overseers? The heart excuses itself from all admonitions by pleading necessity: And many make use of the same cunning excuses in matters of godliness that have so often succeeded for them in worldly affairs. # On the Maintenance of Human Corruption #

### Zii ###

...which are naturally pleasant to them, never become more fiery than when difficulties pile up in the pursuit of obtaining them. The value of things is increased by the effort their acquisition costs. A person sets aside everything else that usually tempers and restrains their desires when they see the desired object moving further away from them than before. The very misery that people endure doubles their longing for variety and pleasure. And when they finally attain it, the enjoyment of even a moderate indulgence is far more sensitive and pleasant to them—because they are exhausted by constant toil—than the sensation of the greatest pleasure is to those who are able to enjoy their lives with some freedom and comfort.

Hence it happens that they retain a restless desire to renew the enjoyed pleasure as soon as possible. They exert all their strength to satisfy this desire; and, since they see no other hope of tearing themselves out of their poverty, they are all the more willing to sacrifice the small remainder of their laboriously earned goods to their lusts. <note>The author suggests that when social mobility is impossible, the poor spend their meager earnings on immediate gratification rather than saving, as a psychological response to hopelessness.</note> 

In the state of corrupted nature, one desire or craving usually fights with another, and one is often the death of the other. For instance, the love of wealth resists the power of lust in a person. As long as one retains the hope that they might perhaps gather a treasure and leave it to their family, they often find within themselves the antidote by which the impact of the sweet images of the "pleasure-plague" <note>original: "Lust-Seuche" — a strong metaphor comparing the obsessive pursuit of pleasure to a contagious disease.</note> is withdrawn. But if this hope dies out—if a person becomes certain that they will leave nothing but want and misery in the hut where they will eventually close their eyes—then the love of pleasure alone takes the upper hand in the soul and incites them to try everything without ceasing to satisfy it. 

Despair and lust are so closely related that one generally follows on the heels of the other. What benefit can those who must work on souls <note>Likely referring to clergy or moral reformers.</note> expect from their efforts when dealing with people who think of nothing more than how they might escape the power of the law through cunning and deceit, and drive away the taste of their misery through animalistic lusts? Those who, by a special stroke of luck, are preserved from these diseases of the soul despite their laborious state are nevertheless kept from zeal in godliness <term>original: "Gottseligkeit" — a life of active devotion and piety</term> by other circumstances. Their spirit clings so much to the earth that it treats heavenly things, of which it hears, merely...

## The Second Chapter ##

...recalled as if in a dream, and can awaken no true desire or longing for them within themselves. They perform the exercises of divine service <note>original: *Gottesdienstes*; referring to formal religious rituals and worship</note> little differently than the other duties that compulsion and their profession demand of them. They gradually become so sluggish and sensitive <note>In this context, "sensitive" likely refers to being easily irritated or defensive, a psychological state of being "thin-skinned" due to constant stress.</note> that the most moving exhortations and warnings can no longer disturb their wretched security. They concern themselves more with how they might soon be rid of their own [children] than how they might lead them to the Lord and raise them in the fear of God. And these children are harnessed to the yoke of their fathers so early—so poorly instructed and so ill-armed against the temptations of their lusts—that they enter the service of sin and the world almost at the same time. 

Could we be more expansive here, we would add that the miserable life which most people lead provides many who are inclined toward unbelief with a plausible reason to justify it. We wish only to touch upon the doubt derived from this. It is as follows: 

If we look into the Scriptures and consult our reason <term>Reason (Vernunft): In 18th-century theology, reason was considered a God-given tool to be used alongside the Bible to understand the world.</term>, we hear that a wise and benevolent Providence <term>Providence (Vorsehung): The protective care of God as a spiritual power overseeing the destiny of humanity.</term> rules the earth and determines the fate of its inhabitants in a manner both holy and loving. If we look into the world and consider the adversities and sufferings under which the greatest part of humanity groans, experience tells us that a blind fate deals out fortune and misfortune, and that the unjust power of a few individuals is to blame for the agony and sorrow of the vast majority. 

Can we believe that a loving and kind Creator has chosen the greatest part of his rational creatures for a life that is, as it were, a constant struggle against plague, misery, and poverty? Who will settle this dispute? Should we trust Scripture and reason, or should we trust our experience? We do not deny that we are more inclined to listen to the latter and to cast doubt upon divine Providence. At the very least, it is much easier for us to reconcile the misery of most people with the doctrine of those who attribute everything that happens to blind fate and necessity <note>This refers to fatalism or deterministic philosophies that deny God's active involvement.</note>, than with the opinion of those who entrust the governance of the world to the power and goodness of an omniscient God. 

We are always ready to give a clear and sufficient answer to those who seek to strip the doctrine of the Providence of the Most High of its dignity in this way. They assume that the Providence of the Lord [leads/governs] men...

## On the Maintenance of Human Ruin ##

This is just as absurd as if someone were to claim that an intelligent ruler must lock up and confine the subjects of his land so that they do not violate his laws. Would even a shadow of a government remain if a prince focused on this nonsensical conclusion? How greatly we fear that those will find it much harder to answer the accusation of their conscience in this life, and the inquiry of the righteous Judge in the life to come, who through their unmercifulness and negligence give cause for this reproach against Providence!

### §. XXIII. ###

A good portion of the obstacles that arise for the progress of godliness <term>Godliness (Gottseligkeit): A central concept in 18th-century German piety, referring to a life of active, sincere devotion to God.</term> from the misery and poverty of most people would disappear if the spirit of those whom God has blessed with power and wealth would allow itself to be softened, to come to the aid of the great need of so many afflicted people through charitable institutions. How much good could the ministers of the Gospel <note>original: *Diener des Evangelii*; a Latin-derived term for clergy or missionaries.</note> who work among the poor achieve if a generous hand distributed Bibles and other godly books among those who could not afford them themselves? 

How greatly would godlessness, unfaithfulness, and coarse vices among servants and other lower orders of the world decrease if, in every land, the powerful and wealthy dedicated some of their goods to the establishment of well-ordered houses <note>The author is likely advocating for the creation of orphanages or charity schools, a major social movement of the time.</note>, in which the children of the completely destitute would be well-instructed and honestly raised until they reached the years of understanding <note>The age of maturity or discretion.</note> and could serve the world? How noticeably would improvement show itself in many external matters if schools were established in which the children of people of moderate means—who can spare little for their own—were guided more thoroughly and better than commonly happens, and were prepared for all stations and trades <term>Trades (Handthierungen): Handcrafts, manual labor, or professional occupations.</term> of the world? 

How wisely would one act in particular if one snatched the children born out of wedlock <note>original: *unehlich erzeugten Kinder*; in this era, illegitimate children were often excluded from society and legal protections.</note>—so many of whom grow up in all lands without discipline, supervision, or order, in all manner of wickedness to the detriment of the common good—from the shame under which they are born in time, and [reared them] in special houses against sin...

# The Second Chapter #

What a rich increase <note>original: *Wucher*; here used in the older sense of a "return on investment" or "fruitfulness" rather than the modern sense of usury.</note> would that wealth yield, which would be applied to support those who fall into misfortune through no fault of their own, and to lift up again those who have incautiously fallen, so that they and their families do not fall into the snares of ruin? How deserving of the congregation of the Most High would those make themselves who, out of their abundance, added something to the salary of school-servants <term>School-servants (Schul-Bedienten): A common 18th-century term for teachers, who were often treated as low-ranking church employees with very meager pay.</term> in most places, so that the important office of the education of youth would no longer have to be entrusted to incompetent people and those whom the world has, as it were, excluded from their offices? What a service would be rendered both to the **Lord** and to a country if the freedom to beg were abolished and the needy idlers were encouraged to create something good with their hands? 

All these wishes are of such a nature that we can hardly expect their fulfillment in our times. Our little care for the poor and the lowly will, by all appearances, remain in most places one of the causes why godlessness will retain its free dominion among these people. The Providence of the **Lord** has here and there in our Church awakened some upright men who have applied themselves to removing this cause in their part, and who still continue their begun efforts with an honest and faithful zeal. They cannot boast of very many followers. Some of them have received so little from the world—which nevertheless cannot deny the benefit of their institutions—that they have barely been acquitted of self-interest and other sinful intentions. 

Others would have grown weary and long ago returned to their former quietude if they had not weighed the reward of the future world against their labor, and drawn from it a powerful comfort against the slander, and even against the persecutions, which they must endure because of their love. Almost all who have set their hand to this wholesome work have experienced that the help of the mighty and high of this world, which they need most, is almost nowhere harder to obtain than for works of love and mercy. And it is certain that their example [would lead] far more faithful servants of the **Lord** to follow...

# Preface.

This second part of our Moral Teaching <term>original: *Sitten-Lehre*; refers to the study of Christian ethics and conduct</term> contains nothing but the doctrine of repentance <term>original: *Buße*; in this context, it refers to both the internal change of heart and the outward practice of penitence</term>. How can a doctrine be difficult, obscure, and wordy when it is intended to serve as a light for the whole world—be they sharp-witted or simple—to find the one path that leads to salvation <note>original: *Seligkeit*; literally "blessedness" or "happiness," commonly used for eternal salvation</term>? However, we set a far greater plan for ourselves when we undertook this work. We first intended to explain the nature of that change which the Scripture calls repentance, and which it prescribes everywhere as the sole means of righteousness <note>original: *Gerechtigkeit*</note> and holiness <note>original: *Heiligkeit*</note>, from its very foundation; and by doing so, to halt the progress of so many erroneous concepts and opinions regarding it that circulate among Christians. Is it not heartily to be regretted? It is repentance alone that makes us Christians and disciples of our Savior. And countless people, who would consider themselves insulted if one were to doubt their conversion <note>original: *Bekehrung*</note>, do not even know it. Furthermore, we are bound to this effort by the title, or rather by the intention and purpose of our work. In a system of ethics <term>original: *Sitten-Lehre*; the study of moral conduct</term> based on Holy Scripture, the Scripture must rightly occupy the primary place and impart light and life to all its propositions. And how would it be able to perform this service for the presented truths if one merely set down its words and left the task of interpretation <term>original: *Auslegung*</term>—which so few among them are able to undertake, and even fewer wish to—to the readers alone? 

We have, meanwhile, contented ourselves with those passages of Scripture <term>original: *Oerter der Schrift*</term> that seemed to us the most complete and emphatic. If we had wished to dwell upon every passage belonging to the doctrine of repentance as long as we did on those we selected as the best, we would have caused more annoyance through our excessive long-windedness <note>original: *Weitläuftigkeit*; refers to an overly detailed or rambling style of writing</note> than we would have provided benefit. Two passages of Scripture that are explained thoroughly and in an orderly fashion are as good as a light that spreads its glow over twenty others. And one can take it for certain that a person who has carefully read what has been noted about them will understand the remaining testimonies of Scripture that belong to the same teachings without further citation.

These two intentions have filled approximately half of the space that this portion of our work occupies. # Preface.

Perhaps one or another will find it difficult to forgive us for certain liberties we have taken in the explanation of things pertaining to the doctrine of repentance <term>Buße: in this context, the Protestant concept of heart-felt repentance and turning toward God, rather than the Catholic rite of penance</term>. We have set aside, in several respects, the common and customary presentation found in most of our usual textbooks; instead, we have treated the faith of our churches somewhat more freely, at times using words that have not yet been introduced everywhere. This was done so that we might present the meaning of Holy Scripture more clearly and distinctly, and remedy all obscurity and misinterpretation. 

The unconverted person often hides his wicked and impure opinions behind the names and terms we commonly use when speaking of conversion <term>Bekehrung: the spiritual turning point of a believer</term>, because they are ambiguous; he utters gross and intolerable errors while repeating the signs and divisions of the truth. The inexperienced person <note>literally "the unpracticed"</note> frequently grasps the meaning and sense of phrases made venerable by long use only imperfectly and incorrectly, because these terms represent more than just a single concept of the understanding. At times, he even mistakes the usual divisions of words and concepts for true divisions within things that are, in themselves, indivisible. 

How long have those appointed as guardians of the Lord's congregation <term>Gemeine: the community of believers or the local church</term> complained about these abuses? And how are they to be remedied? We could devise no surer means against them than this: the words and phrases that give occasion to these errors must sometimes be exchanged by an intelligent teacher for others that cannot be so easily twisted or misinterpreted. No word should be placed or used in books from which the whole world is meant to learn without having a clear explanation attached to it. The distinct concepts underlying a single word must be set apart and designated with specific and proper names. The divisions of words and concepts must be carefully distinguished from divisions grounded in the matter itself. We have followed these rules <term>Reguln: guidelines or principles of logic and teaching</term>, keeping a sharp watch that we did not cause the slightest harm to the truth itself. Let the wise judge whether we have done well or poorly.

# Preface.

No one can more sincerely honor the memory of the great men who planted our Church and set its doctrines in order than we do. Those who value their merits lowly, or even despise them, do not know them. And those who, in our times, recount and cry out with bitterness and heat regarding the errors they might have committed, only reveal the blind pride of their hearts and make us understand that they would have stumbled twice—and perhaps three times—as much had they been in their place. These tireless people have, with unspeakable effort, sought out the gold of truth from the thickest dust, carefully cleaned it, and so cautiously preserved and enclosed it that we need not fear any new poverty as long as we protect the boundaries they have drawn around this treasure. We therefore advise all who are to lead the youth being prepared for the service of the Lord <term>Dienst des Herren: the ministry or pastoral work</term> that they should never, without necessity or great cause, leave the paths that those men have paved to seek new roads, or introduce unknown ways of teaching and foreign modes of speech. It generally happens in the Church of the Lord as it did at the Tower of Babel. When the language of the builders is confused and one speaks this way while the other speaks that way, they no longer understand one another. And what else can arise from this evil but dispersal and confusion?

However, it seems to us that this rule of prudence has its exceptions in certain cases, and can be set aside in those writings intended either for the service of the completely simple-minded or for convincing the whole world that the Christian faith is just as rational as it is holy. The ears of the world have, in any case, become delicate and longing since wit has been sharpened, taste refined, and almost all sciences <term>Wissenschaften: in this era, this refers broadly to all branches of academic study and systematic knowledge, including theology and philosophy</term> have been advanced further. And "How long," it is asked, "will people sing the same old song to us that we have heard for so long?" whenever we explain divine truths using the language of our fathers. What is to be done about this disgust? Our stubbornness will not overcome it. And we must therefore often speak differently with the world than we do with those who are to become the salt of the earth (*Matthew 5:13* <note>original: "Matth. There prevail among the teachers of our churches some minor disagreements regarding several matters belonging to the doctrines we have treated. We necessarily had to come upon these. And since our chosen order of presentation has led us this far, we did not wish to remain silent regarding our opinion on these disputed questions. We believe, or nearly so, that the manner we have chosen to decide them will, of itself, clear us of all quarrelsomeness <term>Zancksucht: a tendency toward theological bickering or litigiousness</term> and of all pride. We remain devoted to both sides with equal esteem and love. We have sometimes ventured to compare the disputants; at other times, we have preferred one party over the other. The former, if we are not mistaken, happened without any self-exaltation; the latter without any contempt for those whose views we have moved away from. Whenever we intended to undertake either of these, we diligently encouraged our soul and sought to truly awaken the feeling of our own weakness within us, so that self-love—which almost never ensnares us more easily than when we wish to defend or refute ourselves—might not lead us astray. If those to whom our judgments might seem unfounded follow our example in this, we shall receive either no opponents at all, or else only those who are gentle and loving.

We cannot well conclude this preface without offering public thanks to those who received the beginning of this work with much love and deemed our weak attempt to contribute something to the service of the Lord’s community <term>Gemeine des Herren: the congregation or the body of the Church</term> worthy of their approval, and even their

People who blame without grounds so that their unnecessary praise might not strike anyone as particularly moving? The intentions of a man who seeks the **truth** alone, and those of a person who can neither resolve to praise sincerely nor to blame openly and boldly, are so far apart that both may argue against each other for a long time and yet never meet. Of what use are such disputes?

In this sense, he believes, one can not only attribute insatiable desires to souls, but also accept these insatiable desires as a sign of their **perfection** and **immortality**. We wish to join him in the explanation of these two words without excessive elaboration, so that we may more easily escape this minor difficulty. Otherwise, we take these terms in another sense, which we have indicated elsewhere.

We have two questions to answer. The first: Are **infinite desires**—or desires that now fall asleep and then awaken again—a sign of perfection or of imperfection? The second: Do such desires provide a secure foundation to prove the **immortality** of our souls? Either we are greatly mistaken, or one can answer "No" to both of these questions without danger of error.

People in whom desires are sometimes quiet and sometimes active are constantly alternating between rest and restlessness. Is this state a condition of perfection? Are those not far more blessed and calm in whom desires are always peaceful and soothed—those who have reached the goal of their wishes, who desire nothing more, and who take pleasure unhindered and incessantly in the enjoyment and possession of the goods that have filled the space of their souls and satisfied their spirits?

We wish to use the very same metaphor <note>original: *Gleichniß*</note> that our gentle opponent—or rather, our affectionate teacher—has chosen. Are we blessed or physically perfect because we can never completely quench our hunger for as long as we live? Would we not be more blessed and tranquil if we felt no hunger or thirst at all? And is our insatiable hunger not a sign of the decay and fragility of the **wretched cottage** <note>A common 18th-century philosophical and biblical metaphor for the human body (referencing 2 Corinthians 5:1), suggesting the body is a temporary, flimsy dwelling for the soul.</note> with which we are surrounded? We imagine the state of the spirits who have been received into the bosom of blessed eternity as a state of everlasting pleasure and stillness, in which desires will no longer have a place.

He concedes that this potential misuse could by no means be blamed on us. He even adds this brief and emphatic defense of our heart and will: "Who can help it if a sharp-cutting knife comes into the hand of someone incautious?" How much discord would be avoided in the **community of the Lord** <note>referring to the church or the body of believers</note> if all rebuked their brothers so wisely and gently, and separated a man's intentions from the means he uses to achieve them, his way of teaching from the doctrines he treats, and his delivery from his opinion; and if they did not immediately transform certain representations and explanations of thoughts into errors and crimes. The spirit can be free and pure of all false opinions; the will can be animated by a legitimate and sincere purpose; and yet the **imagination** <note>original: *Einbildung*; in 18th-century psychology, this referred to the faculty that forms mental images and can lead to emotional "heat"</note> can nevertheless perform its office poorly and have either too much or too little heat and fire. It would have been pleasing to us if the nature of the publication in which this judgment appears had allowed the author to carry out and explain this point somewhat more extensively. Had this been done, we would have drawn more benefit from it for our own improvement. If we understand him correctly, his opinion is this: our style of writing is at times altogether too lively, and we have not always watched sharply enough against our imagination.

# Preface.

If we have not yet succeeded in this effort as well as we ourselves wish, then the errors arising from it should be attributed not to our will, but to our capacity. If it pleases the Providence of the Lord to lengthen our years a bit more, then old age will presumably completely extinguish the excess fire and bring the imagination entirely under the rule of the understanding.

[He] says: All these things are produced by the one and the same Spirit. 1 Cor. XII. 11. <note>The author is quoting 1 Corinthians 12:11, where Paul discusses how the Holy Spirit distributes different spiritual gifts to believers.</note> (*)

We want to sincerely confess that it is difficult for us to find the error that we are supposed to have committed in these words. As far as we know, it is unanimously taught in our churches that eloquence <term>original: *Beredsamkeit*; the art of persuasive speaking</term> and erudition <term>original: *Gelehrsamkeit*; deep scholarly learning</term> are, in themselves, attained through the natural powers of man. And this doctrine is founded in Scripture, in reason, and in experience. Regarding the *use* of eloquence and erudition, the matter is different. We willingly admit that many righteous men of our community have spoken the truth when they taught that the Spirit of the Lord sanctifies these natural gifts in His instruments and servants, and grants them wisdom and understanding to use them beneficially and for the best of His church in their office. We thus in no way deny the gifts of office <term>original: *Amtsgaben*; the belief that God provides specific spiritual abilities to those called to ministry</term>. Meanwhile, the passage from the Apostle Paul seems to us to deal with the extraordinary gifts of the teachers of the first congregation. And how can it be hidden from the learned man, to whom our words seem offensive, that in this interpretation we agree with the most famous biblical scholars <term>original: *Schriftforscher*</term> of our community?

We have called the knowledge of God that resides in an unregenerate person <term>original: *Unwiedergebohrner*; a person who has not undergone a spiritual "new birth" or conversion</term> a "dead knowledge." (**) This adjective seems offensive and contrary to Scripture. (***) "We would rather say," it is claimed, "that the man is dead, but not the divine knowledge that remains in him and is always living." In a dead mother, a living fetus can still be found; in a dirty lantern, a bright light can burn. We would have to be very mistaken if this reproach were significant. It is a living and powerful seed lying in a stony and unprepared field. However, it is dead because it is prevented from bringing forth fruit and proving its inner life. Moreover, we are not even speaking of divine truth itself. We are only speaking of the knowledge and conception of this truth. If man is dead <note>referring to the state of "spiritual death" before conversion</note>, as is admitted, then the knowledge of his spirit is likewise dead and cannot be called living. And does not Scripture expressly say this with us? Faith, so speaks the Apostle James, if it has no works, is dead in itself. James 2:17. Who denies that knowledge <note>original: *Wissenschaft*; in this theological context, it refers to the intellectual or "scientific" grasp of doctrine as a component of faith</note> is a piece of faith? If, therefore, according to the words of the Apostle, the entire faith of an unconverted person is dead, then his knowledge is, without dispute, of no different nature. It is dead because it bears no fruit in him. We do not write all this because we are absolutely unwilling to let go of the use of the word *dead*. If this explanation does not suffice to satisfy those who find the word *dead* in this meaning offensive, then we will gladly put another in its place that offends no one. How could the Spirit of Peace dwell in us if it were difficult for us to sacrifice a word for the love of the brothers and the peace of the community of our Savior?

# Preface.

This is not entirely criticized. It is only desired that readers might not misuse our presentation. Does this not imply that it was not composed with enough care and caution? Before setting this down, we have read through it again deliberately to judge whether anything in it could be drawn toward a foreign or false meaning. Regarding the matter itself, there is likely little to be improved. We have indicated, as clearly as possible, that we wish to see banished from the Church of the Lord no disputes other than those that are unnecessary—those stirred up over small and innocent missteps and conducted with bitterness and vehemence. Nonetheless, we do not hesitate to repeat the aforementioned wish ourselves: 

> May the Lord grant that neither this, nor any other single part of our well-intentioned work, be misused by anyone! 

We do not deny that we have inherited the spirit of peace and love from the great and worthy men who formerly held the dignities and offices with distinction, which we now administer according to our ability. However, we shall always be on our guard so that we never stain ourselves with a dangerous leniency <term>original: *Gelindigkeit*; here meaning a soft-heartedness or tolerance that might compromise the truth</term>. Truth is holy. And we know that he who willfully denies or abandons it sins just as much as he who transgresses the duties of love.

The latest reminder has taught us anew what has already been noted by many: one can take upon oneself the suspicion of error when one presents a completely common and well-known opinion in an unusual way. It is more than sufficiently known that some sins of man have their seat more in the blood, in the **vital spirits,** <term>original: *Lebens-Geistern*; in early modern medicine, these were subtle fluids or vapors believed to circulate through the nerves and regulate both physical movement and emotions</term> and in the constitution of the internal parts, rather than in the soul. Irascibility <term>original: *Jachzorn*; a sudden, violent temper or prone to outbursts</term> is such a sin of nature <term>original: *Natur-Sünde*; a concept suggesting that certain moral failings are rooted in one's biological temperament</term>. ## §. I.

A person, who is by nature constituted as he has been described up to this point, must be entirely changed if he is to find his delight in the Lord and His law, and spend his life in obedience to God. Matthew 18:3; 2 Corinthians 5:17. The means to this blessed change is **repentance**. <note>The German term "Busse" can mean both the internal feeling of remorse and the outward act of penance; here, the author emphasizes it as a transformative process of the soul.</note> John the Baptist (Matthew 3:2, 6), our holy Savior Himself (Matthew 4:17; Mark 1:15; Luke 24:47), and His apostles and witnesses (Acts 2:38, 3:19; James 4:9; Hebrews 6:1) pointed those whom they wished to lead to the Lord toward this, as the only *medicine* for their souls. One must either strip these testimonies of their divine authority, or one must believe that repentance is the origin and the beginning of all true godliness.

### Explanation.

Those who have not forgotten the outline and context of our work will find the reasons for themselves that compel us to present and elaborate on the doctrine of repentance here. This piece of divine truth is commonly reckoned as part of **Dogmatics** <note>original: "Glaubens-Lehre," referring to the systematic study of Christian beliefs.</note>. And we admit that it must not be omitted from there, if the entire "Way of Salvation" is to be described in its true order. However, it is just as indispensable in the study of **Ethics** <note>original: "Lehre von der Gottseligkeit," literally "the doctrine of godliness."</note>. Repentance is the beginning of the "state of grace" and the source of all the power that makes us

<column-break/>

capable of performing pure works that are pleasing to God. Whoever remembers this will be more surprised that the consideration of it is missing from most books dealing with **Moral Philosophy** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre."</note>, than ask for the reasons behind our decision to deal with it in such detail. Who would think ill of those who are meant to instruct certain servants in the will of their master, if they first describe the means that can make them fit for his service?

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the doctrine of repentance, specifically addressing a potential academic objection: why include repentance in a book on ethics (Sitten-Lehre) if it is already covered in dogmatics (Glaubens-Lehre). The author argues that while the subject is the same, the perspective and purpose differ between the two disciplines.</meta>

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>On the Nature and Character of Repentance.</header>

It is easy to see what those who are otherwise minded might object for their part. They will willingly grant us that repentance is the foundation of a godly life: They will conclude with us from this that those who wish to please the Lord must always be directed toward the same: They will reject with us those who separate faith and love from one another and make the kingdom of grace into a kingdom of law and fear. However, they will add, all this can remain true and take place even if the doctrine of repentance is omitted from the instruction on godliness. One can assume it as a truth that is established and proven elsewhere, and need only remind one's readers that they must look around and ground themselves well in the doctrine of truth that leads to godliness, if they wish to know the nature of upright worship. Of what use is it to say once more what is orderly and exhaustively explained in the **Dogmatics** <note>original: "Glaubens-Lehre," the systematic study of the articles of faith.</note> and to expand the already extensive realm of **Ethics** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre," the study of moral conduct and Christian living.</note> to the annoyance of the learners through vain repetitions? Repentance has already been assigned its proper place among the doctrines intended to enlighten the understanding. One should leave it there and not shift the boundaries that so many teachers of enlightened understanding and unfeigned loyalty have established! This objection seems to be well-founded. And we therefore did not decide to disregard it until we had weighed it carefully and found legitimate reasons to deny it victory over our undertaking. We hope—

<column-break/>

—that most will take our side once they have read these reasons and considered them as attentively as we have.

Both those who present the **Dogmatics** and those who treat the **Ethics** <note>original: "Lebens-Lehre," or "Life-Doctrine."</note> must appeal to repentance. Both would erect a foundationless building if they did not mention it. Yet both do not view it in the same way. The teacher of truth envisions it as a necessary piece of the order of salvation prescribed for humanity. The teacher of godliness considers it the foundation and the means of **sanctification** <term>Sanctification (Heiligung): The process by which a believer is made holy and transformed by the Holy Spirit.</term>, from which all duties of man must spring. This different perspective allows both to speak of it and yet not be forced to say the same thing. The former connects it in his understanding and in his instruction with the remaining parts of divine truth that God has made known to us for our comfort. The latter unites it immediately with the sanctification and renewal of man that God demands. The former presents it as a means to **reconciliation** with God: the latter as a means to obedience toward God and His laws. This difference of intention gives both the ability to distance themselves from one another in a certain way, so that they awaken different concepts in the minds of their students and can counter the distaste that grows out of the dry repetition of a doctrine. Regarding the main matter, they both remain on one path. The truth is unchangeable and always retains its form, whether it be from the right or—

The former—we understand this to be the **Teacher of Faith** <note>original: "Glaubens-Lehrer," a theologian focused on dogmatics and the formal articles of faith.</note>—is closely confined by the method of teaching, by the divisions, by the descriptions, and by the words themselves, which have been introduced since long ago and have been, as it were, hallowed by so many great men. He must always keep his eyes upon the footsteps of his predecessors. Should he wish to conduct himself somewhat more freely than they, he would have to fear that some might consider him a secret friend of those against whom one wishes to guard oneself through the customary way of teaching. It is fitting that divine truth be handled by everyone according to the same rule and prescription, provided no great causes stand in the way, so that the inexperienced are not led into the delusion that the old doctrines have either already been confused with new and unusual ones, or would soon be exchanged for them. The latter—we mean the **Teacher of Morals** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehrer," a teacher focused on Christian ethics and practical living.</note>—has permission to explain his thoughts somewhat more unboundedly, freely, and extensively. It is not demanded of him that he maintain the arrangement most exactly, which was established in the textbooks for the purpose of allowing truth and error to be distinguished all the more certainly and easily by the learners. One knows that he wishes to instruct the weak and the strong, the experienced and the inexperienced at the same time. Therefore, the sensible world grants him the right to set the concepts apart more clearly and to explain and draft them according to the understanding of all people,

<column-break/>

proceeding through a new path toward the goal he has set for himself, and to dispel the darkness through many and more common words, which can grow in many people from the brevity and order of the usual teaching method. The former presents **repentance** <note>original: "Busse," referring here to the theological process of conversion and penitence.</note> like a piece of the truth, and is only concerned with showing how firmly it is connected with the remaining parts of the same, and how thoughtlessly and uncertainly he must step into the kingdom of faith who understands it erroneously or even leaves it behind. The latter dwells solely on the benefit it provides to one who wishes to attain holiness: He strives to demonstrate that all impulses of the heart that unite us with **GOD** are worked through it. He shows that the entire spiritual strength of the righteous is generated and maintained through it. To say this same thing in other words: The former looks at repentance as a concept of the understanding that must be properly purified and enlightened; the latter regards it at the same time as a power of **GOD** that must renew the will and subject it to the law of **GOD**. Perhaps one will learn to understand this more easily from our treatment of this doctrine than from a longer explanation.

Namely, we shall deal with repentance in such a way as a teacher of godliness may and must deal with it. From the teachers of faith, we shall borrow nothing more than the kernel of truth, which they themselves have taken from the **Scripture** <note>The Holy Bible.</note>.
