# On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

...to think. We will always remain in the fellowship of those who hold to the pattern of sound doctrine <note>original: "Fürbilde der heilsamen Lehre." This refers to the standard of orthodox Christian teaching, likely within the Lutheran tradition.</note> as to an invaluable jewel. However, we will not venture into the narrow streets and sections through which others are accustomed to leading their disciples so that they might escape their adversaries; instead, we shall seek a leveler path alongside them, which everyone can follow—and especially those who, for lack of the necessary strength, are unable to force themselves so strictly. It is enough that we finally reach the same place toward which they are heading. At the end of the road, we will part ways. We will let them draw the conclusions that benefit the truth, while we present only the advantages that flow from our work for the sake of godliness. If all this does not happen as successfully as we wish, we hope to find a certain refuge in the love and gentleness of our brothers. We will always remain united in will and heart with those from whom we may be separated by words, by the division of concepts, by the explanation of certain passages of Scripture, or even by a few errors of weakness.

Man is, as we have proven, by nature afflicted and infected with defects of the understanding and with diseases of the will. Even if the understanding occasionally thinks purely and correctly, this light is soon darkened and stifled again by the violent and disorderly lusts of the will. If a desire arises in the will that in itself cannot be called evil, the darkness and blindness of the understanding ensures that,

<column-break/>

before one realizes it, the desire vanishes like a dream. And yet, this so corrupted man is supposed to pursue holiness and peace if he wishes to see the **Lord**. *Hebrews 12:14.* He is to practice love toward **God** and men from a pure heart, from a good conscience, and from unfeigned faith. *1 Timothy 1:5.* From this, who can conclude anything else but that he must be transformed and renewed in spirit and in all the powers of his soul? If Scripture did not teach this clearly, the matter itself would teach it to us. If a will is to be governed by noble, pure, and holy impulses, the understanding must first recognize—unhindered and vividly—the glory and beauty of those things toward which the will should be directed with zeal and constancy. The will decides on nothing great unless the understanding first moves and encourages it through its representations. However, the understanding of the natural man is dim. He sees divine things either only imperfectly or unclearly. And where he occasionally recognizes them better and more clearly, he is faced with a rapid change that will bring back the old darkness. Where is the man who need not fear a change of light and darkness in his spirit, and who can maintain a constant day in his soul? Therefore, a change must occur in the understanding of a person who is to leave the state of nature. The concepts of divine things present within him must be freed from the shadows surrounding them and presented to the mind in their true form, so that they may take effect.

> If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature. 2 Corinthians 5:17.

To be in Christ means nothing other than being a member of the spiritual body of Christ, a true disciple of the Savior, and a part of His community. Those who attain this privilege are, as the Apostle says, so changed as if they were new creatures. When the Lord created this world, He gave all things their essence and their particular nature. Generally speaking, then, to "create" means as much as giving a thing its nature and essence. And what, then, is a new creature? One must take care not to understand this as if the Spirit of the Lord intended to teach us that another soul is actually infused into us, another life given, a new essence granted in place of the old, or that the old spirit were, as it were, recast and incorporated into the essence of God. The Apostle speaks metaphorically <note>Original: *Gleichniß-Weise*.</note>. He does not claim that the change by which the children of God are distinguished from the unconverted world is actually a change of essence. He only says that it resembles such a change, producing such effects as usually grow out of a change of essence: those who compared the inner stirrings of a sanctified person and his external deeds with his former behavior would find him as noticeably changed as if he were newly created and had received a completely different spirit. This repentance, therefore, whatever it may be, must be that through which the heart of man is cleared, prepared, and arranged for the great change that distinguishes a member of the Kingdom of God from other men; it is that which gives the power for this spiritual transition. John <note>John the Baptist</note>, who was called by God to remove the obstacles from the minds of the fallen and worldly Jews—obstacles that could resist the voice of the Son of God himself—awakened the people to repentance: *Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand* <note>original: "Thut Busse, das Himmelreich ist nahe herbey kommen." Matthew 3:2</note>. He compares himself to the heralds whom Eastern kings used to send ahead when they intended to undertake a journey, to urge their subjects to level and improve the streets and paths so that their procession might continue comfortably and without hindrance <note>John 1:23</note>. This image explains the office of John as well as the nature of the matter he prescribes to the Jews. Those heralds cried out that the paths should be cleaned, widened, and purged of stones, sand, filth, and other things that might delay a traveler. In place of this command, John proclaims repentance. Who can conclude anything else from this comparison but that repentance is that through which all obstacles are removed from the grace that wishes to occupy and change the heart of man—obstacles that could stop or delay its work, its progress, and its path? The Savior himself, whose arrival John announced to the wayward Jews, repeats the command of his forerunner at the beginning of his own teaching ministry.

<column-break/>

Jesus began to preach, says Matthew, and said: *Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand* <note>Matthew 4:17</note>. In the Gospel of Mark, the words of the Redeemer sound somewhat different: *The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent and believe in the gospel* <note>Mark 1:15</note>. The meaning, however, is perfectly identical in both passages. Our Savior undoubtedly presented one and the same thing at different times with different words. He, just like John, gives this as the reason why repentance must be done without delay: because the Kingdom that the Lord intended to establish here among men—the kingdom called the Kingdom of Heaven because the inheritance of heaven and future blessedness is promised to its citizens—would be established in a short time. This reason again reveals to us the nature and power of repentance. No one can enter the kingdom of heaven except he who is entirely changed. This is the pronouncement of Jesus himself <note>Matthew 18:3</note>. This change must happen through a certain means. Yet Jesus prescribes no other means of preparation to those he invites to his kingdom than repentance. In this, therefore, must lie the power we need for the change required of the citizens of the Kingdom of God. The time has come in which the long-promised kingdom of grace shall be planted among you. Its King has already appeared and awaits those who wish to become his subjects. However, the holiness of this King and the promises of this kingdom do not tolerate souls that are stained and filled with blindness and malice. You must first sanctify, change, and purify yourselves if you wish to be accepted. You ask, what means is there for this purification, which is far too difficult for us? I answer: Repent <note>The German term "Buße" carries the weight of both "repentance" (a change of mind) and "penitence" (a sorrow for sin).</note>. This will prepare your heart as it must appear before the face of the all-knowing King.

What Jesus himself did among the Jews, he commanded his witnesses to perform among all nations as he was ready to take his leave of them and was diligent in instructing them in their office: *Thus it is written, and thus it behooved Christ to suffer, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations.* Luke XXIV. 47. Repentance is presented here as the means to the forgiveness of sins and to all the goods for which an innocent and acquitted person can hope. No one can imagine that his sins will be remitted by God if he retains the desire to renew them and the unwisdom of the spirit that produces and maintains this desire. This is a new proof that repentance effects the change of the soul which creates for us a right to the gifts of grace of the Lord! Is it not undeniable that that which brings about the forgiveness of sins must also be the cause of the state of the soul that

<column-break/>

moves the Most High to this remission of debt? The witnesses of Jesus observe this command of their Lord and King most exactly. Peter proves with a divine eloquence in his first speech to the house of Israel that the Jesus whom the unbelief of the Jews crucified like a criminal is the only Savior of mankind. The startled and moved listeners inquire at the end of the speech as to how they might become partakers of the redemption that this Jesus has earned. The Apostle answers briefly: *Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus for the remission of sins.* Acts II. 38. ->### On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.<-

<note>original: "Busse"</note> the words of the Greeks and Hebrews, which we have rendered in our language through the word **Repentance**, initially indicated nothing more than the clear and distinct recognition of one's misery and sins, along with the consequences that arise from this recognition. This meaning was afterward extended by some who wished to express with a single word everything that brings a person to reconciliation with GOD and a holy walk of life. We all have a desire to say much with few words, so that we may more easily and conveniently converse with one another about invisible things. This inclination is, if we do not err, the primary reason why the names of our souls' conceptions have so quickly lost their simple meaning in all languages.

The Second Reminder. What has been noted regarding the word Repentance must also be said of the word Faith. This latter word likewise does not always stand in the same sense within the divine Scriptures. *Faith properly means the divine power of the soul, which is worked through the teaching of the Gospel in the souls of those who convert*, or the means for the transformation of the heart and our condition, which lies in the teaching of the merit of our Redeemer and the promises of God founded upon it. However, one still finds passages of Scripture in which the word "believe" simultaneously designates the transformation of the heart that springs from the word of the Law, or Repentance in a narrower sense. The

<column-break/>

terrified jailer at Philippi <note>A city in Macedonia where Paul was imprisoned; see Acts 16.</note> asks the Apostle Paul for a brief instruction on the way to salvation. The Apostle answers: "Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house." Acts 16:31. Those who would wish to prove from these words that faith without repentance could open heaven would be reproaching the witness of the Lord—who so often insists upon repentance—claiming that he was at odds with himself and demanded now this, then something else, from those who submitted themselves to the Lord. To prevent this, one can do nothing else but concede that under the word "believe," **Repentance** is here also understood. *Thus, the word "believe" and "becoming a believer" must be taken in this way everywhere it stands alone regarding those who allow themselves to be moved to obey the preaching of the Apostles.* The noblest among the Jews at Thessalonica believed: also of the honorable Greek men and wise ones, not a few. Acts 17:11–12. Several pagan men at Athens, and among them Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a judge converted by Paul's speech.</note>, became believers. Acts 17:34. Crispus believed with his whole house and many Corinthians became believers. Acts 18:8. Either the order of salvation established by Christ and the Apostles cannot remain unviolated, or it is necessary to believe of all these people that they first recognized and regretted their sin, and afterward sought in Jesus the remedy for all the anguish and unrest of their conscience.

All languages allow for a part of those things that constitute a single essence and cannot be separated to be named in place of the whole matter. These ways of speaking cause no obscurity in the presentation. Those who are well-instructed immediately envision the whole matter if only something belonging to its concept is mentioned, because they know that the part named stands in an unchangeable connection with the remaining things from which the whole matter is composed. Rather, through such names that indicate only a part of the matter, its image is more clearly illuminated and more strongly awakened in the human understanding than if only the general name were used. Therefore, no wise person will reproach Scripture as a fault for instructing people through such figures of speech about **repentance** as well as other doctrines of **faith**. The meaning of these words is this: In Peter's soul, a clear image of his great misdeed appeared, and it brought forth the most violent terror, fear, sadness, and tears.

The Baptism that was administered to those who accepted Christ was a sign of the repentance and faith that the preaching of the Word had worked within them. The Scripture, therefore, sometimes says nothing more of the new Christians than that they were baptized, and remains silent on the causes for which they were deemed worthy of Baptism. Those who read these passages must add these causes in their thoughts. Our Savior, as He is about to depart, leaves this ordinance to His disciples: **Go forth, and teach all nations, and baptize them.** Matthew 28:19. <column-break/>

The keeper of the prisoners at Philippi <note>Commonly known as the Philippian Jailer.</note> was baptized, and all his household immediately. Acts 16:33. Here again, the sign of the repentance that has occurred stands in place of the repentance itself. This man, along with his household, regretted the sins they had committed and took hold of the Savior whom Paul proclaimed to him. When this had happened, he received through Baptism the assurance that he was an heir of life, and a strengthening of the faith already present within him.

->The Fifth Reminder.<-

Where the fruits and effects of a thing are, there is the thing itself. The rules of all languages therefore permit the fruits of a thing to be put in place of its cause. The Scripture does this as well when it speaks of repentance. It often demands the fruits of repentance in place of repentance itself, because the former cannot follow where the latter has not preceded. The conversion of souls arises from faith, which is ignited in repentance and brings it to perfection. Let no one wonder, then, if in certain places of Scripture, where the word **faith** should stand, he encounters the word **convert** <note>German: *bekehren*</note>. # On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

<columns>
...can properly be called kinds, are linked together within it. Repentance is commonly divided into that in which **God** alone works, and that to which the penitent himself contributes something. <note>original: "Poenitentia seu conversio activa & passiva." Translated as: Repentance or conversion, active and passive.</note> One calls the former "conversion," and the latter "repentance" in its proper sense. The first is an effect of **God** in which the soul of man has no part. The second is a movement stirred up in man through the power of God and can therefore be viewed as something belonging to the man himself. We do not reject this separation of things that manifest themselves in the soul of a penitent. It has its value. It serves especially those who wish to establish themselves firmly in the knowledge of the truth and wish to rebuff certain people who think to advance their incorrect opinions through the ambiguity of a word. However, it will be shown in our explanation that these distinctions are not entirely necessary when one considers repentance only in its connection with <term>godliness<note>original: "Gottfeligkeit." This refers to a life of active piety or "godliness," a central theme in 18th-century Pietist literature.</note></term>. Because of this, we have been moved to believe that we could set them aside. Even without this, these two types of repentance follow one another in such a way that they can only be separated by our thoughts. The movements of the soul, which are properly called "repentance," are inevitably there as soon as the **Lord** works "conversion" within it. And no law of reason forbids us to combine two things in one description which the intellect only separates for clarity. Could all this not excuse us, we would still have sufficient protection in the example of Holy Scripture.

<column-break/>

There are very few passages in which repentance is so distinguished; on the contrary, there are very many that, with the single word "repentance," encompass both what **God** does and what man feels and experiences when he is rescued from the state of nature. The fair-minded and sensible, who might think we could have spared these and other excuses, will bear with us for having taken care of the <note>The "weaker ones" refers to laypeople or those "weak in faith" who might be confused by technical theological jargon or suspicious of new ways of explaining traditional doctrines.</note>weaker ones and those concerned for the truth, and for wanting to cut off every opportunity for suspicion and offense. The entire work of the **Lord**, which is called repentance, divides itself into two main operations. First, the **Lord** clears away the obstacles of nature that resist sanctification. Afterward, the **Lord** gives us new and supernatural powers to begin inner and outer cleansing and sanctification.

and to continue. The person who is to be converted is, according to the words of the Apostle, God’s field-work. <note>The original term "Acker-Werk" refers to 1 Corinthians 3:9, often translated as "God’s husbandry" or "God’s tilled field."</note>

No image is better suited to explain this matter than this one. A field, if it is not to receive the seed in vain, must first be cleaned and purified. How groundless is the hope of a sower who throws his grain among stones, thorns, weeds, and wild plants? A field that has been cleaned must further—if one wishes to rejoice in its fertility—be manured, warmed, and prepared, so that the seed buried within it may be brought to life and can manifest its hidden power.

The hindrances to <term>sanctification<note>original: "Heiligung." In this context, it refers to the ongoing process of a believer becoming more holy and aligned with God's will after their initial conversion.</note></term> lie in all the powers of the soul. <margin>Romans 7:25</margin>

<column-break/>

is not a tyrant who commands without cause, and only gives laws so that his subjects might be tormented. And what have we gained if we have won this much over ourselves or others? The most necessary thing is still missing. The clarity and conviction necessary for a person who is to direct and govern himself in all things according to his thoughts and opinions cannot be awakened. The truth is there; the understanding sees it. It shrinks from denying that the truth is worthy of love and obedience. And why, then, do love and obedience not follow? Why does it stop at merely praising its beauty? It is because the understanding only glimpses it, as it were, from a distance and through a cloud, which it cannot drive away or scatter by its own power. This is an extraordinary hindrance to our improvement and sanctification! If repentance is therefore a means for the transformation of the soul and one’s conduct, then it must remove this cloud and grant the understanding the ability to see and contemplate divine truth closely, clearly, in all its parts, and in its perfect glory and beauty.

The understanding would be able to progress much further in the knowledge of truth if only a longing for it resided in the will. How many difficulties does even a very weak spirit often overcome when it is strengthened and driven in its efforts by the desire of the will? This or that person, of whom we believed they would never rise from the ranks of the ignorant, can often, after a few years, be paired with the learned, the sharp-witted, and the wise.

# On the Nature and Character of Repentance

<columns>
<margin>NB</margin>
It makes us slaves to sin and robs us of all spiritual freedom. It does not allow our intellect to exert its powers to rightly know the spiritual life and the means that lead to it. It creates and maintains in us a loathing for all those things that alone can refresh and satisfy the spirit. It disturbs us in all the activities and exercises of <term>piety<note>original: "Gottseligkeit." A state of living characterized by devotion to God and moral uprightness.</note></term> and drives away good impulses and thoughts through the images of <term>sensual pleasures<note>original: "Wollüste." If <term>repentance<note>original: "Busse." The process of turning away from sin; a fundamental change of mind and heart.</note></term> is a means for the transformation of the heart and conduct, then this great obstacle—this restless and violent love of the world—must be restricted by it and **made subject to the love of God:** Thus, the yoke in which this love harnesses us must be broken therein, and the freedom to choose the good and follow it must be restored.

To this love of the world must be added the unwise and disordered love of ourselves. Who is clean of this poisonous plague? And who does not feel that he would be an entirely different person if he could rid himself of it? The inclination that man bears toward himself, the desire that drives him to seek and maintain his happiness, belongs—so long as it is considered on its own—to the order of the Creator.
<sig>Part I. Section II.</sig>

The human race would be a society of lethargic and lost people who would consume and exhaust themselves through their own laziness if no one had a desire to retain the good that he has and to make himself always happier and more perfect. However, in the state in which we now live, so many stains and faults cling to this inherently good impulse that it can be called a disease rather than a commendable and useful quality of our nature. God has presented us with a twofold kind of happiness toward which we should strive. These we first separate from one another. We direct our desires toward only one. What is even worse? We choose the worst and least kind: the perishable instead of the imperishable, the temporal instead of the eternal. From our earliest youth, we strive to establish ourselves firmly and arrange things in this <term>inn<note>original: "Herberge." If we still occasionally look higher and remind ourselves of the happiness that shall begin when this one ends and never cease, it happens with an unheard-of negligence, and not much differently than how we long for a good that imagination has shown us in a dream. The care we devote to the lowest kind of happiness is, moreover, irrational and perverted. We consist of two parts: a spirit and a body. Both can enjoy a certain happiness in the world. ## On the Nature and Quality of Repentance

<columns>
...that his will receives new desires? We answer: It is true, if it is understood as the Spirit of God himself has explained it. The rules of language allow us to say of those who are made fit to use their natural power well, that they receive a new power. One gives credit to a physician who, through his art, frees an eye from a cataract <note>original: "Staar"</note> or other defects, saying that he has given the eye a new power. It can be said of a prisoner whose dark dungeon is illuminated by a light, that a new ability has been communicated to his eyes through this light. And yet everyone knows that neither the physician who heals the sick eye, nor the jailer who carries the light into the dungeon, grants the sick person and the prisoner the ability to see, but rather they only remove the obstacles which prevented these unfortunate ones from making use of this power. With the same right, one can say of an intellect to which a pure and clear knowledge of the truth—which it could not provide for itself—has been brought, that it has its teacher to thank for a power that it previously lacked. It is not forbidden to attribute new desires to those who, with their natural inclinations, fall upon other things which they previously did not regard. He who lets the desire for wealth go, and instead makes honor and high esteem the goal of his wishes, actually adopts no new desire. He loved at the time when he desired goods; and he does just the same after it seemed more advisable to him to strive for honor. His love has only chosen another object <note>original: "Vorwurf" - in this context, it refers to the object or aim of one's attention, not a modern "reproach."</note>.

<column-break/>

And yet one does not speak wrongly when one says of such a person that a new desire reigns within him. An honest servant <note>term: Knecht - a laborer or servant</note> who is moved by his master to a higher position retains the old desire to act faithfully and to observe his duty. He satisfies this desire only in another way. He proves it through new works and business. And yet no one forbids us from describing this promoted servant as a person who has cast off his old inclinations and is driven by new impulses. What then hinders us from saying of those whom the Spirit of the Lord has moved through the power of truth—so that they no longer strive after that which is on the earth, but after that which is above (*Colossians 3:2*)—what hinders us from saying of these people that they have received new desires and have put off the old?

This explanation will be able to serve more than one purpose. It will be useful to those who think nothing certain or definite of the changes which grace effects in us through repentance <term>Busse - repentance or penance</term>, and who tie their faith to words they cannot explain. A person of this sort is overwhelmed by the first adversary and falls now to this side, now to that, as he is pulled by ignorant or crafty people. It will repel the bold blasphemers who reproach us, saying that our teachers speak of conversion <term>Bekehrung - conversion</term> as unintelligibly as they do absurdly, and that daily experience refutes our great promises of the power of enlightenment and rebirth. If there dwelt in these arrogant ones a sincere desire to rightly know <note>The text cuts off here, continuing to the next page with "know".</note>

# The First Principal Section

<columns>
...to learn <note>original: "nen zu lernen"; the suffix of 'beginnen' (to begin) from the previous page</note>, and if they took the time and patience to ask people who are experienced in the Scripture and understand what they believe, they would soon learn, to their great astonishment, that they have not been attacking the doctrine of Christians, but rather their own false imaginings of this doctrine. It <note>The doctrine of Repentance</note> will correct those who persuade themselves as if God, in **repentance**, performed such a work of **omnipotence** as He did then, when He let all things come into being out of nothing; imagining that He overturns the essence of our souls and increases every faculty with certain additions, that He creates new powers in our spirit and partially destroys the old, innate ones. If this were the opinion of Christians, then we would indeed have to fear those who threaten us with the evidence of experience <note>i.e., critics who argue that humans don't physically or psychologically change their basic nature upon conversion</note>. It will finally convict those of error who dare to assert that the **Lord** takes the spirit of people who are being converted into His own essence in an incomprehensible way and equips it with His own perfections and attributes. That is to say, making "little gods" out of converted Christians. And if those who are devoted to this delusion understood their supposed rights, they would surely demand a kind of worship from other people who do not wish to open their heart to the Lord. What does a creature not deserve who has, as it were, lost its nature and been drawn into God?

The gifts and attributes that are bestowed upon man in repentance, so that he can achieve internal and external holiness, we do not wish to recount and describe extensively here. This will happen in the following sections. And here we will

<column-break/>

therefore be able to get by with few words. If the natural blindness of our spirit is the greatest obstacle to our improvement, then it is certain that a person who is to dedicate himself to the Lord must recognize the truth purely and clearly. A light must rise in the understanding that convinces just as much as it enlivens. If the will is sluggish in approaching the truth because it is afraid that its light might disturb its peace and pleasure, then it is necessary that this sluggishness be transformed into a desire for learning and diligence. This happens through the very same light which illuminates the understanding. If it is naturally vexing and repugnant to us to hear the will of the Lord because innate lusts cling to earthly and transitory things, then we will never turn back and seek the Lord unless a desire and love for things that are eternal, imperishable, and truly good is awakened in us. If we are foolish worshippers of ourselves, who cast ourselves down by wanting to exalt ourselves above everything, then we must perish unless we learn to value ourselves rightly and condemn the immoderate veneration of ourselves. If we possess a natural inability to perform what is good, then we will never break forth from the darkness of ruin unless we are clothed with a power to bend our will under the will of the Lord and to sacrifice the desires of nature to the recognized truth and justice. **Repentance** <term>Busse: in this context, the word implies a total "change of mind" or transformation of the inner life rather than just a feeling of regret</term> is the means by which man is prepared and made fit for true sanctification. Once this is established, then all these gifts and perfections must be worked and brought about within us through it.

## §. III.

The beginning of this general concept of repentance—wherein the same is called an effect, or a **work of God** <note>The author uses 'work' (Werk) and 'effect' (Wirkung) to emphasize that repentance is something performed upon the human soul by a higher power, rather than a self-generated change.</note>—is already proven by the following description of this effect itself. Is it possible that a human being, who is by nature as we are, could free themselves from the obstacles that keep them from **God** and endow themselves with light, wisdom, order, and obedience through their own powers? It is easier to imagine a sick person making themselves healthy, or a blind person giving themselves sight without any help, than such a person as we are sanctifying and purifying themselves. (Ephesians 2:1; Colossians 2:13). And if it is proven that the power by which we are converted cannot lie within ourselves, to whom else but **God** can we attribute this great work? The Scripture states this most clearly in many places. (5th Book of Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> 29:4; Psalm 51:12; Jeremiah 31:18, 34; Hosea 6:5; 2 Timothy 2:25, 26; Ephesians 2:5; Philippians 2:13).

If so, we would not be what we are, and the measure of our powers would have to be depicted incorrectly in Scripture. From God? Then God will ultimately be the one whom the saints and the converted must praise for their change and conversion. And Scripture does not allow us to doubt this in the least. # The First Main Chapter

The Spirit of God gives the name of "fools" <note>German: *Thoren*. In 18th-century theological German, a "fool" is not just someone lacking intelligence, but someone morally and spiritually blind.</note> to sinners and the disobedient. This word expresses all the wicked qualities that defile their souls. (Proverbs 10:20, 12:15, 16). On the contrary, the sanctified are called "understanding." This name, in turn, encompasses everything that adorns the soul of a godly person and makes it pleasing to God. Moses, in the following text, explained the concept we must form of this "understanding heart" and specifically named the parts belonging to it. The first is an **enlightened intellect**, the second an **obedient will**. The former is indicated by "eyes that can see," the latter by "ears that hear." Those familiar with the writing style of the Holy Scriptures will not dispute this explanation. The matter itself shows that Moses is speaking metaphorically. For what else can the eyes he mentions be but the intellect? And what could the ears signify, if the other power of the soul—the will—is not meant by them? The Scripture compares human intellect with the eyes of the body in so many places that we can spare the effort of citing them. Therefore, healthy "eyes of the mind," or eyes that see, can indicate nothing else here than an intellect that recognizes the truth purely and vividly. "Hearing" is, in many places in the Holy Books, synonymous with "obeying." Consequently, when ears are mentioned in a spiritual sense, and it is added that they are "ears that hear," it is clear enough that the subject is the inclination to obey and to do the will of God.

<column-break/>

All the prophets of the Old Covenant agree with this testimony of Moses. David, in the anguish of soul stirred by the wrath of the Lord over his transgressions, desired that he might never again violate the covenant with God from that time forward. He saw, in this regard, that the root of sin lay within his soul. From this, he concluded that he would always remain in danger of displeasing the Lord through disobedience if this root were not killed and the heart cleansed of it. And who is it that could make it barren and stifle it? Grace, which enlightened him toward **repentance** <term>Busse: In this context, it refers to the total internal turning of the soul toward God, rather than just an outward act of penance.</term>, and experience join together to assure him that he can expect nothing from his own strength. He therefore seeks help from the Lord and prays that He might cleanse the foundation of his corrupted soul and uproot the weeds that might sprout and spread at the slightest opportunity.
> Create in me, O God, a clean heart, and give me a new, steadfast spirit. (Psalm 51:12).

The meaning is: whether they might perhaps one day grant their soul entry to the grace that wants to change and sanctify them. Whether perhaps one day the

<column-break/>

"Giving" here must mean either: *being able to give*, or: *willing to give*. Whoever is able to give and does not give must either be prevented from sharing his treasures or not be inclined to enrich others. The latter meaning is unbefitting of the holiness and love of God. Reason and revelation rebel if we try to imagine God as a being who has no pleasure, no will, and no desire to save certain people whom He is able to save. Therefore, the former meaning alone must hold true. What means does the Lord use to give repentance and soften the heart? None other, the Apostle answers, than the **Word of Truth**, which He has allowed to be partly repeated and partly more clearly proclaimed through Jesus and the Apostles. The servants of the Lord are therefore exhorted not to grow weary in their instruction of sinners and the stubborn, so that the way to their souls may not be closed to God. By this explanation, we provide a guide for those who wish to use and weigh the passages of Scripture—whereby the truths of faith are established—in such a way that neither they nor others may have any grounded doubt remaining regarding their true meaning.

His **Omnipotence** knows neither what we call effort and labor, nor what is called resistance and hindrance. <meta>This page continues the argument regarding how God works within the human heart. The author is transitioning from the debate over whether repentance is purely a work of human reason to explaining why God, in His wisdom, chooses to work through the natural faculties of the human soul rather than through raw, overwhelming power.</meta>

# ->Of the Nature and Character of Repentance.<-

In all cases and circumstances, the Lord acts according to a rule. His power could, in a single moment, accomplish everything that pleases Him, if it did not have an accompanying attribute that cannot permit the laws He has made to be destroyed, nor allow confusion to be introduced in place of the order we so admire. In the work of **conversion**, the Lord deals with creatures to whom, according to His wisdom, He has granted a power to recognize the **truth** and to arrange their conclusions and counsels according to that recognized truth. His wisdom and justice demand that He deal with every being in a manner consistent with the nature He has given it. What would it be if He made His will alone the measuring-stick of His actions and took now this path, now that, without seeing whether it harmonized with the nature of things? Would this not be, as it were, a silent punishment of Himself? Would His works not bear witness against His own perfection? Would He not, in a certain way, accuse Himself before the eyes of the world of having established the arrangement of things we see, and the distribution of various gifts and qualities, without ground or cause? Would His power not contradict His wisdom? From this, it is indisputably clear that the Lord cannot give **repentance** <note>original: "Busse." In this theological context, it refers to a transformative "change of mind" or "turning back" to God.</note> to mankind through a mere pull of His power that nothing can withstand. Outside of Him, there is nothing that could prevent or stop Him from changing and forming our will all at once, so that it might maintain order in its desires and take away all power from the stubborn movements of the blood, the **spirits**, and the **vital humors** <note>original: "Geister und der Lebens-Säfte." This refers to the early modern medical understanding of physiology, where "animal spirits" and bodily fluids (humors) were believed to govern physical impulses and emotional states.</note> to disturb its conclusions.

<column-break/>

However, within His essence are certain perfections that set boundaries for His power in this matter. His holiness, His wisdom, and His justice require that He guide and convert human beings in a manner that is consistent with the nature and qualities of their souls. A soul is a creature that the Lord has made capable of grasping the truth, of distinguishing the false from the true, and of holding as good and useful that which is provided with clear marks of truth. It is a creature into which the Lord has placed an invincible drive toward perfection and **bliss** <note>original: "Glückseligkeit." Often translated as happiness, but in a religious context, it implies the ultimate state of joy in God's presence.</note>, and which is therefore always ready to decide upon and carry out that which presents itself to its understanding as a certain means to bliss and perfection. What must happen if a being so constituted is to be won over—in a way that agrees with its nature—to renounce its ordinary inclinations and to swear eternal obedience to a law to which it was previously averse? We are certain that no rational person will answer differently than we do: Such a being must be improved through the power of truth, through a pure and certain conviction of the understanding, and through a lively recognition that its true welfare requires a change of its will and conduct. And we conclude from this that the Lord, who always acts wisely and can never undertake anything that is at odds with His great perfections, must perform the work of repentance through the truth and through the enlightenment of the understanding.

Reason gives us, as anyone can see, this proof. Should anyone fear to trust it completely, all of Revelation stands ready to grant it value and authority. Is there a single example of **conversion** <note>original: "Bekehrung"</note> to be found in the Old or New Testament that was accomplished by anything other than the strength and the light of Divine Truth? The earliest times of the Church of the New Covenant show us all kinds of people who were brought to faith in a sudden, swift, and extraordinary manner. And in this entire multitude, not one can be seen whom the Lord drew to Himself through a blind coercion; not one whom the Truth did not compel to confess Jesus. The miracles, by which Jesus and His witnesses proved their Divine mission, did not conquer the disobedience of the Jews and heathens: the **Truth**, which they proclaimed, did so. The miracles only dispelled the blindness, the inattention, and the natural resistance of the nations, which had prevented the Truth from proving its strength upon their souls. The Spirit of God has remained silent regarding the things that occurred with this tax collector before Jesus called him. It is more than probable that he was already prepared and nearly won over by the Truth before the Savior commanded him to leave his place. At times it pleased Him to reveal Himself to Abraham, Moses, and other prophets in the first manner. At other times, He had that which the people should know placed upon tablets or composed in writings. He acted in the same way at the beginning of the **New Covenant**. And what would it cost Him if He wished to proceed no differently until the end of the world? We will allow the name of a prophet to those who, in addition to the three specified characteristics, are equipped with these that we have added. And in what part of Christian history, which stretches from the second century to our times, can people be seen who have passed themselves off as prophets and were of such a character? We have reviewed the host of people who have either assumed this dignity for themselves or received it from their friends and admirers. We have specifically considered one after another those who have presented themselves among us as messengers of **God** to men since the time of **Luther**. And yet, none have been found among them to whom we could not challenge this honor for valid reasons. We see that many among them were not evil-minded and carefully avoided the vices that they punished in others in the name of the **Lord**. We see that others burned with a true zeal

<column-break/>

to stop the ruin of those who call themselves **Christians** without cause, and who recognized the causes of the decay of **godliness** <term>Gottseligkeit: a state of living in a way that is pleasing to God; true piety</term> and wanted to root them out. We acknowledge that some can be acquitted of all suspicion of sinful deceit and truly believed themselves to be, without malice, what they claimed to be. And we wish that some of this kind had been treated more mildly and gently in the past and not mixed in with the deceivers and the false. But we see just as certainly and clearly that these people, who wanted to deceive no one, were themselves unhappily deceived. We see that their imagination was strong and their understanding much too weak to resist its attacks. Their prophecies and history bear witness against them. Yet it can be overturned in another way. <note>The following sentence is underlined in red ink in the original</note> It is thought that **God**, because of the complacency <note>original: *Sicherheit*, implying a state of false spiritual security or overconfidence</note> and wickedness of men, must occasionally add extraordinary teachers to the ordinary ones. **Jesus** himself denies this and says that the ordinary ministers of truth can accomplish everything that is in accordance with **God's** intentions. People who could not be healed by the ordinary means of grace would be just as little set right by an extraordinary one. If they hear not **Moses** and the **Prophets**, neither will they believe, though one rose from the dead. Do we act wrongly if we draw this conclusion from these words of the **Lord**: If the writings of the **Prophets** and **Apostles**, which are daily read and preached among us, cannot move the heart of sinners, then neither will any new **Prophets** and extraordinary messengers of **God** do so. A raised dead man is without doubt a far greater witness than a **Prophet**. Will he then accomplish what the other cannot do? # On the Nature and Character of Repentance.
## Part I. Section II.

->H<-

So it must follow that the written Word—the word left behind by the Prophets and Apostles of the **Lord**—is the only means of repentance <term>Busse; a term encompassing both the internal act of repenting and the outward turning toward God</term> and conversion. How this teaching is to be understood will already be known to those who have read what preceded. A word is actually nothing more than a sign by which a concept of the understanding is indicated. In this sense, a word is distinct from its meaning and the concept connected to it. We do not use the name "Word" in this manner when we say that the Word of **God** converts, sanctifies, and regenerates mankind. Our opinion is not that the words of Scripture, insofar as they are nothing but words or signs of thoughts, change and purify the heart. And we wonder not a little that some, who think themselves sharp-sighted enough to despise the faith of all Christians, understand us so, or rather *wish* to understand us so. We are accused without hesitation of viewing the words of Scripture as a magic song <note>original: *Zauber-Lied*, referring to an incantation or spell</note>, and of being so bold as to pretend that the names, syllables, and letters of which they consist could accomplish the same thing in the minds of men as certain foreign and barbaric words were able to do among the spirits, according to the opinion of the ancient Egyptians and Syrians. Among these peoples, deceivers were found who persuaded the light-minded commoners that evil spirits feared the sound and noise of certain words and, as soon as they heard them, fled in terror. And if we believed what is attributed to us—if we taught that **Satan**, who dwells in the soul of man, or the innate wickedness, must take flight

<column-break/>

and vacate the heart when someone pronounces some words of Scripture with emphasis—then we would be compared with these supposed magicians not without cause. However, if there is anyone among us who thinks so absurdly and insanely and will not allow themselves to be corrected by reason, then they are not a healthy member of our congregation. We do not wish to deny that some Christians in older times entertained something of such a foolish delusion. And if we were to search, we might perhaps still find various traces of it in the Roman Church and in the Eastern congregations. We are completely clear of it. We do not instruct our people that it is the *words* of Scripture, but rather the *teachings*, the *divine truths*, the *divinely inspired and revealed wisdom*—which is presented through the words as signs and lies beneath them—that establishes the change in souls which we call repentance and conversion. The letters and words of which the Law consists do not crush the sinner’s heart. The words of which the promises of grace are joined together do not heal the wounds that the Law has struck. Rather, the commandments and threats of the Law itself, and the promises made known through the words, perform this.

If the serene and pure spirit were still present, which was imparted to man by the Author of his life at Creation; if there were in us...

They may prove things correctly. Yet, they live impurely and, as it were, refute through their conduct the teaching that they publicly profess. We would not be able to face this difficulty if we claimed that truth, as truth—viewed alone and by itself—could change and improve mankind. We know just as surely from experience as from the **Scripture** that a natural man <note>original: *natürlicher Mensch*; a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:14, describing a person acting on human instinct without the Holy Spirit</note> can neither perceive the teachings of the Spirit of **God** nor apply them to his conversion. # The First Principal Chapter

<columns>
[whi]ch the power that must convert us is to be found in our own souls, Scripture, reason, and experience oppose with equal strength. We do not wish to use the arguments now that we could take from those sources. It will be enough to uncover from history the impure origin of the so-called **internal word** <note>The "internal word" (innerliches Wort) refers to a mystical belief that God's primary communication happens directly within the human soul, sometimes seen as superior to the written Bible.</note>. What will people say when they see that this famous word grew out of an absurd and long-rejected explanation of the doctrine of the **Trinity**, which only pleased those teachers of the early ages who wanted to know more than God has allowed us to know? What will people say when they learn that the doctrine itself, which gave birth to this word, did not long withstand the reproaches of its adversaries, and would undoubtedly have pulled its untimely fruit down into ruin with it, if some good-hearted and simple people, who knew nothing of its lineage and origin, had not taken it up? Will this not be just as good as a thorough refutation of this so strongly defended and just as strongly contested word, to which many attribute the enlightenment of the whole world? What can one think of a doctrine that must be ashamed of its origin? We want to show this as briefly as possible. Those who demand a scholarly proof of the things we wish to present shall be served at another time.

In the second century after the birth of our Savior, the principle was accepted here and there among Christians as certain and established—the same principle from which **Plato** derived his entire wisdom—

<column-break/>

that man is, as it were, a brief summary, a sketch, an image of God and the world. The body of man is, in the opinion of this wise man, the **small world** <note>original: *die kleine Welt*; also known by the Greek term *microcosmos*. It is the idea that the human body contains all the elements of the universe.</note>. And whoever, therefore, wishes to understand the nature of the visible world, its arrangement, its connection, and its order in general, and to judge it sensibly, must learn to know himself and the natural arrangement and condition of his own body. That which happens and takes place in the great world has been represented in the body as if in an extract, or as if in a mirror. The soul of man is the image of God. To speak more clearly: just as the body is a small world, so the spirit of man is a **small God** <note>original: *kleiner GOtt*; sometimes called *microtheos*. This suggests the human mind reflects the divine mind in miniature.</note>, a being in which everything is pulled together briefly and narrowly that is spread out more perfectly, grandly, and extensively in God and His nature. From this seemingly poor and small, but in fact fertile ground, flows everything that Plato wanted to teach us about God and the world. Man is his key, with which he wants to unlock all the secrets of nature and the divine essence. And if one takes this single rule away from his wisdom: **He who truly knows man, also knows God and the world**, then everything he presents with so much eloquence and confidence is mere chatter without life or proof, a fleeting shadow in which no rational person will find pleasure. How much unnecessary effort could the mighty army of his interpreters, who are much darker than he himself, have saved if they had thought of this simple sentence in their explanations? # Of the Nature and Quality of Repentance.
<note>The header "Busse" (Repentance/Penance) appears here, though the text continues to discuss the nature of the soul. In 18th-century theological works, the nature of the soul was often considered the necessary foundation for understanding how a person "turns back" to God.</note>

<columns>
...about the writings of the first Fathers just as much light as it spreads over the works of Plato, let us not linger. Our purpose allows us nothing more than to note in few words the consequences he drew from the similarity between God and our souls.

Whoever wants to know what **GOD** is, says Plato, must learn to know himself and his spirit. And on what is this rule grounded? On the essence and nature of the soul. Careful observation of souls will teach everyone that they have nothing to do with matter, that the soul is something special that can exist by itself—a being that has its own life and acts through itself. If this is certain, then it is also clear that it is from **GOD**, that it belongs to **GOD**, and that it has arisen from the nature of **GOD** himself. There are no more than two general sources of all things: **GOD** and **Matter**. That the soul does not belong to the latter is indisputable, and is proven by everything that experience daily makes known to us about it. It must therefore be a part, a birth, a child, an *outflow* <note>original: "Ausfluß"—often translated in philosophical contexts as "emanation," the idea that the soul flows out of the divine substance.</note> of **GOD**. What is born of **GOD** must be similar to him. All things provided with a **generative power** bring such creatures to light that bear the image of their parents. Can one think otherwise of **GOD**, if one wishes to remain rational? And would it not be absurd to believe that humans and animals beget other humans and animals that resemble them in all parts, and yet **GOD**, on the other hand, has produced things of a completely foreign kind and nature? Should that which is otherwise so correct and certain be false here: that the effect

<column-break/>

testifies to its cause and the fruit bears witness to the quality of the trunk? If souls come from **GOD**, they must represent the one to whom they owe their essence and origin, and be, as it were, his extract. Therefore, whoever wants to know **GOD** must learn to know his soul. What is in his spirit must be in the Father and origin of all spirits in a far greater and more perfect way.

In our spirit is a natural life, a power to move of itself. No earthly thing can come into motion unless it is driven by another and lifted out of its rest. One thing lives and moves through another. Our soul does not need such external means for its movements. It acts through its own power. It moves without a foreign impulse. This is a sign that it has its own and natural life within itself. And this is also a proof that it cannot die. In our spirit is, as it were, a space in which countless images and concepts are gathered and mixed together. This army of so many images and concepts has a commander who governs it, who orders it, and who arranges it for the best of the whole person. This is called the **Understanding** <term>Verstand: the faculty of the mind that organizes sensory data and logical thoughts</term>. There is a power in our souls to assemble the manifold images of things that dwell within it, and to separate them from one another. And this happens in the souls that are masters of themselves, according to eternal and immutable laws that **GOD** himself cannot abolish. Finally, there is in our soul a power [to arrange] the patterns of concepts which [are] in the understanding...

All this must also be found in the first cause of all things <note>A common philosophical term for God as the "Prime Mover" or origin of existence.</note>, because the same is mirrored in our spirit. **GOD** thus has an independent life—a life that no one has given him and no one can take away. There is in him an infinite place that encompasses all images and representations that are only possible. There is in him an understanding to govern and arrange these representations according to the unchangeable laws of truth, justice, and beauty. There is in him a power or a spirit through which he executes what his understanding has found to be good. This spirit needs something in which it can work and labor. Just as the soul of man requires a body, so he needs a certain substance <note>original: "Zeuges"—referring here to the raw material of the universe.</note> with which he can unite to carry out his counsel. There is thus an eternal matter, and **GOD** makes use of it just as man uses his body. He has a power to govern and direct matter, just as we have a faculty to move our body. This is the so-famed **Trinity** of **Plato**, which so many wish to explain, and so few can explain. This man, who lacked no gift of nature less than a lively and fiery imagination, has through it adorned and elevated his style of writing much more than is usually done by those who are full of reflection and who wish to become known in the

<column-break/>

land of invisible things <note>The realm of metaphysics and abstract philosophy.</note>. He speaks, therefore, of these three attributes—which he distinguishes in **GOD** and in the soul of man—no differently than if he were speaking of three special natures or persons. There are few who know how to separate this ornament of his writing style from his true meaning. From this the opinion has arisen as if his doctrine of **GOD** were related to the faith of the Christians: as if he had made just such a separation in the Godhead as we must make if we wish to trust the pronouncement of the Spirit of **GOD** in the Scripture: as if he had heard something of the three persons in **GOD** in a school of the Jews and had either not dared to present this truth clearly, or had understood it poorly and indistinctly.

This opinion has found followers all the more easily in modern times because it was seen that the scholars of the earliest Christians believed this and, as we have already considered, allowed themselves to accept this fundamental principle of **Plato** with all its consequences to the extent that they explained the doctrine of the Scripture concerning **GOD** from it. We say with diligence: the *scholars* of the Christians. One cannot attribute to the whole community of Christians what was believed and often written down carelessly enough by the few scholars among them whose writings are still extant. The faith of most Christians was simple and encompassed nothing more than what is presented in the Scripture with clear words. Here and there a school-philosopher <note>original: "Schul-Weiser"—meaning a scholastic or academic philosopher.</note> arose who allowed himself to long for giving a human addition to the simplicity of revelation, and the words of the Holy Spirit...

A human being begets and, as it were, gives birth to his reason <term>Vernunft: the faculty of logical thought and understanding</term> when he gathers his concepts and thoughts together and brings them forth through intelligible words and signs. He then brings the children of his soul to the light and gives life to his mental representations. This is what God did when He begat the Son and gave birth to Him from Himself. The Son is the Reason and Wisdom of God—that which the intellect is in the human soul. God brought forth this inner Word from the depths <note>original: "Abgrunde"—literally the abyss or the profound, bottomless nature of God</note> of His essence from eternity, spoke it, and, so to speak, distinguished it from His nature. And so that humanity might perceive and hear it, He clothed it in time with a body and provided it with the instruments of speech. This distinction, this birth, this pronouncing of the Word does not abolish the unity of the Father and the Son. A person who presents the images of his intellect to others, or composes them in a writing, is not actually separated from

<column-break/>

All of this is all the more certain because Plato himself mentions a King or Father, a Son of this King, and a Spirit.

We refrain from judging this particular doctrine. We only wish to show that the inner Word, which is meant to live and move in the souls of all people, is a fruit of the same. And how easily will we be able to do this? The human spirit is an extract, a small concept, a mirror of the Godhead, because it originates from God. Therefore, what is in God is, in a certain measure, in our soul; and what is in our soul is in God. In God are immutable concepts of good and evil, eternal laws of truth, holiness, and justice. Our soul, whose father is God Himself, must therefore also be provided with these, as far as its nature permits. In God is a faculty to represent these unchangeable and eternal concepts to Himself, and to connect them with one another or separate them from one another—in a word, an intellect. It is a foreign fruit; we mean to say, an imagination which some Christians, enamored with worldly wisdom, have fetched from a human school and thoughtlessly transplanted into the field of the Lord's congregation. The first inventors of it meant nothing other than natural truth, the first basic teachings of wisdom and virtue, and at the same time the power of the human soul to rightly use these truths which are implanted and lie within it. These they have named Christ, the Word of the soul, the Son of God, because they imagined, out of an excessive veneration of Greek science, that what *Plato* calls the Son of God is our Savior and Redeemer, and that this second person of the Godhead is therefore nothing but the Reason and Wisdom of God. <column-break/>

# The First Principal Section

...teachers <note>The OCR text begins with "ren," likely completing "Lehrern" (teachers).</note> had so emphatically assured, better than their adversaries, noticed that their answer would no longer hold weight once the adversaries had read the books of the New Testament for themselves.

In the great disputes among Christians concerning the Trinity <note>original: *Dreyeinigkeit*</note>, which Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336) was a priest in Alexandria who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, distinct from and subordinate to God the Father.</note> stirred up in the fourth century, the explanation of this doctrine—from which the "Inner Word" had emerged—lost the prestige it had previously enjoyed. Arius or his followers sought to use this doctrine to their own advantage and appealed to the great Origen, who had presented and developed it most skillfully and clearly. Those who wished to suppress his party opposed this undertaking in two ways. Some, in order to save the truth, became accusers of Origen and charged him with great and significant errors. Others believed that the truth must be cared for in such a way that the honor of this highly deserving man remained intact; they therefore denied that he had ever taught what the Arians claimed to find in his writings. Both the former and the latter admitted that Scripture contradicted those who interpreted the distinction of the Persons in God in the manner we have shown above. Consequently, both parties united to overthow the previously popular concept of the Trinity and to denounce it as a distortion of Divine truth. Therefore, the "Inner Word," which is a necessary consequence of this concept, had to fall at the same time and be stripped of all its dignity. After this period, it can be seen either not at all, or only in a completely disguised and transformed state, in the books

<column-break/>

of those who present Divine truth rationally and, in particular, who wish to protect the doctrine of the three Persons in God against all the artful tricks of the Arians, the Sabellians <note>Followers of Sabellius (3rd century), who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely three different "modes" or "masks" of a single God.</note>, and other inquisitive teachers. Origen was publicly condemned as a corrupter of the wisdom that God revealed through Christ, and teachers and students were forbidden from reading his writings. Once this had happened, who would have dared to praise the "Inner Word" in the schools or in writings, since it was nowhere more clearly portrayed than in the books of Origen? Furthermore, it was no longer needed as much as in previous times. The heathens <note>original: *Heyden*; refers to practitioners of traditional Greco-Roman religions.</note> could no longer cause unrest for the Christians once the Emperors themselves confessed Christ. Thus, one was spared the effort of resolving their inquiry through an ingenious detour: namely, the question of what had become of their ancestors who knew nothing of Christ. Instead, all pretense was cast aside, and they were told plainly to their faces that all their great men had gone into the kingdom of Satan, and that their descendants would follow them and never see the light if they departed from this world without faith in Christ.

Under these circumstances, the "Inner Word" would have perished entirely had there not been people found among the Christians who were enemies of all "school-wisdom" <note>original: *Schul-Weißheit*; refers to formal academic or scholastic theology.</note> and who wished to learn the way to salvation not through books and rational investigations, but through a perpetual devotion and a withdrawal of the spirit from all visible things. Thus, he was read incessantly among the monks and hermits: his teachings were approved: and, among other things, the **Inner Word**, or the Christ who is in all men, was received with willing hearts. It is indisputable that very few of these people, and perhaps none among them, grasped or understood the entire doctrine of this man, along with its causes and intentions. To do so requires far more erudition, far more knowledge of the propositions of Plato <note>original: *Platonis*. Plato’s philosophy, particularly regarding the soul, heavily influenced early Christian mystical thought.</note> and his later students, far more information about the state of the church in the second and third centuries and about the objections with which the heathens attacked the doctrine of Christ at that time, and far more discernment and reflection than these good brothers had or wished to acquire. ### On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

We do not hesitate to claim that those who have presented the workings of grace in the souls of men through images taken from the birth, life, and suffering of the Redeemer would have performed greater service to piety and truth if they had said no more than what they found in the Holy Scripture. And we have such a good opinion of their integrity and love for the truth that we do not doubt they would have spoken differently had they known the ground from which such manners of speaking arose, and had they read the books of certain people—who allow themselves to be led astray by their own imagination—with more caution. Those who nevertheless wish to continue speaking as these people do must, if they do not wish to lose their reputation for wisdom, first settle this question within themselves: Is a man who loves pure and true <term>piety</term> <note>German: "Gottseligkeit", referring to a lived, heartfelt devotion</note> permitted to express his thoughts and teachings through such signs and images? These are images that can give the imagination of the untrained and simple-minded an opportunity to wander; they have already been misused countless times and applied against the pure service of God as confirmed in the Scriptures; and perhaps they would never have been devised or introduced if some of the ancient Christians had not attached altogether too much value to <term>heathen wisdom</term> <note>A reference to Greek philosophy, particularly Neoplatonism</note>. It is time for us to conclude our history of the so-called "Inner Word." For those who have read it with deliberation, it will provide occasion for all sorts of thoughts and reveal the causes of various events, manners of speaking, and opinions that have caused great movements and disputes. If the Son of God, or the second person in the Godhead, is the same as the Reason of God, then the rest is also correct, which the ancients added to this opinion: I mean to say, then the first person, or the Father, is the same as Life, and the third person is the same as the power and effect of God in his creatures. Aside from these attributes, there is nothing in God that could be called the Father or the Spirit. The Father is therefore, as Origen and his followers said, in all things that have life and being. Since Jesus calls his Word a seed, or compares it to a seed, he undoubtedly teaches that a power is hidden within the Word to produce spiritual fruits in the souls of men. The power to bring forth fruit always lies within the seed and is not first communicated to it only when it has been scattered by the farmer into the bosom of the earth. The Savior says that his teaching is like the seed. Does this not mean a rejection of those who consider the truth of the Lord to be empty and fruitless until the heart of man has opened itself to receive it, or who believe that the union of the Spirit of God with the Word does not happen until the human being himself wishes and longs for it? We do not expect that a sensible person will ask: how can that which Jesus says of the Word, which he himself and the Apostles presented to the world, be applied to the Word that is composed in writing? Anyone who reflects that the Word which has been written down is distinguished from that which was formerly preached by nothing other than the mode of presentation; anyone who considers that the mode of presentation can neither give nor take anything from the truth itself; anyone who remembers that he who speaks a truth conveys his thoughts to others through the very same signs by which another, who puts it on paper, explains his meaning, will easily [overcome] <note>The sentence is completed by the catchword on the next page</note> this doubt.

To understand this more quickly, imagine two doctors: one suggests a healing remedy to the patient orally, the other presents the very same remedy in writing. What would the medicine lose of its intrinsic power and utility simply because of this difference in how it was proposed? Will the person who follows the written prescription not find health just as surely as the one who observed the doctor’s oral advice? And why then should the teaching and truth of God, which alone can improve and sanctify our souls, have less ability and effect—less power and impact—when it is brought to the understanding through visible signs and strokes <note>meaning the written characters of the alphabet</note> than when it is conveyed through the sounds and vibrations of the air? The field only provides the seed with the opportunity to express its fertility. According to this common way of speaking, our Savior says: those people who have received the Word with a willing soul bring forth fruit. # The First Main Chapter

[God] gives birth to man anew <note>original: "Wiedergeburt." Therefore, what is attributed to the Word by the Apostle must also be understood as those truths which we read in the Scriptures and hear from the mouths of the ministers of the Most High. With this explanation, we have prevented all doubts and objections that might prevent anyone from accepting our interpretation as certain. Now the words themselves can be explained without offense.

The Apostle attributes to the Word, or the divine truth which he and his fellow workers proclaimed to the world, a power to give birth to men anew. <column-break/>

ployed. The Word is a seed: it is not a perishable, but an imperishable seed. The seed has an internal life, a hidden power to bring forth fruit from itself. If the Word is like a seed, then it must likewise be provided with an internal life and a strength to produce fruit. The life of a natural seed can be smothered. It can fall into a poorly prepared land. And this field can be to blame for the seed rotting and perishing. It can be killed by all sorts of other accidents and afterwards, when it is sown, deceive the hope of the farmer. It is a perishable seed—a seed whose natural power can be taken away. In this respect, the Word of the Lord does not resemble such a seed. It is an imperishable seed. It can be hindered from bringing forth fruit. An impure and ill-prepared heart can hold back its power. Disorderly desires can inhibit its fertility. However, no violence, no accident, and no cunning can rob it of the life it has from God. If the field is lost through an earthquake, through a flood, or through other changes in the world, then its seed is perished and lost along with it. This does not happen to the Word of the Lord. Men fall down and die. The Word that dwelt in their souls does not die. It accompanies them into eternity: and it finds at all times a new land in the world again, upon which it can grow with its power. The truth of God remains truth: and it remains a strong and living truth, even if all the powers of heaven and earth joined together for its weakening <note>original: "Entkräftung." # On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.
L 3

...had applied more diligence to investigating the nature and character of the image itself, and thereafter to conclude from it what kind of operation of grace <term>Gnaden-Würckung: a theological term referring to the way God's grace actively works upon the human soul to transform it</term> was being indicated. In our view, there is no surer way to place the understanding of scriptural passages—in which divine things are depicted through earthly and natural ones—beyond the danger of all misunderstanding than this: One must first learn to rightly know the natural thing that the Spirit of the Lord uses as an image. 

And whoever does not wish to fail in this must set aside the common meaning that words have in our daily languages and strive to discern the particular understanding they have in the divine books. It is a common error to think that the words with which Scripture indicates human and natural things mean nothing more or less than they do in the learned and currently common languages. And what false explanations has this so common error not caused in both ancient and modern times? 

One must then, once the image itself and its properties have been rightly clarified in one's mind, judge what kind of spiritual concept must lie beneath it. For this purpose, we look to the operations and properties attributed to the matter in Scripture, which are made known to the understanding through an earthly image for the sake of our human weakness. We wish to follow this instruction and seek to explain the nature of rebirth <note>original: "Wiedergeburt"</note> as clearly as possible by comparing natural birth with the things assigned to spiritual birth. The benefit of this effort will 

<column-break/>

extend over all the passages of Holy Scripture in which rebirth is mentioned.

It is necessary that we first investigate what "birth," "to bear," and "to be born" indicate in a natural sense in those passages where rebirth is mentioned as a divine operation of grace in our souls. Or, to put it another way, we must rightly set before our eyes the image with which the Spirit of God compares that which He calls rebirth. 

"To bear" <note>original: "gebehren"</note> means, in most languages of the world, as much as placing a creature of its own kind out of itself into a world that it has not previously seen nor known. And "to be born" means to be placed into the world by a creature of its own kind and nature. Birth is thus the action or movement by which a certain creature separates from itself and brings into this world another of its own kind, which was previously formed and animated within it. 

In the language of the Greeks, the word which we translate as "to bear" <note>This likely refers to the Greek verb *gennaō*, which covers both begetting by a father and bearing by a mother.</note> is applied both to animals and to humans. It is used both for those who come into the world with a power to live and move, as well as for those who are dead and without life and movement. This general meaning of the words "to bear" and "to be born" must, in the context of the word "rebirth," be restricted on one side and expanded on the other. It must first be restricted: the word "birth" in this manner of speaking does not mean just any birth, but specifically the birth of a human; and not even the birth of every human, but—
