...encourage [their senses] toward the truth and prove the internal change of your heart through an active love. This connection immediately strikes anyone who is willing to read these words. Accordingly, the Apostle attributes to rebirth the power both to sanctify oneself more and more inwardly and to fulfill the law of love outwardly. If rebirth grants this ability, then it must be that which endows the human being—who is by nature lifeless and dead—with spiritual life. And if this is true, then it is proven that it is not merely natural birth (which does not give life) but rather begetting (which is the origin of life) that is the earthly image the Lord's messengers have in mind when they speak of rebirth. And is it not known that in other places, a spiritual begetting is expressly ascribed to the word which is here assigned a type of birth? God has begotten us, says Saint James, according to His will, through the word of truth, so that we might be the firstfruits of His creatures. <term>James 1:18</term>. These words are all the more remarkable because the two images contained within the word "rebirth" are here set apart and specifically named. Begetting <note>original: "Zeugung"</note> is clearly considered. Birth is indicated by the latter words. Whoever becomes a "firstfruit" of a certain kind of creature must be born and brought into the light. One can further add that elsewhere in Scripture, that which is here called rebirth is named vivification <note>The act of being made alive or endowed with life.</note>, <term>Romans 6</term> and <term>Ephesians 2:5</term>, and the "new creation," <term>Galatians 6:15</term>. These names would

<column-break/>

not suit the matter if the word "rebirth" referred only to birth, or to the entry into the world and into life. We have finished with the outline of rebirth when it is considered in an earthly and natural way. To be reborn, in the natural sense in Scripture, means to receive the power to think and to live and to be placed into the world with this power.

Whoever wishes to know what rebirth means in a spiritual sense must never lose sight of this image. He must imagine, one after another, the parts that belong to natural birth in the broad sense in which Scripture takes this word, and conclude from their nature what must happen and occur in those whom the Spirit of God calls "spiritually reborn." We shall attempt to do this without error and in this way bring forth a clear and pure concept of rebirth. Those who are begotten in an earthly manner receive their essence and their life indirectly from God through their parents. Life is nothing other than the ability to move and perform such things as are in accordance with the purpose for which a person was created, according to certain rules and laws of nature. One must be content with these general descriptions of begetting and life. The Scripture, which intends to instruct the wise and the unwise, the learned and the unlearned alike—and which in fact cares more for the simple and inexperienced than for the sharp-witted and practiced—provides no others in its [teachings].

# On the Nature and Character of Repentance

...are presented, they fit together so well that one can perceive almost nothing unequal—no deficiency, no excess—be it on one side or the other. Now it can be said with certainty what rebirth is, which Peter ascribes to the Word and which our Savior presents as the only way to the Kingdom of **God** (John 3:5). Rebirth is the effect of divine truth in the soul of a sinner, whereby he is clothed with faith and the power springing from faith to live spiritually, and is transferred from the kingdom of Satan into the Kingdom of **God** for a new life. In the strict and proper sense, this parable <note>original: Gleichniß; referring to the metaphor of birth</note> designates only the blessed change that arises in the human will during conversion. This will be immediately apparent to those who are familiar with the writing style of the holy books. Rebirth is the divine communication of spiritual life and, at the same time, its actual beginning. Spiritual life means, as already mentioned, primarily the capacity in Scripture to do good and to pursue <term>sanctification: the process of being made holy and following God's will</term>, just as spiritual death indicates the inability to align oneself with the will of the **Lord**. Both actually belong to the human will. The fruit which the Word produces in the intellect <note>original: Verstand</note> is called "Enlightenment" in Scripture. Yet, since no capacity to do good can exist without enlightenment—as the light of the soul that rises in us through the power of the Word is the cause of all the divine strength that manifests in our will—no one is forbidden from expanding the concept of the word "rebirth" and including everything that happens both in the in-

Scripture itself sets this image in this extensive meaning. And it is permitted in all languages to name one of two or more things that are indissolubly linked together and to understand the others with it.

Perhaps it is not unnecessary to give a brief answer at the conclusion of this digression to those who might ask whether this explanation of the nature of rebirth agrees with what the teachers of our church generally say about it. Many of our teachers, who for a hundred years or more have dealt with rebirth in their writings, say that it is the communication of faith, which makes us righteous and blessed. We have nothing to object to this description. It can keep the place it has held until now with our goodwill. We hope, on the other hand, from those who prefer their description to ours, that they will recognize that the difference between us and them does not concern the matter itself, but only the manner of the presentation. Faith is the means, the origin, the source of spiritual life, or the power to sanctify oneself inwardly and outwardly. As faith is ignited in us, the capacity also arises to fear the **Lord**, to love Him, and to honor Him through sincere obedience. In the first way of speaking, the means and the cause are named; in the other, the fruit and the effect. And when does a sensible person ever accuse another of an error for naming the cause instead of the effect, or the latter instead of the former, in his instruction? In the descriptions of <term>rebirth: the spiritual transformation of a person by God; also called regeneration</term> that are composed with some detail, these two things are taken together, just as in our own description. It is stated in these that **God**, in rebirth, transfers man from the state of spiritual death into spiritual life through the gift of faith. Is this instruction not exactly what we have presented thus far, only explained and proven somewhat more clearly and thoroughly than is usually done? The few things that one might still remind us of are so easily resolved and cleared away by what has been previously reported that we do not wish to be delayed by them, but rather proceed to the third of the passages <note>original: Oerter; here referring to "loci" or specific scriptural proof-texts</note> which we have set apart for proof.

This third passage belongs to the Apostle Paul and reads as follows: **So faith comes from preaching, but preaching through the Word of God.**
*Rom. X. 17.* <note>Romans 10:17</note> Our purpose does not necessarily require that we consider these words in their context, as they can be viewed as an isolated sentence that always retains a certain and clear meaning, whether it be placed alone or joined together with other truths and doctrines. Paul means to say this: Our preaching, the announcement of the Evan-

<column-break/>

-gelical message which **Jesus** has entrusted to us, is the cause why the nations believe in **Jesus** and recognize Him as their Savior. And we do not preach without a call and command. We are sent and chosen for this purpose. The Word or the command of **God** and our **Lord** urges and drives us to preach and to reveal the Son of **God** to the unbelieving world. The proof that we wish to draw from this saying lies in its first clause. The latter clause belongs to a different matter. Paul ascribes the faith of the nations, who accepted **Jesus** as their Savior, not to the miracles which the apostles of the **Lord** performed, but to their preaching. He names, according to a common way of speaking, the preaching itself instead of the truths and doctrines that were presented through the preaching. This is so clear that we would have to imagine quite unintelligent and thoughtless readers if we wished to prove it further. Preaching itself is a sound, a certain movement of the air. Who could imagine that such a natural thing could bring about knowledge, conviction, and confidence in the souls of those who hear it? The faith that is awakened through this preaching is, without any doubt, the one of which the Apostle speaks in his entire letter: the faith that <term>justifies: makes a person righteous in the eyes of God</term>, the faith that is the means of sanctification, the faith that leads to salvation. Anyone who would interpret this word differently and understand "faith" as nothing more than an opinion and a certainty of the heart that **Jesus** is the Messiah, would give the Apostle's statement a meaning that anyone who merely hears it...

That part of divine Truth or the Word which instructs mankind regarding their duties and the punishments of those who neglect them—the **Law**, in a word—reveals to the sinner the hideous shape of his heart and conduct, and the danger in which he stands because of it. What can this knowledge awaken in him other than an abhorrence of himself, and with it a violent fear and anxiety regarding the wrath and judgment of **God**? ### Explanation.

We have once taken the innocent liberty of presenting the doctrine of the **Scripture** regarding repentance somewhat more freely and clearly than is commonly done, and to adhere more to the power of the words and classifications <note>original: "Eintheilungen," referring to the formal systematic categories used in scholastic theology.</note> with which it is described by the teachers, than to the words and divisions themselves. We continue to maintain this liberty and assure ourselves that no sensible person or lover of truth will take offense at it. The **Church** has prescribed no laws of teaching-style to those who wish to instruct others. And she has omitted this for wise and well-founded reasons. One cannot prevent, through any art or caution, the fact that time and the changes that occur in languages, opinions, and other worldly things, [from causing] the words and turns of phrase with which a doctrine was formerly presented,

<column-break/>

to be enveloped in a certain obscurity. This unavoidable obscurity gradually becomes a cause of many errors and abuses. And whoever wishes to remedy these failings must often leave the well-trodden path and first enlighten the understanding of men before he can permit them the use of the established words and sections. It is just as impossible to bring it about that all who wish to make the **Truth** known to others perceive it in the same way and carry it out according to the same order. How is it possible to draw such diverse temperaments of men under a single and immutable law? One must therefore suspect that as many various presentations of divine truth will result as there are people of reflection and **Reason** who undertake its explanation. And does it not matter little in what kind of

# The First Main Section

We do not wish to mention the remaining reasons why one must consider it harmful and inadmissible to set a specific limit on the natural freedom of minds in the presentation of spiritual truths.

In the doctrine of **Repentance** <note>original: "Busse," a term covering both the internal change of heart and the theological process of conversion.</note>, besides these general reasons, there is a particular circumstance that obliges us in certain cases to set aside the usual treatment and arrangement of the subject. The teachers of our churches are divided over the number and the nature of the things that belong to repentance. Many count three parts of repentance: the recognition of sins, sadness or remorse over sin, and faith in the Redeemer and Savior **Jesus**. Others distinguish only two parts within it: the recognition of sins and faith, or the sadness over sin and faith. Some are of the opinion that one must make four parts of it if one wishes to counter all false concepts and imaginings of repentance with complete certainty: the recognition of sins, the remorse and pain over sins, faith, and the new obedience of the heart, or the soul's resolve to align its movements and deeds according to the Law of **God**. This disagreement in the division of the parts of which repentance consists must cause a difference in the descriptions of these parts. The recognition of sins

<column-break/>

cannot mean the same thing to those who view repentance as a matter composed of two parts as it indicates to those who dissect it into four parts. It is no different with remorse or sadness over sin. Besides this, there is no part of repentance that is described more uncertainly or inconsistently than this one. We might add that many explain this remorse and sadness in such a way that one may justly doubt whether they have presented the matter intended by it purely and clearly to their understanding. This person speaks of it as if it were a fruit of the **Gospel** <term>Gospel: the "Good News" of salvation through grace, often contrasted with the "Law."</term> promises of grace; that person seems to reckon it as an effect of the **Law** <term>Law: the moral commands of God which reveal human sinfulness.</term> in the mind of the sinner. Some present it as a movement that is worked partly through the Law and partly through the Gospel. And many seem to intentionally leave us in uncertainty as to whether they wish to derive it from the Law or from the teaching of the Gospel. This conflict does not actually affect the matter itself. Those who divide and describe it so differently immediately reach an agreement when they are to summarize the concepts of their understanding in one main description; they then sketch for us, with a few exceptions, a picture of repentance that everyone recognizes as their own. One person draws the concept of repentance in his mind as narrowly as possible and separates from it everything that can be considered either a cause or a fruit of it. The other expands it as far as the nature of the matter will allow and includes everything that gives life to repentance or arises from it.

The wise person easily scatters these small clouds through the light of his understanding and finds in all places the core of the doctrine that is necessary for him to know. However, there are not only the unpracticed, who cannot help themselves so quickly, but also the reckless, who neither want to nor can be convinced that a departure from the style of teaching to which they are accustomed is not a departure from the truth. <note>The author is addressing a common 18th-century concern: that changing the "formula" of a doctrine like repentance might be mistaken for heresy.</note> Whoever wishes to instruct the former and keep the latter from unkind judgments and errors cannot act more safely or certainly than by deriving the doctrine itself from its true foundations and showing it in its simple form, without concerning himself with the various styles of presentation. Whoever does this establishes wavering minds in the science and knowledge of truth and, without bickering or strife, brings those who are eager to learn to a point where they can tolerate their brothers—who may think somewhat differently than they do—with gentleness, as fellow partakers of one faith.

All who treat **Repentance** <note>original: "Busse," referring to both the internal change of heart and the outward turning from sin.</note> agree that repentance springs partly from the **Law** and partly from the **Gospel**; or, to speak more clearly, it arises partly from what is found in Scripture concerning man and his duties, and partly from what is written therein concerning divine love, benefits toward mankind, and His promises. And one cannot deny this unless one either wishes to take the word **Repentance** differently than it is generally

<column-break/>

used in Scripture, or if one wishes to present Christian doctrine in an entirely false and incorrect manner. The whole of repentance thus divides itself naturally into those dispositions and movements of the soul which the **Law** awakens in the soul of the sinner, and those which the **Gospel** brings forth in the same. Whoever wishes to separate these two categories from one another without error and precisely determine the true nature of the movements belonging to each must look to three things: First, the nature of the **Law** and the **Gospel** from which they arise; second, the nature of man himself, in whom they are worked through the Word; and third, the characteristics which, according to the pronouncement of Scripture, must show themselves in those who perform repentance. Each of these three things reinforces the consequences and conclusions provided to us by the other two. And all together they open to us, so to speak, the heart of a penitent and teach us the origin, the distinction, the connection, and the order of the qualities and movements that accomplish in him the divine change of spirit and conduct. We wish to follow this guideline as much as we can, so that the entire number of the various stirrings of the soul—which we are accustomed to encompass with the single word, **Repentance**—may be rightly distributed, and each may be clearly recognized according to its origin as well as its kind. The beginning must be made with the explanation of the two words, **Law** and **Gospel**.

The word **Law** <note>original: "Gesetz"</note> signifies more than it otherwise generally signifies in **Moral Doctrine** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre," the study of ethics and human behavior.</note> when one says that the **Law** brings the sinner to repentance...

Ordinarily, one designates with this word the entire collection of the rules and commandments of **God**, according to which a person must arrange their deeds and their conduct toward **God**, themselves, and others. In the doctrine of repentance, this word signifies not only this, but also the light and the order that must be and remain in all the powers of our souls if we wish to please our Creator; moreover, it includes everything that has a kinship and connection with this law of the soul and of life. To the Law belongs, first of all, everything that the *Scripture* *teaches* of those divine perfections which moved Him to give a wise and holy law, which bind Him to punish the despisers and transgressors thereof, and which give Him the power to take vengeance on the souls and bodies of sinners in countless ways, in time and in eternity. In short, it includes everything we read in the Scripture concerning the wisdom, the holiness, the justice, the omnipotence, and the truth of **God**. These infinite attributes of **God**, which give emphasis and authority to His law, are presented to us partly through words and partly through histories and examples. And thus, the entire record of sinners who, from Adam onward, have brought the wrath of the Most High upon themselves through their disobedience, and all reports of the sufferings and evils that befell them on account of their malice, must be included under the general word "Law." Who does not easily grasp this? These wretched ones are, as it were, the visible law of God, the interpretation of the words of which the law—which only the understanding grasps—consists; they are the proof and the confirmation

<column-break/>

of the teachings that are presented through words. To the Law belongs everything that **God** has let us know of the depravity and the natural corruption of man, of the causes of this misery, and of the guilt that lies upon all people because of it. These pieces provide us with a certain explanation of the Law. The person who recognizes their sin, their deficiencies, and their worthiness of punishment, sees within themselves the will and the meaning of the Law—just as a sick person, who knows the nature and the causes of their suffering, simultaneously sees what the physician must undertake to remedy their ill; and as a person who notices their crooked and incorrect steps simultaneously perceives the rule by which their gait must be directed. <note>The author uses medical and physical metaphors common in 18th-century devotional writing to explain how self-awareness leads to moral correction.</note> These elements increase in sinners the conviction of the holiness and fairness of the Law, of their duty to obey it, and of their inability to fulfill this duty. When they are rightly understood, they give the Law—properly so called—the power to humble and crush the proud heart. They increase the fear and reverence for the Law-giver and move the sinner to concern themselves with the means against this consuming fear. One must, therefore, reckon the history of the Fall of the first humans as part of the Law, and attach to it all scriptural examples of sinners who showed a hard and stubborn heart toward the long-suffering love of the **Lord**. What are these sinners but living witnesses to the truth of all those passages that speak of the corruption and the innate sin and malice of mankind? We wish to be brief: "Law" signifies not only the rule according to which the powers of our souls must be governed and our external life led, but also everything in which the Law is founded, and everything, in turn, that is founded upon the Law.

One can misunderstand the opinion of those who speak of the power of the Law in sinners if one does not remember this extensive meaning. We say: The Law makes the beginning of repentance; the Law breaks the heart of the sinner; the Law brings about the knowledge of sins. What do we mean by this? Do we understand this only as the commandments of **God** that serve as a rule and guide for life? Do we mean to say that the Ten Commandments, which Moses gave to the people of *Israel*, must be heard and perceived whenever a sinner is to be converted and recognize his sin? We assert neither this nor that. We know that in some churches people teach as if they believed this.

<column-break/>

And it seems that from this opinion arose the custom common in the English and other churches of always reading the Ten Commandments and the curses of the Scripture against sinners in the daily and weekly assemblies. Everything belongs to this same category: what is promised regarding the fruits of faith and grace in the souls of the righteous, and regarding the eternal glory and rest of those who have kept loyalty and faith until the end. The examples of great sinners to whom the **Lord** granted forgiveness and righteousness for the sake of their faith, the conversions of unbelieving Jews and heathens <note>German: *Heyden*, historically used for non-Christians, usually translated as "pagans" or "Gentiles."</note>, the spiritual and earthly rewards of the righteous, and the testimonies of patience, contentment, hope, and godliness which the believers have given to the future world—these are all confirmations of the divine power, the truth, and the certainty of the Gospel. Therefore, they are considered parts of the Gospel when it is understood and viewed in a broad sense. The smallest of these things can bring the first seed of faith, which purifies and changes the heart, into the soul of a penitent. One diminishes the power of divine truth if one binds the beginning of spiritual life to a certain specific piece of it, and especially to the word that actually proclaims the redemption that occurred through **Christ**. It is possible that the passage from Saint **John**: **God is love**, the story of the converted **Paul**, or something else from which divine grace and the truth of His promises shine forth, may lay the foundation for the remorse, the conviction, and the trust

<column-break/>

of a sinner. What this small amount has established and worked will afterwards be strengthened, nourished, and fully formed through the remembrance of the entire doctrine of grace. In the doctrine of faith, there is nothing but order, connection, and harmony. The very smallest piece of it relates to its entire composition. A sentence, an example, a promise is the thread that leads an understanding that wishes to follow, imperceptibly, through the whole household <term>Haushaltung</term> <note>In this context, *Haushaltung* refers to the "Divine Economy"—the way God manages and administers His grace and plan for humanity.</note> of the **Lord**. Whoever has rightly grasped it is drawn from one compartment into the next, until he has peered through and learned the entire wealth of the grace of **God** and the complete mystery of His love. To continue speaking by way of a parable: a ray of the sun that falls into a dark room gives the eye of its unfortunate inhabitant so much joy and pleasure that his spirit does not cease seeking until he discovers the entire sun from which this small gleam sprang; and at the same time, it helps him to partake in this wish, however small and slight the ray may be. And a glimpse into the kingdom of grace—a truth that belongs to the work of redemption—sets the whole heart in motion and does not cease to work until the weak faith has grown to its true size and has accomplished everything it can and must accomplish.

If one of these parts is missing, then repentance from the side of the Law is incomplete and can therefore bear no fruit. The evildoers of this world draw some hope and confidence from their tears, from the compassion of a judge (which often overcomes justice), from the skill of their defenders, from the intercession of their relatives and friends, or from the instability of earthly things, which often saves those who least expect it. And what if something could be devised to satisfy the angered Judge? Would the danger then be overcome and entirely driven away? All that we have said can be brought under three main points. In the sinner, the Law brings about: I) An enlightenment of the understanding in things pertaining to the Law. II) A sincere examination. The truths of the Gospel, which man previously grasped and understood only superficially, unclearly, and vaguely, are clarified in the understanding of the troubled person through the power of God’s Spirit, who works through them. The love, compassion, goodness, and mercy of the Most High allow themselves to be seen by him with all their works, and they make the terrifying image of divine severity and justice, which had frightened him, bearable. The suffering of Jesus and the redemption of the world, which were accomplished through it, show themselves to his spirit so brightly and clearly that he is at once thoroughly instructed and livingly convinced of them. And this enlightenment of the understanding gives birth in the will to a hunger and thirst, as the Scripture says, *Matthew 5:6.* <note>A reference to the Beatitudes: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness."</note> a heartfelt and longing desire to become a partaker of the fruits of these benefits and to reconcile with God through Jesus. Is it possible that a sick and tormented person, who feels his misery and has the means of his salvation before his eyes, could remain without longing and desire to take possession of it? The Spirit of the Lord satisfies this desire, which He Himself has fathered. He leads the sinner's understanding from the knowledge—from the living and powerful knowledge of the Gospel's teaching—to the approval, to the specific conviction that he belongs to the innumerable multitude of those whom the Lord loves, whom He has chosen from eternity for salvation, whom He has

<column-break/>

reconciled to Himself in time through the torture and death of His Son, and whom He is ready to glorify and make heirs of His kingdom. What a life, what a confidence, what a joy must arise from this inner conviction and certainty? On one side, the person feels the greatest trust in the merit of the Redeemer and, in this trust, claims this treasure and the **righteousness** <note>original: "Gerechtigkeit"</note> that lies within it as if he had earned it himself. The remedy for his debt is there. He has taken possession of it through the new power that has been granted to him. The Lord accepts this claim to the righteousness of Jesus by virtue of the <term>Covenant of Grace<note>A theological concept describing God's promise of salvation based on Christ's sacrifice rather than human works.</note></term> which He has established, and releases the sinner from the punishment he deserves. This is exactly what we commonly call <term>Justification<note>The legal act where God declares a sinner righteous through faith.</note></term>. On the other side, a tender love for God and for the Redeemer stirs in the soul of this penitent. This enlightenment presents the Redeemer to him as the single source and inexhaustible fountain of all well-being, all grace, and all happiness, which the entire human race—and he in particular—is to expect. Whoever is as purely and livingly convinced as a sinner (in whom the Spirit of the Lord transfigures the word of the Gospel) that he has been saved from the greatest misery and made an heir to an unspeakable happiness through the unmerited and yet infinite love of another—and whoever feels the beginning of this salvation in the certainty of his justification given by the Spirit of the Lord—he would have to be a completely different creature than a human being if he felt no counter-impulse, no drive, no inclination toward

# The First Main Part

...to Him, whose fullness has made him so rich. The justified person <term>justification: the theological concept where a person is declared righteous before God through faith rather than their own merits</term> thus embraces the Judge, who declares him innocent, as his Father; and the Redeemer, who earned the gracious verdict of the Judge for him, as his Lord, who has shattered the chains of his bondage and paid his debt—as his Friend, as his Brother. The first fruit of this love is a divine repentance, a sorrow born of love over the ingratitude with which he has stained himself until now, over the vanity and blindness of his mind that commanded him to despise the hand offering him life and grace, and over the malice that inspired defiance and outrage against Him who has loved him from eternity. Though the eye may remain dry, the heart nevertheless sheds tears over its previous stubbornness and false sense of security. The second fruit is a desire—a desire that is both awakened, strengthened, and maintained by love for **GOD**—to dedicate oneself and one's entire life to the **GOD** whom he previously resisted, and to offer henceforth to the Author of his welfare the sacrifices that were formerly paid to the waywardness of nature and the world. Following this resolution comes the surrender of the heart to the **GOD** who alone can sanctify, govern, and guide it in the way one now wishes to be guided and governed. The light that the person has received does not let him believe that he can, of his own power, think, desire, or walk in the way he has resolved. He knows himself to be a wretched and needy creature, fit for nothing but errors and sins. He therefore submits his soul to the divine government and assures himself that the same [divine power]

<column-break/>

alone can complete the work it has begun in him, and can both purify and sanctify the spirit. And through this same power, he immediately receives the beginning of the ability to satisfy the delight he feels in the Law of the **LORD**, and to practice the obedience he has sworn. This is what we commonly call sanctification <term>sanctification: the process of being made holy and being renewed in character after conversion</term> or renewal. All of this, which is accomplished in the sinner through the truth of the **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelii," Latin genitive</note>, can be fittingly organized into four main points. The **Gospel** gives (I) to the understanding of the sinner an enlightenment regarding those things that belong to the means of salvation and the redemption of humanity. (II) A particular conviction that the grace proclaimed by the **Gospel** also applies specifically to him. (III) A living appropriation of this grace of **God** offered in **Christ** <note>original: "Christo," Latin dative/ablative</note>. (IV) A love for the **GOD** who has reconciled Himself with us through **Christ**. From this love arises sanctification, which drives the person toward obedience.

The new obedience, or the resolution to henceforth direct oneself according to the rule and precept of the **LORD**, is a movement of the soul to which both the **Law** and the **Gospel** contribute their part. The **Law** first awakens this God-pleasing will. Whoever sees a misfortune hanging over his head, which he has prepared for himself through his own iniquity, cannot help but form the conclusion within himself that he wishes to avoid the causes from which his current danger arose, should he have the fortune to escape it. # On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.

*“I shall go softly all my years because of such bitterness of my soul.”* <note>original: "Ich werde mich scheuen alle mein Lebtag für solcher Betrübniß meiner Seelen." This is a citation of Isaiah 38:15, reflecting King Hezekiah’s humility following his illness and recovery.</note> Yet this resolution is dead and powerless in the soul of a corrupt sinner. <term>The Law: the moral commands and requirements of God, which in this context serve to show the sinner their failure and the threat of punishment.</term>, or the fear of the punishments that it threatens, can set him on the path, but cannot sustain, strengthen, or complete it. It can instill the will to do good, but it cannot break the power of the desires that pull that same will in the opposite direction. This is achieved by the doctrine of the grace of the Lord, or <term>the Gospel: the "good news" of salvation and forgiveness through Christ, which motivates through love rather than fear.</term>. From this arises faith and love for **GOD**. And these give to the lifeless obedience of the Law the strength to overcome the corruption of the heart and the world. Both, Law and Gospel, maintain this resolution to walk according to the Spirit through daily <term>repentance: (German: *Busse*) a transformative process of recognizing sin, feeling sorrow, and turning toward God.</term>. The former presents the wrath of the Most High over sin to the mind; the latter presents His grace and mercy in Christ. And the sluggish and negligent will requires this double enlightenment and reminder to maintain and establish itself in the order into which it has entered. How quickly a deadly slumber would overtake us if we entertained our soul only with the memory of divine love during our hours of devotion? And what else would we perform but the servile works of fear and anxiety if we sought to drive away our distaste for godliness through the mere contemplation of the Law?

We do not mean to say that every sinner is first enlightened by the **Law** <note>The "Law" refers to the moral requirements of God, which reveal a person's sinfulness.</note> and remains on this first step of repentance for a time; that he afterwards comes to an examination and is again somewhat delayed by it; and that he finally falls into terror and sadness after completing the examination, remaining there again for some time without comfort or grace. The Jews who heard the first sermon of the Apostles <note>A reference to the crowd at Pentecost in the Book of Acts.</note> are brought through repentance to faith, and through faith to the true sanctification of the heart, in just a few moments; they hardly feel the blessed change taking place within them. None of those things of which repentance is, so to speak, composed can be absent or missing in the sinners whom the **Lord** draws into His fellowship. We are therefore authorized to properly separate these parts from one another in our thoughts and in our instructions, and to describe them clearly. However, it remains up to the wisdom and love of the **Lord** how far they should remain separated in this or that person who is actually being converted, and whether the heart of the sinner must be led gradually from one step to another or—like hard bodies struck by lightning—be melted and transformed in an instant or in a very short time.

# The First Main Section

...teaches how to connect things properly and leaves the soul under the dominion of its desires.

The Scripture presents this to us in a very engaging way through an image that moves and convinces all the more because it seems to contradict itself. To be blind and to see are two things that rhyme as little as light and darkness. And yet the Spirit of the Lord attributes these two conflicting qualities to those who recognize the Lord’s will and yet do not carry it out—those who think purely and correctly about God’s Law and yet walk as if they were stuck in the greatest ignorance. No one can explain these passages in any other way than according to the rule we have provided. They mean nothing if they do not indicate that the Spirit of the Lord must enliven the grasped and recognized truth in a special way and convince the understanding through it, if it is to bear fruit and change the heart. Our Savior says: *He has come into this world for judgment, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.* <note>original: "Joh. IX. 39." John 9:39.</note> In our languages, such ways of speaking that contain something ambiguous are not so common. However, the Easterners <note>original: "Morgen-Länder." This refers to the cultures of the Near East, where Jesus’s listeners lived. The author explains that "Oriental" rhetoric often used paradoxes to provoke deeper thought.</note> use them frequently, with the intention that the attention of the reader and listener might be sharpened and encouraged. And Jesus aligns Himself here, as elsewhere, with these ideas. It is well known that "seeing" in the books of Scripture means as much as knowing and understanding something, and "blind"

<column-break/>

being means as much as suffering from a lack of understanding and knowledge. These words of Jesus differ from other places where this figure of speech occurs, in that the word "seeing" or "to see" has a twofold meaning in them. In one sense, it means to recognize and know. In another sense, it also means to understand and know something in such a way that one is simultaneously moved and livingly convinced by it, and directs oneself according to one’s knowledge. When our Savior says: He has come so that those who do not see may become seeing, the phrase "become seeing" is used in the latter sense. One can give these words no other meaning than this: Those previously ignorant and inexperienced in the divine truth that leads to salvation—the simple ones who enjoyed no grounded and clear instruction—shall come to such a pure and bright knowledge that they accept me as their Savior and Redeemer. And when He adds that those who see shall become blind, He takes the word "seeing" in the first sense. Beyond dispute, He wishes to teach nothing but this: Those who are well-instructed, who have practiced the truth, who have well-grasped the counsel and will of God regarding the salvation of men according to the letter, will be prevented by their senseless lusts and desires from drawing fruit and benefit from their knowledge and from doing what it requires of them. One cannot well understand the words "those who see" as referring to an imagined knowledge, as they are explained by various interpreters.

If Jesus had wanted to say this, as these learned Scripture-scholars believe: "Those who imagine themselves to be wise and understanding, although they are not, shall become ignorant or blind," then there would be no contradiction in his words—and actually, he would have said nothing at all. Those who persuade themselves without basis that they are learned and understanding are, in fact, already ignorant. They therefore cannot *become* blind and ignorant. One cannot set them in opposition to the simple and ignorant. What spirit and power would be in the words of Jesus if we interpreted them thus: "Those who are in fact blind and ignorant, although they falsely think they see and understand, shall become ignorant"? Can one fall into a state in which one already is? Moreover, our Savior says in the following that the Pharisees condemned themselves by admitting they had knowledge <note>original: "Wissenschaft und Erkenntniß"</note> or that they were "seeing." <note>John 9:41.</note> And this refutes the cited explanation of these words just as certainly. He is punishable and pronounces judgment upon himself who has knowledge and admits he does not lack it, and yet holds back the fruit and power thereof. But how can he be condemned by his own knowledge and by the confession of his knowledge, who only dreams he knows God and His will, and in fact has understood and learned nothing of it? And who would deny that the Pharisees generally knew and correctly understood God's counsel regarding the salvation of mankind from Moses and the Prophets, since Jesus himself exhorted the people to follow their teachings and commands, because they sat in Moses's seat? <note>original: "Stul Moses." Man sees the great perfections of the Lord—which are the ground of His Law and must simultaneously give it emphasis—only from a distance. That which Scripture reports of it and reason confirms does the same for him as an undeniable report of the power and justice of a ruler who reigns in a far-off region of the world does for us. One does not doubt the truth of this report. One praises the qualities and virtues of the King whom it concerns. One occasionally forms a sketch of the state of his subjects in thought. Yet because one does not have to fear him, one remains without concern in the habits and ways to which one has become accustomed. As long as we leave our restless and rebellious hearts their freedom, we lack the convincing clarity that alone can impart to the will a lasting movement toward the good and the power to maintain it. This very same distance prevents us from being able to awaken any kind of feeling of this impending agony within us, however skillful the images of Scripture—with which it represents such agony—otherwise are at stirring and moving the imagination. We will set aside the other reasons that can be drawn from this passage of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> against this cited explanation of the word: **Law**. This single point will suffice for people who have no desire to persist in their blindness. The Apostle denies this Law a certain power: **It cannot justify before God.** Conversely, he attributes to it another capability: **It can enlighten a person so far that he clearly recognizes and perceives the misery of mankind, the nature of sin, and his own injustice.** The meaning of the word justify <note>original: "rechtfertigen"</note> is well enough known. It means, in general, to declare one as pure, innocent, and worthy of salvation. Paul thus denies that a person can reach the point through the works of the Law that the Lord must recognize him as innocent and a lawful heir of His promises on account of his obedience. The **works of the Law** can generally be no other than such works as the Law commands and which correspond with the Law. These works are

<column-break/>

of a twofold kind. There are true: there are false works of the Law. The former are those deeds that are in all parts according to the Law, which spring from a holy and faithful heart and are performed with a good and righteous intention. The latter are actions that indeed seem according to the Law, but are reprehensible and impure, both in the causes from which they flow and in the intentions toward which they are directed: they are apparent deeds, which either fear of the threats of the Law, or the hope of a human advantage, or an impulse of nature brings forth. We can leave it to those who wish to understand this passage correctly whether they want to connect this or that concept with the words of the Apostle. The understanding of them will remain the same on both sides. If it is the true and righteous works of the Law that Paul means, then two propositions will lie in his words, one of which is tucked inside the other: The first: **Man can perform no true works of the Law.** The other: **Therefore, man cannot attain righteousness before God through the works of the Law.** Could man accomplish such works that truly and properly are called works of the Law, then God's righteousness would not deny him the reward of his obedience. It would have to declare him righteous and capable of salvation. This clearly shows that one must give this meaning to the Apostle's words, where one wants to understand them as the true works of the Law: because man does not obey the Law as he is obligated, because he cannot keep and fulfill it, because he [performs] no such works as

->### The First Principal Chapter<-

...than what the Law of the Lord requires, it is impossible for him to acquire righteousness through his obedience to it or through **works of the Law**. If these are the "false works" of the Law of which the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> speaks, then this same truth need only be presented with slightly altered words. One says nothing different than what we have already stated when expressing the sense of the witness of **Jesus Christ** in these words: Man cannot attain righteousness through the Law. For the works that he performs by his own strength according to the Law's prescription are only works according to the letter, works without spirit, power, or faith—works which the Law forces from him. We do not grant our readers the freedom to choose between this or that explanation because we are uncertain which is preferable. We have no hesitation in siding with the former. It is natural and agrees better with what precedes and follows. Furthermore, we recall no passage of Scripture where the phrase "**works of the Law**" must necessarily mean false works forced from man by fear of the Law. We are only being so fair-minded as to prevent all objections, so that those who have become accustomed—without cause—to always understand "false good works" when they hear of "works of the Law," may have no cause for doubt left. If the Law itself cannot give righteousness because man cannot fulfill it, it does nevertheless have the power to bring the sinner onto the

<column-break/>

way of true **justification**. One will never decide to seek a **foreign righteousness** <note>In Lutheran theology, "foreign righteousness" (iustitia aliena) refers to the righteousness of Christ credited to a believer, as opposed to one's own "proper" righteousness earned through deeds.</note> unless they have first certainly and thoroughly recognized the corruption of their nature, the Law's demands upon us, and what is called sin. This knowledge is provided by the Law. **Through the Law comes the knowledge of sin.** <note>A quotation of Romans 3:20.</note> The Apostle here expresses two connected truths through a single short sentence. Whoever is to comprehend what sin is, and how much lies beneath this word, must first know what Law is and what belongs to it. Who can say what is crooked and uneven if he does not know what is right and straight? Who will be able to discover errors against the rules of an art or science if the rules of that art are not properly known to him? This word of the Apostle must therefore be accepted and explained in this way: The Law reveals to man what the **Lord**, by virtue of His holiness and righteousness, requires of him, and how great the perfection must be in one who wishes to appear before the judgment of the Most High without worry or terror. As this happens, as it enlightens the understanding of man in this way, it simultaneously instructs him on how far the dominion of sin extends, what is indicated by this word, and what misfortune awaits him who surrenders himself to its rule. The **knowledge of sin** spoken of here cannot be the common, natural, and ordinary knowledge that a rational and attentive person can acquire from observing the Law.

It is an understanding that compels man to hasten toward the grace of God and the righteousness that Jesus earned; an understanding that stops the sinner's mouth and brings all the world to the point where it must confess that it is guilty. Rom. 3:19. Such a blessed and salutary fruit cannot be expected from the science of reason and nature, as was already reminded above. This simple explanation is confirmed by the matter itself and by constant experience. Those who hold to it can easily answer the doubt raised by most interpreters: Whether the Apostle speaks here of himself or of a third person? and need not join those who have persuaded themselves that the Apostle treats only of a certain kind and genus of Jewish teachers of his time, who considered the rising lusts of impure nature to be innocent. If there is an order and a consistency in the speech of the Apostle—which no one will deny—then what comes before must agree with what follows. One finds this necessary agreement in this interpretation. One does not find it in any of the others, and especially not in the one we have chosen. Therefore, that former interpretation must be held as the most valid and certain. 

However, it will be easy for us to set aside this proof, as strong as it may seem. An explanation of the Scripture from which an obviously absurd and false proposition follows must be rejected, even if it has the appearance of agreeing with the sequence and all the circumstances of the speech. Such is the case with this interpretation. Those who confess to it must at the same time concede that the Apostle gave this teaching: A person who knows nothing of the Law of God does not sense the power and strength of the evil desire in his heart. Even according to our interpretation, a certain order and unity remains in the ideas of the holy man. One will easily perceive this from the brief explanation of his words that we intend to give.

Where the light of revelation is lacking, one will always believe that a disordered lust—which one neither awakens with diligence nor maintains with deliberation—deserves the displeasure of a just and kind Judge no more than a careless word. From these words of the Apostle, one can draw a correct and clear conclusion. That which gives man a clear and distinct understanding of his ruin, the magnitude of his guilt and transgression, and the nature of sin, cannot in itself be a spark for sin or plunge man into sin. The Law does this. It shows that sin has taken possession of the whole person and that much belongs to sin which, to reason, appears at most to be a weakness. Therefore, it cannot of itself give occasion for sin, nor lead man to evil deeds.

For sin took opportunity from the commandment and stirred up in me all kinds of lust. For without the Law, sin was dead. That "sin" in this answer signifies innate sin—the inclination toward evil that we inherit from our parents—is clear. One need only note that the *Apostle* presents the sin of which he speaks as the mother and cause of inner cravings and lusts; thus, one cannot doubt the truth of this explanation. This inherited sin, which the *Apostle* represents as a person—as a tyrant who rules violently over man—is, as it were, afraid that its reign will be over when it notices that the understanding <note>original: "Verstand" – the faculty of the mind that perceives and processes information.</note> of its former servant has been more clearly instructed in its duty by the Law than before. The sinner, who has been enlightened by the Law, is moved by this new knowledge to think of his improvement and to watch more sharply over his heart than before, in order to strip the lusts of their power. Sin becomes, so to speak, uneasy over this decision of the enlightened reason <note>original: "Vernunft" – the higher human faculty of logic and moral judgment.</note> and worries that it will lose much through it. It therefore gathers all its servants, all its power, to destroy the same and to darken the light that has dawned. So miserable and corrupted is man. The evil will, which loves its disorder, never becomes more violent and active than when the understanding arms itself against its tyranny and dares to oppose it with valid reasons. And in

<column-break/>

this struggle, sin usually keeps the upper hand, unless a supernatural power strengthens the understanding and scatters the army of enraged desires. For without the Law, sin was dead. If "being dead" here meant not moving at all or having no capacity whatsoever, then this word of the *Apostle* would seem to lack truth. This way of speaking must therefore be understood comparatively. *Paul* <note>original: "Paulus"</note> wants to say: sin did not have so much life, so much capacity before; it did not stir so strongly and violently before. Those who are familiar with the writing style of Holy Scripture know that a considerable number of such passages can be collected from it, which sound as though they must be understood simply and without regard for anything else, and yet are more narrowly defined by the subject matter itself and the circumstances. Sin, or the naughtiness of nature, is powerful and lively enough in those who either have no revealed Law or live as if no Law had been given to them. However, it lets its presence and its natural power be noticed much more clearly and strongly by man when the Law enlightens the understanding and appears to create the resolution to improve oneself. In this state, a difficult struggle arises between Reason and Sin. The latter renews the old pleasant sensations that one felt during the practice of certain evil deeds. It gives the imagination the power to represent past pleasure to the understanding so vividly as if it were actually being enjoyed, and thereby ignites a culpable desire for the repetition of the deeds that caused it.

It is true that some do not allow themselves to be completely overwhelmed in this examination and govern their reason so cautiously that it must finally deliver a sharp judgment against their master. Genesis 3:9–10. Memory recalls past deeds without hindrance or difficulty. It renews the traces of sensations caused by the enjoyment of sins in the years of childhood and ignorance; it brings long-buried and forgotten crimes to mind just as quickly and easily as the fresh and clear footprints of recently committed misdeeds. It becomes easy for the imagination to bring the ugly features of man’s inner nature and his outward life and conduct into a pure and true sketch. Self-love falls silent and appears to become orderly and rational. It is as if it calmed itself with this conclusion: It is wiser and better to confess one's misery and wretchedness so that one might escape an infinite misfortune, rather than to excuse and gloss over it merely to enjoy a false glory and a short-lived satisfaction. Conscience can therefore administer its office with the sincerity proper to an upright judge. It places the man, who shows himself openly and honestly, against the Law. It searches for how much the former resembles the latter. It wishes to find a similarity and must finally confess that it can find none. The parable of a mirror, which the Apostle uses, places this beyond all doubt. What is a mirror other than a means to investigate the state of one's face? It is called a "law" because in its essentials it is the same ancient and unchangeable law that was imposed upon the human race from the beginning. It is called a "perfect law" because the person who could obey it would be perfect and without blemish; because everything in the Law of Moses that had the appearance of imperfection was abolished by it; because the eternal commandments of love for God and neighbor are explained and presented therein according to their perfect definition; and because all misinterpretations and false explanations of the Law

However, this is not as correct as it seems. Faith, considered by itself, can bring the heart to a certain pain, to a kind of regret, before it becomes so complete that justification and the forgiveness of sins must follow. To understand this, one need only remember that faith consists of different parts and has its stages. Remorse is an unpleasant sensation of the soul that manifests when one cannot deny that they have acted against their duty, against themselves, and against their own welfare. Sadness is slightly different from this movement, though it is usually linked with it. It is a vexing movement of the soul that arises within us when one sees that our happiness, or a part of it, has been withdrawn. Can such a person be free from these movements? And where else do they come from than from the **Gospel** or from the illumination of the understanding, which is worked within us through the word of the **Gospel**, and is the beginning of saving faith? It is certain that the Law contributes its part indirectly to this remorse. The truths of the **Gospel** would not be able to shatter and move the heart on their own in this way if one had not previously recognized their crimes and their punishability through the Law. However, the most immediate and primary cause is the revelation of the grace and love of the **LORD**, which is granted to the understanding through the word of the **Gospel**. No one can regret or mourn the loss of a great good if that good is unknown to them.

# The First Principal Part

...say that in those people who find themselves in these circumstances, there is a kind of **general love** toward **GOD**. Anyone who truly knows a **LORD** who is filled with love, and who sees the richness of His mercy and goodness opened up before them, must draw a particular esteem and reverence toward such a loving benefactor, regardless of whether they themselves know if they will ever attain the enjoyment of His grace. This reverence, which arises from the contemplation of the goodness and love of another, is a species of love. It is commonly accompanied by a feeling that has something of that emotion within it which we call love. In the world and in common life, one does not hesitate to give it the name "love," even though it is distinct from love properly so-called. Who can deny that in those whom the **Gospel** has enlightened and prepared for saving faith, there is a clear and bright conviction of the divine perfections which bring us so much salvation and grace? And how could one believe that the effect of this conviction—the veneration of divine love, which is the root and the beginning of **reciprocal love**—could be lacking in them? Meanwhile, one in no way casts doubt on the truth found in the books of faith <note>original: "Glaubens Büchern"; referring to the official confessions of the Lutheran or Reformed church</note> of our churches, that love follows **justification** <term>Justification: The theological moment when a sinner is declared righteous before God through faith, rather than by their own works.</term>. This truth is eternally firm, if by the word "love" one means true and proper love—the love that grows out of the feeling of divine love: the love that drives us to love **GOD** back as our Father and Benefactor, and which instills in us the diligence, desire, and strength to obey Him.

<column-break/>

This love would have to arise without grounds and without cause if it could stir and manifest itself in a person before that person was assured of their reconciliation with **GOD** and the forgiveness of **sins**. We add further that this general love, which can precede justification, cannot even be considered the cause of the **repentance** <note>original: "Reue"</note> which we call "Evangelical." This repentance is produced rather by the love we bear for ourselves, through the innate desire to be happy. The **Gospel** unlocks the abyss of divine love to man. Yet he knows that he has made himself unworthy of access to it, and he doubts whether he is permitted to draw comfort from it for himself. Meanwhile, he cannot help but wish and long for his own welfare and happiness. What remains for **self-love** <term>Self-love (Eigen-Liebe): In this context, not "selfishness" in a modern sense, but the natural human instinct for self-preservation and the desire for one's own eternal well-being.</term>, which sees itself so deceived in its hopes, other than a deep pain and a violent remorse? This is the only sorrowful means through which it can, as it were, somewhat satisfy and soothe itself. We have been moved by nothing to include this reminder—which our project did not strictly require—other than our desire to maintain peace and harmony among our brothers. We have seen some old and new writings in which the **penitent sinner** is depicted as if he were capable of a love for **GOD** before justification. It is believable that the authors of these works had this "general love" for **GOD** in mind, and not true "filial love" <note>Filial love: the love a child has for a father.</note>. It would therefore be a hasty judgment to burden them with the suspicion of an error against the pure truth.

# On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

It seems to us that King David composed the Psalms—which he set down as a monument to his repentance through the impulse of the Holy Spirit—at a time when the truths of the **Gospel** <note>In this context, "Gospel" refers to the "Good News" of God's mercy, contrasted with the "Law," which brings awareness of sin and fear of judgment.</note> had already begun to soften the intense terror of the **Law** through their light, and to awaken the sorrow caused by the loss of **God’s** grace. In these Psalms, he speaks as a man who fears the punishment and wrath of the Most High, yet still hopes in the goodness of the **Lord**. He speaks as a sinner who indeed trembles, but who nevertheless sees the greatness of the Judge’s mercy so clearly and distinctly that he almost dares to consider his redemption and **justification** <term>Justification: The theological state of being declared righteous or "in the right" before God.</term> as certain. **O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, and do not discipline me in your wrath.** These words, with which the sixth Psalm begins, are a clear testimony of the anxiety that God’s justice and the threats of the Law stirred within him. But what do the following words mean: **Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for the sake of your goodness?** Do these words not come from a soul in which a pure image of the Lord’s goodness has been established—an image that produces a repentance and sadness accompanied by some courage and hope? The first half of the thirty-eighth Psalm consists of bitter complaints about the terror and unrest that exhaust and consume a convicted sinner. The other half is the sketch of a heart that does not yet feel the powerful comfort or the living effect of grace, and yet expects it; a heart that grasps the infinite love of the offended **God**, and not only grasps it, but also prom-

<column-break/>

ises it to itself. How tender and confident these words sound: **But I wait for you, O Lord. You, O Lord my God, will answer.** In the fifty-first Psalm, which is rightly presented as a model to those who wish to know the nature of true repentance, one perceives only a small remnant of the anxiety and terror that the Law strikes into a person who "comes to himself" <note>This phrase refers to a moment of self-realization or awakening, similar to the Prodigal Son in the Bible.</note>. On the other hand, one sees a significant measure of strengthened confidence in the grace of God. This confidence is only hindered from reaching its full growth by a sensitive melancholy over having offended this grace, and by the fresh footprints of a half-conquered fear. In the remaining songs of this great King, which are testimonies of his fall and his resurrection, the situation is no different. We believe it will be easy even for the most inexperienced readers to instruct themselves in this matter.

Many consider it permissible to expand the meaning of this word and to include under it the first stirrings of love that lead to true and God-pleasing obedience. And is it not advisable and useful in all things to set apart with understanding things that are of a different kind and character, even though they seem in reality to be so closely linked as if they were inseparable? Among the great multitude of people who daily arise and seek new roads to heaven and find them to the confusion of many innocents, there are not a few who stumble and fail only because they either do not know repentance or they explain the necessary parts of it incorrectly, or shift and displace them. This part of Christian doctrine depends on many others that are indispensable to the knowledge of salvation. We express much in a single word when we say that the **Law** <note>The 'Law' (German: 'Gesetz') refers to the biblical commandments which serve to show humans their sinfulness before they can receive the 'Gospel' or grace.</note> produces **contrition** or **terror** in the heart of a repenting sinner. In the soul of a person who clearly and distinctly recognizes his connection and duty, his frequent transgressions of this duty, his inability to fulfill this duty, the justice of the Lawgiver to whom he is subject, the danger in which he stands, and the greatness of the punishments he deserves, various movements must arise. ### Of the Nature and Character of Repentance ###

...overflow the mind like a violent stream, such that the mind itself does not know which of them has the upper hand. It may be that they are stirred one after another and alternate with one another, so that only one always reigns alone and after a while leaves the dominion to another. Whether this or that happens, it is nevertheless indisputable that all these unpleasant stirrings must be present. And we encompass them all at once under the single word **remorse** or **terror** <note>In Lutheran theology, the "terrors of conscience" (*terrores conscientiae*) refer to the overwhelming fear and sorrow a person feels when they realize their sinfulness in the face of God's judgment.</note>.

<margin>more on page 137. <note>original: "plura p. 137."</note></margin>
**Remorse** is an inner pain that one feels when one is certain that they have committed something that runs against their duty and obligation. **Sadness** is an inner unrest over the loss of a thing upon which our welfare depends entirely or in part. These two sensations are very similar. And they are rarely separated from each other, because generally that which conflicts with our duty is also a hindrance to our happiness. How could a person remain free from these movements of the soul who sees himself convinced that he has acted against the greatest and holiest duties and, through his misdeeds, has forfeited his hope, his right, and his claim to the most perfect salvation? **Shame** is an unpleasant sensation that strikes us when we cannot deny our ugliness and failings and, moreover, know that they are just as visible and known to others as they are to ourselves. Can a sinner defend himself against this vexing movement, to whom the Law <note>The "Law" refers to the Ten Commandments and God's requirements, which "reveal" the sinner's failings.</note> has most clearly revealed his nakedness, his misery, and his follies, and who cannot doubt that God, the angels, and the true children of the Most High are witnesses to all the disgrace and shame that clings to him?

<column-break/>

**Hatred** is a restless surge and sensation of the soul, accompanied by an abhorrence and repugnance toward those things or persons who have hindered, or if not destroyed, then diminished our welfare; it is also accompanied by a desire to remove them, where possible, from one's path. To the sinner, whom the Law of the Lord has enlightened, two causes of the misfortune he fears present themselves. The one is himself; the other is the sins he has committed against the will of the Lord.

He must confess that he has brought himself into misery and has willfully neglected the means by which he could have attained true and infinite happiness. He must regard his transgressions as so many snares that have pulled him back from the goal of true life and sole contentment into an abyss of destruction.

How can he remain his own friend under this conviction? How can he hold back the repugnance toward himself? How can he refrain from cursing the sins and the moments in which he allowed himself to be led into sin, and from condemning the misdeeds that have robbed him of the grace of his Creator and Sustainer?

Besides all this, he has every reason to suspect that the common enemy of mankind, Satan, contributed no small amount to this, having promoted his misfortune with lust and pleasure and ensured he persisted so long in his blindness and folly. How can he think of this author of so many disorders without feeling the most violent hatred at the same time?

This suspicion has countless friends in our confused days. It is generally the favorite and first excuse seized by those who wish to enter the Kingdom of God without constraint or difficulty. It promises special transformations and such changes of the soul and all inner powers that have no similarity to any known and common movements and changes of the mind, and which the spirit of man therefore does not recognize. Whoever wishes to explain and make comprehensible such high and unknown things to other people—things known to him and others only through sensation—must take the changes of nature as an aid and speak in nothing but parables. The greatest masters of this secret art boast themselves that they have renounced all reason and imposed an eternal silence upon their understanding, and they wish that their students might follow their example.

At the time when the truth of the **Gospel** <note>German: "Evangelii." Referring to the Reformation era when Protestant teachings became prominent.</note> broke forth from the night in which it had lain for so long, both the German word *Verzweifelung* and the Latin *Desperatio* were used in common speech in a twofold sense. It meant, on the one hand, a state devoid of comfort and hope—the condition of a heart that expects no happy end to its misery. Later, it also indicated a mistrust

<column-break/>

in oneself, or a conviction of the soul that one is too weak to rescue oneself from a certain misery or misfortune. It was said of Judas that he fell into despair; yet this same word was often on the tongue when one wanted to report of David, of Manasseh, and other **penitents** <note>Those seeking forgiveness through repentance.</note> that they had renounced all hope of earthly and natural help in their repentance. One can, therefore, collect many passages from the books of the first teachers of our churches <note>The early Reformers of the 16th century.</note> which appear to contradict one another, because in some, despair is demanded of the penitent, while in others, it is denied that a penitent must despair. It is unnecessary to show that here "despairing" is the same as banishing all hope for grace and the forgiveness of sins from one's mind. It is easy to cite many more such places from the books of the first teachers of our churches which seem to contradict each other because the word "despair" is placed therein with a twofold meaning.

# On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

Disagreement disappears if one pays attention to this double meaning of the word **despair**. In those passages where **despair** is required of the sinner, "despairing" means as much as laying down all confidence in oneself, in one's own merits and works, and taking refuge alone in the grace and mercy of the Most High. In the passages where the scholastic theologians <note>German: "Schul-Lehrern." Refers to the "Schoolmen" or medieval academic theologians.</note> are accused of teaching despair—because they claimed that one could earn something from God through the terror and anxiety felt under the Law and its punishments, and thus penitential sorrow is distinguished from despair—"despairing" means as much as giving up all courage and all hope for grace and salvation. The first witnesses of the pure **Evangelical truth** <note>The early Protestant Reformers.</note> found in the circumstances of the times in which they lived a particular reason why they thought it necessary to mention despair occasionally in their instruction on **repentance** <term>Busse: The internal process of turning away from sin and toward God.</term>. The delusion regarding the merit of so-called **good works** had still taken quite firm root in the minds of most who had come out of the **Roman Church**. It was difficult to truly convince these people, who had previously heard so much about the great benefit of their outward works and exercises, that they must appear before the judgment of the Lord stripped of all trust in their merits if they wished to obtain grace and forgiveness. And even those who had grasped this holy faith with their intellect were nonetheless often led astray by all sorts of external and internal things, so that their hearts fell away from it. The teachers who daily

<column-break/>

saw and regretted this therefore held it advisable to repeat this sentence to wavering minds: that a sinner must despair and lose heart—that is, renounce himself and his supposed merits—and must expect all salvation and the power to do good from the grace of the Most High alone. And indeed, in the language of those times, no more convenient word was found through which that which they found so useful for people could be presented in brief. There was no danger of misinterpretation. Most people knew that by this term, often nothing more than a complete mistrust of oneself was intended. And in general, one was safe at that time from the kind of people who counted a **Cain-like or Judas-like remorse** <note>Biblical examples of "false repentance" where the sinner is overwhelmed by guilt but does not turn to God's mercy.</note>, or a true despair in God and His grace, as essential parts of repentance. Our language has changed since that time. And the circumstances of the churches have likewise shifted. The word **despair** now, on its own, never means anything other than a completely comfortless and hopeless state, unless something is added to restrict its general meaning. We have almost more reason to restrain those who wish to see the Lord without **sanctification** <term>Heiligung: The process of living a holy life following conversion.</term> and good works, than those who oppose the righteousness of God with their merits and good works. And what is more? We must take care that we do not open a free path for certain gloomy and ill-humored minds—who give the healing doctrine of repentance a cruel and terrifying appearance—to sow their weeds among the simple and to frighten the weak and fearful.

The passages of Holy Scripture that speak of the **sorrow of repentance** <term>Buße: The internal process of turning away from sin and toward God, often involving deep emotional distress.</term> are as well-known as they are easy to understand. This holy King can be presented, without any exaggeration, as the one in whom the troubled and restless stirrings of the soul—which a clear and convincing recognition of iniquities brings forth—rose to the highest degree. Never has a man displayed more certain signs of the greatest trepidation and anguish of the soul to the world than he. During the day, he holds back his tears in order to be fit for the business necessary for the government of his country. This restrained storm breaks forth at night, at the time when others rest from their labor, only with all the greater force:
> I drench my bed all night. I soak my couch with my tears. <note>original: "Ich schwemme mein Bette die ganze Nacht. Ich netze mit meinen Thränen mein Lager." Psalm VI. 7.</note>

The internal unrest of the soul, which beset him during the efforts of the day, and the lack of rest which creatures usually enjoy at night, exhausts the **vital spirits** <term>Lebens-Geister: In older medicine, these were subtle fluids or "vapors" believed to circulate through the nerves to provide energy and health.</term> and consumes the juices that give color and appearance to the human form.

Health itself suffers in this troubled state.

Decay seems to take its beginning in the fleshy parts of the body:

The flow of the blood in the veins is hindered and stopped; and the bones are therefore attacked with a painful sensation:
> Let me hear joy and gladness, that the bones may rejoice which you have broken. <note>Psalm LI. 10.</note>

He <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> is often accustomed to mixing general principles and truths into the specific exhortations and warnings he gives to the congregations of his time. His office required this. Therefore, he also inserts a principle here that deals generally with the **repentance and sorrow of a Christian**, and does not solely relate to the Corinthian incident. The words we have cited can be taken out of the rest of the speech and viewed as a self-contained truth that he only happened upon by chance. They contain more than what is found in the specific event that gave rise to this instruction. Anyone who does not pay attention to this can hardly use this passage as a proof in the doctrine of the **sorrow** produced by the **Law** <term>Law: In this theological context, the "Law" refers to divine moral standards that reveal human sinfulness and create the guilt necessary for repentance.</term> during the initial repentance. The sin of the Corinthians was not one of those transgressions through which a person completely loses the grace of the Most High. It was a fault to be attributed to weakness, inattention, or haste; a misdeed that required improvement and regret, but not a repetition of the "great repentance" <note>The author distinguishes between daily repentance for small faults and the "great repentance" required for a total conversion or return to faith after a total fall from grace.</note>.
