It was a sorrow of love, in which the Law had a share only insofar as it presented the committed mischief to the minds of the fallen. And if, accordingly, our words were a special rule that extended no further than the displeasure that had arisen in the Corinthians because of their lapse, then they would have to be struck from the number of scriptural passages that deal with the **sorrow of the Law** during the first conversion.

When these words of the Apostle are considered as a distinct doctrine, they teach us *the necessity, the nature, and the fruit of repentant sorrow.* And whoever is rightly instructed in these three things knows everything he must know about this matter. The *necessity* is easily proven from the fruit that this sorrow brings. It effects a change of spirit and mind. # On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

...which *produces a repentance* that no one regrets, who then would deny that it is necessary for a sinner? The nature and character of this repentance is explained primarily by the single word *godly*. It is a godly sorrow. This word allows for more than one meaning. *Godly* <note>original: "göttlich"</note> refers to something that comes from God, something that is in accordance with the will of God, or something that arises because of a matter concerning God, His honor, or His service. We see nothing in the words of the Apostle from which we could conclude that he associated only one of these three meanings with the word "godly." Indeed, all three are so united with one another that they cannot be separated except in thought. These are reasons enough to justify our taking the word "godly" in the broadest sense it can encompass. The sorrow of repentance is called "godly" because God is its author, for His Spirit gives birth to it through the voice of the Law. It is called "godly" because the Lord demands it of those who wish to come to justification <term>Justification: The theological concept of being declared righteous before God through faith.</term> through faith. Finally, it is called "godly" because it springs from the offense against God, from the conviction of the Spirit that one has transgressed the will of God and thereby lost the friendship of the Most Holy Being. What the Apostle mentions in contrast regarding the sorrow of the world reveals to us another quality of this blessed remorse and sorrow of the soul. *The sorrow of the world*, he says, *brings death*. And that which brings death is terrifying, consuming, and intolerable. If godly sorrow is the opposite of this harmful and danger-

<column-break/>

-ous sorrow, then it leads to the true life of the soul. And that which produces life and satisfaction of the spirit can be neither terrifying nor unbearable to the soul. It casts down the spirit, yes; however, it does not suppress it. It is an unrest that is sensitive and painful; however, it is not an unrest that gnaws at the spirit and robs it of all joy, freedom, and confidence. It is an anxiety that imparts a strong desire for rescue and redemption; however, it is not an anxiety that despairs of the hope of redemption. *The fruit of this sorrow* is presented in these words: *It produces a repentance leading to salvation, which no one regrets.* One understands this without further explanation. Yet, one understands it even more clearly when it is translated thus: *It produces a change of mind <note>original: "Veränderung des Sinnes." This is a translation of the Greek word "metanoia," which literally means a change of mind or heart, rather than just "feeling sorry."</note> that no one regrets, leading to salvation.* Those who are knowledgeable in the Greek language will all agree that this translation is consistent with the words. The Apostle has a twofold benefit in mind. A sinner who is made sorrowful according to the will of God becomes differently minded than he was before. New and God-pleasing inclinations and desires enter his soul instead of the old sinful lusts. And these bring a sense of satisfaction and peace of mind with them. This is the power of the words: *which no one regrets.* This manner of speaking is one of those with which eloquent people are accustomed to give their discourse a certain ornament, a "proper color"—if one may speak this way. One often says less with the words than one intends to give the listener or reader to understand, in order to give the matter greater weight and to move the mind

# The First Principal Chapter

...to maintain attention by varying the presentation. This is called a reasonable diminishment <note>The author is describing the rhetorical device of "litotes," where one affirms something by denying its opposite (e.g., saying "not bad" to mean "good").</note>. The laws of eloquence <term>Eloquence: The art of persuasive speaking or rhetoric.</term> allow one to represent the happiness of a person who has attained a degree of perfection as smaller than it actually is, saying no more than that he has been freed from a certain evil. One can say of a wealthy man: "He is not poor"; of a powerful man: "He is not weak"; of a strong man: "He feels no infirmity." And everyone knows that this means: This or that person is rich, he is powerful, he is strong. 

Thus speaks the Apostle here. He reports less than the reader is meant to think. He says that a converted sinner knows nothing of displeasure, no dissatisfaction, no regret over the change of his soul; and the reader should understand this as if he had said that his mind is pleased with the new formation of his heart and feels a true peace and contentment of the soul. What a pleasure it is when the restless desires, which martyred the spirit and drove it hither and thither, cease and give way to other inclinations that disturb no one, because they are satisfied and calmed by an infinite good? Salvation <note>original: "Seligkeit." This term encompasses both a state of spiritual "blessedness" and the ultimate state of "salvation."</note> is the second fruit of this sorrow. It is a word that indicates two types of salvation at once: the salvation of time, which flows from the certainty of peace with God, and the salvation of that eternity which is granted to those who have partaken in the first.

The contrast to these excellent words will occupy us for a shorter time. "The world" in this context can mean either the unbelieving and unconverted people,

<column-break/>

who are so often called "the world" in Scripture, or it can signify that which this world encompasses: the goods, the pleasures, and the honors of this world. These two meanings must be united here to properly understand the Apostle’s meaning. Worldly sorrow is a torment of the mind that arises in unsanctified hearts, devoted to vanity, over the loss of earthly and worldly things. This "brings forth death." It is well known that "life" and "death" are two words that in Scripture often generally indicate all kinds of happiness and misfortune. One has found the key to understanding these words when one notes this. "Death" here signifies all kinds of suffering, weaknesses, and dangerous incidents from which death can follow if they persist and continue. 

What is more certain than this word of the Apostle? Grief over the theft of things that make this life and this earth so sweet and pleasant to the "children of the world" attacks the natural strengths of the body and often ignites a secret fire that gradually wears a person down and delivers them to the grave. And even if death does not always result from the mental unrest of a person whose idols have been taken away, there nonetheless follow plagues and evils that can rightly be called a death, a deadly pain. What is a daily torment of the soul, which draws all cheerfulness and strength from the body and strikes down the whole man, other than a daily death?

This is not a separate part of repentance <term>Repentance: In this context, "Buße" refers to the entire process of turning away from sin and toward God, encompassing both internal sorrow and external confession.</term>. This desire, thus strengthened, is called the **new obedience**, to which both the Law and the Gospel contribute their part.

### The First Principal Section

He presents these <note>original: "dieselbe," likely referring to divine truths or consolations mentioned on the previous page</note> to his mind. He strives through them to appease and quiet the agitated spirit. And he works in vain. The spirit admits their truth, and yet does not perceive their power. He knows that they are infallible, and yet does not taste the pleasure that must arise from their certainty. He hovers between light and darkness, and is always—he knows not how—held back and bound when he wishes to approach the rays he sees in the distance and satisfy the desires of his heart through them. He sighs that the Lord might forget his iniquities, renew the life of his soul through the revelation of His grace, and speak into his heart—through the word of the Gospel—the comfort that he cannot bestow upon himself. The Lord hears him at the time that pleases His wisdom. That which happens to him is as unexpected as what occurs to a man whose eyes are freed from a transparent bandage, which allowed him to see his master’s **letter of freedom** <term>Freyheits-Brief: a legal document granting manumission to a slave or a formal pardon to a prisoner</term>, but did not permit him to read and understand it. He recognizes that He has reacquired peace and reconciliation with God for the whole world, the evil and fallen world. And all of this is impressed upon his understanding so vividly by an unknown and secret power that he simultaneously sees it clearly and believes it without doubt. The science <note>original: "Wissenschaft," here meaning systematic study or intellectual knowledge</note> of these things, which we gather through our own diligence, fills the understanding and leaves the heart empty. In our minds, it is worth little more than the testimony of a stranger who gives us the news that an important inheritance will fall to us. We believe and we doubt. We believe as long as we remain our own teachers, because we wish that everything we hear might be true. And what am I saying? We believe. We can say with better reason: we *think* that we believe. In truth, we doubt because the testimony that comes from ourselves and other men is a testimony that can deceive and does not carry with it the true conviction to which everything must yield. But the knowledge that comes from the Lord Himself carves itself into the soul with pure and indelible strokes. We must often content ourselves with general and indefinite ways of speaking—for example, attempting to draft and depict for others what a well-ordered and rational speech achieves in the minds of the listeners. Is it then any wonder that all the richness of our wit and all the abundance of our languages is not sufficient to make a work of the Spirit of God—which is only felt,

<column-break/>

which has no equal, and which is known only by its effects—completely known through words to men who consist of flesh and blood and **do not perceive what is of the Spirit of God**? <note>original: 1. It is the **Morning Dawn** <term>Morgen-Röthe: Literally "morning redness" or "aurora." In 18th-century spiritual literature, this frequently symbolizes the first light of spiritual awakening or the breaking of divine truth into the soul.</term> that announces the rising of the day in the heart of man. One person sees it earlier, another later. One is moved, as it were, in a single moment from darkness into the light and learns all the truths upon which the certainty of his salvation depends so quickly that he can sense no increase or growth of knowledge within himself. Another is held back longer by the wisdom of the Lord and, like an ignorant pupil, is led slowly from one level of knowledge to the next. The former finds himself unexpectedly so strengthened that he can oversee, judge, and admire the entire counsel of the Highest as if from a height. The latter understands piece by piece what he must know, and finally brings together all the parts that have become known to him little by little, in order to make a whole from them that is joined together and can stand on its own. This diversity of enlightenment must be attributed partly to the wisdom of the Spirit of God, and partly to the natural character and disposition of the men whom the Lord enlightens. The Spirit orders and fits together what the salvation of each person requires. And the salvation of man often requires that he be led gradually to clarity,

# On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

If we wished to prove everything we have reported so far regarding the first power of the Gospel <note>original: *Evangelii*</note> with passages from Scripture, we would have to set out and prove three points in order. First, we would have to show that neither faith nor love could arise or be maintained without the systematic knowledge and cognition of the teachings of the Gospel. Second, we would have to demonstrate that the systematic knowledge of divine truth, which we can acquire for ourselves, is not sufficient on its own to produce these healing fruits; rather, only a divine systematic knowledge—an enlightenment of grace—is fit for this purpose. Finally, we would have to establish that the truth of the Gospel itself is endowed with the power of God to manifest its glory within the sinner’s understanding and to ignite the light that he requires. And it seems almost unnecessary to us to give any of these three things more strength and clarity than they either possess in themselves or have already received in the preceding sections. The first proposition proves itself to all those who merely know what the words of which it consists signify. It remains as we <margin>p. 161.</margin> noted above: A believer and a righteous person without systematic knowledge and the cognition of God is nothing but a phantom <note>literally "a vision"</note> that vanishes at the first glance of reason, because it is composed of two things that no understanding can bring into fellowship. Scripture rejects this absurd image whenever it places the essence of religion in the cognition of God. Our Savior does this in John 17:3. Peter does this in 2 Peter 1:3. John does this in 1 John 2:6 and elsewhere. If there is any sense

<column-break/>

in these passages, it is undeniable that the cognition of God is the foundation and beginning of justification <term>Justification: The theological concept of being declared righteous before God through faith.</term> and sanctification <term>Sanctification: The process of being made holy and growing in spiritual character.</term> or the whole of religion. One often names the most prominent and first part of a matter instead of the whole thing. This manner of speaking is common in all languages. This being presupposed, let us see what Jesus intended to teach when he said: Eternal life is nothing other than to know God and His Son. The way to life is called the cognition of God because no one can set out upon it or walk it unless he has seen and recognized the truth. To deny this is not much better than saying, without redirection, that our Savior spoke words that mean nothing certain. The third proposition has already been secured and proven above <margin>p. 76.</margin> by means of clear passages of revelation, where we showed that the word of the Lord is the only means of conversion and rebirth. The second proposition has just as much testimony from experience as from the books of Scripture. If it were enough for faith and godliness to understand the counsel of the Most High regarding the redemption of humanity and to know its reasons, why then do many walk so disorderly and wickedly, who surpass many a child of the Most High in systematic knowledge and cognition? Why, then, do those who do not do the will of the Father in heaven doubt so little the truth of Jesus' mission that they even prophesy in His name and cast out devils? Matthew 7:21–22. John derives the systematic knowledge of a true Christian from the anointing. *You have the anointing from Him who is holy, and you know all things.*

Who can conceive that a person who fears the wrath and punishment of the Most High, and at the same time knows that his evil heart will never cease to sin and provoke the wrath of the LORD, should remain without pleasure and desire for a steadfast godliness? Who can believe that a person who is gnawed by a violent annoyance over his previous mistakes and sins should not long for any change in his vice-ridden inclinations? The Pharisee concerned himself neither with the forgiveness of sins nor with the strength for a holy and perfect walk. It is nowhere common to compare every desire, every wish of the heart, with hunger and thirst. One never says of a person who, without any special emotion, wishes to himself that he might be in the place of certain people who are exalted above others through honor, prestige, and wealth, that a hunger and thirst for honor and wealth plagues him. # Of the Nature and Character of Repentance. <note>original: *Busse*; in this context, it refers to the process of spiritual turning and the internal change of heart rather than just external penance.</note>

Faith is understood here only insofar as it brings about the inner conversion of the heart and sanctification <term>sanctification: the process of being made holy or being set apart for God's purposes</term> in a person. However, for the sake of order and so that we may serve those who always wish to understand the entire connection of the teachings of Christianity, we will not leave this part entirely untouched. And perhaps the little we intend to remind you of will contribute to the things we must still present being more easily understood and accepted.

We first find it necessary to note that the fruit of the Gospel, which we call the confidence and appropriation <note>original: *Zueignung*; the act of taking a spiritual promise and claiming it as one's own</note> of the merit of **JESUS**, is not different or separate in reality from the preceding or specific conviction of the sinner that **JESUS** especially earned salvation for him; it is different only in name and in our concepts. To be certain that a desired good belongs to one, and to appropriate it to oneself, are only two ways of speaking that represent one thing, albeit in different ways, and awaken the same concept in those who hear them. The son, who is undoubtedly assured that the wealth of his deceased father belongs to him, appropriates it at the same time

<column-break/>

in his mind and accepts it as his rightful inheritance. And while the sinner recognizes with unshakeable firmness that **JESUS** has paid off through his obedience not only the debt of all people, but also his own debt, he simultaneously accepts this repayment and this payment, which he so longingly desires. The enlightened understanding <term>understanding: in 18th-century thought, the *Verstand* is the faculty of reason and logical perception</term> draws the will after it with such speed that the assent <note>original: *Beyfall*; the intellectual agreement with a truth</note> that comes from the understanding and the appropriation, which is a work of the will, can only be separated through our thoughts. Regardless of this, we do not act without cause when we consider the specific assent as something distinct from the confidence or appropriation of the merit of **JESUS**. Both powers of our souls, understanding and will, work together on this business. The former, the understanding, grasps the truth of the sentence: **JESUS** is my redeemer. The latter, the will, grounds itself and relies on the truth of this sentence or makes use of it. Both unite here, as we have reported, so suddenly and without delay, that no one can imagine a true space or difference in this matter. But this does not deprive us of the right, for the sake of clarity and correctness, to divide, as it were, this simple movement and effort of our souls. A work of our spirit, to which both understanding and will contribute their part, can always be rightfully considered from a dual side. And this happens here. If the power of the Gospel over the mind of the sinner, who approaches for his justification, is viewed from the side of the understanding, then its effect is called assent, or specific conviction.

# The First Main Chapter

W<note>The letter "W" here refers to the start of the German word *Wird* (If/When).</note>hen faith is considered in such a way that it moves the will and brings forth action, it is called **trust**, **confidence**, or the **appropriation** <note>original: *Zueignung*; the act of claiming a spiritual promise as one's own</note> of the merit of **JESUS**. Those who first devised this division of terms did so partly for the clarity of the concept—which is of no small importance—and partly because they wanted to separate themselves more precisely from those who turn faith into a mere "assent of the intellect" <term>assent of the intellect: simply agreeing that something is true without it changing your heart or behavior</term>. Who would be so unfair as to criticize such a commendable intention? This observation, which seems to concern only words and standard categories, actually affects the heart of the matter and proves its truth. If confidence or trust is nothing more than a specific conviction or "assent" when viewed from the side of the will, then all the reasons we use to prove that a sinner must accept **JESUS** as his Savior and Redeemer are also strong enough to demonstrate that one must place their trust in him and his merit. What is more? This observation can be used against those who place the essence of justifying faith <term>justifying faith: the type of faith that makes a person "right" in the eyes of God</term> in things other than trust.

One can, if one wishes, look at justifying faith from a twofold perspective: first, from the side of the sinner who is to be justified; and second, from the side of the Judge who must acquit the sinner. If it is viewed from the first side, it can be regarded as a condition that is absolutely necessary for the goal the sinner seeks. If it is considered from the side of the Judge, it is the cause by which he must be moved to

<column-break/>

pardon the sinner. Whether one looks at it this way or that, it will always remain true that the confidence and trust of the repentant sinner in the merit of the Redeemer is the "Main Piece" <note>original: *Haupt-Stück*; the central or most important part of the doctrine</note> upon which everything depends. One can understand this more easily by imagining a human example: the image of a prisoner who can obtain his freedom in no other way than through a "foreign payment" <note>original: *fremde Bezahlung*; a ransom or debt paid by someone else on the prisoner's behalf</note>. The law, which limits the prisoner's hope and the judge's compassion, is this: whoever has forfeited his own freedom shall never be released unless another pays a certain sum of money for his redemption and delivers it to the Lord of the Land. A person who has fallen under this decree through his own fault will first wish from the bottom of his heart that someone might be found to take his place and pay the ransom. If a benefactor exists who has declared that he will help all unfortunate people of this kind through his own loss, it will be necessary for the prisoner to obtain news and certainty of this, if he is to be saved by him. This general knowledge <note>original: *Wissenschafft*; here meaning awareness or information rather than the modern sense of scientific study</note> is not yet sufficient. It is further necessary that he be specifically convinced that the generous and wealthy person, who promised his assistance to all, also wishes to share the fruit of his love and mercy specifically with *him*. Finally, it is necessary that he accept the offered benefit and make it known to the judge that he has found someone who will fulfill the law of the land and, by virtue of that foreign payment, demands his release. Which of these things is the most important?

# On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.

What is the element upon which the very most depends in this case? It is easy to see that, from the perspective of the unfortunate person, the specific conviction that someone is there who will take over his debt and pay the **ransom** <term>ransom: in this context, the "price" paid by Christ (his suffering/death) to free humanity from the legal debt of sin</term> is the most important and greatest thing. The mere desire for a savior and the general conviction that such a loving man has been found cannot set him free. The Law has not promised this grace to those who only wish to change their miserable condition and know that the means to do so exist. It demands an actual payment. Trust in the love of the Savior, whom the miserable person knows, and the acceptance of this unmerited goodness is only an effect of the specific conviction that He is ready to help him in particular. From where would the prisoner’s confidence, from where would the joy of spending another’s property as if it were his own arise, if the conviction were lacking that the owner of this property had, as it were, dedicated and gifted it to him? However, this conviction is distinguished from trust—as we have proven—only in name and according to our concepts. One is therefore justified in placing the essence of the condition under which freedom is to be granted to the guilty party in his trust. It is no less clear that this very confidence, when the matter is viewed from the side of the Judge, is the primary cause by which He is moved to announce the requested grace. Without payment, He may grant no freedom. The sinner presents himself to the Judge with the required ransom that another has offered. This causes the Judge to

<column-break/>

change his severity into gentleness. To be sure, if we wish to speak precisely and properly, it is not so much the guilty party's trust in the magnanimity and **satisfaction** <note>original: *Gnugthuung*; the theological concept that Christ's death "satisfied" the requirements of divine justice</note> of the Redeemer, but rather the actual acceptance and presentation of the ransom that is the ground of the judicial sentence. However, is this acceptance, is this handing-over not an inevitable consequence of the preceding trust? Can anyone use something that belongs to another as his own if he is not first certain and sure that it is permitted and allowed to him? And will a person in distress, who is assured of this, not immediately feel the courage he needs to apply it to his own benefit? How little the state of a sinner who is being **justified** <term>justified: being declared "not guilty" or "righteous" in a legal sense before God</term> differs from the state of the person we have presented here as an image is well enough known. It will therefore not be particularly difficult for anyone to derive from this what we wish to have concluded from it. In the meantime, we do not care much whether someone wants to use the word "trust" or "confidence" in this matter or not. We gladly allow it if one prefers to say, as some in fact do, **that the essence of faith consists in the specific conviction, or in the grasping and acceptance of the righteousness of JESUS Christ.** This change of names does not change the doctrine itself. The former—conviction—is the cause of trust; the latter—the grasping of Christ's righteousness—is the fruit of trust. It has never been forbidden to name the causes instead of the effects, or the effects instead of the causes.

# The First Principal Section

Those who either accuse us, or at least fear, that this doctrine of our churches regarding the essence of the faith that justifies might strengthen the complacency <term>complacency: the original German "Sicherheit" refers to "carnal security," a state where a person feels falsely safe from God's judgment and stops trying to live a moral life</term> and credulity of people who wish to be saved without effort or care, either do not understand this doctrine or are more fearful than is necessary. If it were taught among us that the faith to which we ascribe justification produced nothing else in the souls of the repentant than assurance and trust, and that a person who felt this trust within himself could no longer doubt his salvation—regardless of what his character might otherwise be—then we would indeed be guilty of the fall and ruin of many people. However, we all unanimously assert that this trust is not the only fruit of true faith; we maintain that this very faith, which fills the heart with joy and assurance, also kindles within it a pure and unadulterated love for God, from which flows an earnest desire to please Him. We teach that true faith is recognized by two characteristics: by trust and by obedience. What can a person who wishes to plunge himself into ruin use from this instruction for his evil purposes? If we taught our people that any kind of trust in the grace of God, which was earned by our Savior, justifies and saves, then at the very least one could accuse us of great carelessness. But who among us has ever said this? We have declared ourselves so often and so emphatically that we do not mean a vain and unfounded trust, but rather a founded and divine one, when we make trust the cause of justifica-

<column-break/>

tion. A vain and unfounded trust is a confidence that grows from an opinion adopted and accepted without reflection or consideration. A person who lets himself be talked into it by a chatterer <note>original: "Schwätzer," implying a gossip or someone selling false ideas</note> that a certain wealthy man wants to name him heir to his estates, and who squanders his own property in the hope of this imaginary inheritance, allows himself to be deceived by such a futile trust. His hope is based on a pleasant dream which he allows himself out of a love for sin and disorder. A firm, secure, and certain trust, however, is built either on clear and irrefutable reasons or on a testimony that cannot deceive. Such a trust is that to which justification is granted by grace. It is wrought by God in the soul and stands upon the internal, irrefutable testimony of the Spirit of God. It is impossible for a person who sincerely wishes to examine himself to confuse these two types of trust with one another.

And yet it happens, some will undoubtedly object, who regret the self-deception of so many people! Thousands go lost because they mistake a delusion <note>original: "Wahn"</note> of their heart—breathed into them by the desire to sin and by self-love—for the divine trust which is the soul of faith. Were we determined to dwell at length upon this matter, we could, with no small appearance of truth, call into question this alleged experience which is so often brought against our churches' usual presentation of faith. It is said, it is repeated, and people do not stop repeating it, that the abuse of our <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "srer" indicates the next word is "unsrer" (our).</note>

# On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.

...teaching of trust delivers thousands and thousands into the hands of Satan! And is this even proven? Perhaps among the thousands put forward, nine hundred are lost for entirely different reasons. Whence does this misuse arise? What is the cause that so blinds and misleads these people that they make the purest and healthiest doctrine—which is carefully guarded with all the necessary explanations—into a cover for their security <term>security: the original German "Sicherheit" refers to "carnal security" (securitas carnalis), a state of false peace where a person continues to sin because they believe they are already safe in God's grace</term> and carnal rest? This answer is enough to justify those who consider it unnecessary to introduce other words or to bring the doctrine of faith itself into another form. We may speak and instruct as we wish, yet this evil heart—which persuades the sinner to hold his hollow trust for the true confidence of faith—will remain there. And it will not only remain there: it will also not set aside its malice and will always continue to deceive the one in whom it dwells. <column-break/>

Would we have thereby uprooted the evil root that drives man to twist and despise the counsel of the Most High regarding his salvation? Would we have thereby prevented all errors and mistakes that the understanding of sinful man can commit in this matter? Will the heart change if we change the words? Will not rather the very same cause—whereby true trust is confused with false—bring man to pass off a natural zeal, a faint desire to become pious and different, a wavering and inconsistent resolution to improve, a weak wish to become righteous and blessed, for the true longing and the upright obedience of the heart? It is the man who wishes to understand the doctrine wrongly: the doctrine does not cause the man to form this will. If we could find the means to keep the impure and perverse will from its resistance, then no one would turn the doctrine we present from the Scripture into wantonness. One can give back one thing to this. It is true, one can say, that man's wickedness is to blame for the false interpretation of the doctrine. However, it is also certain that one manner of presentation and teaching contributes more to it than the other, so that man errs so dangerously. One must therefore choose the one in which lies the least opportunity to stir up corruption and, as it were, to arm oneself against the light of the understanding. In order that we might distinguish this movement—which we only obscurely comprehend—from other internal stirrings, **we look partly at its origin, and partly at its effects.** It arises from an opinion of our <term>understanding<note>The 'understanding' (Verstand) refers to the rational faculty of the mind that processes information and forms judgments.</note></term> that the basis of our <term>welfare<note>Wohlfahrt</note></term> and <term>happiness<note>Glückseligkeit: a state of supreme, often spiritual, bliss or beatitude.</note></term> lies either entirely or partially in a certain thing or person. If it is rational creatures upon whom our love falls, then generally a conviction of the understanding precedes it: that they are either naturally inclined to increase and secure the peace and happiness of other people as much as they can, or that they have actually already established, built up, and rescued our own welfare from all danger, or at least are able to increase and establish it. This kind of love, which we dedicate to such beings in whom there is understanding, will, and the capacity to serve, can therefore conveniently be divided into the general and the specific. We call a **general love** that stirring which rises within us when we imagine a being that is always ready to use its entire capacity for the service and peace of other creatures. However, it touches the heart differently than reverence does, and produces other impulses and movements. This specific love has its stages and is greater or smaller in its impulses and effects, depending on either the nature of the happiness we have received and expect, or how our imagination represents and estimates it. The strongest love expresses itself in those who, with a complete clarity of understanding, see and comprehend that a person—whom they have nevertheless despised and offended—has earned infinite merit on their behalf and, moreover, intends to continue without hesitation or end to delight them with the greatest happiness. # Of the Nature and Character of Repentance

Whoever circumvents this rule robs themselves of the light they need to understand countless passages of Scripture. And what, then, shall the love of God be, when it is viewed as an <term>affect<note>Affect: in this historical context, a strong, moved state of emotion or feeling that prompts action.</note></term>, as a movement of the heart and the will? It can be nothing other than a supernatural and divine stirring of the soul, which is produced through the clear knowledge of the infinite grace and love that God has shown us both in general and especially in Jesus Christ, and which entices and drives the person who feels it to dedicate their entire life to Him whom they recognize as their highest good. The doubts and difficulties that can be drawn from some places in Scripture against this explanation will be easily answered by those who are knowledgeable in the language of the Holy Books. And we shall, at the place where this part of our work actually belongs, come to the aid of those who cannot easily give themselves the answer they would like to provide.

<column-break/>

How easy is it now to demonstrate the connection between faith in God and love for God? Or to show that the love of God must necessarily grow out of true faith and arise within us? God has so arranged our nature that we cannot refrain from casting our love upon those in whom we perceive the origin and the source of our peace and happiness. <margin>Nº 343</margin> The faith that is awakened in us by the Spirit of God through the teaching of the Gospel shows us in God an infinite abyss of love and mercy toward us—we who, through the Law, have come to a living recognition of our nakedness, our misery, our ingratitude, and our folly. It makes us beyond doubt certain that this immeasurable Being has, from eternity, regardless of our injustice and sin, destined us in Jesus for the greatest possible happiness, and in time has partly fulfilled and partly intends to fulfill this eternal counsel toward us out of pure grace. It presents to us a divine Redeemer who did not allow Himself to be hindered by our shame and unworthiness from coming down to us from the bosom of the highest happiness, to bear the punishments that the justice of the Lord had decreed for us, and through His sufferings to acquire for us access to the grace of God and the inheritance of heavenly goods, whose value is immeasurable. We shall triumph over all because the Lord loves us and has loved us in Jesus from eternity. However, we remain certain that our interpretation will be given preference if one does not wish to reject this most necessary and certain rule of explanation: The easiest and most natural explanation, the explanation that first occurs to us as soon as the words are read, must always be held as the best.

Paul says: **Nothing shall separate us from the love of God.** If the "love of God" here is the love that God bears toward humans, then these words mean this much: God will always stand by us whenever a misfortune befalls us, because he loves us. If the "love of God" is the love which humans dedicate to God, then the meaning of the words is this: No suffering, no misfortune, will be able to extinguish our love for God. Which of these two interpretations must first come to the mind of those who read the Apostle’s words? Without any doubt, it is the latter, which the words themselves provide, as it were, without force or effort. If something were found in the context or in the other circumstances of the speech that could not support this understanding, then it would have to be exchanged for the first—even though it seems so easy and clear—despite the fact that the first interpretation must be extracted through art and reflection. But nowhere is an obstacle of this kind to be seen. One finds instead, if one follows the thread of the speech with attentiveness, another reason that leads us from the first explanation to the other. Suppose that Paul speaks of God’s love for humans and intended to say in the last five verses of this chapter that God will not leave his believers in all tribulations because of the love he has placed upon them; how would one have to view this conclusion of his speech in that case? It seems to us that these five sections would then be nothing more than an eloquent and lively elaboration of the words immediately preceding:

<column-break/>

We stand under the protection and supervision of a God who is powerful enough to preserve us, and loving enough to apply his whole power to our advantage. ### Of the Nature and Character of Repentance. ###

Among the passages we will cite to prove the following truths, there will be one or another that can be added to these points in a certain way.

(II) The love of God, awakened by faith, is the root and foundation of internal sanctification <note>Sanctification: the process of being made holy or being set apart for God's purposes</note>, or those impulses and movements aimed at the godliness of both the soul and one's life. Our own experience speaks for this truth just as clearly as revelation does. Who does not know the power of love? Our nature gives us no rest as soon as we are assured that a certain person has set aside their own self-love to save our peace and happiness. We immediately feel diligence, zeal, and a desire to show ourselves helpful and pleasing to them. And anyone who felt none of these stirrings toward such a great benefactor could not, without reason, be denied the name of a true human being—or at least a rational and thoughtful one—by the entire human race. We double this diligence and zeal when we are convinced that our future happiness rests solely in the hands of the very person who pulled us from danger. The more clearly and better we know the greatness of the happiness that another's love and favor has bestowed upon us, and the less we doubt their ability to fulfill what they have promised, the more carefully we strive to align our inclinations and paths according to their will. How often does the ambitious man prescribe difficult rules for himself, to whom the grace and love of his prince has promised a high-

<column-break/>

-er position after a certain time? And how do certain fools torment themselves so that they might please those whom their sick and delusional imagination presents as the only pillars of their happiness? These things are so certain and established through constant experience that people generally measure the greatness of another’s love by the magnitude of the effort with which they seek to serve the one they appear to love. No one has ever dared to dispute the truth of these conclusions: *Paul* spares no care, no diligence, no labor to satisfy the inclinations of *John*; therefore, it is true, as he claims, that he is possessed by a strong love for him. *John* does what seems good to him and cares little whether his deeds are pleasing to *Paul* or not; therefore, he claims without cause that he loves *Paul*. Whenever the imagination <note>The "imagination" (Einbildung) was considered a specific faculty of the mind that could visualize spiritual truths or be distracted by worldly ones</note> withdraws from the visible world, it sees a sketch—albeit an imperfect one—yet a magnificent outline of the glory that belongs to the righteous. And should **sanctification** <note>Sanctification (Heiligung): the process of being made holy and aligning one's life with God's will</note> be lacking amidst this enlightenment and love? Should such a moved and awakened person remain sluggish and negligent in surrendering his soul to the governance of God, whom he adores with the most perfect reverence? And should he allow his nature's will the freedom to resist the will of the Lord, in whom he seeks all his joy and salvation? We confess it, for we cannot contradict experience: that natural love works more vehemently and strongly in most of those who are sanctified than the love of grace or the love for God that comes from faith. Where are those who, with the same patience and joy, are willing to undertake for the Lord's sake what they take upon themselves to please those whom they love by nature? The father, who joyfully gives up his entire fortune to save his child's life from the hands of murderers, draws back with fear and impatience when a third of his goods is demanded for the support of the needy members of Christ. The woman, to whom her blood does not seem too dear when she must protect and defend her husband, often denies the

<column-break/>

Lord who bought her, if she can only preserve the freedom to confess Him by losing a small amount of prestige. Yet these examples, which are so common in the world, do not prove the weakness of God's love. This love has sufficiently proven and glorified its divine power in so many **witnesses of Jesus Christ** <note>Witnesses: a reference to martyrs, from the Greek 'martys', who stood firm even under the threat of death</note> who ended the greatest and bloodiest struggle with victory and glory. They only prove the impotence, the sluggishness, and the disorder of our soul. If the soil into which the seed of truth—from which love grows—is entrusted were better, the fruits would undoubtedly be more beautiful and powerful. Our heart is so soft and impure that the representations coming from the senses and the imagination penetrate far deeper into it, stir up far stronger desires, and leave behind far more certain footprints than the truths that the intellect only grasps and recognizes. And even if the Spirit of Grace strengthens the dim eyes of our intellect, the deep-rooted impulses of nature still oppose this light with such emphasis that the spiritual and holy affections remain faint and can hardly reach the highest stage of perfection.

The first movement that manifests in those who are forced by a living conviction to confess that they have offended their highest Benefactor and have opposed the purest love with a hard and defiant heart, is an inner discontent, a kind of hatred toward oneself, a displeasure over one's own folly and naughtiness, which one is accustomed to calling **repentance**.

The most remarkable example among those we find in Scripture regarding this repentance of love seems to us to be the sinful woman, whose story Luke relates in Luke 7:36-50. We will not concern ourselves extensively with the identity of the person <note>Historical debates often identified her as Mary Magdalene, though the text here avoids taking a side</note> whose love wrung out so much sorrow and tears, nor will we illuminate the specific circumstances of this event one after another. Whoever is eager to be more accurately informed of this has so many well-known writings of learned people at their service that one can hardly count them all. We wish to view and explain this story only insofar as it is useful for our purpose. A woman, who by her sinful way of life had scandalized all the inhabitants of the place where she lived, and who was known to everyone as a person who had acquired her fortune through one of the most hideous vices <note>A common euphemism for prostitution</note>, pushes her way into the chamber where JESUS sat at the table with various people of learning and reputation. From the wages of her unchastity and sin, she has procured a jar of precious ointment. She throws herself with this jar, full of sorrow and bathed in tears, in the presence of the entire assembly to whom she was an abomination, at the feet of JESUS. She wets his feet—which were extended from the couch upon which the Savior lay at the table, according to the Jewish custom of the time <note>Referring to the Roman-style reclining at meals where feet were positioned away from the table</note>—simultaneously with the tears of her eyes and with the ointment that the jar contained. She dries the wetted feet again with her hair and kisses them.

<column-break/>

JESUS says himself that these were no signs of fear and anxiety, no marks of a terrified heart sighing for mercy, but rather effects of love. From this it must be concluded that this woman is to be seen as a converted and justified <term>justification: the theological act of being declared righteous before God</term> sinner, as a person who has already survived the struggle of repentance, who has already received her forgiveness and been absolved by God, who has already become a partaker of faith and love, and who wished to offer the first fruits of her conversion. One cannot derive a pure and certain understanding from the answer JESUS gave to the Pharisee—who was taken aback by the woman’s boldness and Christ’s gentleness toward her—unless this is presupposed as indisputable. This sinful woman thus teaches through her outward behavior what the Scripture presents in words elsewhere. She teaches that love for God follows immediately upon justification and out of faith. She teaches that this love is the ground and origin of all work employed by the converted to please God. She teaches that this love, when it takes possession of the heart, excites a blessed and pleasant sorrow and repentance of the soul, which often betrays itself in the present through tears and other signs. She teaches finally that all other inclinations, all natural impulses, must yield to this dominant love; that fear of men, self-love, shame, and whatever else keeps us from godliness are smothered by it, or that the denial of ourselves and of all earthly things is produced through it. # The First Main Section

The conclusion is this: Either JESUS knows that this woman is a sinner, or he does not know it. Whether the former be true or the latter, I cannot consider him a messenger of God. If he knows it, then he is no prophet for that very reason, because a messenger of the Most High must not enter into any fellowship with gross sinners. If he does not know it, then I cannot accept him as the person he claims to be, because a prophet must know people and see their secret sins. This conclusion is absurd because it presents two false premises as true and correct. It is false and unproven that a prophet must know every person who approaches him. And it is just as untrue that he must avoid association with all those who are wicked. One might suspect, upon reading these words of the Pharisee, that the Savior would dismiss him with the saying he usually gave as an answer to those who slandered his fellowship with sinners:

> The healthy <note>original: "Die Starcken" (the strong/sturdy)</note> do not need the physician, but those who are sick.

This suspicion is mistaken. He takes an entirely different path to shame the ignorant pride of this Pharisee and tailors his answer to the specific circumstances of this Jewish scholar. He first presents him with a parable of two debtors who are indebted to a creditor in unequal measure. One owes a great deal, the other a moderate amount. The creditor takes pity on the need and inability of these two people and forgives the debt of both. From the difference in the debt arises a difference in the obligation and the gratitude. The Savior asks the attentive Pharisee: Which of

<column-break/>

these two, in an orderly and natural way, would love his benefactor the most and show the greatest gratitude toward him? It was easy to answer this question. And the Pharisee therefore answers correctly that the one to whom the greatest debt was forgiven would, according to the common course of nature, be most moved and brought to reciprocal love. The Savior then applies the parable to him and the woman presently labeled a sinner. He reproaches the Pharisee that, since He had come into his house as a guest, the Pharisee had given Him so few marks of his love; indeed, he had even failed in the duties of politeness that were customarily shown to foreign guests among the Jews and Eastern peoples. It was established among the Jews who wished to be held in high regard that one should receive guests they intended to honor with a kiss upon entry into the house, that one should have their feet washed before the meal, and that one should anoint their head with fragrant oils—partly so that the heart might be refreshed and cheered, and partly so that the brain might be strengthened against the vapors of the wine <note>Ancient hospitality customs often had practical health components; the cooling oil was thought to counteract the heating effects of alcohol.</note>. Whoever omitted these things silently signaled that he did not hold his guests in special esteem, or was at least quite cold and indifferent toward them. The Pharisee had honored the Savior with none of these duties of politeness. This was a clear sign from which one could see how little love and reverence for this great guest dwelt within him. And the reproach with which he secretly attacked Him showed more than clearly that he had invited Him not out of love and high esteem, but out of curiosity <note>original: "Fuͤrwiz" (impertinence or nosiness)</note> or from other motives.

...had invited him to the meal with even worse intentions. To this proud Pharisee, Jesus contrasts the sinful woman. How does this conclusion harmonize with the preceding parable to which it belongs? In the parable, the Savior presents love for the creditor as a consequence and effect of the prior generosity and forgiveness. Since they had nothing with which to pay, he forgave them both. Tell me, which of these two will love him the most? The cancellation of the debt comes first. Love follows it. In the conclusion of the parable, as it reads in our <note>The author refers to the standard German Bible of the time.</note> and in other translations, this order is reversed. Love comes first. The dismissal of debt and sin follows. Love is the cause, and the forgiveness of sins is the effect. Who can find their way through this reversal? One will be able to help oneself out of this difficulty in no other way than through a different translation. As many have long suggested, these words can also be rendered thus:

> Many sins have been forgiven her. **Therefore**, she has loved much.

His pride held him so captive that he thought he needed no repentance <term>original: "Buße," meaning both the internal change of heart and the act of penance</term>. That is why he esteemed **Jesus** so little. And he was thus still unholy and unconverted.

Our Savior teaches that this commandment is the greatest and foremost in the Law, Matthew 22:38, and that he who loves Him will also keep His word, John 14:23. To these general passages, which are understood without further explanation, we wish to add a few others, according to our custom, which are somewhat less known and require greater attention.

The first part of this passage we understand thus: In the community of Jesus Christ, in the kingdom of the Redeemer, neither circumcision brings anyone preference and honor above others, nor does the lack of it <note>Original: *Vorhaut*, literally "foreskin," used here to mean the state of being uncircumcised</note> bring shame and dishonor; or more clearly: The uncircumcised person counts in the kingdom

It can surprise no one who is experienced in the writing style of our holy books that we here take the name "Jesus Christ" not as His person, but as His community—the multitude of those who recognize Him as their Redeemer and Lord. How often is the most noble member or the best part set in place of the whole? Jesus is the head and the Lord of His community. Why should the head and the Lord not be named in place of the community that stands under Him? And we quickly add that this passage cannot well be explained otherwise than we have explained it. The other part, upon which we alone have to look here, contains this truth: Faith and love are the only marks <term>Merckmahle: identifying signs or characteristics</term> by which one can know the true members of Christ's community and distinguish them from other people. The word "love" stands here alone and is not so restricted by any addition that it must be drawn to only one kind of love. It is therefore right that it be understood generally of all love, both of love toward God and toward one's neighbor. However, Scripture uses the word "love" in a twofold sense. Sometimes it signifies the internal love that dwells in the soul; sometimes the external works that are performed through the impulse of internal love. # The First Main Chapter

We have decided to move from this passage of scripture, which can be applied to our purpose with less effort, to another, which we will not be able to use until we have driven away the darkness with which it seems to be surrounded. We hope that the diligence we intend to apply here will be rewarded by the benefit that may arise from it. The Apostle wishes for the converted Ephesians an increase in faith and love, and at the same time recounts the fruits they would obtain if his prayer were to be heard. Both of these he does for the most part with figures of speech and words taken from earthly and visible things, so that his thoughts may become all the more comprehensible and vivid: <term>Ephesians 3:14–19<note>The author uses this specific New Testament passage to illustrate how spiritual strength is built through divine grace rather than human effort.</note></term>. The wish or the prayer itself reads as follows:

> I bow my knees, that God may give you power to become strong through his Spirit in the **inner person**, and for Christ to dwell through faith in your hearts, and through love to be rooted and grounded.

The first words briefly encompass the entire wish: I pray to the Most High that He may daily grant more spiritual power and strength to your souls, which are sanctified through Him. The image to which these words refer is quite suited to represent the state of the newly converted. Paul compares them to people who have just survived a great illness, and who must gradually regain the strength lost through the violence of the ailment through care and medicine. The following words break down, so to speak, what the Apostle had expressed in general, and

That an increase in faith is requested for the Ephesians with the first words is immediately clear as soon as it is noted that the Greek word <note>The author is referring to the Greek verb *katoikēsai* (κατοικῆσαι), which signifies a permanent, settled habitation.</note>, which our translation renders as "dwell," signifies something more than this. It actually means: To have a certain, constant, unchanging dwelling in a place. The meaning of the Apostle can therefore be none other than this: I implore the Most High that your faith may increase more and more, so that the communion and union with Christ in which you stand may become inextinguishable, or that Christ may make your soul His constant dwelling. The union with Christ shall be so sealed and confirmed that it never ceases. The means by which this can happen is, as the Apostle himself says, faith. To be "rooted and grounded in love" (as we translate it) can, as we believe, hardly signify anything other than becoming more complete and rich in love. Love is represented here under the image of a soil or fertile ground. Believers are depicted partly as trees, which spread their roots further and further into this ground and thereby become ever firmer and more immovable; and partly as houses, whose foundation—from which the entire durability and stability of the building grows—lies in this soil. This comparison is not one of those that must be justified by the nature and character of Middle Eastern languages <note>original: "Morgenländischen Sprachen." The author suggests that while many biblical metaphors require knowledge of Hebrew or Aramaic idioms to make sense, this specific image of "rooting" is universally understood.</note>. It can also be used in our own languages without error. And which love is it, then, in which the Ephesians were to be grounded? If human authority and the consensus of most interpreters counted in the explanation of Scripture, we would have to admit that the love meant is that which **GOD** has shown to mankind in **Christ**. The majority of the most distinguished scriptural scholars <note>original: "Schrift-Forscher," referring to the academic and theological commentators of the era.</note> maintain that **Paul** intended to say: I wish for you that you may daily recognize and understand the love of **GOD** toward you more clearly and plainly. We could allow this explanation the approval it has received from so many great men, and yet still prove from this passage the truth we are striving to derive from it. Those who perceive the love of **GOD** toward them ever more purely and completely also increase, at the same time, in love for **GOD** and their neighbor. The further one sees into the depths of divine

<column-break/>

grace and mercy, the more strongly and vehemently one is driven and moved to love Him back with all the powers of the soul. It could therefore be naturally asserted that the Apostle’s prayer is directed as much toward the love of **GOD** for mankind as toward the love of the believers for **GOD**. However, after having most diligently weighed the circumstances of these words, it seems to us that everything fits together better, flows more clearly, and is more suited to the Apostle's purpose if one sets aside the common opinion and understands it primarily as the love for **GOD** and neighbor, which is born in the saints through faith. First, it is certain that the wish commonly found in this passage is already included in the preceding words. Where **Christ** has chosen His permanent seat, or where there is a close and inseparable union with **Christ**, there is no lack of clear and distinct knowledge of the infinite love of **GOD** toward mankind. And whoever asks this of **GOD** for another also wishes this for him at the same time. Furthermore, we can recall no passage of Scripture in which the word "love," simply and without any addition or explanation, is used for the love of **GOD** toward man. **John** uses this word alone when he speaks of the love of the Redeemer shown to mankind in *1 John 3:16*. <note>The verse states: "By this we know love, because He laid down His life for us."</note> But that which immediately follows these words—that He laid down His life for us—removes all misunderstanding and defines the kind of love he is discussing. The **Apostle** holds the undoubted hope that the answering of his prayer would create a threefold benefit for the newly converted **Ephesians**. They would first comprehend, with all the saints, what is *the breadth and the length, the depth and the height.* They would, secondly, recognize that *loving Christ* is much better than knowing everything. <column-break/>

without explanation. The first is obscure for two reasons. First, it is clothed in a metaphor <note>original: "Gleichniß." While often translated as "parable," in this context of biblical exegesis, it refers to a symbolic or metaphorical comparison.</note>. The **Ephesians** are to comprehend the breadth, the length, the depth, and the height of a certain thing. And what is this thing? Is it the love of **GOD**, which he mentioned shortly before? Does **Paul** mean to say that the **Ephesians** would see and grasp the entire size, the full extent of **GOD’s** love for them and their love for **GOD**? That they would recognize the infinite expanse of divine mercy and their entire duty toward **GOD** and their neighbor if they increased in faith and love? Or is it the temple and the congregation of **GOD**? Does he mean that they would comprehend the true nature of the spiritual house of the **Lord**, the right manner and form of the **Church of Jesus Christ**? The most distinguished and astute interpreters are divided between these two opinions. Yet some are uncertain whether this or that one has stronger reasons behind it, and they therefore try to see if they can pull both together and take the **Apostle’s** words in such an extensive sense that includes both explanations. Having weighed everything, we join without hesitation those who believe that it is the **Church of Christ** being spoken of. The words themselves—which refer to a building that can be measured according to its length, height, breadth, and depth—are best suited to this interpretation. And with such a building, or with a temple, the **Apostle** had compared the **Church** shortly before.

The **Apostle** first instructs the **Jews** that they have no reason to exalt themselves over the **Gentiles**, because they were called by pure grace just as the others were. **vv. 3-10**. He then turns to the **Gentiles**. To these he presents partly the wretched state in which they previously lived, and partly their current rights and freedoms. He assures them that the distinction between them and the **Jews** has been abolished through **Jesus**; that one people has no preference over the other in spiritual things; that both peoples constitute a single **Community**; and that they should not listen to those who would only have them regarded as guests in the **House of the Lord**. Rather, they were **fellow-citizens**

<column-break/>

and members of the household with the **Saints**. **vv. 19, 20**. To what end were these careful reminders and teachings necessary if things had been quiet and peaceful in **Ephesus**, and if the two peoples, gathered into one flock, had known nothing of the strife in other congregations? In our view, the words of the **Apostle**—the meaning of which we are examining—refer to this disagreement. To comprehend the **breadth, height, length, and depth** of the **Temple of God** means as much as recognizing that the **Temple of God** is far more spacious and larger than was believed in **Ephesus**; that the whole world belongs to the **Community of the Lord**; that the foundation of this holy building is **Jesus** alone and faith in Him; and that all who would ground themselves upon this **Cornerstone** would be incorporated into it. **Ephesians 2:21, 22**. We cannot say how much more probable this explanation might appear to others, for we must fear that the love each person carries for their own opinions might blind us, just as it does other men. To us, however, it seems easy, natural, in accordance with the words of the **Apostle**, and provided with all those qualities that an interpretation of an obscure passage must possess if it is to count as more than a mere guess. And if we are not mistaken, the added words "with all the saints" themselves serve to increase its weight. These **Saints** are, in our opinion, the **Jews**. They called themselves "the Saints," or "the Holy People." And the name was due to them because **God** Himself had separated them from all other remaining peoples and chosen them for His own possession. ...in this very letter, he uses this designation. The second sentence causes the reader some pause because it can be appropriately interpreted in a twofold way. One can first render it thus: **"That you may recognize that the love of Christ surpasses all knowledge,"** <note>original: "Wissenschaft"; in this 18th-century context, it refers to systematic knowledge or scholarship rather than just modern natural science.</note> or, that human understanding with all its effort is far too weak and incapable of grasping the magnitude of the love of Christ toward mankind. And we believe that he chose wisely when he exchanged the former for this one, although the most skillful of today's interpreters are of the opinion that he would have done better if he had kept the first. To give power and light to this explanation, we again assume something that can hardly be disputed. We imagine that exactly what happened in **Corinth** and elsewhere also occurred in the congregation at **Ephesus**, where a portion of the congregation boasted of their **knowledge** and **insight** and, for the sake of this supposed scholarship, deemed many things permissible that were offensive to the weak and untrained, and in part punishable in themselves. If we could linger, it would be easy to demonstrate from the first chapter of this letter that there were such "imaginary wise men" in **Ephesus** who chattered much about their great insights into the foundation of truth and wisdom. The word **Love**, in the question upon which we wish to give our opinion, can mean two things. It can indicate the *ground and the cause of love; it can indicate love itself.* No one doubts the latter meaning. The former is somewhat rarer, and yet not entirely unusual. One says: "Peter is rich in love." This way of speaking does not mean that love is always actually active and revealed in Peter. Its meaning is only this: Peter is of such a disposition of mind, of such a kind, that love can very easily arise within him. He lacks none of the causes which must necessarily produce the emotion of love. If the word **Love** is used in this sense when one says that **Faith** or the teaching of the **Gospel** brings forth trust in the **merit of Jesus** and **Love** at the same time; that **Love** is present in the **Faith** that makes us righteous <note>This refers to the doctrine of <term>Justification</term>, where a person is declared righteous by God.</note>; that no other faith justifies but that which is active through love—or however else one wishes to speak—then, as we believe, this proposition is irreproachable. *One can aptly say that things themselves are there and present* when one sees the causes from which they must inevitably arise. One can say without error that the blossom is present, even though it still lies in the buds; that the harvest is there when everything is so prepared that it must begin without delay. It can therefore also be said that **Love** is present in the soul of a person

<column-break/>

in whom <term>Faith</term> is powerful. No other faith justifies than the true and living faith. **The true and living faith is the ground, the sole source, and the cause of love for God and the neighbor.** Love is thus present beyond dispute when faith grasps the righteousness of **Jesus**, insofar as it lies within faith as if in its cause. It is present because that which will soon give it life and movement is there, and must give it. It is present because it cannot fail to appear and is already seen by **God** in all its fruits and labors. We cannot easily persuade ourselves that anyone who rightly knows the doctrine of our Church, or rather the doctrine of the Scriptures, should deny this. Whoever dares to deny it must at the same time prepare himself to maintain that a faith without power and life—a faith that lacks one of the greatest properties of faith, namely the ability to purify and sanctify the heart—an imperfect faith, in a word, is the means of <term>Justification</term>. And which <term>Evangelical</term> <note>In this 18th-century context, "Evangelical" (Evangelisch) refers to the Lutheran tradition.</note> teacher would want to take this blame upon himself? One can also teach without danger of error that **good works** are present with the faith that makes one righteous, if only one adds the explanation that one means the *capacity* to do good works. Certainly, good works are present because that is there from which they must infallibly follow and arise. And whoever separates the power to perform them from faith, let him see whether he can derive renewal with its fruits from the same. But whoever gladly avoids misunderstanding and suspicion...

# On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.

...to prevent the confusion of the weak, he does better, in our opinion, to present his thoughts in other words.

If the word **Love** in the matter we are discussing is meant to signify love itself—which is an *affect* <note>An "affect" in 18th-century psychology refers to a strong emotion or a movement of the soul.</note> or a movement of the soul directed toward God—then one must judge differently, unless we are very mistaken. The question, if one wants the word **Love** understood in this way, would be phrased thus: Does a person, at the very moment the Lord assures them of the forgiveness of sins through the testimony of His Spirit, actually feel that blessed movement of the will which we call love for God? Is the affect of love powerful in the soul at that time, in that very instant, when they are gladdened by the certainty of their spiritual freedom or <term>Justification</term> <note>Justification is the theological term for God declaring a sinner righteous.</note>? One cannot thoroughly answer this question unless one first clearly envisions both the divine decree of grace, by which the sinner is justified, and love for God, and then holds these two things against each other. This comparison must ultimately show whether it is possible for the one to arise and occupy the soul simultaneously with the other, because, to our knowledge, there is no scriptural passage so clear that this doubt can be resolved without extensive explanation.

<margin>p. 185.</margin>
It has already been noted above that the so-called judicial decree of God in justification is actually the certainty of the heart, which we receive through the internal testimony of God’s Spirit, that for the sake of Jesus’ merit, our debt

<column-break/>

has been canceled and the deserved punishment remitted. We add here that this assurance must be seen as nothing other than a conclusion of the enlightened intellect, strengthened by the Spirit of grace. By this we mean the following: The Holy Spirit does not speak these exact words in our souls: "You are acquitted by God for Christ’s sake and are thus an heir to the salvation that Jesus earned for His members." Instead, through His assistance and grace, we ourselves derive this conclusion from the word of the **Gospel**, which has achieved a divine and unshakeable certainty in us that nature cannot give. This truth presents itself to the intellect with a clarity and distinctness that no human imagination can reach or describe: *Jesus has earned salvation for me through His suffering. His righteousness belongs to me. In Him, so to speak, I have been sacrificed to divine justice.* This divine light of the intellect tolerates no laziness in the will. The conclusion of the will, which we call **Confidence**: *I want to accept this righteousness, which is mine, and make it my own; I want to clothe myself with it and approach the throne of the Judge in this finery without fear*; this conclusion follows so quickly that one can hardly think of it as a separate action of the soul.

The spirit, thus enlightened and moved, cannot stand still. The power of God working within it bids it to proceed immediately in its work and to add this consequence: *Therefore I am saved from the curse of the law; therefore my sin is taken away; therefore the judgment of...*

One will be able to take everything needed from these explanations to pass a well-founded judgment on the controversial question regarding the presence of the love of God in the work of justification. All who have researched the nature and powers of our **intellect** unanimously assure us that our spirit is far too narrow for two clear and distinct perceptions to dwell within it at the same time and produce different conclusions. And all who have the desire may learn from their own experience that this claim is certain and true. Two thoughts can indeed rise within us at once, but one will always hinder the other, preventing it from either properly clarifying and expanding itself or achieving anything firm and certain. What one gains in brightness and clarity, the other will lack. And if one succeeds in reaching a certain level of clarity that enables it to draw new conclusions or set the **will** in motion and heat, the other will be obscured and vanish before one even realizes it. To the assurance of divine **grace**, which is granted to us in justification, there belongs—as we have shown—a pure and clear per[ception]...

This enlightenment must instill a love for the law, as well as the courage, delight, and desire to obey it. ### §. VIII.

None of these components belonging to <term>repentance</term><note>German: "Busse." In the 18th century, this referred to a structured body of doctrine or learning rather than modern experimental science.</note>—things which can only arise from a clear, bright, and convincing understanding. **Approval, trust, and love can dwell nowhere else than where there is an infallible and engaging knowledge of certain doctrines and truths.** If these movements of the heart could renew an unenlightened spirit, they would either have to arise from nothing or be created by a miracle that would be unbecoming to the perfection of **God**. To know, to know without doubt by virtue of a testimony that can never deceive nor has ever been deceived, to believe that an inestimable and most-desired good has been acquired for us and belongs to us, and yet not to recognize this good as one's own, nor to accept it as one's own, are two things that cannot stand together. These two pieces, which we separate in our thoughts, are in themselves so undivided and inseparable that they constitute only a single piece. If the latter is missing, then the former is also not present. If the first is present, then the last is as certainly there as heat is accustomed to be with fire. And what would we see if we separated love from the fruits of the **Gospel**? Defects on both sides. On one side, a powerful thing that is nevertheless powerless. On the other, a living movement that has arisen without a cause. If the divine knowledge testifies that **God** is our highest good, **that Jesus is the only source of our righteousness and salvation**, and yet produces no love, then it is "living-dead" or powerless despite its power. If the voluntary and emphatic resolution of the will to serve **God** and live for Him alone is without love, then it has proceeded from itself and without a cause. **Law** and **Gospel** give birth to and maintain the <term>new obedience</term><note>The outward change in behavior and lifestyle that follows a true inner conversion.</note>. Suppose that this is absent and does not follow repentance; then one consoles oneself without reason or proof with the opinion that one has been reconciled with **God** and has performed the repentance required by Him.

We wish to use these general reminders to show in more detail that **repentance** can be equal for everyone neither in the measure of the parts of which it consists, nor in regard to its duration.
