Regarding the things that cause the duration and length of the **stirrings of repentance**, these can be dealt with without great long-windedness. *Often it is grace, often it is nature, often it is the sins* of men that are the cause why some come slowly and with difficulty to the enjoyment of divine grace and the true joyfulness of the spirit, whereas others, in a short time, reach the contemplation of God's goodness through all mists and clouds. Often nature <note>The author uses "nature" here to mean a person's natural temperament or psychological makeup.</note> is the cause of this. Many minds are of such a constitution that they struggle to move away from the thoughts they have once earnestly embraced and to exchange them for others; they find it just as difficult to change the movements of the heart they have once adopted and to swap them for others. Once they have properly grasped certain doctrines and truths, it is easy for them to spend days and months in the contemplation of the same, and almost impossible to turn their thoughts so soon to something else. If sadness, if love, if joy, or another emotion has seized their heart, it maintains its dominion for a long time and effortlessly rejects all other stirrings that one might wish to put in its place. It strives against nature that a person of this sort—unless the Lord wishes to act

<column-break/>

extraordinarily upon him—should traverse the path of repentance quickly. He will linger for a long time in the contemplation of his dangerous state and the sins from which it arose, and will be slow to resolve to go further. He will persist for a good while in the sadness that follows it, and sometimes almost fear the end of that sadness. This same thing will happen to him with the remaining parts that are counted as belonging to faith. His soul will, for a time, take pleasure in the contemplation of divine love in general, and only gradually gather the courage to apply this general knowledge to himself. And it may be that days and weeks pass before divine confidence, which takes all fear from the heart, reaches its necessary greatness in him. One finds people in whose understanding nothing invisible will take root *unless they have weighed it piece by piece and considered it from all sides for a good long time.* Anyone who wants to teach such people, for example, what meekness, what love, or what gentleness is, must first take everything apart, present one piece after another to his pupils, repeat what has been presented more than once, grant them space and time to consider each thing for themselves and look at it closely, and finally fit everything together and emphasize it until the weak spirit has made itself properly acquainted with this new concept. They learn nothing if one proceeds with them in haste and presents all the things they are to grasp and retain at once. The conversion of such a person will last longer than the repentance of another who can contend with many things at once with his understanding and quickly oversee a complex matter.

# The First Main Chapter

Often, human sins are the reason why people remain so long in anxiety and terror before the wrath of God. Is it not right that David should mourn longer and more intensely—he who endeavored to cover one of the ugliest sins, adultery, with another even more abominable, an assassination <note>The original German "Meuchelmord" refers to a treacherous or clandestine murder, specifically King David's plot to have Uriah the Hittite killed in battle to hide his affair with Bathsheba.</note>—than a person who, moved by the greatest danger to their life, allows their mouth to deny the truth that their heart cannot deny? Suppose that Judas, who maliciously and willfully delivered Jesus into the hands of his enemies for a handful of silver pieces, had taken refuge in the unfathomable mercy of God: would this traitor not have wept longer over his appalling crime than Peter, who had indeed fallen deeply out of an unfounded confidence in his spiritual strength, but had soon risen again?

Grace is often the reason why the repentance of some people is continued for a long time with no common intensity. God, who always arranges His chastisements according to the strength of men, will not leave a weak spirit—to whom sadness can easily cause harm and bring about dangerous accidents <note>In this context, "Zufälle" or "accidents" refers to sudden medical or psychological episodes, like fainting or fits of despair.</note>—for long in anxiety and unrest. And the very love that moves Him to shorten the suffering of this person will compel Him to let another, who can carry more and must endure longer if they are to be rightly purified, wait longer for His comfort. The spirit of many people is fleeting and light-minded. When the pain subsides, the memory of it and the causes from which it arose are half lost—

<column-break/>

Those who are of such a nature easily fall back into their bad habits if no deep wounds are inflicted upon the heart that cannot heal so easily. What the flightiness of the spirit does in these people is accomplished in others, who are nonetheless stronger, through a multitude of business affairs and through a restless way of life. How long does the pain of the "great ones" of this world last? They go through so many changes and are surrounded by such manifold impressions that an occurrence which is unbearable to other people appears tolerable and slight to them before one knows it, and is soon entirely forgotten. This is experienced by all those who cannot remain long with one and the same thought, or find so much to do that they can direct their mind to something specific for only a short time. One concept pursues another and is itself pursued by a new one, once it has killed and smothered the first. The repentance of such busy and restless people would not be steadfast if the Lord did not delay and test them longer than others. They must climb slowly and go gradually from one step of conversion to another, so that they do not plunge back down in the midst of the effort and return to their old state. Cheerful and lively temperaments, who seem to be born for joy, exert all their strength to completely root out the sorrow that has perhaps befallen them as soon as they have drawn just a little breath. Nature drives them to tear the ropes that have held their spirit for a time. How soon would these people again give ear to the lure and attraction of the world and its lusts if the Lord did not [apply] the Law more than...

->§. IX.<-

Those who are reconciled with God and have received the assurance of His grace are not, for that reason, exempt from the entire duty of humbling themselves before God and being brought low by the contemplation of their forgiven misdeeds. The evil heart, which unwillingly bears the chains placed upon it, often unexpectedly returns people to the slavery of sin—those who, immediately after completing their repentance, retire to rest and seek to completely forget the sorrow they have endured. Therefore, whoever wishes to firmly ground and strengthen his conversion must occasionally renew the regret and unrest from which the Lord delivered him, and reopen the healed wounds through the power of grace, so that the fear of God may remain in him and preserve his soul from falling away amidst so many temptations.

# Of the Nature and Character of Repentance.

### Explanation.

We almost believe that the doctrine we have provided here will seem new, strange, and unheard of to many. We claim that repentance, even when it has been completed, must nevertheless be continued. Does this not mean: that the means which leads to improvement and conversion must also be used at a time when it has become unnecessary and the sought-after goal has been attained? And is this not—if not entirely absurd—then at least dark and incomprehensible? A repenting sinner and a converted Christian who has been accepted into grace by God are two contradictory persons who do not fit together. He who is the latter no longer requires repentance; and he who still requires repentance, or stands in a state of penance, cannot claim the name of a converted Christian reconciled with God. It is well known and admitted by all that *a justified and renewed Christian* <note>Justification is a central Protestant concept where a believer is declared righteous by God through faith in Christ, rather than by their own works.</note> must do *daily repentance* and recognize the manifold failings that overtake him with remorse and erase them through faith. However, we are speaking of the repentance that is usually called "The Great Repentance." <note>The "Great Repentance" refers to the initial, profound transformation and turning away from sin that marks the beginning of a person's life as a Christian.</note> We want a Christian, to whom God has granted justification for Christ’s sake, to periodically step out of this blessed state in his thoughts, to give the Law back the power to confuse and terrify his soul, and to desire grace and mercy from the Lord anew. Is this necessary? Is it reasonable? Indeed, is it possible? Can a person divest himself of the grace he has received and feels within him, and gather a storm in his

->Part 1, Section II.<-

<column-break/>

mind, which is otherwise bright and enlightened? Can a person who has been healed and strengthened take back upon himself the pains he has lost, and long anew for the help and deliverance he has already obtained?

It will be necessary to completely uproot these doubts by first explaining what we mean by the continuation of the first and "Great Repentance." <margin>scribbled symbol</margin> To continue or renew repentance means nothing else to us than to imagine once again the unhappy state of wrath in which one lived before conversion; to recount to oneself in detail the sins committed therein; to thoughtfully weigh the displeasure of the Highest over these sins and the punishments that His justice must appoint for transgressors of the Law; and to hold before one’s spirit the invaluable grace received in justification through Christ. This is done so that one may be all the more secure against the snares of spiritual enemies and remain steadfast in faith. He who does this retains the assurance of his reconciliation with God and the spiritual peace in his soul, yet he possesses, in a certain way, the appearance of a penitent for as long as he remains in this contemplation. For his own benefit, he withdraws his thoughts for a short time from those things that refresh and uplift the heart, and instead shows them the things that previously caused him so much anxiety and unrest. Meanwhile, the conviction of his righteousness remains unshakable. He

VI. 17** <note>1 Corinthians 6:17: "But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with Him."</note>, can neither deny the light that has dawned within them, nor command the Spirit to cease being active in their souls.

This explanation of the matter at hand will let no one doubt the possibility of the counsel we have given. Just as it is possible for a man who has overcome a severe illness to represent to himself in thought the causes that brought him into this misery, the pains he endured, the love of those who willingly took on a portion of his distress, the skill and effort of the physician who snatched him from the danger of death, and the burdensome sensations caused by the remedies through which he regained his health—just as it is possible for one redeemed from death to imagine all these things, partly to awaken within himself care and caution to prevent new suffering, and partly to maintain love and gratitude toward his friends and benefactors: so too is it possible for a Christian united with God to set out of sight, in certain hours appointed for this purpose, the happiness in which he lives, and to renew within himself, as it were, the past restlessness of the soul in all its parts. We need therefore only show the necessity and the utility of this spiritual exercise, or demonstrate the obligation of the converted to this duty. We wish to give this proof all the clarity of which it is capable, and to lay down nothing as a foundation but such truths as every rational person has become acquainted with through his own experience and interaction with other men. It is first of all well known that we humans generally tend to forget nothing more gladly or easily than those things which have brought us shame and dishonor, and have moreover placed us in pain, sorrow, and unrest. # On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.

...which have given us honor and status, leave such deep traces in our brain that we hardly lose their memory and restore what might have been lost without effort. And because we find a new pleasure in the memory of enjoyed delights and honors, we refresh these traces so often and so eagerly that they can be erased neither by time nor by the accidents of life. However, the sufferings we might have to endure, and the signs of our weakness and vice, do not occupy our memory and our imagination with such force, because they are vexatious and unbearable to nature and self-love. And we are never particularly concerned to maintain them in the possession they might have gained. We feel again, to a certain extent, what we previously felt so reluctantly, and therefore we stop, as it were, our present pleasure when we occupy our spirit with the endured shame and anxiety. Therefore, we only rarely and reluctantly impose this work upon it. And if the old tragedy presents itself to us again, we are but negligent spectators and change the scene as soon as we can. The most intense pain and the greatest dishonor thus become as unknown to us over time as a long-vanished dream-vision, while a minor delight always remains known to us. The old proverb, that it is joyful and pleasant to remember one's past evils <note>This refers to the classical sentiment *Haec olim meminisse juvabit* ("One day, it will be pleasing to remember even these things") from Virgil’s Aeneid.</note>, is false if it is meant to signify that a person gladly dwells on the contemplation of his endured suffering. It can indicate nothing more than this—where it is to remain true—that a person rejoices when he

<column-break/>

thinks about how he was rescued from the evil. The end of his sufferings, the memory of the victory over his adversity, pleases him: and not the adversity itself, or the memory of the plagues that previously overwhelmed him. If we are so constituted, we must fear that our sinful way of life and the anxiety and unrest that the Law <note>In this theological context, "the Law" refers to the divine commandments which serve to show humans their sinfulness and their need for grace.</note> brought upon us with its threats, and the effort we applied to establish our reconciliation with the righteous Judge, will be diminished in our thoughts from day to day and finally be entirely withdrawn from our memory. The Saint <note>A term for the converted believer or one living a life of faith.</note> does not cease to be a human being who loves himself and his peace, and thus, as people are wont to do, he will be reluctant to let himself be disturbed in the enjoyment of divine love and grace by an image of his endured terror and the causes that produced it. Time will assist him in more easily defeating this supposed enemy of his contentment. And if, after the passage of several years, he considers it necessary for his encouragement to earnestly and devoutly remember the days of his spiritual struggle, he will perceive with wonder that the footprints of the same have almost entirely vanished in his soul.

We know further from an infallible experience that those who no longer know the misery and the danger from which they have escaped are closer to misfortune than they themselves think, and can be pulled back into the old evils by a minor temptation. # The First Main Chapter

...to visualize <note>The German *vorzustellen* here means to represent or vividly imagine.</note>, he possesses the most certain means of avoiding new sufferings and dangers. On the other hand, he who no longer knows what he had to endure before he was brought to the rest he now enjoys, is deprived of the greatest support upon which a weak person must <margin>H7</margin> lean when he is tempted to fall. How many would remain healthy if they did not forget that they had been sick, miserable, and plagued? And how many would conclude their remaining days in safety and peace if they remembered how unsafe and restless the days already lived through had been? For a Christian, nothing is quite as advantageous for his steadfastness in goodness as the contemplation of the state in which he found himself before he was enlightened, and the sorrow that overcame him when he received the first light of grace; and conversely, nothing is more harmful than the inability to remember those past hours of danger and unrest with emotion and vividness. One wakes up again, alert and refreshed, from the dangerous slumber that imperceptibly overcomes even the most sincere Christians amidst the daily alternations of work and rest, if, in the moments set aside for devotion, one can again take on the guise of the miscreant <note>The term *Missethäter* refers to a criminal or wrongdoer; in this pietistic context, it refers to the sinner standing before God's judgment.</note> who previously pleaded so longingly and eagerly with the Lord for compassion. In this state of humiliation, one draws fresh strength to meet temptations and to pursue sanctification. One stirs up a wholesome terror within oneself that makes us, for a time, insensible to our own lusts and the inclinations of the world. One blows, so to speak, the dying fire of love

<column-break/>

for God back into flame—for He took pity on us at the time when we were most unworthy and opened the entrance to His kingdom for us. One can easily imagine this if one only reflects on the behavior of a person to whom, in the midst of his disorder, the troubled and painful sickbed is shown, upon which he had to atone for the former errors of his life. How quickly, for such people, does the desire to continue the newly begun pleasure disappear? How easy it becomes for them to find reasons to withdraw from dangerous company? How swiftly do all the powers of reason gather to resist the impression of the senses and the imagination? And how happy are they generally to end the conflict between lust and virtue to their own benefit? Those, on the other hand, who can only remember in a general way that they were formerly sinners and enemies of God—who work in vain to form a pure and clear outline of their old malice, danger, and unrest—who have diligently cleansed their minds of all footprints of overcome anxiety in order to enjoy their present contentment all the more freely—they often fall when they think they stand, and find themselves without armor when the battle is most fierce. Daily repentance <note>original: *Busse* — This refers to a continuous process of penitence and turning back to God, rather than a one-time ritual.</note>, which is considered so necessary by all, must draw its best nourishment from that *first* repentance which pulled the person out of the dominion of sin. He who is to truly repent and atone for his daily sins must know how much the Law <note>In Lutheran theology, "The Law" refers to God's commands that reveal human sin and the need for grace.</note> can exert over the soul of a person who cannot deny his guilt, and how difficult it is to endure the sight of an almighty and righteous Judge whom one has offended.

# The First Principal Section

...consider useful, you may enjoy yourselves! Our imagination may be as capable and our memory as fortunate as they ever can be: yet they remain the powers of a spirit that is enclosed within certain boundaries and must yield to the power of the senses more than it would like. Daily new ideas, new sensations, new concepts, and images! Who can receive all these new guests so cautiously and carefully that the old ones still keep their place and are in no way offended or damaged? In a spirit as narrow as ours, the old must make room for the new if we do not wish to become unfit for this life; it must either give way entirely or contract so much that it can hardly move or expand when we wish to call upon it. And so, whoever finds a certain matter so pleasant and necessary that he considers its loss or damage to be his misfortune, must prepare a place for it within himself that cannot be disturbed. He must dig its foundation so deep that it can withstand time and daily changes. This occurs through nothing other than a slow and frequent repetition of all relevant things, which one must undertake at the time when the movements of the spirit have not yet entirely ceased. This effort, as it were, compels the soul to try whether it can connect this matter, which is so diligently and emphatically recommended to it, with the great and universal truths in a certain way that it cannot lose. ### §. X.

The benefit of repentance reveals itself in both the inner and 
outer life of the Christian. The converted person feels inwardly an 
inexpressible peace and satisfaction of the soul (Romans 14:17), 
a living drive to bring his heart into order, to always 
enlighten his understanding more, and to subject his inclinations to the will of the 
**Lord** (Romans 7:22, 24), and a divine capacity 
to carry out this drive and thus to become daily holier and more 
perfect (Philippians 4:13; 1 Thessalonians 4:1, 3). The external 
life of the converted person aligns itself with this inner change of the 
soul. It becomes ever purer, holier, more useful, and more 
similar to the life that our Savior led here below (Ephesians 4:13, 14; 
Matthew 3:8). In short, to summarize everything that belongs here: 
<margin>p. 455.</margin> The inner fruit of repentance is sanctification <term>Heiligung: the process of being made holy through spiritual growth</term>; the outer fruit 
is holiness of life or active godliness (Philippians 1:9f; 
2 Peter 1:8).

## Explanation.

We wish here only to speak generally and in common terms regarding the fruits of true repentance <term>repentance: the German "Busse" refers to a total change of heart and mind (metanoia), rather than just feeling sorry for sins</term>, so that we might not disrupt the order of things which we have resolved to treat in succession. Were we to involve ourselves more deeply here and present each new quality of the enlightened understanding and each new inclination of the sanctified will in particular, we would be presenting matters ahead of their time, which we shall have to speak of in detail in the doctrine of the State of Grace. Everywhere, the Scripture describes a Christian to us as a completely changed and inverted person; as a new creature; as a person who has become like a child (Matthew 18:3); as a warrior who is always watching against his enemies and daily obtains one victory after another over them; as a person who no longer lives for himself, but for—or according to the will of—Him who died and rose again for him (2 Corinthians 5:15); who is crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:19). And when the means is asked for, through which this great transformation must be effected, nowhere is any other named than repentance. What more is needed to convince anyone who is willing to see that repentance must produce special fruits both in the mind and in the conduct of a person? And how great, therefore, must be the blindness of those who know not how to name any fruit of repentance, and yet can claim that they have entered into the Kingdom of **God** through it? The world would laugh

<column-break/>

if someone said of a certain medicine that it had indeed made him healthy, yet had neither lifted the pains with which he struggled, nor the incapacity, nor removed the remaining causes of his illness. And yet this very world thinks that it speaks understandably and truthfully when it says that it has been healed and led to **God** through repentance, even though it can boast of no decrease in its former defects and impure inclinations. The Pharisees committed this absurd error in the times of John <note>John the Baptist</note>. They came to John, who preached repentance. They confessed their sins (Matthew 3:6). They allowed themselves to be baptized by him. However, they took the sins which they had confessed and, to all appearances, repented of, back with them again. They let them keep their former seat: and yet they claimed that they had performed repentance and comforted themselves with this imagination. John, who through a divine revelation looked into the souls of these foolish people and perceived this strange delusion therein, attacked it with a divine zeal and taught them what they themselves ought to have known: that repentance must bring forth fruits, and that where these fruits were lacking, no repentance had occurred. "You brood of vipers," he says, "who has warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" These words mean as much as: You fools, who are begotten of evil parents and have the same impure and absurd opinions regarding the service of **God**, the same sinful inclinations in you, which your fathers...

# On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.

...the fruits that are worthy of repentance, could they mean anything other than deeds that bear a certain witness to the internal good quality of the person who performs them? These few words thus contain almost everything that belongs to the essence of repentance. It must occur inwardly in the soul. It is a change of the thoughts and the counsels of the soul. The external signs of repentance can appear in a person, and yet he can still be without repentance. Repentance produces the resolution to fulfill the divine will. Repentance gives the power to carry out this resolution. From true repentance arise holy works pleasing to **God**. Whoever says they have repented and continues their usual way of life deceives themselves and others. All these teachings, and several others, can be derived without artifice from the words of John <note>Referring to John the Baptist</note>. We look here only at this truth, which is most clearly contained therein: Repentance brings inward and outward fruits. The Pharisees despised this instruction of the Baptist and learned its truth through a most lamentable experience. The Spirit of the **Lord** has allowed it to be incorporated into those books <note>The Holy Scriptures</note> that are meant to instruct us toward salvation, so that this misfortune might not befall us. And how many are there for whom the written word accomplishes no more than it previously did when spoken orally? Countless people, who condemn the disobedience of the Pharisees and are terrified by their misfortune, nevertheless retain their own opinion of repentance—the very opinion that brought about their disobedience and the misfortune that followed.

If only that which is called repentance is considered 

<column-break/>

and weighed, it will immediately become clear that it is a work from which great changes in a person must follow. Whoever has believed for a long time that nothing was lacking in their perfection and nothing stood in the way of their welfare, and unexpectedly realizes that the former was imagined and the latter is nearly lost, must—because he is a human being—feel the beginning of a strong change within himself. Just as those upon whose body a great weight falls that could crush them, pull all their life-spirits <note>Original: "Lebens-Geister." In early modern medicine, these were thought to be subtle fluids or gases that moved through the nerves to provide strength and animation to the body</note> together into their hands and arms without knowing how, and thereby become twice as strong as they are by nature in order to hold back impending death: so the intellect of such people gathers all its powers and sends them all at once after the rushing desires of the will, in order to bring them back from the road upon which they travel and at least bring them to a standstill. And they must obey, however strongly and violently they proceed. Even if they cannot be immediately steered onto another path, they are nonetheless prevented from continuing their usual course. What a commotion manifests in the soul of a man who wishes to die only in extreme old age, when a physician <note>Original: "Arzneyverständiger," one skilled in medicine</note> informs him that the cottage of his spirit <note>A metaphor for the physical body</note> is very dilapidated and will shortly be torn down due to his intemperance and disorder? He feels a capacity he has never felt. And the love of pleasure, which otherwise seemed invincible to him, is in a moment overtaken, shackled, and subjected to reason. # The First Main Part

...unless these new conceptions are again diminished or even erased, it is impossible for the old law, according to which the will was formerly directed, to regain its power. It may stir. It may strive for its old mastery. It may raise a mist through the imagination and the senses, whereby the insight of the understanding is darkened for a time. The truth that it sees will provide the rules according to which the will shall henceforth govern itself. It will instill in the will the desire to work against itself and grant a capacity to gradually take the life from its inclinations. If one finds a means to bring a hot-tempered person <note>original: "Jochzornigen," an archaic variant of "Jähzornigen," meaning one prone to sudden, violent rage</note> to believe, undoubtedly and constantly, that his violence will soon disturb his welfare and shorten his life; or to impress upon an ambitious man as an infallible truth that his ambition will shortly cast him down; then one has also found the remedy against the sicknesses of these people. Even if they do not yield immediately, they will nonetheless be gradually weakened and subdued wherever the understanding maintains its clear insight. We are no less moved when, so to speak, a previously unknown light spreads over things

<column-break/>

that promise us blessing, welfare, and peace. Who remains unmoved when pure truth forces them to confess that someone, who owed them nothing, applied everything they possessed—their life and their satisfaction—to ensure their safety? If nothing stirs of a desire for gratitude, nothing of a zeal to please his benefactor, nothing of reverence and love in the soul of such a person, then it is either false that he rightly recognizes the greatness of the kindness that has happened to him, or it is certain that he resembles unbridled beasts more than men. Who remains cold and negligent when he has been convinced by his own reason and the experience of many others that he must always remain unhappy unless he carries out a certain plan for his future conduct that has been presented to him? If, in such circumstances, one feels no drive toward a different life, no resolve to walk according to the prescribed rule, no power to make a beginning toward improvement, then the conviction of which one boasts must either be imperfect or the understanding must not be master of itself. How many people can be cited who have adapted to an entirely new way of life and gradually denied their most pleasant lusts <note>In 18th-century German "Lüste" refers generally to strong worldly desires or appetites, not exclusively sexual ones</note> after they were thoroughly instructed by a dangerous accident or through painful sensations that it was absolutely necessary for their peace and welfare to turn back? ### Of the Nature and Character of Repentance.

In some people, there is a drive for holiness, a will to improve, but it lacks power and life. In others, there is a certain capacity to produce some good thoughts and impulses—from which works follow that have the appearance of virtue—yet they are without delight and love. The former promise everything and fulfill nothing. The latter fulfill something but can promise almost nothing, because there is no ground for a firm hope and confidence, no true love within them. The former are stirred up by the weak light of literal knowledge <note>original: "buchstäblichen Wissenschaft," referring to intellectual book-learning without spiritual experience</note> and by the desire to be saved here or there—a desire innate to all men—to form an impotent resolution to purify their soul and dedicate their life to God; a resolution that is renewed daily but never takes root, passing away as quickly as it arose. The latter allow themselves to be brought by the threats of the Law, which they imagine, to the point that for a time they force their thoughts, restrain their impulses, and arrange their outward deeds according to certain commandments. The spirit, which loves its freedom, sighs under this bondage and seeks to disentangle itself. And it succeeds more than is good. What is extorted through fear and coercion is not lasting or constant. Therefore, nothing is more common than for these people, when they think they stand firm, to fall away and be led so far by a small temptation that they themselves doubt whether a capacity to sanctify themselves ever reigned within them. This inner sanctification extends to both powers of the soul. The understanding <term>Understanding: "Verstand," the cognitive faculty of the soul responsible for discernment</term> is sanctified to the Lord when the convert works untiringly to expand and deepen his knowledge. The dawn is so beautiful,

<column-break/>

that the saintly person wishes to see the full day and to behold the Lord ever more clearly. And the extraordinary benefit that this knowledge provides in the sanctification of the will strengthens and increases his longing. Thus, he never thinks his knowledge <note>original: "Wissenschaft"</note> is pure and perfect enough. 
<margin>p. 280. 286. 304.</margin>
He remembers that his previous misery grew out of his former blindness; that this alone held him fast in the snares of sin and the world; that this life is full of clouds and vapors that can imperceptibly fog the understanding again and rob it of its clarity; that within himself, his evil desires are the natural and greatest enemies of his enlightenment; and that a weak and fragile creature living in so dangerous a land as this earth is can never acquire enough light and clarity in the things concerning his highest welfare. He therefore strives to sanctify his understanding more and more to the Lord and perceives the progress and benefit of this effort. His drive is powerful. He does not labor in vain. One truth is gradually added to another. One part of faith after another is further transfigured and illuminated through the grace that assists him in his devotion and meditation. This is what the Apostle says: *We come from one glory to another. 2. Cor. III. 18.* <note>original German: "Wir kommen von einer Klarheit zu der andern," usually translated in English Bibles as "from glory to glory"</note> The understanding thus enlightened sanctifies the will. This power receives through the light that illuminates it a zeal to order and arrange its impulses according to the prescription given to it by the understanding. Knowledge and the skill to judge or to examine. The latter arises from the former. The former is the cause; the latter is the effect. Knowledge <note>The original German word 'Wissenschaft' here refers to a systematic body of knowledge or understanding, rather than the modern definition of 'science.'</note> is, in turn, twofold: what is properly called "knowledge" and "experience." This division does not distinguish the knowledge itself so much as the means by which it is acquired by humans. The entire holiness of the will, which is produced in repentance <term>Busse: In this context, the internal transformation and turning back to God</term>, is called love. The outward fruits are indicated by the phrases: "being pure and blameless" and "being filled with the fruits of righteousness," which we shall soon explain. The correctness of this division of the Apostle’s words will be obvious to every reader if we slightly alter the beginning of the usual translation. In our view, this beginning must be rendered as follows: "I pray for this, that your love may become richer, stronger, and more complete through all kinds of knowledge and experience." We give only a single small word—the word *through* <note>original: "ἐν" (en). The author is debating the translation of this Greek preposition, which Martin Luther translated as 'in' but which the author argues means 'through' here.</note>—which Luther translated as *in*, a different meaning, and we believe that here it is the same as *through*. It must be taken this way in many passages of the books of the New Covenant <note>The New Testament</note>. This is so well known to all scriptural researchers that the time we would spend proving it would be wasted. And that it cannot be explained otherwise in this place is set beyond all doubt by the subject matter being discussed. Knowledge is the foundation and the cause of righteous and true love. The darker it is, the smaller and more incorrect the love is. And the purer, greater,

<column-break/>

and clearer it is, the more faithful, honest, and well-founded the love is. Whoever wishes for another that love might become more perfect, constant, wise, and orderly in them must simultaneously wish that the things that must give love its heat and nourishment may become increasingly clear, familiar, and certain to their understanding. From this, it is simultaneously evident that the Apostle requests a twofold growth from the Lord for the Philippians: a growth of faith and knowledge, and a growth of love. The former is indeed explicitly named; but who does not see that the latter is also intended? If love is to become richer through knowledge, then it cannot remain as it was. It must also grow in both magnitude and clarity. Who does not know that causes must be reinforced with new strengths if they are to produce greater things and work and accomplish more than before?

He teaches that those who are converted and enlightened through both knowledge <note>original: "Wissenschaft"; in this 18th-century context, it refers to systematic or theological knowledge rather than the modern natural sciences</note> and experience attain an ability to distinguish the good and the true from that which has the appearance of the good and true, and to separate that which is more useful and blessed from that which brings no benefit and is not without danger. And this doctrine is one of those that prove themselves as soon as one simply knows what the words mean. A Christian has to do with two kinds of things: some concerning faith, others concerning conduct <term>Wandel: One's daily behavior, lifestyle, or moral path</term>. The former are judged according to the precept of the divine truth revealed to us; the latter are judged according to the rule of the law. Doubtless, the Apostle means both. It is just as dangerous to regard an error as truth as it is to hold an illicit act as permissible. He who has been rightly enlightened by the Spirit of Grace, through the Word and through experience, will fall neither on this side nor on that, and will just as easily recognize whether that which is presented to him as a matter of faith is in accordance with wholesome doctrine, as see whether the law permits him to undertake certain things. And the higher one rises in knowledge, the more proficient one becomes in this so useful and necessary testing.

It remains orderly in its intensity and never separates itself from wisdom.** The mocker—who compares this holy emotion with the reckless surges of certain people who allow themselves to be not so much governed by their imagination as carried away by it—finds his dismissal in these words of the Apostle. **The Spirit of the Lord says that the love of Christians toward God and their neighbor is a fruit of enlightenment and becomes more complete and richer through knowledge.** A person to whom one mystery of truth after another is unlocked, to whom one perfection of the Most High after another becomes clearer and more intelligible, who [sinks] ever deeper into the abyss of divine grace and love—

The other two words aim at one’s life. The first indicates the care taken to avoid forbidden works. The Greek word <note>The Greek word is *aproskopos*</note>, which in our translation has been explained by the word **Blameless** <note>German: *unanstößig*; literally "un-stumble-able" or "without offense"</note>, signifies sometimes a person who gives no one offense or opportunity for sin and error, and sometimes someone in whom no stain or fault is seen. One of these meanings is grounded in the other and refers to the other. He who causes no one offense or scandal is himself free from coarse and obvious faults; and he who cannot be reproached for sins and coarse faults

<column-break/>

will never lead others into sin and error through his conduct or through his words. There is a simile in this expression taken from travelers or wanderers. It can indicate a person who does not delay anyone else on the path they travel, as well as a traveler who himself proceeds incessantly and meets no hindrance on the roads he walks. Both meanings can therefore fitly be united here. A blameless person is a Christian who is diligent in omitting all deeds, words, and works that could either make him punishable or instill in others the desire to sin. The added words: **Unto the day of Christ**, do not place the true sense of the Apostle clearly enough before one's eyes. One should translate: **On the day of Christ**, that is, on the day when Christ will hold judgment over mankind; thus everything is much purer and clearer. We would only waste time to no purpose if we wanted to take the trouble to prove that the Greek little word <note>The preposition *eis*</note>, which was rendered by Luther as "Unto" <note>German: *auf*</note>, also signifies "On" or "In" in very many places. To whom among those who have read the New Testament in its original language is this unknown? And that it cannot well be taken otherwise in this passage of the Apostle is set beyond doubt even by the simplicity and clarity of the sense which these words yield when "On" is substituted for "Unto." # On the Nature and Quality of Repentance

...of the witness of Jesus Christ should be presented somewhat more extensively: so that you, when the Lord comes to judgment, may appear before His **judgment seat** <note>German: *Richter-Stul*; referring to the *Bema* or judgment seat of Christ</note> as people who have preserved the salvific teaching unadulterated and pure, who have sincerely renounced the sins and vices that the Lord hates, and through His grace have fulfilled all the duties He has prescribed according to their ability. The final figure of speech—*to be filled with fruits of righteousness*—presents the converted as good trees that have brought forth much fruit; as people who have not only guarded themselves against sin, but have also diligently performed the works that the Law requires. The Law commands, and it forbids. He who takes care not to act against the laws that forbid something is called **blameless**. He who observes what is commanded in the Law is a tree that bears **fruits of righteousness**. Scripture calls the works of the saints, which they perform according to the order of the Law, "fruits," because they—just like natural fruits—stem and sprout from an internal power. Here, they are specifically called fruits of righteousness. This name can be explained in two ways. A fruit of righteousness can just as easily mean a **righteous fruit** or a **righteous work**, as it can mean a work that is wrought and brought forth by righteousness. If we prefer the former explanation, then "righteousness" here is equivalent to the Law which commands righteousness: and a work of righteousness is nothing but a work that agrees with the Law, or, as Scripture otherwise speaks, a work of the

<column-break/>

Law. If we accept the other meaning, then it may be asked: whether the internal righteousness to which fruits are attributed here is the **righteousness of faith**, or the intention of the saint, wrought by faith, to walk and live righteously? Scripture uses the word "righteousness" sometimes in this sense, sometimes in that. If we choose the first, then the effect is named here instead of the cause, which happens in countless places. We wish to say this: the righteousness that follows from faith is established, and the faith must be understood. A work of righteousness will thus be a **work of faith**, or a work of love that has arisen from faith. If we choose the second, then a fruit of righteousness is a work that has sprouted from an internal drive to fulfill all the righteousness of the Lord. One can claim with a fair degree of certainty that the first meaning is the correct one, or that "righteousness" here signifies the **rule** <note>German: *Regul*</note> according to which good works must be framed, and not the cause through which they are performed. A fruit of righteousness is a work that is similar to the pattern of righteousness presented to us in the Law: a work that righteousness demands. And a person who is filled with fruits of righteousness, or bears many fruits of righteousness, is a Christian to whom the testimony is due that he has practiced **godliness** <note>German: *Gottseligkeit*; a term implying both inner piety and outward religious devotion</note> from the heart and has proven his faith through many works pleasing to God. We appeal, in order to confirm this explanation, to the words that are added: which [come] through Jesus...

We can therefore leave it undecided and safely use our translation. In the Scripture, the Greek word <note>original: "epichoregēsate," usually translated as "supply" or "add to"</note> never means anything other than "to provide" or "to grant." And here, we should not strip it of its usual meaning without a pressing reason. Imagine first that the word "soul" or "spirit" has been omitted, and that the Apostle meant to say: "Supply to your souls, through faith, the recounted gifts and virtues," or: "Adorn your soul with them." If one then replaces the little word *In* with the word *Alongside* or *With*—which can be done legitimately—then no further difficulty remains. We are surprised that some interpreters, to whom the reputation of scholarship and cleverness is otherwise gladly granted, have been unable to see any trace of a wise order in the listing of the qualities with which the spirit of a Christian must be adorned, and have therefore claimed that the Apostle named them indiscriminately, just as they occurred to him. How easily would one have set aside this somewhat offensive opinion if one had been willing to consider the words with proper attentiveness? There is more connection and order in this register than appears at first glance.

The holy man <note>referring to the Apostle Peter</note> divides all the perfections of a Christian's soul into the general ones, from which all other virtues flow and grow, and the specific ones, which are based upon the former

<column-break/>

and which in turn are the foundations and sources from which the specific duties of a Christian arise. There are three general perfections: Faith, Virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" (Tugend) implies moral excellence or spiritual power</note>, and Discernment <note>original: "Bescheidenheit," which in 18th-century German often referred to "discretion" or "judgment" rather than "modesty"</note>. Everything belonging to godliness—whether it remains within the soul or is brought to light—draws its life and its value from these three great perfections. And no matter how great a virtue or a work may be in the eyes of men, no matter how glorious or useful it may seem, it counts for nothing before the Lord and is of little use if it was not animated and sired by those three principal virtues. The specific qualities are divided into three categories, just like the duties that spring from them. We owe certain duties and works to ourselves, to God, and to other people. And these duties must have their roots in the mind of the Christian, or burst forth from certain internal qualities of the spirit, if they are to please the Lord. The roots of the duties we are bound to pay to ourselves are called, in Peter’s words: Temperance and Patience. The source of the duties directed toward God is called, in a word, Godliness. The internal causes of the duties owed to one's neighbor are brotherly love and universal love <note>often referring to "charity" or "agape"</note>. We hope that the correctness of this division will prove itself even to those who are not lazy in their reflection. We shall seek to promote conviction through a clear explanation of all the words.

To say much in few words: it is the confident conviction of a spirit enlightened by God regarding the truth of the Gospel’s teaching. This faith produces love, and through love, virtue. General virtue, of which we speak here, is nothing other than a powerful and unshakeable resolution of the sanctified will to carefully conduct itself according to every part of the divine law. This virtue, or this sincere resolution to obey the Lord, must be accompanied by prudence and governed by prudence if it is to bring the desired fruits to us and others. What is virtue without prudence? It is exactly like a ship left to the wind without a steersman. Such a vessel can just as easily be driven off course as it can be led into the harbor. It is exactly like strength and bravery used without order and without purpose. Jesus therefore commands His followers to pair their honest zeal with prudence. His Apostles repeat this command everywhere. And Peter thus places prudence among the first and greatest qualities of a Christian. The Greek word <note>original: "gnōsis," usually meaning knowledge</note> which we translate as "prudence" usually actually means "knowledge." In this context, it cannot retain that literal meaning because it refers to a quality that follows faith and stands alongside virtue. Luther, therefore, expressed its true value with the word "discretion." <note>original: "Bescheidenheit"</note> In his time, "discretion" in our language meant as much as "prudence"; and a person to whom we now give the name of a "prudent man" was then called a "discreet man." <note>The author is explaining a shift in the German language; in the 1500s, "Bescheidenheit" (now meaning modesty) referred to the ability to "bescheiden" or discern/decide wisely.</note>

It should not particularly surprise anyone that the Apostle says "knowledge" instead of "prudence." Knowledge is the mother and cause of prudence. And who does not know that in every language of the world known to us, it is permitted to name the cause and imply the effect? Furthermore, in Scripture as well as in secular books, it is very common for the words "knowledge," "wisdom," and "prudence"—by which the perfections our intellect is capable of are indicated—to often lose their specific meanings; they may indicate now one, now another of these three qualities, or sometimes several at once. The nature of prudence will be discussed elsewhere. Another remark regarding the words: The phrase *“Not lazy, nor unfruitful”* contains a graceful style of speech which orators usually call **understatement** <note>original: "Verkleinerung," referring to the rhetorical device of litotes, where an affirmative is expressed by the negative of its contrary.</note>. Those who wish to give their words a certain ornament and emphasis are permitted to diminish the thing they are dealing with, as it were, in order to make it all the greater and more significant. Being “not lazy nor unfruitful” thus means as much as: *Being very diligent and uncommonly fruitful.* That being fruitful means the same as performing many good works need not be told to anyone familiar with the writing style of the Holy Books. When these reminders are taken together, this meaning emerges from the Apostle's words: *Where these virtues are in you, and always grow, and always become more perfect, you will undoubtedly apply all diligence to sanctify your whole life to the service of God and [strengthen] your faith...*

The orders and constitutions which they prescribed for the great societies they accepted as their leaders are all based on this general reflection: No people can be peaceful and happy where everyone retains the freedom to act according to his own inclinations and impulses. **The First General Error.** All rational people who wish to establish the kingdom of virtue and piety in the souls of men in a certain way have presupposed that it only depends on the human will whether one wants to become pious and virtuous, or that one can improve and change oneself. The world must be very unknown to those who harbor the hope that a <term>doctrine of virtue<note>In the 18th century, "Tugend-Lehre" (Ethics) was often debated as a science that could be derived from reason alone, independent of religious revelation.</note></term> built on rational grounds—no matter how clear and distinct it may be—will seem easy, understandable, and well-founded to even a tenth part of a country.

These and several other errors, which we set aside for the sake of brevity, have not remained hidden even to those who otherwise, in their entire lives, cared for nothing so much as how they might

<column-break/>

draw people away from vice and move them toward a rational way of life. Socrates set aside all other learned questions that had been stirred up by the wise men, and maintained that man should concern himself only with how he might govern his heart. "What do we care," he said, "for nature? What do we care for the course of the heavens? What do we care for plants, animals, and so many other things that have hitherto been so sharply and precisely investigated?" Let us call our thoughts back from the world and turn them solely toward how we might improve our soul and arrange our deeds according to the eternal law that the highest God wishes to see observed. He reinforced this exhortation through his own example. He taught only virtue and lived according to the teachings he gave to those who entrusted themselves to his <term>discipline<note>Here "Zucht" refers to the ancient Greek concept of "paideia" or moral training and upbringing.</note></term>. Should one believe that this great man, who wished to hear of no science other than the doctrine of virtue, himself first doubted whether his instruction would accomplish much? And why "doubted"? He even believed that he, as well as all others, would labor in vain to draw the ill-natured man and bring him to an orderly and decent conduct. And yet nothing is more true than this. Socrates, that constant friend of virtue, is the first who raised the question so vigorously pursued among his successors: Whether man could be made a lover of virtue through discipline and instruction? One can divide those who wish to open and pave the path to virtue through reason into two main types. Some have taught the immortality of our souls and depicted the future world as a land in which these immortal spirits would receive the reward for their behavior in this world. Others have presented spirits as being just as mortal as bodies, and therefore denied all future punishments and rewards. It goes without saying that these two categories must be just as far apart in their rules of virtue and in their motivating grounds for virtue as they are in their opinions on the essence of the soul. The latter <note>Those who believe the soul is mortal</note> can be further divided according to the different intentions they had in their exhortations. Some have wanted to make a person virtuous in a certain way only so that he might obtain honor, dignity, and

Others for the end that they might create for him an inner satisfaction and true greatness of mind <note>Likely referring to the Stoic ideal of "apatheia" or emotional fortitude</note>. Others for no other reason than that joy and stillness might be preserved in civil society and that nations might be brought into a flourishing and blessed state. From each of these intentions, a distinct and special kind of moral teaching must necessarily grow. Yet, since those who have endeavored to achieve these intentions have been very different in their knowledge, their mental gifts, their experience, and their natural inclinations—and moreover, must very often frame their proposals and means according to what the countries in which they taught and the people they worked with would permit—far more such types have arisen. And these people, one will say, are nevertheless rational in very many things and act like the wise when their house must be managed, their children raised, or their servants hired.

We answer: Precisely this will be found in many of those who deceive the world with their false prophecies. It happens very often that reason is deposed from its rule in some of its territories—if we may speak this way—and yet continues to reign in the rest, because the advantage of man requires that it not be driven entirely out of its domain.

Those who preach virtue because it protects man from bodily pain, from vexatious and unpleasant sensations, and from the torment of the soul, are rightly held in higher esteem by the rational than the first ones we spoke of. Their intention is more laudable, and the virtue they demand is more honest and sincere. They cannot be satisfied with the appearance of virtue, because only the thing itself can provide the benefit they hope for. On the other hand, the means by which they wish to win friends for virtue are not so strong or powerful. For them, everything depends on this teaching: "Strive for virtue and flee the vices that oppose virtue."

People who surpass others in the capacity of the power of **imagination** are generally also more capable than others of feeling pain and **delight** vividly. It is not so very difficult to present a future **delight** or an impending pain to them so that they already believe they feel the beginning of it: however, it is uncommonly difficult to provide this painting with duration and constancy. The first **voluptuous** sensation, through its strength, clears the representation of a future pain out of the mind, and the first painful sensation clears the sketch of a future **delight**. What is the remedy against this flaw of nature? We will stay no longer. Matters stand poorly for the cause of virtue if **reason** knows nothing greater and stronger to dampen the charms of vice than the fear and hope of the punishments and rewards that **virtue** and **vices** carry with them.

...they claim that virtue must be sought and loved only because it is beautiful, because it provides the soul—alongside true nobility—with an inner satisfaction, a greatness that only a wise man can perceive and taste, and a tranquility that no external pain can disturb. "The madness of men!" he says, "who expect a reward for virtuous deeds outside of themselves, whether in this world or another, and who exercise violence upon themselves only with a view toward this reward. That is to reach for a painted cloud <note>An allusion to the Greek myth of Ixion, who tried to embrace the goddess Hera but was deceived by a cloud made to look like her; it signifies chasing a hollow illusion instead of reality.</note> and let the goddess herself go. A Sage strives for virtue because she is endowed with an essential beauty, and he is calm, satisfied, and composed in her possession, whether good or evil befalls him, whether he be honored or insulted, whether he lives in or out of pain." Reason teaches the Sage that virtue and vice are as certainly and naturally distinct from one another as light and darkness, and that the former is good and the latter evil. This same Reason instructs him that he must exert all his strength to attain perfection if he wishes to maintain the name of a Sage. And since there is no other way to perfection than virtue, it is clear in itself that a Sage must desire and seek nothing more zealously. He has everything once he has acquired it. He needs,

<column-break/>

in order to be comforted and calm, only to look upon himself. The order that he will find in his soul, and the harmony with nature and reason that he will encounter in his deeds, is a sight that will please him indescribably. It will equip him with a magnanimous contempt for all earthly and visible things, for all pleasures <term>Wollüste: In this philosophical context, it refers to "delights" or "exquisite joys" of the mind rather than carnal lust.</term> and all pains. An architect is delighted when he sees a palace that is built according to all the rules of art, even if it is inhabited by someone else. What delight, then, will the virtuous man not taste, who finds within himself—within his soul and his conduct—an imprint of that immutable perfection which no one but an ignorant person could undervalue? If there is a God, how great then is a Sage? He is equal to the Origin of all things; he is equal to God through his virtue. Does this thought suffer any discontent or unrest? If there is no God, then the Sage himself is a God. He is what God would have to be, if a God existed. What can displace such a man from his peace of mind? This speech sounds magnificent. And who can remain entirely unmoved when they first hear it? We could, if necessity required it, point out the passages from the Stoics and other ancient and modern Sages from which this is composed. And it would be just as easy to lengthen it through all sorts of thoughts—which sound even higher and more beautiful—from Seneca, Antoninus <note>Refers to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, the Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher.</note>, Confucius, and others. It will be more useful to investigate how much power lies within this to move men toward virtue, and whether it is possible to lead the world toward a rational conduct <insert>conduct</insert> according to this precept.

...the person, before he can make use of their instruction with benefit: Ignorance and **blindness of the spirit** <note>original: "Blindheit des Geistes"</note> prevent man from recognizing the beauty of virtue and his connection to it. The ambitious man will admit everything presented to him regarding the emptiness of the goods for which he strives so hard—provided he is not without reason—and yet he will not allow himself to be led astray in his course. He senses a secret pleasure <note>original: "Wollust" — in this context, it refers to a deep psychological delight or satisfaction rather than carnal lust.</note> when he sees that many regard him with wonder, and notices that this respect brings him great benefit in many other things. From this side he values honor, and not from the other, where it reveals itself as a passing dream or as a night-shadow. He can despise and love it at the same time, depending on how he views it: despise it when he judges it according to its essence, and love it when he considers it in view of his circumstances.

"If you have," says the Emperor Antoninus <note>original: "MARCVS ANTONINVS," better known today as Marcus Aurelius.</note>, (*) "an excessive desire for certain foods, then think to yourself: This is the carcass of a fish, of a bird, of a sow. It is sheep's wool dyed with the blood of a snail <note>A reference to Tyrian purple, a dye harvested from murex sea snails, which was an immense luxury in the ancient world.</note>. "Great Emperor!" the voluptuary and the lover of splendor will answer, having heard and weighed this teaching that sounds so respectable and wise: "Everything you say is true. My food is slaughtered animals. My wine is a lowly juice drawn from the earth through the vine into the grapes, cooked by the heat of the sun, and forcibly pressed from the clusters. <column-break/>

natural color. However, these contemptible foods refresh and delight me. This earthly juice cheers and gladdens me. This worthless garment gives me status, patrons, and access. And I myself feel a joy within me, which I cannot express, when I put it on. Were this not so, I would heed the filth not at all and gladly let it rot. What does it matter to me how the things I find in the world are constituted in themselves? It is enough that I become pleased and happy through the enjoyment and use of them. My desires do not arise from an error of my intellect; they arise from an internal feeling that neither you, nor other men, can stifle."

For many hundreds of years, the world has admired the saying of Epictetus: (**) "The things of the world themselves do not make men restless. Rather, the opinions of men regarding these things disturb their peace." And does he deserve such uncommon high regard? In our opinion, it is praise enough if one says of him that his statement is neither entirely true nor entirely false. Sometimes only our imagination tortures us. Yet, in countless occurrences, it is not the opinions that grieve and delude us, but the good and bad sensations that we either actually feel or wish to feel.

Why should we not follow this king, enlightened by **God**, in our teachings and exhortations, rather than certain melancholy enemies of the world and of mankind, who want to kill a person before he dies and would make the world a wilderness if they could?

Regarding the people who have taught virtue only insofar as it is a means to secure the peace and welfare of a whole nation, an entire work could be composed that could give occasion for many pleasant and useful reflections. He who wants to see quite clearly and distinctly how weak the reason of man is without a divine revelation, when

<column-break/>

"The folly and blindness of men!" a wise man will exclaim once he has completed this learned pilgrimage. How poorly have those who want to rule over the hearts of other men often known their own hearts? How unfortunately have even the most cunning spirits calculated, who wanted to determine and arrange the future fate of their countries through their commands? How poorly things would stand for the peace and security of the world if our **Jesus** had not torn the veil from the eyes of men and shown the world the foundations upon which everything in our times still rests that can be called happiness in a land? It cannot be denied that among the lawgivers of the ancient world, who wanted to make their nations virtuous in a certain way so that they might become happy, there were men of uncommon spirit who thought sharply and purely, understood the nature of our hearts, and through reflection and experience often arrived at praiseworthy designs. And what is more? Men who were driven by a sincere love of mankind and gladly wanted to put an end to the misery we bring upon ourselves through our restless desires. *Lycurgus* <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, credited with establishing the city's military-oriented social system.</note> was no ordinary mind. He thought, and what is even greater, he thought clearly and orderly. His plans hang together, all aiming at a certain purpose, all flowing from a few fundamental principles that can generally be accepted as indisputable truths, and they were, moreover, put into effect with a singular consistency and wisdom. We will concede even more. It is clear that this man did not mean ill by his fatherland, that he was master of himself and his impulses, and that he did not lack magnanimity, courage, shrewdness, and several other virtues necessary for important undertakings. However, what use are all these great qualities if a person has no other guide than his own reason? It happens very often that instead of the glory he hopes for, they bring him dishonor and shame in the eyes of posterity. Before *Lycurgus*, *Sparta* had been a sad theater upon which one bloody war and one internal unrest after another was performed, to the unspeakable harm of the inhabitants. *Lycurgus* took it upon himself to root out the causes of these great evils and to introduce such a government and way of life that eternal stillness and security would have to follow. Who can refrain from praising this intention? A man who strives to purchase the pleasure and peace of other people with his own danger and unrest seems to be something more than a mere human. # The First Main Section

...of the fatherland arose, and he soon found that they resided solely in nature and in the hearts of the citizens. He concluded from this that his people would never be happy if they retained their innate impulses and drives of nature. His first fundamental rule was therefore this: If my citizens are to be invincible against their enemies and peaceful within themselves, I must be intent on how I might change their nature and their hearts, making them into such people who have nothing more in common with other humans than their physical form and their ordinary weaknesses. All the institutions and orders that come from him are so many testimonies that he presupposed this rule and steadfastly directed himself according to it. And had he been able to find safe and certain means to carry it out, then perhaps the structure he established would still stand undestroyed. We wish to present his thoughts in the order they follow one another, so that one might have less trouble judging his entire work and its value. (*) The desires of men, which are directed toward honor, toward pleasure, toward wealth, and toward status, give birth to all the sufferings and unrest that plague the people themselves and ruin the prosperity of entire nations. However, these desires normally arise from the

<column-break/>

natural drives that reside in the souls of men. Therefore, if the desires are to cease, the natural drives must first be smothered, and the human must be transformed into a half-monster <note>original: "Unmenschen." In this 18th-century context, it refers to someone stripped of natural human feelings or "human-ness," rather than necessarily being "evil."</note>. To achieve this, which seems so difficult and almost impossible, two things are necessary. First, one must give such laws that are set in opposition to the impulses and drives of nature. Second, one must tolerate and permit nothing in the land through which these laws can gradually be deprived of their power, or through which the drives of nature—which are to be held back by the laws—might be provoked and awakened. Yet, how strong is nature? Will it not, regardless of how it is suppressed, rise up in a short time and shame all the diligence of the lawgiver? This concern can also be met. The fear of the wrath of the gods is stronger than nature. One must use the former so that the latter might be deprived of all desire for rebellion. If this cannot accomplish everything, then one must take self-love <note>original: "Eigen-Liebe." Here meaning vanity or the desire for social approval.</note> to one's aid and proclaim as shameful and indecent that which is actually in accordance with the nature of man. If, in addition, the intellect is suppressed so that it can gather no strength, then there is absolutely nothing more to fear.

# On the Nature and Character of Discipline <note>original: "Busse." In this 18th-century context, this term—usually meaning penance or repentance—refers to the rigorous moral and physical correction required to reshape human nature.</note>

The first natural impulse, which causes much evil, is the love of life and comfort, which is regarded as the cause of a long and contented life. Wherever this impulse reigns, timidity <note>original: "Zaghaftigkeit," referring here to a lack of courage or military spirit</note> first arises, which is the most harmful quality in a people who are to remain free and not fall under the dominion of the other nations that surround them. With this, many other desires are linked, which disturb the person themselves and set the citizens in strife and enmity. When does a man who wishes to live well and live comfortably ever stop wishing and desiring? When does he cease seeking new means to satisfy his cravings? How can a person so constituted remain free from envy toward those who live more peacefully and contentedly than he, or from malice and treachery, from hatred and resentment? And what is secure in a land where these inclinations rule? This impulse must therefore be uprooted before all things. It arises, however, primarily from two causes: from the sickly constitution of bodies and from a tender and soft upbringing. Thus, the entire community of Sparta must first consist of nothing but perfectly healthy and strong people, and no weak or powerless individuals—other than those whom age has enfeebled—shall be tolerated within it. To ensure that no weak and frail people sneak in, the newborn children must be put to the test by certain people appointed for that purpose. If it is found in this examination that they are not of a firm and durable nature, they must be immediately removed from the world and thrown into a certain abyss <note>A reference to the "Apothetae," a chasm at the foot of Mount Taygetus where the Spartans practiced infanticide for the sake of eugenics.</note> without mercy. It is

<column-break/>

better to destroy such weak creatures immediately than to burden the commonwealth with citizens who are fit for no great things and who might, by their example, instill in others the desire to live a quiet life. The strong and healthy must be raised from youth in such a way that they become ever harder and learn to calmly bear and despise both the greatest hardship and death itself. Away with all branches of learning <note>original: "Wissenschaften," meaning organized fields of study</note> that may indeed adorn the intellect but, in contrast, can soften and corrupt the heart! Sparta needs no orators, no doctors, no philosophers <note>original: "Weltweisen," literally "world-wise ones"</note>, no poets, no artists, no legal scholars. Away with all pleasant foods and playthings! A young Spartan must be drawn and accustomed to the hunt and to the most arduous exercises, to combat and strife, to audacity and boldness, as soon as he can walk properly. The greatest pain must be made tolerable and easy for him. To achieve this, all grown boys must be scourged and whipped until they bleed every year at the altar of Diana <note>The author uses the Roman name Diana for the Greek goddess Artemis. This ritual, known as the *diamastigosis*, was a Spartan test of endurance.</note>. And honor must season this sensitive pain. Whoever demonstrates the greatest patience in this sharp chastisement must be praised and lauded. Whoever flinches, cries out, or gives in must be mocked and scorned by all as an unworthy member of the fatherland. The female sex must not be exempt from this strict upbringing. Fearful and tender mothers give birth to timid, volupteous, and unhealthy children who harm the state more than they benefit it. Unmarried women must therefore, just like the young men, fight, wrestle, dance, and work, so that

### The First Main Chapter

...that they may become strong and not one day, through their untimely laments and tears, rob their husbands of their courage <note>original: "Herzhaftigkeit," a quality of being "stout-hearted" or possessing physical and moral bravery</note> and undaunted spirit. A people who are so led and educated can find no particular pleasure in this life, and will therefore forgo and surrender life itself—and whatever serves the preservation of life—without resentment. And who would dare attack such a people? Who would be able to overcome them?

The other impulse of nature, which causes much disruption in the commonwealth <note>original: "gemeinen Wesen," the 18th-century term for the public state or "common weal"</note> through the desires it generates and the vices that spring from those desires, is the love and inclination of one sex toward the other. Who can count the enmities, the crimes, the wars, the devastations, and the frenzies that have arisen from love and from the jealousy born of love? Who does not know that this passion <note>original: "Affect"</note> strips the boldest and bravest heart and turns heroes into children? And how often has a man in love betrayed and sold his fatherland—even his own kin—to reach the goal of his desire? No wise man would think of a complete eradication of this impulse. Nature, as well as the best interests of the state, oppose such an undertaking with equal force. However, one must work toward the goal that it never reaches such a vehemence that it can harm the peace of the commonwealth. It must not die entirely, because the people themselves would die out with it. Yet it must be half-killed and weakened. Love, in a word, must not remain a true love or a natural impulse. It must be turned into a state duty <note>original: "Staats-Pflicht"</note>, into a

<column-break/>

habitual custom, to which one submits more out of love for the welfare of the fatherland than out of personal inclination. And what is to be done to moderate the impetuous and boiling heat of youth to such an extent? The laws concerning the education and lifestyle of young people of both sexes are already as effective as a strong rampart against the assaults of love. People who are granted no time to feast their eyes, who are kept in constant labor and unrest, who must always strive, fight, and hunt with one another, who cannot be seduced by orators or poets, who receive no more food and drink than the highest necessity of nature requires—and even then, are permitted to consume only poor and poorly prepared nourishment—will not be so strongly tempted by the lusts of the flesh. If these laws cannot do everything, because nature is too powerful, then certain other regulations shall complete the work. One must first establish a kind of enmity and reluctance between the two sexes. To this end, on certain days, the youths and maidens must compete most sharply with one another in the presence of the authorities and the elders, striving to overcome each other. The less one party spares the blood of the other, and the more strongly they strive to triumph, the more they must be praised and lauded. Through these public and earnest combat games <note>original: "Kampf-Spiele"</note>, a quiet and perpetual jealousy and enmity will be maintained between both sexes, which will not easily allow any strong affection to break out. Therefore, if the state is to be happy and peaceful, if no internal war is to arise, and if no external enemy is to find anxious and fearful opponents, then all love of parents and children must be entirely banished from it. ...mysteries! That Lycurgus was of such a character as we have described him here is shown by his life, his death, and his entire state constitution.
