If one takes the trouble to examine the history of the Spartans, as far as it is known, one will realize that things never looked as beautiful and quiet among this people as is claimed; that the laws of Lycurgus <note>Lycurgus was the legendary lawgiver of Sparta, credited with establishing the city's rigid, military-focused social system.</note> were indeed read, praised, and in part upheld, but never fully observed; that nature always asserted its rights against them and made its strength known through all kinds of vices. The ethics <term>Sitten-Lehre: literally "teaching of customs," referring to moral philosophy or the code of conduct</term> of the Chinese is of a completely different kind and character than that of the Spartans. One can almost say that the one is diametrically opposed to the other. The lawgiver of the Chinese—whether it was Fohi <note>Fohi refers to Fu Xi, the legendary first emperor and culture hero of China, credited with creating the first laws and the writing system.</note> or someone else—built almost everything upon the very foundation that Lycurgus wanted to tear down. We might put it this way: if the latter [Lycurgus] wanted to dampen and kill the impulses of nature, the former [Fohi] believed that one could most safely use some of these impulses to make the people quiet, orderly, modest, and, if we may use the word, virtuous—and that one must therefore elevate these impulses and strengthen them with the utmost care. It seems that the oldest founders of the Chinese state concluded thus: nothing is more powerful and mighty in man than that which is natural to him. Whoever wishes to tame his heart and make him a peaceful and rational citizen must not set himself against man's nature. Rather, he must overcome man through himself and skillfully use the most common and usual stirrings of his heart, so that through these, he might be preserved from gross errors and excesses and brought to a state of stillness. It cannot be proven that the Chinese lawgiver actually thought this way. There is not enough light or sufficiently certain records to undertake such a proof. However, it is highly probable that he judged roughly so, because a large part of his ethics consists of certain inclinations, which manifest in all people, being elevated and driven almost beyond the bounds of reason. # Of the Nature and Character of Repentance <note>While the header mentions "Busse" (repentance or penance), the text focuses on the social and political motivations behind Chinese and Spartan moral systems, suggesting a broader context of moral correction or discipline.</note>

Take away the love of parents for their children and of children for their parents, the love of wives for their husbands, the love of brothers and sisters, and you have simultaneously removed the most essential means that the legislator deemed necessary to accustom the people to a decent and honorable conduct. One will be far less surprised by this peculiar distinction—which otherwise opens a wide field for many thoughts and reflections to a sharp mind—when one notices that these two lawgivers did not have the same intentions. The Spartan <note>Referring to Lycurgus, the legendary lawgiver of Sparta, who designed a society entirely focused on military readiness.</note> wanted to establish a state that was not only internally peaceful, but also capable of facing all external enemies through its strength and the bravery of its members. The Chinese <note>Likely referring to the legendary founders of Chinese civilization or Confucius, whom 18th-century European scholars often characterized as a "legislator" similar to those of Greek antiquity.</note> seems to have looked at only one of these two things. He strove only to cleanse the state he wished to found of internal enmities, unrest, and disruptions, and was, as it appears, entirely unconcerned about external enemies. We well see that this introduction will already sound quite new and unheard of to many, especially those who have persuaded themselves, or allowed themselves to be persuaded by others, that no people under the sun has more thoroughly investigated or more skillfully presented the teachings of virtue <note>original: "Tugend-Lehre"</note>, which can be recognized through reason, than the Chinese people. Having heard us, one may reject or accept this opinion. We shall count the former as no shame and the latter as no glory. It will surprise others that we have placed the ancient Chinese in the order of moral teachers who believed in no immortality of the soul, no punishments, and no rewards after this life. It is well known that various great and famous people in our times <note>A reference to the "Rites Controversy" and Enlightenment thinkers like Leibniz and Wolff, who argued that ancient Chinese philosophy was a form of "Natural Religion" compatible with Western reason.</note> have applied the utmost effort to present the faith of the first inhabitants of China as a brief summary of true natural religion. ### The First Main Section

...wanting to deter from vices through the fear of an eternal punishment. In this investigation, he can therefore be regarded in the same light as if he had denied the immortality of souls. We intend to explain our conception of the nature of Chinese virtue and the means intended to promote it as clearly and orderly as our ability allows, and as impartially as possible. And we can—if we may allow ourselves this boast—do so with some confidence and certainty. We have read all samples of Chinese wisdom published thus far with the intention of making ourselves thoroughly acquainted with its foundations. And if we have not miscounted significantly, we have not many more writings left to read in which the most capable people of our times have debated the nature and constitution of this wisdom. One will perhaps see from the matter itself that we have applied ourselves to sincerity in this effort and never intended to please one or the other of the contending parties. If, despite this, we have not been able to escape all errors, these should be attributed more to the weakness of the human intellect—which can err nowhere more easily than in such investigations that many have confused with great diligence—than to a culpable inclination of the will.

One can hardly judge the ethics <term>Sitten-Lehre</term> <note>Literally "doctrine of customs"; this refers to the systematic study of morals and social behavior.</note> of the Chinese at all if one does not first divide it into the ethics of the people and the ethics of the scholars who are meant to govern the people. This necessary distinction

<column-break/>

is so blindingly obvious to those who attentively and reflectively peruse the reports and accounts of this people that we must wonder how it could have been forgotten by so many acute and famous individuals. These two kinds of moral doctrine stand as far apart from each other as those which Plato and Pythagoras <note>Ancient Greek philosophers known for their "esoteric" (secret) teachings for a select few and "exoteric" (public) teachings for the masses.</note> presented to their weak and sluggish students (and through them to the common man), and those they presented behind a veil or in silence to the witty and great minds. The moral doctrine of the common man consists of a few duties necessary for keeping the people in peace, quiet, and industry, and for drawing them away from coarse vices that could be detrimental to the general tranquility. Its purpose is not to cleanse the heart of its natural disorder and to prepare it for a well-founded and righteous virtue. It is only intended to ensure that the external peace and prosperity of the empire remain inviolate and may grow at all times. It is as probable as anything can be that this is as old as this great empire itself, and that the first legislator of the Chinese—whoever he may have been—was a naturally clever and far-sighted man who wished to make the people who voluntarily submitted to him happy through their own efforts and to create a lasting and healthy body politic <term>Staats-Körper</term> <note>A common Enlightenment-era metaphor comparing the organization of a state to a living biological organism.</note>, if we may speak thus. No nation of all those who now inhabit the earth has an older or more certain history and chronology than the Chinese. To put it briefly, it is a doctrine of how a man who wishes to rule others wisely and rationally must be constituted, so that the happiness of the people and the well-being of the commonwealth are in no way disturbed, but rather built up and elevated through him. The father of this doctrine is the famous sage, Confucius, as the Jesuits usually call him, (*) whom all of China has revered nearly as a God and as the prince of all its wisdom until our times. (*) This name is, as far as we can judge, only an honorary name given to this great man for the sake of his virtue and merit. What this honorary name actually means is difficult to say with certainty because of the great disagreement among those who try to explain it. It is almost as uncertain how it should be written and pronounced. It is agreed that it consists of three distinct words: and the last two are, in the opinion of most, nothing but a title. It is well known that in the Oriental languages, honorary titles are not placed before the name, as with us, but are attached to the end of the name. Perhaps the titles explain it best, telling us that the whole name is best rendered in our language by these words: The venerable teacher or Doctor Cum or Con. However, how one should write and pronounce it is highly doubtful. He is called by some CVM FV CV, by others CONG FOV TSEE, by others CON FV SE, and by the Japanese KOOSI, or simply KOO. Despite all this, it is clear that this highly esteemed man bears a completely corrupted and false name in Europe. And for this, we believe, the Portuguese are to blame, who have immensely transformed and distorted all Oriental words and names.

# The First Main Chapter

...reclaiming the kings of the people and wishing to oppose the encroaching corruption.(*) We have neither the desire nor sufficient reason to dispute this claim. Rather, we must admit that he renewed, through his authority, the way of living and walking that had been prescribed to the people since the oldest times, and that he did not entirely invent the art of governing—which is especially considered his own invention—from nothing. As obscure as it appears in the writings of the Chinese (which are much older than Confucius), various passages within them are nevertheless of such a nature that they can be accepted as the first fundamental principles of his wisdom. These small sparks he has, by all appearances, fanned through his intellect and through love for his fatherland, until the light—or to speak more clearly, the science—arose from them, which has seemed so wonderful and excellent to the Chinese for more than two thousand years. He can rightly be called the father and author of a science who first brought it into a certain and clear order and arranged it skillfully, presenting it more clearly and extensively than had been done before.

The virtue that the founder of the Chinese Empire wished to instill in his people, in order to lay a secure foundation for the welfare of this great society, can be learned almost more distinctly and clearly from the common way of life introduced from time 

<column-break/>

immemorial, from the customs and habits of the land, from the education of the youth, from the examples presented to children and young people in schools for imitation, and from the laws and the manner of government, than from the ancient writings—which are valued in China almost as much as the Holy Scriptures are among us—and from the books of Confucius. In these writings and books, there is little clarity and order. If one reads them as attentively as possible, it will still be exceedingly difficult to extract a certain and coherent image of the people's oldest moral teachings <term>Sitten-Lehre</term>. One proceeds more easily if one pays attention to the things we have named, and afterward seeks out the fundamental sources in the understanding of the Legislator, from which these must necessarily spring. We will try to see if we can use both as we wish, in order to draft a sketch of Chinese political theory and ethics <term>Staats- und Tugend-Lehre</term>. If a great empire—these, in our opinion, were the thoughts of the first Chinese Legislator and his oldest successors—if a great empire is to enjoy a constant and everlasting happiness and never collapse within itself, then the entire people must be provided with and possessed of an infinite reverence, rooted in the soul itself, toward their ruler and all those who are employed by him for governance. ### On the Nature and Character of Discipline.
<note>original: "Busse." In this 18th-century context, this term likely refers to the "rectification of conduct" or "self-discipline" rather than religious penance.</note>

...reverence toward the Monarch, which is based on his splendor, his power, his birth, and other such external advantages, exists only in the imagination and can therefore be diminished by many causes, or even driven from its seat entirely. One must therefore, above all things, be intent on how such opinions might be planted in the mind of the people from which reverence toward their head flows like a natural and certain consequence. All families <note>The German word *Geschlechter* here refers to lineages or extended households</note> of such a state, whose peace and prosperity should not be interrupted by any great changes, must in themselves be well-ordered, satisfied, quiet, and content. It is absurd to imagine that a body can be healthy whose members are sick and faulty. And it is no less foolish to believe that a whole people can fare well when things look desolate, disorderly, and perverse in the small societies of which the people consist. If, on the other hand, all members of a body are well-constituted and fit to perform their tasks, then the health of the whole body is present: And if all houses of a great empire are peaceable, quiet, and inwardly well-connected, then the whole society cannot be afflicted with any particularly dangerous plague. One must therefore endeavor to introduce such a virtue and way of life into all houses that permits no discord, no disorder, no cares, and no unrest. These two things will accomplish very much, and yet not quite everything. The families, even if they are united and peaceful within themselves, can fall into enmity with other families over many matters; A

<column-break/>

person can conceive a hatred against another and, to satisfy this hatred, unite with others to suppress his enemy. These small wars can spread through many families and not only shatter their internal peace but also gradually draw large parties together, which bring the entire empire into distress and danger and can tear down all its welfare. How often has a slight enmity between two persons or two houses destroyed in a short time that which seemed, by all appearances, imperishable? One must therefore apply all diligence so that a certain general friendship and a mutual high esteem for one another be established throughout the entire people.

All duties belonging to the common and ordinary moral doctrine of the Chinese people relate to these three things: reverence toward the head of the country, the internal well-being of each family in particular, and the general friendship of the people—if this word is appropriate in this matter. There is no duty, no part of the established prosperity, no ancient custom, that could not be derived without coercion and effort as a consequence from these three main rules, or viewed as a means toward these three main objectives.

# On the Nature and Character of the Laws.

...which, the nature of the government, the education of the youth, and the other matters already mentioned above, into a sharper focus. The boundaries we have set for ourselves do not allow us to delve as deeply into this matter as might be done.

One will be satisfied that we show in general the manner in which the founders of the Chinese Empire connected their skillfully designed **clockwork** <note>In the 18th century, the "clockwork" metaphor was a popular way to describe a state functioning as a complex, self-regulating machine</note>, by what **driving-springs** they set it in motion, and what **weights** they hung upon it to maintain its course.

And since we concern ourselves only with the oldest and first establishment of the state, which was undoubtedly not as complex as the current one, no one can demand more from us.

Who will deny that, over time, many pieces were added to the initial design of the government by the kings and sages of the land, which the fathers of the Empire could neither think of nor dared to think of for lack of experience?

We wish first to see what paths were taken to achieve each of the three great objectives held to be absolutely necessary for the welfare of the country.

We will thereafter recount the general reasons by which they sought to move the people to a willing and sincere observation of the duties prescribed for the sake of these objectives.

It is here presupposed that we have not been deceived by those who have provided us with reports on the internal state of the Chinese Empire, the customs of the people, the rules of government,

<column-break/>

and other things.

We can presuppose this without fear, because all witnesses precisely agree on most of the things we shall cite, despite the fact that they are otherwise far apart in many matters and opinions, and indeed sometimes argue most vehemently against one another.

The people must first be instilled with the most perfect and deepest reverence—a true reverence of the heart—toward their ruler, toward all persons who hold power and authority from him, and toward his regulations and commands.

**Fear** is a bridle <note>original: "Zaum"; the author uses the metaphor of horse tack to explain that fear is a restrictive and fragile method of control</note> that breaks easily for the very reason that it is too hard and uncomfortable.

The reverence that arises from the senses and the imagination vanishes when dark clouds gather, and it never truly takes deep root.

A people that is to live happily and prosper must honor its regent externally because it is internally convinced that he deserves the greatest honor and esteem.

The person of the one who reigns must, therefore, be made as venerable in the eyes of the people as can possibly happen through certain opinions and institutions: And he who governs, on the other hand, must himself spare no diligence to make himself great, respectable, and venerable.

# The First Main Chapter.

...the people should believe that no one besides the Emperor could move Heaven to benevolence and mercy. And through the many hundreds of years that have passed from the time of this book until our own days, the many great changes that have occurred during these times have been unable to weaken or erase this ancient state doctrine. The Emperor sacrifices alone. His prayer alone is considered the pillar for the entire welfare of the land. All eyes are on him when a part of the empire looks gloomy and dangerous. And upon the first report of a great misfortune occurring here or there, he conducts himself according to the opinions and the will of the people. He shuts himself in his palace. He fasts and prays. He abstains from all pleasure and luxury as long as the plague lasts. And he alone receives the honor once the suffering has been overcome. It is said that Heaven allowed itself to be swayed by the humiliation and intercession of its Son <note>original: "Sohnes" — a reference to the title *Tianzi* or "Son of Heaven," the Emperor's role as mediator between the divine and the earthly</note> to set aside its wrath and displeasure toward the people.

These two opinions give the person of the Emperor an extraordinary luster, a more than human dignity, and a divine reputation that cannot fade as long as its causes remain immortal—that is, as long as the opinions themselves are held to be true. However, these are still only opinions resting on a weak foundation, which can therefore be corrupted by time, disgraced by reflection and reason, and conversely, cannot be rescued from this danger by any convincing proof. A single bold and daring mind, who has a desire for innovation and would rather rule than

<column-break/>

obey, is strong enough to lead a good portion of the people to the point where they cast away these errors and lower the ruler in their thoughts. He must never be unready to hear and receive the complaints of his subjects, never weary of answering them and helping everyone, and never so tired that it would be difficult for him to stand by those in need and raise up the fallen. He must always be watchful so that no unjust person can use his name and authority to oppress the people, and if a misfortune should occur, he must forget his own peace to restore the destroyed contentment of his own. It is not surprising that many among the Chinese rulers have lost sight of this great state doctrine—to which all rulers should reasonably bind themselves—and thought more of their own pleasure than of their people. ### On the Nature and Quality of Penance.

U u
<meta>catchword: Peo-</meta>

...love and esteem of their people through their tireless concern for the welfare of the same. The Tartar dynasty <note>original: "Tartarische Stamm" — referring to the Manchu Qing Dynasty (1644–1912), who were ruling China when this text was written</note>, which now sits upon the throne, yields in this matter to almost none of the older monarchs. A Chinese Emperor is a lord whom everyone serves with an inexpressible reverence so that he may serve everyone without ceasing; one who places his entire honor in the fact that his people might love him, and who is almost never at rest or left to his own devices, so that he may convince his subjects that he is not unworthy of the great privilege he enjoys. He does not cease to depict his paternal love with the most emphatic turns of phrase in all his writings and commands; and he lets no opportunity pass to show, through his arrangements and ordinances, that these words are not signs without meaning. Hardly does a shadow of a danger or a misfortune appear in any corner of his extensive empire than a swift message is sent to the court by his command. And hardly has the same delivered its report than he is in the deepest mourning and in the greatest labor to stand by those who suffer, or may suffer, with counsel and help. His face must not brighten, and his lamentations must not cease, until the tears of his citizens are wiped away, their need stilled, and the danger driven off. A father, he says in his public commands, must weep and work so long as it takes for his children to be comforted and satisfied.

And if one were even to add that this commendable behavior of the Emperors was an infallible sign of the excellence of the wisdom of <term>Confucius<note>original: "Confucius" — The Latinized name of the Chinese philosopher Kong Fuzi (551–479 BCE), whose teachings on ethics and governance formed the bedrock of Chinese statecraft.</note></term>, in which they are instructed from youth and which they themselves explain and present to certain state officials at specific times, then the mistake could rise no higher. This lord is despised if he is indifferent to the happiness of his country, and would be utterly lost if he wished to increase his highness and power through the misfortune of the people. The people value the greatness of their rulers much differently than we do. Among us, a monarch is called "great" if he strives to expand his dominion through all kinds of means and ways—whether they be according to justice or contrary to it—who overcomes those who wish to block his path to glory through cunning, prudence, and guile; who successfully leads and completes great and bloody wars; who strikes terror and fear into his neighbors; who erects magnificent works and palaces and forces nature through art; who maintains a numerous and richly dressed court; and who introduces every conceivable kind of amusement and draws people to himself through gifts and honors—

<column-break/>

—those who know how to invent new varieties of pleasures; who is diligent in filling his treasury and, to that end, is intent on how he might bring money and wealth into his lands. The Chinese person can be persuaded by no effort to recognize these things as the qualities of a great ruler. He measures the greatness of his Emperor by the magnitude of the work and burden that he undertakes and bears for the benefit of his people; he knows no other description of a great king than this: "A great king is a faithful servant of his subjects, who demands no more rest and ease than his concern for each and every one of his citizens will permit, and only takes a moderate portion of their surplus so that he may partly spend it on their protection and satisfaction, and partly set it aside." Therefore, those Emperors of the Chinese who formerly wished to eternalize their memory through the things by which our rulers generally become immortal—who built, who waged war, who loved splendor and luxury, who established costly and unnecessary works—have been portrayed in their history as little better than senseless and ill-intentioned rulers who forgot their purpose and disgraced and lowered themselves. This concept of the true greatness and perfection of a ruler is very closely connected with the opinions upon which the infinite reverence they pay to the head of the country is founded. He alone has the right to approach <term>Heaven<note>original: "Himmel" — Here referring to the Chinese concept of *Tian*, the supreme guiding force of the universe and the source of political legitimacy.</note></term>. He alone can move Heaven to grace and mercy. But a <term>Son and Deputy of Heaven<note>original: "Sohn und Stadthalter des Himmels" — Referring to the title *Tianzi*, implying the Emperor rules as the earthly representative of divine order.</note></term> must be like Heaven. Heaven is kind and loves humanity. It is never angry, except when mortals forget their duties. He who represents Heaven here on earth must therefore be of the same nature. From these thoughts follow others that have even greater significance. If he is of a different character, how can he please the loving and just Heaven? And what will he, who displeases Heaven, be able to achieve? What use will his sacrifices and intercessions be? And what purpose will a regent serve us who has no influence over the spirit of Heaven because of his own lack of virtue? We honor, we fear, we adore him because Heaven deems him worthy of its trust and blesses the people through him. If he has fallen from the grace of Heaven, then the reasons for our reverence are abolished. And do we not act sensibly in this case if we renounce our obedience to him and give his place to another who performs the will of Heaven more sincerely? Is it any wonder that a lord, who rules over a countless people who can think this way—who have often thought this way, and who have more than once acted according to these thoughts—seeks to win their love and reverence through constant concern for the welfare of the empire? <term>Confucius<note>The Latinized name of Kong Fuzi (551–479 BCE), the philosopher whose ethical system the author is scrutinizing.</note></term> does not populate the Chinese throne with such wise and virtuous Emperors alone. Fear and the desire for honor are the two most prominent teachers to whom these lords mostly owe their virtue.
<sig>Uu 2</sig>

<column-break/>

We wish to be brief: If the most vigilant and virtuous Emperor who ever governed China were moved to our lands and named the ruler of a European people, the entire treasure of wisdom that he brought with him from the school of Confucius would not prevent him from living as is customary at our courts, and seeking fame and power through the very same deeds and efforts by which they are acquired in our countries. And if the administration of the Chinese Empire were given to one of those who rule the European peoples, he would not first need to learn the moral teachings of Confucius to be fit to imitate the great examples of his predecessors: His own mindfulness would soon show him that his first and greatest care must be directed toward the welfare of the people if he himself wished to possess the throne peacefully and leave it to his descendants.

This is by far not all that we can bring to mind to demonstrate clearly that the peculiar love of the Chinese Emperors for their subjects is a quality that can only be called a "virtue" in a very broad sense. One can show from the internal constitution of the government that these lords must tear through a hundred strong bonds, with which they are surrounded on all sides, before they can become entirely negligent, lazy, and vicious. # The First Principal Part

*Kangxi* <note>The text uses "Chamhi," an older European transcription of the Kangxi Emperor, who reigned 1661–1722.</note>, who died only sixteen years ago, issued a decree to the governors and state officials when the fruits of the land were being consumed by locusts and other pests. (*) "Why is it," he asked, "that the fruits of our fields are spoiled and taken away by drought, by floods, by locusts, and by pests? Perhaps the Emperor himself is the cause of this misfortune, because he governs unjustly and poorly, thereby forcing Heaven to punish the people so that he might wake up and improve himself. Perhaps the high-ranking officials who govern the land so afflicted are to blame, thinking more of themselves than of the common welfare and losing sight of justice. Often distress arises from those who represent the person of the Emperor in the cities, if they do not proceed according to equity, and neither through their verbal instruction nor through their example do they guide the people as they should. Often everything in a land is lost because the laws are transgressed, ancient customs are neglected, and lives are led in a disorderly fashion. In such cases, the communion between Heaven and mankind is shattered and severed because hearts are darkened and corrupted. And then, plagues heap themselves upon us. Heaven, which is always inclined

<column-break/>

to do good, transforms its favor into hatred when men seem to have entirely forgotten their duties." The final proof is given to us by the last monarch of whom we know anything, *Yongzheng* <note>The text uses "Yong Tchingh," referring to the Yongzheng Emperor, reigned 1722–1735.</note>. It is well known that in the year 1731, the capital of the empire, *Beijing*, along with the surrounding area, was shaken by a terrible earthquake and almost entirely devastated and overturned. *Yongzheng* received the first news of this almost unheard-of misfortune while he was enjoying himself in a small boat on a branch of the river that had been diverted through his garden. Hardly had he heard it when he threw himself to the ground as a sign of his deepest reverence toward the Spirit of Heaven, and lifted his eyes and hands upward, full of humility and sadness. Some time later, he became his own public accuser. He had a document sent throughout the entire empire in which he confessed that his misdeeds and faults had kindled the wrath of Heaven upon his people, and that the misfortune would never have occurred if he had governed better and presided over the people with more wisdom and care. (**) One could not ask for stronger testimony that this ancient opinion <note>The <term>Mandate of Heaven</term>, or *Tianming*, the idea that a ruler's right to lead is granted by divine favor based on their virtue.</note> has not yet been extinguished in China. This belief is the reason why governors and judicial officers are punished and generally removed from their positions if important crimes and misdeeds are committed by some of the people in a province, city, market town, or village.

### On the Nature and Character of Repentance

...committed. The people, it is said, would not act so recklessly and wickedly if their guardians and overseers were not negligent, unjust, and vicious. And these wicked shepherds <note>The author uses the metaphor of "wicked shepherds" (*unartige Hirten*) to describe corrupt officials who fail to lead their "flock"—the common people.</note> could cause the ruin of the entire flock and prepare Heaven against them for vengeance, if the power that was given to them for the good of the land were left to them any longer.

It is easy to investigate why the oldest kings and sages wanted to see a doctrine introduced and constantly propagated that, by all appearances, is so detrimental and dangerous to the peace of the country and the majesty of the regents. A man who is aware that he will be burdened with the guilt of all the plagues that might arise will generally take the utmost care to ensure that no valid cause for hatred can be found in his actions and conduct; he will be intent on nothing so much as how he might prevent all evils and dangers. It was therefore considered useful and beneficial to give course to a harmful proposition <note>The "harmful proposition" refers to the idea that the ruler is personally responsible for natural disasters, which could technically incite rebellion.</note> in order to tame the highest heads of the land and their powerful ones. This was done to keep them from the abuse of their power and to accustom them to constant care and vigilance over themselves and the land. The intention has been partially achieved. The Emperor, as well as most of those who take part in the government under him, are eagerly occupied with winning the love and esteem of their subjects and either preventing all plagues or suppressing them in their first beginnings.

<column-break/>

Yet the greatest care of men is too weak to stop those evils whose causes lie in nature. One therefore prepares in time to make the storm that might arise bearable and to calm the discontent of the distressed people. One collects both money and stores of all kinds of fruits and things that might be lacking. And one distributes these so richly to those who suffer, as soon as their grievances become known, that the complaints cannot last long. The Emperors, as well as all those who bear the burden of government with him, do not wait until the people accuse them and proclaim them the authors of their distress. They present themselves as if they were the sole and true evildoers and testify to their repentance <note>original: "Busse"</note> and remorse through fasting, through tears, and through promises of improvement. The people are moved and won over by this because they conclude from these signs that their regents feel no less pain and unrest than they themselves feel. And since the people also see the diligence of their rulers in restoring the old state of peace and abundance through generosity and other good arrangements, the desire does not rise within them to take revenge on those who do not wish to deny that they have provoked Heaven through their sins and mistakes. We wish to conclude this section. It is, in our opinion, made clear enough that the virtue of the high and low authorities in China is not a virtue of reason and the heart, but rather a zeal generated and maintained by the fear of downfall and by the particular constitution of the state.

# The First Main Section

The second objective of those who established the Chinese Empire pertains to the prosperity of every household and lineage. Every house must be internally peaceful and well-ordered, and externally free from necessity and want. If every small society is so constituted, then the great society of the Empire must simultaneously flourish and be at peace. The virtues from which the external prosperity of households grows, and through which poverty and want are driven away, need not be sought far afield. If all members of a lineage are industrious and satisfied with what is available—if no laziness, no love of comfort, and no extravagance dwells in the houses—then enough is easily gathered for one's needs. Therefore, from ancient times, people have endeavored to recommend **industry** and **contentment** as the primary virtues to the people, and at the same time, to resist the vices that oppose them through wise laws. According to the will of the Lawgiver, a lazy person must be viewed as a plague upon the land and as a human being who shames himself. One lineage, just like any other, must be constantly occupied. The men must till the fields and never grow weary of improving their portion. The women must tend the silkworms, which spin the material for the people's clothing, and themselves weave and prepare the garments of the entire house from silk and cotton. A house must find all things it needs within itself: and no one belonging to it must desire more than can be provided and made through the diligence of the household members. This is how the old-

<column-break/>

-est design for the way of life appears, which the Lawgiver deemed necessary for the external prosperity of every lineage. Time, the infinite growth of the population, trade, many inventions that have emerged over time, and various other causes have immensely altered this simple sketch, introducing superfluous splendor, extravagance, and vanity, as well as lust and indolence into the cities and especially into the houses of the great. Yet a good portion of the people still generally follows the old rule. And the teachers of youth, along with the poets, constantly praise the times in which the entire people behaved in this way, no less than the Greeks and Latins are accustomed to praising the reign of Saturn <note>In Roman mythology, the reign of the god Saturn was considered a "Golden Age" of agricultural abundance and social equality.</note> and the so-called **golden age**. The Emperor himself does not cease to insist upon this constantly. Among the famous Imperial Edicts, which are continually recited and explained to the people, the fourth reads as follows: *The people shall, above all things, honor and hold in high esteem those who till the land and tend the mulberry trees, upon whose leaves the silkworms live. If this is done, one will never experience a lack of grain to nourish oneself, nor of clothes to cover the body.* The fifth decree is composed in these words: *Let everyone strive to maintain a prudent household and, to that end, practice contentment, moderation, and decorum. Whoever is endowed with these virtues will avoid a thousand foolish expenditures.* (*)

# On the Nature and Character of Repentance.
<note>original: "Busse." In this 18th-century context, "repentance" or "atonement" refers to the moral self-correction and the restoration of order required to maintain social and spiritual harmony.</note>

Without any doubt, it has required much reflection to determine those human qualities through which internal prosperity, peace, unity, and the connection of every lineage—which have been considered the surest foundation of the Empire’s happiness—could be established. The Lawgiver judged that every small society must resemble the entire Empire, or the great society of the whole people, if it were to persist on its own and if the Empire were to be preserved from danger and unrest. In the Empire, there is a single head, to whom all members show a reverence that has no equal; he, in turn, responds to this reverence with perpetual and untiring love and care. This harmony between the head and the members is the soul that gives life and orderly movement to the entire immense body. The members are all connected to one another in such a way that the smaller serve the larger without compulsion, because the latter are closer to the head; that the larger care for the smaller, because the former would themselves suffer and perish if the latter were disregarded and abandoned; and that those who are similar to one another in rank and dignity honor and love each other. This connection resists the evils that could attack and gradually consume the health of the body. Every house must be arranged according to this pattern. The father of the house must hold as much authority within it as the Emperor does in the Empire and must be served by all household members with the same reverence. He, on the other hand, must conduct himself toward his own in no other way than the Em-

<sig>Part I. Section II.</sig>

<column-break/>

-peror behaves toward the people, and he must constantly think of how he might build the happiness of both the entire lineage and all those who belong to it. Those who stand under this head must likewise be subject to one another in a certain way, so that the bond of unity may hold firm. After the husband, the wife must enjoy the greatest honor and love. Among the children, the eldest brother must have a privilege over the rest and be honored by his siblings as the third person in this small state. Both, on the other hand, must observe toward their children and younger siblings what the so-called <term>Mandarins</term> <note>Highly educated officials in the Chinese imperial bureaucracy who managed administrative affairs on behalf of the Emperor.</note> or Imperial servants are obligated to do in regard to their people. The others, who cannot be easily distinguished from one another by privilege or honor, must be united with one another through a sincere love. From people who are led in this way from youth and live in such a connection with one another, evil and disobedient subjects cannot easily arise. Rather, they will be willing of their own accord to observe in regard to the state and outside the house exactly what they have been accustomed to doing and observing within the house. All those who have seen <term>China</term> and are knowledgeable about the affairs of this great Empire agree—however much they may argue over various other things—that the founders of the same thought in this way and placed their hope of establishing a firm, peaceful, and imperishable state upon these thoughts. And even if they were in disagreement on this point, many other things, and primarily the books of the <term>Chinese</term>, which we can now read, would not [fail us...]

...cause one to doubt it. What has happened to carry out this great undertaking of bringing peace and unity to every lineage within itself?

First, those natural impulses and drives that bind parents to children, children to parents, brothers to one another, the wife to the husband, and the husband to the wife, have been declared the greatest and highest virtues, through which a human being must become truly perfect. It has further been deemed necessary to extend these inclinations, which nature itself instills in man, much further than reason demands, and to set almost no limits upon them. Finally, that particular impulse from which the most benefit was hoped—the love of children for their parents—has been fortified by so many supports and external fortifications <note>original: "Aussenwercke." A metaphor comparing social customs to the defensive works of a fortress.</note>, by so many customs and laws, that its effects must remain even if the love itself should die out and completely vanish within the soul. Among all the nations of the world who do not let their reason grow completely rusty, it is considered just and fair that a child should love and honor his parents, that a father should raise his children well, that a wife should be submissive and obedient to her husband, that younger brothers should defer somewhat to their elders, and that the entire house should guide itself according to the will of the head. Yet those who perhaps fail in these duties in some matters retain their reputation in common life and are at least safe from public shame and contempt. And nowhere is anyone offended if a child complains about the turbulence of his parents, if

<column-break/>

a wife considers it permissible to gently <note>original: "mit Glimpf." This implies using tact, mildness, or propriety when correcting someone.</note> set her unreasonable husband right, if younger brothers maintain against their elders that birth has given them the same rights, or if grown and married children believe that paternal authority has ceased and often prefer their own opinion to the advice of their parents. In China alone, those who commit even slight and common errors in these matters are immediately stripped of all respect and honor. And whoever acts more coarsely or simply persists in his small misdeeds is condemned by the unanimous voice of his entire country as a monster unworthy of life, and must fear that the laws will punish his moral failings <note>original: "Untugend." Literally "un-virtue" or vice.</note> most severely. The obedience and reverence of children toward their parents is almost more an act of worship <note>original: "Gottesdienst." This highlights that filial piety in China was viewed with a religious intensity that transcended mere civic duty.</note> than a duty commanded by nature and reason. The slightest violation of this obedience—a small resentment, displeasure at a strict command, a short delay, a thoughtless word—is a state crime that is tolerated just as little as disobedience toward the highest ruler of the Empire. What is more? Heaven, or the Spirit of Heaven, who is held to be the primary author of all the people's happiness, can be attacked and offended through words and deeds. Justice does not stir when this happens, and the laws do not forbid it. # The First Main Chapter

...allow it to be done: it is not enough that they set aside all their business and abandon their offices and services when those who sired them die, so that they might have the leisure to pursue their righteous grief unhindered; it is not enough that they spend three whole years after the death of their parents in the deepest silence and solitude. They are also bound to prostrate themselves before their lifeless bodies with signs of the utmost sorrow, to visit their graves, to place food upon their graves at certain times, and to preserve their images or at least hang small tablets in their houses upon which their names are written, which are called the seat or throne of their spirit <note>These are known as "spirit tablets" (*shenzhu*), which act as a focal point for the presence of the deceased relative during rituals.</note>. What is greatest of all: they are obliged to venerate their parents and ancestors up to the fourth generation in certain small chapels built for that purpose, using special ceremonies, sacrifices, incense, and other signs of the greatest reverence, just as if they were gods. It is easy to estimate for what end these ordinances were given. Through the service rendered to deceased parents and ancestors, the lawgivers intended to firmly ground and make inextinguishable the reverence of children toward the living within their minds. Is it to be presumed that anyone would dare to despise and offend a living person whom one must honor so carefully and holily after their passing?

<column-break/>

And they were not deceived in this opinion. No one denies that these customs are a proven remedy against disobedience and one of the principal reasons why examples of rebellious and insurgent children occur so rarely among such a vast people. The imagination is so moved and ensnared by these rituals that the heart cannot summon any strong impulse toward disobedience.

Doubtless, our opinion will be expected regarding this famous service that the Chinese render to their lifeless parents or their spirits. We shall therefore briefly disclose it. It is known to the whole world with what intensity the legates of the Roman See <note>original: "Römischen Stuls," referring to the Papal authority in Rome.</note>, who were sent to China to proclaim the Christian faith, fought for many successive years in the past and current century. They argued whether the honor which Chinese laws commanded to be shown to the deceased was a form of idolatry <term>Idolatry: the worship of a physical object or person as a god, which was strictly forbidden in Christian doctrine.</term> and a harmful superstition that newly converted Christians must renounce, or whether it was an innocent custom brought about by the statecraft of ancient lawgivers and therefore could in no way dishonor the faith of a Christian. The Jesuits maintained the latter. The Dominicans and Franciscans defended the former. (*) The former have,

This service will nonetheless remain reprehensible because it is very dangerous and can give rise to actual idolatry <term>Abgötterey: the worship of a false god or idol, as opposed to the "true" God.</term>. It is certain that the customs belonging to this service are all of such a nature that those who perform it can think of almost nothing else than that the spirits are actually there and acting as spectators. Even if it is not commanded to believe that they are present, it is certainly not forbidden to anyone either. And everything is so arranged that the Chinese are, as it were, invited to fall upon these thoughts. 

It is certain that no service can be more similar to a true and proper idolatry than this one. The Emperor, who is also the High Priest of the realm, does almost nothing else when he sacrifices to Heaven than what happens in the assemblies of the lineages <note>The "assemblies of the lineages" refers to the family or clan gatherings for ancestral rites.</note> who must honor their ancestors and parents. And there is a special circumstance in these customs that can uncommonly promote this conclusion. The Master of Ceremonies <term>Ceremonien-Meister: an official who directed the complex ritual protocols of Chinese state and family life.</term> gives, when the act is completed, a short speech to those who attended it, and assures them that they can henceforth promise themselves all earthly happiness, health, wealth, abundance, long life, and whatever else is pleasant to man, after they have paid their ancestors the due reverence. 

He does not say that the spirits to whom they brought the service would give or request these goods for them. It is highly believable that the meaning of his speech is only this: that Heaven will let them lack no happiness because they showed themselves so humble and reverent toward the spirits of their fathers. However, how soon does the common man mix two things together that are so closely related as these two? What help has it been in the Roman Church <note>The author, likely a Protestant, is using the "Chinese Rites" controversy to critique Catholic practices regarding saints.</note> that its most sensible teachers have so often reminded the people: "The saints whom you call upon are not those who give you the good you wish for. The vast majority of nations in the world have drawn from **religion** the greatest motivation for an honorable and orderly life, and through their leaders, have had the vengeance of the **gods** in this world and the next proclaimed to the wicked, and their grace to the **pious**. The matter becomes even clearer if one adds to these passages the customs still in use today, the common opinions of the land, and the public service performed by the **Emperor** and his officials. It all comes down to roughly the following propositions.

In the visible **heavens**, which span the earth like a vault, a living and powerful Being has dwelt from eternity, much like the soul within its body. At a certain time, this **Spirit** dried the earth—which was then a shapeless mass flooded with water—through his powerful influence and the force of his rays, bringing it into its current state and order. Scarcely had this happened when living creatures arose, able to inhabit and further cultivate the cleansed soil.

From the Earth, eleven other men were born who reached an equally great age. From the lineage of Heaven descend the first **princes and founders** of the Chinese Empire. Heaven loves mankind and is very inclined to do them good, because they received from him the power to think—or **reason**—and would never have emerged from the womb of their mother, the Earth, had he not made them fit for procreation. He therefore continues to shine upon and moisten the earth so that it may further produce the things that human life requires. Beyond this, to prevent all disorder that might hinder the fertility of the earth, he has placed certain spirits, sprung from him, over the mountains, valleys, rivers, forests, and other things. He demands no special worship from the people for these benefits. He is honored enough if the laws and rules are observed which he has made known through his son, the **Emperor**. And these are easy and all aim at the welfare of mankind. No one else is so high or worthy that they could perform an acceptable service to him. He who is sprung from Heaven himself, the Emperor, is the only one who may lift his hands to him and offer the **sacrifices** that please him.

All new and unusual phenomena in the visible heavens are, as it were, the voices of the Spirit that animates the heavens, through which he reveals his will. Therefore, the heavens must be carefully observed by certain people appointed for this purpose, so that everyone—especially the Emperor—may quickly learn how the Spirit of Heaven is minded and might avert the evils that may strike the land. We ask that particular attention be paid to this latter point. It is the true reason why the Chinese have, from time immemorial, placed such great value on astrology <term>Stern-Seherey: literally "star-gazing"; in this historical context, it refers to the state-sponsored observation of celestial events interpreted as political omens</term> and have observed the course of the heavens with such diligence. Will those who have rightly considered this passage and various others that are just as clear, be able to continue praising the ancient religion of the Chinese as a perfect and divine religion? The number and the magnitude of the attributes and perfections which the oldest Chinese sages attributed to the Spirit of Heaven <term>Geist des Himmels: a translation of the Chinese concept of 'Tian' (Heaven) or 'Shangdi' (Supreme Deity)</term> can hardly be determined. Yet one may think as well and favorably of him as one wishes; one must still admit, if one does not wish to reject the most certain reports, that compared to the God presented to us by revelation and sound reason, he is a very small and insignificant God—a God who lacks the very best and most important attributes—and that the fathers of the Chinese took no pains to correctly explore the nature of the eternal and infinite Being from whom all things come. Is it then impossible for a people to be pure of polytheism <term>Vielgötterey: the worship of many gods</term> and of idol-worship, yet still be ignorant of the one true God?

One must therefore fear that he <note>Referring to "Heaven" or the divine influence</note> will withdraw his kind and powerful influence if he notices outrage and rebelliousness. However, the first of these motives has never been touched upon by the <term>moralists<gloss>Sitten-Lehrer; teachers of ethics and social behavior</gloss></term>. And if it is permitted to speculate—as is likely in such an obscure matter—the **Emperor** in the most ancient times was not appointed as the first and sole teacher of the empire so that the people might be more conveniently and easily steered toward virtue through his authority, but rather so that the people would not be presented with all sorts of teachings that could harm the peace of the **commonwealth**.

The other reason is made almost entirely unusable by two things. First, because it is never asserted that Heaven punishes individual families, persons, or humans for the sake of their vice, but it is always claimed that the greatest part of a community or a country must be corrupt if Heaven is to pour out its wrath over the inhabitants. Afterward, it is because the guilt is shifted onto the **monarchs** and their servants when great plagues break out over the land; the leaders of the people are even identified as the sole cause of the vices and misdeeds of the **subjects**. It is therefore certain that the bond which connects virtue with religion in China is almost invisible, and that neither one nor the other would be lost if it were cut entirely.

In place of religion, two other helpers and assistants have been joined to virtue, which over earthly-

<column-break/>

minded and fleshly men indeed possess no small power. Those who judge best of the **ethics** of the Chinese nonetheless unanimously admit that one is accustomed to fire up the minds toward obedience through the hope of **fame** and **honor**, and partly through **examples**. No people in the world is more careful than this one to single out those who distinguish themselves through their virtue and to honor them both in their life and after their death. 

For these reasons, they have never wanted to know anything of <term>hereditary nobility<gloss>Geschlechts-Adel; status passed down through birth rather than earned through service or character</gloss></term>. Virtue alone ennobles: and he who is born and raised in a wretched hut often climbs through his commendable conduct to the peak of the very highest dignity of the empire. The high and low magistrates are bound to keep the most diligent watch whether some in their territory show special proof of their industriousness, their love and reverence toward parents, their politeness and modesty, and other virtues, and to give report thereof to the court. 

And the court does not delay in testifying its high esteem toward these people through great titles, posts of honor, and indeed even through gifts. It is nothing unusual that a countryman who farms his field better than others, or a craftsman who through his untiring industry and skill provides well for his own, is moved into the highest ranks of the country through the title of a **Count** or **Duke** <note>The author uses European titles to approximate Chinese ranks such as Gong (Duke) or Hou (Marquis) granted for merit.</note>. ...deceased, made immortal through triumphal arches and honorary columns, which are adorned with great words of praise. And all of China is filled with such marks of honor, which the Emperors themselves or their officials have erected to the glory of the heroes and the virtuous of the land. Often the deceased are elevated to higher dignities after their death—titles they earned during their lives—in order to stir the envy and ambition of the living. Is it not more to be wondered at that in a land where virtue is so highly valued and rewarded, so many vicious people are still found, than that many spare no effort to earn themselves a place among the virtuous? 

The examples, which are the other great means of helping virtue forward, are partly dead and partly living examples. <note>The "dead examples" refer to historical biographies and recorded deeds of ancestors.</note> Young people are told from their earliest childhood, both in schools and in homes, of the praiseworthy deeds and actions of the famous and great people of old that the country can boast of, and they are encouraged to take these as models for their own conduct. And this is almost the most distinguished part of the instruction that the youth enjoys. They are not held back with abstract rules, doctrines, exhortations, logic, or causes. The teachers all believe that one can accomplish much more with youth through examples, and therefore they rely almost exclusively on this path. The living examples, upon which the whole people should look to learn virtue, are the Emperor with his house and court, and all those upon whom he has laid a portion of the burden he carries. According to the fundamental principles of the empire, the Emperor himself must do what he demands of his sub-

<column-break/>

-jects. His house must be so ordered and arranged as he wishes the house of every citizen to be ordered and arranged according to the principles that he constantly has preached. And the counselors, the governors, and other officials must, in turn, take the pattern of their whole conduct from him. The oldest laws therefore command that the Emperor himself cultivate the field at a certain time, <note>This refers to the ritual plowing performed by the Emperor to emphasize the importance of agriculture.</note> that he himself instruct his children and court officials and urge them toward a decent life, so that the fathers of households may see their own duty reflected in him. 

They also intend that his consort <note>The Empress</note> should show the women how they are to behave in their houses through manual labor, by tending to mulberry trees and silkworms and other such things. <note>Silk production was considered the pinnacle of female domestic industry in traditional Chinese thought.</note> They demand that the Emperor, as well as all who belong to him, observe the ancient customs—and especially those ordained for the remembrance of parents and ancestors—as precisely as the lowest citizen, and that he encounter his mother or grandmother with no less reverence than the least child of his subjects is duty-bound to do.

Has this then always happened, one will undoubtedly ask here? And if it has happened, by what arts could such great and powerful lords be brought to such a forced and tiresome way of life? We answer to the first point: that it has neither always happened so perfectly, nor does it happen now, as it should have occurred according to the strictness of the ancient laws. At times, lords have ruled over China who held their personal freedom higher than the wisest regulations of the Fa- <note>The text cuts off here; likely leading to "Fathers" or "Forefathers."</note>

Since the beginning of the empire, to prevent ill-intentioned rulers from ascending the throne, the **Emperor** has been given the power to choose his own successor, from whom he can expect a restoration of the example of **virtue** to the people—a virtue they will one day lose when he passes. And if an **Emperor** even now wished to set aside his love for his kin in this manner, he would find no resistance anywhere. If the hope the **Emperor** has placed in his successor fails, and if the latter shows a total aversion to the old lifestyle of his predecessors once he has reached the government, he finds so many obstacles in his self-chosen path that we cannot recount them all. All respect and love for him are lost: and yet upon this depends the entire peace and security of his reign among a countless people, who would rather die themselves than witness the downfall of their ancient **customs**. He is worshiped as a god so long as he walks according to the **ways** of the fathers, and hated as a plague upon the land if he abandons them entirely. Everyone knows how much power these two reasons have over the minds of men. Yet they are surmountable. One only needs to put new and different opinions into the heads of the people than those they have heard from youth, and their concept of **virtue** and true honor changes. And what use are examples once this has happened? Precautions have therefore been taken against this danger. From ancient times, the people have been forbidden all communion with other nations, and all travel to foreign lands has been most strictly prohibited, so that they might learn nothing other than what they ought to know, and might not be led astray in their thoughts concerning virtue and honor. They have even sought to root out the desire to see anything strange or foreign, which naturally arises in many. This is undoubtedly the reason why the **Chinese** were convinced from the beginning that all other nations were beastly, irrational, and foolish, and that wisdom—

<column-break/>

—had settled nowhere but in their own land. From this has arisen the unbearable pride with which this people is afflicted, and their contempt for all other men, about which all who have become acquainted with them complain.

All who are not entirely incapable of thought may now judge how much praise and esteem this common **Chinese virtue** deserves, and how fine and glorious the means are by which they have sought to make it popular. The virtue itself is no virtue of the soul or the mind. It requires no wise or rational arrangement of the thoughts, movements, or desires of the heart. It presents man with no noble or grand purpose. It consists of a small number of certain duties that are not particularly difficult, which aim solely at the peace and security of the empire and the earthly welfare of every generation, while allowing the impure desires of our heart as much freedom as they wish. What is a virtuous **Chinese**? A man who honors his **Emperor** and all who stand directly beneath him as if they were visible gods; who carries natural love for his kin so far that it almost turns into folly and irrationality; who hates idleness and luxury; and who, in common life as well as on special occasions, deports and conducts himself according to the prescriptions of the **Register of Ceremonies**. <note>The *Liji* or *Book of Rites*, a foundational text of Confucianism that details the social forms, administration, and ceremonial rites of the state.</note> These qualities do not prevent him from granting his desires everything they want. Man is by nature lazy and disinclined to exert the power of his understanding. He loves himself immensely in this and thus wishes to be as great in the minds of other men as he is in his own heart. # The First Main Chapter

...one might consider the causes which destroyed the remaining empires of the world. China possesses such an advantageous location that it can hardly be overrun and conquered by other peoples. It is protected on one side by a stormy and impetuous sea, and on the other by arid and rugged deserts that stretch far and wide. A long time passed before the inhabitants of these deserts, the Tatars <note>The author uses "Tattaren" (Tatars) to refer to the Manchu people who established the Qing Dynasty in 1644.</note>, became so powerful that they could venture against such a formidable nation. Because they had gathered so much strength, a Great Wall was set against them, which they could not easily scale. They finally became masters of the empire anyway, after they were willingly let in during the previous century <note>The 17th century.</note> to serve as allies in an internal war. This change of rulers, with a few exceptions, was unable to cause any particular change in the government. Prudence drove the new regents just as strongly as the simplicity and ignorance in which they were raised; they resolved to become "Chinese among the Chinese" so that they might rule the Chinese. Is it any wonder, when one considers this, that the Chinese Empire has endured much longer than the other ancient empires that have long since passed away? If one gave this empire the same location as Greece, Egypt, Syria, or Persia, and then asked whether it could have maintained its original state in those parts of the world for so long? Whether it would not likewise have been destroyed long ago? That the internal form of the empire, the laws, and the style of government remained intact in their main essentials is no greater miracle. One generally stays—

<column-break/>

—with established and ancient customs as long as one learns no others. The ancient laws of the Chinese forbid all trade, all communion with foreigners, and all travel to foreign lands. This order has ensured that the court, as well as the people, have always remained in love with their own customs and laws and have never thought of improvement. Those who have made themselves somewhat familiar with ancient and modern history will agree with us on this matter without resistance. It cannot be unknown to them that almost all the peoples of the world do not abandon the institutions and laws of their ancestors until they are either led astray by the customs and instruction of foreigners who have settled among them, or have seen new opinions and practices on their travels which please them better than their paternal ways. And perhaps we would be a good deal happier, healthier, and more peaceful if this could not be proven from the recent history of our own fatherland! Our descendants will, unless we are entirely mistaken in our conjecture, see the truth of this reminder much more clearly. China has stood open to Europeans since it was conquered by the Tatars, and trade with foreigners, which was previously forbidden, is now permitted. In all likelihood, this communion with foreigners will gradually weaken and tear down one piece of the old way of life and government after another, and create no fewer changes than among other nations.

# On the Nature and Character of Repentance
<note>The original heading "Von der Natur und Beschaffenheit der Busse" refers to moral reformation or penance. In this context, the author uses it to introduce the moral "reformation" of the Chinese state through Confucian ethics.</note>

*Catchword: more; Marker: Part I, Section II.*

...of those which Confucius prescribed for those who are to rule the people. This man is so famous among us, and has been portrayed in such different colors, that we believe our error would be overlooked if we were to depart from our main purpose for a time in order to provide a detailed report of his life, intentions, and teachings. We rightly hesitate to take full advantage of this liberty, and will content ourselves with mentioning as much about him as we deem necessary for those who wish to reasonably measure his greatness and merits in general. Who was Confucius? How great and wise was he according to his understanding and science? How virtuous and orderly was he according to his will? There are not yet so many reliable accounts of him among us that these questions could be answered fundamentally. Yet we know enough of his circumstances that they should not be left entirely unanswered. One can assemble a picture of his virtue and wisdom from his history and from his books, which at least very much resembles them, even if it does not represent them perfectly. Confucius was by nature a profound man, very inclined to order and stout-hearted, of a physical constitution that allows for no violent and strong passions, gives almost no inclination to the lusts of the senses and the imagination, and tolerates no lightheartedness or instability. The natural love for order that dwelt within him awakened in him a strong aversion to the perverse way of life that was then in vogue in China, and especially against the vices of those who

<column-break/>

ruled the people, and an earnest resolution to restore the innocence of the earliest times and to give a new life to the almost forgotten orders of the fathers. His profundity opened the way for him to this great and laudable undertaking. His reflection led him to the root of the vices he hated, and showed him that the wise laws of the ancients would achieve little if the heart were not first brought into order and provided with a sincere inclination to obey the laws. He therefore resolved to devise and present an art of governing the heart. He considered it unnecessary to burden the common people with his rules of virtue, partly because they were too weak and dull to grasp them properly, and partly because they follow anyway if they have great predecessors. The oldest laws of the Chinese demand it anyway of the regents, that they should instruct the people through their example. We have seen above that from ancient times the common maxim: **As the King, so the people** <note>The author refers to the Latin proverb *Qualis rex, talis grex*, meaning the people mirror the character of their leader.</note>, has been accepted as an indisputable truth, and therefore the freedom of the Emperors was so carefully restricted. Confucius retained this opinion of the fathers, which is confirmed by constant experience, and judged that he need only betake himself to the courts, or offer his wisdom to those who were one day to be used for government. His natural courage supported this intention and broke through all obstacles that stood in his way. And his innate constancy—we had almost said stubbornness—drove him to continue the work he had begun incessantly and not to give it up entirely before his end. Another, who

# The First Main Chapter

...seeks, and that which the orator and historian have added from their imagination is set aside, then errors appear in his intellect, errors in his will, errors in his way of living and interacting, which can hardly be excused.

What shall one first judge concerning the intellect of a man who never concerned himself with the things from which all connection of people to a virtuous and orderly life must arise, and yet wants to lead them to virtue and wisdom? Who leaves standing those important questions from which alone something certain can be concluded about the purpose of man, his nature, and his duties: What is man? To what end does he live? Does he have a law? Or has he none? Is he entirely perishable, or only in part? Has he something to fear when he dies, or nothing? What is the nature of the Highest Cause <note>A common Enlightenment-era term for God or a Creator</note> that gives him life and origin? He, I say, leaves all these great questions undecided—and what is "undecided"?—entirely unexamined, and yet wants to show the way to true happiness and contentment. We do not wish to agree with those who consider him an enemy of God and all divine service. It may be that he maintained within himself a vague concept of an eternal cause of all things. It is said that he taught that men received their reason from Heaven and that Heaven must therefore be feared and honored. If that is so, then he apparently believed exactly what his countrymen have believed since the earliest times of their empire. However, would a

<column-break/>

sharp and penetrating intellect have allowed itself to be satisfied with this meager science? Would he not have risen higher than the common people <term>Pöbel: The uneducated masses or "the mob"</term> and exerted himself to the utmost to get to know this world, mankind, and the author of the world and mankind more precisely? Would he have done it differently than the great minds of the Greeks and the Romans, who established schools and invented new types of wisdom? All these, as well as the rest who became great and famous through their shrewdness among other nations, allowed themselves no rest until they had worked their way out of their doubts regarding these things in one way or another. Confucius alone among all the sages lived and taught as if he never thought of them, or as if they concerned neither him nor other men. His best friends admit that he mentioned God and His attributes, the soul and its nature, and the future state of souls with hardly a word. One may think what one will of the cause of this strange behavior. We have not been able to refrain, when we compared his entire life with the same, from concluding for ourselves that it lies in the constitution of his intellect. The intellect of very many people is only bright from a certain side and otherwise dark everywhere else. Generally, these are people who are naturally gifted with mediocre powers of the mind and afflicted with a certain strong inclination of the will that suppresses all other desires. This inclination of the will encourages the intellect to turn all its strength to the side toward which it is itself directed. Through this effort
