# On the Nature and Quality of Repentance <note>original: "Von der Natur und Beschaffenheit der Busse." This header is unusual, as the text continues to discuss Confucius; it may refer to the broader theological section of the book or a printing error in the original volume.</note>

...the spirit, bestowed with a fair measure of ability, gains a great insight into some things and remains in the rest as dull and simple as the spirit of a shepherd or a plowman. He is like a piece of iron that the craftsman has sharpened only in one spot for a specific purpose and has otherwise left raw. The science of these people fills the eyes of most, who have neither the time nor the capacity to sharply examine the depth of their understanding. And thus it often happens that they achieve uncommon fame and, especially after they have died, seem to entire peoples and lands like earthly gods. Their weaknesses, which kept many from venerating them as long as they lived, die with them: and the good qualities, which made them so respectable to many during their lives, remain alone in their writings and teachings. No wonder, therefore, that their honor increases after their passing and is ever more elevated by time, which otherwise tears everything down. If we are not greatly mistaken, the great Confucius <note>The Latinized name for Kongzi (551–479 BCE)</note> belongs to this category. An innate, strong drive for order, to which no other violent natural desire was added, forced him, as it were, to draw together all the power of his understanding—which in itself was not the least—to invent reliable means against the confusion that had greatly corrupted his fatherland in his time. To that end, he read the books of the ancients and found some instruction for his undertaking therein. He followed these tracks with his understanding and did not cease reflecting until he had devised the rules of art <note>term: Kunst-Reguln; here meaning systematic principles or social mechanics</note> that, in his opinion, could restore to the shattered China that state of

<column-break/>

rest and happiness in which it had stood at the time of its childhood <note>A reference to the idealized early dynasties of Chinese history, such as the early Zhou</note>. Everyone who has looked into his writings or considered his deeds knows that he did not wish to invent a universal wisdom. The narrow space of his spirit could not accommodate such extensive intentions, and the work commanded of him by his will occupied all its powers so strongly that he could cast his eyes nowhere else, nor fix his thoughts on anything else. He thus became wise and sensible on one side and remained ignorant and simple on the other: wise in things concerning the earthly happiness of his fatherland, but blind and senseless in the important matters that a prudent man must rightfully investigate and explore first.

We find another sign of his constrained and mediocre intellect in his doctrine itself and in the manner of his presentation. His teaching consists of all sorts of propositions and rules that are neither properly connected among themselves nor derived from certain and clear reasons. Furthermore, he has let many rational sayings be heard which are so little related to the first principles of his teachings on virtue and government <note>term: Tugend- und Regierungs-Lehre; the core of Confucian ethics and political philosophy</note> that one can regard them as children without father or mother. He often says what should happen: and that which he commands is sometimes entirely in accordance with reason. However, the weight is missing. He has named no cause why his command must be kept. And in the few general doctrines that he most diligently impresses upon others, one also seeks in vain for the ground...

### The First Main Chapter

->The basis of the duty he prescribes.<- Who will deny that in this disorder, one recognizes a man who could not properly organize his own intellect? He was indeed so rich in reason that he could perceive the distinction between good and evil—which is written into the hearts of men—better than many others, and could discover many individual truths of the law; yet, at the same time, he was so poor that he could never collect and arrange them in the way necessary to convince and captivate the mind. He is no Zeno, no Euclid, no Aristotle, no Plato <note>Refers to the great systematic thinkers of Ancient Greece; the author argues Confucius lacks their logical structure</note>, who, as wise master-builders, laid a specific foundation and applied themselves to linking all the pieces of their teaching correctly and rationally. He is like an artisan who can neatly craft many individual pieces belonging to a comfortable dwelling, yet can neither hew and lay the foundation stones nor assemble his supply into a whole; or like a general who is skilled at recruiting soldiers and leading them toward the enemy, but unskilled in forming a proper battle array. We readily admit that it may be possible for a practiced and sharp-minded man to bring the wisdom of Confucius into a systematic arrangement and set it up in such a way that it resembles a thorough science <term>Wissenschaft: In this 18th-century context, this refers to a structured, academic system of knowledge rather than just the physical sciences</term>. However, whoever wishes to take this effort upon himself will have to add much from his own treasury if the building is to become firm and steadfast. And on the other hand, he will have to cast away various teachings entirely, because they would distort his building and displace its order. And even suppose that neither this nor that were necessary—suppose that everything fit together easily and naturally—is it not itself

<column-break/>

bad enough already that this wisdom requires such an artisan, and does not become truly useful until a foreign master has shown how the Chinese man *ought* to have thought, if he had been able or willing to think rationally and wisely?

A man, however clever he may be, who demands that people improve themselves according to his prescription as soon as they have heard his instruction—obeying truth and virtue and never straying from them again—knows human nature very imperfectly and betrays his own lack of understanding. A wise teacher, who rightly examines his own heart before he sets out to work on the hearts of others, knows beforehand that he will have to sow seeds abundantly and wait a long time for a good harvest. What is more difficult to tame than nature? And what is our naughtiness other than our nature? Those who are of a different mind and imagine that everything must yield to their words and reasons without resistance cannot complain of injustice if they are reminded that they have left a large and necessary piece of true knowledge untouched, and must sharpen their intellect far more. And this, after all, was the mistake of the great Confucius. As wise as he believed himself to be, he was yet so simple-minded <note>The author uses "einfältig" (simple-minded) here to critique Confucius's alleged naivety regarding human stubbornness</note> that he thought everything must lie down at his feet as soon as he spoke, and live and walk just as he saw fit. He was raised to one high office after another. He soon became a judge, then a governor, then a privy councilor. The King of Lou <note>original: "Lou," referring to the State of Lu, the home state of Confucius in ancient China</note> made him

He was not dismissed because of his virtue; rather, he resigned and fled as soon as he noticed that everything could not be tuned exactly as he wished. After leaving the court of *Lu* <note>Original: "Lou," referring to the State of Lu, the birthplace of Confucius</note>, he traveled from one land to another and refused to settle anywhere, because he found nowhere such willing inhabitants who were ready to turn back <term>umkehren: Literally "to turn around," this word is often used in a religious sense for repentance or conversion</term> and follow him immediately. At last, weary of his unrest, he shut himself in his house, satisfied himself with a moderate number of students who came to him, and finally died full of resentment and displeasure at the disobedience of the world—especially the great lords, who would not allow themselves to be guided by him. "What is the use?" he said at last to his students. "Kings do not wish to guide themselves by my teachings. Of what further use am I in the world? Nothing remains but for me to die." He departed the world with these thoughts: Kings and their peoples must become wise and virtuous the moment truth and wisdom are presented to them. If they improve slowly, or not at all within a certain time, they do not deserve for a wise man to remain with them. He must move on and seek another court that is more eager to learn. His historians <note>Original: "Geschicht-Schreiber"</note> know how to artfully frame this behavior and depict it as a sign of a noble and sublime spirit. <column-break/>

This—which we have taken as testimony that his intellect was not properly enlightened, and perhaps could not be enlightened in all respects—serves us at the same time as a key to his heart. We ask all those who have closely observed the ways of men and the causes of those ways: whether it cannot be clearly inferred from this that the desire to rule and to be the sole authority contributed immensely to his great movements, and was the fire that chased him from one country to another? He overlooks the common folk and attaches himself only to those who can grant him great service and offices. We admit that this does not make him entirely guilty. The old rule of his country comes to his aid here, which dictates that teachers of virtue should conduct their business at court. However, he becomes quite suspicious when one considers this: He seeks a country or a court that is inclined to leave the entire government to him alone and to follow his head in all things. And he finds what he seeks. This alone brings us almost to the thought that the courts in *China* in his time were not as fundamentally vice-ridden and evil as his friends depict them. In a few days, these destroy everything that Confucius had built. However, this cloud will pass with time. My Lord will gradually come to himself again from his current intoxication. His previous rational behavior shows that his heart is neither entirely evil nor his understanding incapable of distinguishing between good and evil: And this very fact is as good as a guarantee that he will not always be in a frenzy. I will, as long as his delusion lasts, remain quiet, do as much for the good of the people as is permitted to me, and watch for every opportunity to set him right again. This steadfastness is even commanded by the laws of the Chinese. The Overseers <term>Censors; officials in imperial China whose duty was to monitor and criticize the conduct of the Emperor and the government</term>, who have been assigned to the Emperor since ancient times, must not allow themselves to be deterred if he will not immediately grant a hearing to their exhortations. They are bound to repeat their requests and representations without ceasing—now in this way, now in another—and not to relent, even if they see the utmost danger to their lives before them. Confucius takes the measure of his duty neither from reason nor from the ancient laws of his country. He attempts it: And who knows how wisely and cautiously he may have attempted it? He tries to see if he can lead the King back to the path he has abandoned. And since the King will not immediately follow, he resigns his office, leaves the court, and sets out again on his old pilgrimage. Does one not clearly see here a stubborn and haughty man who could bear no resistance and believed that an injustice was done to him if everyone did not recognize him as their sole master and conqueror

We must not particularly oppose those who are perhaps of the opinion that the natural love for order, which we granted him above, contributed much to his becoming immediately vexed and rebellious when he saw disorder and disobedience. This opinion is nothing but a detour that ultimately leads to the same goal. He who loves and promotes virtue and order only because it pleases him by nature, loves them for his own sake and for the sake of his own pleasure. He actually loves himself, and not virtue: and what he seems to endure for its sake, he endures to please himself. Such people, when considered on their own, are not much greater than those who cannot tolerate any weeds or confusion in their gardens, or who walk away in a huff if a lute player offends their ears with false notes.

We are persuaded that the latter can be surmised with much justification, and that Confucius, through his untimely and incautious speeches of punishment and exhortation—and perhaps even through some other things that are even harder to excuse—brought so many enemies and persecutors upon himself. We have already remarked that the courts in China could not have been quite so vicious and depraved in his time as his friends are accustomed to claim. How could such a strict and serious teacher, a man who could tolerate no appearance of lust, pomp, injustice, greed, and other vices, have found so many friends and patrons in such a decayed country who elevated him to the highest positions of honor for the sake of his wisdom? Is it common, in lands where vices—and indeed the worst vices—have the upper hand, to place an itinerant <note>original: "herümlaufenden"; literally "running about." The author uses this somewhat dismissive term to describe the wandering nature of philosophers who traveled from state to state seeking patronage.</note> sage at the head of the government as soon as he merely lets himself be heard? And if he has resigned from a court and place out of stubbornness, to be accepted again elsewhere immediately? From whence, then, could these great persecutions and sufferings have arisen? How could it have happened that he was nearly killed by a nobleman at one time, and at another fell into the throes of starvation? <note>This likely refers to the "Starvation in Chen," a famous episode where Confucius and his disciples were trapped without food between the states of Chen and Cai.</note> Doubtless because he poured out his wisdom without rule or order, rebuked the great and powerful without shyness or consideration in the presence of the lowly and humble, and perhaps even presented the faults of the rulers so hideously to the people that one had to be concerned about insurrection

<column-break/>

and rebellion. One hardly finds even among the wildest peoples of the world such monsters who would want to kill and execute a man who harms no person's advantage or honor, who wishes to heal the sicknesses of humanity with gentleness and modesty, and who leaves the religion of the country unchallenged, for no other reason than his wisdom and virtue. Even if we cannot present this cause of the sufferings encountered by Confucius as undoubtedly certain, it is nevertheless so probable that it can never be entirely rejected.

We wish to assemble a portrait of this man from these remarks, to which some others could be added, which will make him fairly recognizable. Confucius was neither the greatest nor the smallest mind. The eye of his spirit was sharp enough to recognize and distinguish a part of the truth, yet far too weak to survey the entire realm of wisdom and truth. He was strong enough to choose a certain rational purpose for himself and to judge in general what ought to be done if it were to be achieved. However, he lacked the skill to draft a correct and well-consistent plan and to devise the means that could lead to it. He saw well enough what ought to happen according to reason; but he did not grasp by what means it could be brought about so that it actually occurred. He was not a man who could advance in the land of truth without a staff and a guide, and he therefore occasionally went astray. The ancient sages of the Chinese were intended to serve him <note>The text implies that Confucius relied heavily on the authority of the "Ancients" rather than original philosophical innovation.</note>...

Without doubt, he would have brought things much further if he had possessed one of the great people who lived in Greece in former times—a **Zeno**, a **Socrates**, or an **Aristippus**—as a predecessor. He possessed some of those qualities in himself which tend to make great and excellent people. However, some of these were entirely lacking in him. And some among those he did have were not present in the proper and just measure. Therefore, he appears sometimes great, sometimes small, depending on the disposition of the one who wishes to judge him. His abhorrence of coarse vices, his love for order and for the welfare of his fatherland, his diligence in improving the great and powerful, and his regular and naturally virtuous life bring him prestige and honor. The great self-love that one perceives in him, his stubbornness, the resentment <note>original: "Unmuht"; refers to a state of ill-humor or indignant restlessness.</note> that leaves him no peace when everything will not immediately settle as he wishes, and several other things, demean him. He is great when he is placed in his own times and in the lands in which he lived. A man of moderate stature appears a giant among dwarves. He becomes small when he is taken out of his land and set against other wise men. The uncommon reverence that has been shown to him for so many hundreds of years by all of China, in Japan, and elsewhere, is no proof of his greatness and perfection. A squint-eyed man easily becomes king among the blind. <note>This is a variation of the proverb "In the kingdom of the blind, the one-eyed man is king."</note> And who can depose him once he has climbed so high? Who does not know that many deceased persons are wor-

<column-break/>

shipped as saints by entire nations who, in their lives, were held by the wise to be madmen, and indeed truly were?

The **Moral Philosophy** <note>original: "Sitten-Lehre"</note> of this so famous man is neither a science that stands for itself alone, nor a wisdom that is meant to subject the hearts of all men to itself. It belongs to the **Art of Statecraft and Government** <note>original: "Staats- und Regierungs-Kunst"</note> and is, so to speak, only a servant of the same. It is actually an instruction on how a ruler, who wishes to govern well and make his people happy, must make himself skillful and prepared for this great work. The master of this philosophy intended to change and enlarge the common virtue of the Chinese people—as it is determined by the ancient laws and orders—so little that he rather believed it to be unimprovable; he confirmed the ancient customs and ways (some of which were nonetheless unjust, others absurd) through his teaching as well as through his example. He was a teacher of kings and of their present and future servants. According to the fundamental rules of the Chinese **Art of Government**, those who rule over the people and hold offices in the state must acquire the high esteem of the people more through their virtue and wisdom than through their external advantages, and moreover, they must provide the people with a model for their life and conduct. This ancient teaching had fallen quite into oblivion by the times of **Confucius**. In the four remaining school books <note>The *Sishu* or "Four Books" of Confucianism, which traditionally include the *Great Learning*, the *Doctrine of the Mean*, the *Analects*, and the *Mencius*.</note>, which were published by his disciples, there are very many sayings, thoughts, and teachings that originate from him. Is it indisputably true and correct? Is it unquestionably true that no one can rule a land well except he who rules his own house well, and that he who rules his house well can also skillfully rule an entire people and land? How many kings does history show us who managed their houses poorly and yet presided over their peoples with glory? Who has ruled more wisely and virtuously than **Marcus Antoninus**? <note>Marcus Aurelius (r. 161–180 AD), the Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher. One knows many regents of both ancient and modern times who allowed their imprudent wills an impermissible freedom, and yet despite this, they provided for the prosperity of their realms with vigor and procured abundance, security, and peace for their subjects; and on the contrary, others who plunged themselves and their peoples into misfortune, even though they never stained themselves with vices and watched over their hearts with no lack of diligence. He who has come this far carries within himself the only medicine against the excesses of his desires and will not so easily surrender himself to vice. This is one of the greatest commandments of the **Stoics**: and **Confucius** says exactly the same. How highly this instruction in virtue can be esteemed has already been proven above. And we shall therefore have nothing remarkable to remind the reader of anew here. The doctrine that one must cast off his erroneous opinions and must value the things with which we are surrounded according to their internal worth, and not according to the price of our imagination, can lead a person who follows it blindly to dangerous abysses. Whoever practices this work for a period of time will experience how much his spirit increases in light and discernment, and how much his evil desires decrease. Meanwhile, he himself must not rest. As soon as he senses the beginning of his freedom, he must shake off the chains that hold him captive and strive to elevate himself above everything that partly plagues and partly refreshes mankind through sharp devotion and contemplation of celestial and invisible things. These are the fundamental rules of almost all the people of whom we are now speaking. Their entire doctrine of virtue <term>Tugend-Lehre: the philosophical study of moral excellence and character</term> is easily grasped. It requires only two things: the taming of the body, which proves so burdensome to the spirit, and the elevation of the spirit, which has been unhappily entangled within the body. Whoever is willing to commit to these two things need no longer ask after wisdom and virtue. They find their own way and break forth from the innermost depths of the soul, no differently than the sun emerges when a strong wind has driven away the clouds.

One would have let the matter rest with these two rules, had it not been observed early on through experience that while they are easy to understand, they are difficult to fulfill. The senses of man resist them and overturn even the most honest intentions. The eye, the ear, and the sense of taste bring pleasant and vexing sensations into the soul; and the soul becomes, as it were, so intoxicated by them that it follows wherever it is led by its desires, and

<column-break/>

refuses to cause the body any torment or hardship. Therefore, a third rule had to be added to the first two: every opportunity for the senses to seduce the soul and distract it from its intent—to restore itself to its ancient freedom—must be cut off. By virtue of this command, he who seeks virtue must despise the world, avoid the society of men, and flee all occasions that might give the senses cause for rebellion. In places where people reside, this is exceedingly difficult to observe. Thus, nothing is better than to vacate the world if one cannot well trust one's own soul, and to lead and conclude one's life in the clefts of rocks, in remote wildernesses <note>original: "Einöden"</note>, and among wild animals. Yet, for many, it is uncommonly hard to deprive themselves of the sight and company of other people, especially those to whom nature has bound them. These individuals may use another means to reach their goal—a means that is inherently somewhat more difficult and vexing than the first, but which still allows a person the pleasure of enjoying the company of his peers. A man must place chains upon the members of his body or confine them in such a way that they cannot enjoy the sensual pleasures <term>Wollüste: intense physical or carnal pleasures</term> to which they are urged by their senses and by other people. <column-break/>

life, as the monks are supposed to lead, penance. (*) The Egyptian, Syrian, and Indian wandering brothers, hermits, and saints still use this word for their self-chosen discipline, and are called penitents. And this naming is based on the old opinion, which Plato and Pythagoras learned from the Eastern sages: that the human soul sinned in the invisible world, was cast into the body as punishment, and, if it wishes to reach its old home again, must atone and do penance for the sin of its former life through all kinds of arduous exercises. An Eastern penitent, therefore, and a monk, who is the same, or at least, according to the original intentions, should be, are people who must think of nothing for the whole time of their lives but how they might dissolve the bond that joins the soul to the body and, through the plagues they inflict on the body, restore to the spirit the virtue and purity it formerly possessed. How unknown is this description to those who have stepped into the footsteps of the first monks and hermits? Yet again, this is a clear example that the old habits and customs of people often remain unchanged, while the reasons for them are completely forgotten and lost. # On the Nature and Character of Penance.

Once Christians had moved away from the opinions that first introduced and popularized the solitary life and the voluntary torment of the body, they were forced to either completely abolish these "bodily exercises"—as Saint **Paul** calls them in 1 Timothy 4:8—or place new doctrines in the stead of those abolished, so that these practices could be maintained in honor and esteem. The former was forbidden for all sorts of reasons, none of which can be praised. Therefore, the latter had to occur. Consequently, the concept that pure reason as well as revelation gives us regarding the nature of **God** was altered. The kind Creator of mankind was depicted as a being who finds pleasure in the torture of his rational creatures and loves to see them destroy their bodies and make them unfit for the service of other people as a sign of their repentance <note>The German word *Buße* implies both internal repentance and external acts of penance. The author argues that monks emphasize the latter to the point of self-destruction.</note>. Scripture and reason command us to view **God** as the kindest and most loving Being, who has surrounded man with countless things through the moderate use of which he can feel the love of his Author in advance. Both maintain that we have no power to destroy or harm our body, but are rather bound to tend to it so that it may be useful to us and others. But what is impossible for superstition, especially when it is strengthened by certain other desires? It is easy for it to overturn the purest and clearest truths and **God** himself

<column-break/>

into an unmerciful ruler, if it sees no other means to strengthen itself in its dominion?

How much is the virtue worth that is attained through these means? How much are the means themselves worth, which are supposed to lead to this virtue? If this virtue were a true virtue, it would still deserve very little praise, because it can only be acquired by a very small number of people. How many can bring themselves to hate one part of their being and torture it to please the other? And if all, or most, could achieve this, what would become of the world? A wild land, which **God** had largely created in vain because no one would want to make use of His benefits. However, it is wrongly and poorly spoken when one calls the supposed perfection of those who have declared eternal enmity against their bodies and renounced the society of other people a "virtue." The state of these people is a middle-state, which can be called neither a virtuous nor a vicious life. They are not truly vicious because they have removed all temptations and opportunities for vice; they are not virtuous because they cannot practice any virtue <note>The author suggests that virtue requires the presence of temptation and the active choice to do good within society, rather than mere withdrawal.</note>. They are people of a special kind, who perform nothing evil because they cannot, and do nothing good because they neither can nor will. Meanwhile, the evil desire retains its dwel-

### The First Main Chapter

...of men become so virtuous and orderly that his outward righteous works are nothing but the inevitable consequences and fruits of his inner inclinations, then the natural powers of the soul must be elevated as far as is necessary for virtue and <term>godliness<note>The original German "Gottseligkeit" implies a state of being blessed or pious through a relationship with God.</note></term>. The <term>understanding<note>The "Verstand" refers to the cognitive faculty or intellect.</note></term> must think and judge more purely than it is accustomed to by nature in matters concerning piety, and must not allow itself to be led astray by the perceptions of the senses and the imagination. The <term>will<note>The "Wille" refers to the faculty of choice and action.</note></term> must form an unshakeable resolution to direct itself according to what the understanding recognizes as good and to become master of its desires.

**The third truth.** If the will is to attain this strength and perfection, it must be clothed and possessed with a fierce hatred and aversion toward everything called injustice and wickedness, and with a sincere and fierce love for everything that can be called order and virtue.

**The fourth truth.** All hatred and all love spring from the knowledge of the understanding: And the purer and more certain this knowledge is, the stronger and more constant these two inclinations of the will also become. The understanding must, therefore, be enlightened above all things, and not only know the will of the Highest itself, but also see the true nature of both virtues and vices without hindrance, in order to move the will through this living knowledge toward an inclination for the former and an abhorrence of the latter.

**The fifth truth.** In the current

<column-break/>

weakness of our nature, the mere knowledge of the beauty of virtue and the ugliness of vice is not sufficient to fill us with an earnest hatred for the latter and a sincere love for the former. We spend most of our days in constant confusion and among nothing but visible and earthly things; and therefore the image of holiness and unholiness in our spirit, even if we have grasped it correctly, is distorted and darkened every day. Furthermore, man meditates on nothing but his own <term>happiness<note>Original: "Glückseligkeit." In this context, it refers to a state of ultimate well-being or eternal felicity.</note></term>. Whatever he is to truly love or hate must, therefore, present itself to him as a cause of his happiness or his misery. And so, if man is to become inclined toward righteousness and an enemy to injustice, he must be certainly and clearly convinced that an uncommon happiness depends on the former, and an infinite misery on the latter. In short: the will of man will remain sluggish unless he learns to view virtue as his highest good and vice as his greatest evil.

**The sixth truth.** The more distinct and clear our perceptions are of the evils that will encounter us if we remain devoted to a certain thing, the more we will be incensed against it. And so, if the hatred against sin is to become truly alive in us, then the plagues and sufferings that will follow it must show themselves to us without a cover.

A spirit that perceives and learns through the senses of the body, and is burdened every day with countless earthly concepts, loses—before it realizes it—the knowledge of truths that have no fellowship with the visible and perceptible, unless it diligently tends to them. Whoever, therefore, has become a friend of virtue and an enemy of vice, and does not wish to change back again, must daily renew the knowledge to which he owes this happiness and cleanse it from the dust of this world, if we may speak so.

We shall proceed. To pull man out of the snares of sin and his natural wickedness, God has had a clear and complete rule of his life and conduct set down, which is called the **Law**. Man would have wandered around forever in his thoughts and gone astray countless times if he had been required to determine and establish for himself all the duties to which he is bound. 

To this Law, God has added punishments for the transgressors and promises for the obedient. He has had His perfections and attributes—which the human spirit sees only from a distance, and yet which must give the greatest weight to the laws as well as to the punishments and rewards—vividly and clearly drafted and described. Finally, He has explained His commandments through examples, so that they might be more easily understood, and shown through instances how infallible His promises and threats are. 

Thus, man knows the will of God. However, this knowledge of the divine will, which he can acquire himself, is like a **distant light** that pleases the eyes of travelers but gives no courage to continue the journey in the darkness. This knowledge is content merely to maintain its place, and it attempts in vain to bring the human will under its dominion. God has therefore connected a portion of His divine power with the Law He gave and equipped it so that it is not only capable of instructing, but also of enlightening the understanding to such an extent that it can penetrate the most secret corners of the heart and give a completely new course to the natural impulses that dwell therein.

This would never happen if it had to happen through man himself. God, therefore, has willed to be powerful once again within the weak themselves. He has imparted to the doctrine

<column-break/>

which we have indicated a supernatural strength to convince the understanding of its truth so emphatically that a person can no more deny it than he can the rays of the sun which he feels; through this, he can bring his whole heart to an unshakeable confidence. A person who has been so changed and prepared by God and by the truth—which God has equipped with His power—carries within himself the inexhaustible fountain from which all virtue and <term>peace of mind<note>original: "Gemüths-Ruhe." A central concept in 18th-century philosophy and theology, referring to an internal state of tranquility and emotional stability.</note></term> flow. 

He loves virtue: and he loves it because he loves the One who commanded it, because he clearly perceives that it alone is worthy of love, and because he cannot doubt that in practicing it, he loves himself and his own welfare. He hates all disorder and sin: and he hates it because he honors, reveres, and loves the One who forbade it, *because his knowledge does not allow him to love it, and because he sees that he would have to hate himself if he wished to love it. This hatred and this love grow just as* his faith grows, and they allow him no standstill on the path to perfection. 

He falls daily and must regret his fall, for no one can remain calm who falls into the hands of that which he hates and is delayed in his hope. Yet he composes himself again because he finds in his spirit the assurance that he has no accountability to fear so long as he holds to the One who has borne the sins of all men. His life flows on in these circumstances: and he does not fear its end. Has a single wise man ever presented a guide to virtue and peace of mind that can be compared with this doctrine?

He has had His perfections and attributes—which the human spirit sees only from a distance, and which must give the greatest weight to the laws as well as the punishments and rewards—vividly and clearly drafted and described.

It is content to hold its place and attempts in vain to bring the will under its mastery. 

God has therefore linked a portion of His divine power with the Law He has given, and equipped it so that it is not only capable of instructing, but also of enlightening the understanding to such an extent that it may penetrate into the most secret corners of the heart and give the natural impulses residing there a completely new course...

# The First Principal Section

...people choose / can be undertaken, and therefore they postpone it from one time to another. And among these fools, the greatest are those who intentionally and deliberately set aside this work until the final hours of their lives. What should one think of a person who intends to defy his Judge for as long as it remains permitted to him, and not conclude his madness until he can no longer carry it on?

### Explanation.

The whole world must confess that no errors in matters concerning faith and <term>godliness</term><note>German: *Gottseligkeit*. This refers to a life lived in active devotion and reverence toward God, a central theme in 17th and 18th-century German theology.</note> are more harmful to people than those that touch upon the foundation of all true godliness—its origin and its source. A person may otherwise err as crudely and dangerously as possible; yet the way to life and to improvement remains open to him, so long as he retains a pure and sound concept of the means through which he must reach communion with God and a living <term>sanctification</term><note>German: *Heilgung*. The process of being made holy or being set apart for God's purposes.</note>. One can always hope that he might one day make use of this knowledge, and that the grace he then receives will remove the remaining filth of his intellect and correct his false opinions. But what is there to hope for if he does not know the entrance into the Kingdom of God and entrusts his welfare to blind and inexperienced guides? Or, to speak more clearly, if he does not know in what manner and way his heart must be renewed and made pleasing to God? The most stubborn and disorderly patient leaves his friends some comfort and confidence as long as they notice that the true medicine for his ills and weakne-

<column-break/>

-sses is not unknown to him. One thinks it is not impossible that he might finally grasp the remedy known to him and thereby recover. But all confidence vanishes when he views poison as medicine, or seeks to achieve health through things that must increase his suffering. How much is it therefore to be regretted that the complaints of the ministers of the Gospel regarding the errors of Christians in the doctrine of <term>repentance</term><note>German: *Busse*. While sometimes translated as "penance," in this context it refers to the internal turning away from sin and toward God.</note>—which is the foundation of all godliness—are more than well-founded? And that so many people, who all believe they cannot enter the Kingdom of God except through repentance, hide opinions under this word that are as absurd as they are erroneous and harmful? We do not wish here to recount or refute the errors regarding repentance through which some communities separated from us partly corrupt or defile the holy truths they profess with us from Scripture. We have enough weeds to uproot in our own land. We only want to say something about those false opinions of repentance that circulate among those who boast of the Gospel, holding countless numbers of them in the snares of sin and destruction.

# On the Nature and Quality of Repentance.

We do not even promise a complete register of these incorrect thoughts. The evil heart of man knows so many remote paths to escape the light of truth that one can hardly discover them all. One must therefore be satisfied that we point out and warn against the most common and well-known ones.

All errors into which men can fall in the doctrine of <term>Repentance</term><note>German: *Busse*. In this context, it refers to the entire process of turning from sin to God, encompassing both sorrow for sin and faith in forgiveness.</note> can be conveniently divided into two main categories: general and specific errors. We call "general errors" those which pervert the entire doctrine of repentance and completely overturn the concept of repentance given to us by the Scriptures. We call "specific errors" those which falsely and incorrectly describe and represent only certain parts of repentance. These latter errors are again of a twofold kind. Some concern repentance itself; others concern the **fruits of repentance**. In repentance itself, both the **Law** and the **Gospel** take part. We often err greatly regarding those things mediated in us by the Law, and often regarding those which the Gospel works within us. One can therefore make a new division here. Some of these specific errors shall be touched upon here only in passing; this is partly because they have been dealt with elsewhere, and partly because we will be able to speak of them more conveniently in the following main section. The foolish and godless opinion of those who believe it is permitted to save their repentance and postpone it until a convenient time shall be specifically 

<column-break/>

attacked by us at the end. It can rightly be placed among the general errors because it falsifies the essence of repentance and changes its entire nature and purpose. However, we intend to take it into consideration last and separately because, in folly and danger, it exceeds all unhealthy representations in this part of <term>Moral Teaching</term><note>German: *Sitten-Lehre*. This refers to Christian ethics or the study of how a believer should live according to divine law.</note> and is more than a mere mistake or error of the understanding. In this opinion, a <term>sacrilege</term><note>German: *Frevel*. A term implying a deliberate, defiant transgression against God's will.</note>—a particular malice and naughtiness of the will—combines with an erroneous opinion of the understanding. These two things together produce a certain damnable disposition of the soul which deserves its own specific name and is labeled too mildly if one calls it merely an error.

We have perceived three general errors or three false primary concepts of repentance in our dealings with people, which we wish to present and reject one after another.

All three focus exactly on how they might make these so-called days of repentance as sad, burdensome, and unpleasant as possible. It is not enough that they fast, not enough that they forbid all noise in their dwellings, not enough that they leave all business and work aside and distance themselves from all society. They strive to plunge their spirit into the deepest melancholy it can bear and to sensibly torment and weary their bodies. One deprives himself of light and veils the windows of his chamber, so that the rays of the sun might not perhaps brighten the soul and delay the entry of sadness into his heart. Another calculates the faults a human can have, and all the sins someone can commit, and forces himself to believe that he is guilty of all of them. The third wraps himself in coarse and rough linen. All three spend most of their time on their knees and rejoice when the skin on this part of their body becomes hard and unfeeling. When the days are over in which they have so martyred themselves, they mix with free and cheered faces among the crowds of those who walk according to their lusts and repeat without shame what they have, in their opinion, atoned for. In these examples, which are not so unusual in our times, one sees quite clearly the false delusion of repentance spoken of here. These people believe that one can punish oneself to escape the punishments of God, and that this is the repentance which Jesus demands. In very many people, this ill-advised description of repentance does not manifest itself so brightly. ...bore the punishments of sins and perfectly reconciled God’s justice? It is very easy to answer, and for more than one reason. Self-love and the pride of nature lead many so far astray. No matter how beautifully our mouths speak, our hearts are loath to accept that we owe our salvation and redemption entirely to God. We like to appear as if we had worked on it ourselves, calling ourselves "unprofitable servants" <note>A reference to Luke 17:10, emphasizing that human effort adds nothing to God’s grace.</note> only out of modesty and humility, though in truth we do not wish to be called entirely useless. A weak spirit imagines God only from the side that is terrifying to our eyes, or imagines God’s justice as the quality we usually call severity and hardness in the world. And how many such weak spirits are there? Indeed, how many are there among those appointed as guardians over their brothers <note>likely referring to clergy or spiritual directors</note> who diligently seek to set up such an image of the Most High in people’s minds? A person, I say, needs only to think of God and His justice in this way, and he will weave scourges and rods for his own discipline, even though he otherwise does not doubt that Jesus is his only Savior and Redeemer. <column-break/>

God will be more easily moved to grace and will more quickly blot out your iniquities if you do more than is necessary and punish your own misconduct yourself. Should God, who is just, leave your zeal for penance unrewarded? How quickly this absurd imagination can be coaxed out of the hearts of many who impose a strict penance upon themselves, if one only takes some trouble to ask them precisely and in detail? Many among us do not know what to say when they think of the great multitude of those—among the heathens as well as among Christians—who rage against themselves so that they might move God to compassion and grace. It has long been suspected that this lineage would die out and that the world would gradually be moved by reason itself to do away with the error that God, who is a Spirit, could be softened by the plagues of our bodies. And nothing happens less than that. Why is this? Because the secret pride of our hearts remains, and fearful superstition seems far safer to many than a free and pure wisdom.

God demands that we should practice now and then and behave for a few days as if we were rational and wise people. He has the power to command such things of us. We obey Him because we must fear Him, and afterwards we live again as we please, once we have proven our obedience.

### The third false concept of repentance.

Repentance is a ceremony through which man must testify to his humility and abasement before his Creator and Judge. Reason, as well as Scripture, dictates that man should humble and abase himself before God—to whom he owes his being and everything he possesses, and from whom alone he can expect all true happiness. And no wise person has anything to object to this teaching. One is horrified by the madness of those who, as it were, rebel against God, and one scolds the foolish ingratitude of people who accept the good that the Lord gives without acknowledgment. However, we often commit childish errors when it comes to the practice of this duty toward God, which no one wants to transgress. # Of the Nature and Character of Repentance.

### [Column 1]

...satisfied with external signs of humility. Our impure imagination is to blame for this, among other things; it never allows the understanding to work out a pure and perfect image of the Most High Being, and it constantly mixes the weaknesses of men—whom we call kings, the powerful, and heroes—with the attributes of the **Lord**. One error follows another. And those who first judge so incorrectly regarding the true humility and abasement that **God** demands of us are almost forced to believe that this work has its certain days and hours, and must be repeated from time to time. How we wondered when we first unexpectedly encountered, among certain people who otherwise walked respectably and orderly, not only this opinion but also the delusion that the hours of repentance are those in which man must testify his reverence to **God** and give proofs of his humility toward Him? And how could this wonder not increase as we gradually noticed that the group of people who allow themselves to be captivated by this is not so small and insignificant? 

Repentance—to present the opinion of these people more clearly than they themselves can—repentance is, in their thoughts, roughly what a **ceremony of homage** <note>A "Huldigung" was a formal ceremony where subjects swore an oath of allegiance to a new sovereign in exchange for protection and the confirmation of their rights.</note> is in the world, in which the subjects indicate, partly through words and partly through other customs, that they recognize the one to whom they pay homage as their sole and lawful lord, and promise him obedience and loyalty, while he, in return, takes each into his protection and allows them to be most firmly assured of his grace. There is no better simile to explain the shapeless and dark concept of 

<column-break/>

### [Column 2]

repentance that many hold within themselves! Man lives in the kingdom of **God** and is His citizen and subject. He enjoys His protection, lives by His benefits, comforts himself with His mercy, and hopes in His promises. What is more just than that he should confess this in the face of his Creator, recognize himself as **dust and ashes**, and **God** as his King and Lord, and vow to Him an inviolable loyalty and an unbreakable obedience? 

However, man does not keep his vow and cannot keep it because of his inability. He is more a rebel and an unfaithful citizen than an honest and obedient subject. How does he manage, then, so that he is not excluded from the kingdom of **God** and not only robbed of his freedoms and rights, but even punished for his disobedience? **God** Himself, according to this opinion, has removed this difficulty. He wants to always accept us in grace for **Christ's** sake. But He also wants one to do repentance from time to time—that is, to renew the homage and, in doing so, confess one's wrongdoing, present **Christ** as one's **Mediator and Advocate**, and promise improvement. 

Therefore, what subjects in the world must perform when they are solemnly readmitted and pardoned by their lord from whom they had defected, that is what those who do repentance must achieve. And whoever performs it best does the best repentance. These people are accustomed to confessing their defection as eloquently as possible and thinking so little of excuses that they would rather make themselves more guilty than they actually are. They are accustomed to pleading movingly for forgiveness and grace.

## On the Nature and Character of Repentance

...no errors can easily creep into the fruits of <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "Busse"; here referring to the lifelong process of turning from sin toward God, rather than a single act of penance</note>. Scripture has said nothing more clearly than this: that the internal sanctification of souls and the external godliness of one's conduct are the only things that deserve this name. It has, moreover, accompanied this instruction with several parables taken from such well-known things and so easy to grasp that no one can misunderstand them. What can be more comprehensible than the parable of the trees and their fruits? And what is clearer than the image that **JESUS** himself takes from a field, in which a good seed finds no obstacles to revealing its inner power? This clarity has achieved so much that man has not entirely perverted or overturned the doctrine itself. However, it has not been able to obtain enough from him that he would abandon all desire to deceive himself even in this matter. We shall remain silent about those who leave the doctrine itself standing but deny its power. We mean those who have, to their own misfortune, persuaded themselves that **JESUS** and the Apostles only intended to teach what repentance would work in us if we were different and better-natured people, not what it must work in our current state of weakness. This delusion, which shames the power of grace and turns the doctrine of godliness into a mere mirror—in which one can glimpse a well-rendered image of a perfect man that this world will never produce, an image that one may indeed behold for pleasure but must not adopt as a model—this delusion has been contested so often and so successfully that it would be superfluous

<column-break/>

to expose its folly anew. We wish only to note a few opinions that carry a more secret poison and can more quickly befuddle and captivate the mind. The heart must be changed; the life must be improved. From these two pieces, one recognizes that repentance has occurred. Man takes occasion from this holy and certain doctrine to consider every internal and external change that has an appearance of conversion as a mark of his repentance. It is a common thing in the world that people withdraw the inclinations of their souls from certain things and direct them toward entirely different matters which they previously did not esteem. It happens just as often that many prescribe an entirely new order for their conduct and continue to live as if they had been formed differently. Do these transformations always come from supernatural causes? Is it grace alone that has such power over us? Many, who gladly call themselves Christians and yet do not wish to fulfill the duties that cling to this name, do not allow the slightest doubt to occur to them regarding these questions. In their opinion, no one can contest this conclusion: "We are changed; therefore, we are converted." And they deceive themselves because their inordinate desire for salvation and self-love prevent them from paying attention to the causes from which this supposed conversion arose. We are fickle creatures who can easily be retuned by all sorts of things and brought into a different course without **God** needing to intervene directly and guide us. # The First Main Chapter

Fear and hope—sometimes through certain examples that no one should reject, sometimes through other things that we often do not even know ourselves—twist a person around so much that his old fundamental laws become completely unknown and foreign to him. And the worst part of these natural changes is this: often those changes that seem best and most laudable to us and others are actually dangerous plagues, which kill much more certainly and quickly than the evils they have replaced. <term>Plato</term> <note>Ancient Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BC); the author likely refers to a passage in the *Phaedo* regarding the "trading" of virtues</note> says that human virtue is a trade. If everything this philosopher proposed were as easy to prove as this, he would deserve the highest place among those who have used their reason well. For what is more truthful than this: that we only trade our faults and vices and imagine that we have become virtuous when we have bartered lead for counterfeit gold? The change of our customs and outward conduct happens even more easily. A single respected man, who has managed to establish the opinion that he undertakes nothing without ground or reason, becomes master over the customs of an entire country; he often gives the most sacred laws to a great multitude at the very moment he only wishes to amuse or entertain himself. We shall soon present this matter somewhat more clearly and orderly. The rest of this main chapter shall be used against those senseless and perverse scoffers who allow themselves to be ruled by the foolish imagination that man has the freedom and the power to perform <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "Busse"; a transformative spiritual turning toward God</note> whenever he pleases, and therefore they postpone their repentance. These are harsh words. However, the facts will show that they are not poorly chosen.

At times, it seems as if they are waiting for a proper and pleasant opportunity to execute what they have not entirely renounced or have generally intended to do. At other times, it seems as if they hope for a supernatural impulse that shall one day enclose their indecisive hearts and enliven the will to repent. Meanwhile, they follow the fulfillment of their desires from one day to the next without care or anxiety. They answer those who wish to lead them to better paths by saying they are not at all disinclined to convert, but that the hour of their visitation <note>A biblical term referring to a specific time of God's grace or judgment</note> has, by all appearances, not yet come; they claim they wish to offer **God** an open heart as soon as His grace announces itself more strongly at the door. In the meantime, they generally do not neglect the common exercises of outward public worship, so as not to make themselves entirely unworthy of **God's** grace. In most of them, there is no settled malice, no formal intention to resist grace. # On the Nature and Quality of Repentance

<column-break/>

...maintain the resolution within us to serve Him one day with all our strength? Those who wish to appear more cautious and modest plead the fear of falling. We know ourselves far too well, they say, to believe that we could remain constant if we converted in our strong and healthy days. Our early <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "Busse"; in this context, it refers to a total change of heart and mind, rather than just a feeling of regret</note> would, because of the violence of the desires that dwell in our nature, be as much as the beginning of an apostasy from God, and that apostasy in turn as much as the beginning of a new repentance. How saddened we would be by this constant change? And how dangerous would it be for us?

What kind of accountability must a person take upon themselves who vows obedience and faithfulness to God ten, twenty, or thirty times, and breaks his promise just as often? It is therefore better that we save our repentance for the years in which a person can much more easily resist temptations, and in which the fire of nature will no longer assail us. The most crude and senseless of all are those who say without shame that they intend to settle accounts with God during the illness that will take their lives, and think to still His anger over their sins in the final moments of life through the merit of His Son.

If one wishes to look at the causes from which this shameful error of delaying repentance arises, one can make another division of the people who are devoted to it. Some are so blinded by the desire to sin alone that they seize and accept it as a truth. Their knowledge would soon bring them to a better path if

<column-break/>

they took the trouble to consult it. But the ill nature of their heart does not let it come to that. This heart speaks so strongly and drives so vehemently that they can no longer see or perceive anything other than what it shows them; it dresses up the ugliest propositions that serve its purposes so skillfully, as if they were dictates of reason and truth. Others are brought to this punishable conclusion almost as much by the ignorance and simplicity of their intellect as by their love of sin and disorder. How many are found even among those who are otherwise rightly honored for their status and their offices, who understand so little of the main truths of faith and religion that anyone who wishes can infect them with their dreams and visions? Others of these people have been deceived by a false concept of repentance and of the life of a Christian. 

What do the strict legalistic teachers do, who describe repentance as the most terrifying and saddest work in the world, and the life of a Christian as a state of misery, unrest, and melancholy—what do they do other than pervert many and incautiously lead them to the resolution of putting off their reconciliation with God as far as possible? The first group is the hardest to win over. An error that lies in the will alone is much harder to eradicate than a delusion that only sticks in the understanding. It is advisable for those who have to deal with such people to always remember these two divisions, so that they may see more clearly in what manner and with what reasons their [arguments should be met].

# The First Main Section

...insanity must be attacked. Many who are otherwise faithful and honest in their intentions wage the wars of <term>godliness</term> <note>original: "Gottseligkeit"; refers to the practice of a devout Christian life</note> unsuccessfully, only because they believe that the same weapons can be used against all its enemies who come dressed in the same clothing. We set the latter division aside for now and hold only to the former, because we wish to contest the error in itself, without regard for the persons who are afflicted by it.

Our reflections against this error will, in part, strike all those in general who intend to save their <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "Busse"; a total turning away from sin and toward God</note> for a certain time; in part, they will strike only one of the three types into which we have divided them. That is to say: we first want to examine the resolution in general, without concerning ourselves with the particular circumstances of those who have formed it. Afterward, we want to look a little more closely at the additions with which each of the described categories restricts that resolution. We begin with the general reflections.

We can hardly believe that those who intend to postpone their repentance until a certain time—whether it be fixed or indefinite—actually understand what they are thinking and saying. One need only explain the words: **"I will postpone my repentance,"** to convince all rational people that nothing more godless or absurd could be said or thought. What does this unfortunate phrase mean? It means: "I will continue for a certain time to do what displeases God and what His justice must punish, regardless of the fact that I know I am thereby drawing His

<column-break/>

wrath upon myself; and at a time that seems convenient to me, I will allow Him the freedom to bring me to better thoughts and ways." Can one read this explanation without horror? Does not almost everything that can be called malice, wantonness, contempt for God, ignorance, and folly flow together in this one thought? The person who speaks this way, or thinks it to himself, decides on two things. His first conclusion is malicious and damnable: **"I will sin."** The other is unwise and presumptuous: **"I will let myself be converted by God at a convenient time."** And the connection of these two conclusions is absurd and ridiculous. They belong together so little that one contradicts and overturns the other. The first conclusion is certain. The person carries it out, and therefore lets no one doubt its certainty. However, this certain and firm conclusion testifies against the other and proves that it is uncertain—or rather, that it is not a true conclusion of the <term>will</term>, but only a false and groundless promise that one does not intend to keep. If the latter conclusion were certain and serious, the first would have to fall and be overturned. Anyone who is so clearly and plainly convinced of the necessity of his conversion that he has truly resolved to do penance one day can no more remain in the will to continue sinning for a long period of time than a person who is firmly resolved to pay off his debts one day can maintain the intention of continually making new debts. Therefore, let no one believe that people are telling the truth when they assure themselves and others that they will one day cast off their sins and [serve] God...

### Of the Nature and Condition of Repentance

...wanting to obey. They deceive themselves and others most shamefully. The two resolutions, which they bind together, do not agree with one another. If the first gains real power, the second is lost; and if the latter keeps the upper hand, the first must yield. The true meaning of their heart is that they want to persist in the service of sins for as long as possible. This intention appears all too godless and evil. They therefore wish to make it somewhat more tolerable by adding an attachment, and they add that this damned intention should nonetheless cease within them at a certain time. This is the same as if they wanted to unite these two sentences, which stand directly opposite one another: **I want to convert**, and **I do not want to convert**. Must not one of the two be false? 

One of these two hostile resolutions, which seek to link the ruin of men, accuses and condemns the other. The first resolution—*I want to sin for a while longer*—represents the fulfillment of the second as unnecessary and superfluous. No one can resolve to sin without taking it for certain that **God** can overlook and endure malice, defiance, and outrage, if the evildoer only retains the will to turn back one day. And if this is true, why then is it necessary to convert one day? It will be enough for <term>salvation</term> <note>original: "Seligkeit"; refers to the state of eternal spiritual health and the soul's arrival in heaven</note> if one only does not let go of the will to submit to **God** one day. Whoever dies with this will shall have nothing to fear in eternity. The final resolution—*I want to convert one day*—accuses the first of the greatest folly. It presupposes that no one can

<column-break/>

see the **Lord** without <term>conversion</term> <note>original: "Bekehrung"; a total turning around of one's life and priorities</note>. If this is indisputable, then it must be irrational and foolish to linger diligently in the state of <term>unrepentance</term> <note>original: "Unbußfertigkeit"; a state of being where a person refuses to admit wrong or change their ways</note> and sin for an uncertain time. 

The first resolution would itself, according to the confession of those who make it, be highly punishable and damnable if the latter were not joined to it. This is the "anti-poison" through which the poison of the first resolution is supposed to be moderated. However, the first of these two resolutions is in our power; the second is not. We know that we can sin and fall; we do not know whether we will have the capacity to lay aside sin one day and rise up from the fall. A doubtful and uncertain intention, which perhaps can be carried out and perhaps not, is thus supposed to excuse and justify the most godless undertaking—an undertaking that *will* certainly be carried out and must cause the inevitable misfortune of man if the other resolution, which does not stand in our power, should remain unfulfilled. 

What an absurdity! How would the judgment of reason sound regarding a man who decided to make the streets unsafe for a time through robbery and murder, and yet did not doubt that the Prince would not prevent him in his godless work and would ultimately grant him full pardon, because he had intended from the very beginning only to carry out this business until he had enriched himself by it? And is there any difference between such a man and those who, through the uncertain hope of their future conversion, allow themselves to be led into the resolution to resist **God** and to continue their life in all kinds of sins?

### On the Nature and Character of Repentance ###

...are, in those times when the spirit has its full strength, and to undertake that difficult and unpleasant work at the very time when the spirit will be exhausted and powerless. We all know that the powers of our souls generally decline along with the powers of the body, and that sensitivity <note>The author uses "sensitivity" here to mean a person's vulnerability to pain and emotional distress, which often increases with age.</note>, on the other hand, increases and grows with the years in the vast majority of people. It is unbelievable, judging by the rules of probability, that these people will ever bring themselves to repentance. If they were deterred in their stronger years by the effort and displeasure they imagined it would take, where then will the resolution and the will arise in their weaker years? Is it to be expected that powerlessness will give birth to what power itself could not produce? Therefore, if someone says: "I want to start my repentance toward the end of my life because it is difficult and tedious," it is the same as if he confessed clearly and plainly: "I never want to repent." We understand what one might answer to this: "Our good intentions will not find as many enemies and obstacles in old age as in the years of youth and strength. No matter how weak we may be, we will still be able to carry it out more easily than before."

-> Part I. Section II. <-

<column-break/>

What simplicity and thoughtlessness! We shall close off this excuse further below. Here it will be enough to say, in general, that just as many obstacles to repentance present themselves in the final years of our lives as in the first. We are so foolish that we think it is all over with the adversaries of our happiness <note>In this context, "happiness" refers to "eternal blessedness" or salvation.</note> when one kind of adversary withdraws, only to let another kind—one that is not quite so impetuous—move into its place. The enemies of our repentance do not become more reasonable just because we choose "the other side" and view repentance as a business that can be completed with few, or perhaps just mediocre, strengths, and which causes the soul no particular unrest. Is it not recklessness and folly to delay a matter that must happen eventually, and which could happen without particular hardship, from one time to another, thereby putting oneself in danger of a great—indeed, an infinite—loss? Because we feel our own weakness, we often make allowances for those who hesitate for a long time before picking up a heavy physical load. # The First Main Part

The second point: **The measure of remorse and sorrow which repentance brings forth is proportional to the measure of sins that the person has committed.** The pain of a penitent <note>A "penitent" is someone seeking forgiveness through religious transformation or "repentance" (German: *Buße*).</note> who for many years in succession has intentionally and willfully plunged from one sin into another must be much stronger, much more vivid, and much longer-lasting than the mental anguish of another who has served sin for only a short time.

He who does not wish to doubt these two propositions can easily estimate how capable and ready even the most fortunate old man would be for the work of repentance. Let it be remembered that we are not speaking here of all elderly people, but only of those who have intentionally saved their repentance for their final years. In repentance, the dark and false opinions and concepts of the intellect are to be eradicated, and the desires and cravings of the will are to be directed toward entirely different things. Will this happen easily with people who have maintained and nurtured these opinions and desires within themselves for sixty, seventy, or eighty years?

Will an aged man—however lively one might imagine him to be—easily agree to attack these dearest companions of his life, who have pleased and delighted him for so many years, and banish them from his spirit? Even if he does agree to it, will he accomplish much against them? Will it go much differently for him with these thoughts and impulses—which have become most secretly entwined with his own nature—than it usually goes with old servants whom the household cannot do without, but whom one nonetheless wishes to dismiss? These servants laugh at the displeasure of their masters and let

<column-break/>

themselves be cast out without worry, because they know that they will be called back the next day and be served and honored even better than before. How difficult and sorrowful must a repentance be that extends over a long life spent diligently in nothing but sin? What kind of turmoil must arise in a soul to which the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the biblical moral requirements and commandments which, in this theological context, act as a mirror to reveal a person's failures and sins.</note> presents a countless multitude of sins and misdeeds, all committed intentionally and which therefore cry out, as it were, to God for vengeance?

How will an elderly man, who is an enemy to all compulsion and unrest, endure this sight? How will he hold out in this "heat"? Is it not more than believable that he would immediately withdraw as soon as he feels the first onset, and that he would either entirely renounce the will to repent or else beg for one delay after another, until death finally overtakes and takes him away in the midst of his preparations for repentance? 

In short: we have viewed the intention to convert in old age from every angle. And we have not been able to find a single side from which it did not seem irrational and absurd, hateful, malicious, and highly unbecoming of a wise person—let alone one who hopes in Christ.

The reason used to gloss over this childish intention is true only in the sick imagination of the people who propose it. In itself, it is false and as contrary to experience as it is to reason. It is thought that one will find fewer obstacles in old age. And it seems as if some of those who refute these people have left them unguarded in this opinion...

### On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

->Iii 3<-

...strengthen them. In many books and public exhortations, people are warned against this evil and perverse way of thinking: that a Christian should not wait until his sins leave him, but must leave them himself before they depart from him. How so? Do sins leave us in old age? If this were true, our final days of life would be blessed. And those people who wish to approach God only in old age would have at least a small appearance of an excuse. It shall immediately be shown that this is spoken poorly and carelessly, even if it is perhaps understood well and correctly <note>The author suggests that while the advice "leave your sins before they leave you" is common, it is logically flawed because sins do not actually "leave" a person just because they grow old.</note>. We can grant the imagination of these people so little that we must rather maintain the direct opposite and say: it is absurd to postpone one's conversion until the end of life, because in old age one encounters far more obstacles to conversion than in younger years. 

There are more obstacles on the part of the **understanding**, which in old age—as everyone knows—is dull, tired, and unsuited for any sharp reflections. There are more obstacles on the part of the **will**, which in old age lets itself be bent as little as a dry tree, and continues along the path it has walked for so many years. There are more obstacles on the part of the **body**, which draws to itself a good portion of our worries and thoughts because of its constant infirmities; which often, through the pains it must feel, shatters the spirit and moves the mind back and forth from fear to hope, and from hope to fear. There are more obstacles on the part of our **earthly business**, which takes up much more time in old age than before, because the loss of the strengths of the body

<column-break/>

and the spirit teaches us to walk slowly. There are more obstacles on the part of the **circumstances of our household**, which must be arranged and set in order so that we may not grieve our loved ones, whom we have loved in life, after our death. There are more obstacles on the part of our **friends and relatives**, who often rob us of our best hours in old age—partly because they consider it a part of their duty to sweeten the years that do not please us, and partly because they wish to become wiser and more prudent through our experience. These are only the general obstacles of old age that befall most people. Otherwise, almost every station and every gender has its particular hindrances, which press much more heavily in the final years than before.

<margin>Note well</margin> But, one will doubtlessly say, is it not a great thing that a person, when he has turned gray, stops sinning and is liberated from his lusts <note>In this context, "lusts" (*Lüste*) refers to any strong worldly desires or passions, not just sexual ones.</note> which otherwise drove him to sin? We have heard this a thousand times and have never been able to understand it. "The person stops sinning in old age. Sins leave him. Lusts depart from him." What does this mean then? If one must not doubt the truth of these words, then old age is repentance itself. And one would be able to say this just as well as people are accustomed to say that old age is the sickness itself. Why does one need repentance if one commits no more sin, nor can commit any? We have learned, not without dismay, that many of those who save their repentance for the final section of their life are indeed devoted to this opinion, and so think to themselves...
