## The First Principal Part

...burden: Repentance puts an end to the sins of men. Old age does the very same. Why should we, therefore, torment ourselves before the time? Why should we force ourselves into a hatred against sin? Let us wait until we turn gray. Old age will accomplish, without our effort, that which we must now perform with great toil. And we will then please GOD no less than we would please Him now, if we martyred ourselves with an untimely repentance. This delusion is grounded in another error that misleads countless Christians: the idea that godliness is nothing more than the omission of external works and deeds that run contrary to the law of GOD. We, who are meant to lead the perverse and disorderly world toward truth and godliness, often do not penetrate deeply enough into the intentions of their hearts; we therefore sometimes give them answers to their excuses that so little destroy their false conclusions that they seem, rather, to confirm them. We assert plainly that it is not true that a person ceases to sin in old age, or is "left" by their sins. Our sins are of a twofold kind. Some require a certain measure of bodily strength in those who wish to commit them. Such are <term>unchastity</term> <note>original: "Unzucht"</note>, certain foolish and sinful pleasures, violence, and others more. Others can be perpetrated by even the very weakest and sickliest. One can be suspicious, slander, lie, and cheat, all while barely maintaining the smoldering wick of one's final strengths for a time through medicine and moderation alone. Do these, or do those sins—if we have practiced them throughout the time of our

<column-break/>

lives—cease of their own accord when we have reached a certain goal in our life? Neither these nor those, unless we have labored entirely in vain to explore the ways of men. To prove this more easily and briefly, let us call the former the "unquiet" sins and the latter the "quiet" sins. The unquiet sins can no longer be carried out once the natural strengths have vanished. An eighty-year-old man can normally no longer satisfy his lewd passion, and must naturally leave off from scuffling and striking because his limbs tremble. Yet the sins remain with him nonetheless, because the lusts and desires, which are the sources and causes of the sins, remain stuck in the heart. He does not cease to sin, because one can clearly perceive from his words and behavior that he is an enemy to his own weak nature, which prevents him from sinning further, and that he would take up the abandoned game again if his nature could be rejuvenated. An exhausted old man must, to a certain extent, let his drive for unchastity rest. Meanwhile, he does not leave it entirely unsatisfied. He reads with pleasure the writings in which the "heroic deeds" of the unchaste are described, and laughs when he is told a story of a cunning adulterer, or of a foolish woman who deceived her parents and overseers only so that she might all the more severely deceive and shame herself. An old brawler must leave his sword in its sheath out of necessity. Yet he wishes that he could take to the field, and he breathes into younger men those ridiculous and absurd rules of honor, according to which he, in his younger years...

### On the Nature and Character of Repentance.

...has directed [their lives]. Are these people no longer sinners? They are just as much so as before. According to the teaching of Jesus Christ, he who nourishes the desire to sin within himself and wishes to sin gladly is just as great a sinner as he who carries out this desire. And he who looks at a woman to lust after her has, as He Himself teaches, committed adultery with her in his heart. Matthew 5:28. <note>The author uses this famous verse from the Sermon on the Mount to argue that sin is a matter of the internal "will" rather than just the external "act."</note> We readily admit that some, once they have turned gray, also seem to lose the inclination toward the sins they once loved, and do not deny that they acted unwisely and foolishly when they indulged in them. However, one should not think that in these people the evil desire has entirely died out and turned into a true aversion and hatred. One finds enough signs in them to see that it is merely stirring somewhat more weakly in them than in others. And why do they resist those who follow their old example so little, if the desire were entirely removed from their heart? Why is it that when they hear something of the disorderly conduct of the youth, they only say so coldly: "Youth rages; it will become just as tired of folly as we are"? *It is well known enough that the quiet sins of the years of strength are not cast off when old age comes.* We wish only to call to mind something that is not so well known. These sins, which we have called "quiet," <note>The author distinguishes between "active" or "restless" sins (like violence or lust) and "quiet" sins (like pride, greed, or resentment).</note> generally become stronger and more pleasant in the years of incapacity than they were before: and this for two reasons. Firstly, two evil qualities generally set in among the elderly that previously either did not rule over their minds at all, or did so much more mildly. The one is

<column-break/>

greed; the other, pride. The former arises partly from fear, which is almost always a companion of weakness, and partly from love for our own kin, which is commonly never stronger than when we are soon to depart from them. The latter grows partly from the honor that nearly everyone shows to the elderly, and partly because we are conscious that we have experienced, lived through, perceived, and examined more than others who are younger, and are thus wiser than they. These two mental illnesses <note>original: "Gemühts-Kranckheiten." In this era, "illness of the soul/mind" was often used to describe moral or spiritual failings.</note> require for their necessary maintenance all sorts of those sins that can be committed in silence and without [apparent] sin. To satisfy and nourish greed, one must deceive, offend, and *falsify the truth.* To please *pride, one must slanderm blaspheme, suppress and remain silent about the gifts of another, judge recklessly, and diminish the best of deeds.* Secondly. Quiet sins are often thwarted and held back in younger years by restless ones. A person who chases after honor and goods is so heavily occupied that he does not look so sharply at other people unless they wish to block his path; and he therefore does not let his tongue wander so far. A voluptuary sinks his imagination so deeply into the delights he seeks that it must push almost all other things out. However, in the final years, we are unfit for the vices that require effort and labor. And therefore, all our strengths fall upon the sins that one can pursue without movement or unrest. On this side, we generally wish to recover from the loss we have suffered on the other. The proverb— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "Sprich-" (proverb).</note>

# The First Main Part

...word says: The elderly gossip and talk a lot. And why? Because they can do very little. A person who was once secretive and quiet often becomes a boisterous chatterer in old age, because he can no longer enjoy the lustful pleasures that previously kept his tongue tied. And is it not indisputable that he who speaks much—especially when he speaks with a weakened mind, as the elderly do—generally sins a lot? Let us be told, once all this has been considered: do those people have a grounded reason for comfort and excuse who want to glorify the last period of their lives with their repentance simply because it is freer from sins and obstacles? We remain who we are as long as we live—unless the Lord sanctifies us—unclean, evil people inclined toward sin. After fifty years, we will be surrounded by just as many, if not more, enemies of our conversion than we are today. Old age merely "paints" our skin, so to speak. But the leprosy of nature <note>A common theological metaphor of the era, "leprosy of nature" refers to "Original Sin" or the inherent corruption of the human soul that remains regardless of outward behavior.</note> remains stuck in the juices <note>original: "Säften." This refers to the "humors" of the body, reflecting the medical belief that character and health were dictated by bodily fluids.</note> of life.

### The Third Kind.
**"We will repent when we are about to depart."** <note>Meaning, repenting only on one's deathbed.</note> They think a task that is so vexing and unpleasant is performed early enough if it happens at the end of life. They argue that God is unchangeable and always maintains the same grace and love toward sinners who take hold of the merit of His Son. He will—they say—receive us just as willingly at the end as He would today. If there are people whose salvation one can fundamentally and rightly despair of, it is truly these. They are open mockers and despisers of the Most High, to whom the word of the Apostle, in its strictest sense, can be applied:

<column-break/>

They are ungodly and turn the grace of our Lord Jesus into license <note>original: "Muhtwillen," referring to intentional or reckless sinning based on the assumption that God will forgive anyway.</note> and deny God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the only Sovereign. Jude v. 4. Without a doubt, unless they have become completely insane, they must grant to all people the same right that they take for themselves. If one person can postpone his repentance until the end of his life, then it is undoubtedly permitted to everyone. And what abominable principles follow from this? First, this: All people who apply themselves to a godly walk of life are fools. Moses, David, Abraham, Paul, and all the saints acted with simple-mindedness. We alone are wise, we who have decided to sin our whole lives long. Indeed, it would be foolish to plague one's own nature and struggle against the flesh if one could finish the business with such a late repentance! Furthermore: everything the Scripture says about virtue and godliness, all exhortations to repentance, all the sermons of the Apostles—who first insisted on repentance and would admit no one into the Kingdom of God without it—are merely wind and superfluous. It would not matter at all if the entire part of the Scripture called "the Law" were cut out and lost. What purpose does it serve, since no one needs to live godlily or get along with God, provided they just repent at the last moment? Jesus would have instructed His Apostles poorly when He commanded them to preach repentance; and the Apostles would have done poorly to preach as He prescribed to them. They would have acted more wisely if they had given the people this single teaching: "Live however you yourself wish. Only do not forget, if you happen to become dangerously ill, to make use of the merit..."

# Of the Nature and Character of Repentance

...to comfort [yourselves] in JESUS and to regret your mischief. More still: through his suffering and death, JESUS has earned for mankind the freedom to sin. <note>The author is sarcastically describing the logic of those he criticks; he does not actually believe Jesus died to allow people to sin.</note> One can, with intent and wantonness, commit sins for the entirety of one's life—the punishment for which He took upon himself—and nonetheless be safe enough from the wrath of GOD in the next world, if only one throws one's trust upon Christ when departing from this world and confesses that one has done wrong. Let us be shown that one of these conclusions does not flow naturally, easily, and without any force from the intention of these people? We do not wish to pass a judgment of damnation. Let the LORD alone remain the judge. *However, we cannot deny that we must often doubt whether the justice of the LORD can spare such transgressors and mockers, as often as we imagine that justice as it is depicted in the Scriptures.*

We are strengthened in this doubt when we examine the words of these people more closely. We, they say—we who hold that we can commit all sins unhindered that we wish to commit, if only we repent at the last—we wish to reconcile GOD through our repentance in the face of death. Unless we are completely deceiving ourselves, these words are composed of contrary and conflicting things: And they therefore have no meaning at all. Can one then consider all sins permitted under the condition of future repentance? Can one then repent with such a state of mind? To repent <note>original: "Busse thun." In this context, "Busse" (repentance/penance) refers to a total internal transformation of the heart, not just an outward ritual.</note> will, without doubt, mean to these people: to recognize one's sin, to earnestly regret the same, to reconcile it through

<column-break/>

faith in Christ with GOD, and finally to make the resolution to desist from the same and to live in the future according to the will of the LORD. And how then shall a living recognition of sins and a heartfelt regret over them arise in a dying person who is certain that it was permitted for him to commit all the sins he had committed until then? To believe that one has done nothing inadmissible or punishable, and yet to confess that one has sinned—not only to confess this, but also to be distressed because of one's misdeeds—these are things that cannot possibly be reconciled. Turn whichever way one will, one can never escape this reproach of a manifest contradiction. If a person who saves repentance for his final days thinks that he will certainly carry out his conclusion at the time he has set, and will then repent, then he cannot believe that he can save his repentance for so long: And if he believes that he can postpone his repentance for so long, then he cannot believe—if he wishes to think rationally—that he will then repent. And what shall we say of the resolution to walk holily from now on, or of the <term>new obedience</term> <note>original: "neuen Gehorsam." A theological term (Nova Obedientia) referring to the voluntary and sincere desire of a person to follow God's laws after being justified by faith.</note> which unquestionably belongs to repentance as an inevitable fruit? Does it not sound absurd and childish when a person says that at the time when death will rob him of the ability to sin in a few hours, he wants to make a holy promise to GOD to sin no more?
